I purchased eight of these power strips based on the Belkin name, the build robustness and their ability to be mounted securely. I'll be looking elsewhere to replace the whole lot of them soon. If I though it was a single defective unit, I'd try to get a replacement. But, so many bad units tell another story.

I also bought the smaller version of this surge-protector which is rated at only 1800 Joules, so I got this one because I figured it would be the same with just a higher Joule rating. Well, I’m kind of disappointed in this one. Unlike its smaller sibling, this one isn’t rated by UL or ETL, there are no markings or ratings of any kind on the body of the strip itself. Additionally, this one doesn’t have any indicators to let you know if it’s still protecting or even grounded. The only light is the on/off switch which is also supposed to be a resettable circuit breaker, but I have no way of knowing what’s going on inside… It could just be a bare power-strip. The arrangement of the outlets is also too close, as you can see in my photo, I intended to plug a bunch of different things to it in my workshop, but out of 10 outlets I get six, maybe seven useable ones. The clincher came when I plugged-in my Ryobi sliding compound miter saw. The saw is rated at 14 amps and the only other thing plugged-in at the time was a 500mA charger for a cordless driver. After about 15-20 seconds, I lost power to the saw and realized that the switch had tripped on this thing. Since it’s not certified, and there are no indicators on it, I wouldn’t use it as anything other than a glorified power-strip. The 1800 Joule version is OK, but if you need the 2800 Joules of protection, you should look elsewhere. Update 09/21/2019: The seller reached out to me about the lack of ETL/UL listing on the surge-protector. It turns out that the device is indeed ETL listed and I was able to verify that on the ETL online database, but I couldn't have done that without knowing their internal model number for this unit (LTS-10TS). They just forgot to put the stickers on... smh! Also, they've promised to add/include a surge-protection indicator in a future revision. So high marks for customer outreach, but it still doesn't explain why mine trips, even when running my saw a half power. Perhaps just a faulty unit?

First let me say that the high resolution of this monitor looks beautiful- text is extremely crisp and easy to read, and high resolution images look great. This 23.8" monitor is smaller than some of the other 3840x2160 monitors out there, giving it very high pixel density, resulting in very crisp images. You will likely have to increase your text and icon sizes though, since most desktop environments weren't designed with this high of DPI in mind. I did experience a number of problems getting the monitor set up. When I tried it for the first time, the monitor did not correctly auto-detect the input source, and I was left with a black screen until I realized the problem and selected it manually. Also, when I first started using it, half the screen was noticeably redder than the other half. I discovered though that if I went into the monitor menu and changed "Color Settings"->"Preset Modes" from "Standard" to "Color Space" then the image would appear correctly. I'm willing to live with this, but someone who cared about different color calibrations might not find this solution acceptable. Also note that if you want full 3840x2160 at 60 Hz you'll have to use a DisplayPort connector (not HDMI), and also go into the monitor menu and enable DisplayPort 1.2- otherwise you'll be limited to 3820x2160 at 30 Hz. In order to support 60 Hz, the monitor acts under-the-hood as two half-resolution monitors side by side. This is supposed to be transparent to the user, but seems to cause various problems on some people's systems. Personally I was able to get it working at 60 Hz under Windows 7, but under a Linux installation on the same machine it would only be recognized with DisplayPort 1.2 disabled, restricting it to 30 Hz. I've been using it at 30 Hz and find it perfectly fine for watching movies, desktop applications, and playing some types of games, but people playing fast-paced action games would really want 60 Hz. Overall, if you want to be an early adopter and spend some time fiddling with the monitor, you'll probably be able to everything working correctly and you'll be able to enjoy beautiful high resolution. If you're looking for something that will work 100% out of the box, I'd recommend waiting another year or so for the technology to mature.

For the price, this is a good deal. You will probably only use the charger. Take all the critical reviews of the FM transmitter with a grain of salt. People reviewing them extremely negatively apparently have their hopes up WAY too high. An FM transmitter is self explanatory. It transmits the device through your FM radio. WHICH MEANS, it will SOUND LIKE a radio signal. ALSO, it requires a clear signal to work. Obviously it cant transmit on a radio station that has a signal already coming through. So if you live in any sort of major city, you can forget it. You probably have a small signal coming through each and every setting. In summary, the FM transmitter cannot be complained about because it DOES do what it is supposed to do....It just doesnt sound like how everyone is hoping it will. Transmitters are generally NOT the way to go. Buy this kit just for the charger. Toss the transmitter.

These Tozo NC9 make listening to my music truly enjoyable and the dynamic sound allows you to enjoy the full sound range from lows, mids and highs without my having to raise the volume to an excessive level. I have small to mid sized ears and the NC9 ergonomic design proved both comfortable and held well in my ears while going for my 5 mile walks and working around the yard. Did fine with phone calls. Easy to link with my phone and my computer. Negatives: the Transparency Mode is not too good; I find that if you are listening to music, you need to maintain the volume low in order to hear a person who is speaking to you even with the Transparency Mode on. The product warranty from Tozo is 12 months, not 18 months on this product. Overall, a very nice product at a great price! I would recommend this product to a friend. If you love music and are looking for a well made pair of Bluetooth buds at an affordable price, these NC9's are for you.

This is an easy upgrade from the Toshiba tray-loading drive of a Dell Inspiron E1705. The drive fits great. Has read some DVDs that none of my other drives will read, but has gotten stuck when inserting about half of my inkjet-printable Sony DVDs that I've stored a lot of data on. Definitely prefers a disc with a smooth top. See my posted image of DVDs it does not like. Update: continues to be hard on discs when being inserted. Have added two pictures of damage to a brand new Sony CD (smooth top, not printable) that got stuck on insertion. Manually removing it resulted in major damage to disc on both sides. Unless someone can recommend an insertion trick to avoid discs getting stuck, I can't recommend this drive. BTW, after this disc was stuck and got ruined, I inserted another from the same set and it worked perfectly. But who can live with that kind of uncertainty? Update2: I did some experimenting and may have found the "trick" I was looking for. It appears that this drive is not good at moving a disc to the centerline when being inserted. The user has to carefully feel that the disc is properly centered (left and right) while inserting. The drive won't grab the disc until it is almost fully inserted, so you can move the disc left and right to get the feel of center well before the disc gets stuck. By the time the disc is half-inserted, be sure there is an equal amount of left-right wiggle room before pushing farther - and if you encounter any resistance, stop immediately and try to re-center. I'm used to more expensive slot-loading drives, where this centering is not an issue.

I'm an engineer and after some research online I believe the device is not signaling to the source to provide sufficient power. There seems to be a difference in power delivery specifications between US and Chinese standards such that current level is not correctly negotiated when using anything but the provided cable. I reached out to the seller for information, link to a technical specification, hoping to buy a longer cable or adapter that would meet my needs but they did not respond. Another problem is that the color output is quite different from another model I have of the same brand. Based on the marketing material and reviews I watched, I expected these two devices when set to the same numeric color value (in Kelvin) to output the same color. AC 110/240v capable works everywhere in the world, PAL /NTSC capable. 7. DVD Component Output is great (Must have HDTV Capable TV), SVideo and RCA outputs also available for Non HDTVs 8. Progressive Scan Output is also available. 9. Accepts virtually any cheap DVD+R media, and DVD+RW media, tried with Cheap GQ DVD+R and Memorex DVD+RW works great. 10. Plays commercial DVDs okay, But do not expect it to play all badly scratched Rental DVDs, Plays cheap VCD 2.0 (PBC ON/OFF), 1.1 and 1.0 Flawlessly UPDATE !! -- Converts and plays cheap PAL VCD/SVCD to NTSC TV output easily and displays on NTSC HDTV capable TV without change in Aspect Ratios or color mangling. Cons: 1. It is very basic DVD recorder, No fancy Editing is possible, Even the Title name does not go beyond 8 characters!!! 2. Does not play WMA media. No ID tag display for MP3s, No menu structure for MP3 playback selection like Panasonics DVD players. 3. JPEG image viewing produces little darker pictures no aspect ratio is maintained if the image size is small (It streches picture to fit the screen) 4. Included TV tuner induces noise on TV channels when connected to CableTV on certain channels when the unit is on, I had to connect the unit seperately rather than the pass thru' option to avoid this interference, Looks that the powersupply in this unit is producing noise which interferes with TV tuner. 5. Limited editing capablities once recording is done, the only option is to delete and or edit the title name and or finialize the VR to DVD video. 7. Do not attempt to fill the disk to the brim, It will surely confuse the player, It might hang on you if you do not enable chapter markings, If you enable Chapters (5-15 mins) it does not hang but the last chapter is lost, Remember, After the DVD recorder fills the DVD, It must have atleast some space left to write the Index mark, Lead-in Lead-out, hence plan ahead to avoid Coasters. For the price, I would say it is good product, It is too early to comment on the reliability of the unit, However, the unit looks well built, Hope it lasts long. Very bright. I can't tell you how many lumens or lux, but it was much brighter than I expected it to be. As Jerry said, you're never going to beat God, so these would be useless during the sunlight (try a reflector), but will add kick on overcast days, failing light, or as is often the case, a dark, cavernous church or reception hall. I've read some people complaining about having to increase ISO to get an exposure. Imagine how much you would have to increase your ISO without it. And again, I'm in the professional game. If you are complaining about your ISO, it may be time to consider an updated camera body. Build quality - I expected the unit to feel a bit "cheap", figuring the manufacturers would have cut corners to increase profitability. I was wrong. Everything about the unit feels great. There is a little "play" between the black handle front and back (probably where the battery compartment would be serviced by a tech) but that's a minor gripe. The buttons, the frosted light shield, the threaded coupling plates, all of it feels sturdy, well-built and durable. Color - I have some 500 LED video lights (very popular and sold under a number of different names) which produce a very green shifted image. Even my 160's have a shift. The constant color on these is unlike any other light I've used. They are dead on daylight without any color cast. I'm guessing the higher quality LEDs and color temp control are part of the cost of these - and they are worth it. Imagine trying to color correct a number of images in post with a unit without color temp control. Battery life - at full power, I got about 70 minutes out of the light. Just as reported and expected. I had heard that the battery didn't hold a charge for more than 48 hours. I just checked now and the light came on and the indicator showed full after more than a week since charging. Perhaps that claim came from an early production run or was defective. I would always check my gear the night prior to an event, but it appears to hold a charge. I do wish there was a field serviceable battery, as we all do, but I work within the constraints as presented. Perhaps in the next version. So is it worth it? Should you buy one? I think so. Heck, I'm buying a second one.

This drive appears to use DM-SMR (Drive Managed Shingled Magnetic Recording). SMR technology can increase drive capacity at a low cost, but with very low (5-10 MB/Sec) write speeds. The drive has a small high-speed write cache which supports 150-100 MB/Sec transfer speeds, but once that cache runs out, speed will plummet and the drive will become unresponsive. The screenshot shows what happened when I attempted to transfer 100GB of files at one. So if you're only downloading games bottlenecked by a 10-20 MB/Sec internet connection, you'll probably never experience this. But if you're trying to move an entire game library to the external drive, or trying to do any other type of large-scale file transfer - forget about it. To make matters worse - once you've saturated the cache, drive response time skyrockets to 4-30 seconds! Since the drive manages it's own cache - stopping/pausing the transfer will not solve this, and the drive will continue to trudge along at low speeds until it clears the internal cache. This will severely impact reading from the drive and has already caused application crashes and data-loss on my end.

I am including my complete review for this OOSSXX Wi-Fi extender and the full OOSSXX HD Camera System which i also purchased because I needed this extender to make the other system work. Overall I am happy with the OOSSXX HD Wireless 960P Video System but it would take 3-4 hours to get it to reliability function in my house; if you did not make any mistakes, have poor wireless signals or need to order parts (I had all those things and it tool me much longer). It could be considered very easy to install the system if all the cameras were separated from the NVR by a single interior wall and <30ft away. The initial set-up with everything in the same room was really "Plug & Play". I must complement OOSSXX for a much better than normal instruction manual and very good YouTube videos on many aspects of the installation. They were KEY in getting the system to work well for the final camera locations. Once I moved the cameras to their permanent locations the signals were constantly dropping out on 3 of the 4 cameras. The front porch camera only connected ~1/2 the time. It is 28ft from the NVR and the signal must go through an interior wall and diagonally through a brick exterior wall sheathed with 1/2" OSB (11-12" thick). Even when I used the Repeater function from the nearest camera to the porch it still dropped out several times an hour even though it was only 16 ft. away but still diagonally through the brick wall. You can tell when there are connection problems by looking at the time field for each camera. A bad connection will not be synced with the others. I solved the problem by using the OOSSXX IPC Router Extender (reasonably priced at $20 at Amazon) placed in a central location and separated from the NVR by a single interior wall and 16 ft. away. The IPC Router Extender is only 6 ft. from the porch camera and the signal goes perpendicularly through the brick wall. The worst thing was that I had to un-install the cameras from the exterior locations and place them in the same room as the IPC Router in order to match the IP codes of each of the cameras to the Router. The instructions and VIDEOS were very good on this fairly complex task. On the other exterior camera I had drill through the brick wall (12.5" thick) and use the supplied antenna extension so that the signal only had to go through one interior wall to reach the IPC Router which is ~ 15 ft away. The final camera is 30 ft away from the IPC router extender and goes through one interior wall with a signal strength of ~50-52 (3 of 4 bar). I also tried multiple channel selections to determine which one provided the highest signal strength. The videos and the instructions on setting up the IPC Router Extender were very important in getting everything to work. Once I finalized on this arrangement; I have not had any dropouts in the signal (1 month use). The wireless capability of this network is probably equal to a router from 10 years ago; but that is to be expected for what we are paying for the system. (Just the wireless router for my home network costs as much as this whole system.) In daylight or a well lit room the resolution of the 960p cameras is great. In low light and under infrared conditions the static items (not moving) are very clear but it is difficult to see facial features in detail unless the person stops moving or is close to the camera. Setting up the Video Detection recording does take some experimentation to get it to work without false alarms(recordings). My suggestion is to limit the detection area to the specific areas of interest; then adjust the Sensitivity. Don't include trees or bushes or blowing wind will trip the recording function. The infrared mode does seem capture "fairies", "ghost" or dust darting around the scene; but not all the time. That is another reason to limit the detection area and the sensitivity; but sometimes they are nearly constant. There are lots of forum discussions on what is the cause but nothing definitive. I just ignore them. I am continuously recording one camera and the other 3 on motion trips. After 1 month, the 1TB drive is 1/3 full. The IP Pro3 phone app works great! Just don't use a password with a special character for your account. The app will not work if you do. The E-see.com web access would only work for me using the NVR Cloud ID and not my account ID; no big deal for me since I use the phone app to remotely view the video.

BE WARNED! YOUR LAPTOP WILL PROBABLY NOT WORK WITH THIS CARD BECAUSE THE LAPTOP VENDOR WON'T ALLOW IT! I am reviewing this with only one star to get your attention. The product may work perfectly but many laptops will not allow this device to work once installed. Many laptop vendors, including HP, only support wireless cards that are shipped from HP. This is enforced by having the PC BIOS look for a special vendor code being returned from the wireless card. If the code is not found then the laptop will not boot at all. There are good reasons for laptop vendors to have these limits such as reducing warranty support calls and keeping the hardware compliant with FCC electromagnetic emissions requirements. Still, it puts customers at a disadvantage so don't waste your money.

I bought this router for my new apartment thinking I'd use something better in the future. I'm sure the turbo g works fine because the computers I had on the network were able to communicate within the LAN, but this item is not compatible with my cable company's setup and WAN is unaccessible. I subscribe to Comcast in the SF bay area and new service comes with an Arris telephony modem. Apparently, with Comcast and this modem, Comcast requires you to use the MAC address associated with the modem they lease to you. After hooking this unit up, you realize that the unit knows only to report the MAC address associated with this router. The conflict lies in that Comcast does not recognize this new MAC address. Calling Comcast will get you confused customer service reps that won't change the MAC address associated with the account. Calling Buffalo will get you a knowledgable rep, but can only tell you to ask Comcast to change their MAC address on file. Now, since I had to get wireless set up for this place immediately, I went to Circuit City to buy a standard D-Link g router. The D-Link router knows how to clone the MAC address of the modem for the router so that Comcast does not get confused. Before buying this unit, check with your cable internet ISP to make sure they can change MAC addresses if you want to be able to use it for world wide web. It seems to have special features for logging onto DSL, but I personally have not tried. This compatibility issue made me conclude that it's definitely a 1-star modem, especially since D-Link recognizes the same problem and has a built in feature to accomodate. Aside from that, the 1-star rating also reflects the 3 hrs wasted on tech support and another hour wasted on going to Circuit City to buy the new router and to go to UPS to return this thing to Amazon.

FIRST 2 DAYS OF USE: Pros -Excellent for small wrists!! (I’m 5’4 and 105lbs on a good day, so it’s been hard to find anything that fits my tiny wrist) -Beautiful design, very elegant, and does not look like a smartwatch! -Super lightweight and thin -Feels great on wrist -Easy to use -Can be used to find iphone and to control music -Arrived quickly in 2 days Cons. Serious connectivity Issues - The bluetooth connection would break multiple times a day, which means that I missed calls and messages. The range is very short, maybe 20 feet. Sometimes I would lose the connection going from my room to the bath room a door away. Battery life is not as great as advertised. -It took about 15 min to charge it the first time I used the watch. However, the battery was at 10% after 28 hours of moderate use. Fully charged it the next day at 7pm, and it was already at 50% at 9am the following day. Mind you, I slept 8 hrs during which the watch obviously was not used. Of note, the second recharge took over 30 mins using my iPad charger (which is way more powerful than a normal outlet)!!! Wrist band has poor quality -Leather is nice, but it started showing signs of use after 2 days! ONE MONTH UPDATE. SOLVED connectivity issues ( by resetting, turning off standbymode and keeping pebble app running in the iphone background) -I reset the watch to factory settings, deleted all unnecessary apps in Pebble app, and turned off the standby mode. That seems to have taken care of the bluetooth issues. On standby mode the watch basically stops the bluetooth to conserve battery energy, but then the watch seems to have trouble reconnecting afterwards. Right now, I only lose bluetooth connection if I go too far from my phone or if the Pebble app is not running in the background on my iphone. - Battery life still poor It was initially better after I deleted all the unnecessary apps. I would get a solid 2 days with light use and 36 hours on average with mod-heavy use (meaning lots of notifications etc). At the beginning a full charge would start at 2d 4h, but now the watch displays 1d13h. I'm worried that the battery will not hold a charge for a day in a month... -Esthetic The watch looks really good. I love it, and that it does not have the bulky smartwatch vibe. I changed the wristband to a plastic one and can work out with it without issues. Overall: Overall I still LOVE this watch. I love that I can used it to find my phone or to control the music remotely while I am driving or working out! This is a great watch for newcomers to the smartwatch world. It is SIMPLE, easy to use, STYLISH and lightweight, great for skinny wrists too. It is a watch first and foremost, a simple smartwatch that does not try to do everything. It's great for the basics (notifications, alarms, find my iphone etc). However, if you care about fancy cardio features, water resistance, or long battery life this watch is NOT for you. Also, navigating the bluetooth connectivity issues can be very frustrating. I removed one star because of that and the battery. 7MONTH UPDATE: Still going strong! Battery same as new.

Acer made a good name for themselves by providing reliable desktop computer components, and that reputation carried over when several years ago, the company advanced into providing laptops. Now after owning three of them, I have never been disappointed in the operation or reliability of any of them. This one is very small and solidly built and it has a brushed aluminum finish I really like in contrast to the nice shiny metallic finishes usually associated with Acer laptops. So now we enter into a new era of Tablet computing and Windows 8, and it is a definite change from the previous computing we learned so well. Advancing cautiously with the help of Acer's desktop, Windows eventually revealed that it is still the same old Windows inside with a new graphical sugar coating and some new enhancements that make it very appealing for use with the new Touch Screen Tablets that are steadily gaining in popularity. Windows 8 has your back if you still find better use for a computer than a Tablet, so this Acer has the familiar touchpad mouse built into its keyboard, but I still prefer using a BlueTooth mouse whenever possible. Additionally, many Android users may find Windows 8 is very similar to using the data provisions of their cell phones, complete with an endless number of available apps. This little 11.6 inch wonder in electronic wizardry will always remain readily available whether I am at work or travelling. Sized the same as the newer Tablets, I consider this laptop to be better provisioned, and best of all, it sells for about half the price of a top-rated Tablet. It is provisioned with the least expensive version of a set of three new CORE Intel processor configurations that increase in cost at each level of complexity, but really don't provide enough in additional abilities to warrant a higher price over what I already have in this very basic laptop computer. This i3 runs very cool and is built into the smallest laptop frame Acer provides, and I even have a little accessory carrying case for it. This laptop is too small to accommodate a mounted optical disk drive, but that is easily fixed since there are several external CD/DVD RW drives available at a nice price, all provisioned to plug into a laptop's USB ports for immediate use. Regardless, Acer Support provides a Recovery Flash Drive for this computer that can be plugged into one of its USB ports if a recovery to factory specs ever becomes necessary. With a little more time researching some of the other similar laptops available from Acer before purchasing this one, chances are I would have also seriously considered the Acer Aspire One laptop. That would have saved another couple hundred $$ since it is a very close duplicate to this one. The only real difference is its slightly slower Intel processor, but it also has a smaller but more practical 320 Gig hard drive, which for all my needs is still HUGE. Either one of these laptops is perfect for students who must store and do their work on a fully provisioned computer, and there are also some AMD provisioned 11.6 Acer laptops as well at an even lower price.

I bought this camera about a week before my honeymoon, on the strength of its specifications and the positive reviews. We wound up getting some great indoor and outdoor pictures of Barcelona, and couldn't be more pleased with the camera. My wife, who isn't interested in fiddling with aperture and shutter speed, used the excellent Auto mode; I was able to get some nice results with the aperture and shutter priority settings. This camera has an excellent lens - the wide-angle end is as wide as you're likely to need, and the zoomed-in end is sufficiently tight for most uses. The maximum aperture of f2.0 gives you more flexibility with exposure time than any other point-n-shoot of which I'm aware. Coupled with a sensor that's usable at reasonable ISO, and with auto-stabilization, the fast lens lets you take fantastic indoor shots with available light. The included flash is pretty powerful, but I almost never used it. The only things I didn't like about this camera were its lack of an optical viewfinder (you can purchase one that fits in the hotshoe) and the need for a lens cap. Otherwise, this is a fantastic camera, and arguably the best current-generation camera in its price range.

At first I was very negative about this product - it doesn't come with a power cable to plug the adapter into the wall - and that fact isn't 'clear' on the listing. However, I have a box of 100's of these power cables so it wasn't a bit issue. I know I am in the minority there ;). After persisting and working through getting these things to work, I am happy to say that they work great!. I am running mine (I have two now - ordering more) running off of a Raspberry Pi using CGminer 4.9.0. I will post the steps and command line at the end of this review, but I am not seeing any heat issues with the included power supplies - at least yet - been running them for about two days now. The big key to these is getting a really good USB hub to plug them into before plugging them into your PC or Raspberry Pi. Get a good USB hub - the one I got uses a 4 amp power supply. A small fan blowing some air under them to help the heat-sinks cool better also helps. I am running mine at 243Mhz and 780mV and getting an average of 62Gh/s out of each one of them - so far no issues (knock on wood.) Getting these guys to run on a Pi was key to keeping the power consumption low - which is key to maximizing ROI - such as it is with a miner that doesn't do over a terrahash ;). For the money, I think these things are a great deal - but they are not plug and play. There are some good articles out on the interweb about using Windows (cgminer shows up as a virus - I think this is a false positive but was nerve wracking nontheless), but not a lot of stuff out there on using the Raspberry Pi and CGMiner to control the Antminer U3. After doing a lot of twidling, below is the list of steps/commands I ran to get these things to work well: Get a Raspbian image and burn it to a SD card for you Pi (lots of tutorials out there on this - won't bore everyone with those steps here) Get remote access or console access to your PI - login as Pi and do the following: ================== sudo apt-get update sudo aptitude install git autoconf libtool libcurl4-openssl-dev libncurses5-dev pkg-config yasm make libusb-1.0-0-dev sudo aptitude upgrade <reboot> git clone git://github.com/ckolivas/cgminer.git cgminer cd cgminer ./autogen.sh export LIBCURL_CFLAGS=-I/usr/local/opt/curl/include export LIBCURL_LIBS=-L/usr/local/opt/curl/lib ./configure --disable-libcurl --enable-icarus make sudo make install (This step is optional) ========================== To start mining, use this command - if you leave the au3-volt and au3-freq out it will use the default of 225Mhz and 750Mv which is good to start with: sudo ./cgminer -c <yournameorwhatever>.conf --au3-volt 780 --au3-freq 243 A few troubleshooting steps: Execute 'lsusb' to see what your Pi see's on the USB bus - you should see the following or similar if your Antminer's are properly connected: Bus 001 Device 006: ID 10c4:ea60 Cygnal Integrated Products, Inc. CP210x UART Bridge / myAVR mySmartUSB light Make sure you execute the proper 'configure' command - icarus is required for Cgminer to use the Antminer U3. I would 'highly' suggest building cgminer yourself - there appears to be some questionable images out there and I think it's better to know for sure what you are running than using a canned image. Minepeon doesn't appear to be updated to anything new enough for you to get the most out of the Antminer U3's. Bgminer at this time does not support the Antminer ASIC mining rigs. Use a dedicated USB power cord to power your Pi - do not use the hub that you are using to connect the Antminer U3's to your Pi to also power your Pi. While the Antminer's do have dedicated power supplies, they do also draw a considerable amount of current through the USB ports as well. Hopefully that will give some help to people who are stuck with these. Happy mining!

Purchased this board ten months ago and got maybe two months of use out of it before giving up on it and ASUS. Sent it back once after it bricked itself and they reflashed it and sent it back, minus some of the stuff I sent with it. Used it for a bit longer and well after upgrading to the newest available firmware, attempted my memory OC again...immediately bricked itself in the same manner. By this time I had modified it to the point that another return would have been too much of a hassle to bother with. Replaced it with a an MSI board that was a quarter of the cost Pros: - Solid power delivery and VRM cooling - USB-C header - POST code display - Dual M.2 4.0 slots - Stiff as a board Cons: - $430 - Two fans, meaning two potentially noisy points of failure. Common issue with X570 boards, which is silly since we were cooling chipsets with three times the TDP passively a decade ago. Barely excusable on a SFF board. - Single, non-removable, BIOS ROM chip. - Self erases it's ROM chip when attempting to POST from a particularly bad memory OC or when delving too deeply into the AGESA settings. - BIOS flashback feature that should make a second ROM chip redundant, won't work on badly corrupt firmware. - POST code display often spits out post codes that aren't listed, or are listed as 'reserved'. This is not helpful. - Single sided memory retention clips make it almost impossible to remove DIMMs without 'zippering' them at an angle. - Chipset run silly warm for how much cooling it's got, probably because of the 1.5mm thick thermal pad between it and it's heatsink. Didn't cause any problems, but was still worrying, given that it's got fans. - CMOS battery is hidden under the heatsink and taped to the side of the I/O ports. It's also packaged in heatshrink with the terminals connected to the motherboard via two wires and a tiny header...this makes it vastly more difficult to replace than it should be. The battery was also half dead (2.95v...3.3v is normal for a full charge) out of the box. - Themal pad connected SOC VRM to motherboard backplate making almost no contact. - The M.2 riser, with heatsink installed is very heavy and would almost certainly break or damage the SO-DIMM slot it sits in if the system were roughly handled. - M.2 heatsinks warp the M.2 riser and installed M.2 drives when secure. Lessons learned: - You don't always get what you pay for.

I was extremely happy with this purchase. I will start off with the pros. - The listing shows the computer coming with an i5-3470. But mine actually came with an i5-3570. It's the same generation and build architecture, but its base clock and turbo clock are both 200MHz (0.2GHz) higher; so this processor is better than what it was supposed to come with. - The computer did not require ANY cleaning inside. It had been thoroughly cleaned inside so there was no dust or dirty spots. I did replace the thermal paste on the CPU, as it was likely pretty old, but I would not expect the seller to have done that themselves. - I didn't need it, but it came with a mouse and keyboard. The Mini Tower (MT) case is far better than the Small Form Factor (SFF) case versions for a few reasons. (1). Air flow is much better. Although the SFF don't have bad airflow, it isn't as good as the MT cases. (2). Full size PCIe slots allow for full size cards to be installed (SFF require half height cards) (3). More HDD/SSD spots and connections. MT has 2x3.5" and 2x5.25" bays to go with the 4xSATA connectors (4). The MT use a full size, standard, ATX power supply instead of the proprietary power supply units in the SFF. That means you can spend like $30-$40 and get a nice power supply unit and go with an even better GPU like a GTX 1060 6GB. There was really only one con for this machine (or at least the one I got), and that was the RAM setup. I got the listed 8GB, but it came installed at 4x2GB. That means if I ever want to upgrade, it will cost more because I will have to replace everything instead of just adding a few sticks. That being said, I don't really think I'll be upgrading, so the RAM isn't a huge deal. I paired my machine with a Zotac GTX 1050 Ti 4GB Mini and this thing can game! I can play GTA V on HIGH settings @ 1080p while still getting over 60 fps. That's without any overclocking with MSI Afterburner. Keep in mind this is about the best graphics card you can use in this computer without upgrading the PSU because there are no PCIe power connectors. The GTX 1050 Ti 4GB Mini just uses the power from the PCIe slot and does not require any extra power. Total price of the entire rig was about $360. That is an EXCELLENT price for modern 1080p gaming at 60 fps. If I was to spend any more money, it would be on a new PSU, but just for reliability sake. I have included pictures of some of the components inside the case, along with a Cinebench test of the CPU and GTX 1050 Ti 4GB Mini. Here are the specs of the specific machine I received. It seems like they are not all the same, so I can't guarantee you will receive the same: CPU: i5-3570 (4 core, 4 thread, 3.4 base clock, 3.8 turbo clock) RAM: 8GB (4x2GB) DDR3 @ 1600MHz (maximum speed supported by CPU) HDD: 1TB Seagate BarraCuda 7200RPM PSU: Dell 275W OS: Windows 10 Pro 64-bit (with sticker code on case if you want to install on new SSD) I added the GTX 1050 Ti 4GB Mini and the 250GB Samsung 840 Evo SSD.

In a business where companies are competing to shove as many drivers as possible into their flagship products, I am very glad I gave the single BA Klipsch X10 a try. If they were $200 I would never have gotten them, so thank you Amazon, for the $95 deal. I've had a number of higher end IEMs, such as Shure SE535, Ultimate Ears TF10, 700, Etymotics ER4-PT, ATH-CK10, Monster Turbine Pro Copper, etc. Some of these are more expensive or technically superior than the X10s, but I find myself grabbing the X10s more often ever since I got them. I find that they work well with just about every genre. After a few days of testing, I can honestly say that the X10 is up there with some of the best universal fit IEMs out there, a truly first-tier sound that comes in a very tiny and comfortable housing. The sound is involving, fun, natural, and smooth. There is more bass than most single BA driver IEMs, and an enveloping sound that reminds one of a speaker-like sound. It is amazing that these small earphones can produce such expansive and big sound. The X10 proves once again, just as the ER4s has proven, that a carefully tuned single balanced-armature driver can sound just as good, if not better, than IEMs with 3 or 4 BAs. ___Packaging___ I think the Black Friday $95 X10s come in a different packaging than the regular priced ones. It is cheaper and more flimsy, not representative of the MSRP. I have a habit of keeping the box as like-new as possible when unboxing. This was not possible with the X10, as the box was designed to be torn open. ___Accessories___ You get an assortment of ear tips, a cleaning tool, airline adapter, 1/4'' adapter, and a very nice carrying case. The carrying case is hard shell and very compact. ___Comfort/Fit/Isolation___ The silicon tips are oval shaped, which is much more ergonomic than your usual rounded ones. I find that they provide better fit, as well as prolonged comfort. I tried the bi-flanges, but reverted back to the original medium sized tips. The X10's elongated housing reminds me of my ER4-PTs, and enables a deep insertion, which provides better isolation. Personally I prefer deeper insertions over those barely-in-ear ones. ___Build Quality___ Meh. I've heard stories about the very thin cable and strain relief break in a few month. I can really see that happening. These earphones feels fragile. And the build quality is not perfect or seamless. ___Sound___ Klipsch headphones are known for their overpowering bass, such as the Klipsch Image One. However, that is totally not the case with the X10. The X10 still has a very strong bass, very good texture, impact, and weight. It is also slower and not as punchy as other BAs, such as ER4 and CK10. The X10 definitely is one of the more bassy IEM I've heard, including dynamic driver ones. But the bass does more to bring out the fun and emotions, rather than dominating everything else, which is really impressive. The soundstage is not so big or open. The sound is more in-your-ears with the X10, rather than right there in your brains like most IEMs. I like it because the music is more laid-back, and not as intrusive. You can listen to them, and just let the music play in the background. That is not to say the X10s have bad soundstage. As a matter of fact, the X10 positions all layers of sound extremely well. The vocals, the instruments, the little details. The soundstage is awesome at imaging vertical displacements and horizontal positioning is just so so. Vocals and treble have taken an obvious step back, because of the bass and soundstage. They aren't recessed. They are just not as forward as other IEMs I've used to. As a result the X10s are a bit darker, natural, smooth, and laid-back. That is, if the ER4s represent the perfect neutral sound, then TF10 and CK10 would be the bright IEMs, and X10s would be dark but leaning very closely to being neutral. However, after months spent with my ER4-PT, which is known for its unfailing ability to present details and accuracy, the X10 surprised me several times already with details in my music that I haven't noticed before on the ER4-PT. I switched back to the ER4s, and whaddaya know, these details are there, but they aren't as well fleshed out, or as defined and well positioned on the ER4 as they are on X10. Because of their please-all soundsig, the X10 is good for most genres. I'd miss IE8's enormous soundstage and grand bass on some large classical ensembles, and I'd miss the pitch-perfect, crystal clear, and bright sounds the ER4 has when I listen to Les Miserables, but there isn't a case of music with which the X10 sounds bad at. In fact, they've rekindled my passion to some genres that I hardly listen to anymore but used to love, like The Beatles. ___Final Words___ As you can see, I think very highly of the X10. I've had mine for 3 days, and I cannot imagine my IEM collection without them. They are truly amazing, and unique. The X10's sound is one of a kind, and top-tier in its class. $95 is a real steal, but $200 is a bit too much for them. For their performance, I'd pay up to $150 for them.

I never write reviews, but my experience with this product has been so negative to an extent that I hope my efforts here prevent others from wasting their time as I have done. The enclosure performs its advertised functions, but exhibits flaws that will likely result in its return for a refund. Three significant flaws have been observed so far: two of the three case to chassis screws were stripped by their ports, the enclosure vibrates and emits an incessant low hum while running, and the drives do not spin down to idle, which has opened Pandora’s Box when attempting to address the lack of an idle function. The firmware shipped on the device is outdated, and one must update to a new firmware version in order to set the drives to idle when not in use. Glotrend’s firmware update software is only available for Windows computers and is flagged by antivirus and browsers as being unsafe. Specifically, it appears their firmware software contains a WIN32:Vitro virus. Based on another review, it appears that there is a new, virus-free firmware available outside of Glotrend support but it is unclear which firmware update is applicable for this hardware, and thus is a non-starter to resolve the lack of an idle. When attempting to contact Glotrend support for 2 consecutive days, their website returns an error and advises the user to try again later. This reviewer will give it a few more days for resolution, but will most likely have to return the enclosure to seek a product that can reliably provide a simple RAID array without all the fuss and the likely premature destruction of its hard drives due to excessive vibrations and use.

I purchased this item for easily switching computer displays at the church I attend. I am a volunteer that works in the media booth. As it is a non-profit and in this economic climate, the budget is very small. Basically any and all equipment is donated by the volunteers. That means I footed the bill for it. So I was extremely pleased that it didn't cost hundreds of dollars! I have two overhead projectors and a flat panel TV that all receive signals from two laptop computers in the media booth. I was seeking something that would allow me to easily send a signal from one of two different computers to any of the output devices. Perhaps displaying a PowerPoint slide show in the lobby on the flat panel TV while presenting a live video feed from the two ceiling mounted projectors. The device works beautifully. So if the LED is red, you have to rapidly press the switch twice in order to get back to the A device. * I wish there were a way to retain settings when power is lost. Everything reverts back to the A setting. So if you have a configuration where some devices are operating from the A side and some from the B side, when power comes back on everything reverts to A. Additionally, I have the two input four output model. I'm presently not using the fourth output. I typically power that fourth off by pressing the button. I also have two overhead projectors. It would be cool to somehow lock those together so a single press changed their two outputs. Overall it seems to have been a very good investment.

Love it. Finally, designed to be held in one hand… for hours! I traded in my Kindle Paperwhite for the Oasis and am really glad I did. The Paperwhite was not objectively heavy, by any means, but the Oasis is infinitely more comfortable to hold in one hand for long periods of time. It is noticeably lighter, which makes a difference. More importantly, though, it is designed for one-handed reading with its tapered form factor and dedicated page turn buttons. It really does feel completely different. I'm not one to buy into advertising hype, but I can attest to it feeling like a new, better reading experience. It feels like you're holding a stack of index cards, or a CD/DVD case with a booklet inside (for those old enough to be able to visualize those) instead of a tablet. And I love the new shape, the shorter size with the larger bezel on the side for holding it is much more natural. I read for hours each day while commuting on often uncomfortable mass transit. If you primarily read at the kitchen table or in some other comfortable environment, this may not be worth the upgrade for you. For me, however, it makes all the difference. I can hold it in the same position (again, one-handed) for hours and do not have to awkwardly re-position my hand to avoid fatigue or turn the page. I can hold on to the subway pole with one hand while grasping my Kindle securely with the other and never risk dropping it or annoyingly juggling it in my palm while trying to turn the page. I read pretty quickly and this new design helps me power through books even faster. I can't compare it to the Voyage (which I was considering because of the page turn 'buttons' before the Oasis came out), but am very happy with my upgrade from the Paperwhite and believe the new form factor is totally worth it. I appreciate that this is not simply an incremental upgrade where they are trying to get us to pay more for marginally better performance specs that no one really cares about, but rather a truly updated experience. If you read a lot, or if you read while commuting/traveling, I think you'll appreciate the difference. I even appreciate the difference when reading in bed while laying on my side. I love the ability to get comfortable (or as comfortable as one can get while commuting) and stay completely still while flipping through page after page after page. I am extremely happy with my upgrade. The price is high (and at this price it should not include advertising) but is worth it for me because I use it, literally, for hours every weekday. Pros: Packaging is pretty, the USB cable and aux cord come in a cute little baggy for me Good bass for a small, Bluetooth speaker 360 degrees of sound is pretty cool Pretty cool on/off guy talking to me (my friends all mock me now whenever I turn it on - maybe this is a con now? hehe) Very sturdy. My friend accidentally kicked it while cliff diving (thankfully it didn't fall into the water) and I hardly noticed a scratch on it. It tells me when the battery is low whenever it's on, and gives me an estimate of how much battery is have left. The microphone actually works!! Cons: These cons may be a bit nitpicky, but I do feel they were definitely significant enough to comment on (i.e. they're the reason I gave 4 stars instead of 5). I also tried to give each con a decent reason why I thought they were cons. The power and Bluetooth buttons are in an awkward position on the speaker. I have to really dig my finger into the crevice in order to turn it on. I would really have liked the power button to be on the top with all the other buttons or at least somewhere more accessible on the speaker. Whenever the battery is low, the speaker will tell me "Battery is low", but it will always tell me at a constant volume. As in, there is always a set volume the 'announcer' will report things to me, instead of the speaker raising/lowering the voice in order to match whatever volume I'm on. I use the speaker at an extremely low volume when I'm sleeping, so when the speaker tells me the battery is low, it sounds like he's yelling, "BATTERY IS LOW" at me when I would rather him whisper it to me instead. This is the biggest reason why I gave the speaker four stars, honestly. Why would you not match the volume I have my music at, Fugoo pls I would like more precise battery estimates. I've only noticed that he will only tell me four options: Battery is full, about 3/4, about half, or low. I'd like it to be precise to at least 10% maybe? Reporting the exact percentage like my iPhone does would be ideal. Maybe a little bit of nonslip grip on the bottom to keep it from sliding around would help it out. Overall, despite my extremely nitpicky reasons (except for my big paragraph), this speaker is definitely still worth the money. Definitely invest in a quality Bluetooth speaker, because the cheaper ones will die on you quickly.

I've purchased a lot of cams over the years, many in the $100-$300 price class and also larger surveilance systems with POE and an HDR in the $2000-$3000 range. I can say that ALL of them were a major pain to setup and install, and most of them had problems requiring them to be reset after a day or two, eventually frustrating me to the point where I stopped using them. The Amazon Cloud CAM was a piece of cake to setup! It worked right out of the box, and delivered impressive high quality video immediately. I was pleased that I ddin't even have to re-enter my wifi router's password - it apparently learns it from the app on the iOS which is already connected! The one negative I've found so far: The ir emitters for dark viewing are also good...EXCEPT...if you try and aim the cam out a window. In that case, the ir emitters just reflect back off the glass and you see nothing outside. Unfortunately, there isn't a way through the setup app on iOS (not sure on Android) to disable the ir emitters! The cam is not rated for outdoor use so I'm not sure what to do for this issue. You can move the cam around from place to place simply by unplugging the power adapter and taking it all to the next location. It comes back up in a minute or two just fine, every time (so far). The motion sense is cool, and the cloud storage is great. You can see video snips of the motion events on the app, and since the video is stored in the cloud if a burglary occurs and they steal the camera, the video should still be there in the cloud, although I'm not sure how to access it if the camera is gone since the app appears to marry the videos with the cam. I was surprised that I could talk 2-way to the cam, and although it is half-duplex (you have to press a button on your phone to talk) it is still a decent feature for a low-price cam. I was about to buy some more cams, but when I bought the first cloud-cam is was $119. I tried to "buy it again" and it is now $199. I think it is worth $119, but not so much $199. Not sure what's up with that - maybe I got a special pre-order price? Anyway, my GF told me to get it out of the house cause she doesn't like being "watched". I imagine much of the world wonders if Amazon is spying on them but that's for you to decide. I noticed that the microphone is quite sensitive, and does a good job...BUT...the iOS app sounds stays on even when the MUTE switch on my phone is on (the app seems to ignore the switch). I was surprised (ok, shocked) to learn the that Cloud-Cam doesn't have the ability to 'flip' or mirror' the image. You are forced to mount the cam upright which doesn't work in all desired cases.

This case is a good value, especially if you're looking for a case to hold a lot of drives. It's almost ideal for my purpose; building a small file and media server for my home network. I am mostly pleased with my purchase, and even with a few items displeasing me I couldn't find any other case that met my needs for less than double the price. My requirements: Room for a micro-ATX motherboard, a big CPU heat-sink, and as many hard drives as I can stuff inside the box. Ventilation adequate to keep the drives and CPU cool while transcoding video. Graphics card fit or cooling was not a consideration. The server does not contain a graphics card (other than the one embedded in the chipset). Most of the time it doesn't even have a monitor, keyboard or mouse attached. Pros: Lots of space for drives. I put eight 3.5 inch hard drives in the case. In addition there are two 5.25 inch bays and three places to mount 2.5 inch drives. Lots of ventilation. The front is fully ventilated with room to mount two 120mm fans so I can blow outside air over all those drives. There are also vents on both sides and the top. Most vents are filtered (though see the cons below for more on those filters) No frills look. This thing is sitting in my home office. I do not want a computer that looks like a gaming system. I do not want a window on the side nor do I want LED fans. This case looks nice but doesn't look like it should be in a game room. Comes with two basic (no PWM) fans mounted. I replaced them with PWM fans (and added more PWM fans elsewhere), but I didn't really need to. Motherboard mounting plate has an opening for mounting a cooler back-plate. Cable management is decent. I've never worried about this before (I don't care to see inside my computer) but I suppose it makes airflow within the case a bit cleaner. Cons: Fit and finish leave a bit to be desired. One side panel was bent at the corner when I received the case. I straightened it, but it still doesn't sit squarely on the side of the case. It's not worth the trouble to RMA, so I'll live with it. Filters are difficult to remove for washing. All require you to remove one side panel or the other to access. In some cases, if you mount a fan, the filter ends up between the fan and the case side (meaning you must remove the fan to remove the filter). Little headroom between the motherboard and the top of the case. I use a downward blowing CPU cooler (Scythe Kabuto II). There is so little space between the cooler vanes and the top of the case that it's impossible to mount standard 25mm thick fans to the top vents. I think I can make thin (15mm) fans fit, but I'm not certain. It would have been nice if the case had a little more headroom.

(Dec 2019 update below) First, don't be scared off by "refurb". The seller (StallionTek) provided a nice clean system - in this case the specs were nicely dragged toward current-day (as of 2018/2019) within the constraints of a 2013 platform. Yes, there are some small scratches / dings on the case, but as noted, the system was clean. No dust bunnies or dried coffee spills. This has a healthy dose of RAM (128GB) and disk (500GB SSD + 2TB HDD), cooling like an overclocked game rig - but not too loud. Plenty of USB, a firewire port plus some old-school PS/2 and DB9 serial COM. There's extra internal drive bays if the time comes to get more disk storage. Dual Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPUs and dual nVidia Quadro FX 3800 Graphic cards are admittedly a bit dated, but capable. It's running a fresh/current OS and - best part - none of the typical HP bloat ware. As advertised, the system does come with a mouse and keyboard, but both are wired USB. And while they're good for initial bring-up and will be great to have on a shelf as spares for when yer in a bind, they are a bit minimalist, clunky and cheap. You'll want to pick up a proper mouse/keyboard. Ask yourself why you are considering this system. I personally had need for a modest/starter workstation-class system for number crunching, light CAD, and software development, etc. but I wasn't interested in jumping into a $2K to $3K system only to be potentially underwhelmed given the price. (If you need a modern-day, top of the line workstation, then you should probably move along.) And don't forget it's *WAY* cheaper than if you had bought the system new, at full price, and then paid for all the current day upgrades. ****** Update: Dec 30, 2019 ****** Hate doing it, but I had take back one star regarding SSD/HDD. One concern I had on receiving the system was the "Super Talent" brand 500GB SSD. Despite all my tech purchases over 30 years, I had never heard of them and was a bit concerned it was junk. But a few quick searches turned up nothing negative and a few "pretty good value" comments, I figured I was falling victim to "brand name" prejudice. Fast forward 5 months of limited use, I started getting blue screens daily/weekly, but system checks, diagnostics turned up nothing. Then one day, my SMART check came back with a panic report (out of the blue) the drive was failing. Reallocated sector count was maxxed and pending sector count was climbing. I was able to partially image it, before the drive completely failed - fortunealye my SOP is to regularly snapshot drives. The last successful SMART report showed the drive failed with only 96 hours of power on time (!!!) Then on closer scrutiny, I noticed the 2TB Hitachi HDD had over 58000 hours of power on time, so it's well used. Hitachi makes good drives, so I'm not as concerned. Power-on hours is the drives "worst" reported attribute, all others are still very good. But still, I had naively hoped that the perhaps most vulnerable components would be what was renewed. So cheap junk SSD (personal sample size of 1), and a well worn HDD. I had to pony up for a new SSD and will sooner-than-expected need to replace the HDD. So far, in spite of this disappointing episode, I *still* think the system, as purchased has value. it might stack up a bit differently against other options given the necessary component replacements. But I will probably still make this purchase again. I contacted StallionTek for comment on 12/18 (admittedly, the week before Christmas wasn't the best time). But as of 12/30, I've gotten no response.

I have some pretty good telescopes, and I have a few pairs of the little pocket binoculars that are so common, and quite a few items in between. The problem that I have been tolerating for a long time is that of not having an "optimal" pair of binoculars for routine use. These would have fairly bright optics, fairly good magnification, fairly light weight to carry, a reasonably sleek, non-clunky shape, a moderate size, reasonable sturdiness, and a comfortably sharp focus. I only received these "Byakov" binoculars today, and in addition to all of the above, I find that they also solve the ages-old problem of what to do with the lens covers. It is desirable to protect the lenses well when not looking through the binoculars, but it is always such a pain to pull off the caps, put them safely somewhere, and then be able to take a look. These eyepiece covers attach to the neck strap, so they simply swing out of the way, and the objective lens covers are held by tabs, and they just fold downward, out of the way. Removing the covers is not extremely fast, but it is faster and more care-free. The other items included in the package, the phone camera mount, the tripod binocular mount, and the tiny tripod, are nice to have as well, just in case one wants to use them. No, they are not super sturdy, precision equipment, but they are also not mere junk. For the price, I have no right to say that anything here is less than great. If I were being picky, I would say that, on my instance of this product, the lenses are not absolutely free of distortion, but I can read quite fine print at quite a distance, in a neighboring room lit moderately from a side window. The view is comfortable and clear, and I don't feel that I am being robbed of detail that I want to see. This is in comparison to many cheap binoculars that, when they are in focus, you still can't make out details. Again, for the binoculars that I received, the weight seems good, and the feel of these binoculars is solid, in contrast to what I think I have read from some users. Nothing here is loose or floppy, nothing rattles, and nothing feels fragile, even though the few exposed, hard plastic parts would probably not withstand a high impact, more than one would want to give to a pair of binoculars. The focus dial moves without difficulty, but it also feels smooth and firm, and it brings the view into precise focus. The right eye focus compensator is also firm and smooth, reaching a precise focus and not changing position without effort. A smaller and even more portable size is always preferred, of course, but that would be hard to achieve without losing either magnifying power or brightness. The feel of these binoculars is serious, like a real tool, yet not cumbersome. I don't see a better compromise between carrying convenience and general capabilities than is in this basic design of binoculars, and it is a delight to find this degree of quality at a price that does not make a person reluctant to use them regularly.

This could have been a great headset for sleeping. While it has no noise cancelation, the earbuds isolates fairly well and has a large battery. However, the firmware nearly ruins it. The first problem I noticed with the firmware pertains to incoming calls. When someone calls, instead of the custom ring tone or the registered name being spoken by the phone assistant, the headset cuts all audio and the voice notification reads out the phone number. That is incredibly useless as I have custom ring tones set that can wake me up for emergencies. Next, Ill cover the volume and control issues. This headset does not report as a Bluetooth headset to my phone, but instead is listed as a media device. This probably wouldn't be an issue if it didn't also set the volume to 80%. I typically listen to the earbuds at 35% volume, and my phone doesn't allow other wireless or wired headphones or headsets to go past 60% volume without confirming that I understand the risks to my hearing. This product bypasses that by not reporting properly to the source. If you connect the headset while you have media playing you'll get blasted until you lower the volume which requires repeatedly pressing the volume down button since holding the volume buttons changes tracks! The worst aspect of the headsets firmware involves the battery. This headset is supposed to have 25 hours of battery capacity during active use. Imagine my surprise when I was listening to a podcast while getting my morning coffee and heard all audio cut out and then heard the notification voice say "Battery Low" while the battery was reporting 20% charge. 20% of 25 hours is 5 hours. Yeah, that was really annoying to hear the low battery warning cut through every 5 minutes until I got so frustrated that I turned the headset off an hour later. This meabs that you can only get 2 nights of uninterrupted sleep before having to charge the headset sin you'll be awoken after 4 hours of the third night by the obnoxious warning.

This review might be a little long, bear with me. A few points to note first: 1. The monitored temperature displayed on the T units is NOT the same as the max temperature on the top of your equipment. I’ve found as much as a 12 F difference after the equipment has been on for a while. Keep this in mind when selecting a setting temperature. 2. The fans are NOT particularly quiet. In a quiet room it is possible to hear the fans at speed 1. They aren’t loud, but you can hear them. Anything above 3 is unusable in my opinion. Actually anything above 2. 3. Since the unit sits on top of your equipment, it should NEVER be powered off as it does impede normal convective cooling. For this reason I will never turn off the front panel display so that I can always be sure the unit is on. I’m using a T8 to help on a Denon X4400 which is in a location without really open ventilation. My goal is to try to keep the temperature somewhat lower than without the T8 and to stabilize it as much as possible. After experimenting for a bit, I found the most important goals were: 1. Keep the fan speed as low as possible, but more importantly, 2. Keep the fan speed from shifting between speeds as this is VERY noticeable when it happens. My current settings are: Alarm at 100 F, Setting at 91 F, Sensitivity at 4 F, Max fan speed at 2, Mode on SMART. At these settings with normal viewing, listening, the fan stays at 1 for about the first 4 hours or so. After that the AVR is getting warm enough that the monitored temperature begins to hit 91 F, and the fan starts to switch between 1 and 2 to pull the temperature down. At this point fan speed switching gets pretty regular and if you’re watching/listening to something with quiet passages or dialogue, it’s pretty audible. I’m still experimenting. At first I wasn’t sure I was going to keep the T8, but in the end I still feel it’s worth some work and compromise to keep the AVR temperature more stable. Of course your situation may be quite different than mine, so YYMV.

The concept of the headphones is good - they are slim enough not to be obtrusive when laying on a pillow. However, with that said, I feel that there are several design inadequacies that keep this from being a quality product. PROS: * Very slim profile * Sound quality is good * Battery life is adequate * Paring is good CONS: The headband is very poorly designed. * Placement of the Bluetooth component: --- It is located at the back of the band which places it under your head. After as little as 15min when laying on a pillow, it creates a pressure point that is extremely uncomfortable. Prolonged use (1hr+) results in a headache and soreness the following day. If you tilt your head to either side on the pillow, the pressure point of the Bluetooth component becomes even more apparent. --- The controls for the Bluetooth component (paring and volume) are positioned at the back and under your head. To access the controls you either have to sit up or completely remove the headband for any adjustments you need to make. To solve the two component issue above, I have had to wear the headband backwards (rotated 180 degrees) so that the Bluetooth component is at the front of my head. This has made the headset somewhat usable and eliminated most of the discomfort. But now, the band is reversed. The widest portion of the headband is at my forehead and the narrowest portion of the headband is at the back of my head. * Access to charge the unit and adjust speaker locations: --- The band has an access slot that way to small to properly access the Bluetooth component and the speakers. The narrow slot is further restricted by a large velcro strip. --- The Bluetooth component needs to be accessed which involves removing it because the location of the USB port is approximately 2 inches away from the tiny access headband slot. This places a lot of stress on the wires and the USB plug when trying to get the unit in and out of the headband. --- The adjustment of the speaker location for optimal sound is extremely difficult. The headband is cloth, and the speakers are covered in cloth, so the friction between the two make it very difficult to work with. --- To wash the headband, you have to remove everything (Bluetooth component and speakers) through the tiny slot in the headband which is extremely difficult but not as difficult as trying to get it all back in place. With a little additional thought, these flaws in the design could have easily been avoided - especially for a product that sells for $100.

I love my Sky Smartpen. I have been a longtime user of Evernote and I'm so pleased that the sky pen works with Evernote, which I think is one of the best organizational tools out there. I am primarily using my Sky to take online Chinese Language lessons with teachers in China by Skype. I use the (sold separately but very inexpensive) 3D earphones made just for these Livescribe Smartpens. For the Skype lessons, I use the 3D earbugs and then I use a logitech wireless headset with soft padding over the earbugs. The padding is standard on most logitech headsets and makes it so that the double setup doesn't bother my ears at all and the recording is crystal clear. I was really unclear with the data online about the ability to record phone meetings versus live meetings and lectures. Unless I'm doing it wrong, the answer is: you can wear just the 3D earphones during a meeting or a live lecture, they will pick up what you hear and also what you. If you're recording a phone/skype call you need to have a second layer which is the headset. I was using the headset anyway so adding the earphones has been nothing difficult or notable. I was worried about recording all of these classes because I only got the 2G version of the pen and I read online that in order to get data OFF of the pen, you have to archive the entire notebook; that erases all of the recordings from the pen but makes it impossible to keep using audio recording with the same notebook (though you can continue to use the notebook for writing notes). But then I realized that you get about 200 hours of recording even on the minimalist 2G pen and that should be more than adequate for each notebook and even using multiple notebooks for multiple subjects (which I'm also doing). If you archive one notebook and not another, it only deletes the archived notebook from your pen. The other notebook is not affected. NOTABLY, ALL OF YOUR NOTES ARE STILL IN EVERNOTE and readily available to you. In short, my concern about running out of recording space on the pen before I was actually finished with the notebook is not a legit concern. (The notebooks are very very reasonably priced). Also, I just clicked on one of the audio recordings in Evernote and a web-browser-based app opened up that had all of my notes in conjunction with the recording, so if you want to review your audio and written notes without having your notebook with you- it's completely possible. Great for travel or if you move on to a second notebook and don't want to cart the old one with you to class. Or, if you have your notebook with you, you just tap on the part you want to hear again while you're reviewing your written notes. It's really an extraordinary device. I don't know how I made it through law school without it... but back then we only had slate and chalk... The reviews that dislike the product seem largely to be from people who don't like Evernote or who were happy with other versions of the pen and thought that the sky was an expansion on the same pen rather than the introduction of a different pen with different features. For those who aren't afraid of learning the incredibly easy and intuitive Evernote system and who don't already have one of the other livescribe smartpens, I strongly recommend the Sky.

I bought the DragonFly Black about a year ago for my mobile music production setup, as I wanted a high quality portable DAC for my mobile music-making setup. It outputs a very strong signal, and it gives a lot of power to my mixing headphones and portable monitors. HOWEVER, I've started noticing that the onboard DSP on this DAC will sometimes do what appears to be very aggressive peak limiting on the signal. I started noticing this when I was doing some drum sound design. Transients would sound muffled or they wouldn't even appear at all sometimes (pure impulses don't seem to want to come through). I A/B'd this with other usb DACs I had lying around, and confirmed that the issue was indeed confined to the device. I recorded the output of the DAC back into the system, and sure enough, the output waveform confirmed what I was hearing: the transient of my test signal was smashed by some process and then replaced with a fade-in attack, an instantly recognizable signature of some kind of compressor. I've attached the before and after photos. Furthermore, what is interesting is that the peak limiter will only kick on with peaks that are spaced far enough apart by relative silence. It seems to be that a peak from silence will "wake up" the limiter, and then take a few seconds of silence to go back to sleep. This peak limiting behavior is persistent on mid-2015 macbook pro, an m1 apple air, as well as a computer running Alpine Linux, so it safe to say that this is a firmware related problem. I also bought and tested the DragonFly Red, and it also applied the same peak limiting on my test signal. So far, I've only encountered this issue in music production related tasks, such as previewing drum samples and other short audio files. For more long-term music listening, this doesn't seem to happen. I've been trying to communicate with Tech support about this over the last few weeks, but so far it has been a slow and unhelpful process.

I had a few questions about the board after install and so I contacted ASUS's 25/7 Tech Support. So far, they have answered quickly and have been knowledgeable, professional and polite. This board is positioned as an entry level board to ASUS's "Republic of Gamers" motherboard series of high performing, feature rich motherboards targeted exclusively at the gaming community. After having looked around and researched MOBO's extensively for a new rig I was building, this one stood out as a great deal for the money (under $200.00) and for it's design, quality and features. ASUS also adds a lot of extras that make owning this board all the more appealing; the SATA connectors are really high quality, the packaging is some of the best I have ever seen, they even include a front end connector adapter so you don't have to worry about trying to line up and plug in all those tiny front end wire pin connectors on the board itself. One drawback is that the board does not support 1394 fire wire connections. I do use that feature with a video editing software suite I often use that has a 1394 cable connection for transferring video from a video camera to the computer. I can only assume that perhaps 1394 fire wire is being gradually phased out(?) Anyway, this is not a huge deal for me, as I can always use my other computer that does support it for that function. Not good for inputting raw, full-spectrum audio. The item is compact, simple and works as described. However, I must note that as this piece of equipment utilizes the phone's / tablet's native microphone TRSS jack, the audio inputted will be subject to any internal audio processing applied by the phone's / tablet's operating system. For example: Apple iOS applies a rather sharp high pass filter to all audio arriving via the microphone TRSS jack which, unfortunately, makes this product rather useless for anyone looking to input (and then perhaps stream) raw, full-spectrum audio. The signal is delivered reliably by this product; however, because it is delivered to the microphone TRSS jack, the resulting audio has no low end and sounds rather tinny--due to the iOS high pass filter. In conclusion: the product is simple and straightforward; however, if you are looking to input raw, full-spectrum audio, you should first determine how the input signal will be treated by the device you are plugging into. If that is your desire and your device is Apple brand, unfortunately this product is not for you.

I bought this sound bar for purpose of being a speaker. It is a SOUND BAR. But still, I reluctantly did that too. * It asked me for permission to know my location. I denied it of course. It is a SOUND BAR! It does not need to know my location. Without granting it permission to read my location, I still could not use the app. And hence I cannot use the sound bar. This was finally too much to consider. I am not going to tell a sound bar my location so I can use it as a SOUND BAR. In the user interface, I did click on "Why does this app need my location?" (or words to that effect). The resulting explanation made no sense. I then tried to use it without the app, but could not. I am a computer security professional and researcher. So I can confirm the common sense conclusion that most everyone would come to anyway: There is no good excuse for a SOUND BAR to make any of these demands. Perhaps there is additional enhanced functionality that would be enabled by these extra permissions --- though the explanation offered by the app made no sense. But even if true, the sound bar should still have its basic functionality --- all I needed --- without these privacy destroying permissions. These privacy destroying "requirements" were also not disclosed in the description. Hence I am returning.

How young and naive I was a mere three months ago. Since then, this contraption has managed to make me look incompetent and unprepared every time I teach my classes. And yesterday in class, the tablet refused to rotate to the correct orientation (rotation lock was not on). While I was working on my slides, it zoomed in and refused to zoom out, completely unresponsive. A few minutes later, the word "Shift" was following my cursor around and the zoom behavior continued. Anyway, the moral of the story is that I ran to my office mid-class, came back with whiteboard markers, and finished my presentation on the board. By the way, I teach electrical engineering classes. Wireless mouse batteries that came installed int he mouse were almost dead on arrival. If you are experiencing flaky mouse operation with the wireless mouse (e.g.- flashing, wobbly on screen mouse pointer), then replace batteries. I use these on my rides on the BART (San Francisco Bay Area Transit) which can get awfully loud. I also use them on my infrequent plane journeys. They are excellent. Having had these for almost two years, I can comment that they provide all the above: they cancel noise perfectly, and they are affordable.
