I initially used the "auto" power function but i had to stop using it. It takes a second to turn on, which is very annoying since it is only one channel of my system so i could hear when it turned on, and it creates a strange discharging sound when it powers down. I could only describe it as the sound of a dog whistle going from inaudible (20kHz) down to about 10kHz for a second. Not that big of a deal, but it would auto turn off after only a minute of use. It would often auto-off when browsing through menus and the sound would startle me. Plus it makes a weird blip when it turns on. I did find these sounds are only a function of the auto power feature, and do not happen when the unit is plugged in or the power switch is turned on or off. So now i have the amp hooked up to an "energy saving surge protector" that turns on all the amps when the receiver draws more than the standby power. I wish this amp had a 12v trigger but i cannot reduce star value for that, images are clear it does not have a 12v trigger. Now everything works like a charm. Plus other reviews have mentioned that the standby power is essentially the same as the on power usage, so now that its being disconnected after each use I know its "standby" power usage is 0. So if you are not creative like me, you may want to opt for "always on" and use the front power button or deal with the weird start-up/power-down noise.

First of all I'll say that I am happy with the softbox. As a preamble I'd say the lack of instructions is a little perturbing but I found it fairly self explanatory. So now I'll talk about the physical aspects of it. The mount seems pretty sturdy and is made of aluminium. The ribs seem tough enough but time will tell. The interior reflecting surface is a rough silvery texture and the overall outer seems to be relatively thick. The mount part of the cover is made equivalently. It's hard to gauge the velcro but it feels strong enough and isn't exactly under a great deal of tension. The grid seems acceptable and again, given that it's under almost no tension I suspect it'll last. Overall I feel like it is well made enough. Next onto putting it together. Based on the reviews I'd seen a lot of people seemed to find it difficult to put together. My thought upon reading the reviews was that perhaps they weren't doing it correctly but I've come to the conclusion the complaints are well founded. The ribs are need to be bent relatively far before they can be inserted into the mount and, combined with the glossy/slippery coating they have, this is harder than your imagine. Additionally, with 8 ribs in total the amount of flex you have when forcing them into place decreases meaning the last one is the hardest. Once they are all inserted, clipping in the internal and external diffusers, adding the rear reflector and mounting the box are all fairly straightforward. Also, thankfully, taking it apart is easier than putting it together: I removed the ribs from the mount, starting with the one that was inserted the least deeply. I could imagine it taking about 5 minutes to construct for someone who has done it many times with my first attempt taking me just over 10 minutes. In use I tried it with one studio strobe and (along with a [[ASIN:B00JAAXH1A Neewer S-Type Bracket Holder with Bowens Mount for Speedlite Flash Snoot Softbox Beauty dish Reflector Umbrella]]) a speedlight. For those wondering, with both diffusers my speedlight (guide number 120ft, 35mm, 100 ISO) gave me f8 at about 8 feet at full power (100 ISO); this means it consumed about 2 stops of light which is about what you'd expect. The flash seemed to illuminate the full front diffuser though I didn't try it without the internal diffuser. My suspicion is that without that diffuser I'd gain about a stop of light at the expense of less uniform illumination. My 160Ws strobe gave f11 from 8 feet at full power so again it took about 2 stops though I suspect even without the internal diffuser it would uniformly illuminate the front diffuser meaning f16 at 8 feet (100 ISO) which would definitely afford more flexibility. Given the size of the box I'd be unlikely to use it further than about 15 feet form the subject so my speedlight would give me f4 (with both diffusers) and f8 on my studio strobe (with one). With my stobe that's around EV13, so about 1 stop above open shade on a sunny day (i.e. usable). With my speedlight in a similar situation I'd have to bring it in to about 8 feet for similar effect. Basically I'm saying this is usable with a (single) speedlight outdoors in the shade, on a very overcast day or near sunrise/sunset at fairly close range but don't expect miracles in brighter settings or from greater distances. As you'd expect, with a studio strobe it works fine with the additional benefit that it can be reasonably used without the interior diffuser giving you about an extra stop of output. On to the quality of the light. As you'd expect, given the two diffusers, the illumination is very diffuse. At sufficiently close range the light will wrap around but at typical working distances you get pleasant, soft shadows and a very nice catch light (not your standard umbrella spider web). I mounted the front reflector as far into the box as possible to minimize the spill but even then (without the grid) you get a very broad area of illumination with a very soft fall off. The large penumbra of the box allows for some potential for feathering light but you should expect a lot of spill. With the grid fitted the output tightens up considerably. The penumbra shrinks considerably allowing much better control over where the light falls. For a low key shots this is extremely important (and the reason I opted for a box with a grid) and in that regard I'm pleased. Overall I am happy with this item for the price. If it were a little easier to construct I'd give it five starts but for now I'm subtracting one because of that. Barring and hardware failures in the upcoming months I'd definitely recommend this.

Disclaimer: A pair of these were bought solely for the purpose of a home theater set-up for a guest room and that’s how they’ll be reviewed. PROS: (This part’s quite short) These speakers sound fantastic for the size. They definitely punch above their weight. Even without the sub, the bass delivered from a stereo pair is adequate and punchy although not as low-frequency as one would hope. Mids and treble are distinct generally until around 90% volume after which distortion occurs. Will that’s it for the pros. CONS: As a “home theatre” alternative this is HORRIBLE. Maintaining connection is a major issue. Again these are in stereo pair and a home theater created with my fire stick 4K. Multiple times during the week one speaker in the pair will stop playing. I’d have to tap the physical volume button or unplug the speakers to get them working. In the 2.5 months playing these I’ve also had to delete and re-add my Amazon home theatre set up over two dozen times to get them playing again. The hardware of these speakers is impressive but honestly the software is a tremendous deal breaker. The software also occasionally affects the audio quality. On multiple occasions there’s been a quite noticeable and horrible reverb from the speakers making it sound as though there was an echo in the room. Now let’s talk Dolby Atmos. You may be tempted to buy these as an Atmos system based on the price. I’d definitely avoid that option (note, Atmos is only available wirelessly through your fire TV and not through optical). I’ve played Atmos content from multiple streaming services and there IS NO DISCERNIBLE BETWEEN ATMOS AND STEREO CONTENT! Quite frankly the fact that these speakers are listed as Atmos, is laughable at best. OPTICAL? Yes indeed. These are connected to the TV (LG NANO Cell) via a toslink to mini toslink adapter. That reverb I mentioned earlier, we’ll that always happens when I use the optical connection, no matter what audio options I use on the TV. This happened to a buddy of mine too so I know it’s not just my speakers. The only place where this sort of shined is as an optical output for my Xbox series X. The audio quality and consistency far exceeded that of Amazon’s bogus “wireless home theatre”. It wasn’t without issues however as there was a bit of a lag between the Xbox’s video and the audio. VERDICT: If you’re looking for a smart speaker that packs a bit of a punch (DEFINITELY WAY MORE THAN A HOME POD) then this may be for you. But as a home theatre, this is a definite flop!

I love everything about this projector! The first thing I noticed as I was taking it out of the box is that the remote is easy to use and feels solid. And the design just looks modern. :) The projector boots up very quickly and the picture is very bright. I was running it indoors for the first time against a wall that wasn't white (just as a first test when I got it) with lots of sunlight coming into the room and the picture looked really good on it. The 4K video being streamed from the HDMI looked awesome. I tried the wireless casting from my Macbook and it worked as well as I had hoped. I would use this only if I was sharing presentations that didn't rely on video because the HDMI connection is really what you want to use for that. I love the fact that I can connect the audio wirelessly using Bluetooth to my Sonos speaker - which was a really easy process. There is VERY slight delay in the audio sync when using Bluetooth, but this is the BEST syncing that I have seen from a projector so far. My old projector had a much longer delay that made it impossible to use Bluetooth audio without it being annoying - so this is an awesome benefit. The headphone jack is also there and hooks up right to my speaker, so I'll be using that personally, but having the option to use Bluetooth is really nice. The speaker on the projector itself is also really nice and it gets loud enough to use if you don't have an external speaker. It really helps that the projector is really quiet. Anyway, the screencasting from the Macbook was simple. I tried to cast from my Android phone, but my phone doesn't support Miracast. (That's not the projector's fault - it's my phone that is the problem.) It is really nice that I can use Miracast though. I am sure it works as great as the casting from my Macbook. Connecting to the casting was very simple too. The keystone feature is important since you'd want to either mount this projector to the ceiling or lower on a table. (This is ideal for that purpose.) There is a button on the remote that makes rotating and flipping the projection SO easy. My last projector had that feature buried in the menu, so that made it a bit more difficult. But with this projector, it's just one button that you can use to cycle through the different options. SO EASY. This makes setting up the projector for rear projection simple. That's typically what I like to do so that the projector isn't in the way of anyone watching the movie. This thing has 2 USB ports as well which will let you show photos and videos (and also play some music) on a flash drive. Cycling through the photos with the remote is awesome and it loads everything really quickly. You do have to wait a minute while the USB flashdrive loads though - which isn't bad at all. There are icons on the home screen menu (which is very intuitive) which will tell you when the USB drive is ready to go. By the way, connecting to the wifi is really easy too. No problems with it at all. There was also something else on the menu that I didn't realize it had: Office Suite. I figured it would show documents that you load onto the flash drive. I loaded some PDFs, a Microsoft Word document, and a spreadsheet. Using that, I was able to show those documents directly on the screen and use the remote to scroll through them. Super cool feature that can come in handy when you need it. The projector comes with a really well-made fabric case with great padding. My old projector didn't have that, so this is really nice for storage. I'm usually not someone that reads manuals - I just dive right in. Which was fine because this thing was so easy to use. But I did peek at it afterwards to see if I had missed anything while playing with it. The manual was well-written and very clear. There was also a cleaning cloth and some long cleaning swabs that came with it. I did have to refer to the manual for the swabs to see what they would be for and it seems like it would be for cleaning the inside if it gets dirty. The manual shows that there is a place on the bottom of the projector that you can easily open to clean it out if the lens shows any dirty spots over time. That's a really convenient feature that I haven't seen before. It also came with an HDMI cable and a stereo speaker cable. Glad to have had those included! Like I said at the beginning of my review, I love everything about this projector. For the price, you really do get a lot of bang for your buck! Thrilled with the purchase and I highly recommend this projector if you're looking to get one with a great picture and lots of features.

First of all, you can't have surround sound and voice chat both running wirelessly via bluetooth. Apparently this is just a thing bluetooth can't handle? This was not made clear in any reviews or product information anywhere. So if you are running discord and your game both from your PC, the only way to get surround+chat is to use the wired connection. Second of all, this headset doesn't connect to the Nintendo Switch wirelessly. You still need to plug it into the headphone jack. This means you can't use this headset when your Switch is docked, unless you get an extension cord or your couch is really really close to your TV. The only time the bluetooth becomes handy is when you are playing Switch in handheld mode with the headset plugged in, and would also like to use the nintendo chat app or discord on your phone. You can then connect to your phone via bluetooth while staying plugged in to the Switch and hear both game sound and discord at the same time. So to reiterate, this isn't really a wireless gaming headset except in very specific situations. This is not really the headset's fault, more a weakness of bluetooth and how stupid Switch online features are. That said, I do find it to be a superb wired headset. It is extremely comfortable, sounds great, the mic works very well, and I like the on-ear controls. Discord did struggle to recognize my mic until their support team gave me a beta of the next version to try. And WoW in-game chat is still not recognizing the mic, which is very annoying, but I have discord now so not a huge deal. In summary: high quality gaming headset, not quite plug-and-play setup, not quite useful wireless. 4 stars.

Set-up tip #1 (this was not clear in the instructions): When adding whatever type of sensor (magnetic, infrared, etc), be sure to send the synchronization test trigger signal *WHILE THE UNIT IS MAKING THE CONFORMATORY 3, 5, OR 7 CHIRPS*. Put another way, after you plug & unplug 7-times to allow addition of a magnetic sensor, the main speaker makes 7-chirps ... this is key... while it makes those chirps, trigger the magnetic sensor IMMEDIATELY! If you wait until after it stops chirping, the unit will NOT accept the sensor & it will just be a frustrating process where you assume, incorrectly, that the unit is defective. You must walk through the 3-5-7 chirp programming procedure for each and every unit. You cannot do the 5-chirps, for example, and expect to program all two infrared sensors at the same time....you've got to go through the process two times total. Otherwise, its an insanely bargain unit that works fine for very basic "scare the intruder off" type protection.

I live on the first floor of an apartment building and there are obstructions to my signal all around me. The only location in my one bedroom apt that gets any signal is the top of my bedroom window so that’s where I have my mobile hotspot Velcroed to the glass. I am lucky to get 1Mbps, maybe two in the right weather or at 4am. I’ve been desperately trying various things to get more bandwidth: Hotspot antennas, new APs, Wi-Fi extenders/repeaters... I even looked into signal boosters which were far more expensive than I thought they would be, and I live in an apartment building so looking back, I have no idea what I was thinking or where I was planning to install them. This little device was less than ten bucks so I decided to give it a shot. And after I installed it, the adapter did just what I thought it would do: nothing. I tried every conceivable permutation of configuring this device and scoured the troubleshooting pages on TP-Links website and researched forums, blogs, and tech sites. I learned so much about IPv4, IPv6, DNS, etc. I feel I could start a job in I.T. tomorrow and perform reasonably well. I was all ready to return it with all the other items I had tried, but gave it one more shot from start to finish and here’s what I wish I had known for my installation nightmare: -The disk they gave me was – for whatever unknown reason – incorrectly configuring the adapter. I downloaded the driver from their website directly instead of using the software on the disk, even though it was the exact same version. -I turned off my native network adapter but did not uninstall it nor disable it. I can use that adapter as a hotspot AP. (If you don’t have a functional adapter installed, you can still use the hotspot setting but you will also need an Ethernet connection.) -Specifying a Domain Name System (DNS) service was not worth the hassle involved in configuring and then reconfiguring the adapter properties. Best just to leave it set to DHCP. But even if I had known those things (and many more), it wouldn’t have helped a single bit. The few times I was able to get it connected to my Wi-Fi, the best I was able to get was about 200Kbps download speed and most of the time it was around 50Kbps. When I switched back to my installed Qualcomm adapter I could pull in almost 1Mbps. Then I remembered that one of the troubleshooting suggestions was to isolate the device from Bluetooth signals, and I have a dongle for my wireless mouse and keyboard that is Bluetooth enabled sitting in the adjacent port. I unplugged the dongle and rechecked my connection speed. My download speed had shot up to over 9Mbps! I know that’s not really a speed to write home about (and the upload speed is pretty weak) but I can’t believe how overjoyed I was to get that much. So, to make an incredibly long (and very boring) story short, if it’s not easy to get it going, keep at it… the tech is sound and the device worked, even if it did take my entire weekend to get it set up properly. Best of luck to you.

October 16 Update: Two months later and still very happy with this computer except for one annoying feature which I fixed. My den is very quiet and a few weeks ago I noticed a slight grumbling noise from the fan. I found a disassembly video on YouTube, removed the fan assembly, and pulled out the fan from its base (it just pulls out, nothing to loosen). With my magnifier I noticed a small raised burr on the plastic base the fan rode on and smoothed it with a small fingernail file. I added a drop of light oil to the hole the fan goes into and put it all back together and haven't heard any noise since. I even put my ear to the computer and could barely hear the fan. When it works, this drive works well. It's quick (maxes out at ~2.9 GB/s on my system) and is easy to use. I bought the drive in October of 2019 but the drive started having issues in August of 2020 and fully died in September of 2020, which means it only lasted 11 months and that's where the issues come in. First, PNY doesn’t provide any diagnostics tools. When I first started having issues the S.M.A.R.T. reports all said everything was fine, but Dell's utility was showing issues. However there was no way to do further tests to confirm Dell's utility info. Talking to support was fine, and they gave me an RMA number so I could send the drive back but with two major issues: 1) They would not send a replacement ahead of time. I did an RMA for Western Digital years ago and they took my payment info and sent a new drive with the understanding that if I didn't send back the defective one, they would charge me for the replacement. No such option exists for PNY so I had two choices; Go without a computer for the two weeks needed for the RMA or, buy a replacement myself and… try to re-sell it later? 2) Return shipping is paid by the customer, and not by PNY. This isn't a huge cost, but again, it's a strike against them, especially since the issue is that the drive failed, so it’s not my fault. So, I ordered a cheap temporary drive and it thankfully arrived the day after this drive fully gave up the ghost (again, the day just before that, the S.M.A.R.T. reports all said everything was fine, but Dell's utility said there were issues). I shipped the drive back Monday, it arrived Friday and they shipped the replacement Tuesday and it arrived Saturday. So a total of 13 days for the turnaround from the time I shipped the drive until the replacement came. The replacement is brand new and appears to be an updated version (thinner flash modules and they are only on one side rather than both sides). It's working well and I'm hoping for multiple years of service from it, but I'm not holding my breath. If they paid for return shipping and gave me an option of getting the replacement before shipping back the defective drive, this review would be glowing. But because of those issues, I can’t recommend buying any hard drive from PNY because if you need to use the 5 year warranty, it’s a pain.

I find these cameras to be increasingly frustrating, likely correlates with recent software updates. Seems they don’t test things all that well before release? Ring has been far more solid software-wise. Starting a couple months back, they must have been attempting to fix notification issues. Well they made it worse IMO. Now the number of events in the badge notification seems to sum up over time. ie, 10 motion events, go into app to view, clears.. next time you get 5 more events, the badge now says 15. And it keeps going. Only way to fix is to kill the app and relaunch. Then very recently, I get false notifications. At least I think they are false. Motion detected in back yard, view it within seconds, nothing there, no video in the cloud.. nothing that explains why I received a notification. It keeps going notification every few minutes.. and I have to disable the camera. Restarting the camera doesn’t resolve. Either they are throwing false notifications (never see anything when going live) or they are failing to save the videos that I pay a monthly subscription to see.. —— original review ——- I had trouble deciding which camera brand to buy. I tend to go right to the bad reviews to see what people are saying. Problem with that approach is every product out there, someone has something bad to say ha ha! So what I did was purchase 1 Arlo, 1 Ring StickUp and 1 Blink Outdoor. Figured I'll decide for myself what's what. The Blink went back pretty quickly because their audio sucks and their support wasn't great. There was a constant interference type static noise. Arlo and Ring had great audio, could easily hear the birds in the morning. The Blink also required a little 'base station' whereas the Arlo and Ring do not. Both Ring and Arlo have decent apps and decent notifications. Arlo has a more flexible mount system straight outta the box, for the Ring I had to purchase an extra mount to get the adjustments I needed. Arlo has better images/video/field of view, that is one of the main things I like about my Arlo cameras. (I purchased a second Arlo when I returned the Blink) Arlo also has some good recognition features. I have gotten several notifications of an 'animal' in my driveway.. I'm skeptical, but look at the video, sure enough.. a squirrel running by or the neighbors cat late at night. About here is where the positive things kinda stop with the Arlo cameras. The battery life is pretty terrible for the one in front of my garage. It probably sees a tad more motion than the one in the back yard, but the one in the back yard seems to last twice as long. Maybe the one in front of the garage has a defective battery or something? In any case, I've had these cameras since I moved into my house about 4 months ago. I've charged one of the cameras 3 times already, the other one I charged twice. Meanwhile I have yet to charge my Ring camera, and it's still sitting at 73%. That's pretty impressive for the Ring. My next area of frustration with the Arlo is the activity zones. I have had these set up how I want them from day 1. You can only define boxes that are square to the camera's field of view, that sucks. On the Ring I can make diagonal lines and better define the area. I could deal with the boxes if they actually worked properly. I think the camera has different moods. I have a few boxes set up so that it should only notify me of motion if detected in my driveway or the front yard. I specifically am trying to avoid notifications from vehicles driving by on the street. I can go several days without an erroneous notification. Then all the sudden on certain days, it's like the activity zones decide to stop working. I'll get notification after notification, view the video, it's a car driving by in the street. Not anywhere near my activity zone. I reached out to Arlo support early on, and they were not really helpful. They just suggested that I set up my activity zones incorrectly. Well guess what, they are extremely easy to set up, and they work half the time. sounds like a software issue to me. I'm guessing the faulty activity zone motion detection contributes to the poor battery life on that camera. A nice thing that Ring offers that Arlo doesn't seem too.. If the notifications are going nuts one day (when the activity zones aren't working properly and cars are driving by). you either have to disable the camera or get a buzz for every one. The app appears to have a global mute option that I could select for a certain duration. But I'd prefer to just mute the camera that's being stupid. Can't do that though, I have to disable it altogether.. Then remember to go enable it again later. The Ring on the other hand, I get out the mower and walk by it, I get the notification on my watch, right there convenient as can be, along with the selection to dismiss the notification is an option to snooze notifications from that camera for 30 minutes. Just enough to finish mowing! So all in all I do like the Arlo for it's better picture quality, but software-wise and battery-wise it's just not quite as solid as the Ring is. I have had a few experiences though where the Ring failed to notify me of a package being delivered to my front steps.. so who knows. Nothing is perfect.

As my star rating and review title states, I LOVE this cooler. I bought this to update the stock CPU cooler on my I7-7700. I was concerned about internal temps as I play games that utlize a lot of CPU power. I haven't actually measured the temps before an after my install, but on the surface I feel much more confident in using this, rather than the stock CPU cooler. As other reviews have suggested, this thing is HUGE and the picture doesn't really do a good job in representing its size. Luckily it fit inside my case (Meanit: 4PM), For reference, its two or three inches higher than my Geforce 1070 card when installed. Installation of this was a pain, when installing the stock CPU cooler for my CPU for the first time on my Motherboard (ASUS Z170-E), I did not have to work on the underside of the board, instead, all I had to do press the plastic screws in and turn to tighten into place. However, installing this CPU cooler required me to basically take my PC completely apart to be able to remove the motherboard to screw in the mounting bracket on the underside. This took up most of my time, but once I got it in and everything else back together, all I had to do was attach the Intel mounting brackets to the cooler and screw it in to the mounting holes. The Cooling fan is a separate part and it attaches directly to the radiator of the cooler using metal brackets (no screws needed). This method keeps the fan firmly in place and I have no worries about it falling off. The fan is very quiet but I believe it's doing a very good job keeping things cool. When I get actual temps I'll update this review accordingly. Of course my favorite thing about this cooler is the RGB functionality. In addition to the fan being RGB, the cover of the radiator is also RGB. Its able to cycle through a variety of colors to match (or contrast) other lighting in your cabinet. I've been experimenting with different color combinations with this and my 9 other RGB fans, and so far my favorite combination is purple front, top, and rear fans, with this being orange. My only complaint with this device, is that the controller that controls the colors, and modes, and brightness is difficult to mount outside the case. I have it on the other side of the case so I don't see it, but it looks tacky and takes away from my stealth look of my case. Even better, I wish they included a button bracket that I could put on the back of my case. Other than that, this is a great buy for me. The colors get very bright, but I have tinted tempered glass on my case, so its not hard on my eyes, even at the brightest setting.

Compared with the last version of the Audio Technica nose reduction headphones, these provide much better noise cancellation when set at its highest level. There are three modes which are selected by pushing the button below the power switch. Changing modes take about 2-3 seconds as the noise cancellation turns off then turns on again in the new mode. Each mode has its own color light but which is which is not mentioned on the headphones themselves so you need to remember. Also comparison between modes is difficult because of the lag in change and the fact that noise cancellation turns off completely for a couple of seconds when you switch. If the switching between modes was instantaneous and without turning off it would make the headphones much better. Another down side for travelers is that for some reason the case has become noticeably fatter. Where the old case slimmed down a bit where the headband portion of the headphones was stored, the new case does not and instead has about a 3/4 inch shelf for the band to rest on and a commensurate increase in case size. The headphones themselves are a bit bigger also so the rest of the case is also fatter. This is a definite negative for frequent travelers. Another negative I have found it a humming feedback when I use on the highest level with my notebook computer. When I touch the notebook case the hum goes away so there is a grounding issue with the headphones or my notebook and I am not sure this is happen to everyone. I have been using the Audio Technica noise canceling headphones for about 10 years and this is my third pair. I have the Bose ones but like Audio Technica better and they are a much better value. If you are inclined to upgrade, you may want to wait until the next model when hopefully the above problems are solved and the case slimmed down to its former size.

Basically a 50mm f/1.4 prime lens when used on APS-C. That's about the ideal single-prime configuration. Couldn't be happier! Camera body tested: Sony DSLR-A700 (APS-C) PRO: -Standard lens! 30mm has the same field-of-view as a 45mm lens on an APS-C sensor. This is in "standard lens" territory, a solid approximation of a 50mm f/1.4 lens on a full-frame body. -focus is smooth and solid. -focus window (if you're into that kind of thing) -inexpensive -quick AF (due to the poor close-focus performance inherent to the design. Everything's a tradeoff) -very sharp, even more so when stopped down to f/2.8 (2 stops) CON: -limited to APS-C bodies due to internal design decisions. I prefer lenses that work equally well on full-frame and APS-C. (NOTE: consider the Sigma 28mm F1.8 EX DG Macro as an alternative, if you shoot both APS-C and full-frame) -magnification 1:10, oof. That's pretty rough. Don't expect to focus on close subjects. (near focus distance is 0.4m, 1.3ft) -Discontinued, replaced by the Sigma 30mm f/1.4 DC HSM A (more expensive) -Optically not as good as the Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM A (way more expensive), which is one of the best wide primes lenses available for the Sony A-mount, and is full-frame. When used on APS-C, I'd take this lens over my full-frame 50mm f/1.4. The 50 is just too long, as it is equivalent to 75mm on APS-C, compared to 45mm for this one. I like it. I use it. I'd recommend it to any APS-C shooter. If you shoot both full-frame and APS-C, consider the Sigma 28mm f/1.8 EX DG Macro. it'll work about as well as this one on APS-C, but double as a fast wide prime on full-frame. Only 2/3 stops slower aperture, but about 5x better Macro, no complaints there either.

This is a pretty great Bluetooth mini keyboard! It was recommended to me by Lew from Unbox Therapy, the tech YouTube channel. It looks cool and has a few cool features. It has a backlight that you can toggle in case you're working in the dark and can't see the keys. It has a mini mouse pad, so you can move the mouse on whatever device you're on. If it's a PC with a high-resolution screen, however, you may have quite a way to go before getting the mouse across the screen. I bought this for my Fire TV because my last mini-keyboard of another brand broke on me. This is a good replacement, though the different layout will take a bit of taking used to. The backspace, for example, is on the top row next to the function keys for some reason. The shift key is also smaller than I'm used to. The click buttons are great since there's two for both right and left-click. There are the ones below the mouse pad and the ones that look like triggers on a game controller. It's also easy to set up via Bluetooth like any other Bluetooth keyboard. If you've never set up a Bluetooth keyboard, yes it's easy. I do have a couple of complaints, however. One is the battery isn't the greatest. I turned it on to use it one day only to have it not turn on. Not a problem since it has a rechargeable lithium battery as all modern devices should be. My biggest complaint is that it's missing the menu button. You know, that hamburger ≡ symbol on the keyboard that nobody seems to use? Well, that's one of the few buttons that the Amazon Fire TV uses, which uses it as its options button. The fact that it's missing is a bit annoying, so I have to use another controller whenever I need that one button. Other than that, it is a great mini keyboard.

This was purchased as a gift for Father's Day and we could not be more happy with it. We also purchased a dog harness and a road bike holder for it and it has worked perfectly in both occasions. As someone who is not that into video, this is a great way to get into filming. We have been looking at purchasing a GoPro for awhile, but spending $300-$400 on one was out of the question as we didn't know how much we would use it. We paid $105 for this and are very happy. It's much smaller than I thought; it fits almost in the palm of your hand. It's very easy to move between accessories. The clips and wires to upload the materials to your computer come in the package, however, you will need to purchase a Micro SD card separately. Make sure you purchase a 32GB or below as the HERO is not set up to handle the 64GB. This is not a problem for us however as this holds about 4.5 hours of footage on it. It took a little bit of understanding and reading to get how to work it, but once you do it once or twice, you should not have any problems going forward. I enjoy the fact we can take both video and pictures but the difficulty is that since there is no viewfinder or screen on the back, you have to kind of "cross your fingers" that you're getting the correct shot. It hasn't been a problem for us though as it films in widescreen/fisheye so you always get more than you probably really needed. The one difficulty we have found with the camera is what has already been stated in previous reviews regarding the sound and the back of the camera. It's very difficult to pop the back off so I always let my boyfriend do that as I don't want to break it. Also, if you're looking to record both sound and video, you should absolutely leave the back cover open as having it closed muffles the sound a bit. We aren't looking for the sound aspect for our use, so this wasn't a problem for us. We plan on using this in the future for vacations and purchasing more accessories to go along with it. Overall we are very happy with our purchase and can't wait to see what else we can find to film with the GoPro!

This lens had and continues to have serious issues with its lens stabilization system. The Panasonic "X" lens series was touted by Panasonic as a harbinger of future premium lenses (without Leica's help); and the new Panasonic Power OIS was claimed to be twice as effective as the previous Panasonic lens stabilization system in certain situations. The reality? The 45-175mm lens was fielded with serious issues with the new Power OIS, evidently picking up shutter vibrations at certain shutter speeds and producing double images. Panasonic issued firmware Version 1.1 to fix this, but in my experience the issues remains. I tested the lens using firmware v1.1 on an Olympus P2 body ... handheld at 1/50, 1/160, and 1/250 of a second. Double images occasionally occurred at 1/50 and 1/160 of a second; on other occasions they were sharp. The images at 1/250 were always sharp. For Olympus micro 43 users, there is another issue: the OIS is always ON; there is no way to turn it off. I also own the Olympus 40-150mm zoom lens. I've had no lens stabilization issues with the Olympus lens (and you can turn the IBS on and off). Recommend that Olympus users pass on this lens and buy the Olympus 40-150mm instead.

Update- after my initial review below, Tozo customer service contacted me and wanted to be sure I was satisfied. I just received the T9 model and find their fit works much better for my ears. I am totally satisfied and ended up with a great product. For that reason, I am bumping my rating up to 5 stars. The initial review and my concerns with the fit of the T6 model are still applicable, so I will leave my original review intact below. If you think you may have the same fit concerns as me, I recommend checking out the T9s instead. The added "q-tip" stick really helps fit them and hold them in my ear better. --------------------------------- Disclaimer: This is the first set of wireless earbuds I have used. Some of the issues I describe below may be common to all earbuds and not specific to these. I don't know. My rating is based on comparing to what I think headphones should be, not comparing these to other earbuds. ***The Good*** Nice Case Long battery life Good connectivity to my phone Waterproof (though not tested first-hand yet) Comfortable ***The Bad*** Don't stay in place very well Touch sensor gets hit accidentally too often Fit is finicky I'm pretty picky about my headphones. Unlike most people, however, I'm not very concerned with their sound quality. I bought these for listening to podcasts in the car and while out walking or jogging or working in the yard and making the occasional phone call. Podcasts don't need high fidelity. In most of these cases, I only use one ear bud as I want to be able to hear other sounds around me, like cars and stuff. I'm not a fan of the in-ear design and how insecure it is. Maybe that is specific to these headhpones or all ear buds. I don't know. I have had headsets with over the ear hooks and like how they fit much better, but they aren't very compatible with sunglasses. The hooks interfere with the glasses arm and result in comfort problems. These particular ear buds never really feel like they are seated well in my ear. I have tried all the different sized ear tips that came with it and none give a secure fit that feels right. They tend to work their way loose over time. I can usually tell when it is getting loose and push it back in before it falls out, but there are a few times where it has fallen out. That brings me to the next problem: I hate the touch controls, too. I wish it had physical buttons. Every time I need to adjust it and push it back in, I end up triggering the touch control and skipping ahead or backwards or stopping the playback. Maybe the Q-tip design of air pods works better as you have something to hold onto and the stick portion can help hod position in your ear? The rest of the performance of these earbuds is better. The battery life is great. Having the charge indicator lights on the case is handy, so I know when it is time for me to recharge the case. I've never run out of battery in these. I have done a few road trips with these and will say that sitting in a car and not moving is a good application for these. Unlike with walking or working, they stay in place well enough and are comfortable for long duration listening. Connectivity with my phone is very quick and seamless. I rarely get any interference, which is more than I can say for previous bluetooth headsets I have used. I haven't had any complaints about the mic when using these for phone calls, so I guess that works well. Overall, I give these 3 stars. They perform OK, but I was hoping for better.

Do you really need this kind of product just for analog-type connections? The answer is you do especiallly need this product for analog connections. 1. Dual-balanced conductors means your left and right connections are receiving equal audio signals. Is this important? Well if you want louder left or right signal reaching to your audio equipment due to faulty construction, then it may not be important. This may be an exaggeration, but if you care for sonic quality this product is for you. 2. Protective shielding. Analog signals are very much susceptible to interference. This interference can and will enter the cables and onto your audio where it is amplified and introduced as distortion. Worse, poor cables will introduce audio loops where buzz and hum are heard. Any audio engineer will know never to cross audio cables with one another. Worse, no audio cables should be crossed with electrical plugs. Why? all these signals against one another produce electrical resistance and audio contamination in the analog signals. But no average Joe/Jane will know this. So what's important to know is that this product meets THX-certified guidelines, which means you won't have to worry so much about audio distortion and poor quality and performance when buying something like this. And at this price, compare it with other audio cables and they can even be more expensive with cheaper and thinner construction and NO THX-certification. For example you can compare this with Monster Cables iCable for the iPod, which is more than twice the price than this produce. I admit it has an even better construction and excellent build, but it isn't THX-certified. Well, I can bet that product does surpass THX-certifications but with half the price of the product you can be assured of excellent sonic quality. For your iPod, these cables will suite you more than fine. Another example is Sony's RK-N215PM, which is the same price as this Monster cable. It's very flimsy and the cables are very thin. If you're asking for electrical interference, then this is the product your looking for. Worse, at the same price this Sony isn't THX-certified. I had to buy three of these Sony cables because the Monster THX i-mini cables are so thick that my Logitech Z-680 THX speakers can't accommodate three of the connectors side by side. It's a shame I had to get non-THX cables for the THX speaker set. Believe me, this product is a steal. Get it while they still offer free shipping.

Let me preface this review by saying that I'm a hude proponent of smart everything and use Echo products daily. I think the future will hold AI in almost every aspect of life and like it or not I think that's where we are headed. So clearly the next logical step was to have AI in our cars. I see this as a great step and wanted to get in as an early adopter. That said, version one products have always and will always have some problems, the echo auto is no different. So let's start with the good. The unit is very compact and although the chord is kind of an eye sore, I dont think it's that big of a deal. Furthermore, I think the unit looks fine in the car, almost gives it a futuristic vibe which I really dig! The device is also so easy to set up. This is something Amazon has really perfected over the years. I remember setting up the original Echo and how much of a pain it was. Now if you buy a new echo device, it's likely that you can have it set up in minutes. The echo auto is no different. I had it set up and working in under 5 minutes which is really a pleasure. Now onto usability. The device is very responsive to the wake word and even if you have music playing it still picks you up. It also is a full on Echo meaning anything you would ask your normal echo you can ask the echo auto. Also very nice! So far I've had no problems with it hearing me wrong or doing something I didnt ask for. Overall there is a lot going for this product but there are some complaints I have right off the bat. For one, it is not very quick with responses. You ask it to play a song and it could be 10 seconds before that song starts playing. This makes sense though as it has to send your message to your phone then back to the auto to play through the speakers. It essentially adds a middle man to the process which adds time. This isn't really a huge deal in my opinion. A much larger problem is one that I actually have yet to experience. I have read other reviews saying that the connection is spotty or that they have to reconnect every time they turn off the car. This is a problem but I assume that Amazon can fix this through software. It's an early product and needs some polishing before it is perfect. So far the auto has been a great product. I really like having alexa in the car and i really think it is safer than using your phone while driving. It has some bugs but give it some time and I see this as a very promising product and would definitely reccomend buying one. I will also try to update this review as I use it more.

I'm a long time Fitbit customer. I previously owned Versa, and Versa2. Prior to that I had a couple of Pebble smartwatches. So I quickly upgraded to Sense when it became available. All the features I love about Fitbit watches, sleep stats, fitness stats, continuous heart rate, notifications, are there and working very well. Initially I found the new UI a bit confusing. Not having the physical 'Back' button on the watch set me back a bit. I struggled for a while on how to get back to the watch face from various situations. Things improved much better when I eventually discovered the "VIRTUAL BACK" button. If you gently press the middle left side of the watch, it gives you a haptic feedback and puts you right back to the previous screen. Otherwise most existing features work similarly. Swipe to the left, you get the application list. Swipe down you get the notifications. Swipe up you get the enhanced fitness statistics as well as weather widget and EDA widget. Fitness stats have been broken into two: CORE and ADVANCED. You have to load the ADVANCED stats separately if you want to see it all. NEW FEATURES: If you swipe to the right, you get the most commonly used settings. 'Do not disturb', 'Sleep', 'Always on', 'On when arm moves' buttons as well as watch face dimmer and music volume. These are very useful to have easy access to. I'm keeping the 'Always on' mode on at all times and turn off the 'On when arm moves' setting. This way I can always see the time at a glance and use the 'virtual back button' to light up the watch face when I want. I put my watch to sleep mode before going to bed. I use the virtual back button to wake the watch up and turn off the sleep mode when I wake up. With these settings, my battery lasts about 5 days. ECG: This is an app in the application list. When you want to take your 30 second ECG, you start the app, place two fingers on the watch face corners and let the watch measure your ECG. After 30 seconds measurement, the watch tells you if you had a-fib during the 30 second time it took the measurement. It doesn't continuously monitor your heart rate looking for a-fib. I guess the idea is when you are not feeling well or having heart palpitations, you will manually start this app and measure it. SKIN TEMP: The watch measures your skin temperature while you sleep and compares it to your baseline temperature. The idea is that a large variation in your sleep temperature may be an early indication that you are soon to get sick. EDA: Allows you to relax and measure your stress level for two minutes at a time. Afterwards it gives you a number indicating your stress level. You can also log your mood periodically and the Fitbit app keeps track of it. I find this feature marginally useful if at all. CHARGER: The new charger is much smaller and slimmer than the old versas. It has four small pins that connect to the watch on the back side. It reminds me of those old pebble watch chargers, where after a while dirt and sweat got in between the pins and contact with the watch became difficult. I had to frequently wipe clean the charger and the backside of the watch with wet wipes so that it could continue to charge. It remains to be seen if this new charger will develop those same problems as old pebble watches. I was hoping for touchless charge, like those of apple watches. Unfortunately not in this release...

I did a lot of research before actually replacing my old 500 GB Hard Drive with the 3TB Hard Drive provided in the Avolusion (AVPS4HD-N3T) Package. I wanted to save and transfer all my Gaming Data (Profile, Games, Updates, Apps, Trophies, Saves, etc.). Everything you need to replace the Hard Drive is provided in the Avolusion package except what you will need to save all your Gaming Data which exists on the old PS Hard Drive. The USB Thumb Drive provided is not for this purpose, it is loaded with the PS4 Operating Software and will only be used to install the PS4 Operating Software to the new 3 TB Hard Drive. I bought a "U32 Shadow 1 TB USB 3.0 External Backup Hard Drive for Sony Play Station 4" (Sold by Amazon). I had a "full" 500 GB Hard Drive I was replacing and the U32 Shadow has enough space and is already formatted and ready to receive the Gaming Data from the PS4 (Apps, Games, Updates, etc.). Before I did anything, I saved my Gaming Data from the old 500 GB Hard Drive to the U32 Shadow using the Menu Options on the PS4. Once this was done, I removed the old 500 GB Hard Drive and installed the new 3 TB Hard Drive using the tools and easy instructions provided by Avolusion. After installing the new 3 TB Hard Drive, I used the USB Thumb Drive provided to update the PS4 Operating Software on the new 3 TB Hard Drive. The Thumb Drive had the latest software already loaded on it. With the new 3 TB Hard Drive installed and the PS4 Operating Software loaded, I then transferred the data from the U32 Shadow to the new 3 TB Hard Drive. Once I transferred the Gaming Data using the PS4 Menu Options, I rebooted the PS4 and everything was like I had left it on the old 500 GB Hard Drive (Everything in its place and nothing missing). Great quality product with easy to follow instructions!!! The process is straight forward and easy enough but does take some time when transferring data. Just remember, you will need to consider what you need to do if you want to save and transfer your Gaming Data.

First of all before I even say anything MAKE SURE YOU ARE ACTUALLY USING A GIGABIT SWITCH. I understand that they sell a "fast ethernet"switch which is extremely outdated nowadays and is only valid if you have dialup speed internet which if you are shopping for a switch you most likely dont. I mean it is pretty self explanatory plug it between a end device (computer/ gamesystem etc) and an ACTIVE ROUTER that you have either assigned static IPs of the end devices or has DHCP active. This does not assign anything. I saw some people rate it 1 star because they connected it from a modem to other devices.. most modems are bridge adapters from the cable provider coaxial to an actual router. Some companies like comcast have dual purpose modem routers but bottom line is you need a switch to add connections to a router assigning IPs not to connect from a raw modem signal to multiple devices that have no IPs assigned. I thought this was somewhat common sense seeing as mainly tech savvy related people buy network switches but alas it still needs to be said. I am writing this review under having purchased the 5 port switch but as I have multiple devices and game systems in the viscinity on a upstairs floor, I am seeing the need to get a 8port switch to extend connectivity. I would advise against crossing switches (1 switch connecting to another switch for more ports) and suggest just getting a larger port unit. Crossing switches has a tendency to result in mismanaged bandwidth unless it is managed through a web portal which these are not. Chose these over the netgear ones due to design and history I have with it. Again the main issue people are having is not realizing they did not purchase a gigabit switch.. fast ethernet version is cheap for a reason. It is an antique at this point and is not worth the few dollars discount over a full gigabit speed switch.

As all the other reviews indicate, this is not a router for the average consumer. This requires some pretty advanced knowledge of networks. But with that said, this product is still a ROYAL pain to setup simply because of how they chose the default/reset configuration. Only having the router initialize if it can connect to a DHCP server on its outward facing eth0 port means that you have to disconnect the router from the installation and connect it up to something that has a DHCP server and will tell you what address it assigned to the router. So you need to plan ahead (before you disconnect from the web) and get a laptop with a second NIC to run a DHCP server. Linux to the rescue. Then you can configure the router's down stream ports and save the configuration. Now you have to redo all the wiring to get the laptop connected to the downstream port and the web to the upstream. Now you need to use that laptop to connect to the router and get served an IP address from its DHCP server (the laptop is now the client). Now you can program the router from the downstream side. EXCEPT if you want to change the subnet address of the downstream side you are connected to. Try to do that and it goes out to lunch and you are back to reseting the router and starting all over again. The simple solution would have been for the router to act as a DHCP server on a downstream port with the upstream disabled till programmed. That would save 6 hours of farting around. But once installed it does route. I have had it up for a few weeks with no need to reboot. I unleashed a remote computer to attack my network and they were unable to get past the protections. So that I am happy with.

I have sent a few customer service requests to Neewer directly about this and have yet to receive an answer, which is a shame. I bought these because they are gold plated where the connectors touch the chassis ground. (A well built USB 2.0 mini B connection) But there is no conductivity between the two ends on the shield. What good is gold plating the connectors if there is no connection to shield ground? I tried other "non gold plated" USB 2.0 cables and they conduct fine on the shield. If you simply want a 4 wire connector, (possibly USB 1.1 only) this might work. When the chips are down at 70 mph in traffic, you don't want confusion from a GPS. This one has too many hiccups. It took me a while to figure out what it's doing, and in part I learned it by using my Garmin nuvi 65. The 65 and 55 appear to be the same design, and they do the same screwy things. The major flaw is what it does at selective highway intersections (not all....but you will rarely know which ones!). A junction is characterized by 3 graphics: upper left corner has the "turn left/right" graphic. The main part of the screen shows the traffic lanes division and your path. Another inset graphic shows the signage to expect. At various intersections (I found 3 in the LA area, one in Phoenix) the graphics are wrong. The one I travel all the time is I-10 eastbound, intersecting the US60 eastbound. The main graphic showing the lane pattern is correct, but the insets for turn (upper left) and signage are both wrong. I couldn't repeat the LA junctions (I didn't have hours to kill on that trip), but I do the I10/US60 several times a week. However, I now know that the junction instructions might be wrong....and "might be" destroys the value of a GPS. Other gripes: first, the data base doesn't recognize many breaks in the median as a pathway (the graphic shows a white line at the median break, so it "knows" something is there). So if I want to go to McDonalds (it's a free country), the GPS tells me to take this roundabout pathway. I know the median break (I'm an addict) so I take it, and get in line at the drive-up. Sitting 24" from the building, the GPS never recognizes that I've reached the destination. Nor does it "let go" once I've gotten close to the destination (earlier versions deleted the waypoint after you pass it). The nuvi 55/65 keeps giving instructions to go back to that waypoint miles down the road (and days later, after I turned it off and next used it a couple days later, it still wanted me to go to McD's). The earlier design had this feature done right. And it didn't screw up the junctions. Another: I'm sitting in a gas station; one that's obviously been here for years. Garmin doesn't list it. I wonder if you have to pay them a promotion fee to be included in the data base? This one's going back and I'll use my old garmins for another year hoping these guys figure out what they're doing. Update: tried to find a post office; GPS took me to a building that once WAS a PO, but the paint job says it's not been for a couple years. That's the second PO in the last year that the data base got wrong. I think "lifetime maps" means you might find something in your lifetime. They don't charge much for the "lifetime" option. It's worth even less. I think I'll take the money from the return and invest in a better cell phone, and give up on a separate GPS. Google found the nearest Post Office right off the bat.

*UPDATE Dec. 18, 2014 I highly recommend these. I mentioned in my original review that these would be great 'phones for travel, and then I went ahead and flew on a plane (my first time in a plane since 1998! it was very exciting!) to prove their worth. They're great. Great at noise isolation and produce great sound. I do have one tip to share. You might look a little goofy, but it's worth it if you are interested in dampening the vibration/banging traveling up the cord (which is by far my biggest complaint with these). All you have to do is, after inserting into your ear, tuck the cord over and around your ear so that it's going up behind your ears. The key is that all the vibration will stop where the cord touches your ear, and the remaining line isn't going to be touched or moving by much of anything. To give you a visual, the end result might look like the sports-marketed earbuds that wrap around behind your ear. It SIGNIFICANTLY helps. One other thing. I really like the braided cord, and my color is bright blue. Again, great for travel: it's easier to spot and distinguish from your other myriad cords, and the braided texture doesn't seem to tangle as badly as some other cords. *ORIGINAL REVIEW Nov. 13, 2014 These are killer earbuds. Does the wood help? Maybe, I don't know. But these sound fantastic for the price. Does the braided cord reduce banging noise? Probably not, but it feels great, looks great, and is easy to untangle. I am not an audio professional by any means -- I'm not a "super hearer" -- but I do listen to a wide variety of music and produce the occasional music track/ video track / podcast episode. I don't know if I would use them as studio monitors -- and I'll explain why in a moment -- but for playback, for convenience of slipping these in your pocket or having a pair in your glove box for emergency listening... these put out some great sound. There's a bassy punch, but it leaves plenty of spaced for nuanced mid-range tunage. (That's the only convoluted audio-babble sentence I'll use, I promise.) The honest to goodness, only downside of these earbuds: they're still earbuds. The little silicone rings that seal off your ears feel great, like the start of an amazingly-comfortable Q-tip entering your canal, and do a lovely job of sealing off outside sounds. (Thus the "noise isolation.") They also do an amazing job of sending every single vibration, every miniscule amount of friction that touches that braided cord, into your ears. This is very noticeable to me during quieter songs, extremely noticeable during moments of silence, and not too bad during louder music. You'll never notice if you're sitting very still -- passenger in a car, a plane (which is why I purchased these!), or laying in bed. Here's what it comes down to: I will probably never use these at work, where I am often using my arms for typing and computery-stuff. (I also use a standing desk, so I'm probably shifting my weight back and forth more than if I were sitting in a chair.) But the subtle motion of moving my arms, shifting around, or whatever, is more than enough to send the annoying vibrations up the line. I listened to about two songs at work before pulling out my trusty pair of Sony MDR-7506 studio monitors. But I want to end this review by clarifying that I didn't buy these to replace my regular "big" headphones... I just needed a small pair of 'phones for travel and other situations where I didn't want to stuff a huge pair in my bag, but it would have been nice to have some. (Hiking around on trails, for instance.) I totally expected these to have the "vibration downfall", but what I did not expect was the killer sound that these puppies can rock out and the really nice quality design. Thumbs up!

I think these gloves are intended solely for coloring or drawing with pencils on paper, and for that purpose, they work just fine. However, I purchased these gloves for drawing on my android tablet and phone because the seller said they work for palm rejection. This is misleading and simply untrue. They may work differently on apple products, but my android devices reacted to them as though my hands were bare. U-P-D-A-T-E: A few days after my purchase, Customer Service reached out to inquire as to whether I was pleased with the gloves. I curtly explained my disappointment and thought that would be the end of it. The reply I received was patient and kind, expressing concern and the desire to make this right and possibly improve the gloves for the future. I learned that there is padding on one side of each glove to help avoid the screen detection from movement on that side of the hand. Because of that one glove is suited to the right hand, and the other to the left. All I saw initially was black gloves and used them on the opposite hands. After using a tablet with the gloves on the proper hands, they did protect the screen from hand movement as long as the fingertip didn't touch the screen. The padding doesn't extend to the fingertip,and it was explained to me that is so the fingers can breathe. I suggested the padding extend to the fingertip, and that is under advisement for such time as it is determined that changes would be warranted. For my trouble and feedback, I was refunded my purchase price and may keep the gloves. Therefore, I revised my rating from 1 to 5 stars. There is room for improvement, but their Customer Service is a 5.

For $10 I didn't have very high hopes for this mouse. I'm extremely happy with what I received, although I did have one issue. The mouse looks as good as my previous $50 Road Mice Mustang mouse. Fit finish and quality are on par with each other. The battery has been fine for month that I've been using it. The scroll wheel feels quality. It looks terrific. I did experience a couple of issues that were mentioned in other reviews. I've resolved them both and here is how to fix them: 1. The mouse powering off after a few minutes. Yes, it shuts down after a few minutes of not using it. If you simply roll the scroll wheel one click either way, it instantly turns on. Not an inconvenience and it took a day or two where I do it without thinking about it. 2. One headlight worked intermittently. This one might be an issue for some. I took the mouse apart (1 screw) and found that the issue was where the led was soldered onto the circuit board. I simply used a soldering iron to reflow the solder at the led and it works 100% now. Super simple if you know how to use a soldering iron. If you don't/can't solder, yours will probably have the same problem when you get it, thus my 4 star rating...

This player has some tricks to it. Hit stop once and the player will remember the location even if you play another disk and put the first one back in. I love that. I bought the Magnetek because it advertised that it would play more formats. The Sony never played old disks well. I have an old VCR/DVD combo machine and it plays any the Sony wouldn't play. It won't play more recent DVDs. So, need to know: 1. It may not play old DVDs 2. If you hit pause and forget about it, it will restart the DVD eventually. 3. If you hit stop once, it will remember the place on the disk even if you play another disk. Had it remember after two other disks once. If you turn the machine off without hitting stop once, it doesn't remember. I also like that you can hit play when the unit is off and it will turn it on and play. Also, eject will turn it on and eject. So, a little quirky, but I like it better than another machine that earned five stars, so this one has to get five stars, right? And the price is a real winner.

En términos generales son unos audífonos bastante buenos, bien construidos, de gran estética, duración de batería y sonido pero con algunos puntos que los empañan: Pros: *Excelente construcción de los audífonos. * La estética, el color negro brillante y los LEDs le sientan genial en mi opinión (acá es cuestión de gustos si te parecen bien que sean de acabado brillante y tengan LEDs, aunque estas se pueden apagar con una simple configuración). * Gran batería, con los LEDs apagados y algo más de la mitad del volumen cada carga completa de los auriculares te dan fácilmente 7 horas. * Gran sonido. En este punto parto de los gustos, el sonido se siente algo lejano, particularmente vengo de los One Plus Buds y su firma de sonido (más cercana y con más brillo) me gusta más, al principio no podía adaptarme al sonido de estos Razer pero luego de unos días me acostumbre y debo decir que su sonido esta realmente bien. Los compare frente a unos AirPods Pro de ultima generación y la calidad del sonido es sumamente similar. *Aplicación sencilla y fácil de usar, permite reajustar los gestos según se requieran. Contras: * Tamaño grande los auriculares y algo pesados (se entiende por el tamaño de la batería), aun así comparados con unos AirPods Pro de ultima generación que son similares en tamaño (de la zona del driver), los de Apple se sienten mas ergonómicos y cómodos, al final te acostumbras a su forma pero no es su mejor cualidad. * Mala calidad de construcción de la caja, su material se siente de baja calidad con un plástico delgado y poco solido, al cambiar las almohadillas se siente un ligero desajuste en los auriculares en su interior. Totalmente diferente a los audífonos que si se sienten totalmente solidos. * La aplicación aunque es sencilla y bien diseñada, es lenta con cada apertura, ya que requiere sincronizarse con los audífonos y es proceso que toma aproximadamente 10 segundos (cada vez que la abres). Por otro lado no se entiende que se requiera de una aplicación independente solo para configurar las luces LED, esto debido a que Razer tiene su propio entorno de gestión LED (Chroma) pero igualmente es poco eficiente que solo para los LEDs de los audífonos debas instalar la aplicación completa de Chroma. * Falta de sensor de proximidad, para mi tal vez el punto más critico de unos audífonos de este precio, como comentaba tengo unos One Plus Buds que me costaron la mitad y si incluye esta funcionalidad (al quitarlos de los oídos se pausa el sonido y viceversa) no se entiende que los de Razer no provean la tecnología para hacerlo. * ANC testimonial, aunque incluya dicha tecnología la verdad es que su funcionamiento es muy muy bajo, en mi opinión la cancelación esta alrededor del 20-30%. No es un gran problema para mí porque la verdad no es algo que use pero si estas pensando en estos audífonos por dicha tecnología no deberías comprarlos.

Just a note about myself that is relevant to this review: I own a DSLR and have owned many point and shoot cameras, I am well versed in using a camera (iso, aperture, shutter speed, white balance, etc) Pros: - Very good pictures under sunny and outdoor conditions (it saturates greens/blues so the pictures have quite a punch, but honestly in a positive way) this is really the best part of the camera, you can take it to the beach without worrying too much, or to the jungle (I went to the Amazon River with this camera) and the pictures for the most part were great. - Smaller than it looks, easy to carry - It takes pictures faster than a lot of other point and shoots - rugged feel with glass sunken in, so you'll never accidentally hit the lens unless you stick a thin object in there. - waterproof (they note that you have to change the rubber seals every year to keep the waterproofing working) Neutral: - glass is always exposed, which seems rather strange and maybe damaging for the camera. Most cameras either come with a cap, or close/hide. I'll give them the benefit of the doubt and say it's so rugged that it doesn't matter. Cons: - Absolutely terrible, unusable pictures under fluorescent lights (automatic setting is terrible, I tried various manual settings and got it a little better, but still unusable pictures, I don't think I've seen a worse camera under this conditions - with flash it was a little better for close things, but in general this is the camera's biggest weakness. - Video is terrible too. But this time even under the best sunny conditions, it is grainy and shaky even with image stabilization on. It is so terrible that even watching it in a small screen (much less than HD) it looks grainy. A cellphone (I took side by side shots with my samsung epic 4g) takes much, much better pictures under fluorescent lights than this camera. This was basically the reason I returned the camera, it was meant to replace completely another point and shoot, not just for outdoor sunny adventures. And seeing a cellphone handle the white balance so much better than this camera's auto setting and even manually optimizing and playing extensively with the white balance to make it work in this lighting - was what ultimately convinced me to return it. The only way I would recommend this camera is if you plan on taking pictures on the beach or out in the sun, and have another DSLR or point and shoot for any indoor activities. And you don't care for video, since even under the best conditions it was terribly grainy and the image stabilization doesn't seem to do anything for videos.

This cable is way over-the-top stiff and will loosen and eventually destroy your USB-C I/O ports if you move your laptop around frequently—especially if used on your LAP, or possibly a conference table. It may even happen to any laptop used anywhere since they are not designed to sit stationary. The cable will bend and tweak the female connection on your laptop (the ports). Once this happens enough, no cable will be stable on that port because the internal parts have been compressed and bent. This can be a very costly repair if you are using a MacBook Pro or similar high-end computer. AGAIN, this cable is WAY too stiff for any mobile device unless you never move or bump it. You will start noticing "Disk Not Ejected Properly" error messages when you move your laptop ever so slightly. After this enough times, you may not be able to charge your computer once all ports have been degenerated. Finally, you may experience shorts within the electrical connections that will fry your I/O board. This happened on my 2017 MacBook Pro using this very cable, and Apple was gracious enough to cover the $1200 repair under their warrantee—knowing full-well the problem was caused by an extremely stiff USB-C cable. They've seen this happen with many braided cables of this nature. The USB-C connectivity architecture is somewhat delicate. A lot of information travels through small contacts at high speeds. You could say this cable it "too sturdy" and that's why I gave that feature 3 stars. As for value, you might consider this a $1210 cable if used carelessly. I would only recommend this cable for use with a desktop computer or "stationary" hub. In that case, this cable will outlast your computer or peripheral. As for the speed, I cannot speak with great authority, but it felt slow to me. This is likely due to the length of 2 meters, though. Shorter USB-C cables are always going to be faster. As for the one I purchased, it has now been sliced into 6 cables, approximately 1 foot each. Unfortunately, there are only two of those 6 cables that have a connector. None of them have connectors at both ends.

I've been using the 8000NEX for 2 days and I'm happy to report that a lot of the bad ratings on here are completely bogus. I purchased this unit to take advantage of CarPlay but also wanted a separate navigation system so that I don't have to constantly use my mobile data for directions. So far I am very pleased with my purchase! A couple of observations from my 2 days of use. Installation - fairly straight forward. Installation was done by a friend who is a professional installer and he did not incur any issues. Interface/ergonomics - read through some reviews were people were complaining about the interface being cluttered/not intuitive and the buttons being too small. I'll just chalk that up to "can't please all of the people all of the time." I just don't see the clutter or lack of intuitiveness that others have complained about. You can easily navigate through the various parts of the unit via the top menu screen. A reviewer mentioned that the setup for Settings is confusing. Totally untrue! The main settings for the unit are indicated by two gear wheels. Then each individual feature will have it's own menu which is indicated by the bulleted stacked lines icon. Not sure as to what's so confusing about that!!! I also like the buttons as is. Pioneer can only do so much given that they're limited by the dimensions of the standard double din. Bigger buttons = smaller screen and I personally would rather have a bigger screen. Navigation - it works as it's supposed to! Not much to add here. And unlike another reviewer stated cross streets do appear before you get to an intersection. CarPlay/iPhone 6 integration - CarPlay is one of the major reasons why I got the 8000NEX. It is a little buggy (which is expected given this is version 1.0) but for the most part it does what it aims to do. No learning curve - if you've ever used iOS you'll feel right at home. At first I couldn't access my Contacts via CarPlay but eventually it sorted itself out. I've also have not had any issues using my iPhone 6 with the 8000NEX. I actually prefer Pioneer's interface for music and navigation and then I'll use CarPlay for hands free calling and messaging (you can easily switch between CarPlay and the Pioneer interface via the Mode button). One quirky thing I noticed with the iPhone is that if I try to plug my phone via the Apple Lightning to Digital AV Adapter I get an "Incompatible USB" error message. But the HDMI feature (which allows you to mirror your phone's screen) works just fine when using the AV adapter. I could be missing a setting somewhere but for now I use the Lighting Digital AV adapter only when I need to mirror my phone on the unit through HDMI. AppRadio - I don't use the AppRadio feature as CarPlay supersedes it when the iPhone is plugged in. I was able to access it by plugging the phone via the Digital AV adapter, turning on Bluetooth, and switching the input setting from USB to Digital AV. I've heard a lot of complaints about this feature being buggy but I can't add much to that since I haven't tried using it. HD Radio/CD-DVD/Bluetooth - works exactly as it's supposed to. You can also trick the 8000NEX into thinking your parking brake is engaged while you're driving if needed. All in all I really like this unit. A more appropriate rating would be 4.5 but I'm not going to penalize the 8000NEX with 4 four stars because of Amazon's rating system. I highly recommend the 8000NEX!!!

We were planning a driving trip with our 3 kids, 15 month old twins and a 3 year old, and I knew I needed to get a dvd player for our SUV to get through the drive! After a lot of in depth research, I decided that this would be the perfect one, and it has!! This is the first portable dvd player our family has had, so I hope it lasts a long time. The things I love about this is that it can play 2 different dvd's at the same time, or you could hook it up so that the second screen plays the same dvd. I also love this because, with our daughters still facing rear in their car seats and my 3 year old faces forward (she is in the middle of the 2nd row and the twins are on the side of the door), I was able to get one screen behind the drivers headrest (for the 3 year old facing forward), and the other screen went on the middle headrest of the 2nd row (so that our twins could see it). This was PERFECT!!! Everyone was happy, including me and my husband who had a quiet drive! We adjusted the volumes on each monitor so that it could be heard for all the girls. Now in putting the second screen on the middle headrest of the second row, this made the wires hang all over the car. But if I was in the car by myself, this would definitely be an issue...this is why we only use it for long car trips (anything more than an hour) so that it could entertain them. I would definitely recommend these dvd players!!! It worked in our Honda Pilot, so I can assume it would work in any SUV/minivan that had 3 rows of seats. I have no doubt if we had our 3rd row up, I could still put this on the middle headrest of the 2nd row with no problems! This really is a must have for any family looking to entertain their kids on long car trips!!
