I have tried many ear buds for running including on the road and trail. You don't want too much noise cancellation unless you want to be hit by a car or passing cyclist or bit by a dog. You also do not need audiophile pure sound since there is plenty of noise around you and you are running and breathing somewhat hard. You want reasonably good sound and comfort so they feel good, don't fall out and do not hurt your ears. That said, these are just great. They sound very good and after trying them on a bouncy trail run, I could not even notice I was wearing them. I just heard the sound. No pain, no discomfort, no falling out, no blocking of essential environmental sounds. They were clearly the best activity ear phones/buds I have ever tried. If you want the purist sound for sitting and just listening, get full headphones. If you want the super ear phones that jam into your ears and block the outside sounds, that is fine, but they are worthless for activities. These sounded very good, among the best I have heard, although I admit I have not tried the audiophile ear buds since I think they are not necessary. Also, keep in mind that ipod (or other MP3 players) compress the music so much that I doubt even great earphones can fix that degradation in the sound. An album on a cd with 600 mb compresses down to about 60 mb on itunes. If you think you will get purist sound from 90% compression, you are dreaming. When you wake up, if you want to run with comfortable clear sounding earphones, these are a great choice.

I'm not a professional photographer - aspiring to even be "amateur" in fact. Since I tend to shoot outdoors most often, lighting has not been too much of a concern up to this point. But having quality lighting at my disposal when I need it is something I've been thinking about for some time. With the anticipated arrival of our first grandchild, and having been asked to shoot baby's first photos, I felt now was certainly the time to invest since I can't exactly perch the kid on a fence post somewhere with glorious sunlight. My requirements: Affordable Versatile Portable This kit met all three requirements during my searches and the initial reviews left me optimistically hopeful. I unpacked and set everything up for a functional check. Everything worked and I liked the relative ease of assembly. Relative being the operative word, but I'll get to that. Lighting was very adequate during some eBay photo shots. It all fits nicely back into the provided carry case for storage and portability. Here's the negatives: The boom was a bit clunky to set up and the boom arm is just lying loose in the carry case. Everything else has a box to go back into. The boom light head differs from the other two having only a single bulb, but that's understandable given that it must be lighter weight, and is permanently fixed to it's softbox (VERY easy to set up this softbox though). But the switch for this light is right up next to the light head. Great if it's down low, not so great if you've got it up over your subject and want to turn it on/off during a session. The other two softboxes themselves, though, are a bit tricky to put together. There's a video available that makes it look as easy as putting butter on bread, but I have to ask myself how many takes it took them to do it so smoothly. Prepare yourself for a bit of a struggle. Once assembled, however, they are pretty secure. Bottom line: if you want decent lighting that's affordable and portable, this is a pretty decent option. And while there are certainly better lights for a permanent studio, a small starter studio might do well with this set. When set up, they were pretty stable even to move around with the boom being the only part that's a bit wobbly when fully extended. Bang for the buck - 5 Stars. I just wish it didn't take almost an hour to set it all up.

Previous Review: Still the best Wifi adapter for Linux. Update: Based on my recommendation a friend who lives in a remote area recently purchased one. It did NOT work out of the box on Linux Mint. Turns out that up until a short while ago v1.10 that uses Atheros drivers was what was being shipped for many years and worked perfectly. They are now producing and selling v2.1, it uses rtl8188eu drivers and they are not included in recent kernels. Your best bet is to search the forums for your distro for specific instructions.They are easily obtained from github and installed IF you have an alternative method to connect to the Internet with Linux. My friend did not. Fortunately, I was able to email him the drivers and he got them with an old Windows machine and transferred them. However, this has left a sour taste in his mouth for Linux. Yes, not Linux fault, I get that, but most new users won't. Also, while this is with Linux Mint 18.2, I also run Kali occasionally and have heard on their forums that it no longer can be put in monitor mode.

Almost all SSDs are designed for use in laptops and not PCs or workstations. The issue is that on a low battery condition, a laptop will shut down or stop nicely so data loss from power faults is rare. On a PC, though, power faults and hard stops do happen from time to time unless you have a dedicated smart UPS that also can shut down your machine. These are more expensive than most home users want to pay for. I worked in IT for 5 years at a location that bought almost a thousand SSDs and the Crucial ones were far more reliable in desktop PCs than the other brands when it came to recovering from crashes or the machine suffering a problem/having to do data recovery. In general only the file they were accessing would be mangled, same as a mechanical drive. On other brands like Samsung, it was a die roll if the thing was corrupted. This is a short note about GNU/Linux performance. I purchased this because my Geforce 1050ti was not waking from sleep in Fedora 26 using the open-source driver stack. I keep seeing how good the open-source drivers are for AMD cards so I decided to try it. My whole purpose in this test is to use the open-source, not proprietary drivers. The issue with the 1050ti was the computer would wake from sleep but the screen would not, otherwise it worked fine. OK so on this RX550 the driver loaded up automatically no problem. Desktop acceleration (Gnome 3) seems a little snappier/faster, but I did not run benchmarks so this is just my impression. I set the machine to sleep after 15 minutes and walked away. Came back later, woke the machine and the screen came on. I've had no hiccups since. I feel a little dumb.... I've been complaining that Linux doesn't sleep/wake properly for a while but all this time I've used NVIDIA cards. I thought it was a motherboard power management issue, not the video driver. Anyway, I am happy to have a great little Fedora Linux desktop working as well as any computer should in 2017. Thanks to AMD for opening up and assisting a great community is creating great open-source drivers!

UPDATE: After couple months of usage (quite light, total 10 hours maybe) unit quit working, it short circuited battery and emitted bad smell. I decided to fix it by myself, I've opened it and discovered that IRLR8103V MOSFET failed and was shorting circuitry. I've replaced it and now light works fine. Some specs you'd like to know but not found online: 1. Made in China. 2. Comes with Sony NP-F960 compatible battery (7.4V 6000mah). 3. Design and features mimick Sony camera light. 4. Has considerable weight even without battery. With battery, you simply can't use it with cheap, handheld camcorders - light weight will turn your hand upside down. 5. Has additional barn doors, diffuser, condenser, color filter. All of them are useless, since their usage considerably shortens light output, which is not great at all (more on this later). All these bells and whistles are removable, so removing them will save your weight considerably. 6. Has built-in battery charge indicator, which is also almost useless - always shows full charge, then rapidly drops down, 5 minutes earlier before shutting off. Overall, this is not bad video light, has 10 pieces of 1W led, which deliver very neutral white color, not warm, not cool, just as it should be. The problem is, that 10W of LED seems to be same power as my 10W Sony halogen camera light. I was expecting just more output. And considering not a toy price tag of $179, you should think 10 times, before purchasing this light. For that price, you may get other, more lumens per buck output enabled camera light. Conclusion. Not bad, but $179 is way too much. For $79 - this would be a good purchase.

A few things to note about this product: 1. It works well and does exactly what it is supposed to: transmit audio to a bluetooth device (i.e. headset/speakers). Audio quality is perfectly adequate for watching TV/movies. 2. The photo shown is not the product. The photo seems to show a mini HDMI connector implying this is for video. It is not...this is an audio transmitter only. 3. The unit comes supplied with an adapter cable that has two RCA jacks (Red and White for stereo audio). The other end of this cable is an RCA receptacle. The instructions imply that you can plug in the 3.5mm mini plug into this receptacle, which you cannot. If you don't have a 3.5mm minijack (headphone jack) on your TV, then you will need to go get an adapter so you can connect the 3.5mm plug on the unit to the RCA connection on the Y-splitter cable supplied.

I am more than thrilled with the performance of this practical "walk-around" lens. I have used it most extensively on my Nikon D7000 and its performance was everything I needed. I do two kinds of photography primarily, urban/street, and wildlife/nature/landscape. When I travel by car I can take all the lenses I need for all of the above, but when I fly and have room for just one rig, and when I hike and can't possibly lug a super-zoom (mine is the Tamron 150-600 which I have also enthusiastically reviewed on Amazon) this meets my needs perfectly for those kinds of ventures. The lens is light weight, the barrel moves smoothly for focus and zoom. The 16-300 range is very versatile, focus is fast and sure (in my experience at least, all the way out to 300 mm), not as much problem with vignetting as some of my Nikon lenses (I'm eager to try it on my new body, D500 which has built-in vignetting compensation which should make it even less of a problem). There is of course distortion especially at wider angles, but that is a problem with all lenses. I just go with the flow and consider it part of the photographic drama (more recent processing software than mine may offer corrections for this lens). It functioned surprisingly well for what a I call a "pseudo-semi macro" for butterflies and other insects - the butterfly is a crop, but the subject is amply sharp enough to make that work well. Highly recommended for a really good lens, especially if you can have only one.

I've had a Kindle 2 and a Kindle 3 (Kindle Keyboard). I tried out the Kindle 4 but thought the screen contrast was a step back and continued using my trusty keyboard. I avoided the Kindle touch because of complaints about the over sensitized screen. I was excited for the Kindle PW after so many months of being envious of the Glow Nook. Finally, I received the Paperwhite on the day it was released and was immediately greeted by a glowing pixel in the middle of the screen. I'd already seen some of the other complaints and was happy that mine didn't seem to have all of those issues. Still, I talked to customer support right away, because the manual said that the light could be turned all the way off (which it CAN'T). Customer service told me that it should turn be able to turn off and offered to send out a replacement. The replacement came a few days later, and this one had loose dust that glowed under the screen, a few bad pixels, and the ever so attractive psychedelic colors people keep mentioning. I called customer service again and they offered to ship out a second replacement. This one has an issue with a pixel, the color problem, AND a light leak at the bottom left corner. I decided that I might just live with the first one and spent 5 hours adding books. It took this long do so because of a flaw with the cloud that only allowed some books to be downloaded with covers. After five hours, I discovered that my eyes were severely fatigued. This has NEVER happened to me on any other kindle device. The next day I tried again (for a shorter period time) and had the same issues. As much as I like the case, and the size, I think this one is going back too. Thankfully, I still have my KK!!! There are a few things that Amazon did right. The cover feature is cool (though the large portion of the screen being taken up by recommendations is incredibly annoying). The screen responds well to touch. Highlights and book error reporting are very easy. Honestly though, it seems like the Paperwhite is a prototype. I'm returning mine until Amazon gets the kinks worked out. My Dad has always had a rule about waiting 6 months before buying new technology. I hate to admit it, but I think he is right.

UPDATE 4/4/2014: After two years' experience, I've read a ton of books on the Kindle Touch, and I'm still using it. I bought another for my mother, and she's enjoying hers. Amazon has updated the software a couple of times, and it's significantly better than it was at the initial purchase. I'd buy another one in a heartbeat, but really don't need to -- this unit seems like it will last forever. Battery still lasts about 2 months! ORIGINAL REVIEW: This is my first e-reader, and I'm nearing retirement age, so read my review with that background in mind. The Kindle Touch is an excellent e-reader overall. I really like using it, and find it very easy to read (my vision is not the best). I enjoy having a whole library in my hand and being able to pick what I feel like reading at the moment. Each book opens to the page I left off. Variable font size is a great feature; I can have more on the page when I need to, or blow it up for ease of reading when I need it. It's very accessible also, with the two-finger touch sensor. Speaking of which, I'm enjoying the touch interface more than I thought I would, and now I wouldn't want to be without it. Why not five stars? Some of the features could be made more easily accessible. The table of contents requires several touches to access, and the "buttons" on the overlay menus aren't as touch-sensitive as the device normally is. Sometimes it takes two or three taps to activate a button. The worst thing about the Kindle Touch was my initial (first day or two) experience. It comes very well-packaged, but there is NO instruction in the packaging for how to use it; only how to charge the battery. There is a User's Guide pre-loaded in the Kindle, but you have to figure out on your own how to use the device to access the Guide, which then tells you how to use it! Bad idea, Amazon!! I also had difficulty figuring out how to naviage a two-page long home screen; it's not the same as navigating a book, and it can be frustrating at first. Warning: if you load e-books from sources other than Amazon (Gutenburg Project, for example), you may not find those books as easy to navigate as you will the Amazon books. I've already tried some of those, and deleted most out of navigational frustration. I have not had negative experiences getting around in any of the books I got directly from Amazon.

Update: it’s been almost two years since I bought this laptop, and it hasn’t held up at all. The software glitches have become unbearable. Context: I bought this laptop on Black Friday, 2016, for $899. Update: I've owned this laptop for more than 6 months now. Here's how it holds up... GOOD - The laptop has great hardware. 16GB of RAM is more than enough to tackle everything I've thrown at it. - The 1060 is a beast and runs most games at great/max settings at 1080p, 60FPS. - Open slot for m.2 SSD card (only m.2, unless you plan on swapping the current 1TB HDD) - Very quiet, very cool. Have had literally zero issues with it even warming up, let alone getting hot. - Sound is incredible. Multiple speakers and the audio is very crisp. BAD - Worst trackpad I've ever used in my life. I've used trackpads extensively for the last 8ish years, finally had to buy a mouse. Very sluggish feeling and not good at picking up small movements. - Arrow keys are bad. Still not used to their awkward placement/size. - 1060 is a beast, but this is the 3GB version, which actually makes a big difference in some games. In RE7, for example, this laptop runs it flawlessly at 1080p, 60+ FPS, max settings with ease... most of the time. Whenever you go to a new area, though, and stuff starts to load in, the games stops responding for a few seconds. I found out this is because RE7 caches shadows in the video RAM. When I turned this feature off, it only stutters when entering new areas, which is very tolerable and 100% playable. Something to consider, though. - The software on this computer is buggy as hell. I'd say 1/4 times I open the lid, I'm met with a black screen. I then have to turn the display off, and open it back up again to get the monitor to turn on. It only takes 5-10 seconds, but it's annoying, especially in a laptop with a ~$1000 price point. Also, there's been a few times I've been met with weird glitches, such as context menus that won't go away until a restart, and sometimes the entire bottom task bar not responding to anything. Overall: Very good laptop for the Black Friday price I paid ($850 after rebate), and most of the issues I have with it are minor, but if I I had to pay the $1000 tag on it, I think I'd look for a 1060 with 6GBs just so I'd feel more confident going into the future.

I would give FIVE stars if only there were the documentation you need to get started. This board is a close relative of the WeAct black pill board. It's like a Maple board. It has a 10 analog inputs and 16 PWM pins. Plenty of SPI/I2C pins. Lots of GPIO on a board faster than an Arduino Due. It's frustrating because you don't need "pinouts" to use this, you need a map of pin functions like the ones you usually get on an MCU board, not a mechanical with label names for pins. But if you have the label names you can map them to other boards with better documentation. You do not need an st-link or a serial board if you want to use the Arduino IDE. It's ready to use. The only major thing you lose using Arduino is the interactive debugger. I would love to use an interactive debugger but using Arduino has its perks, too! You do need to make sure your USB C cable is a 'data/sync' cable, not just a power cable. When you plug in USB to the board, you will see a red power LED and it will be running a test program to cycle the blue LED from darker to brighter. Follow the instructions given by others here to set up the stm32duino programming environment. If you are an Arduino/Teensy user, you will be happy to find familiar coding capabilities.

Four stars for features and sound quality. Misses the 5th star for brain dead firmware and instructions that are just flat out wrong. VERY IMPORTANT: If you are connecting the sound bar to a TV that supports ARC (I have a Samsung model), do NOT use the HDMI pass-through mode illustrated in the skimpy instruction pamphlet that comes with the soundbar. It will NOT work correctly when installed like this. Instead, plug your video source (cable box) directly into the TV and then use the ARC-enabled HDMI port from the TV and plug that into the soundbar's HDMI OUT port. This is the *only* configuration I found that actually worked correctly... the soundbar will automatically detect the ARC input and use it consistently. Trying to use the HDMI passthrough mode, the soundbar would routinely start up in "D.IN" input mode and have to be manually switched to HDMI. Why not just default to the mode it last used??? The HDMI passthrough mode also stopped ARC from working when trying to watch other sources (DVD player, media player, etc), which is exactly the opposite of its intended behavior. It's possible that Soundshare would also work as well as TV ARC, but my TV does not support that so I cannot say.

I tried to be short, but this review just kept on going! Sort of therapeutic to write. It's my first, I think. I hope it helps someone make a purchasing decision. I bought this for four main reasons: 1) It has a standard USB jack so would hook up easily to the existing set of speakers (high quality) that I purchased years ago to work with my old Creative Microphoto. It also means I didn't need a separate proprietary cable since any USB cable would work. Hardly any device can claim this, I don't know why they all need their own types of cable. 2) My music collection is around 50 GB and growing as I continue to convert old vinyl to wma or mp3 files. I needed 64 GB. 3) All my music is in wma or mp3 format and works with Windows Media Player and therefor Windows Media Center and can be shared over my network to our PS3 and other computers. 4) Very positive experience with the Microphoto that just won't die but is too small and battery life after many years of use is too short to even mow the lawn with. At the time of my purchase of the X-Fi2, it was the only player that met the first three (most important) requirements. It was also $100 cheaper than an iPod Touch that while attractive, would have required iTunes, which for me was a step backwards in several ways. So I purchased the X-Fi2. I've tried to like it. Really, I have! Understand that I have it very full of music; I don't really want it for photos or video. But there are too many problems with it. Let me explain some of them: 1) It takes several minutes to turn on. During this process, you don't really know if it's coming on, as after an initial welcome, the screen goes dark and you wait. Eventually, usually anyway, it turns on and the main menu appears. Sometimes, nothing happens, and you try to reset the silly thing but you don't really know what's happening because the screen is still dark. Sometimes plugging it into the computer helps, but I can't explain why. Plug it in, the thing starts, unplug it, and go exercise or mow or whatever. 2) I just saw another post that states that there is an 8000 song limit. I'm not quite at that limit, but I'm very close. 3) Indexing my music collection takes a LONG time. Several minutes. It feels like 15, but that is probably longer than it actually takes. The progress bars are deceptive; just when you think it's done the bar goes back to the beginning and it happens again. This happens every time you sync, or when the batteries get too low, or sometimes just randomly. 4) Playlists. I've spent a lot of time in Windows Media Player creating various playlists. I save them in M3U format. I can select which playlists to sync with the X-Fi2, and it sends the songs but not the playlists. Other players (such as an older Archos 5 I have) send the songs and the playlist. I know that I can create playlists two ways: on the X-Fi2 or on the PC if I use Creative's application. Have you looked at their app? It's junk, and I have everything working so nicely in WMP. I don't want to run their app just to create playlists. I have looked at the playlist files on the PC and on the X-Fi2. They are both text files and with some work I might be able to translate one into the other. But I feel quite strongly that this is a very silly approach for something that should be provided. 5) Play by Genre. I do this frequently, but not on the X-Fi2 because it's difficult and occasionally causes a lock-up or shut-down (interesting phrases, one is up and the other is down... but both are bad... isn't English strange?). From what I can tell, I cannot just select a Genre and say "play all". Instead, you have to "add all." First, you must empty the queue of what's playing. My process is to pick a single track from the genre I want, and play it. While it's playing, go to the genre, show all tracks, then "add all." It works, but it's much harder to do than expected. My old Microphoto does it better; in this regard, Creative took a step backwards. One must be prepared for disappointment during this process, for it often doesn't work well and results in a reboot, and often a rebuild of the index, which I've explained takes minutes. 6) Other minor problems. Battery life seems to have dropped quickly. The screen is not visible in bright light. The volume is very difficult to control. The auto-lock is hard to turn off if sweaty or in bright light, and it must be off to adjust the volume. Cover art isn't always transferred properly. My kids want more games, but that's not a big deal to me. What does all this mean? Let's say I want to do something as simple as shuffle through my Classic Rock collection. About half the time, I can do it, but it takes several minutes to get started and a bit of frustration with various slides and taps. The other half the time, it won't turn on or will need a restart and re-index. It has taken me up to 15 minutes to get it going. I'm frustrated and disappointed. I really want to find the ideal player, and I so badly wanted the X-Fi2 to be it. I've applied firmware updates and continue to hope that eventually I'll be happy. Updates, by the way, are very rare, which leads me to believe that Creative has moved on and I've very little hope for this any longer. I guess if I wanted to get this playing a certain genre, and leave it on, hooked up to the speaker/recharger I have, and never turn it off, it would work well. But I'm too energy conscious to do that, and others in my family use the speaker too. It does sound great. It's light weight. It's built well. It looks good. It does have some apps on the Internet that work well on it. It has potential to be what I want. But unless there is a major update to it, it's mostly just a piece of junk. If anyone out there has comments on what I'm doing wrong, please let me know.

I initially thought the handling would feel awkward because of that shape, but not at all, it is just fine. - Contrary to another review, I actually like its light weight. When you do that to drag text, then the piece of text you are moving finds itself inserted in the middle of a random word or sentence. Every time, the only resort is Ctrl-Z when it is available. It's very annoying. This is the main reason why I'm only giving 3 stars. - There is no LED light to warn you in advance that the battery is about to be empty. There is no LED light to tell you when the mouse if fully charged. There are various LED lights but the manual does not explain their roles. - For the mouse to last for more than one week, it seems that you need to charge it for 24 hours. It could be less, but again, there is no LED light to tell you how long. - The bottom surface of the mouse is not even, which makes the mouse wobbly on a flat surface. As a result, the mouse feels "cheap", which is eventually a reflection of its price. NEUTRAL: - When the mouse is in sleep mode, and you wake it up by pressing one of the buttons, it takes about one second for the cursor to appear. So during that time, don't start moving the mouse to see where the cursor is, because in this process, you end up losing track of where the cursor could have gone. Overall, I don't regret my purchase for its price and for my intended secondary use of this mouse.

Update: Mon 29 Dec - received replacement GoPro4 this evening and it works as expected. It would appear that all of the issues experienced below with the previous GoPro4 were a result of a hardware issue(s). Thank you Amazon for replacing it so expeditiously, very impressive! I'm very satisfied to have a working Hero4 now. Giving it 4 stars instead of 5 due to the issues experienced below and also because it does not support a true RAW shooting mode for stills. Would like to see support for Adobe DNG in the future, or at least a GoPro RAW standard that they release a RAW codec for in ACR/Bridge. ----------- BLUF: Awaiting replacement, thank you Amazon for being such a reputable marketplace; GoPro - in need of quality control/manufacturing improvements. Background: After receiving the GoPro Hero4 Black I went to Gopro.com to register the device and associate it with my account and it had me download the 1.2 update to install. Unzipped this on the card and powered on the GoPro4 which sat in a "Busy" state for 40 minutes. Had previously installed a newly charged battery along with the Sandisk 64GB UHS-1 95mbps card. After approximately an hour, I hard powered off the GoPro 4 Black via holding the power button. After powering back on I was able to set up the iPhone app that I used with my Hero 3 Black. Of serious concern however, was the purple live view video I was seeing. No issues with wifi or getting the iPhone app to work with it initially, but then the Hero 4 Black would stop responding completely. Again hard powered off and took the SD card out, tried simply navigating the menu system of the GoPro 4 and it would freeze after attempting to change mode/navigate to the next menu option. Tried several other variations of the above and other desperate attempts at getting normal function out of a piece of electronics that I no longer had any faith in whatsoever. A few times I had to completely remove the battery as the power button would not respond. Contacted GoPro via the chat, but no response, left a message. At this point I decided it was a better use of everyone's time and resources to exchange for another unit that may work properly. I know these units work as I see the GoPro team using them each year at the Vans Triple Crown of Surfing. Just not sure why the consumers are having such hardware issues? I'm guessing issues regarding manufacturing runs, hardware, and quality control. If you get one that works, they're awesome, the challenge is getting one that works. If the replacement that I receive courtesy of Amazon's upstanding and impressive service works I'll be happy, if it also has issues I'll be refunding. On the bright side, my Hero 3 Black never gave me any of these problems. Hope this helps someone out there, but this was my experience with the hero 4 Black on the 2014 Christmas Holidays.

The big story on this camera is the amazing lens coupled with nice, bright aperture, and a huge sensor (bigger than micro-four-thirds), giving truly amazing low-light performance. I can take excellent pictures with this camera indoors with no flash, photos impossible for most other cameras. The glass on this camera is huge, and it closes with a built-in lens cover!! It also has great macro performance; you can take wonderful close-ups of flowers etc. Auto-focus is very good, giving nice sharp pictures. Another notable feature is the pop-up flash, which is hinged, so you can easily put your finger under it while shooting to tilt the flash up and get "bounce" lighting from the ceiling indoors. Much better than the usual flash lighting. The camera is quite compact and comfortable to hold. There are a multitude of menu options for shooting, with all kinds of cool special effects including fish-eye lens effect, HDR, starry sky, and special background defocus mode, which shoots two fotos at different focus points, and combines them to blur the background, for great artistic portraits etc. Although the lens and sensor are big enough to achieve very good "bokeh" even without this special feature. The tilt-screen is also pretty amazing. Not only can you shoot holding the camera low to the ground, or high up in the air, but you can also flip the screen completely up to 180 degrees for taking "selfies." This is the only camera I know of with this capability. Also, it's a touch screen, and you can tap on the screen to select your focus point. Best all-around camera I've ever seen. The combination of lens range (from 24-120mm), sensor size, bright aperture, compact size make this camera truly unique and without any real competition. It even takes pictures in RAW. The only camera I would compare to it is the Sony RX10, which has a longer telephoto lens and bright aperture, but the sensor is smaller, and the Sony is twice as big.

I bought these to upgrade from my previous setup, which was a medium sized set of logitech computer speakers with a separate sub, similar to the z313, which were around $50 at the time of purchase. At more than twice the price, it would make sense that these are better. My experience so far: Sound quality: is good, great even by comparison to my old unit. Mids lows and highs are all there and a lot of those subtle production values come through. It won't get really loud but gets plenty loud for me. One thing I like is that it doesn't feel like it will pop its own speakers. I've listened to a variety of music on it from hip-hop to jazz to classical. All sounded really sweet. Bass: Not amazing but plenty of feel and tone. That being said, i bought this because of the ability to add a sub and I will be doing just that. Setup: Easy. Open it, plug it in, turn it on. Bluetooth: Easily switches between devices, 2 iPhones, an 11 and a 7, a 2015 macbook, a dell laptop. There is a button on the remote that kicks off whatever is connected if you want to switch devices. It's sweet. So far, it isn't having trouble being recognized by these devices but I do have to completely turn off the unit and turn it back on to get it to work right with my mac. The machine connects but doesn't play sound loudly enough unless i go through this ritual. Likely a problem with the computer, which is easy enough for movies. It is not my common listening device for music. Movies: No problems with latency on any streaming platforms or dvds, only watch films on the mac, haven't tried the dell. Sound is clear and big when sitting about 20' away. Very clear. Often times, these smaller systems seem to muffle out the dialogue when the movie rumble gets going. This, so far, has not been the case with these Edifier speakers. Everything is nicely balanced. Remote: This is why I gave 4 stars. Though the remote does control all devices just fine, play, pause, forward, etc...the buttons don't always work. You have to be right in front of the unit and press the buttons hard, which makes the cheap feeling remote feel like it is going to snap in two. Whatever the case, it isn't long for this world. price: If the remote was sweet, and the system got a little louder, this would be a perfect buy. As is, I feel like this unit is a smidge over priced. I would buy again.

After inordinate amounts of research, I ordered and used the K7 on a shoot and was greatly disappointed, primarily because of the qc and the sensor's obvious malfunction. So I guess I got a bad one, but that doesn't excuse anything, nor does it relate to some of the other issues. It would overheat all the time, resulting in video shut down, more noise in the images, and lines through the stills. Bad sensor. The Pentax is built well, one of the most solid constructed slrs available, but so what? For this price it should be solid and that is really the only impressive thing about it. It takes very neutral pictures, which can be good. It has some nice tweaker features, in camera control of many parameters, but in the age of photoshop, who cares, give me a nice clean neautral photo, I'll tweak it later. It's video is almost useless. The 720p is functional, but like I said the sensor overheats very easily, and unpredictably. It also is a moire pattern beast. Stay away from roof tops, patterned clothing or window screens, lest you want moire hell. The full frame video has horrible interlace jaggies, so don't even bother. You have to be in paranoid mode to make use of it, meaning, only plan on shooting ten seconds-twenty seconds max, or you might have a shut down in mid shot. The stills are nothing special, no matter what your setting. Honestly my nearly three year old Sony 350 takes just as good stills and that cost $600. That extra money cannot be justified by limited video capabilities. I guess I was somewhat biased by my partner who was shooting with a Canon T1, which cost $700 less and had a crappy kit lens yet it put the Pentax to shame in lowlight. And come on, the ability to shoot in available light is really what makes a digital camera. A $200 point and shoot can shoot good pictures in sunlight. Yes the larger sensors and lens choice are just as important...but my Sony cost $600 not $1500. Slrs need to be able to produce good pictures in low light and the Pentax has no excuses. We kidded that the t1 is an x-ray camera. It shot in near complete darkness, with a fast shutter and virtually no noise. The results looked like it was shot at magic hour. On the same exact settings, the equivalent on the Pentax, mine were dark, extremely grainy, out of focus and embarrassing. And I have a faster lens. Oh and the t1 shoots better video. The Pentax also has the worst auto mode for those get-it-fast-or-it's-gone situations. So if the Pentax cannot even stand up to a camera costing $700 (what am I getting for that money, better build?) than forget it. Pentax is basically the turtle in the SLR race, but here slow, steady, and more expensive doesn't win the race. If you are going to take pictures of still life or landscapes (daytime) and have time to adjust, tweak, fine tune etc, because honestly what dslr works the same way as a film camera, and you want a tank on your tripod, then get the Pentax, otherwise looks elsewhere. Canon and less so Nikon have rightfully left Pentax in the dust of the digital realm. check out the finished video from the shoot and see for yourself. [...]

I received this antenna this afternoon and decided to throw it up to test. After the poor performance of my last antenna, I wasn't holding out much hope. Installation was the same as all of the mast mount antennas, so nothing special there. The aiming was pretty simple using the signal meter on my 4G modem. As for the performance, that part is awesome! After finding our cell tower and getting the positioning just right, the results were: Signal Strength: Built-in Antennas: -113 dBm This External Antenna: -91 dBm This is in an area where all of the cell maps show no signal available. Speed Test: Built-in Antennas: 1-3 Mbps down/0.3 Mbps up This External Antenna: 40 Mbps down/17 Mbps up Obviously I am very happy with the results, and wish I had purchased an external antenna earlier. If anything changes (antenna failure or weather damage), I will update this review, but as it sits, easily a 5 star antenna.

I have a Ring doorbell, 4 blink minis, and a geeni cam and this Tapo outdoor camera is probably my favorite out of all of them. It's the only one that doesn't lag on live views and the picture quality is better than my Ring. I don't like the view range though. With my ring doorbell you can see EVERYTHING outside. Ground, sky, and almost everything left and right of it. With the tapo camera I have to choose whether I want to see my porch OR parking area. I do like the different settings, like "person detection", "line crossing detection", "motion detection", "alarm", "flood light", etc and the night vision is FAR superior to my Ring doorbell. You don't miss alerts either, unlike the "person detection" with the ring doorbell. Tapo will pick up on a person that's barely within video range, and Ring sometimes won't pick up on a person even if they're right in front of it. I don't like that you aren't able to set up motion alerts for Tapo through your alexa devices, although you CAN do live view and have all notifications (or whichever ones you choose) sent to your phone Via the Tapo app. I don't like that tapo doesn't have an option to continuously record like Ring does. But I like that tapo is wired so there's no charging it up everyday like I have to do with the Ring doorbell. I also like that you can speak through the Tapo cam like you can the Ring doorbell. Tapo is also very bulky which makes it more difficult if you're going for subtle. All in all, it's a great camera and I'd purchase another!

Granted, the outlets in my apartment are more "well-used", but this was not an issue with my Gen 2 and it's mount in the exact same outlet. So there I am, overseas in need of an IPod dock that also plays CD's and has an alarm clock. I get on Amazon and start searching. Many great products for reasonable prices come up and this is one of the cheaper ones, so I add it to cart. It arrives in the mail about three weeks later and I'm as happy as a kid getting the exact Christmas present I wished for. I open it up. Not bad; nice sleek looking glossy plastic body with a smooth finish. I plug it in and start reading the quick start guide. It shows me how to set up the time and alarm, adjust the brightness on the clock, how to switch between radio and CD etc. I plug in my IPod and play around with it. It works just fine. I put in one of my CD's and it plays nicely. I try to tune in the radio but then remember I'm in the middle of a desert and there's no way I'm catching 103.7 KAMEL middle eastern radio station on this thing so I switch back to CD and listen to some music. Great! Two weeks later the CD starts to skip. I stop playing it, eject the port, pull the CD out and re-insert it, close the port and push play. It plays fine. Another week later it does the same thing, so I do the same thing to fix it and it plays again. Yet one more week and it does the same thing again, so I do the same thing again to fix it and it doesn't play. I try to adjust the surface angle and ... ... ... it's ALIVE. It works fine and since then hasn't given me any more problems but I'm pretty sure if I move it from the crooked position that it's in, it'll stop working. I've had this product for about 2 months now and am happy with it but I'm in a desert so I'm happy with most everything I have. Could I have done better? Yes. Should I have spent another ten or twenty dollars to buy a name brand? Maybe. Don't waste your time or hard earned money on this product. It isn't worth it. The volume goes up and down in high quantities, so if you're sharing a living area with a friend you can't turn it low enough to where it won't disturb your partner. I know, you're probably thinking "why not use headphones"? Because you can't always use headphones. Sometimes you just want to listen to some George Michael's "Careless Whisper" and slow dance with an imaginary partner while your roommate is asleep in low volume and this thing doesn't allow you to do that. It's either high or mute. The brightness of the clock set at the lowest level is bright enough to be used as a rescue signal. We've already determined that, trust me. The radio antenna is a wire, not a metal antenna, a wire. It doesn't come with a remote. Kind of gets annoying when I have to constantly walk over to adjust the volume or switch to another song or something (all that sand getting in between my toes) gets old and annoying after a while. There are a lot of better products out there with remote controls. I might end up using this as a paper weight or a toilet. This is MY review for this product. Hopefully it helps you make the right decision.

I'm just the average collector.. or vinyl / HiFi Enthusiast... who strives as any to build a better HiFi system, one piece @ a time. Over the years I've come to a better understanding what the numbers are all about, and am more than happy to share my experience with you :) A little about My current TT Setup. *ATLP140XP Turntable *SCHIIT MANI Preamp *KLPISCH RP600 Bookshelf Speakers *PIONEER VSX D509S AV Receiver (this is an older model, which I use only for music, 100 x 5 @ 8 ohms, over the years it has handled every combination of Speaker / HiFi Component I threw @ it, one of the last few models which have a fiber optic digital out, perfect to pair with my Pioneer Cassette Deck CTW806DR, which has a digital in, for clean hiss-less recordings) *ORTOFON RED / BLUE / BLACK Cartridge (I climbed the upgrade ladder just like any other HiFi enthusiast, I keep switching between the blue and black Cartridge, but at most times the Blue is always on.) So I've been reading a lot about this little powerhouse of a preamp, watched a couple of YouTube reviews, everyone seems to agree on one thing, for its price and flexibility in functionality (MM & MC Compatible) the output is Phenominal. The option to switch Gain / Load, is great. Mine came set at the below setting: *Gain 1 and Gain 2 both L: 30dB of gain 30db of gain is a pretty good starting point, so I left it at that and run it thru a couple of records, Hendrix, Floyd, Portishead, to name a few, while switching between the 3 cartridges. I found that firstly, other than your regular surface noise, there's no added hiss, no hum. The answer lies in the details as they say, this Preamp breathe's new life and tonal balance to whatever music you listen to, the highs are defined but don't distort, the mids sound balanced but yet soulful, the bass is punchy, quick and sounds fuller. Further experimenting with records by Type O Negative, King Crimson & Sinatra, I decided to bump it up, now running @ Gain 1 = H, Gain 2 = L: giving me 48dB of overall gain, this is where the Mani shines for any MM Cartridge. First noticeable difference was the bump in standard loudness and added clarity in highs, I had to reduce the volume down at-least by 10db (in layman's terms that would be, say if you're listening to your music @ Volume 30, you will now have to reduce it to 20, yup that's how much louder it gets, a very noticeable difference without any distortion) The Channel separation comes through beautifully, many-a-time making me turn my head left and right. The bass sounds more meaty, a more whole sound. The jump in db, after switching to *Gain 1 = H, Gain 2 = L: 48dB of gain, also helps in preserving your main amplifier, when the standard loudness increases, you would naturally reduce the volume on your main amp, therefore, now you aren't pushing it as much! Even at lower volumes, the details shine through. Advise to anyone who has a TT/Preamp setup, if you're thinking of upgrading your cartridge, try upgrading the preamp first, I was in awe of the output on my Red Cartridge, it made my system sound almost like those Yamaha studio monitors, super balanced, yet dynamic. I'm assuming the most commonly used cartridge on HiFi systems is MM, so the settings out of the box either the 30db or 48db are your best bet. You may bump up to Gain 1 and Gain 2 both H: 59dB of gain, if you are using a lower output amplifier or receiver, however anything that's 100w x 2 @ 8 ohms will be good to go @ 48bd gain settings. Lastly I'd like to add this is a quality built product.. its top notch sturdy, strong connectors, not at all flimsy! a very minimal design with just the one led light in front. works for me tbh. Its small size allows it to be tucked right behind my turntable. Schiit are quite reputed when it comes to their products, and this preamp, besides exceeding my expectations.. is no exception. It gets the job done and then some, for a fraction of the cost you'd pay for any other preamp. All I'd say is, I now have a piece of Schiit that I love! A few tips on connections, if you are going to connect all your components to 1 power strip, make sure it is surge protected, this will help in maintaining a stable current going to all your devices, at the same time the surge protector will act as a firewall against any spikes in voltage.

The quality is of the plywood is a little questionable, and the top layer seems to be some kind of laminate (you can see the pixelation sort of pattern up close). The stacked layers of plywood have some chipped out holes like other reviewers have shown in photos. I plan to fill mine with wood filler and sand it down--maybe add some danish oil for protection. Not a huge deal--especially for the price. The overall execution is super clean though. I love how light colored the wood is, with just enough texture and warmth to make it perfect for a minimal desk setup. It's actually a shade lighter than my desktop, which is an IKEA GERTON for reference, with no stain or finish added. There's plenty of room to store and keep exactly what I need at my fingertips (my DAC, headphone amp, audio interface, and closed 16" macbook pro), while hiding a majority of the black metal electronic boxing and cables from sight. This makes a big difference in how cozy the setup feels with that much going on. I don't plan on putting my monitor, or anything else, directly on the stand. The main function of the shelf to me, is to hide what I want to arrange under it. That said, it feels extremely sturdy, and sits very flush on my desk with no wobble (contrary to other reviews I read). I did have to use quite a bit of strength to force the cork legs into the openings on the underside of the wood. I suspect people who reported a wobble may have no wedged all of their legs in completely. A few positives over the Grovemade, if that's what you're comparing this to: - The open underside is far more practical for storing things. Grovemade's current desk shelf now has a metal shelf running along the entire length, which limits what you can put under it to a max height of 2" on the bottom, and about 1.6" on the metal shelf. For me, this would have made storing all of the electronics (minus my laptop) impossible, and ultimately became the dealbreaker on the Grovemade for me. I asked if they would be willing to sell me their previous design (it had JUST changed online), and they wouldnt. - The cork legs are a more typical cork color--like you'd see on a wine bottle. Grovemade's cork legs on their light version of their desk shelf are more of an orange hue. Just an observation--take that how you will. ** This is in no way meant as a knock on Grovemade's shelf. I desperately wanted to make their shelf work for me, and was willing to pay the premium for their beautiful build quality/finishing. When it comes to build, this product doesn't even compare to Grovemade--and the positives that it DOES have, should really be attributed to GM as they pretty much stole the design from them. But if you're like me... willing to compromise with the quality, potentially patch some chips in the plywood (or live with them as is) and prefer the open underside, I would definitely recommend this shelf.

I bought this to use on my Trek hybrid bicycle. As a speaker, it sounds great, better than I was expecting, including good bass, for its size. Even tested it on my Harley Road King motorcycle. The two reasons it didn't work for me was 1) the mounting, and 2) the battery life. For the mount, the back mounting surface is flat, and so a rubber strap stretches across the handlebar to hold this in place. The strap itself is secure, no concerns with the speaker coming off, but on the 7/8" diameter polished chrome handlebars of my bicycle, the speaker kept rotating, so it was impossible to keep aimed at me for best sound. Seems like if this was meant to mount to a round bar, it would have some sort of U-shape bracket with high-friction rubber. For the battery life, the ad said 8 hours battery life. I'm guessing that's rated at like half volume, but at 3/4 volume, which is where you need it if you bike with any background noise, I was barely getting over an hour. Guessing I had a defective unit, because when I charge it, it only charges for a bit, then shuts off before the battery indicator goes all the way up. Tried it with multiple cords, and multiple chargers, same result. I saw a number of questions about whether this could work on a motorcycle, so I decided to give it a try. I've got a 2004 Harley Road King, with a windshield and an aftermarket exhaust that's probably slightly louder than stock, but not by much. Granted, not designed for this purpose, but wanted to see how much power you'd need for a motorcycle speaker. For lower speed, in-town cruising, you could hear the speaker easily over road and exhaust noise. At highway speeds, you're aware there's a speaker on, but it doesn't have enough power to overcome road, wind, and engine noise, especially if you've got a 3/4 or full helmet on (which cover your ears). But I found it decent for lower speed riding with a half-helmet (ears aren't covered). On the motorcycle, the speaker didn't rotate, likely because of the larger diameter handlebars, and the fact that there were some brake lines and a throttle cable behind the speaker, preventing it from rotating. If it wasn't for the battery life, I would have kept it for its intended use on my bicycle, and I would have figured out a way to overcome the speaker spinning on my handlebars. I likely just got a bad unit, but my review is based on the product I received. Hope this helped! EDIT 8/29/2021: Bumping up to five stars because of the great customer service! Tribit representatives reached out to me, and arranged for a replacement unit that works great.

After having a home computer for over 6 years the old computer finally needed replacing, & I decided to go the way of a laptop for a new one. I had to get used to Windows 8, but it didn't take long to figure out how it works. I actually really like it because you can go between the "Start" page & a regular desktop screen. The "start" page is customizable so you can put all your favorite programs on one page without having to navigate through other stuff to get the program/s you want to use. I do not use my laptop for anything fancy: regular internet stuff such as checking e-mails, hanging out on a few forums & my favorite websites, Netflix (hence why I bought a laptop with such a large screen), editing my business website, search engines when necessary, etc. Once you get used to everything its very easy to navigate including settings. Im not very techy so I cant give a fancy review about RAM & RPM, but for what its worth the computer runs smoothly, quickly, & I haven't had any issues so far. The touch pad took getting used to as well, & like any laptop it makes scrolling a little difficult & slow, but I bought a wireless mouse for when I need to do stuff with extra speed. The screen is bright (when you set it to be), & all pictures/images are clear & crisp. A full battery lasts a little over 6 hours at full screen brightness (which is a big battery killer), & charging a dead battery takes no more than 2 hours. This laptop comes with a battery monitor so it tells you percentage & how much longer your battery should last as well as battery health (so you know when the battery needs replacing), & there are settings you can change if you plan to keep the laptop plugged in for extended periods of time, plan on frequently charging it with a not low battery (ex: 50%, 75%, etc), etc. Shipping wise it was packed well & arrived on time. The only con is the size of the laptop can be be a bit bulky, but I think its worth it so its not a huge deal for me. Overall VERY happy with my purchase!

When power is restored it will charge the batteries and switch to float charge. The benefit of this system is that you can run your full size sump (I have 2 in my pit) and it will run off grid power (even when plugged into the inverter. If/when the power goes out it uses the automatic transfer switch to seamlessly switch to battery power. Then back to grid power when it is available. I have not put the system together and tested the inverter yet, this review is just based on opening it and reading the owners manual. After I add the batteries and hook it all up I will test it and update my review. ****UPDATE**** after spending several hundred dollars on 1 AWG cables, 3 deep cycle batteries, etc. I plugged the sump pump in and the inverter beeps and can not run the pump. This should not be the case, it is a 1/3 HP pump and is only 7.3 AMPS. That is only 803 running watts, well under the 2000 rated watts. Even at start up it does not even come close to the 4000 surge watts this inverter is supposed to be rated at. I know the pump doesn't go over the supposed 4000 watts that your inverter is supposed to have for surge because I previously ran the pump off a 2000 watt generator during power outages. To add insult to injury I wrote a very polite email soyond over a week ago and thus far have recieved no response.

If you love listening to HAM radio or if you need a reasonably stealthy antenna outside of your vehicle for a low-power HT, this will probably do the job. For anything else, it's not ready for prime time. I can only imagine the SWR on this to reduce a strong 2m signal to two miles while my cheesy 5w Boafeng hand-held will crush that even from inside my SUV.

Bought this Nikon HB-34 Lens Hood when the original [[ASIN:B000OV16JO Nikon HB-37 Lens Hood]] was bumped off the end of my Nikkor zoom lens by someone with protruding elbows while shooting photos from a bridge. That original hood had served me well, though the fit was a bit loose. But as I saw it sailing off the bridge into the water below, was glad that at least I had a good camera strap. It was a lesson learned the hard way. Saw the [[ASIN:B0009HN588 Nikon HB-34 Lens Hood for 55-200mm DX Nikkor Lens]] listed here on Amazon, and though it wasn't the same as the original one for my [[ASIN:B000O161X0 Nikon 55-200mm f/4-5.6G ED IF AF-S DX VR Nikkor Zoom Lens]], thought that it might be worth a try. After two years in constant use, can say that it was a was a good choice. Not sure why, but the original 'round' HB-37 lens hood never was a good tight fit on my lens. At the time that I bought the zoom lens, this HB-37 hood came with it, so I shrugged it off and kept using it. There was a bit of looseness to it in the way that it fit even when double checked; the bayonet mount wouldn't go as tight as one might hope. But this HB-34 lens hood has always had a good precision fit, one that one would expect from Nikon, and it continues to do so to this day. As far as lens performance goes, it's flower-type design works well for reducing the non-essential light falling onto the front lens element, especially when a filter is attached. Using a circular polarizer can be a bit tricky the first time, but the bayonet mount helps quite a bit as you can remove the hood, rotate the polarizer for maximum saturation, then mount the hood again without having lost the optimum position with the polarizer. It should be noted that I've never experienced vignetting with this hood or with the original HB-37 hood when used with the 55-200mm Nikkor zoom, but it's not advised to use it with shorter focal lengths. The HB-34 hood can be reversed on the zoom lens when you're ready to stow it in your camera bag, but you'll have to run the lens out slightly towards it's telephoto range when you do so, or it won't fit. Have been doing this since the time that I bought it here and have had no problems storing it that way. The [[ASIN:B0009HN588 Nikon HB-34 Lens Hood]] has been a good one for the 55-200mm DX Nikkor lens, and is a far better fit than the HB-34 lens hood. For some the HB-34 hood may have more of a professional cosmetic appeal, but its real benefit is in its functionality. Highly recommended as a replacement. 10/14/2012

First, the hardware is great. It has big touchscreen that's responsive. It has a CD/DVD slot that always available with no drop down faces, or sliding machinery to break. As others have mentioned, it takes a second to start up. If you jump in your car, and quickly start backing out of your driveway, don't expect your reverse camera view to save your kid's bike. This same startup "lag" is more obnoxious with DVDs. It has to startup, enter DVD mode, read the disc, and start back where it was playing. If you turn the car on and off often, or maybe from "run" to "accessory" (getting gas, stopping to park) it may bug you. We just decided to install a "road trip" switch that overrides the ignition, and keeps the head unit turned on full time. If we stop for gas, or have to turn off the car, the movie keeps playing. This is critical for a 4 y/o in the middle of Despicable Me. ipod vs. Android - This head unit plays much nicer with Apple. Your best bet is to use a standard ipod cord. Unless you want video. I did pair the head unit to an ipad with bluetooth. It read the files, but it sticks to your current playlist, with limited folder navigation options (forward and backward?). Visualization - very limited. Sure, you can change the background image, and pick a custom backlight color to match your dash. However, once you do that, the home screen, and the now playing screen kinda suck. I figured there would at least be a EQ or visualizer, or...something. In their effort to make this unit simple to use, they may have made it grandmas-new-buick simple. Parking brake override - you don't need to buy anything. Just attach the "parking brake" wire to the frame of the head unit. Done. This is not a "smart" unit that needs the parking brake to be reset. Remote Included?? The ad says this unit "comes with a steering wheel remote..." NO. INCORRECT. NOT EVEN CLOSE. It has a remote WIRE that can be used to connect FACTORY steering wheel remotes if you buy the connector / black box. No big deal, but it's not true, so don't expect a remote to be in your box. OMFG, my ipod has no sound, is something broken??? NO!!! Many devices require you to set the unit's ipod input to "AV2" rather than ipod. This may be blacked out. If so, turn the unit to standby. Push Menu > Setup > Input > AV-2. Boom, sound. I'm sure there's more... Bottom line, it's worth the price, especially if money is cheap, and you really want a couple of the features. If you're on a budget, maybe hold off on the bluetooth, and get the 370 model...

I have a bit of a headphone/earbud fetish, and these are the new object of my desire. The initial impression was amazing. The box was large and stuffed with goodies, but best of all, the first thing you saw were these gorgeous earbuds when you open the box. They were nicely displayed, and they unpacked in seconds. If you want to rock the default tips, you're set. The included cable is just the right length and of great quality. The fit was amazing even with the default tips (there's a whole array of options included). The somewhat deep fit simply stays in place without undue fatigue or slippage. These are less bulky than the FH7 and more balanced than the UE Triple Fi 10s I used to use. Sound isolation is great. I also use Bose Quiet Comfort 35 II at work, and these really don't lose out at all despite being a passive solution. These add a driver to the Triple Fi and use a different quad setup than the FH7. It's a smashing success. Sound is subjective, and no experience can be all things to all people, but these are perfect for me. Quick, lively, and able to hit all of the notes with finesse. The FH7 will get lower and provide a bit more grunt, but these feel much livelier. I couldn't imagine being happier with a set of earbuds. Great build, wonderful accessories, and divine sound.

The amp sounds great, and there is a noticeable increase in volume, BUT BE ADVISED. I checked the speaker wires coming from the amp with a circuit tester and discovered that the polarity for the wires for the rear speakers coming from the amp were reversed of what the manual says. The manual states that the positive wires for the rear speakers are green and violet while the negative wires for the rear speakers are green with a black stripe and violet with a black stripe. Upon checking with a circuit tester, I discovered that the positive (hot) wires for the rear speakers were green with a black stripe and violet with a black stripe while the negative wires were the green and the violet. I hooked the speakers up in accordance with what the circuit tester showed rather than what the manual stated. Have no had any problems with the amp as a result. Someone at the factory just hooked the wires up inside the amp wrong.

This review is for [[ASIN:B002ZCXK0I Western Digital 2 TB Caviar Green SATA Intellipower 64 MB Cache Bulk/OEM Desktop Hard Drive WD20EARS]]. I've been looking for the largest and the least expensive external hard drive on the market without compromising quality. I seem to use about 1.5 TB -2 TB about every 2-3 months. The last 2 TB drive I purchased from Amazon few months ago was [[ASIN:B002QEBMCI Western Digital WD Elements 2 TB USB 2.0 Desktop External Hard Drive WDBAAU0020HBK-NESN]]. Suddenly I got a better idea when I saw those hard drive docking stations. Instead of keep buying External hard drives and USB hubs - I already have 9 External Drives hooked up to my iMac 27"-Why don't I buy those "less expensive internal drives" and just plug them into the docking station as needed to access the content. I read a lot about these "GREEN" drives and how cool and quiet they run. I am happy to confirm that it's all true! I received the new drive in 2 days as promised with Amazon prime. It was packaged in a brown box with no cable or anything else. I guess that what you call "Bulk" or bare drive. If you're simply replacing your existing drive on a fairly new computer this should be fairly easy and you won't need anything else. For me, I am using it mainly with a Mac. With an External docking station (I bought the [[ASIN:B002MUYOLW Thermaltake BlacX Duet eSATA USB Dual Hard Drives Docking Station ST0014U]] and this allows me to simply insert the WD Caviar Green and use it like an external drive. I shoot a lot of raw photography and HD video and I don't need to have all the contents available on the computer all the time. So, the 2 TB high capacity and the ability to plug and unplug these drive into the docking stations seem like the perfect solution for me or anyone who create a lot of digital content in a short period of time. Here's a summary of my experience with these Drives: Pros: 1-Very Quiet - This is an important feature for me considering that some previous WD drives that I bought actually create a loud hum on my desk and I have to turn them off when not in use to avoid hearing the noise continuously. 2-Fast - For an energy efficient drive, It is faster than I expected. I purchased my Catalyst iPhone X Waterproof case at the same time I upgraded to an iPhone X in April 2018. I tested the case and made sure that was fully waterproof before putting my phone inside. I even went as far as weighting the Catalyst case down at the bottom of my pool -about 10 feet- for about a half hour and had no water intrusion. After putting my phone in, I checked the case again, although this time less than 3 feet – just in case. Again, I saw no water or indication that water had entered the Catalyst case. While I don't plan to use my phone for diving or underwater photography other than an occasional photo of the kids, I like the depth rating just in case I drop my phone in water deeper than a meter. The design of the case is very slim considering the impact and waterproof ratings. The rubber or silicone outer case is comfortable in my hand and very slip resistant. I haven't dropped my phone yet, but feel comfortable that it would be okay if I did. My only complaints with the design are: First, that the front facing camera seems a little hazy through the plastic front screen protector. I saw this comment on a couple of other reviews but it doesn't affect my facial recognition. However, it does seem to make FaceTime video or front facing photos of little fuzzy - as if the camera lens is dirty. Since the camera is basically where your face touches the phone while you hold it to your head, I originally thought that it was just oil from my skin. After cleaning it well with a microfiber lens cloth, I believe it is the case. I think a future design with glass or a better (more clear) plastic would fix the issue. Sound quality is good both holding to your head or on speakerphone. I have had a couple of people tell me that they had trouble hearing me but that has been intermittent so I'm not sure if it's the phone, the case, or the connection. My 2nd issue with the design is really a simple fix for the next model. There is a small rubber/silicone lip in the area that allows you to access the charging port. I never noticed any issue until I realized that this small area of the case had developed a tiny tear. Once the tear started, it is impossible to keep it from continuing to tear further without gluing; but I think that may prohibit removing my phone from the case. Since I have only had my Catalyst case for 4 months, I contacted Catalyst customer service directly and received a response almost immediately on the same day. Because I had purchased my case from Catalyst (through Amazon) and not from a 3rd-party seller, Catalyst was fantastic about reviewing my issue as a warranty replacement/repair. I am very happy with their prompt response and fantastic customer service and am an even happier Catalyst customer considering that I had a small issue but they treated me like a valued customer. I have had all of the other big name-brand impact and waterproof/water-resistant cases for my iPhone and Apple products and think that the Catalyst Waterproof iPhone X case is my favorite. Other than the two small issues, I couldn't be happier. (All of my other cases have had issues that could be better...). One issue for all cases of this quality is price - none are cheap! But you get what you pay for and Catalyst went above and beyond with their customer service. THANKS! K

With mixed reviews of this new, improved, and twice as expensive Logitech wireless trackball, I had my reservations about spending $100 on a "new" product. The new Logitech MX ERGO wireless trackball has several useful updates beyond "old green ball" (the M570). The unit feels more substantial with seemingly less lightweight plastic. All in all, I am very happy with the new Logitech MX ERGO wireless trackball. When my other M570s eventually die, I will have no problem replacing each one with the new, improved model.

Great little GPS unit. If you are looking for something that is multi-discipline (hiking, running, biking, etc.) this is a great GPS. Used on my bike now for several rides with the cadence and speed sensor from Garmin and it has worked like a charm syncing and displaying info from those units. The ability to make different profiles for different activities is awesome, so when I ride I can see the important things like speed, cadence, grade, etc., or running i can see more time based info like pace, or hiking more navigational based things like elevation, bearing, etc. or whatever else you choose. Setting up the data screens is very easy.Screen is small but adequate and very readable in daylight. Battery life has been fantastic and I'm still on the same pair that it came with after several bike rides and multi-day backpacking trips. Touch screen has been fairly responsive, maybe not as perfect as a phone's screen but absolutely usable. The computer side software is pretty good. Installing maps can be a little cumbersome, but once you figure it out it is pretty easy. Tons of free maps available online. Base Camp is nice for planning routes, transferring data and updates, and just general PC to GPS data connection. The GPS also shows up as a mass storage device so you can just transfer .gpx or .fit files directly from the file system if you choose. The Touch 35 also works with the Garmin Connect app for your smartphone, and I have been using the version for Windows Phone Mobile 10 with little problem. You can get Garmin connect to automatically link with Strava too so you can get some extra data on your bike rides and runs. Overall: if you are looking for a GPS that does a single discipline very well with all features suited primarily for that one activity, I think there can be some better options like the Edge series for biking or Forerunner for running, but if you want something that can give you good accurate data doing just about anything, the eTrex Touch 35 is a fantastic option. Highly Recommend!

I'll start this review by saying that I'm _VERY_ new to digital photography, and picked up a Canon Rebel T3 in a very aggressively-priced box set about a month ago. The kit came with the standard 15-50mm non-IS lens, and that only left me happy for about two weeks. I picked this up from a used seller to save a couple bucks, but at the price point, it's already pretty unbeatable for features in a low-end lens. While the stock kit lens uses an old (and loud, and slow) gear-driven auto-focus system, this one uses a super-fast, whisper-quiet STM system. Though not as cool as the USM setup on Canon's higher-end units, this is a clear upgrade from what you got in your camera's box. The zoom is smooth, and so far the pictures have been pretty terrific. I've used it more as a macro lens thus far than as a telephoto, but my images have improved significantly as I've been able to achieve a finer focus for day-to-day shooting. One thing I have to mention, and it may just be caused by the old-style body of my T3, but there are some distances where it doesn't seem to be able to figure out what I want it to autofocus on. Since the distances always seem to be about the same, given a specific zoom ratio, and the lens tries to focus one direction, then the other, finally giving up, I am currently attributing this to the lens. It has not been a big issue thus far, as I just adjust the focal length and it will sync in. The non-IS lens produced constantly shaking video when hand-held, and I can't wait to see how this stabilized lens will do when I get it out into the real world. If you're looking for a cheap second lens as a newbie (just like I was), you will be very happy with this one. I can't give it five stars because of the focusing issue, but given the price of the device I feel very satisfied with the purchase.

I was really excited about this gimbal. I love that it folds up, and it is lighter than previous models. But I ran into a few issues, some of which might have solutions, so don't. One of the most annoying things about this gimbal is that when you turn it on, it always starts in portrait orientation. There is no way to change that. Unless you are shooting for Instagram only, nobody wants to shoot in portrait. Further, who buys a gimbal just to shoot in portrait? So, I was forced to double tap the M button every single time I turned on the gimbal. I contacted DJI, and they stated there is no way to change that behavior. Second, I have no idea why, but I recorded video for an entire day using the DJI Mimo app and this gimbal. When I got home, all of the footage was missing audio. Sure, I had some B roll stuff, but that is useless outside the context of the story. It was all useless. That's completely unacceptable. Lastly, the face tracking feature is something I thought would be very handy. And it is handy. Some of the time. But maybe half the time I was using it, the app simply lost track of the subject. That resulted in continuously restarting the scene. The weird thing is that it would track great for a half minute or so before it "forgot" what it was shooting. The entire time, I was in the same general area facing the camera. All of these things added up to the most frustrating experience I've had with a gimbal. I really like every other DJI product I've owned (Osmo Mobile 1, Osmo Action, Osmo Pocket). You are better off skipping this one. The most useful features simply don't work as advertised.

This thing is JUNK. I'm moving from cable (Frontier FIOS) to broadcast/streaming. Bought a Fire 4K (bedroom), Fire Cube 4K (den), and Fire Recast (den.) They all work (although the Recast was finicky.) The Recast requires an external TV antenna. I own 2; the cheaper (unamplified) indoor antenna actually works better than the amplified omnidirectional outdoor one - after a scan, I get 64 channels with about 59 usable. Can't get ABC - problem because of sports, particularly football. Bought this antenna because of the ratings, vendor claims, and aesthetics. I placed it on top of a 6-ft book case. After 3 attempts at a scan, I could - at most - only get 8 channels to show in Recast. Only 5 were usable. I returned it - a real waste of money. Buy a Winegard, Channel Master, etc. Get a name brand - remember, you get what you pay for! P.S. The maximum range of reception for a top quality antenna is really only 50 miles, and more likely less than 40. If you expect to pull in signals from 60+ miles, expect to spend $$$ on a great outdoor antenna and a very, VERY tall mast. It's because of the curvature of the earth - proof the 'flat earthers' are wrong...
