LATEST UPDATE: After messing with these for about 6 months, I've decided these are really not worth the effort. Makerfocus has been very good so far and working with me (sent a new set of chips during the messing around below) and all 4 have failed over the past 6months. Every time it's for a bad checksum error. The below info for flashing them is still valuable, but I don't recommend them at all due to the problems with bad memory chips. Ok, many reviews say contrasting things about these devices and there is a LOT of misinformation. First of all I LOVE THESE DEVICES!!! Now for the removal of misinformation (I have the older style chips): UPDATE: I think I know where the main problem others have had lies!!! The below was working great then everything just stopped working. Programmed and nothing. It didn't seem like anything was different. After 2 DAYS of messing around I found the problem. You MUST HAVE 10k resisters on RST, GPIO 0 and GPIO 2 to 3.3v. Once I discovered this from hours of Googling IT WAS LIKE MAGIC. Everything became stable, every flash worked. Flash mode QIO worked! (one suggestion was to use DOUT). I had problems with OTA and I realized that the default in Arduino for Flash Size is 512. I changed to 1M (No SPIFFS) and OTA update started working! ADDITIONAL INFO: I found that the blue led flickers if you don't add a 10k pullup resistor to the TX line if you aren't using it. #1 - These devices ARE flashable. I have no idea what people mean when they say that. #2 - You CAN use Arduino IDE and upload sketches. You just need a USB serial cable (see below for more info) and use generic esp8266 with the port of the usbserial and 115200 baud. Ok, now for the truth behind the misinformation: #1 - These devices can be troublesome to work with, but I don't think it's the device itself as the fact you have to communicate through serial. I spent an entire day getting to the bottom of the issues. - You must use a USB to Serial adapter to talk to them. - You have to tie the chip enable pin high and the GPIO0 to ground to program. You also have to remember to pull the ground after you flash to run the firmware. - The TX and RX pins are supposed to be 3.3v. I tried several cheap ways of converting TTL (5v) to 3.3v because I didn't want to be a $4 converter for a $4 chip and didn't have great results. I finally (and fearfully) just connected TX <-> RX and RX <-> TX and the chip came alive. I have flashed many times with no problems. The concern is damaging the RX on the ESP8266 but even on the official Arduino.cc website had a Fritz with the TX, RX hooked directly so I'm still not sure about it, but I'm taking my chances and once I'm done playing I'll not be flashing them that much anyway. If you have a USB to Serial that does 3.3v as well as TTL then no worries. UPDATE: I believe my USB to Serial is 3.3v AND 5v logic compatible so be careful on the above. - My USB to serial kept having problems and I'd have to unplug and replug every time I did a new flash. That might be the USB to serial. - I discovered using the esptool with --port /dev/cu.usbserial (I'm on a mac) --baud 115200 flash_id would tell me when I was talking ok to the chip. - The baud rate is 115200. - I used the python esptool and it worked fine. I even installed TASMOTA and ESP-LINK which are cool firmwares to play with. - Plan on powering the chip on and off with everything you do. Hard reset seems to leave the chip in lala as does adding and remove the gpio0 ground. I LOVE, LOVE, LOVE these devices now that I know how to work with them.

I purchased this stand for my PC at home, but have the WALI dual vertical stand at work. Both units are easy to assemble, sturdy, and included all the tools and hardware that I needed. The WALI unit I have at work has a slightly large base for more stability, although the VIVO is plenty stable. On the WALI, the top tube threads directly into the bottom tube, unlike the VIVO that uses a coupler between the top and bottom tubes. This allows more flexibility in monitor height on the WALI unit because you could position the bottom monitor directly over the joint if you wanted to. On the VIVO unit, you can't do that, it has to mount either above or below the coupler. The WALI unit has brackets that are round contoured to clamp around the pipe, versus the square brackets with plastic filler pieces on the VIVO unit. in my opinion, the WALI brackets just look better and are easier to adjust. The WALI unit also includes two bases, the V-shaped base that sits on top of the desk, and a grommet base that can bolt to a hole through the desktop and route the cables underneath. You would have to buy a separate stand from VIVO to do that. Overall, I am still happy with with the VIVO unit and will keep it. But if I ever need to buy another stand, the WALI unit is a better buy for the same price.

I use this case for a workstation with 9 storage drives, and I encountered many thoughtful features when building in this case: 1) Drive cages - The drive cages in the front of the case are oriented such that drives end up with their connectors accessible from the right side of the case. This leaves an pleasantly short and direct path to route SATA power cables from the PSU and SATA data cables from the motherboard. Furthermore, you don't have to worry about anything in the main compartment of the case (the section that houses the motherboard, which is behind the drive cages) interfering with swapping hard drives in and out). 2) Drive trays - It is very simple to install 3.5in drives into the toolless drive trays. The flexible trays have plastic pins on the inner sides that plug into the screw holes of the drive to secure it in place. 2.5in drives sit flush once they are screwed in from holes in the bottom of the tray. The tray's holes are the perfect distance apart, so it is easy to align the drive's screw holes with the tray's holes. 3) Motherboard tray 2.5in mounts - Two removeable foam-padded 2.5in drive trays slide onto rubber mounts behind the motherboard tray for easy installation. 4) Rear-inserted power supply - Being able to remove and insert the power supply from the rear of the case allowed me to simply slide the power supply out to connect an additional power cable when I added more drives to the case. 5) Power supply shroud cable cutouts - This case has many cutouts for cable management. In particular, it has cutouts near the bottom of the motherboard tray and cutouts on the top of the PSU shroud that make it easy to route cables to the graphics card and lower motherboard connectors. 6) Fans and fan controller - The case conveniently comes with all of its fan slots fully populated, so I do not have to buy and install additional fans. Furthermore, they come connected to a series of molex connectors that lead to a fanspeed controller at the front of the case. All you have to do to power the fans is connect the case's assembly of fan wires to two molex connectors from your PSU. 7) Socketed side panels - The side panels are attached to the case by hooking the front ends into slots near the front of the case and popping the rear ends into ball sockets (I don't know the name for such a fastener) near the back of the case. This makes it easy to properly align the side panels with the case when installing them, and it also leaves the side panels flush with the case even without fastening the thumb screws in the rear of the case. 8) Included port plugs - The case comes with silicone (or rubber?) plugs for the front IO ports located on top of the case. Dust and particles really do accumulate in unprotected upward-facing ports over time, so I find it convenient that I do not have to purchase a separate set of plugs. 9) Reversible front hinge - You can change the direction the front panel swings open for your convenience. 10) Noise dampening - both side panels and the front panel are padded with foam. Furthermore, the top of the case has no fan mounts or other openings and is completely lined with foam. This makes my computer very quiet, even when FFmpeg has each of its 22 hyperthreaded cores are under full load. 11) Manufacturing tolerance - I am convinced that this case is manufactured under very tight manufacturing tolerance. When I slotted my graphics card into my motherboard, the holes in my card's PCIe bracket aligned perfectly with the PCIe mounting holes in the back of the case. Furthermore, the mounting holes in all the drive trays are just the right size for screws to fit snugly, making it easy to align a drive's mounting holes with the tray. My list of appreciations is already long, but there are so many more minor things I like about this case, like the visual aesthetics, bottom clearance, and fine fan filters. I haven't discovered anything I don't like about this case, but I hope my review helps you know what kind of building experience to expect from this case. I look forward to this case becoming popular and influencing the design of quiet home workstation cases in the future.

[[ASIN:B00R45XH86 Sony XBR43X830C 43-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV (2015 Model)]][[ASIN:B00LBENEFM Sony BDPS7200 Dual Core 3D 4K Upscaling Blu-ray Player with Wi-Fi (2014 Model)]] Let me start first with stating I am a loyal Sony customer - since I got my first job, I have been always pairing Sony AV receiver, Sony TV and Sony DVD player, later Blu-ray DVD player. At least for my second and third gen Entertainment center, I even Amazon purchasing record to prove this (first set was bought retail).So, actually I am biased, and it is quite possible that rating should be lower. Maybe I learn something along the way, and increase the rating later. In any case, my expectations for Sony entertainment equipment is 5-stars, nothing less. So, I got Sony STRDN860 AV receiver (did not need 1060 multi-room functionality), Sony XBR43x830c and Sony BDPS7200 blu-ray player (links are included). Here are pros and cons for the receiver: PROS: 1) Sound is pretty good. Everything with sound works well, therefore 3 stars baseline. 2) It passes HDMI video, it can upscale to 4K and that works well CONS: 1) Remote is horrible. It is only good for the AV receiver itself, but unlike previous remotes, it cannot pick up any functionalities for TV or Sony Blu-ray DVD player! 2) Perhaps HDMI-CEC can help - one would think. I am not sure if the standard is at fault (why would I care, I am a consumer&customer!), but it is not possible to press power button on the AV receiver remote and have TV power on together with the receiver! Also, it is not possible to power TV off when receiver is powered down. Same for blu-ray DVD player! Curiosuly enough, it is possible to turn on TV with the TV remote, and have receiver turn on, however this is useless, as one needs receiver remote much more. I have played with HDMI-CEC settings on all applainces - the possibilities are very limited (i.e. on the receiver CEC-HDMI can be only on or off). I have also went to HDMI organization web pages, and read about CEC / HDMI standard. For some reason, TV is behaving as a "master" device, and it is not possible to make receiver a master device. Very annoying. 3) So, I am stuck with 3 remotes (except that blu-ray remote actually has a little button for TV, so it is possible to reduce this to two). This is very annoying, and there is no good information on how can Sony customer (a loyal one) get a one remote for 3 devices that are all from year 2015? Even more, why isn't this included? My previous AV receiver remote was able to control TV, receiver and blu-ray! Why would I have to research universal remotes - I have chosen all latest equipment, high-to-highest end, from Sony! 4) uPnP/DLNA functionality - there are bugs. AV receiver is supposed to be able to play music from the uPnP enabled servers. However, this ONLY works if one browses through default uPnP folders (i.e. "Music"). If one is browsing through actual file/folder structure on the NAS server, the files cannot be played. embarassing, ESPECIALLY since Blu-ray DVD player does not have this problem. You may say - OK - it works on the Blu-ray player. However, I always test all the features, and expect them to work. It is not as if consumers are paying with fake dollars. 5) Functionality lag - for some reason I do not understand as an engineer - when I turn on receiver, it takes about 4-5 seconds for the receiver to negotiate with the TV and pass the HDMI signal. I understand that there is HDMI security protocols to be negotiated, but really, on consumer expense??? I think I am coming to CES 2016 again this year - I am going to visit Sony booth and talk more about my experience...

I bought this in order to install an IDE hard drive full of data into a newer SATA computer. The adapter was pretty simple to install on the hard drive, and to connect to the SATA outlets. There was one hitch, however, which is that both the adapter and the hard drive need power, and this adapter does not come with the cables necessary to connect to the computer's power supply. There was no mention of this in the instructions that came with the adapter or in the description online. Bummer. It took a little head-scratching to figure out what I needed. Fortunately, the necessary product is available online (through Amazon in fact) for only $5. Manhattan, 6" SATA 15-Pin Male to Dual 4-Pin Molex Female Y Splitter, 308977 Manhattan, 6" Sold by: WOWparts With that additional adapter there was still ONE MORE THING TO DO. This also was not covered in the instructions with the ULTRA adapter. I needed to set a jumper on the IDE hard drive to "master." The drive had been the "slave" in the prior installation, and it is still a secondary drive in the new system. Still, to work correctly, it needs that jumper. Fortunately I had little jumper pins that I could use. The instructions for setting the jumper were printed on the hard drive (in my case, I needed to jump the pair of pins farthest away from the power supply plug. When everything was set up correctly, the little indicator light on the adapter winks on and off as the hard drive is being accessed. Very nice. With all this done, voila! Success--at least so far for the first couple of weeks. :) So it seems like a good product. It works well, doesn't require that you sacrifice a card slot for an IDE controller card. It's too bad the instructions are not more complete. Better instructions would have saved me about a week of being annoyed--and I would have purchased the power adapter at the same time as the drive adapter.

Really solid- more like 4.5 stars. I have been looking for alternatives to chest strap based heart rate monitors for years. Several months ago I bought and returned the LG electronics HRM, which is also based on the same in-ear monitoring technology, because of glitchy software, inconsistent heart rate measurement, and extremely poor GPS. When this Jabra product came on the market I pre-ordered it hoping it would function as promised and after a week with the headset and 20(+/-) miles running I can recommend this with just a few caveats. Below is an outline of the pros and cons. Pros: No chest strap. In ear heart rate monitoring was the primary factor driving my interest in this product. Set-up was a breeze. I had the headset working within 5 minutes of taking it out of the box (note: it is paired to the new iPhone 6 with IOS8). One slight twist in the pairing process: iPhone's bluetooth will show 2 Jabra signals, and one must pair both of these. Evidently there are separate signals for both the HRM and the music and other functions or something. Very accurate heart rate measurement. Having run with chest straps I generally know where my heart rate should be through various levels of exertion and the Jabra earbuds seemed highly accurate and reflected changes quite quickly. This time out I didn't compare it head to head with a chest strap the way I did with the LG product a couple months ago but I nonetheless felt confident about the readings. Very few dropped readings. Over the course of 4 runs with a total distance of around 20 miles, only once did the earbuds loose my heart rate, and only briefly. In ear, these earbuds are very secure (but not so comfortable- see below). Intuitive music and phone controls. the App: A pleasant surprise to be had on the included Jabra app. Having used Nike+ and RunKeeper for years, I had fully expected to be disappointed by the included Jabra app, but to my surprise it is better than good. Everything is laid out logically including the standard metrics like distance, pace, hear rate and elevation and cadence and even the compatibility with indoors treadmill training. This app could be one's full time fitness app its that good! A couple minor gripes with the app: ok, this is nit picky, but the heart rate interval levels can't be adjusted based on one's own criteria. It appears Jabra uses industry standard levels but some of us are weird enough to do regular heart rate testing in order to fine tune levels which can't be inputted into the app. Secondly when setting up heart rate intervals, the app won't allow for setting a short interval and simply repeating it. Again, minor. So much else goes right with app that I hesitate to dock it. Battery life: 4 runs, 20 miles without a recharge. battery use indicator seems accurate. Better than expected. Ok, so why isn't this 5 stars? well, here are the cons: It isn't that comfortable. There is no way someone would want to make this their day-to-day bluetooth music/phone headset because the unit must really sit deeply in the ear canal and it creates an odd "tunnel" effect where ambient noise is muffled. Further, to stay in place the ear buds put pressure on my ear in ways that aren't so comfortable. My day-to-day headset is the Bose ie2. One can forget they are wearing the Bose and practically fall asleep with them on, where as the Jabra always feel present. The music quality is so so. The headset is 100 times better than standard iPhone earbuds but I would compare the sound quality to the mid-priced Skull Candy line (decent but lack deep base). People definitely won't want these for the sound quality, but my expectations were low on this front. Like life, keeping expectations low can lead to the occasional positive surprise. The bottom line: I would recommend as a great alternative to traditional chest strap based heart rate monitors. The reason I give 4 (really 4.5 stars) and not 5 is mild discomfort with the earbuds and average sound quality for the money.

This is a nice looking product at a good price. The description says that it works on Microsoft Windows, Mac OSX, and Linux. I tested it under Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04 on three computers. It either was not recognized as a USB device or it disconnected when I tried to start video capture. Only twice on one of the computers did it actually start capturing video and then only when I connected it to a USB 2.0 port rather than the USB 3.0 port to which one is supposed to connect it. The most likely problem is that the USB implementation in the firmware is buggy. If they tested it only with Microsoft Windows, they may have removed only enough bugs to make the Windows USB driver happy. If so, then other drivers which issued slightly different (but perfectly valid) commands fail because they hit bugs which have not been fixed. I really wanted to like this device and get it to work. The two times it worked it produced good quality video. But I can't see spending an hour or two fiddling every time I want to start video capture. The seller really needs to get a better firmware on this thing and set up a web site for firmware updates. Until they do and until they actually test it on all the operating systems they claim to support, I do not suggest buying it.

I purchased and quickly returned this laptop. Please understand I'm a longtime Toshiba owner, having purchased my first Satellite T1850 in 1992, and 3 other Toshiba models between then and now. I was looking for a high powered desktop replacement. This might meet that standard if loosely defined, but there are so many substandard head-scratching details about this machine that I decided it wasn't worth the money paid. I was also concerned that the build quality would not hold up over time. The item description I read on Amazon originally made no mention that the screen is not a touchscreen. I don't require one, but it was a surprise to find it missing in a $1000 computer. As others have noted, Toshiba has bogged this machine down with egregious junkware. It is so bad that for this reason alone, I will probably not consider purchasing another Toshiba computer in the future. At the very least, Toshiba should provide an easy means for owners to remove all unnecessary programs from the computer. Because Toshiba fails to describe which are essential and which are not, you don't really know what to remove. This adware slows the computer down a great deal I suspect, adding to the slow boot and wake times mentioned elsewhere. The computer has an odd mixture of high- and lower-end components. A slower version of a fast (i7) processor, a bit less RAM than you might expect in a computer at this price point (12 vs 16GB); no 5Ghz Wifi; a 5400 vs 7200 rpm hard drive; no SSD storage or cache. None of these things are easily upgradable, meaning you're stuck with this machine in its current configuration. Battery life is poor. I have owned other notebooks and ultrabooks in the past few years that got 8+ hours of use per charge. The current $228 HP cheapie I'm typing on now gets 7 or so hours. But the couple times I had the Satellite on battery power, it lasted only about 4 hours. Finally, the build quality of this computer is the worst of any notebook I have owned. The chassis bends in your hand slightly if you pick up the computer with the screen open. The battery on the back hinge wiggles when you handle it. All this movement means that something will eventually crack or fail in some manner down the road. Laptops get handled a lot usually. I cannot imagine this model holding up in a bookbag or soft-side briefcase full of other stuff. And, the edges of the laptop are cheap, cheap, cheap. Plastic, and not even buffed smooth. The left edge scratched my finger, and all the edges are sharp and uncomfortable to lay your arms or wrists upon, causing red marks and pain after only a few minutes. You could use a nylon scrubbie on your $1000 computer to smooth the edges out, but who does that? For only a couple hundred more $$, you can have a lot more computer: You get SSD cache or HD, 16 GB RAM, better quality cases, longer battery life, maybe even a 4K resolution screen. This machine has a DVD burner, but these days for most of us, it's needed so infrequently that it's more convenient to have a separate burner (available from Amazon.com for less than $20). I admit being quite confused and frustrated at purchasing a computer these days. It doesn't seem as straightforward as it used to be. Processor types aren't as easily understood, and clear, concise info on things such as screen resolutions and other details is frequently misleading or lacking when shopping both online and in-store. Just look at the name of this model: "Satellite S55-C5262." These long numbers mean that these "models" are cobbled together from whatever parts are available on the market at a given price point. The notion of design for the end user is forgotten. I recommend doing heavy research if making a purchase of a mid- to high-end computer.

This is a really nice TV, especially since right now the price is just over $1k. The picture is near perfect. That's all that needs to be said there. Set-up is fast, the TV is not that heavy, and the swivel stand is great. Menus are fairly straight forward, although in my opinion there are too many menu options - great if you are a perfectionist and really know what you are doing when it comes to fine-tuning the color. I think there a good amount of inputs. Nintendo Wii through component cables looks fine. Cons: Would be nice if there was a digital coax audio out - there is only an optical out, and it doesn't pump out 5.1 sound (i.e., you go from 7.1 or 5.1 to 2.1 if you run the sound through your TV to your audio system). Standard definition (non-HD) programming looks fairly bad. I bought a cable line power booster, set the HD cable box to output only 480i when on standard channels, set the sharpness to 0, and turned digital noise reduction off. This helped quite a bit, but it still is noticeably bad. There is a lot of pixelation, some channels are passable some are awful. That is my biggest complaint for this TV. Final note - viewing distance means a lot. I sit about 6-7 feet away, and can see pixelation. If I step back another 2 feet, the image is much better. So, if you sit 6 feet away, I would go for the 37" instead.

Despite all the negative remarks about this camera (not professional, oil and dust a on the light sensor, Nikon has dropped the ball), I bought this camera anyway. Why? 1. I have known many "professional" photographers over the last 45 years and many of them showed me photographs that were incredible AND, they were taken with simple point and shoot cameras. Thus, demonstrating it isn't always the camera, but what you can do with it that makes the difference. This camera is sharp, clear, and takes great photographs. As I progress through the learning curve of operating this camera to it's maximum ability, I have seen a big difference in my photos. I am enjoying the challenges this camera poses, and doing my best to get the full potential from myself. 2. I don't care about the oil and dust issues. Things get dirty. I have to wash my car, too. But, cleaning a light sensor is a lot easier and faster than washing the car. So, I bought a sensor cleaning kit. I haven't noticed any problems with the camera, yet. But, I'm ready to take care of business if the sensor shows signs of needing a good cleaning. I find the capability of this camera to be right up there with the best of all 35mm DSLRs. The focus is super fast, I have fast memory cards in place so, the images are stored at lightening speed, and vibrant color are outstanding. As I hinted at earlier, there is a bit of a learning curve that goes with owning one. Don't let this deter you from considering this camera. Buy a good book that is dedicated to this camera and you will be good to go in no time. And, of course, practice with actual photo taking. If you are in no hurry the slope of the learning curve just flattens out. Who would I recommend this camera to? Everyone!! Everyone who has a real interest in using DSLR, that is. Owning and using this camera has been a lot of fun. I always thought I took pretty good photographs (don't we all?) but, this camera has reminded me that I can be much better than I though I was. In oder to get the most from this camera I have to get the most from myself. I love the challenge. March 13, 2013 I wanted to add a few bits of information that I didn't include before. I have a limited budget so, I had to research exactly which lenses I would need the most for now. I finally decided to purchase two zoom lenses. 1. Wide angle zoom: AF-S Nikkor 16-35mm 1:4G ED VR I really love this lens. It has been called the sharpest lens, and in my opinion it is really sharp. Noted to have several types of distortion but, this distortion can be controlled with good handling and software processing. 2. Tele zoom: AF-S Nikkor 28-300mm 1:3.5 - 5.6 ED VR This lenses was highly recommended and I felt this would fit my budget. The lens is sharp, little to no distortion, and has been a very reliable lens. It is heavy but manageable. I can hand hold it alright but, I'm not as rock steady as I was years ago. On a tripod, this lens yields very clear images. The light sensor kit I bought (in case I need it) is made by Eclipse. I purchased a kit that contained a few #3 brushes, a couple o pads, and a small bottle of liquid sensor cleaner. The kit comes in a handy nylon, zippered bag which is easily carried in my backpack. As for the D600, I am going out photographing birds and flowers at this time, and I really like the results I'm getting. The detail of the flowers is incredible. The birds are harder to get but, the camera has come through with its great response. The 24mp sensor makes the difference when photographing the birds. I can't always get close enough to fill the view finder, but I can crop these photos and still have clear and crisp image. ***UPDATE 3/31/2013 I did notice something on my image sensor the other day. So, I took the camera outside and took pictures of a clear sky under the same conditions recommended to search for oil splotches and dust. And, I found them showing up. No problem. I had already purchased the Eclipse cleaning system and, spent 10 minutes cleaning the sensor in the recommended fashion. After testing I found my cleaning had removed the splotches and dust. Thus, I am still happy with my D600 purchase, it still takes incredible pictures, and I have no fear of oil or dust while I travel. Cleaning is simple and quick. I know Nikon should have resolved this issue long ago. However, they didn't! But, I don't really care. I believe we all should learn to do basic things to take care of minor problems like this ourselves. I won't lose a moment of picture taking, nor will I have to search for someone to clean my camera for me. And, I'm glad I made this purchase.

I'm a Canon user and shoot on the excellent but very heavy Canon 5D mii with big glass. After reading the reviews here I thought the Fujifilm X-T1, at half the weight and half the size, would be the perfect camera to carry with me on a trip to Tokyo. I grew up using Fujifilm products and was excited to give this camera a try! It is very portable and light, and slipped into my briefcase with no trouble. The image quality was fine but not outstanding: shooting with the 35mm f/1.4, photos are often fairly sharp and colors are reasonable. With respect to exposure quality, the only real trouble I had was shooting in low light. I am a food photographer by training and was consistently flummoxed in restaurants by the white balance, whether I shot in automatic or manual modes. I like to focus very carefully using the viewfinder on my Canon, which offers a 5x and a 10x optical zoom for fine-tuning focus. The Fujifilm only had one option, which was maybe 5x at best and insufficient for really razor-sharp focus. A more personal note that's odd but perhaps of use to some potential buyers: as someone with long, slender fingers I found the major buttons just a bit too close, too small and too low on the body to operate. When trying to tap one I would often hit another. Likewise, the narrower diameter of the lenses gives less room for fine adjustments when focusing and zooming. I found myself reaching only for my iPhone. It was so much easier to grab and to use and the difference in image quality was not enough to warrant fishing out, booting up and wrestling with the X-T1. After my trip I tried selling it on Craigslist to no avail. Ended up selling this camera back to Adorama at a whopping 65% loss. The next time I want to travel light, I'll slip my phone in my pocket. For excellent photos, I'm sticking with my Canon.

I can pass along that on Dell's 8700 XPS tower PC from 2014, this enclosure does not have the semaphore timeout issue some external enclosures/burners have. This is no guarantee you won't experience it on your PC. It's an issue involving a conflict between the SATA to USB bridge controller in the enclosure and your SATA/USB controller on the motherboard in your PC. The only way, generally, to resolve it is to replace your motherboard or the enclosure. Since it's cheaper and easier to replace the entire PC versus just the motherboard, it's not as easy or cheap, though, as just replacing the enclosure. Unfortunately, the only way you'll know for sure if your PC doesn't have this issue is to try this enclosure. EDIT: 2018-06-10 - Changed my review. It seemed to work fine, but after more thorough testing with different drives, media, and on different PC's, it has one fatal flaw that I cannot recommend this unit for. It randomly drops communication with the device. The drive lights will still be flashing indicating it's doing something, but the actual write/verify rate in ImgBurn will be 0.0x. Cancelling the operation in ImgBurn leaves ImgBurn in an infinite loop until you power off the enclosure. This can, and has, caused me to waste a writable disc because communication was dropped with the device. This has happened on a Dell XPS 8700 and 8930, with an LG and a Pioneer burner, on DVD+RW and BD-R. So, the problem is the enclosure. This unit seemed to work well for a while and then started doing this. I don't know if this means the device always did this and I just happened to get lucky in that it didn't do it before. Or if this unit is faulty or simply this device is not very good quality. Either way, I can't recommend this product anymore after my experiences. I'm going to try the OWC Mercury Pro next. EDIT 2018-09-07 The 0.0x communication drop issue is the fault of the enclosure. I just now tried it with 2 different Pioneer BD-R 2209 drives and the same thing happened. Immediately on the first attempt to write a BD-R in the newer 2209, this enclosure dropped communication with the drive. So, it appears to be a decent product at first, but thorough examination and testing reveals it's pretty much poor construction. And right after the above update, I may need to rethink this thing entirely. It could be the result of a bad USB cable. I was getting these communication dropout issues and finally got a semaphore timeout error. None had ever manifested itself before with this enclosure. So, I tried swapping in an OWC enclosure, but Windows did not recognize the device. So, I put in a different USB cable on a different USB port and Windows recognized the device. I put this new cable in the old port where the old USB cable was and Windows recognized the device. So, it wasn't the port and it was the cable. A bad USB cable could, theoretically, as far as I understand, cause communication dropout issues with a USB device. So, I may need to examine this more closely and re-evalutate my review. EDIT 2018-09-12: After more thorough testing with this enclosure, a 2nd, and a different USB cable, I determined the problem was NOT a bad USB cable. The problems with this enclosure are either the enclosure itself, the Pioneer 2209 used along with it, or the latest 1.51 firmware for the 2209. I doubt it's the firmware because the 2nd enclosure seems to handle the 2209 fine, leading me to blame this Vantec enclosure more.

I've been closely tracking this item ever since it was announced back at CES earlier in the year and I was fortunate enough to get one of the first shipments that came out. Here's a brief look at some of my pros and cons with the item. Previously I had bought a Philips Model: DCP850/37 DVD/iPod portable player and was very happy with it. Albeit the screen was only 7 inch, but it was relatively portable and fairly light and easy to use. Unfortunately it did not support the later generation 160 GB iPod classic, where I store most of my videos (I could only use my 60 GB ipod for the Philips) so I decided to upgrade to the iLuv i1166. My initial impressions are the following: The look of the iLuv 1166 is superior of the Philips. It has a nice, sleek black frame with a very nice large 9" widescreen panel on the face of the gadget. Unlike the Philips, which has the screen on the inside of the clamshell design, the iLuv's screen is on the outside, with a little stand to support it on the other side. When you open the iLuv clamshell, that is where the DVD drive and the iPod cradle is. Like most other ipod/dvd hybrids, there are different adapters you can use for your nano, ipod, itouch or iphone. One definite plus of this item is that it supports many of the current gen ipods, which was lacking in the previous model (i1155) and the other philips players. So if you're like me and you have the 160 GB classic, this is the player for you. I was only able to test the gadget with my ipod and a test DVD. It is very easy to operate (either via remote control or the menu buttons next to the screen) and the menu options are quite simple. The menus are easy to read and it's quite nice to have a battery indicator which gives you a heads up that you're going to run of of juice soon. The picture quality was quite nice. I ran a DVD video and also ran movies, music videos and tv shows from my ipod. The image is crisp and the 9" large screen is definitely a plus. I have yet to test the SD inputs though. But from my experience there is definitely a noticeable improvement in terms of image quality from my philips player. There are also 2 headphone jacks that allows multiple people to watch the same video. The battery took me approximately 3 hours to charge in the first run and I ran 2 movies to drain it out as a test. After running it for about 3 hours (before falling asleep) I noticed it was working fine, so that's definitely good (vs a roughly 2.5 hour play time with my philips). I did have a few gripes that kept me from giving this 5 stars though. First, there is an annoying lack of a chapter search for the ipod movies. So if you're watching a 2 hour movie and want to fast forward, it ain't gonna happen. That's sort of annoying if you want to try and speed through 2 movies on a long trip. EDIT: (I switched up a few movies to test and found that the chapter search worked on one or two of the 6 I tried out. Not sure why this happened and seemed like the rewind function worked more than the fast forward. Not sure if this is another glitch like what I saw with the ipod videos, which I addressed below) I also noticed a strange glitch in which for some reason the menu on the ipod wasn't able to read my music videos in sequential order. Say if you had multiple videos of Michael Jackson in 1 category, for some reason I couldn't access MJ's videos in the order I have it on my ipod. Rather, every time I open up one category, every single video in my ipod appears on the list regardless of category. Again, annoying but doesn't impact the performance of the item. Also there is no video out option (one plus of my philips was that it had a video out that i could connect to my tv). Not a deal breaker for me, but it is a bit irritating for those of you who want to use the DVD option for say, an extended stay at a hotel or at your other home and don't have a DVD there. If you're a gadget freak like me, I think you'll enjoy the item. I also recommend purchasing a cover for this item (I ordered mine from the iLuv/jwin site) as the screen seems very easy to scratch given its location on the outside of the clamshell design. In summary: Pros: 1. Cool, sleek design 2. Works with most ipods/iphones including current gen 3. Decent battery life 4. Huge screen, great image quality 5. Great variety of inputs (dvd, ipod, sd, usb, multiple headphones) 6. Can play in car with car adapter 7. Easy to use menu, remote control Cons: 1. No video out option 2. No chapter search for ipod movies/tv shows 3. Kind of heavy 4. Screen location makes it potentially easy to scratch/damage 5. Gitchy menu at times (at least for me) 6. Speakers not exactly useful (tinny and not really good for playback) But net net, it's a pretty neat item on the go EDIT: So on extended use during a recent vacation ... Simplisafe system purchased by a first time home owner who has never owned a security system Simplisafe has a lot going for it. It's cheap, easy to set up, and functional. I was looking at home security through Ackerman and ADT. I figured, based off the terms listed in fine print on their websites, that I wasn't going to spend less than $1300 for a system for the first year of ownership. ADT had free equipment with a high monthly rate and Ackerman a low monthly rate with expensive equipment up front. Simplisafe cost $15 a month plus whatever you decide to spend on equipment. The Amazon package is cheap but not as inexpensive as selecting the parts on simplisafe's own website through their custom package option (promo code helps too). I could have gone without one of the door sensors included. I saw this after I already ordered through Amazon but decided not to cancel my order because of Amazons easy return option. Still you will save thousands by comparison to other companies with simplisafe. Set up was fairly easy. Placing all the sensors was super quick. It really made me question why someone would ever be paid to do it. The only snag was that my wireless base station cell service did not activate automatically. This is where it went from 5 to 4 stars for my review. The set up for the monitoring service is not really explained well in the instructions. This was a major oversight in my opinion given that their website's forum makes it sound like many people have had the same set up issue. However, I Just called simplisafe and they fixed it in a few minutes. Like many reviewers I agree that the system looks a bit dated or "fisher price." Who cares. It's a security system, not a cool toy. Fisher Price makes very durable products anyway. So far the system has not had a single mishap. I've tested it several times and it always goes off both in and out of test mode. It works. Done. If want to wait around all day for a stranger to come to your house to install something a child could do (though not advised), pay $900 plus for equipment and $30-$50 a month for monitoring via cellular service, then go with a big name security system. But if you do that after reading the reviews here, then you are simplistupid.

I’ve been a huge fan of Garmin for many years. First Garmin was the Forerunner 245 several years ago. In between tried the competition (Withings, Polar) but wasn’t satisfied as they were either lacking in terms of complete overall package or the ecosystem wasn’t as well rounded. Started to get back in more active lifestyle and the integration of Garmin connect with more 3rd party apps (Strava, Zwift), I started to look to return to Garmin. Went with the Venu 2 Plus. Gorgeous screen, good enough battery life, smaller size. Thought I would use the built in speaker more but didn’t. Realized that it didn’t have some of the activities that I wanted, in particular trail running. The 955 dropped and I saw it had more activities, it had more metrics like training readiness, and it had maps. Thought briefly about the Fenix 7 series or the Epix, but didn’t like the weight or the cost. Kept on going back to the 955’s total package of weight, features, and cost. Very happy that I did. Compared to my Venu 2 Plus, it gives me way more data than before. Paired with my HRM Pro the distance tracked is way more accurate. I do a light morning walk/jog on the treadmill in the morning. When I walked with the Venu, it would undercount my distance by 40%. I would have to ensure my arms moved rapidly and over exaggerated for it to count anyway near accurate. When I ran it would overcount my distance by 2x. With the 955 it’s dialed in within the .01 km each time. I love the navigation and mapping. Downloaded a dozen or so local courses and their maps from All trails and each time it’s accurate and redirects me if I’m off. The one thing is that it seems to be overly sensitive to how off track you are, a few steps off and it’ll redirect you. Not a huge deal since I’d rather it keep me on track than let me drift off course. I went for the non-Solar version since I do most of my training in the morning indoors or at night. My outdoor activities are limited to the weekends so I don’t get 3+ hours in the sun to take advantage of the solar charging. I’m getting 9-11 days of charge using for 1.5 hours on average activities a day. Quick to recharge, when it’s low it’ll recharge 50-60% while I’m showering and getting ready after a workout. Great job Garmin!

I did plenty of research for the best value for the money. I had an old Yamaha Avr that was 17 years old so I really wanted the latest technology. This Denon was a 2017 model at an excellent price for a 7.2 Atmos HDR, 4k system which I just bought 3 weeks ago Jan 2019. I have really enjoyed the system. I also bought on Amazon an awesome budget speaker system called Energy 5.1 classic take home it's a theater in a box system. Great reviews online (also reviews on Amazon ) and it sounds awesome! Much better than my old Bose 5.1 system costing 3 times more 17 years ago. This receiver pretty much has all the latest technology like 4k HDR video and a 2.2 HDMI connection for the latest 4k blu ray Dvd. It also has an ARC HDMI connection for the later model TVs but not the latest eARC connection. It's a 7.2 channel system so I can play music, wired as 2 channels in another room of my house, while having a 5.2 surround sound in my main room or I decided to do a seven speaker single subwoofer set up now 7.1. Since this system does the Atmos speaker setup I will add two ceiling speakers for the Atmos 3D surround sound experience if I can figure out a way of not upsetting my wife with holes in my ceiling. There is the Atmos speakers that can go on the floor but I want the best audio experience in the ceiling. The Atmos 3D speaker set up can only be done on a 7.1 or 5.1.2 or higher channel system which this is a 7.2. And can be set up as 5.1.2 or 5.2.2 set up. Which brings me to a set up the speakers using Audyssey. Audyssey is a feature you must use for any setup. Its actually required and you have to connect the receiver to a TV to set up the speakers. It walks you through the entire speakers set up, TV, DVD blue ray player set up etc. The manual is at Denon.com. I am not an audiophile and the online menu speaks to someone who is at least a beginning audiophile. I had to learn a bit of the audiophile language to make sure I set the 5.2 speaker systems set up. I didn't mind learning more and had time to learn more about this system if I wanted to understand all aspects of what the manual was talking about. A layman could set this up without knowing much of the language but you'd definitely wonder what some of the on screen options are during the on screen set up process. Here is why I see people opting for a sound bar set up to a TV directly and not wanting to deal with this more complicated set up process. I did have a sound bar which was fine but I was ready for the next step up and this was a great option with plenty of upgrade options as I learned more or had more money to spend on an awesome system. This is definitely a step up from a beginner surround sound set up. Its definitely upgrade proof. With software updates in the future by Denon you will have a great option here for growth down the road. This has Heos Denons wireless sound systems for whole home speaker systems. This is via wifi for other rooms of my house which also does the online music streaming while I watch streaming TV in another room with a 7.1 surround sound at the same time if I wanted too. It does work fine but requires the Heos application from the play store which is free. I dont have the latest 4k Blue Ray, HDR player yet for the ultimate experience in audio or 4k video yet but it does allow streaming via another source (cable box in my case) of Netflix, Amazon Prime with HDR movies and tv series with excellent sound and pictures. I am using it with a new 4k Tcl 55 inch 6 series TV HDR, with ACR which I also highly recommed for a great value also on Amazon. Now the set up took awhile (an hour or two). I have been having some wifi issues with Xfinity (They finally fixed the issues after 5 times and lots of credits) but after a few tries and a reboot of the router/modem I was able to get the wifi connected. It did need a software update during the set up but I'm not sure if it was required. I wanted every latest technology feature available so I made sure it was connected via wifi for automatic software updates and streaming music. There is a feature called the Multi Eq which is supposed to give me greater control of everything in the Denon but it's from a 3rd party. It's also used by all the Marantz receivers too so you would think it's a great prouduct. It's also a free app but here I had wifi issues trying to synchronize the receiver with the app on my phone. I only got it to pair up once out of a dozen trys and then it still didn't work also it's a 20 dollar one time download. I read the reviews on that product and it had nothing but wifi issues also so I gave up for now. No other product offerings for this feature, which is also recommended in the Denon manual and on screen set up menus. I did however find a fix by connecting the Denon directly to the router modem via an ethernet RJ45 cable but it's not close by so I haven't tried yet since my wife would not appreciate a cable running through my hallway and going through the attic at this time. There is an issue with the ARC connection between the TV and the Receiver. For some reason the arc audio return connection is not playing back smart TV channels. Luckily for me I connected the receiver directly to my cable connection thus running all audio through its HDMI cable connection which they have a way to connect directly to both Netflix and Amazon Prime and audio works fantastic. It doesn't work If I pick Netflix on the TV and try to run the sound back through the ARC. I've read this isn't a Denon or even a TV problem but a widespread issue with all ARCs. Therefore the new eARC is the solution but this receiver only has the ARC on this model. One problem I have been seeing is some distortion on the TV screen when I first connect to Netflix. Each time I work on recalibrating the speakers via the microphone provided by Denon it pauses Netflix and causes errors from Netflix. Also one time I had the receiver on for about 48 hours straight it also started to give me distortion on screen on a normal cable channel. I turned it off and let the receiver cool down for several hours and it cleared up. So there is definitely an issue there when connecting to Netflix and when its overheated I'm assuming. Sorry for the long review. I'd wished for a long review while shopping all the different products. So far I love this system! Looks and sounds awesome. With the 4 year Amazon warranty I'm comfortable with this purchase should there be any issues. Go get this one if you want a system for many years ahead of awesome TV and surround sound.

I purchased this for myself over an iPad. There were a number of things I needed to consider since I am on the road a lot as well as an independent film maker. I need the ability to showcase my work in a board room or in a one on one meeting. The Archos provides an HDMI output and film or movie file formats of .wmv, .avi, .mpeg, .mov.. basically all the necessary formats that I personally require. The built quality is fairly nice and I've seen many folks complain about it being a finger print magnet. Last year, a nearby lightning strike passed through my DirecTv antenna via the coax cable to the DTV receiver and then to my Panasonic Viera TV through the HDMI port. The DTV receiver was fine but it burnt out all HDMI ports on my TV, which is a LOT more sensitive. My bad. I had not grounded the dish or the coax cable. I fixed the TV. I also ordered this device and installed it on a grounding block inline with my DTV coax. While I witnessed the first lightning strike, I did not see this most recent one. But the results were the same in that it burnt out the HDMI ports. As before, the RCA connections were not affected and I can still use the TV with a HDMI to RCA connector. I have since fixed the TV again but noticed that the DTV receiver started having problems getting a signal from the antenna until it finally stopped working altogether. After some troubleshooting, I decided to bypass this device and, sure enough, DTV started working again. So, the good news is that it shunted itself out and worked properly. The bad news is that it failed at it's primary purpose to protect my equipment. The reason I gave it 2 stars instead of 1 star is because I don't know if it prevented any further damage. I have since removed this device. The antenna is still grounded outside with a grounding block, but I have also connected the incoming coax through the UPS coax filter in hopes this will prevent future problems. Now, to wait for the next lightning storm...

Okay, so, let's start off by saying that I'm by no means a super audiophile. But I do love music, tv, movies, and pretty much anything that audio is a huge part of. For several years, I've used various headphones and earbuds. My favorite (and most used) pair of headphones was a nice Skullcandy I got for Christmas. They had good sound and were fairly comfortable. Very durable, too. I'm not a huge fan of earbuds, but I use them at school and when I'm working, or just out of the house in general. I find them uncomfortable in general, though. Recently, though, my Skullcandy headphones broke; I ordered a pair of Bluedioes. They arrived, and I noticed that they were pretty cheaply made. They also malfunctioned about twenty minutes of use; I returned them and just used my Skullcandy ones again.. But that was pretty annoying, since only one side really worked. So, I looked through Amazon again and found this pair. They weren't pricey, and they had great reviews. I compared them with a couple others and then decided to order. And here is what I found: The Pros: These have been great headphones overall. The sound is great; very clear and vivid, which seems to be what most people look for in new headphones. Plus, they're very, very comfortable. I used to get headaches after using my Skullcandies for too long, but these have been no problem. The ears are very padded, and so is the top. Sound and comfort, they most important parts, are totally here. They look great, too. A lot of products exaggerate their product images online; these headphones honestly look just as good, if not better. Very stylish. And, oh yeah, Bluetooth! This is my second time using bluetooth headphones, and they're pretty good. Very convenient. They have a long range; I can walk around most places in my house (and into the yard, even) when they're connected to my laptop. The battery seems to last well, too. Also, they're good at limiting outside noise, which is to be expected. I also haven't experienced any noise leak from these, which used to be a slight problem with my other headphones and earbuds. So, yea, these are a fantastic pair, especially for the price. The Cons: Unfortunately, there are some issues. These aren't the most durable or sturdy headphones. They certainly are much better than the Bluedios I had, but they don't compare to my tank-like Skullcandies. But this shouldn't be a problem for the vast majority of people; heavy headphones aren't great about 90% of the time. Aside from that, they can be a bit spotty if you're a distance away from the source of the music, but this largely depends on your connection and where you are. So, aside from those two cons (which are mostly just opinion based anyways), these don't seem to have many flaws at all. So, in conclusion, these are fantastic headphones. The price ($34.99 when I bought them) is totally fine, and the quality of the music/sound, comfort, and style are wonderful. The Bluetooth capability to convenient to say the least, and the build/weight is also totally fine for domestic use. Thanks for reading, and I hope you strongly consider these headphones! I'm glad that I did.

Overall not a bad watch and should be considered based on your needs. For me I was just looking for a second less expensive option to my main watch (from a competitor). My activities include running, trail running, biking, mtn biking, hiking, and kayaking and do not have too much need for smart watch capabilities (other than message notifications). I got the non-baro version to keep cost down. Here are my pros and cons: Pros - So far so good with GPS accuracy - Good/believable HR data for running (need to crank down wrist strap though) - I find the HR sensor not too protruding or noticeable - Like seeing the projected impact on battery life when changing settings (so far it seems accurate) - Find user interface intuitive - Good size screen (for sub $300 watch) - Like the ability to configure sports mode in Suunto App. - Nice simple way to create routes with waypoints and send to watch. - Native stryd power fields integration - Build quality is good - Training metrics not forced on you or in your way when you don't want them. - Does not artificially limit the activity list for a less expensive model (i.e. hiking activity included). Cons (Bigger cons towards top) - A little large/heavy but okay (not sure I will be wearing this daily once long sleeves returns) - No offline music for road runs (I have a non-phone workaround but would prefer it to be on watch). - Smartphone notifications can't be muted without muting all alerts (prefer a more passive/on demand approach to checking messages and have no desired to be buzzed every message) - Footpod pace changes data seems slightly delayed - No real Map - Wish some settings would persist for an activity (like backlight and wrist HR). - Elevation data just okay for a non-baro. Unfortunately Strava is using this data by default (it's not supposed to for non-baro device) - Elevation profiles for longer activities (10+ miles) are too condensed (need ability to zoom on current climb) - Inconsistent Backlight activation (no dedicated button) Ultimately the cons will probably keep this from being my main watch, especially once I return to the office (no music, no notification only silencing, and too big). I will use it on the weekends and for rougher on watch activities (i.e. I'm okay scratching a sub-$300 watch but not a $600 one) . I give it 4 stars relative to my secondary use case (would be 3 stars if trying to use as main watch). Also I recommend getting the ventilated silicone strap accessory from Suunto (24MM Athletic 1) to go with it.

I like this UtechSmart hub, where the hub is free from the computer, simply tethered via the USB-C port. I recommend the UtechSmart Hub. I'm really happy with it and using it fully now. I have had my Kindle Oasis for 18 months now. Compared to several other Kindle e-readers I've owned over the years, this one is just so inferior. I've had many of the same problems you will read about in other negative reviews. I'm just frustrated in trying to read anything. Before you ask, my past experiences with Kindle readers before have been great, so I didn't read the reviews. My fault. Here are some of the issues I have had: --It is true that this latest model has the absolute worst battery device of any e-reader I have ever used (and I've owned a good number). Hard to believe, but you cannot turn this thing off. --The text does not fade upon turning the page, so you can vaguely see the previous page's print. --Screen lighting will adjust to darker and/or warmer on it's own, without my having manually adjusted it. --Due to it's thin nature, it is hard to hold. If you're using the swipe feature, this creates an issue with unintentionally moving the pages back and forth. It's slightly easier to hold with a cover on it, although it adds some weight. (Not great for those with arthritis issues. This might not be an issue for everyone.) --For no apparent reason, the screen turns off constantly and it has been getting worse. I have to press the wake-up button to wake the screen up, then swipe up to get back to the page. Most of the time, I have to repeat that 3-4 times, only for the same thing to happen 5 minutes later --I've also had a lot of issues with the screen freezing, and difficulty with restarting it. Sometimes it takes 2-3 tries to pull up the "restart" prompt. --I don't know what they did to screw up the storage & organization system of my Library. I can't find my previous collections by author (after downloading my library from my last Kindle). When I start a new collection, it says I already have one, but it won't add to it. I feel like my filing cabinet blew up and I don't know how to clean it all up. Kindle user guide (which is also not great) is not a help in this area. Amazon support on this device is sorely lacking. They are well aware of these issues, but seem to be silent on any type of fix. I see no responses on their part as far as acknowledging the problems or fixes that may be coming. I won't buy another one of these until they can offer a high quality product. Not sure what my solution will be, but will be doing my research!

I've had my collection of Roku devices over the years. When the Roku Streaming Stick 4K+ was announced this year, I immediately ordered one. It has been a pleasure to use. It is only marginally better than the former Roku Streaming Stick+, but the improvements are worthwhile. PROS: - FAST! I find that although the former Roku Streaming Stick+ was fast loading apps, this one is noticeably faster. Apps load up almost instantaneously. - Convenient user-programmable shortcut keys. I primarily watch YouTube on the Roku and set user key 1 to launch YouTube. One press of a button and YouTube is up (even in the TV is off)! - Volume controls and TV power. I have eliminated all of the other remote controls -- I just need the Roku remote. - Voice control. Although I don't use it that much, it's nice to have. If I'm searching for something (especially if it's a long title), it's nice to just press the microphone button and speak what I want. - Great WiFi reception. I don't run into any connectivity issues or spooling issues. It is connected to my 5 GHz WiFi network and works great. - Built-in headphone jack on the remote. I haven't used it yet, but had an occasional need for it in the past and didn't have it then. I'll be ready now! - Rechargeable remote. This is VERY nice! It used to be a bit annoying when the batteries would die on the old remote. Now, if the battery runs low, I just plug it in overnight and it's good-to-go the next morning. CONS: - Can be difficult to plug into the back of some TVs. The stick is a bit longer than the prior stick. It is slightly longer than the recess on the back of my TV. I had to wedge it into the HDMI port. Alternatively, you can buy a short HDMI extension cable, but it would be nicer if Roku didn't have this challenge. Google Chromecast has a short pigtail HDMI cable that makes it easier to plug into tight spaces. Overall, I am very pleased with it. To make it better, I bought a silicone case for it. This makes it so the Roku doesn't slip out of your hands, fall off the armrest, etc. I also added a short lanyard to the fabric tab at the bottom, making it even easier to grab and use. Link to silicone case I bought for the remote: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09BZCTFMR?psc=1&ref=ppx_yo2_dt_b_product_details

I have owned every Kindle since the Kindle 1, except the Kindle with buttons introduced this year -- and I have spent a lot of time playing with that one. There is no sense of stretching to use my finger to turn pages, instead I find I am holding it much more naturally than I have any of the button Kindles. The screen is comparable to the Kindle 3, and that screen is pretty great. The page turns are very fast and I have seen none of the ghosting issues that some reviewers have reported for the Kindle lite. This really does disappear in your hands. The price is amazing, although I may end up choking down the extra $40 to get rid of the ads. Even though they are only on the sleep screen and a small banner on the home screen (kindle contents) I find them deeply annoying. I will wait until the cases come through to see if the adds are less noticible that way, since I'd rather spend the money on books. I wish Amazon would offer heavy kindle users a free ad turn off button, say after the first 20 books. This machine looks nice, feels light, is far more comfortable to hold than the kindle lite, which I find is actually too small. There was nearly no learning curve. Four years ago when customers complained that a kindle needed to be $100 to be affordable, I laughed. I never believed that would happen. Well, here we are at $99 with the nicest Kindle yet. Since I am very attached to my extensive Kindle library, I never considered the nook. I can only tell you that this machine is a dream to use for reading and buying books. Now at 51, I fall asleep with my kindle nightly. On screen typing is a snap. My Kindle keyboard is still in great shape and has been inherited by my 9 year old son. They are right and I agree this is a loss. I also find pdf's much easier to read in landscape - Kindle3 has landscape mode. Cheers and happy reading to all of my fellow Kindleaholics

this is not the type of product one can review quickly. it takes many hours simply to familiarize yourself with the basic operation of the X-50. and it takes time to rip music to the hard drive: for me, close to a month to rip over 1,500 CDs. thankfully the ripping phase is largely complete. i would recommend the X-50 only to someone who is at least a little technically oriented ... or not afraid to spend some time learning functions which are not totally familiar or intuitive. some finesse is required to migrate over (via FileZilla in my case) a small but not insignificant number of tracks which were identified as "bad" during the ripping process. for the past two weeks i've now simply used the X-50 to play the ripped music through my main sound system. the sound is excellent. i chose not to compress any of the music from my CDs ... so most of my loaded music is in WAV format. i have also loaded music on to the X-50 which I had on my PC in MP3 and other formats. in general, the WAV format music sounds much better, but most of the compressed music sounds better than simply "listenable." the interface used to locate and play music is good, but not great. there are some shortcomings in the database. for example, after many operations (including viewing the songs within any particular album), the album list returns to the very top or bottom. you can imagine that when you have nearly 2,000 albums it takes quite a bit of paging up or down to get back the point where you were previously in your album list. there are other means of getting back approximately to your previously place in the list, but those other methods are not totally satisfactory. it's very possible that there are other means of navigating the interface which i have not yet discovered. The product manual is decent but it's fairly obvious that it was not written by someone with a mastery of the english language. that's okay with me. (please, no comments about my english) as far as i can tell, the manual does a decent job of outlining all of the X-50's functions. when I contacted the main office of the manufacturer in south korea via email, i received a reply within 24 hours. i definitely appreciated that. the X-50 is fairly pricey, but i have not seen any other product which offers the same or even similar features. with the X-50 i can listen to any of nearly 2,000 CDs i own with excellent sound quality while banishing all of those 2,000 physical CDs and cases to my garage. that in and of itself is quite valuable. it's relatively easy to locate any particular CD (assuming that you know what you're looking for). my review of this product is still a work in progress ... i'll try to add more later. BTW, if it's not clear from this somewhat rambling review, i am definitely enjoying this product and am glad that i purchased it! it may not be perfect, but it's quite impressive!

iPad mini 4 revised review I own a number of JETech accessories. This product was purchased as my primary protection for my iPad Mini 4. The finish is durable, does not capture fingerprints too easily, marks do wipe off easily with a rag. The fold over cover makes for a good and sturdy stand. The back cover provides plenty of protection, while leaving the speakers and external ports open. Former users of Apple’s authentic Smart Cover should be forewarned that with the extra back/body protection, you do have a little more to hold on to back there. This extra protection does not add much in the form of weight, nor will you likely notice it when you’re holding the portrait in tablet mode, while sitting. You will be aware of it when lying in bed and holding the iPad Mini in widescreen mode. ***Updated*** I am revising this review and removing one star. For all intents and purposes I still think it is a great case, but caution should be taken with those who want protection, but in day to day use you may notice a few design flaws. Of note the Smart Cover inspired front to the JETech case is good while covering the screen but sadly feels a bit bunched when placed in the “open” position, behind the iPad Mini 4. Since most of us will be using our phones in the open position this is of some note. People who like to be as close to their iPad as possible, or who are familiar with the the Apple Smart Cover will notice this the most. With the Apple Smart Cover rests behind the ipad you barely notice it. With the JETech model you picky users will feel it like a bulge behind the case. It is distracting enough to notice, and as cases with cover flaps goes, it is more noticeable than most. The second touch point that that will bother picky users is that the JETech case for iPad Mini 4 is not flush around the body of the iPad Mini 4. This is noticeable most when holding the iPad Mini 4 in portrait mode, or really, just holding it period. To make matters worse the non flush gripping of the case is further made noticeable by it having chamfered edges. it is neither pleasing to look at and it will likely be impossible for many not to notice. All that said I still give the JETech iPad Mini 4 case a 4 out of five. I like the company products and think it is worth considering. Some people could care less and will grip their iPad Mini 4 in a way that makes that less bothersome, it just so happens that both of these design shortcomings are a deal breaker for me and likely will be for people who want the Smart Cover look, but want back cover protection, but will be discerning about the small details. Had I known it would be this uncomfortable I would have looked for a back case that just accommodated the Smart Cover, as an alternative. Outside of that I really enjoy the case, like the weight, it is easy to clean, and for the most part it looks like a very quality accessory for my iPad Mini 4.

This device is basically a laptop power brick, coupled with an oddly designed cigarette-car charger adapter that you use to connect into the power brick and then your plug from your clippers. I assume this is done to keep the cost cheap for the manufacturer or to make it a proprietary connection, so that you can't just buy another power brick as a substitute. However, this is a basic powerbrick that would normally allow you to use a laptop anywhere in the world due to its converter nature. It converts both voltage and frequency, so all you really need is a plug adapter for whatever country wall outlet requires. I just came back from Japan, and took both this and my regular converter from brookstone. I ordered it specifically because it was advertised as specific to clippers. It worked well, but so did the converter, as long as you remember to switch to the proper frequency. The problem I have is the price. This should be priced atleast at half of what it currently sells for, considering what you get. The instructions look like they are printed off of a dot-matrix printer, and at this price, they could have atleast included a carry case or bag, or even a cord strap that most power bricks have to keep the cord wrapped up when not in use, as this whole set up has a lot of wires Although I read the reviews that all gave 5 stars, I was a litlte skeptical as they all seemed a little too similar for my comfort. While I can say that it works, there are other alternatives that work as well that are far cheaper. And considering that they are targeting the military person living overseas, I would hope that a price reduction would happen in the near future.

My wife got me a Fitbit Charge 2 for Christmas last year. I wasn't that excited about it. Over time, I have learned to love its low profile and simplicity. But...I hate the fact that it's a Charge 2. I've had several people ask if I got a new watch and when I explain that no, it's still my dorky Charge 2, they want to know more about the band. Moreover, it protects the outside edge of the screen. I have been through several screen protectors with my watch because they corners will nip something, but I am no longer concerned with that. The band is easy to snap on and the material feels comfortable on the wrist. There are two things to consider: 1) The band sometimes catches and comes unlatched. The reason this isn't a star dropper for me is that it really is no big deal because it doesn't cause the watch to fall off. Even though it comes loose, the initial feed through is big enough to catch it and then you just re-tighten. This is not an everyday thing either. Maybe has happened once or twice in the few weeks I've had it. 2) You have to remove the charge 2 from the band to recharge it. This actually is a bit of a plus for me because when I used to charge it, I would tend to forget it on the charger the next day. Now, I pop the charge 2 out, put it on the charger, and leave the band with my wallet for the morning (like that little string you tie around your finger). On the other hand, If you're super lazy, this might not be the band you. Overall, great product. Very happy with my purchase and highly recommend it.

We bought this product last May when I decided that we should cut cable. It drastically reduced our bill, but I would rather pay for a polished experience than pay for this. To put it simply, this device is unreliable. Here's what you'll have to deal with: Every other day, the recast freezes up. Recordings cannot be deleted and channels cannot be watched. To fix this, you'll have to unplug the device and plug it back in again many times a week to maintain normal function. Speaking of recordings, they must be deleted one-by-one, and it will take 10 seconds per recording if you're lucky. This is a massive pain in the ass if someone else set up recordings for something and didn't delete anything. If the dvr is full, don't expect the thing to handle it well. The device will stop working completely and you'll have to do a complete factory reset, which takes 30 minutes and deletes ALL of your recordings and ALL of your scheduled recordings. Want to use recast to stream outside the home? FORGET IT. Streaming with the fire TV app LOCALLY only works 1/4 of the time, and streaming outside the home has NEVER worked for me. This is just false advertising. Do not expect this feature to improve, because it hasn't for us. Want to watch a recording? First you must click the episode, then click play, then click to acknowledge poor video quality. The recast reports poor picture quality for ALL recordings, no matter what. Every. Single. Time. Even if the quality is PRISTINE (and it's perfectly fine MOST of the time), it will still make you click a window to acknowledge that this product is TRASH and you should have returned the week after you bought it. If you are a techy like me and you live by yourself, then you'll be able to put up with this product. But if you expect RELIABILITY, and you have other people (spouce, children) in your household that RELY on OTA TV, then I STRONGLY do not recommend this. All of your housemates will blame you for this product's unreliability on a DAILY basis and you will regret cancelling cable.

First off, the camera work for what I need. They could, however, work better. Lot better. My biggest gripe is the connectivity issue between the app and the camera. Everything else is minor by comparison. This is an OEM camera, which means someone else makes the camera and Zumimall puts their label on it. There are many brands with the same guts and have the same issues. Cons: * extended live viewing drains the battery fast * motion detection seems delayed (read about it below) * captures AFTER motion is detected * max 30 seconds of video capture * no PC monitoring software, must use app or no access to camera. * uses broadcast packets to find camera (unreliable) instead of the last known IP. * Must have a very strong wifi signal to connect reliably (89% wifi signal is apparently not enough) * 2.4Ghz only. Crowded spectrum, lots of interference from neighbors wifi. * Captured videos live on the camera; cant transfer them without removing the SD card from the camera. Pros: * wireless, no holes to drill through outside wall * decent picture quality (HD) * 3 days @ 14hrs a day of direct sunlight charged camera to full * night vision works well * videos live on the camera's SD card so they're always recorded (good thing given the connectivity issues) So the cameras (I have 2) work but have caveats that people need to know about. One has 100% wifi signal strength (according to the camera) because I moved the router to the other side of the wall. Second camera is forr feet farther down, wifi an interior wall + outside wall between the camera and wiifi router, reports 89% signal strength, and fails to connect 1 in 3 attempts. The failure to connect drive me nuts more than anything else. I mentioned that the motion capture seems delayed. Due to poor documentation, I can't be sure but it seems like the camera "wakes up" and takes a picture to compare to the last time it woke up. Motion sensitivity determines how much of the picture needs to be the same before "motion" is detected. Motion in-between wake ups will be missed. This is seen when the camera captures someone in the yard, but missied them walking onto the yard. Like I said, I can't be sure this is how the camera works but sure seems like it. Once motion is detected, camera takes a snapshot and sends it to the app as an alert. At the same time it starts recording, 10, 20, or 30 seconds max. Then goes through another sleep/wake cycle and will alert/record again. I would rather it record continuously until motion stops but that's not how the camera works. The use of only the 2.4Ghz wifi is an issue where I live. It's a crowded frequency here. There have been times where I couldn't access the camera for a few hours. I will get alerts but can't watch the video since it won't connect. The app uses broadcast packets to find the camera instead of the last known IP; it should try the last known IP first before trying broadcast packets. Upgrades I'd like to see: * use last known IP of camera before trying broadcast packets. This would go a long ways to solving the connectivity issues. * above change would allow me to view camera after I VPN from my tablet to my home router * Video and picture download. You can save a recording or snapshot, but only view them on the app. * Document camera API so 3rd party software can access the camera. * Document the camera setttings AND how they change the camera's behavior.
