I also had to reconfigure the microphone settings every time it updated. The microphone would inexplicably switch from the built-in one to the mic input on my soundcard. (My wife has the same camera for her computer and we have both experienced this problem on our desktop, and both of our laptop computers). It would be fine on a video call and then ten minutes later on another call there would be no mic. The first time it happened it took me a day to figure out how to get it working again. It still puzzles me as to why/how it happens. The update software is too obtrusive...it is too persistent in begging to download the latest updates...there is no option to tell it to ask again in a specified amount of time. Maybe some people like this, I don't like to be constantly reminded by pop-ups when I am working on other things. The Logitech software also does not play well with some other software. If you use Mozilla Thunderbird, the Logitech software will prevent Thunderbird from installing it's own updates which puts Thunderbird into an endless loop trying to install it and then saying that it can't install it. So if you use Thunderbird, you will need to remember to manually shut down the Logitech software BEFORE you go to update Thunderbird. In all, the camera works well, but the software and image quality issues drag an otherwise outstanding product down a couple of notches. But like I said before, this is the best there is on the market and I do recommend it to friends with the aforementioned caveats.

CPE210 2.4GHz 300Mbps 9dBi Outdoor CPE - What I bought - 2 ea. After doing a lot of research I strongly believe these CPE210 units are sold under false pretense and false claims. No one.... NO ONE ever gets even close to the advertised speed. FEW people get 100 mbps or more download speed. 300Mbps = BUNK - DO NOT BELIEVE THAT. So here is what I'm doing and what I'm getting. I have a shop building about 120 ft from my house. I have one CPE210 unit shooting through a window and the receiver CPE210 unit inside the shop so the signal is going through a wood and vinyl siding shop wall. I am getting 45 to 50 mbps download speed. I have these configured as access point and client. I tried every other setup, first being bridge mode. No dice. Access point and client was the ONLY mode that transmitted network connectivity to/from the access point and the client units. My intended usage is: In the shop, there are 4 security cameras connected to a NVR connected to a Cisco 24 port POE gigabit switch. Also, a computer and a TV running ROKU. I want to access the cams from the house. I want to access the internet from the shop. I some times want to put on the news and listen as I work using the ROKU. I want all this to work at once, and it does. Goal met these CPE210 units are doing the job at the 45 - 50 mbps I am getting from them. If I had paid a lot for these they would be going back but at the price point, under $100 for 2 of them and them doing the job well, I am grudgingly happy. Still, I did hope/expect close to 100 mbps connection speed. My internet is around 300 mbps download speed and verified all that is working as expected right up to the access point unit at the house. Any computer, wired or wifi on laptop or phone on my house internet system/network gets 300 mbps on speed test. I have done research and tried every possible configuration for the CPE210 2.4 wireless settings. I did get 60 mbps with security disabled but not going to run without security. If I figure out how to get more transfer speed from these I will edit this review and ad those details. I could go though the trouble of mounting both units outside. Might open the window and then take the shop unit and make up a long cable and move it outside and test them. WIFI - NO BUENO ?? One other complaint, read a review stating there would be wifi on the client unit and I could log on to it and use it. NO.... I had to pickup another wifi router [cheap used but really nice on facebook marketplace] and plug that into my switch and set it up as a access point. After that My ROKU was able to work after inputting the needed wifi setup details. Some day I will trench in a 1" plastic pipe from the house to the shop and run 2 cat6 cables inside that for network connectivity. Until then I got two of these CPE210 units and the piddly 50 mbps speeds but I can live with it, for now. 300Mbps??? how are they testing these CPE210 units and getting that speed? 300Mbps = BUNK, do not expect any more then about 50 mbps. If 50 mbps transfer speed will do it for you then buy a set of these if you need them. I had no trouble getting them to work once I decided to use "access point" for the unit at the house and "client" mode for the unit in the shop. I do have a lot of experience [professional level] with network system setup and installation though. I used to own an internet company.

Seagate Wireless Plus I bought this portable hard drive with built-in wifi capability from Amazon after seeing a review of it at CES. I have been searching for exactly that...a portable hard drive that I could connect to via wifi from my iPad, MacBook Pro or my wife's Window's 7 laptop. And for $200 it sounded like money well spent. I've read many reviews on several websites. They range from very happy to very disappointed. Here's my experience so far: I unboxed the drive, read the quick start guide and powered it up. I downloaded the Seagate Media app while I waited a minute for the built-in wifi to come all the way up. I started the app and connected to the drive. I walked through the tutorial and began to set things up. I also read the more detailed manual on the Seagate site. I attempted to upload pictures from my iPad's camera roll to the drive. I had about 243 jpg's ranging from 1.5-2 mb in size. It managed to upload 13 files and failed to upload the other 230. I thought maybe I had attempted too many at a time. So I uploaded one jpg that was 1.5 mb. It still failed. No real reason given other than it said it failed. I opened a case with Seagate to see what was going on. While waiting to hear back from Seagate I moved on to see if I could backup files from my MacBook Pro to the drive. I was able to to backup all of my media files and documents to the drive without any problems. However, when connecting to the drive from my iPad via browser the file listing changed all the time. In the beginning it was complete. But after several minutes I began to notice pictures, songs and entire albums missing when browsing the drive. It gets so bad that after several minutes the drive would eventually say no files found. Clicking refresh didn't clear things up. Now, this is with the drive fully charged and plugged in. I would have to restart the drive to clear it up. But, again after several minutes it would begin losing files until they were no longer seen. I got the message "No content available in this folder". The next task was to get internet connectivity established on the drive so I could continue to stay connected to the internet and drive simultaneously. This proved difficult. I connected to the drive from my iPad via Safari, then clicked on the wifi symbol at the top and clicked on my home wifi network to connect. I entered the key and waited. After a minute or so a popup message said I had been disconnected from the drive. So, I reconnected to the built-in wifi of the drive and tried to connect to my home wifi network again. Same thing happened. I went to the Seagate site and read about other people with similar problems. I didn't see any solutions other than one. And that was to exchange the drive. They got their replacement drive and were able to upload pictures to the drive from their iPad and establish an internet connection from the drive. So, I decided to exchange my drive. I was still unable to upload my pictures to the drive. But, I worked around this by using a third-party free app to transfer the pictures to my MacBook Pro. I was still unable to connect the drive to my home wifi network. I finally determined that I couldn't use WPA2 on my router. I changed it to WPA and was finally able to connect to it from the drive. I searched the Seagate site for information regarding compatibility but didn't see anything. I did see at least one customer review that said it worked with WPA2, but that wasn't my experience. It may be something to do with my DLink router. I'm still having issues with files gradually disappearing over time. It will eventually say "no content available in this folder" when trying to view the drive. So far, after 2 drives this is shaping up to be a $200 boat anchor. I've had nothing but success with Seagate for my other storage solutions. But this is an epic fail so far for me. I will work with customer support to see if we can work this out. I'd really like to use the full capability of this drive. Jeff ########## Update - 2/13/2013 After working with Seagate support I was able to resolve my "missing" files problem. I did the pinhole reset which cleared the wifi setup. It didn't delete any files so all I had to do was setup the wifi again. It also prompted the drive to re-index all the files. This took several hours. When I first moved files to the drive after purchase, the indexing didn't take more than 10 or 15 minutes, so it appears that it never completed, which is what was causing the problems I was seeing. But, since the pinhole reset and complete indexing of files, the drive has performed exactly as expected. Well, almost as expected. As stated by many other reviewers, the battery life falls well short of the 10 hours Seagate advertises. It has been my experience that the charge lasts about 3 hours after a full charge and no video or audio streaming. The drive was powered on and connected to my home wifi network. I was connecting to the drive from my iPad using the Seagate Media App to check the status of the drive. Hopefully there will be a firmware update that will improve the battery usage. Jeff

I bought these as replacement pads for the pancakes that came on my Fostex T50RP MK3 headphones. After some tossing up between the Shure 1540 alcantara pads, and these, I chose these because they're a but cheaper and me personally I am unlikely to notice that much of a difference. It's a tight fit, but you have to have patience and stretch them gently. It will take time to work them on; they won't fit at first. I found a jar that has a mouth basically identical to the Fostex cans, and popped these on for about ten minutes, then worked them gently onto the headphones and they went on much easier. Patience is a virtue stretching these enough to get them on. Once they're on, they stretch out fine and look like they're supposed to be there. *DO NOT cut the earpads to make them fit better - you'll get them on easier, but they're stretch anyway and then be pretty loose for the rest of their life.* Some people note the sound difference between these and the off-going pancake pads - I didn't notice much of a difference. I can see why it may irk some audiophiles, but the difference is negligible. That difference comes in a slightly reduced lower frequencies and slightly increased higher frequencies. Oh, yeah, very comfy to wear for long sessions of being down with my righteous music.

I had been thinking of getting a WiFi mesh system for several hundred dollars. My house is wired for Ethernet, but not everything is plugged in and the router I have has a lot of dead spots around the house. If you have Ethernet around your house or you can run some to another area where the WiFi is weak, this is the solution you want without spending hundreds on a mesh router. The router I have is relatively current, supporting N networks, but not AC. It wasn't old enough to really need replacing. There is no need to download the software from TP-Link unless you want to have more than one of these and manage ALL of them at one time with identical settings. Just log into your router (Google the brand and model to see how to do this) and look for a DHCP client table. Assuming you JUST plugged the TP-Link into your network, it SHOULD be the one with the highest number to the far right of the IP address. It might even be identified in the list by name. Write the IP address down. Also look at the router's settings for the IP range from which DHCP assigns IP addresses from. You'll probably want to assign a static IP address to the TP-Link so you'll not have to figure out the IP address next time. Just pick anything between 0 and 255 for the last number from outside that range that isn't already assigned to something else such as the router or a printer. Leave the first 3 numbers alone. Open a browser and type the TP-Link's IP address you found from the DHCP table into the area you normally type in an web address. The UserID and password are both admin by default. You'll have to change them as soon as you log in. First, navigate to where the time and date settings are. Set your time zone and tell it to sync to the computer's time and save. Set your daylight saving info if you want it to automatically change and save. Get into the IP address setting area, set it to static, and type in whatever static IP address you decided on, assuming you want to. You don't have to. Type in the IP address of your router as the Gateway, and save. Get into the area where you set the SSID. For both the 2.4 and 5 GHz radios, set the SSID, encryption type, and encryption code or password to be the same as your router. Save. Repeat for the other frequency and save again. Reboot the AP and router. Done. Enjoy much better Wifi signal.

Im a research nut when it comes to buying new electronics. Like you, I check reviews, searched for every picture of the set I could find, posted questions about the set on forums and did the same with all 42inch sets under $1500. I made the plunge and purchased this set saving myself $500. It finally arrived, in one piece. First thing I noticed was how beautiful the set looked without it even being on! It's simple, black frame with Blue LED made the set very classy and modern looking. something I would hang on my wall and be proud of. I could not be happier with the design. Once the set warmed to room temp. I turned it on, it has a v-chip inside which among other things goes through a demo of the TV's features and displays this in full 1080p so right off the bat, automatically the TV showed me what it could do. AMAZING!!!! I have never seen a picture so bright and brilliant in color, I couldn't wait to hook it up to a blu-ray dvd player but I have to wait on that. Next thing I did was test the digital tuner. I connected my Coaxial cable right from the wall into the back of the TV. it took a few minutes to find all the channels (auto program). The first channel I selected was a NON HD channel. The picture quality of regular broadcasts on any LCD stink, this particular set handled it VERY well for it's price tag, more so than some bigger name brand $1400 sets i've seen on display at stores. it is more than barable. Next was an HD channel. The picture was amazing. It lit up the entire room. I liked the picture adjustment options it had, some more expensive sets didn't have these features but this set allowed me to tweak away! I was not impressed with the auto color feature. This basically auto-tweaks the picture depending on the channel your on. I turned this off. Some other features this TV has which compete with much more expensive 42inch sets are the two HDMI inputs, an optical audio output, a USB input (put pictures on a USB memory stick and the TV will automatically play a moving slide show of them), 1080p max resolution, and a universal remote which you can program for your surround sound system, DVD/VCR etc. Lets talk about design for a minute. JVC did a good job with this keeping all connections in the back of the TV (instead of the side which some companies do...and I cant understand why if the set may be mounted flat on a wall...it defeats the purpose). There is a channel in the back to route wires so you can mount the TV as flush to the wall as the bracket you buy allows you to. Other TVs have the inputs flush with the back of the tv. this means the tv must sit away from the wall to allow room for the plugs. JVC thought of this and provided a solution. Thumbs up. Overall I need to ask if this TV was $1,099 with free shipping what makes a $1400 TV $1400? An extra HDMI input? the name "Sony"? certainly its not the quality or build. Also this tv is NOT 120hz, but do you really need the TV to up convert your frame rate? and have you seen 120hz in action yet? if not I suggest you go and see a 120hz tv before setting your heart getting a TV that is 120hz capable..I personally disliked the picture on the 120hz tv's i researched, it looked very processed.

Am a ham over 38 years and have used commercial GMRS radios for decades. Been waiting years for someone to come out with a decent handheld repeater-capable GMRS radio at a reasonable price for the radio hobbyist that's FCC certified for GMRS. So I bought this radio for home use as I have a GMRS license and occasionally use a repeater so this radio fits my needs perfectly. It comes with everything you need including battery, charger and cord, strap, belt clip,speaker mic, antenna, and well written manual. It can also be used as a scanner in "VFO" mode but I did not need this function so all my comments are on the GMRS side of the radio. Has 23 GMRS channels, eight of which are for repeater use and you can use CTCSS or DCS tones. Power levels are 2/5 watts. Well constructed, has a nice LCD display which can be user programmed to show upper and lower frequencies (VFO A and VFO B) or channel name and frequency. Using GMRS is a snap, most of the programming for things like inputting CTCSS, hi/low power, squelch level can be done manually and on the fly. Has dual PTT buttons to transmit on VFO A or B. Pressing one of the function buttons instantly allows reception of the FM radio broadcast band. (You can use CHIRP to program frequencies for the scanner function of the radio if you want). I did program in a NOAA weather channel and it came in loud and clear from 30 miles away. Feels good in the hand and all the soft keys, volume knob, antenna and other parts all are good quality. You can attach an external antenna or another antenna if you wish. I give it a "5" rating as it is well deserved. There's nothing not to like about this radio, and I might just buy another one! Kudos to BTECH for an outstanding product. Update: just bought a second one, am so impressed with this radio!

Turns out, it was this new modem all along. Using the same exact cabling into the same network hardware, the old modem will consistently ping sub 20ms. This Netgear modem is all over the shop with some requests even timing out. I posted a comparison of two pings running on each modem. I also attached my network health stats from my network gateway. Luckily the Xfinity app makes it easy to swap out modems so I could run this test. As per usual, Netgear burns me with their consumer grade hardware. I will be running with my 2014 modem until I can get off of cable internet for good. If I could still return this modem I would. I do not recommend it.

Even without a mobile device, the mini is completely functional, and scrolling through and selecting the various functions is easily accomplished. You can send messages without a mobile device, though it will be a bit more cumbersome than using your phone. It's nice that you don't absolutely need a functioning phone though, in case there is a situation where your phone is damaged and you need to communicate or send an SOS. I was surprised how quickly the GPS acquired a fix when first turned on, and how quickly messages were sent and received. I realize that depending on location, topography etc., that messages may not always be quite as quick, but my initial impressions are extremely positive. My wife and I spend a lot of time, mostly fishing, in areas with no cell coverage. I will update this review after some use in the field. We camp in some areas that are steep canyons. I am anxious to see how long it takes for messages to send with a limited view of the sky. For those considering one of these it might be helpful to know how the messaging works. To me, it seems best set up to send a preset message once you are off grid. You can have 3 different messages, each with their own (and different if you choose), contact list. You can send an unlimited amount of preset messages each month as they don't count against your allotted messages. The way my wife and I plan to use the device is to send a preset message that basically says we are off grid, and to reply if something important comes up. All your recipients have to do is reply to your message and you will receive it. If you choose, each message can also contain a link to your location. If a recipient clicks on it they will see precisely where you were when you sent the message. Obviously if they reply, the reply and any messages exchanged will count against your monthly allotment. My initial impression is extremely positive and I am happy to have this device.

I really wanted to like this monitor, but the power adapter business really turns me off to it. I will most likely be returning it since that was never stated in the description and this is not what I wanted to order.

Unfortunately, Google Android TV turned out to be the worst TV operating system I've ever encountered. It's largely because either TCL or Google decided to strip basic features TVs have had since the 90s. So much for a "Smart TV". For example, typically when you connect an external speaker such as a soundbar via an optical cable, you can go into the TVs settings and instruct the TV to stop outputting sound through the TV's built in speakers and only output sound via the optical line. Here, they decided that it would just do both. So if you plan on using a soundbar it will send sound through both the soundbar as well as the built in TV Speakers. It's impossible to disable the built in speakers. After a lot of online research I found two loop holes. (1) simply turn the built in tv all the way down or (2) plug in a headphone cable into the headphone jack to essentially trick the TV. Two problems with these solutions. One, if you just turn down the volume you sometimes suffer the "mute" symbol on the screen. Second, if you want to use the TV remote or a third party remote, or ANY remote, you will often be increasing or decreasing the TV volume instead of the soundbar volume. Oh and for some reason there is not mute button on the remote even though there are 10 other buttons for dedicated services trying to charge you a subscription fee. [Insert confused Jackie Chan meme] This TV is just plain awful. After realizing that this was an inherit design flaw and not just me getting the setup wrong, I placed an order for a refund. I'll never buy a TCL or Android based TV again.

The X-Grip has two knobs on it: a short screw knob on the upper arm to tighten the upper shoe, and a long screw knob underneath the base to secure the camera. The one on the base is supposed to have been drilled with a 1/4" hole in order for you to mount the X-Grip on a tripod. However, their factory drilled the 1/4" tripod hole in the wrong knob: the shoe tightener. Since the screws are of different lengths, they're not interchangeable. It makes the unit far less flexible. Picture this: I'm out in the field, shooting with the X-Grip, with my video monitor, XLR adapter box, and camera mounted to it. I take my freeform action shots. Now I want to change to a tripod shot. If the hole was drilled properly, I could just attach the X-Grip directly to the tripod. Without that 1/4" hole, now I have to detach everything from the X-grip and remount it on the tripod. This is apparently an ongoing issue with this product, as more than one reviewer has mentioned it as far back as September. I hoped they would have fixed their stock. Obviously, it still has not been corrected. Yes, I can return it. But if I replace it with another one, how do I know if THAT one won't have the same issue? All I want is that one part, properly manufactured. I emailed Opteka several times in November, asking if they could just send me that single knob. I think it's ridiculous to have to spend all this money and effort on postage, packaging, and handling to exchange the unit, when all they would need to do is mail a $1 part with $1 of postage. I received no response. I finally posted it on their Facebook page. I received a response from an M. Coleman. I emailed him that day, on Nov. 25, 2011. It's now mid-December, and I have received neither a part nor a reply. So - that's two stars off for a defective product. Minus another two starts for horrible customer service. And I'm just going to return the unit and get my money back. Thanks for nothing, Opteka.

After trying out 2 other cases and looking at a few dozen others, I finally decided on the iSkin aura2 case for my new iPad. The pictures looked really good (I have to have functionality and pretty) and the reviews certainly supported its claim of quality. I've had it for 2 days now and here's what I think of it. Out of the box, it certainly was a sight! Shiny, blue, and slick. The inside microfiber/suede just felt very luxurious. (I do worry that the lighter color will eventually get dirty with use and I'm not sure how to clean it.) The pattern around the frame where the iPad goes was a nice extra. Usually, I see solids only. The stitching looks good and tight. No frayed ends showing and everything in its place. The magnets in the cover isn't the strongest in the world but it does hold the cover close adequately. One thing to remember is that you must close the cover properly. If you simply slap it close, it doesn't always line up so the cover isn't properly on. You almost have to pull/straighten out the cover and then very deliberately fold it over to close it. I think this is due to the flap that connects the front and back covers. It isn't stiff enough to make sure the front cover stays where it needs to be as you're closing it. Minor quibble and something I can live with. Just have to be conscious of how you close the cover. Not too sure what the shiny blue material really is but it's nice and smooth. However, there are drawbacks to that. Scratches show up easier because of its shiny surface. It came with a scratch right in the middle of the cover. At certain angles, it can't be seen but at other angles, I can see a dark line that is the scratch. Minor irritation. Just a reminder for me to be extra careful in handling the case, which, of course, somewhat defeats the purpose of getting a case if I have to be careful with the case and the iPad as well. The case is supposed to protect the iPad and if I have to be careful with the case, I might as well have gone without it. The other thing I noticed about the material is that smudges show up real easily. My dogs, curious about my new toy, were sniffing the case and, immediately, I saw wet splotches on the shiny blue cover. It went away quickly enough with no visible ill effects but it does show up easily. Wet hands stay away! Also, the black flap is prone to picking up smudges too. Nothing a wet rag can't handle but greasy hands stay away! The fit is really good. It's snug and my iPad stays in place very nicely. The openings all line up where they need to be with one exception. The top opening on the back for the mic is a little off. The mic is almost under the flap of the opening. However, that doesn't seem to have a negative impact on the mic picking up sound. I tested it with a dictation app (while my cat was rubbing up against the mic!) and it recorded just fine. It's something minor but for the price I paid for this case, I would have liked for that particular opening to line up properly. The other issue with the openings is it's a bit of a chore getting to the mute button. Partly, it's due to the curved back of the iPad, I think. But, this is minor and I can live with it. The "privacy shield" in typing mode is somewhat of a joke. I'm not sure it will ever get used. And it wouldn't really work if you're typing on an airplane where you're almost shoulder-to-shoulder with your neighbor. Besides, if I'm that close to someone on the plane and I think they're reading, I would just type a message out for them that I can tell they're reading my stuff. No point in using a privacy shield. Nice thought but somewhat ineffective execution, IMHO. The display mode has 2 angles - I use that mode for viewing and typing (with an external keyboard.) Both angles are good and comfortable but the little "speed bumps" on the front cover that's meant to prop the iPad up isn't prominent enough. At times, I've had the iPad slip off the bumps. Admittedly, this only happens when I'm typing since there's more shaking with the tapping of keys than when I'm just watching a video. But I think the bumps could've been made slightly taller to provide a better catch. The pockets on the front cover are a nice extra but probably won't get used. I just read the description on the box and it was a pleasant surprise to learn that the pockets are shielded. I feel better about putting my credit card in there now but, it's hardly convenient to have my credit card in the case. I won't always have my iPad with me but I'll always have my wallet with me. However, it's good for holding business cards. Just not very many or the cover won't close properly. I tried with only my driver's license and a credit card and that was enough to create a bump that caused the cover not to close properly. Lastly, I have to pick on the branding. It's a bit much. :) I understand wanting the world to know it's an iSkin case but to have the logo just about everywhere is a bit much. (The iSkin logo is on the front, back flap, and inside front cover. Almost like wearing a tshirt with logos on the front, back, and both sleeves. Just one spot will do. If I really like this case, I'm not usually shy about letting people know who the makers are.) Bottomline, this is an impressive case. I like the material. I like the look. I like the functionality. I like the quality. I like the slimness. My issues with it are mostly minor and I can live with them. The price is a little steep, I think but, I'm hoping this is a good investment and will last me a long while. Update: October 3, 2012 Now that I've been using this case for about a month, I've noticed a couple of things that weren't apparent when I initially wrote the review. For one, the dark color of the "frame" portion of the case is rubbing off on the light gray suede where I prop the iPad for viewing. I can see 2 dark spots where the corners rest. Not looking forward to when those spots will either get darker or wear out. Certainly not happy about this. The second thing is the stitching from the card pockets are leaving "imprints" on the screen. I have a Zagg shield on the screen and I can see the stitching on the screen if I hold the iPad up at an angle. It's also visible against a very white surface (like when I'm reading a book.) - it looks like shimmering spots on the screen. Otherwise, it's not visible.

I had three cheap switch boxes on my high-end stereo, and decided this was not acceptable. I needed something to route a CD player, a turntable, and an equalizer to a main system, and to an old Victrola console. I almost bought the Zen, but $400 is a bit pricey. As it turned out, I got this Beresford box to do everything I needed it to. I've always been leery of claims about "greater soundstage", "tighter bass" and my favorite "dark backgrounds" , etc. After hooking up this box, I played one particular song "Pearls" by Sade, and for the first time, I could make out what she was saying in the first line. It seemed to me that everything in general sounded better. My imagination? Maybe, but I think this thing is really a high quality box. I looked inside it, and it is built like a tank. Gold plated jacks, and what I think is silver solder. I wanted a box that had a stereo switch too, for my turntable, and when I looked inside the box, I knew I couldn't re-wire inside. So I figured how to do it on the outside. So, if you want this to do stereo/mono, here's how I did it. I have the turntable in input #2, and output A goes to the EQ then the pre-amp. In input #2, I plugged in 2 y-connectors, one in left, one in right. I also plugged in 2 Y-connectors into output A. The turntable plugs into a right and left lead in input 2, the EQ plugs into the Y in output A. Now, you take the free right and left lead from the Y in the input, and connect it to the free leads on the output, creating a "permanent" stereo connection between input and output. Here's where the mono part comes in: you have to mix the right and left leads that you connect between the input and output. Thus, when you are on input 2, you get L-R stereo internally, but also get R-L on the "outside", thus: MONO. When you switch to a different input, you only have the external connection, thus STEREO. BUT, you have to have a way to switch off your phono pre-amp (which should be in line before the box) otherwise, you may risk some interference on the other inputs like the CD. When I have the turntable off, and the pre-amp box off, I can't detect any crosstalk at all with my CD. Your results may vary if you do this. Anyway, this box is really worth the money.

This transmitter is very, very weak. I am an electrical engineer and the transmission power this thing puts out is pittiful. Yes, it will broadcast to a clear fm channel on your radio. And because the transmitter signal is so weak it results in some other problems: 1) The audio is low and faint. Even with the volume turned all the way up on the ipod, the audio is not very loud, resulting it the background noise being amplified, thus you get a noisey signal. 2) Because the transmitter is extremely weak, the radio has a harder time locking into the signal. That is why people experience static with this device. Think of it like trying to tune in a very weak FM station in your town, or an FM station from 80 miles away - it goes in and out and has static that is very annoying. That is EXACTLY how this device will sound. 3) Does not transmit in stereo, so your music will be mono and not have the full rich sound. So you get mono sound peppered with high background noise and static as the signal goes in and out. I won't mention the quailty of the plug or housing, that doesn't matter. I decided to get this as an upgrade to my current RX-V371, which has been working great for years. In particular, I wanted to be able to upconvert the analog inputs to HDMI output. My setup is pretty simple: 5 speakers; fronts, center, surrounds; and a subwoofer. Inputs are Blu-ray, Chromecast, a PC (HDMI), and a Wii. On the RX-V371, this configuration works fine (aside from the inability to upconvert the Wii). When the RX-V677 arrived, I connected it up in the same configuration that the RX-V371 was in, ran through the setup process, and started testing it. First thing I tested was the Chromecast. It seemed fine at first, but about every 5 minutes, the audio would drop out for about a second, accompanied by the speaker indicators on the front panel flashing off and on. I thought this was a problem with the Chromecast at first, but when moving it back to the RX-V371, the problem went away. Switching back to the RX-V677, I decided to see if the problem would go away over time; instead, it became more frequent. I tried different audio programs and played around with the settings, but nothing made a difference. At this point I was fairly sure it was a problem with the receiver, but decided to test another input source in case the Chromecast was at fault. The second thing I tested was the PC. I switched to HDMI3 and ... nothing. The TV was not receiving a signal (not even the receiver's default background image that normally shows if an input is not connected), and the orange HDMI indicator on the receiver's front panel was flashing on and off rapidly. To try to diagnose the problem further, I connected the PC to some of the other inputs. It worked perfectly and consistently when connected to HDMI4, but not when connected to HDMI3 or HDMI2. Assuming that this was a defect in that particular item, I returned it for a replacement of the same model. When the replacement arrived, I connected it up exactly as before, but had identical issues (except that the audio dropouts with the Chromecast were significantly more frequent, every few seconds as opposed to minutes). I've returned the second RX-V677 for a refund, and am going to try ordering a RX-V675. I didn't actually need any of the additional features of the RX-V677 over the RX-V675, but at the time, they were the same price, so I decided to go with the slightly more recent model. The audio quality is great, user interface is easy-to-use, and composite video upconversion works fine, which is why this gets 2 stars instead of 1, and also why I'm sticking with Yamaha. I hope that the RX-V675 and RX-V677 are different enough that these issues will not affect the RX-V675 as well. Update: The RX-V675 does not have the same issues and seems to work perfectly.

This battery pack contains four 12v 9ah batteries. The batteries are model CSB HR 1234W F2. This battery pack is not made so that the batteries can be easily replaced by the user like the main UPS unit that it connects too. This is disappointing. They could have designed it so that the batteries slid out for easy replacement like they do on the master UPS unit. But you can still easily replace the batteries with a little work. Although you might break off a small plastic tab or two on the front cover in the process but it won't matter or hurt anything. Presumably your two year warranty has expired before you need to replace the batteries so you will have nothing to lose. 1. Remove the 6 screws on the back of the unit. 2. Pry off the front cover. 3. Lay unit on it's side so that the 3 screws on the front are facing up. 4. Remove the 3 screws on the front of the unit. 5. Slide the cover towards the back of the unit to remove it. 6. Disconnect the leads plugged into the F2 terminals on the batteries. 7. Remove batteries. 8. Insert new batteries and reconnect the leads. When I plugged the unit into my BR1500G UPS it basically tripled my estimated runtime per the PowerChute software. Which is exactly as expected since the BR1500G contains two batteries and the external battery pack contain four additional batteries. My reported runtime is now 96 minutes with 233 watts draw. I found no fan inside this external battery. The BR1500G contained 2 Kung Long WP1236W batteries. 12V 9ah 36W. Made in Vietnam. This external battery pack contained 4 CSB HR 1234W F2 batteries 12V 9ah 34W. Still rating it 5 stars. Although I'm disappointed about difficulty to replace batteries when the time comes. Also, I'm really curious to know if the BR1500G is able to inform the user when the external battery needs replacement or if it just gives a general replace battery message for all batteries. Looking forward to seeing future reviews.

I bought this because it has both a back up camera and sensors. I also liked the fact that it attaches to the license plate so I didn't have to drill any holes in my car. Other nice features are that it isn't wireless so you always get a nice clean picture on the backup camera and you don't have to separately wire the monitor to a power source because it gets its power from the backup light wire connection. Note that you have to chase a wire from the back of the trunk to the dash where you intend to install the monitor. I accomplished this by removing the door sill kick plates, which were attached with plastic push pins. I had several minor install problems when attaching the sensor bar to my license plate. First, in my state (MA) you can't attach anything to the license plate that hides any part of the plate. The kit supplies some brackets but they weren't the right size to hang the sensor bar below my license plate. I made some brackets from aluminum bar stock that I got from Home Depot. The brackets were fairly easy to make and only required a hack saw and a drill. Once installed I found that I was getting a false signal because the license plate is slightly recessed on my '09 Camry, which caused the sensors to pick up my stop light housings. This was easily corrected by simply bending the brackets that I made to stand off the senor bar far enough so that the sensors wouldn't pick up my stop light housings. One installed the back up sensors and camera worked great! The back up camera is clear both day and night. The sensors start picking up objects when you are about 5' away. The monitor starts beeping and the display shows some hash marks indicating how far you are away. As you get closer the beeping increases in frequency until you get a steady beep and the display says STOP. On average this happens about 2' from an object. The camera has a wide angle lens so objects appear farther away than they really are. However, with a few uses I can now back up to within 1' from an object using the sensors and the back up camera. If you own a SUV, truck, van or car with limited rear visibility this is a great safety device. I highly recommend it. The quality is top notch.

I bought two of these for reasons many people do...so you can use with an Eyefi card in cameras that do not have an SD card slot.One was for my D3, one for my D700. It goes into the D3 no problem and works, albeit not as fast as I would hope but usable provided you are sending jpegs and not RAW. In normal operation you will not notice a speed drop due to the D3's shoot buffer. However if you switch to high speed bursts your fast 1D/D3 may well turn into a slug once the buffer fills up. The problem multiplies with some other camera's. I used it with a borrowed Sony Alpha 900 recently and the smaller buffer along with the larger file size made the camera unusable. Shoot....wait....wait ....wait....wait....writing speed was embarrassingly slow, so slow I thought the camera was broken until I used a normal CF card which changed the entire nature of the camera. Also check your CAMERA manual to see if you can use it. I didn't check to see if my D700 could fit CFII cards and discovered that it doesn't. The D700 and several other DSLRs only take the thinner CF ONE cards. The difference between a 3.3mm thick CF1 and a 5mm CF2 card means this product is too fat to fit the D700. Check your manual. In SUMMARY I think the card is a bottleneck for speed. Otherwise a good way of adding the nifti eyefi cards to cameras without SD card slots.

I had an old Asus WiFi router and it started dropping signals and I got tired of dead zones in the house...time for an upgrade. I decided on this AX6600 and am glad I did. Setup was easy, just plug it in and go on your way. I have over 50 devices connected (not all are WiFi) and I have not had any issues at all...plus my speed has more than doubled to my ISP. I can now full use the speed that I pay for. I also have not found any dead zones yet. Here's the only "catch" I had with this router. I have a bunch of smart plugs, Roku sticks, etc that operate on the 2.4 ghz and I use Alexa to control them.and I could not initially get them to connect because of the "Smart Connect" option that comes with this router. The "Smart Connect" allows you to broadcast one SSID and the router determines what frequency to set the device to. In order to get everything working, my phone and devices need to be on the 2.4 ghz frequency. So I went into the router's configuration and disabled the "Smart Connect" and set the 5 ghz frequencies to <Your SSID>1 and <Your SSID>2 (There are 2 5 ghz frequencies). I connected my phone to the 2.4 ghz SSID to make sure I had the correct frequency and then I went to my 2.4 devices and reconfigured them. Once I had reconfigured the 2.4 devices, I went back into the router's configuration and enabled the "Smart Connect" again. Everything works smoothly now and I can take advantage of the "Smart Connect" feature. Was it a pain, kinda, but I didn't mind. I also thought the router's configuration page was simple and easy to understand. I love this router and would highly recommend it to anyone looking to upgrade. Oh, it's supposed to work with mesh devices too but I have not tested that out just yet. I will get to that after the Holidays.

UPDATE April 3, 2016: Computer is still great after 4 months. Reallocating space to the C drive hasn't caused any problems. I've mostly been using it for school, so typing a lot of papers and doing research. Nothing too heavy. It handles watching Netflix well, and using Spotify. I haven't had much time for games, but when I do I usually play Civilization: Beyond Earth. The graphics have been great and I haven't had any lag. So, still happy with my decision. I got this computer last night and so far I am pleased, for the most part. I have a desktop, but needed a laptop for school. I plan on using it mainly for school related stuff, but probably will also end up gaming casually. I'm pretty confident this computer will handle all that wonderfully. Pros: -Well packaged -Super fast setup and Windows 10 works really smoothly -The charging cord is so light and small compared to my old laptop. The last one I owned had a two piece charger which was heavy and often pulled on the charging port, causing the port to eventually die. Not so with this thing. -Keyboard is easy to type on even though I'm coming from a bigger desktop keyboard -The track pad is pretty sensitive, but there are easily accessible options in Windows 10 under devices (I think) to adjust it if you want. -The speakers have a good sound -The design is lovely and the cover isn't prone to fingerprints. Cons: -There's some bloatware, as is the norm with computers in this price range. All of it was easily uninstalled, but I had to spend a bit of time googling to make sure I wasn't about to delete something necessary. Not too painful, but annoying anyway. -The biggest issue I had was that I realized the C: drive only had 370GB of storage available, which greatly confused me since this computer is supposed to have 1TB of hard drive space. Well, it does, however 500+GB were for some reason allocated to the D: drive, which made no sense to me as the C: drive is where the majority of people use and store everything. So I started googling again and asking my more tech savvy friends if this could be fixed. The good news is that it can, so you will be able to utilize all the hard drive space advertised (with the exception of the space the system files take up). I recommend taking care of this issue before you get too far into using the computer just in case something goes wrong, or if you feel uncomfortable with messing around with this kind of thing, get a different computer. Here is what I did to fix this: -Right click on the windows icon in the bottom left corner. -Click disk management -Right click on the DATA (D:) drive and select Shrink Volume -You have to enter the amount you want taken out of the drive in MB. I chose to leave 100GB on the D: drive, so I took out 460000MB which equals 460GB. -Click shrink. You will now have however much space you chose free. The disk manager won't let you expand the C: drive for some technical reason I don't really understand, so I ended up googling more and downloading Partition Wizard which was free. There are quite a few free partition management tools out there, so do some googling and pick whatever one feels right to you. For this particular tool, here were the steps. (the tool will also walk you through on their webpage with pictures, but it's pretty intuitive and easy without instructions) -Open the program. It should list all your drives and unallocated space -Right click C:OS (this is your C: drive) -Click Extend (near the top of the menu) -In the Take Free Space From drop down menu, choose the unallocated space option. -Move the slider at the bottom all the way to the right to include all the free space -Click OK -Click the check mark that says Apply in the top left corner of the program. -It only took a few seconds for me and then I had the appropriate amount of space on my C: drive. End verdict: After a day of use, I really like it and think it will serve me well. I love the charger, and now that I figured out the hard drive thing I feel much better about this purchase. There's a chance I just got a weird one with the drives set up the way they were, but it was simple to fix luckily.

Although this radio does appear to be water resistant as advertised, it is otherwise unremarkable and performs poorly. Pros: Water Resistant - I've left it outside in light to medium rain and it continues to function. However, the cord is not grounded so I would advise against letting it get even slightly wet when plugged in. Cons: False Advertising - It does not have the advertised equalizer function. This is listed on Amazon and on advertising materials from the manufacturer website, but is not listed on the box or in the manual for the unit received and there is no combination of buttons I've found to enable it. Poor Reception - Reception is much worse than two tiny handheld radios I own and worse than either of my cars. I'm unable to receive many stations at all, and those I can receive often have some static, even when outdoors. Too Much Bass - This is where the advertised equalizer function would be helpful. This unit is extremely heavy on bass and light on treble. It's alright for rap, R&B, and some rock, but forget about it for talk radio or classical. Talk show hosts all sound like they've been hybridized with James Earl Jones if the volume is above 25% or so, and you'll have a hard time distinguishing some instruments from the background noise in many classical pieces. Rattling/Distortion At Reasonable Volumes - This is related to the heavy bass issue. With volume only half way up the unit will start to distort and even produce a vibrating rattle when playing anything that has moderate amounts of bass to it. Since it's advertised as a work site radio, this is a major flaw. If I want to hear things when I'm 30 or 40 feet away, I'd like to do so without rattling and distortion. Instead it sounds like an oversized bass tube installed in an 80's hatchback.

I've had this watch for about 2 months now and I really like it. I've made a Pros and Cons list below of my opinions with this watch. Pros: -Time: It tells the time, as a watch should. -Background: You can customize the background to have it be a photo of your choice that you've taken. -Phone connect: I had no issues getting the app on my phone and connecting my watch to the app. -Water reminder: I have a reminder set to take a drink of water every 2 hours between the hours of 9am and 9pm, and I like that you can customize the reminders -Battery: AMAZING battery life. I charge my watch maybe once a week. -Water resistance: I wear my watch in the shower and have no issues with it. I had also done an event that involved me jumping into a lake and I kept my watch on with no problems following. When swimming, I will not use it as I'll be submerged in water and this watch is water RESISTANT, not water PROOF. -Incoming texts and calls: I can receive them with no issues and can dismiss calls with the button and quickly glace at the text if I'm unable to see my phone. -Steps: Gives a good read on my step count for the day. I like that it tells you when you were most active in the day and also that it gives you an average of your daily steps. -App: The app is great to use to look at your progress for the day and compare your day with other days. -Breathe: As someone with anxiety, it's nice to have this setting to help with breathing exercises. -Sport mode: There are several options of sport activities to use. -Find your phone: Great to have as I lose my phone all the time. -Brightness control: Great and easy to control. -Alarm clock: I have my alarm set to vibrate and it's subtle enough to wake me up without startling me. -Camera: Watch works great to take pictures with using your phone. -Call log: You can look at your recent calls and dial out without using your phone. -Strap: The strap is comfortable. -Raise your screen: Works great when you lift your hand to check the time or incoming text or call. It does go off when I'm not bothering with the watch at the time, but the screen is on only for a brief moment. -Comfort: 100%! Half the time I forget it's even there. Cons: -Accuracy: I don't believe this is accurate with calculating heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, or sleep. There will be times where I'll be sleeping for the full night and my watch will tell me that I was "fully awake" at points throughout the night. It will also say that I have been "light sleep" in the mornings when I am awake and happen to be having coffee at the table. It will also tell me that my oxygen is at 90% when I have no respiratory issues to have my oxygen be so low. It will also give different readings in one sitting when checking my heart rate and blood pressure. -Time/Date layout with custom background: You cannot chose where the time and date will be placed when using a customized background, it only gives you 1 generic option. -Texts: You cannot text back to incoming messages on the watch. -GPS: All this does is tell you your location in the world using latitude and longitude coordinates. -The button: The only use I've found for this button is using as the "home" button. Why the button twists, I don't know what the point of that is when you have to scroll with your finger on the screen anyways. -Sport mode: I don't do a lot of the sports that are listed and I've found it to be inaccurate with my steps when I use the walking option. -Weather: Also not accurate. -Voice control: It says you can press the button for 3 seconds to activate your voice assistance, but what it actually does is either give you the SOS option or the option to shut the device off. -Swiping: Swiping up shows your recent text messages. Swiping down shows you a menu to access your watch layout, if the Bluetooth is connected, the brightness adjustment, and the watch information. Swiping to the left brings up your watch's application menu, but this can also be done with pressing the button. Swiping left is also like the "back button" to go back to the previous screen you were on. When you swipe to the left, it shows your recently used 4 apps that you've accessed with your watch. The SOS button is there as well. I would rather have the option to change where my watch goes when swiping left or right. -Games: Why? The screen is too tiny for this. -Strap: The strap is a bit big on me, even on the tightest loop, and I need to wear it below my wrist - this could contribute to the accuracy issues. Have not used: -Music: I don't want my music coming from my wrist, personal preference. -SOS: I haven't needed to use it, hopefully I won't need to, but I'm glad it's there. -Notification reminder with additional apps: I don't have notifications turned on for email or social media, as a personal preference. -Siri: I don't use Siri, personal preference. -Stopwatch: Haven't used yet. -Passcode: I don't use a passcode, personal preference. -Calculator: It's a calculator, basic, usually not needing my phone for math use. There's a lot more to the watch that's provided, which I think is great. I do enjoy it and I'm going to keep wearing it. There's the good, there's the downside, there's some annoyances, but no technology will be 100% perfect to your every need. This is still a great watch, especially for someone who's never had a smartwatch before.

First the good ... These are probably the most comfortable 3D glasses I've ever worn. Admittedly, it's a bit like saying "That's the most enjoyable injection the doctor has ever given me", but these are extremely comfortable. The clarity and lifelike nature of the 3D images is intoxicating, particularly with Tron Legacy and Mortal Kombat (admittedly, we're not dealing with a deep bench here in terms of content, so hopefully there will be more stuff on the way). Funtionally, pairing them with the TV was effortless (I think my bluetooth mouse was more work) and they are completely automated after that...the TV knows when you are watching 3D-enabled content and wearing the glasses...if you take them off to set them down and stroll in the other room to get a glass of water, it even seems to sense this and put the glasses to sleep and disengage the 3D display. It's pretty cool if you ask me. We have tried roughly half of the 3D stuff we could get our mits on, video games, blu ray, and VOD/PPV and free stuff via DirecTV. It looks great (better in my home than in any demo kiosk I've seen anywhere, actually). It somehow makes the image not just come *out* of the TV, but (as it should) presents the impression that the TV is many times deeper, and that you are actually peering INTO a 3D world, rather than simply watching it bulge out nearer to your face from the screen. Given the current state of technology and the price point of these, I think I would give these 5 stars. However, I ding two stars as I bought these SPECIFICALLY because to my knowledge no other model on the market allows for my prescription to be installed into the lenses. Though comfortable, they are not particularly glasses-friendly. They don't sit properly on my face and tend to skew away from the nose unevenly when I have my regular glasses on underneath, making the picture a bit contorted (I don't think this has anything to do with the 3d glasses themselves per se, but rather just how they sort of fit snugly and therefore are fighting with my regular glasses for pole position on my face). They say "prescription ready"--and that's about all the website says. Registering them was no help ... in fact, after registering them, the first question someone else on Samsung's website had posted was "How do I order prescription lenses for these?" and it had 0 responses. The documenation says to check the Samsung website (Wow ... I mean really!). I was unable to send an e-mail as their support requests/contact interfaces are all forms-based, and these glasses (much like my new TV) are not available from the drop downs yet ... at least not for support. I called Samsung and they told me to take them to an optometrist. I contacted three optometrists, and none could do this for me (only one knew what active shutter glasses even were) and suggested I contact the manufacturer (yea, well...). I went to Best Buy and they hadn't even heard of the prescription ready option yet. I called Samsung back and they repeated what their screens must have been saying, "take the glases to an optometrist." When I explained the optometrist was unable to help they said they couldn't help me beyond that--no means of escalation or direct contact with Samsung. As of May, 2011, this is still not just a newer technology, but this is a very new product and the only one available (to my knowledge) boasting a prescription-ready lense. I am imagining that I will have to send these in to Samsung (or a delegated partner) at some point, pay an additional fee, wait a period of time, and then have them shipped back. I just wish someone could acknlowledge that this is even a possibility. By the time all that happens, I'll have a new presciption... Until then ... three stars for you! **UPDATE MAY 23, 2011** I finally reached Samsung on a different troubleshooting line, and they put me on hold for about ten minutes then suggested I go to a Hoya Vision website ... I don't think I can put links in here but will try ... effectively, Samsung has partnered with Hoya Vision to provide lenses for these units, and only certain optometrists are set up for this branded style/type of lens creation. So far, I have been waiting 4 days for a response from one of the local Hoya shops I called. They know what the technology is, but have never heard of 3D glasses taking prescription lenses, and so also do not know how it will be done or how much it will cost me. Go to the Hoya Vision website, then click "FIND A HOYA EXPERT" in order to find one locally. Here is the link (if it works): [...] **UPDATE MAY 27, 2011** So I contacted a local Hoya dealer, and they didn't know what I was talking about. They said they would call me back but didn't, so I called them back after a few days and they said I was supposed to have heard back from a Hoya rep (though I had not). They said they would call him again. A day later I got a call from the Hoya rep, explaining how crazy things have been lately (yadda yadda) but that he would be getting back to me with pricing and implementation information--though oddly he asked me about the glasses--are they active shutter? Or passive/polarized (always troubling to have to fill in product reps on the product they represent). I told him these are active shutter/LCD glasses and he said he would call me back shortly. That was earlier this week, and it's now friday. Still no word ... though I must say, the fact that these are advertised as "prescription ready" when they are actually "clip on ready" makes me contemplate calling foul--my face is prescrption ready, then too. I purchased my Sony MRW66E/H1/181 from "Tech For Less" as an open-item "used-like new". I received the item shrink-wrapped in its original packaging which had indeed been open, however, the product did appear to be untouched (still even had the protective blue tape to shield it from scratches). Standard delivery arrived within a week. Reason for my purchase: I needed a reader/writer for an M2 card I bought for my phone (Adapter NOT included). Details the seller failed to mention: Memory Stick Micro (M2) is stated to be a supported memory card under the item's Technical Details. However, as of 24 Jan 2010, what it fails to mention is that you need an adapter for your M2 card to be used as a Memory Stick Duo which the item does not include new or used. After reading the manual, the M2 card is the only card that requires an additional adapter which you can find here on amazon at nearly give-away prices. [[ASIN:B002LQ5B4Q Sandisk M2 (Memory Stick Micro) to PRO DUO Mobile Memory Adapter (Bulk Pack-Memory Card not included)]] Conclusion: Luckily, I own a 4gb Memory Stick Pro Duo card so I was able to test the reader/writer. Compared to my Sony MSAC-US40 which I've used for a few years, the Sony MRW66E seems to read (copy from it) just slightly faster and write (copy to it) just slightly slower to my Memory Stick Pro Duo card. I would like to test this item out with the supported HG cards because I hear those are much faster for reading and writing. Works just fine on my Mac OS 10.4.11. Supports Mac OS 10.2 or later as well as various Windows OSs. Also tested this item on Linux Mint 8 and it recognized my Memory Stick Pro Duo without any issues with both reading/writing. Note: 4 stars was only because I need to buy a separate adaptor for my M2 card which could have easily been stated within the Item Description. Otherwise, this is a 5 star reader/writer and would not have a problem ordering from Tech for Less again.

I bought this 5-degree viewfinder at the same time that I bought my Sekonic 479DR meter (see my review of that). Being very used to using spot meters, this was something I knew I had to have, but I couldn't quite justify the expense of the 700-series Sekonic light meter that had this functionality already built in. It was a bit cheaper to buy the meter, and the spot attachment separately. It's a bit of a pain switching back and forth between the incident light head that comes on the meter normally, and this attachment, but I wouldn't take off more than about a half-star for that. It was my own decision to not buy the one where everything was already in the same meter. In retrospect, I might have considered spending a little more for the 700-series meter that has it built in. This allows the meter to act as an reflected light meter as well as an incident light meter, and to take a reading obviously from a small portion of the shot, so that you can see what the camera is considering "middle gray" and adjust accordingly. I would have preferred a one-degree viewfinder, as I find the five-degrees a little larger an area than I ideally like to check on (maybe because I was used to a one-degree meter for many years). But it completely depends on your subject matter, how brought the fields of illumination are on it, and how wide your shot is (or how far you're standing from the subject). Maybe Sekonic will come out with a compatible one-degree. But in the meantime, this works fine, is fairly easy to read, is FAIRLY easy to attach to the meter when you take the other head off (it could be a little easier) and will work with several of the Sekonic meters out there. It comes in its own little velvet pouch, which helps keep it protected. Another followup -- this on 2/4/14. I recently discovered that the 700-series meter's built in spotmeter is a 1 degree spot. A 1 degree spot accessory cannot be made for the 400-series meters because of design issues. Therefore, if you want a one degree spot, you MUST buy the more expensive 700-series meter. I wish I had known that before I bought the less expensive meter with the add-on.

"Buyer beware", right? Well, you know when you buy a refurb unit that you're getting a lower price because it's not brand new. HOWEVER, it IS supposed to be brought up to all specifications and pass all its QA tests and have functioning components. It's also supposed to include all of the items its promised to come with. The one I received does not entirely fit that definition. I just received this unit a few days ago and I'm going to go ahead and write a review based on my test-use so far with my specific refurbished unit. Once I take it to a tailgate this weekend and test it in that atmosphere, I'll report back and revise my review as necessary. Let's start with the basics: what's in the box? For me, just the main speaker unit. No power cable, no microphone, no mic cable, no manuals. A speaker cabinet placed in a plain oversized box and shipped with nothing else inside--that's what I received. How does it look? Well, this is certainly a used unit and part of why it was returned in the first place was undoubtedly this display screen (photo included). No, I'm not expecting this to be a brand new product, but I would assume that someone in the refurbishment area QA'd these parts before they were reassembled for my unit, no? Rest of the unit looks fine. I'm going to be using it outside anyway so I don't need to it be pristine; but what's pictured isn't even dirt, because I cleaned it thoroughly already. Does it connect easily? Yes, actually as far as connecting to sources it's A+ in my book. Bluetooth was easy and immediate, auxiliary was louder than BT. Radio, all seemed to work fine. Of course, I had a question about connecting the BT and this came with no manual or paperwork of any kind, so I had to go digging on the internet--that was a bit annoying but easily solved. Is it LOUD? Yes, it is loud. It is louder than anything else I happen to own, and while I don't have any measuring devices on-hand, I am willing to bet it is all of the 100W it promises. The problem with mine is, I bet whoever returned this unit before I had it also blew out the speakers somewhat, because if I turn it up past about 70% it distorts so badly that its just loud noise, not anything you'd want to listen to. If you don't turn it too loud though, the sound is rich and great. Don't expect much bass, there is no bass-boost or equalizer and eventhough it's got what should be a competent 8" woofer, its not terribly effective. In fact, I wish this had an aux-OUT so I could connect my old 8" sub I took out of my old '91 Sentra--it was far louder and deeper. How about that battery life? Honestly, I cannot yet attest to its battery life. It arrived almost fully charged! And that's awesome. But also I haven't had the chance to run out the power, recharge, and run it out again. I'm hosting a 6-hour long tailgate in two days and I'll be running this as loudly as possibly, continually, with the light bar, so I'll see how it lasts. Hopefully, the battery they put in my refurb unit is new as is required since old battery cells are both dangerous for reuse and carry a 12-18month maximum effectiveness lifetime. Time will tell! Any other thoughts on functionality? A tone control would be nice, and the buttons are hard to press but overall everything functions as expected. Telescoping handle motion is secure and feels reliable. Rolls smoothly on its wheels. I bet as a brand new unit this would be a very nice product. Do yourself a favor and either buy a new unit or buy something else entirely, but I can't in good faith recommend that anyone pick up a sub-par version like I seem to have received.
