Every other Lightning cable brand I had ever purchased, from $5 generic cables that failed after a week, to $15 Anker's that would last 6 months, had failed. 'Why not just stick with Apple then?', one might ask. Well, my girlfriend has a nasty habit of pulling cables out aggressively, not by the end, but rather just with a strong pull on the cable. This results in the cable weakening about 1/2 inch from the lightning connector end, eventually fraying the white sheath off, and soon after, cable failure. Attempts to correct this have been futile. So, I purchased this cable, which is supposed to be mFi certified, and billed as being indestructible. However, still being a doubter, I kept this cable in my car, away from my girlfriend's hands. This cable is indeed tough as nails. However, about 6 weeks after purchase, I started having problems. I would plug the cable into my iPhone, and nothing. No connection registered. So I would try several more times, with the same result. A few times I would get a connection, but shortly after would get the dreaded 'this accessory might not be supported' message. I would then reverse the lightning end, and get a connection about 50% of the time; only however, after about 5 seconds of being plugged in. So, I sent an inquiry to the company about my problems. The response? Hi Greg! Sorry to hear your cable is acting up. One of the main reasons for our cables to stop charging or have an intermittent connection is due to dirt on the lightning connector or in your lightning port of the phone. Could you try the below for me and let me know how it goes? Thanks! 1. Clean your lightning port. Google for: clean lightning port. This will give you some pointers. Even small amounts of dust or lint can block the contact. 2. Clean the contacts on the Lightning cable. Use a small amount of Ethnoyl (rubbing alcohol) on a paper towel and wipe it down very well. You may need to scrub, especially if you see the gold connectors have dirt/crud on them. Do not do this while it is plugged in and allow it to dry thoroughly after cleaning before use. Now I must mention, after having an iPhone 5, 5c, and 5s through the course of about 5 years, I have NEVER cleaned or had the need to clean either an iPhone charging port, or an Apple brand lightning cable. They simply ALWAYS worked. However, wanting to humor the suggestion of dirt and grime causing the problem, I did as instructed. It seemed to help once or twice. But then, failure began again. I sent a second inquiry to FuseChicken. The response? Exactly the same as the first time. So I promptly replied 'I have done this, does not help.' They never replied to that message, and now, 5 days later, I have decided they must have an auto-responder that sends the same initial reply to messages about failure. But follow ups must be ignored. If you are looking for a tough cable, that will last a reasonable amount of time, keep on looking. This apparantly is not the one. It is past the return period allowed by Amazon, so I guess I am just out my $35. It is nice and strong. Perhaps I can use it for a painting frame hanger or something.

So far the box is behaving itself well and doing what it is supposed to. The comments below are for information purposes. First - use the recommended RAM. Weird things happen with the "wrong" RAM. You have been warned... Kubuntu 16.04 works fine but for one small detail. My Panasonic 1080p TV is connected via HDMI. Turning off the TV causes the display to turn off. The display can be reinitialized with 'xrandr --verbose' or just switching to a console and back (Ctrl-Alt-F1). However, I have found a (for me) better solution using Ubuntu Mate 15.10 x64 which starts faster and does not have the 'TV off' problem. Video tearing is addressed by using compiz instead of the Marco display manager. I also had to create an Xorg config file in /usr/share/X11.xorg.conf.d. Included at the end of review. Google Chrome, downloaded directly from google is now only available in 64bit and plays Netflix and Amazon video just fine. $more /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/20-intel.conf Section "Device" Identifier "Intel Graphics" Driver "Intel" Option "AccelMethod" "sna" Option "TearFree" "true" EndSection $

I hate to be writing a negative review of anything from Garmin, because I've always had great experiences with the company's products and with its support team. But there seems to be a fundamental design flaw with this device: as others have noted in reviews posted here (which, sadly, I didn't read before I purchased mine), the altimeter in my Fenix 3 HR thinks I'm sitting at 65,617 feet. If you've done any mountain hiking, you know how useless that measurement is -- inaccurate by well more than an order of magnitude. In fact, if I were hiking at that altitude, I'd be twice as high as Everest, not to mention... dead. What's more, the thermometer thinks it's 27 degrees right now, even though I happen to be in sunny and comfy Los Angeles today. When I called Garmin to see if I was the weak link in the chain of command, and had somehow screwed up when configuring the device, I was partially relieved to hear this is a recurring albeit sporadic problem; my tech support agent was refreshingly candid, telling me the company didn't yet know whether it was a manufacturing defect or a firmware glitch. I say "partially," because when I called Garmin last week, for help in deciding between the Fenix 3 and the Forerunner 735XT, I was advised to get the Fenix because, according to the pre-sales rep, the Fenix had a much better altimeter. Yikes! I guess these two agents are sitting on different floors, or don't have access to the same database. I am surprised a company that seems as customer-centric as Garmin wouldn't share both good and bad issues with potential buyers -- especially buyers they know have bought many of their products in the past. Ironically, had the pre-sales rep told me there was a problem with some Fenix units, I would have respected Garmin even more than I previously had; now they've damaged their reputation with me, and I have to think long and hard about whether to replace this with a Forerunner, or turn to another brand...

I use this for several backdrops for videoconferencing. The backdrops are variously paper, light vinyl, or very thin cotton. The advantage of this system is the stabilization of the two tripods at either end. This prevents your backdrop from rotating along the axis perpendicular to the floor or seesawing at either end--both common with the T-backdrop stands. I'm very careful with the stand and it's lasted about a year. However, there are some major caveats that discourage me from recommending it. First, the width of the stand is variable thanks to the use of different diameter shallow tubes at the top that slide into each other. But the segmentation of the top bar and the thin, hollow metal mean that after around 5-feet of width, the top bar sags noticeably. If your audience can see the whole structure (like if you're displaying things, not just showing a small central portion on a videoscreen), they'll see the ugly dip/bow at the top. This also means your fabric is uneven at the bottom and may even drape on the dirty floor. This is the biggest disadvantage I've found after a whole year of daily use. A second, but minor, caveat is the large amount of floor real estate the double tripods will take up. If you try to limit this by increasing the base tripod height (taller triangular pyramids), the stand becomes unstable and tips over. So, you'll need considerable floor space--this isn't for a small office. Thirdly, as other reviewers have reported, the vertical poles at the end have a screw component at their tops to secure to the horizontal bar. This component falls down into the top-most cylinders often, compromising securing the stand. A big enough annoyance that, alone, would otherwise deter me from buying another one of these stands. Overall, this was the best I could find on Amazon. If I'd seen a heavy-duty version that at least solved the top-bar bowing problem, I'd have gladly paid for it as I use this stand 6-days a week. As it is, I'm looking into building a permanent track in my ceiling to accommodate backdrops securely. If you intend to show only the central portion of a large backdrop via video, your audience may not notice the above problems. But you could buy far smaller backdrops for that. For large-scale productions, I'd look for a stabler system.

For what it's worth, I manage an enterprise network engineering team of 14 network engineers. I possess 6 current Cisco certifications. I had a need to expand my home network by installing a new layer 2 switch into my basement where I didn't have network cabling. I did, however, have a nearby ceiling-mounted access point providing strong wireless connectivity. So I bought this to connect to the switch so it can connect to my home's network thereby allowing all devices to still be hardwired to the switch with no need for each device to connect via WiFi. It works OK for this purpose. No issues except I cannot get faster speeds than FastEthernet/100Mbps even though all layer 1 links have negotiated GigE port speeds. I use iperf on linux boxes for internal speed testing. It seems like this wireless bridge somehow uses its wired port as a FastEth interface. I can get faster speeds on my raspberry Pis using their internal wifi over this wireless bridge. But again, it works great other than the speed issue. But the far bigger concern to me is that I noticed this device sends traffic to Chinese IP addresses. My firewall was allowing the traffic at first. With this device only needing to be a layer 2 bridge on my network, it has no business talking to anything in China. I created a DHCP reservation based on its MAC address so it always receives the same IP and then I blocked all traffic from its IP address going to the internet. Prior to the block, the only traffic I observed going to the internet was NTP and ICMP traffic, but I still would be wary of this thing. If this was developed by an American company, it would be coded to use NTP from North American sources rather than Chinese sources. But it constantly tries to ping something in China as well as tries to NTP sync to something in China. This tells me it's not just manufactured in China, but the software devs work in China also. And as a network guy, I do not trust it with my data. I'll still use it because I know how to block it. But if you don't have the ability to block it on your network from reaching out to the internet, be aware. I'm going to put this device on a different internal zone on my firewall so I can observe its traffic and what it's trying to talk to internal in my network.

I recently installed two of these no ground plane kits. One was on my motorhome and the other one on a friends cabover camper. Following instructions from the firestik web site, I have 2/3 of the of the 3ft. mast above the roof line with no bends or kinks in the cable. Checking the SWR's on channels 1 and 40, they were just under 3 and around 1.3 on channel19. This was the same on both installations. We normally use channel 4 so the reading on it was also very high. I e-mailed firestik about the issue and for some reason never got a response. I ended up tuning the antenna on channel 4 for the lowest setting and got 1.3. I can use up to channel 21 before the reading goes above 2. This is ok because I never use those upper channels anyway. I was unable to get an acceptable SWR reading on all 40 channels. Firestik does have an excellent tech section on their web site. Look under "off center tuning" if you are having the same issue. The 3 star rating is for the antenna problem and the lack of customer support.

The reason I know about the durability though is one of the unit's many drawbacks, most of which are design failures that would likely embarrass any engineers with a sense of pride (ie. most). It comes across like Sennheiser focused more on speaker quality than most other aspects, and while the speakers are great the ergonomics of these headphones for example are awful. I've had to basically 'train' them by bending them repeatedly to fit my head adequately (by default they squeeze my ears enough to ache after about 20 mins of listening, which is unacceptable). I have a pretty average-sized head by the way, at least according to hat fittings. The overhead portion of these should have been built to be adjustable/bendable, and they are not: there are only notch-based length adjustments near the earpieces. They also slip off most of the time if I tilt my head forward, and they have always done this (before and despite any of my adjustments). The result is usually hitting tile after dropping from head level, and usually one of the pads flies off. All it would have taken would have been some time spent wearing these to realize the flaws here. The other issue I have--and it actually makes me avoid using these a lot of the times--is a design feature that comes across once again like it was never tested. The transmitter/charger is designed so that if there's a sustained period of sufficiently low amplitude/volume in the signal (2 minutes) the transmitter *stops transmitting*. The logic behind this decision still baffles me, because it doesn't serve any purpose like saving battery life because the headphones stay on. What's worse by far though is the result--I'll put together a playlist at my system, start it up, put the headphones on, and go about my business (usually chores around the house that music makes more tolerable). If I remember to keep from pointing my head down and dropping them then all is well until the volume of the music drops below ~15% (at the end of the set, on some songs that have low output for portions of them, or if I have to pause for some reason). What happens is that after two minutes of silence the transmitter stops and I get full volume static in my ears. You can imagine the jolt that gives someone at least, it prevents me from ever putting volume above 40% for any length of time, I can't play some low-output music I own with these, and all the time I have them on I'm fearful in the back of my mind of the signal dropping below 15%. This design flaw is *inexcusable*, especially at this price point. All it would have taken is some measurable amount of testing. The last issue I have is because of yet another lack of testing--transmission/reception. The frequency band of adjustability at the headset seems fine, but the transmitter's band is far too narrow, so the signal is more susceptible to interference in an average environment than it should be. The power output of the transmitter is too low as well, so even close to the transmitter there's audible (very low but still audible) static, and if I wander more than a room away from it the static starts getting in the way of the music. These types of flaws are not acceptable to me. It's not hard at all to design reasonably according to use, and Sennheiser puts this unit at a price point where there is absolutely zero excuse not to. The result is unnecessarily overpriced, sub-par functionality. Update: a few months after writing this, and the internal battery is now losing charge life. After only an hour or so of listening the battery dies. It's obvious that the battery type chosen for this unit was substandard. Overall, these have become not only one of the most expensive pairs of headphones I've owned, they're also the most poorly designed and manufactured. I am getting more use out of my $20 specials now, and I'm debating digging up my old monitor headphones.

Okay, the main issue first: it's definitely not worth spending more for the Canon-made version! This does the job fine, and a little hard-plastic ring is all any maker's version is going to be. Once I figured out how it went on, I had no real problem with the attachment process: just face the filter-screw threading outward, line up the two parts of the guide mark at the side, then push on and turn 90 degrees (until the line matches up with the dot at the bottom on the barrel). It does NOT form a complete seal, though, so you will still need to clean off your camera's lens regularly when dust or moisture gets in behind this. The design has the circle divided in 4, with 90-degree arcs of attached vs. loose, and clockwise/counter-clockwise makes no difference when detaching. On my old camera (a Canon S2 IS, overdue for an upgrade!) there was a release button that had to be held down when detaching the adapter; the SX40 has no such lock or stop, so when I'm changing a filter I worry that I'll turn both layers, and set the adapter loose again. I like the fact that the adapter attaches just below the tip of the lens barrel, and moves in and out with the zoom; my old S2 required a bulky adapter cylinder/cone because it attached at the base! I do rather wish there was some way to slope the abrupt transitional profile, though -- it sometimes feels like you stuck a saucer on the end of the lens barrel, when you're trying to edge the "nose" in somewhere. I actually accidentally "popped" the filter assembly off once when I moved the camera too hastily back from a window frame, and was just lucky it didn't break anything. More plastic wouldn't add much weight, but it would mean a larger item again, a nuisance if you're carrying it in your bag rather than attached. Anyway, if you want to add accessory lenses or filters to the SX40, though, that's the way it goes. The design is what it is, for good and for ill. The particular Vivitar specimen I received has a little molding dimple or "hiccup" in one edge, but it does not affect either the latches or the screw threads. UPDATE: I found one important negative/risk with having it attach to the end of the lens barrel. I didn't always use to make sure to turn the camera off when cleaning and reattaching the adapter-plus-UV-filter (which I leave on as a lens protector), but once when I went to push it back on, the extended lens gave a bit under the pressure -- I'm crossing all my fingers that I haven't stripped the gears! It seems to be OK so far, but I'm not chancing this happening again, and the damage becoming cumulative. (On the S2, no force was required -- simply align and turn, and it clicks solidly into locked position, so this wasn't an issue. <Sigh>) LEARN FROM MY MISTAKE, and always turn the camera off first, so the lens will be fully retracted!!! UPDATE 2, November 2012 -- It just broke. That's within the year, so I'll see how the warranty replacement process works out.

After entering the pairing key it finally connected up. Launched Pandora and pressed the "Media" key on the Audi MMI/AMI to switch to the Ipod connector tune2air, it started streaming Pandora. Here the problems: 1. Volume needs to be jacked up all the way and then even increase via the Audi MMI volume to get some decent volume level 2. The music title was transmitted to the MMI LCD first, but after skipping songs, it did not change the title/artist anymore 3. Contrary to some reviews here, I am not able to skip tracks via the MMI skip (to the right) button, can do this only over the phone, which negates the advantage of having the Bluetooth feature, I could have run a 3.5mm adapter with extension out of the glove compartment as well. I loved eInk, and the fact that I could read outside, even in sunlight. You can't do that on the Fire, plus the lighting can tire your eyes after a while. 2. The device is a lot heavier. Using the SV231DPDDUA2 2-port Dual Display DisplayPort 4k 60Hz unit for this review. Bought it myself for home office use. Initial reactions: - hefty and well-built, and compact too - a TON of ports on the back, like 4 USB ones to plug in devices (i.e. keyboard & mouse or web cam) - no cables (aside from power supply) in the packaging -- **PLEASE** make sure you buy DisplayPort cables (with spares! these things are fickle and I am glad I had some extra laying around) and the proper USB cables to connect your PC to this device Context: I am running two monstrous 1440p displays. I've got a Dell/Alienware AW3418DW (34" Ultrawide 3440x1440 120Hz monitor) and an Acer XB270HU (27" 2560x1440 144Hz monitor). When connected to my main PC with its NVidia GTX 1080, I am able to power both monitors directly through the KVM with no flickering AT THE MAXIMUM REFRESH RATES. That's right, I actually am able to use G-Sync through this KVM -- even when gaming. The Good: Had a bunch of issues during initial set-up so I called the tech support line. My tech, YIPENG from Ottawa(?), was incredible. After an initial text chat, he offered to call me to provide better support, and I am glad he did. For the next forty-five (45) minutes, he patiently walked me through a number of resets and tests to help me diagnose and work around my issue. I seriously cannot say enough about how much Yipeng helped -- I was about to return this KVM, but instead I found joy. The Bad: My other computer is a Lenovo Thinkpad T470, docked in a Lenovo Thinkpad Ultra Dock (model starts with 40A2 and its the weaker of the two in terms of watts -- maybe 135W?). This dock and laptop combination is NOT ideal for for this KVM because the dock cannot put out the signal strength required but I WAS ABLE TO MAKE IT WORK! After much trial and error with Yipeng, we got it figured out: one DisplayPort output from the dock to the KVM, one USB-C to DisplayPort cable from docked laptop's USB-C port to the KVM. It's not perfect but it actually lets me run both of my giant monitors with little to no flickering. The Ugly (main issues): - when switching between the two connected computers, the KVM actually *disconnects* the monitors from the computer that is not in use. This means when you switch back, a lot of your programs/windows will be scattered around your main monitor. This just means I don't switch back and forth unless necessary. - the hardware reset process is a CHORE. You have to disconnect all cables, shut everything(!) down, power cycle the KVM, then slowly begin plugging stuff in again. Only had to do this once or twice during configuration but still it was a drag. - I still get the occasional monitor flicker - every 30 minutes or so - when using my comparatively weak laptop. This is basically a moot point because it's clear that the KVM can work perfectly when my GTX 1080 is sending the signals, but its still something I'd like to see examined or noted somewhere. I am going to test swapping it out so the larger monitor is getting the USB-C/Thunderbolt signal but I am hesitant to change my configuration now that it is working well and has settled. Pro tip: FOR ANYONE USING A LENOVO ULTRA DOCK: the system is likely not strong enough to send out two high-bandwidth DisplayPort signals. If you have it, use a USB-C/Thunderbolt output from the side of your laptop to get a second monitors input to the KVM.

Using the latest Arduino IDE 1.8.10 on Windows 10 and the board support version 1.1.3; the device is problematic to use. The board support currently is annoying to use. 1) Your compile times for the smallest of sketches will take 10 times longer than other Arduinos. I am currently seeing several minutes minimum before I can start the upload. Upload is fast, compile and link is ridiculous. Any small syntax error and you lost another two minutes of your life. 2) The serial connection to the device is problematic. Any time the device resets (after upload, hitting the reset button, etc) the serial port will change. This requires a very specific work flow to not get totally annoyed while you are developing... a) make sure to close all serial monitor windows b) double tap the reset button, then c) select the serial port for the device in the tools menu, then d) compile and upload your sketch, then wait for it to reset (two minutes at least) e) go back to the tools menu and select the serial port again (it will be different) f) finally open the serial monitor e) rinse and repeat until you have a functional sketch And to make things worse, it starts to leave duplicates in the list of serial ports menu. (see picture). You can ignore them as they all represent the same item; but they get in the way of understanding which is the correct one to use. Always look for the one with the name after it (Nano 33 BLE).

I would consider myself a tech enthusiast and an early adopter of technology; so this review is written from an early adopter's point of view with the 2.1 update installed. I will break down the review in several parts to deal with all the features of the headset. Here is the TLDR version: Bragi Dash over-promises and under-delivers at a relatively high price point. The first impressions and aesthetics: The headset is beautifully packaged in a booklet style box highlighting all the features on each flap. Once you unpack and remove the packaging material you have to connect the headset case to a power source to activate the headsets. The case provided has magnetic connectors that connect to each headset. The magnetic connection is nice and secure. Once connected to the case, the dash headset will pulsate a light in various colors to indicate the power level. Blue means full, green means high, yellow means medium and red means low. The case itself has an LED as well to indicate power levels. On the case the green means high to medium and the red means low. There is also an aluminum cover for the case with a slit on the bottom to show LED pulse on the headset. Other accessories include different size fit sleeves and a 6-8 inch micro USB cable, along with the warranty information. The headsets are aesthetically pleasing and snugly fit in the ear with the correct sleeve. Bluetooth range: Something that I was worried about before getting this was the Bluetooth range that I have seen many people complain about. I can personally live with the small range that the headset provides, though I would still describe it as very poor. The right side earbud has the Bluetooth radio so I can place my phone in the right pocket of my pants and still get an uninterrupted audio most of the time; though, not without occasional interruptions. However, if I put it in the left pocket the quality deteriorates immediately and forget about walking away from the phone more than a few feet. In comparison, my Plantronics Voyager Edge headset stays connected for several feet (I would estimate about 25 feet indoors). I must also mention I haven't tried running or any other activity with the headset yet other than listening to podcasts while I stand still. Voice quality: The voice quality on the Bragi Dash is as good as you would expect on a decent headset. Audio quality is clear during the phone calls. The bass and treble have a decent profile when listening to music. I am not an audiophile so I can't say if I am missing out on anything when compared to other, similarly priced headsets. Other features/ sensors: This is perhaps what brings this headset to it's current price point. The headset offers several features other than audio, such as sensing head motion, audio transparency, touch sensors on the individual earbuds, and being water proof. You can shake either earbud to show battery status. Shake your head in yes/no motion to accept or reject phone calls. Tap and slide on the earbuds to control activities such as running, swimming and cycling. I haven't tried the activities yet other than activating them a few times by accident. The audio transparency feature lets you hear your surrounding with amplification. It works great if you aren't really listening to anything. If you are listening to something there is enough noise in your ear already for you to notice and make sense of external sounds. Don't even think about running heavy machinery like a vacuum cleaner or microwave with audio transparency on though, it makes a really loud, amplified clanking / grinding noise and feels like the headset is about to explode. It's actually painful to listen to it. I have also used them in the shower as they are waterproof. Prepping the headset/ Update Process: The headset I got was running on an older firmware and the 2.1 firmware supposedly fixes Bluetooth connectivity issues, though I didn't notice a significant difference in Bluetooth performance from before and after the update. The update process is simple enough. I found their updater program to be useless though. It couldn't update my headset. I used the manual method of copying and pasting the files in the headset's internal memory and letting it update automatically once it's disconnected from the computer. The instructions are on their website in text/ video format and easy to follow. The disappointments: At a price point of $300 this headset lacks a very basic feature of multi-point Bluetooth technology. This allows headsets to connect to two phones at the same time and calls can be taken from either phone and music can be played from one at a time. I use two phones on a daily basis, one for work and one for personal use. With my older headset (Voyager Edge), I could seamlessly switch between the two phones; with this headset, I have to manually disconnect from one phone and connect to the other before making phone calls. This process is not always smooth and adds extra stress in my life. Then another failure happened a couple of weeks ago. For some mysterious reason, my audio stopped going through when making phone calls. I can hear the other side but they can't hear me. At first I thought it could be the mic, so I recorded a voice-clip on my phone. It records voice-clips without a hitch. Next thing I did was delete the device from both phones and paired it again - still no audio. Sent Bragi an email and they replied two days later with instructions on resetting the headset using a different method for updating the firmware. I was already running the latest firmware but decided to follow them anyways. Did as they say but that didn't fix it. And that's where I currently am waiting for Bragi's response (to be fair, I just sent them my reply a few hours ago). I don't know if there are two mics and one of them failed but it has become a really expensive listening only headset. If I had these problems with a headset at a lower price point, I would have been less frustrated. At $300 this is a luxury-priced item with a mediocre experience so far. The Bluetooth connectivity issues, lack of multi-point support and mic failure are three strikes against this super gadget. I wanted to like this headset and I still do. I will follow up with an update if the mic problem is solved. If you are an early adapter and an enthusiast, this might be worth it for you. Not really great for an average user, given how many caveats there are.

I like ever other person here receive a number of pftt calls from unknown people whom I would never want to hear from ever again. Purchased for a non Internet Lane line in a household. We recently upgraded these lines to phone over internet via router and I will post any router based notations with an * in front. Our phone company offers CID with 11 blocked numbers max which is pretty useless to combat these callers. Similar priced alternatives to buying this product: Sentry with the white/black list, the Panasonic multi phone set with 250 Blocked calls, Ooma. However I picked this one over sentry because it was easier to use for non tech savvy people and less confusing for 1st time callers calling twice to get on the white list like with the sentry device. I don't need a new phone system that will only do quarter of the job. CPR allows you to block entire area codes out which is very useful, none of the other phone devices mentioned allows you to do that.. Installation was fast and easy: Literally Wall Jack > CPR > Phone. If you connect CPR to a multiple phones hub station like the Panasonic type with multiple wireless handsets all the associated phones will have the CPR benefits. Phones associated with the same phone number not connected to CPR through other wall jacks will ring once before being disconnected. *With internet router transmitted phone lines there are no noticable differences. The CPR runs off the power from the Phone line so if you are having issues with your phones lines from external elements your CPR may not function correctly. During storm wind & rainy conditions, I had to unplug my CPR for a time because it was blocking all the calls due to issues with our wired phone lines. A battery backup type device might help here however it would not help with poor phone signal strength so therefore I won't hold it against CPR. In fact if your CPR isn't functioning correctly I'd first think it is due to poor signal strength and power transmission. Examples of poor phone signal strength: weak intermittent dial tone, 3 beeps, lots of static, or no dial tone at all.. My phone says "No Line"..Examples for the CPR: blank screen. Screen flickers intermittently on and off. *The phone internet router is powered by residential power thus power outages will probably cut your phone service also interrupting CPR. * Internet signal strength could possibly still be an issue if there are outages and disruptions in internet. CPR blocks 100% Unknown callers.. VoIP ?maybe? FYI Unknown calls come in as "Unknown" no phone #, CID info nothing, just the word Unknown. Much of the time you can not block this number through your phone company because they don't have a record of that number. The first numbers i completely blocked with CPR were the "Unknown" caller and VoIP numbers. After CPR installation those unknown calls have completely stopped. Regarding the VoIP ones maybe? we still receive scam calls from Indian Call centers with spoofed numbers so idk if there is a setting for that.. I thought VoIP was Spoofed numbers, autodialer V#######, or maybe I was mistaken. * No noticable changes from traditional phone lines to via internet phones.. It's possible CPR may need the data through the router from internet to identify the VoIp callers. *I'm not certain if that is the case though. *So far we haven't received any of these types of calls on the new internet based phone setup. Easy Blocking/ Unblocking Blocking numbers can be done by pressing the red button during the call or after from the Call List & Red button.You can also use phone dialed combinations to block during the call but i haven't used it. Unblocking can be done through Block list and find number and press delete. After pressing Block list or Call List.. The block list and Call list buttons act as the UP and Down to scroll through them. When a number is blocked the Line with the CPR does not ring.. However the other lines on other wall jacks not connected to CPR will ring once. Some people are infuriated by this single ring.. however I like hearing it and laugh at them every time they call and it does that. Yes my phones Caller ID (CID) still works through CPR device on the phone. The CPR device doesn't have the Name part of the CID info however your phone set will. CPR still transmits the CID through the device to the phone handset so you can still see who called.. Suggestions to improve the CPR product ..Importance on a scale of (low 1 -10 high) 1) Individual Up/Down arrows. scroll through lists, letters etc. Just to quell the people who want two extra buttons for non tech savvy ppl..4 2) Memory storage for Caller Name editable associated with each stored number.. even 4 letters would be enough but more would be better "SCAM" "WORK" etc..EXGF.. EXBF.. 10 3) # White list. Useful to add phone numbers that may not call frequently and are not bad. 4 4) Battery Backup or Bad Connection power/signal indicator led: I only mention this because the CPR does block all callers.. when there are issues with power / signal strength transmitting through phone lines. The 2 bad connection signals leds would be enough imo. 6

Very nice--now running @ 3200MHz as advertised with my Ryzen 5 1600 system, clocked to 3.8GHz! Got the 8GBx2 package! Recommended! Wanted to add: Here I am many months later and still the performance and reliability is excellent. People should realize that selecting the XMP 2 setting in their bios is the way to go with these--very simple--works ROOB. The bios manufacturers--the company that makes your motherboard--is responsible for implementing the XMP configurations in the board bios, and 3200MHz seems to be easily reached on most if not all Ryzen motherboards by now (Nov '18). If you go for higher clocked ram than 3200MHz, try and verify that your motherboard supports that speed on the highest XMP setting available. If your motherboard does *not* support > 3200MHz speeds via XMP--and you buy, say, the 3733MHz kit, then selecting the XMP setting will only run the ram at the highest speed the motherboard supports--which could be any speed less than 3733Mhz or lower. In that case, it does not mean than the ram will not run on your board at 3733Mhz, it just means that you will have to configure the parameters *manually* outside of using the XMP settings in the bios. The best course is to use the XMP settings, imo, and right now 3200MHz seems universally supported for all Ryzen brands.

This is a nice product, and is useable, but it does have a couple of really annoying design flaws. These design flaws do make using this baseplate feel somewhat awkward, and the cable management is more difficult. 1. When both a Raspberry Pi and a 2560 board are installed, the SD card slot on the the RPi is functionally blocked by a header, on the 2560 board. The small standoffs, that are provided with the baseplate, do not elevate the RPi sufficiently, to clear this header. 2. When both a Raspberry Pi and another board are installed, their USB inputs are on opposite sides of the baseplate, requiring an awkward USB cable connection. 3. The screw holes, for the breadboard retainer clips, are in the wrong place. While each breadboard has an adhesive foam back, these will permanently glue the breadboards in place. If you want to allow the breadboards to be removable, the clips would be used, but with the screw holes in their present position, the clips will cover some of the breadboard holes, when used. Both problems 1 & 2 could be resolved by shifting the 2560 screw-in area to below the breadboard area, but flip it, so that the 2560 board's USB connections are presented along the same edge, as the RPi USB connections. This would result in a more T-shaped appearance. Problem 3 could be resolved by shifting the clips to opposite sides of the breadboards, where they would only press down on the power rail color stripes, and would not cover any holes. If redesigned in this manner, as a T-shaped baseplate, a majority of the cables would be along a single edge,

This is a very nice sounding wireless speaker, overall, I'm happy with it! However there are a few areas where it could improve. Pros: Sound - is on the warm side, with good bass from a small form factor. Highs are pretty good as well. Please keep in mind sound quality will vary depending on the source. Streaming music via Bluetooth is very good, but a bit muffled, and volume isn't as loud. Streaming Internet Radio will largely depend on the source channel, but easily sounds the worst out of the bunch. I can stream Hi-Rez Flacs, up to 192 K, which is great, no need to re-rip anything. Overall, very good sound, good sound dispersal. This thing can get loud without distortion! Design - Light but with some heft, it feels solid and well built. Mostly plastic, with the exception of the cloth speaker cover and the rubberized bottom, which is the unit 'subwoofer' port. The attached carrying strap is a nice touch and swivels in place. Speaker covers are interchangeable. Extra covers are $50, which seems steep. 'Touch Input' on top of speaker is kind of neat, not super responsive, but nice. Slide a finger clockwise/counterclockwise to raise and lower volume. Hold your hand over it and it will 'hush' the unit for as long as your hand covers the button. Unit is also humidity resistant, so you can play it while showering, just don't take it in with you! Connectivity/Inputs - Unit will accept 3.5 mm heaphone jack, and a standard USB port (not tested). External devices/music sources/apps supporting Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, DLNA, AirPlay(not tested). Battery life - seems good, long lasting. Libratone Zipp App shows you remaining battery life. Charges up in about 2 hours or so, for 10 or so hours of playback. Well-made braided power cord supplied for charging. Auto-Shut Off - Unit turns off after a 1/2 hour of no activity. Packaging - Comes in a rigid cardboard tube, Styrofoam on both ends. Speaker is wrapped in plastic. It's well packed and protected. Cons: App - The Android app for this product is pretty spotty at best. App often loses connection with the speaker, requiring a quit/reboot. Once the App crashes or loses connection, you can't adjust volume etc. You can only store 5 Internet Radio Stations in the App. Station information is limited, only shows the name of the station, and location, bitrate would have been nice. However vTuner website will show you more station information. App documentation is pretty bad. Documentation in general could be better, some info in the App, some online, some on paper. Android support seems to be an afterthought, sadly. Color - Ordered Graphite Gray, but received Deep lagoon. it's not a bad color, but it's not what I ordered. I'll probably return it for that reason, after it's a $300 speaker, I expect it to be the color I ordered. Final Thoughts: Overall, I think it's a solid purchase. It needs better Android support and documentation. However if you are using Android, music app N7 supports DLNA streaming via the ToasterCast App. ToasterCast App also let's you stream via Toaster playlist from PowerAmp, my preferred music App. ToasterCast also supports AirPlay. Lastly, I'm also going to run a Rain Storm/White Noise App through this and use it a sleep aid. Just find an app with a timer built in, hook it up to the speaker and that's it. Hope this helps!

I received my MB yesterday and proceeded to build a system with it. Windows 7 64-bit installs and runs mostly beautifully. After some research I found this board does NOT support USB wakup from S3 sleep. If you use a USB keyboard, it will not go into S3 sleep at all, only S1 sleep. S3 sleep turns off the cpu, cpu fan, and much of the logic, just keeping memory and any wakup logic active. S1 sleep does not turn off the cpu or cpu fan, and doesn't reduce the power consumption to very low levels. This also means this board will not work well with USB media center remotes that want to do USB wake via IR remote control signals. Messages on the Zotac website from Zotac customer support confirm this card does not support S3 USB wake. This board WILL go into S3 sleep if you use a PS/2 keyboard (if you enable S3 in the BIOS). It also can power on from a PS/2 keyboard using a key sequence. Due to the S3 sleep issue, forcing me to use a PS/2 keyboard, I'm taking points off the rating. Zotac does make a 9300 based mini-ITX board that is supposed to support USB wake from S3 sleep. Only an updated board rev (that's supposed to ship around November 2009) has this ability. That board is also supposed to support dual-link DVI. The mini-ITX card gives up 2 PCI slots and 1 PCI-x1 slot present on this micro-ATX sized board, and also I believe doesn't have the 1394 port like this board.

I ordered this picture screen so my out-of-state children could automagically send photos and videos of the grandkids, and so far after several weeks, it has performed well. Setup was fairly straightforward despite the semi-ambiguous instructions in the manual, but it was fairly easy to figure out what they meant with a little patience. In addition to sequential or random photo display, the frame can also be used to display weather, time, a clock in various formats (with alarm), music, and videos. Storage can be by cloud, internal memory (8 Gb), USB stick, or SDHC card (full size, micro with adapter, limited to 32 Gb). I use the iPhone app to send files to the frame, but you can also set it up as an FTP server and link to it via a computer. The best feature I’ve found so far is the ability to stand the frame on a table either vertically or horizontally. The majority of photos these days come from smartphones, with an aspect ratio best viewed vertically. The clever simple "1-stick” mount on the back of the device allows you orient the frame “vertically” so smartphone photos are displayed at almost full-frame. I agree with some other reviewers that hanging it from a wall is sub-optimal, given a power cord is required. The controls are mainly from the touchscreen- there are some on the rear- and hence no remote control is included. In actual use, I’ve found that this is not a hinderance- once you set the photos you want, you seldom need to change it. The fact that I got this frame during a $30-off “coupon special” makes it even more attractive. Not sure why some of the Vine reviewers are unhappy with the resolution, I find it certainly sharp enough when viewing from any reasonable distance. So far I’m very happy with it, an easy 5 stars.

This product is for people who want and demand excellent sound quality and are willing and able to pay for it. I have used Shure 530, the Westone 3, Audeo PFE 232, Westone 4 (my former favorite) and now for the last week, the Sennheisers. My home full headphones system includes Beyer T1, Woo Audio WA 2 (upgraded), First Watt J2 amp and Meitner MA-1 DAC (incredible product). I mention these so you know what my reference point and preferences are. Simply put, the Sennheisers are in a class of their own and you can tell that in the first ten seconds. It's that obvious. All the others sound muffled and unenvolving in comparison (apart from the Audeo which sound open but harsh to me). There is no area of weakness. Bass is rock solid and deep, midrange is very involving and the treble is smooth and extended. You hear many more nuances in the recordings driven from iPhone 5 or MacBook Pro 13 inch retina late 2013 model. The beginning of We Belong (Pat Benetar) actually startled me with it's dynamics and clarity. Other tracks were from All the Little Lights by Passenger, Mary Chapin Carpenter, and HD music including Ben Howard (Linn Records), Paper Tiger from Beck or Rebecca Pigeon. All were wonderful with super detail and separation of all the instruments instead of the jumbled mess one often encounters. I know very well that some people cannot distinguish between some free earphones and high quality sound. That's great in a way as you can save a ton of money. But, for those of us who can only enjoy the music when it's well reproduced, these are a wonderful solution short of custom-fitted IEMs. My one criticism is the earbuds. They will not fit everyone and cost a ridiculous amount to replace but I've read that Comply 200 and 500 series fit these and have ordered some to try. Update: I've now tried some Comply tips and they radically affect the sound making it too full and heavy for my taste. You could get that kind of sound for less money. So back to the stock tips and very happy with the product.

When I first purchased this, it was one of several I purchased at once. And to be clear, I have an excellent history with Antec; have been purchasing their aluminum gaming cases for a decade or so, and have purchased/used their cooling fans for a similar stretch of time. Antec is a quality brand, and so long as you pay attention to specifications pre-purchase, you'll never be disappointed if you realize what those specs mean. Here are the cooling fans I purchased on 2012.01.08 (January 08, 2012): Thermaltake Mobile Fan 12 External USB Cooling Fan 12CM AF0007 Thermaltake ISGC Fan 12 Innovative Silent Fan with Advanced Technology, 12CM with Hydro Dynamic Bearing - AF0018 Antec 140mm Cooling Fan True Quiet 140 1 of: Antec 140mm Cooling Fan True Quiet 140 Antec 120mm Cooling Fan True Quiet 120 1 of: Antec 120mm Cooling Fan True Quiet 120 Cooler Master R4 Series Silent 140mm LED Case Fan R4-L4S-10AB-GP (Blue) 1 of: Cooler Master R4 Series Silent 140mm LED Case Fan R4-L4S-10AB-GP (Blue) As those of you who have owned these will probably recognize, these were purchased with silence as the primary consideration, as I had never experienced cooling fans with such low noise levels, and I was unfamiliar with what the CFM numbers really meant with respect to the actual cooling performance, as well as the good old hand-in-front-of-the-fan subjective test of cooling power. To begin with some generalizations, the bottom line is that Thermaltake makes quiet, relatively powerful fans, that Antec had given up far too much power for the sake of silence (silence is useless if it can't cool worth a damn), and Coolermaster's product in question wasn't a master, but a competent apprentice. Both Antec fans were absolutely useless at the low setting. The airflow is barely noticeable with your hand in front of it. If your hand isn't very sensitive, you will probably not realize it's on except for the blades spinning. It's quiet, but USELESS. It couldn't cool a tenth of a degree that mere exposure to the ambient air won't do. Despite its minimal power consumption, the airflow is so incredibly weak, it must be WARMING the target, rather than cooling. Both Antec fans on the low setting are incredibly quiet, but silence is useless with zero utility, and there's no way any honest person would rate these above 0.49 out of ten, so one must necessarily round to zero. These are losers, without question. The Coolermaster was significantly louder, but not nearly as loud as most fans sold prior to this decade, so it was a competent, if not impressively quiet, option. While the word 'SILENT' in the title is misleading, and you can definitely hear this fan even across a reasonable-sized office or living room, provided it's an otherwise quiet room. Within ten to twenty feet, there's no question it's on (again, in an otherwise quiet room), and I wouldn't want it within a couple of feet of my ears with a clear line of sight for longer than a quarter hour at a time. That's a recipe for slow, but certain, hearing loss. Having worked in a class 10 cleanroom, and suffering from that tinnitis ringing that happens when one suffers from permanent hearing loss (thanks a lot, Intel & Micron!), I have no desire to ever make things worse, and the Coolermaster, so long as it is properly placed, is a decent option, although far from the best. But when one factors in its price, it cannot be ignored. If you have need of a 140mm (14cm) case fan, this is a good option, although it lacks speed control. It's either on or off. Now as for the LED lighting, it's a pleasing tint of blue, and it is rather bright. If you want to use this in a room that needs darkness (such as your bedroom or a home theater room), you might want to keep it under wraps, because the LEDs are bright enough to distract in dark environments. But if you want that light, this is a great option. Thermaltake shines in this case, as their fans were decidedly quiet, yet offered a decent amount of airflow even on the lowest setting (more than the Antec fans on low, that's for certain!), and a surprising amount on high, while being more quiet than the Coolermaster. The Thermaltake ISGC Fan 12 (AF0018) was the star of this roundup, and its silence (especially at lower speeds), adjustable fan speed, and excellent airflow (at those noise levels) set a 2012 standard, IMHO, in 12-14 cm 'silent' fans available at Amazon in January of 2012. I purchased another copy of this fan, and if they were still available on Amazon.com, would have purchased two more this month. I still plan to purchase another Thermaltake Mobile Fan 12 External USB Cooling Fan 12CM AF0007 (that's an incredibly useful fan, especially if you're cooling hard drives, in an enclosure or open in a docking bay of some sort, or for cooling an overheating laptop), in addition to newer offerings from competitors (Antec included) to see if they've increased the utility of their offerings. So in closing, the Antec TrueQuiet 120 & 140 were disappointments, and even if you get them at a discount, you will regret your purchase unless you didn't need to cool anything, which is the purpose of a cooling fan. Avoid the Antec TrueQuiet 120 and 140, but I have yet to test the 'Pro' model of each which was released on February 6, 2012, but its specifications likewise fall short of the Thermaltake ISGC Fan 12 (AF0018) by 12 CFM on high, and putting out 2.8 dB more noise on high, but were improved in the airflow department compared to the old model I'm now including in this review. It's too bad the Thermaltake ISGC Fan 12 (AF0018) is no longer available. It was a silent cooling superstar in the 120mm form factor! And finally, the CoolerMaster 140mm blue LED silent fan isn't quite silent, but at under ten bucks, it's great, competent, and while it has no speed control, if it's shortcomings are accounted for, it makes an excellent case fan.

Decided to purchase this one because of all the positive customer reviews. But after receiving the product, I'm not really sure what everyone was so thrilled about. This was *supposed* to be a Christmas present for my dad. Looks like he's getting something else instead. I should have known I'd be in for trouble when I opened the box and unpacked the frame. The front cover of the frame made a "snapping" noise when I first picked it up, as if the black border of the frame was snapping into place. The plastic feels flimsy and not well made. But of course, most people aren't going to carry frames around with them so I didn't let this bother me too much. Besides, I liked the aesthetic of the frame. Next, I loaded up a 16GB Class 10 SDHC card with ~1200 JPGs. Each file was between 250-750kb in size. I also threw on 22 relatively low-resolution 3GP videos that I had taken using an older smartphone camera. I noticed immediately that, when navigating through any menus that read the folder structure off the SDHC card and showed a photo, the device would hang for extended periods of time. Sometimes it would hang for so long (over 60 seconds) that I would assume the device had locked and would just restart it by pulling the plug. So I tried just starting the slideshow. The transitions between photos were absolutely awful; aliased / jagged and jerky. For the life of me, I couldn't find a transition that simply showed the next slide like you would see in a slide show (i.e. no transition effects). The video quality of the device was so-so. I've seen better. I've seen worse. For the price I paid for this thing, I've seen better. Didn't even try the video playback. Of all the 3GP movies I loaded, only a few would actually even show up as "Supported" by the device. So I tried a WMV file that I created using Windows Movie Maker on Windows 7; no luck... the frame said it wasn't supported either. Also, something odd I noticed: Some settings wouldn't stick after unplugging the device. This wasn't consistent; sometimes they stuck and sometimes they didn't. The only setting that I never saw get "reset" from unplugging the frame was the time. Other minor gripes: Boot up time takes longer than I'd expect. The non-photo menus navigated slowly and the kickstand in the back is off-center which will cause the frame to teeter if on a slightly uneven surface. I understand the designer wanted the frame to be used in portrait or landscape mode but there are other ways to design a kick stand that would have made the device more stable. Oh, and the clock defaults to 2010. Could it be that was when this thing was designed and manufactured? Because that would explain a lot... I didn't try the motion sensor or auto-rotate functionality. Sending the device back to Amazon because of the device freezing but even without that problem, I wouldn't pay such a high price for such a mediocre device.

I haven't seen a non-SATA hard drive sold at retail in, what, a decade or so? This page says nothing about the interface of the drive not being what consumers would 100% expect. Sloppy marketing, and now my project has lost a week while waiting for the wrong type of drive to arrive. If you do receive one of these, be very careful inserting them, by the way. New review based on what I learned from Yongnuo support. I deleted my original review in all fairness and deference to the manufacturer to give them time to respond. These seem to be great triggers - I spent more for this version since they have the dedicated buttons and LCD interface which I feel will add value (and hold value) longer. It's nice that they have the ports for wired connections. I *assume* that they provide full functionality for Canon cameras - but I don't have a Canon camera. For folks who don't use Canon or Nikon products (I use Sony a7 with an ISO hot shoe), it's important to note that only the trigger functionality works. I used a YN560-TX mounted on my camera hot shoe, with grouping set, and an RF605C (channel and group matched) connected to a third party Godox/Cheetahlight flash with a PC/minijack cable. >>>Grouping does not work for these third party interfaces - only triggering. This is a disappointment because grouping is not a camera function, and should not rely on special pins on the camera's hot shoe. Grouping originates in the Yongnuo transmitter and terminates in the Yongnuo transceiver, so it is a problem IMHO that they did not enable this functionality between their devices (apparently unless a device senses that it's connected to a Canon hot shoe). After a few email exchanges with Yongnuo and their rep (Eachshot), I still cannot say for certain that this reduced functionality is wholly or in part due to the RF or TX units, but in both cases the manuf talked about old versus new firmware. Firmware cannot be updated by the user, and they were unable to provide information on how to order a newer unit with better firmware. I was not offered replacement units with newer firmware - but only a return due to "customer remorse". Since I can manage having these units only for triggering purposes, I will keep one pair.

Pros: 1: FAST - It's pretty damned fast. I've only seen it hiccup a handful of times, and usually that's only when it's updating some software. 2: Multitasking - It multi tasks like a champ. I'm usually downloading some torrents while watching a movie, and it's never been slowed down by anything I have open or running in the background. 3: Touchscreen is very responsive, perhaps even a little bit too responsive. I've on many occasions accidentally palmed the screen to cause apps and navigation to occur that I didn't want. 4: Ongoing support. This is a biggy. Most tablet makers never update their software to the latest version. Nvidia has stated they'll update this tablet to at least Android L. Overall I'd say this is an amazing tablet, and I can't picture myself getting anything else. That said, it has it's drawbacks. 1: The Micro SDHC card is pretty much a third class citizen. There is no way to change where Apps install by default. They will always go to the 11 GB of built in storage. You will have to manually move every single app to the SD card. This is extremely annoying for a device that only has 11 GB of usable space. 2: In addition to the above issue, when the Apps are moved to the SD card, one of two things will happen. It will either delete the shortcut for that app from your homescreen, or it will leave the shortcut, but bring up an error when you click on it. You will need to re-add all of your shortcuts every time you move an app to the SD card. 3: I plugged in an OTG adapter and plugged a USB 3.0 flash drive to my tablet, and EVERY single shortcut on the homescreen for any app that was stored on my SD card was deleted. The device spazzed out and I had to restart it twice before it finally decided to read the flash drive. 4: The sound isn't the greatest. I'm no audiophile, but listening through the speakers provides sound that is by far inferior to any decent headset. It can certainly put out a lot of sound, but the sound is about average. 5: My Ouya controller did not work for Half Life 2 at all. The game launched, but I just spun around endlessly and was unable to do anything. I was really hoping it would work, since the Shield controller is on back order for the seemingly indefinite future. Anyone know of a place that has it in stock? *Update* 6: I put in a high performance SD card, but I'm only getting 10-15.5 MB/s Write speeds from the internal memory to the card. That's rather disappointing. (It's a Lexar model LSDMI64GBBNL633R) People are getting 41MB/s write speed with this card through USB 3.0, so it looks like getting faster cards might not be all that advantageous. (I don't know how this stacks up with other tablets) *End Update* The Shield Stock Homescreen seems to be the culprit for some of the software issues. Installing the Google Now launcher seems to have cleared up issue number 2. I have not tested issue number 3 yet. *Update* I just got my controller in! So the gaming performance is alright, but so far a little disappointing. 1: Half Life 2 ran OK, I was very disappointed with this port. Right off of the bat I could tell it was a very low effort port, they left in the original menus, and the text is TINY on all screens. I only tried out the first level, where there's almost no action, and I'm getting occasional stuttering. This game is 10 years old and ran perfect on the hardware at that time. With the specs Nvidia gave us, this tablet should really have 0 stuttering issues. 2: Modern Combat 5 also experienced some stuttering in the little amount of time that I played it. Why would there be any stuttering with this title? It's made for tablet graphics and the Shield is far above and beyond the normal tablet level of graphics. 3: Trine 2 and other non-graphical demanding games work just fine. 4: It is pretty awesome to play on the bigscreen, and for the most part it works pretty well. The Android menus and navigation via a controller will take some getting used to, but overall the experience is just fine. 5: With the tablet plugged in, it can pretty much game all day with very little battery drain. I didn't have the controller plugged in, and it did game all day and is still at 75%. That's pretty awesome. *Update 2* I've spent the entire day gaming, and I've come to realize two things. Grid Beta is amazing (AND FREE! OMG!), and GameStream has a long ways to go. Grid: Playing PC games you don't even own, streamed over the internet to your tablet. It is AMAZING. The games play almost flawlessly. I did notice a little bit of input lag with Borderlands 2, but that is more related to my crappy Wisconsin internet and not being on the West Coast, where I believe GRID Beta was meant to be used. GameStream: Ugh! I can play games through GRID almost flawlessly, but my Gaming machine sitting in the room over (780ti, 3770k CPU, 16GB of RAM, hardwired into my wireless router) often ends up down converting the stream, stuttering, and disconnecting from the tablet. I don't understand how I can stream a game from halfway across the country almost flawlessly, but then struggle streaming over my local network. My router is a Single band a/b/g/n with a rated 300mb/s. People are recommending dual band Routers such as the WD My Net N750, so if this crap keeps up, I might consider getting a new router. There's still hope though that nVidia will get there act together and fix the software.

I am a headphone junkie. I've owned more headphones than I can remember for 55+ years. I started as an audiophile, then worked in commercial radio and then as a recording engineer and record producer. Now I'm just an audiophile. I listen to hi-res lossless music mostly as FLAC files on several different DAP's. I own headphones by Neumann, Sennheiser, Shure, Beryerdynamic, Grado, Sony and FiiO. In some cases I own multiple phones from the same manufacturer. Austrian Audio is a spin off from AKG started by some AKG engineers who did not want to follow the company to the US. They are also making studio condenser microphones and several other headphone models. The terms "studio" and "professional" are frequently used to describe headphones. Sometimes they are accurate. Sometimes it is hype. A headphone used to record, mix and equalize needs to be accurate and critical. Unlike some consumer phones which may overemphasize the low end, studio headphones are flat and may seem to lack bass to some ears. The key is flat response, low distortion and high dynamic range. These phones meet my expectations. They have the flat response and dynamic range of a studio phone. They are also quite efficient at 25 ohms. There is a clarity to their sound that is excellent especially in the mid to upper mid-range. The bass response is solid without being heavy. Also, they have good isolation and low leakage. Important in live recording and studio work where leakage could be picked up by the microphone. In comparison to my slightly more expensive Neumann NDH-20's they are at the same high level. They may have the edge on the Neumann's in clarity in the upper mid and high ranges, but barely. They are lighter and more comfortable as well. The Neumann's are less efficient at 150 ohms and need more amplification. Nevertheless, the Austrian Audio phones are comparable. Both are closed back. People frequently comment on the "sound stage" of headphones and consider closed back phones to have a "narrower" stage effect. As an engineer I can say that the "sound stage" is primarily the job of the engineer. Nevertheless, these phones do not sound closed in or restricted. I have tested them on material that I personally recorded and the staging is exactly what I intended. My only negative comment is that the headband can barely extend far enough to fit my large head. Would it have killed them to extend it another half inch? They fit but only just. At $429 they are in the upper price range for me. Are they worth it? Yes, if you are a critical listener with hi-res music and a decent digital player. If you listen to MP3's and AAC's on a smartphone then they are overpriced although they efficient enough to produce a good volume level from a phone player.

The D90 was my first step into DSLR and I chose Nikon because of 20+ years of good past experience with a rock-solid (and very basic!) N2000 and later the digital Coolpix 950. I bought my D90 in June 2009 and for several thousand images it fell in the category "you shouldn't ever feel this close to an inanimate object". I like the way it feels in my hand and its weight isn't a problem for me, although I've seen a few negative comments about that. I'm happy with the bright display. The batteries have lasted well. The controls are where they should be for a Nikon. It was solid: you can easily freeze the hummingbird in the air and the water droplets falling from a dolphin at its apex. It had the kind of responsiveness that you'll recall if you've worked with plain old SLRs (and minus the "lag" of the older non-SLR Coolpix!). It'd be safe to say I love almost everything about the camera...*except* that I've recently run into the F-- lens mount error. I'd read Amazon reviews before buying the camera, but blew off what people had written You can read more about the problem (and 18-135 lens kit) here: [...] and in the results of a Google search of "d90 lens error" or similar. I've removed the lens, cleaned the contacts, etc. but quite often now I'll be squeezing a shot and nothing...sometimes jiggling the lens or remounting fixes the problem. Even slight pressure on the side of the zoom can correct the problem. All I can really say about the problem is that if you don't have it, you'll probably love the D90. If you *do* have it, it's really a deal breaker. In any situation with a moving/changing subject, you almost never have a second chance once you've nudged the lens a bit and tried to clear it. And having that confidence in your equipment that it will work reliably when you need it is unspeakably important. Without the lens mount/electrical contact error, I'd give the camera the highest rating. As is, I now have to figure out what the Nikon terms are on servicing the camera, determine where to send it, etc. All I really want now is to have this camera back working correctly because I think it's a beautiful piece of technology when working.

These earbuds are a major step above any other earbuds I've purchased, in terms of sound quality, level of protection to the inner ear that they provide, and their physical resiliency. These are more expensive than most on the market, but you end up saving money because they are nowhere near as fragile as the other kinds, and the detachable cord means that you don't have to replace the earbuds every time the cord is damaged; you simply detach the cord and send it in for replacement. It's also a lot harder to damage the cord because it's thicker and kind of insulated. I purchased this because I have listened to music, all day at work, for years, wearing earbuds that range in price from $50-$75, and I had begun developing tinnitus as a result. Not wanting to further damage my ears, I switched to,over the ear headphones. These worked really well, but were too unprofessional for work (I looked like an air traffic controller) and didn't work well a at the gym. When I switched back to in-ear earbuds I could really tell how damaging they were; the tinnitus resumed and I began to find it unbearable to listen. I bought these in the hopes that I could find something discreet enough for work, that produced great sound, and didn't damage my ears. Fortunately, these fit the bill. The sound-cancelling element is surprisingly powerful, which helps protect the ears, is great for the gym, and blocks out annoying co-worker chatter. The sound quality is great; not as good as my high-end over the ear headphones, but definitely better than any earbuds I've used before. The sound is buffered to a certain extent which means that it doesn't trigger my tinnitus and, hopefully will help prevent further damage. I have been using these for close to a year now, so this seems to be the case. The only thing I don't like about these earbuds is that they're tricky to remove. This is a great feature for the gym because they do not move, much less,pop out, no matter what I do. This is less advantageous at work, when people come up to my desk and I am unable to quickly slip them out of my ears to answer a question, I kind of have to pause and unwind them and then fiddle with them to get them back on the right way. This is somewhat annoying if I am frequently interrupted, but that's nowhere near as annoying as listening to earbuds with poor sound quality that steadily damage my hearing. The other feature I really, really like about these is that the cord is detachable. With all,of the other earbuds I've used, I found it really frustrating that, as soon as the cord was damaged, the sound would cut out and that was that. No matter how careful I was, this happened a lot, so constantly replacing $50-75 earbuds was really frustrating. With these, the cord detaches from the earbuds; if you damage the cord, you simply send it in for a replacement. Even though these cost more initially than other ones on the market, you definitely save money in the long run. If you like this review please let others know by clicking YES this review was helpful.

Couldn't be happier with this purchase! I was willing to make compromises on this TV as the picture was top notch. Unfortunately there were too many compromises in the end and Hisense support refused to work with me. Picture: Beautiful. 4k, HDR, and SDR all looked fantastic, save for one issue which has been mentioned many times. There is a very noticeable "blooming" around logos or distinct patches of high contrast light. It can be pretty distracting at times, but wasn't a deal breaker. Software/Firmware: Here's where my problems arise. The first issue I ran into was a problem between my Vizio sound bar and TV using ARC. The volume popup box would constantly show up every 3 seconds or so like the ARC connection was reconnecting over and over. The actual sound through the sound bar would be uninterrupted. I was willing to use digital optical instead of ARC as I think ARC can be a pretty finicky technology (in my experience). No issues, I got the sound working with no volume popups. EXCEPT YOU CAN'T FORCE DISABLE THE TV SPEAKERS. Why is this still a thing in 2020? My 8 year old Vizio TV can disable its internal speakers. This leads us to problem #2. Since you can't disable the TV speakers, the remote now increases the volume on both the sound bar and the TV, causing echo. I found YET ANOTHER workaround for this, by plugging in a 3.5mm connection into the headphone jack on the TV. This forces the TV into "Headphones Only" mode which disables the TV speakers. I was willing to deal with this compromise for the sake of the picture. Now on to problem #3. Android OS on this TV is relatively garbage. The first issue that cropped up was trying to play Disney+. I could navigate the app just fine, but when I tried to click Play, nothing happened. No errors or messages, it just acted like I didn't click Play. I learned that a soft restart on the TV fixes this issue. I once again said fine, I can deal with that. Only problem? A soft restart disengages the "Headphones Only" setting, thereby turning the TV speakers back on. If the Disney+ issue was a one time occurrence I would've dealt with it. But it happened multiple times as I used the TV in the first couple weeks. Android OS also froze on me multiple times, with no option but to wait 2 to 3 minutes for it to figure out what it wanted to do, or do a hard restart. Which disengages the headphones only mode. I decided I wasn't putting up with these compromises for the 5-10 years I like to keep TVs. I gave Hisense a chance based on the website Rtings and YouTube reviews, saying they're a legitimate brand now. I'd have to disagree unfortunately - I'm not alone in these issues and their unwillingness to work with me was a big red flag.

I used a Dremel with about a 1/8" thick stone grinding wheel to make this fit a UV-5R+ Plus. When you look at the main photo at the horizontal section of this battery that sticks out under to the front of the radio, there are three raised areas toward the front of the battery. Toward either side there are two raised areas about square shaped. In the center there is a rectangular raised section that goes side to side almost to the raised rather square areas. It was easy using a medium speed on the Dremel to grind down those three areas flush with the bottom of that horizontal area. NOTE that toward the back of that horizontal area on either side against the vertical part, there are two small raised squares. I did not have to grind those at all. I did this with a red and a yellow battery and each fit a red or a yellow Baofeng UV-5R+ Plus. Both batteries fit perfectly each radio. The batteries are difficult to remove however.I use a thin flat blade screwdriver from the front of the radio, to gently slip into the small space at the left add right slighty curved corners on the front to pry the battery lose from the radio. You must of course depress the battery release while doing this. Be gentle so you don't mar or gouge the plastic on the radio and battery.

Works only with Garmin Pilot application on both iPad and Android devices. This new antenna provides synthetic vision to iPad but not on adroid devices at the moment. SynVis is a fabulous feature that essentially replicates my $20,000 Aspen panel PFD and displays terrain, obstacles and traffic in 3D. Not sure what features are available on iPhone. Android version has improved dramatically over the past year or so. It was pretty buggy at first but now solid. Terrain, obstacles, ADS-B weather is available on all devices and operating systems in plan view. Traffic functionality depends on equipment installed in the aircraft. To receive all traffic, the plane must have ADS-B out. My plane added this feature with the Extended Squitter upgrade to the Garmin 330 Mode S transponder. My advice to those who don't have ADS-B out is to use the free FltPlanGo app which works on iPad and android with 5 different antennas, but not this one, so far. It's a remarkable app with most of the features of Garmin Pilot, including geo ref charts, approach plates, airport diagrams. You would get the free ADS-B weather and limited traffic but no synvis, terrain, or obstacles --- yet. You'd get 90% of the features with no subscription charges at all. It also has a number of features Garmin Pilot does not have, such as calculators for temperature conversion, density altitude, runway winds, weight and balance, and pilot logbook. A really good deal and a very slick app.
