I purchased the WD Live Plus HD Media Player to watch movies from my Windows Home server. I got tired of all the DVD's and no where to store them so I built a WHS from an old computer and ordered the WD Live plus. I ran a CAT5 cable to my LCD, hooked up the WD Live Plus and it automatically connected to my WHS. I was up and running in as little as 5 minutes streaming a video on the big screen. The 1st movie played flawlessly until I started to watch the 2nd movie. Towards the middle of the movie, WD Live started to freeze up. At first I thought it was my server so I rebooted the WHS and was back up and running again. Started to watch the movie and froze again. Now I'm getting very upset. Now I powered off/on the WD Live Plus and same issue. Some movies played with no issues and some movies just locked up. Now I'm getting upset with this media Player. I checked WD's website and could not find any solution to the device freezing so I ordered the "Asus O! Player" unit to replace my piece of crap WD live Plus. I was already to mail it back and connect the Asus O! Player but something told me to check the WD support website one more time before I mail back WD Live Plus HD Media Player. I found this on their site: "When playing a movie over a Network location on a WD TV Live HD Media Player, the video may slow down Problem: When playing a high bitrate movie from a Network location (computer or NAS), after a period of time, the video may slow down and jitter. Cause: Samba (the method the WD TV Live uses to read a network location) cannot play back high bitrate movies. Solution: If this problem is encountered there are two solutions: 1. Try playing the content from the Media Server selection on the WD TV Live HD Media Player. This may require installation of a Media Server on your computer. Windows Media Player 11 has a built in Media Server. There are other alternatives such as TwonkyMedia, and TVersity which may also work for these videos. 2. Copy the high bitrate content to a USB drive, attach the USB drive to the WD TV Live HD Media Player and play the content from the local drive". I said Hmmm, "playing a high bitrate movie from a Network location", well this was my problem. I went to TVersity and they explained how the software transcodes any video depending on your network speed and devices for proper streaming settings. So I installed the software on my WHS. During the installation it prompted to install the additional AC3 codec. So I installed it on my server. After installation completed, I configured TVersity to use my Video folder on the WHS and behold video was streaming to my LCD with no issues. Actually I believe the video quality is slighter better now than it was before. So I'll take that back about calling the WD player crap. Now I can say I'm very happy with WD Live Plus and will give it a 4 star rating now. TVersity is excellent software for streaming videos and will help any media player handle video streaming. Oh did it mention that it's free! So go ahead and purchase the WD Live Plus HD Media Player and install TVersity on either your WHS or desktop/laptop and the 2 together they'll make a perfect couple. Enjoy.

I will update this review once I actually get my build completed, but for those wondering, this is a WHITE power supply. POST-BUILD UPDATE: I've now completed my build and have been using my PC for a few days. I still have nothing but positive reviews for this PSU. It's very quiet (my GPU is louder and easily drowns out the noise of the PSU), I've had no issues with any of my components, and the white LED lighting for cables themselves fits my black-and-white theme well. The PSU comes with all of the power cables that you might possibly need with several different connectors (8-pin, 6-pin, 4-pin, etc.), and I haven't had any problems with them so far. They have a nice, thick braiding which looks nice and feels solid. My only complaint is that the 24-pin connector is NOT universal. The 24-pin port on the PSU is weird in that it's actually composed of two smaller ports cables bundled together (I believe a 16-pin and 8-pin). The PSU includes a cable that terminates in a normal 24-pin connector to use with your motherboard, but I wasn't able to use the separate cables that I bought because the 24-pin cable simply won't fit in the 24-pin port on the PSU. There's a tiny bit of space between the 16-pin and 8-pin portions of the port that prevented me from using a standard 24-pin cable. Slightly annoying, but I got over it as the included cables were black and went with my build theme anyway. But something to keep in mind if you were hoping to use custom cables. The rest of the ports are standard and you shouldn't have any issues with those. Definitely recommend for those looking for a white, beefy PSU! I will, of course, update this review if I end up having any issues down the line.

I'm a computer geek from way back. I had systems that dated all the way back to the late early 2000's. The actual systems are long gone sent to the rubbish bin. I kept the hard drives because they contained things I might still want. I kept the SATA hard drives on a shelf in my walk in closet. Just recently after a deep clean I found like 10 of these old SATA drives. All but one still worked. The one SATA drive that croaked had only a backup of the Windows 7 operating system on it. I had no bloody use for that muck. So I set to installing 5 of the old drives at a time in this bulk hard drive enclosure. It was like going back in time. Tons of old files and pictures greeted me. Things I forgot all about but still desperately wanted. By today's standards the drives were tiny most being between 10 GB's, 100 GB's and a few at a whooping 500 GB to 1 terabyte. I downloaded the whole lot to an 8 Terabyte storage brick and again to a back up 8 TB storage brick. I can now safely erase and break up these old drives thanks to this very easy solution. The nice thing is that pulling data off five drives at a time was very much a time saver. I got things sorted in about two days. The fast USB bandwidth moved my files quickly the only limit being the slow old drives. There is nothing difficult about configuring this enclosure to see and access the 5 drives. There is NO special software or geeky knowledge. On Windows 10 it was just plug and play. There are 6 bright blue LED's on the side of the enclosure. One to show the unit is powered. 5 to show the drives in residence are operational and recognized. Windows 10 discovers the drives readily. At first their might be a few minutes before Windows see's the drives for the first time. When in doubt just restart. Be aware that you should remove the USB connecting this 5 Drive enclosure to your computer because often times these old drives have boot sector start ups and operating systems on them. These other OS's on these drives could confuse your start up processes and cause your system to hang. Let your system start first then once the Operating system is fully up and running only then do you plug in the 5 drive enclosure. Wait a few minutes and Windows should recognize the drives. It's your call but at times Windows will ask to scan and correct flaws it finds on the older drives. I'd say unless you know very well what you are doing always refuse to let Windows "Fix" the drives because if the Window's fix breaks the drive it might not be recoverable. I'm advising caution when asked to let Windows repair a drive but of course its your call. Hope this helps. The 5 drive enclosure was worth its weight in gold for me as it brought back pictures and documents of old I'd forgotten about.

So I'm moving and needed something to replace my existing stereo in a smaller apartment. I had a Denon component system with Polk surround sound studio speakers and a 12" subwoofer. I don't post that to brag, rather to give perspective of where I'm starting from. Despite having a pretty nice set up, I would not consider myself an audiophile, rather someone who knows quality and bought accordingly. So back on topic. Bottom Line: For watching TV and movies, this sound bar is pretty good. If you plan on using it for streaming music through your TV, it will need some adjustment. The speech for TV shows and movies is very clear and the sound is somewhat balanced, although the bass is a bit low. The subwoofer is on and fires, but clearly it's not the priority because it prioritizes the highs and mids to amplify speech. As a result, if you put on Amazon music (running it through your TV), the music sounds extremely high and bass even on dance/hip hop is way too low. This is likely because the sound bar doesn't realize it's playing music versus watching TV. When I switched the sound bar to bluetooth and adjusted the equalizer on my phone to compensate for its factory settings, the music sounded reasonably good considering the price of the system. It's not a super powerful system and you will not rattle your windows with the bass, but it should be sufficient for a medium sized apartment or normal sized family room. Does it compare to my Denon stereo? Of course not! But I have about $800-$1000 in that stereo compared to the $100-ish in this sound bar. Is the Denon 10x as good as the sound bar? Also no, but I'd say probably about twice as good, so take that for what it's worth. For additional perspective. I also currently have a Vizio sound bar on a different TV. I added my own subwoofer I had on hand from a previous sound system. The sound from the Vizio with my subwoofer is better across the board. The sound is more balanced for all things (music, tv, and movies). I was going to buy another Vizio with a subwoofer already incorporated, but the price was nearly double of this system, so I first tried Wohome 2.1 system... I do NOT recommend that sound bar (TV and movies were oaky, but music had a strange hollow sound). After returning the Wohome, I figured since I have a TCL TV, why not try a TCL sound bar. This is a big bright spot. Set up was as easy as you could possibly expect. Literally take it out of the box, plug the HDMI into the ARC HDMI on the TV, and plug in the power cords. The TV took care of everything else. In conclusion, if you are looking for a budget sound bar to use with your budget TCL TV, this is a really good option. You are getting a little bit more than you are paying for and it will definitely be an improvement over the TV speakers while giving you an option for playing music from your phone.

After 4 months of anxiously waiting for this product, I finally have it installed in my machine. Was it worth the wait? Well, I guess you will have to keep reading... Upon receiving a notification that my package had been delivered at my door, I was as giddy as a 5 year old on Christmas morning. Accompanying my bracket was a Corsair H90, 140mm for gratuitous amounts of cooling! After settling down after a long day of work, I sat down and began to rip off my XFX R9 290's stock cooler like a high school prom after party. Once I got down to the nitty gritty, I cleaned off the surface, just like after a long long night of making sweet love with lefty. After a year a having a volcano and a tornado, all at once, in my case for the past year, I can tell you I was ready for this moment. I had been saving myself for my whole life for this moment, and it was about to go down. Yanked the stock blower off the old rad and screwed it hard into the Corsair HG10 A1 Bracket. Mounting the shroud around the blower was easy enough, 4 screws and done. Now came time to put the piece de resistance on my naked 290. The bracket slipped on easy enough my 7 year old nephew could do it, followed by a couple screws provided in the packaging. Now it came time for the finale. I had been saving up for this exact moment in time, the moment everything in life is put into perspective. I placed the 4 long stand offs on the board (just like the directions ask of me), and careful set my block onto the jewels. With 4 thumbs screws the job was done, and I had made myself one sexy card. Pros: Back to reality, this product is fantastic. I followed it ever since they announced it in June and eagerly awaited all 3 release dates they promised. On the topic of the bracket, it is super easy to put on and the directions are pretty straight forward. The bracket is made of solid metal; it is definitely made of quality material and you should not have to worry about breakage or bending. It is compatible with every Hydro Series cooler, so your options are still very wide open as far as which water block to use. Cons: The first point of criticism is the placement of the screw holes to mount the bracket to the PCB. I found that when I screwed in all of the anchors, the end of my PCB underneath the blower fan started to bend slightly. In fact, there are no anchoring holes in the bracket past the VRM on the reference PCB. I was concerned at first, but I quickly got over it. My second concern was the mounting hardware used to secure my water block to my GPU. The holes in the intel mounting bracket don't exactly line up with the long stand offs so you have to force the block a little bit to get the thumb screws in. Once I figured out that the standoffs are not meant to fit through the holes, I placed the thumb screws in and had the block tightly secured to my GPU. Thoughts: Corsair had a huge campaign with this card with the idea to beat the NZXT G10 bracket in the GPU AIO mounting catagory, but it took them too long. After the idea was released in the beginning of June, the first release date was set at the end of August (I can't remember exactly, but it was around this time). It was not released and the community brought up many questions regarding the legitimacy of this product and if it would ever come to the market. After another release date was set for the end of September, and again at the end of October, I had all but given up on the release of this bracket. Corsair let me down 3 times and I was literally 4 clicks away from purchasing a custom loop for the card because it had not been release. Finally released in November, and I am a very happy customer. Hopefully this has been a good experience for the Corsair marketing team. I believe they put together too much of a campaign for this card even though it was not ready for market. Atleast the final product came through and met all of my expectations and more (Unlike ESO, that was just awful!). Thank you for the hype around the card, I definitely have to hand it to you for getting me excited for this bracket, but please, it was more of a cock tease waiting forever for this card. I will keep this review at 5 stars because this product really does say what it should; my R9 290 is finally able to hit 100% and not throttle itself. It really does make a huge difference and I can finally unlock the true potential of my GPU. Thank you Corsair for this amazing product, and I look forward to more as the company continues to pursuit more and more to solve a previously unsolved issue.

I like this a lot, even though I don't exactly know what I'm going to do with it. I wanted to type up some parts that were kind of frustrating for me though so you can be sure to be prepared when you order it. I didn't have any problems at all with the image Uniker provided and once I figured out how to assemble it. I've also provided some pictures to help. The pictures of the product on this listing helped me a lot too. As soon as you order this, you should download the rar provided in the FAQ and make sure you have a micro SD card that is at least 8GB big. You will also need the Raspberry Pi 2 of course. While waiting, you'll need to mount the img file in the rar on the SD card, that will be about 20 minutes or so. You'll also want to make sure you've got a plug to USB connector and a USB to micro USB cord. When you get it, you'll notice it comes with no instructions, just some plastic pieces and some screws of varying kinds. Firstly, you'll notice you have four metal spacers with matching small nuts. You'll also notice they fit the four screws that stick out of the LCD board. As fun as that is, you'll only need to do one of them - on the top right of the board. Screw the spacer on the top right of the board, put the screw on the other side of the spacer on the top right hole of the raspberry pi 2, and use one of the small nuts to keep it attached. Then, put the U HDMI connector so it goes on both HDMI ports. Put the micro SD card with the image mounted in the Raspberry pi's micro SD slot. You'll notice you have some hardware that is plastic - take the plastic spacers and plastic nuts and put them through the remaining three holes on the Raspberry Pi, using the nuts to keep them held on. Place all the hardware into the case, pressing carefully to make sure the LCD screen is pushed through the hole all the way. Take the plastic piece with the two longer screws, and line up the screw holes - neither way you position it will match the board, but that part's purpose is to hold the LCD board against the case. Finally, put the back on, using the plastic screws to go through the three holes to the three plastic spacers you put on the Raspberry Pi. You'll need to remove these plastic screws to get at the SD card again, so be gentle so you don't strip the screws.

I'm absolutely loving this monitor. There are number of things that I really like about it: The ultra wide format is especially useful. I can get several full size pages side by side without the annoying gap that you would have when placing 2 monitors side by side. It also occupies less space than placing multiple monitors side by side. I really like the fact that it has 4 USB 3 ports available. A lot of monitors seem to skimp and use USB 2 ports but the Dell has the Super Speed USB 3 ports. For me, this is helpfull because I keep my desktop computer on the floor where getting at the ports is not always handy. I can connect a USB 3 HD off the monitor where it's easily accessible and still get the full USB 3 performance. It's also worth noting that the 4 USB 3 ports are are divided up between two USB input ports. This allows you the versatility of connecting to two different computers if you like and having two USB ports per computer. One of the USB output ports is also a high current (2 Amp) charging port for rapid charging of your cell phone, tablet, etc. Having a stand that is height adjustable is also very nice. I would think that this should just be a standard part of any monitor, much like tires on a car, but for some reason far too many monitors, even very expensive units, seem to omit this feature these days. The general construction of the monitor appears to be first rate. Nothing at all about the monitor feels cheap or flimsy. The glass is almost completely edge to edge with only the slightest of bezel edge on 3 out of the 4 sides. The bottom edge has a bit of bezel and this is where the touch controls are located. I'm also very happy with the most important part of the monitor - the screen. The colors are bright and vived and the screen has a wonderful consistency accross the entire width. The only inconsistency that I notice is that the extreme lower left and right corners seem to have an ever so slight darkening. I notice that I only see this when I'm pretty close to the monitor. Push it back a few inches on the desk and the problem disappears. In normal usage, it hasn't bothered me at all. The only negative thing that I can say about the monitor is that the speakers really are not that great. Don't get me wrong, for speakers built into a monitor they are very good. They provide plenty of volume but they're no match to even a fairly low end set of external computer speakers. There's no real base and the sound is rather tinny. For general computer usage they are fine, but if you are going to be listening to music, or watching videos with decent audio, plan on having some external speakers available. Another plus for me is that Dell stands behind the monitor with a 3 year warrenty that even guarantees that there will be not even one bright pixel. When all is said and done I feel like the monitor is worthy of its premium price and wouldn't hesitate to buy it again.

EDITED 11/17/12: I have now been using my Kindle PaperWhite for about a month, and I love it. It is by far my favorite eReader device, and I find that I am reading much more now that I have this device because it is so comfortable to use and much easier for me to read on than the other eReaders and tablets. The software update that allows me to remove the "recommendations" from the bottom half of the screen solved my main complaint about the PaperWhite. Even my young son prefers it to the Kindle Fire. I think he likes the feel of it, and he also seems to like that the pictures in his books are black-and-white, which makes it easier for him to focus on the words. ORIGINAL REVIEW: My husband has a Kindle Keyboard, and I have a first generation Kindle Fire. I have also borrowed my mom's Kindle DX, which was also very comfortable to read on. The Paperwhite is hands down my favorite eReader. I can read for hours on it, thanks to the ability to change the font size, margins and line spacing to make the print as comfortable as possible. The light makes reading in every lighting condition a joy. Although I do see the slight variation in the screen light at the bottom of the screen, it is very minor and doesn't bother me at all. I don't see any of the weird colors that other people have reported. It's still a much better screen for reading than the regular Kindle Keyboard screen or the Fire. I find the touch screen to be very easy to use, and I really like the page turn capabilities. I also find the "time to read" and real page numbers functions to be excellent additions. Unlike my first generation Fire, I can organize my books into collections, which makes it much easier to find what I'm looking for. I find the touch screen keyboard to be nice and responsive, and the location of special character keys and numbers easy to navigate. I have minor gripes, but nothing that takes away from my enjoyment of the Paperwhite -- I prefer it over print books for the lighter weight, lighting and font adjustments alone, and I prefer it over my old Fire, which is unreadable in sunlight, too heavy to hold for long bouts of reading, and too distracting with the games and internet. I also prefer it over the Kindle Keyboard and DX for the lighted screen and the "time to read" functions. I don't use audio for my personal reading, so the lack of audio is not an issue for me. I have my music on my phone, and I am not a student or visually impaired, so I don't need immersion or text-to-speech functions for my own reader. So, all in all, this is a winner for my reading device. One final comment: I do not have the 3G version because I have access to Wi-Fi at home and work, and can usually find a hotspot when I am out-and-about. I found that this was sufficient when I had my first-generation Fire, but it does mean that I have to make sure I have plenty of reading materials loaded onto my Paperwhite for trips. The memory is more than sufficient to hold plenty of books, though, since they take up a lot less space than movies, games or music.

I originally purchased this so that I could test out what kind of switches I wanted on my keyboard, and for that it was quite useful. It came with 9 switch variations, although most of them are pointless for me, as I was going with a corsair keyboard and only needed to test a few switches. But it's great if you plan on buying alternate keyboard brands with better switch variety. The test kit itself is rather simple: 9 keycaps on top of 9 types of switches. It comes with a keycap remover which was kind of tricky to use because the keys don't stay in the base easily at all. They fall out with a slight pull. And seeing through the keys is trickier for some of the switches that look similar in color, so you have to remove the keycaps to see them properly. The keys felt pretty good, but due to the lightweight base, you don't get a substantial mechanical feel. The base needs to be weighted down with something, as it makes all of these keys feel hollow. You can still get a decent idea of which keys you like based on the smoothness/bumpiness/clickiness of the actuation points on each switch, though, so it serves its purpose well anyway. I ended up going with Cherry MX Browns for my Corsair and I don't regret it one bit. I do wish corsair made keyboards with those Cherry MX White switches though, because those felt amazing on the test kit. It's like a brown with a bigger bump. Overall, I recommend this test kit if you wanna figure out what keyboard switch you're into before shelling out $100+ on one. I just wish it was a heavier product.

I got the 30mm f/1.4 Art and while the focus seemed okay at first, it was clear after a couple of outings my keeper rate was pretty low. When it was in focus it was sharp, it just was usually a bit blurry. After some research, my options were either to send the lens in to Sigma (some folks say they need your camera too) or get this thing. Even though the focus issues are covered by warranty, you still have to pay for insured shipping each way. With that in mind, the dock seemed a little less unreasonable in price. Besides, I like tinkering with things. It took me about an hour and a half of work to dial in the right values, though an hour of that was pretty ineffective. The thing is, they just give you the dock and you download the software, and there is no official recommended way to come up with the adjustment values. I recommend browsing around for focus calibration tutorials. What ended up working the best for me was to be in a bright room at relatively high (but not too grainy) iso, and have a tape measure leaning against a wall at an angle. Then I focused in at the 1ft marker at various distances. After several iterations of trial and error I was happy with the focus at all the adjustable distances, I ended up with +1, +10, +8, +9 from closest to furthest. There are specialized devices, which have a ruler at an angle and something to aim at, and can even be mounted to tripods, but they are pretty expensive for what they do. What would bring this dock up to a 5 star, must have is if Sigma threw in a focus calibration device to accompany it and a guide on how they recommend you do it, a video on the website at least! There are other comments about the choices of adjustable distances (in this case .3m, .4m, .6m, and infinity), but that is how lens focus works, if you look at the range finder, those distances are spaced equally apart. It seems weird, but gives you the best coverage for the entire lens range.

This is my third Garmin unit in the last 10 or so years. My last one was a StreetPilot 2720, which I still use and love, while my wife primarily uses this 765T and I do when we drive her car. This review is based mostly around the NJ/NY metropolitan area. I really wanted to like this unit, but my wife and I both hate it: 1. Routing is really terrible, especially compared to the 2720. The routes are so convoluted sometimes, it makes absolutely no sense at all. This is a frequent occurence, while with the 2720, it was a pretty rare occurence. 2. It's slow to refresh, especially compared to the 2720. 3. It gets caught behind quite a bit. The 2720 lets you know ahead of time that a turn is coming up, then again about 3 to 5 seconds before you actually have to turn. This one warns you the first time, but the second warning comes 1 second before to several seconds AFTER you were supposed to turn. 4. As others have said, the traffic feature is a nightmare. It constantly changes it's mind, and it will take you on the most insane side routes to avoid what it thinks is traffic. The side routes always take longer than your common sense. These avoidances have increased our travel times significantly so many times, we finally just turned it off. 5. The bells and whistles such as lane assist are sort-of useless since it only shows up in about 1 or 2% of situations. So overall, a real piece of crap, I'd say. The basics are so poor, and it has ADDED time to our trip so many times, we cringe when we need to rely on it for a trip, and especially when we think we bought the "Top of the line." For all you out there thinking about a new GPS device, do something I forgot to do: buy something cheap with the basics because all the state of the art technology usually takes some time to iron out, and you can buy it for half price later.

I am an amateur Nikon shooter... that is to say, I don't make any money off of it and it is just a hobby. This is my 3rd Rokinon lens (I also have a Tamron, and many Nikon lenses both DX/FX and pro lenses). When I received this lens I thought the same 3 things I thought when I got my other 2 Rokinon lenses.... 1) It really feels like a quality lens in my hands. 2) What an incredibly sharp image such a "cheap" lens takes... and 3) Worst/cheapest lens cover ever. The first 2 are so good, I end up forgiving the 3rd. These wider angle lenses really let you capture things typical lenses cannot. When shooting in situations like street shots and especially for things like inside museums... they always end up getting my best shots that I just couldn't get with any other lens. These Rokinon's are manual... but honestly, that really helps teach you how to take a good picture and once you learn the nuances of focusing yourself, it is quite easy and sometimes even preferred over an auto focus lens. Did I mention this thing is sharp? The price for Rokinon's are also incredibly reasonable, and at times kind of a steal, largely because they do not have some of the functions like autofocus. This particular 14mm doesn't provide a drastic "fisheye" effect that the 8mm and lower does.... so if you're looking for that strong effect go for a lower mm lens. But this one provides excellent wide angle abilities with out an intense distortion... especially on a DX. It's f2.8 which really makes lower light situations easier as well... again, for inside places like museums and building photography this really comes in handy. I really can't say anything bad about this lens... the only things people will typically complain about is the lack of autofocus, size, weight... but all of that is done on purpose to keep a product that creates a really high quality image while keeping the cost of the lens down... and Rokinon seems to really have that concept down successfully. Don't let the fact that it's not a "brand" name lens deter you... take a little time to get to know it and it'll prove itself to be a more than capable lens in your kit.

I do know how I want music to sound (highs and mids accurate, but with a little bass/rhythm section punch) AND how I want a bluetooth device to work/integrate with my music apps (streaming or local to the phone/tablet). I use these devices almost daily....bluetooth adapter in a pocket, phone usually very close, but sometimes walk out of range. The BTR1 just works as advertised for everything I've put it through for 6 days (several hours/day) so far with 2 different IEMs (Panasonic cheapie and a new pair of FIIO FH1) as well as a full size headphone (Sennheiser Momentum 2.0 enclosed). I've had several conversations outdoors and/or in a noisy environment, and the callers haven't yet made any 'can't hear you now' comments or other voice dropout issues. If something changes as I continue to use the BTR1....I'll update the review. One last tidbit, I wasn't supplied a unit in exchange for a review, nor did I receive any discount for providing a review. June 15 2006 - Unlike some of the reviewers, I couldn't care less about music "services" be they iTunes, Rhapsody, etc. Why pay 0.99 to anyone for DRM crippled tracks? The artist doesn't benefit. I listen to CDs I have bought and ripped. For that purpose, this unit works beautifully with *any* OS including Mac X, WinXP, even Linux. The e270 can act like a flash/keychain drive: just go into the Settings menu and change the USB mode. The e270 also shows the album art (folder.jpg) while playing tracks. The e200 series has a beautiful display, better than the Nano. I wouldn't whine about the design being imitative: the Nano has better quality buttons/wheel, the e270's controls are comparatively flimsy-feeling and are harder for large fingers to operate. Besides, didn't Apple copy from *Creative's* mp3 players in the first place? The courts are reviewing that question now. THE ISSUE. My only issue is that the USB cable is proprietary, mandatory, and irreplaceable. And, Sandisk is currently unable to provide a replacement if you lose it. Without the special Sandisk USB cable, you can't even recharge the on-board Lithium battery, and also there's no wall wart for AC power available either. By contrast, my previous Sandisk e140 player (a 1GB model) uses an AAA battery --and the same USB cable most digital cameras use. Battery- and connection-wise the e140 is a better solution, but the drawback is a dim monocolor display. If you have good eyesight, the e140 is a great economy player; but the e270 is the ultimate luxury toy. Everyone who sees my e270 is smitten. UPDATE July 6th - Sandisk says it is _now_ able to ship me a replacement "e270 to USB" cable, so give them credit for that. Also, according to internet rumor, Griffin makes an e270-compatible wall-wart (AC Power) solution. Finally, no solution is available yet to the "cannot play-tracks-in-album-order" issue, a problem I failed to mention above. This might drive you seriously insane when you play Mozart or Beethoven on the thing when the IV movement isn't played fourth. Or, when an mp3 audio book can't be played in chapter order! We're waiting every day for the firmware update from Sandisk that fixes this track ordering bug.

It's definitely an interesting find. I was reading a lot about this and other USB wires, in attempt to better my existing "cheap" Emotiva USB cable. I have found this wire a pleasurable listen, but lacking detail. I am very price conscious when it comes to wires, so given the price I had to return it. PROs: - neutral sound without coloration reflects instruments and voices correctly - they just sound right - adds significant, but pleasurable sound signature to the music - bass is elaborate, and detailed - wider than average soundstage - classical, electronic and quiet rock sounds fantastic CONS: - biggest con is the lack of detail. it made my system sound pleasurable, but as if i traded in my speakers for a cheaper ones. this also means that despite this cable plays 192Kbps/24bit material, you can't tell the difference between 44Hz and the anything higher. i am pretty sure that AQ decided that this is the exact amount of detail a user is going to get for the price. in the same setup my Emotiva MUSB is far more detailed, and using it i can tell the difference between 44Hz and 96Hz (not hearing the difference above that may not be its fault, as well) - midrange lacks details, and seems dry - despite sounding pleasurable, adds sound signature, so i can't call it being true to the original - on energetic and complex rock tracks tends to sound muddy in midtones, and not dynamic I really want to hear how the really expensive AQ wire sounds, but I am not going to pay that price. First thing to note is that this product does not technically include the case shown in the photos. Many people commented that they received the case. I did not. I reached out to Amazon's customer service. At first they clarified that it is not listed as part of what you'll get delivered. Which is true. But they understood the misleading nature of this product listing and offered to send me the case for free as compensation. Here is that case if you are curious: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0897CMGMD Second. I bought this not because I need a portable machine. I have an excellent MacBook that is super thin and light and has a full-size keyboard. But I have been wanting a basic drawing tablet to help me think through some of my ideas while designing software. I thought about getting a Remarkable e-ink device or one of its many competitors. But those are typically $500 and more once you add in the stylus, case, and so on. I couldn't bring myself to spend that much on something so limited. Even if the reflective e-ink screen is cool. But I could get behind spending $250 for a device that's a full Android tablet with a pressure-sensitive stylus. It turns out that this tablet is much better than I was expecting. The screen is very bright and color-rich. The speakers are decent for playing music with. And the device seems speedy enough to run a web browser and other typical apps. I don't plan to use it for gaming. But for comparison, I have a top-performing $3,500 laptop and various other devices I use daily. As a software engineer I have a good sense of what sort of performance to expect. Battery life seems plenty good too. Although this is a refurbished unit, I don't see any evidence of past use or damage. It is in like-new condition. I downloaded the free Sketchbook app and started painting with it. I was amazed at how cool it is. I haven't done any serious paining or drawing for a long time. This felt surprisingly natural and impressed me. It's not like the ever-incredible PhotoShop and won't do anywhere near the things I typically need from PS. But it is super easy to figure out and use. My wife, who is a daily doodler, also enjoyed using it for this purpose. It's worth noting that it's fairly easy in Android to set up multiple Google accounts so you can each log in and have access to your own email and such. On the whole I'd say this is a success. Especially for a tech nerd who wants an expensive substitute for paper and pencil.

4 stars only due to the active-x control that forces you to set this up using internet explorer. Set up is pretty simple and the wireless has good range. You also need to keep the browser open to save video/images. I use I-Spy which is free and can be minimized to your system tray. Has a ton of features. Camera does well indoors, the IR LEDs provide excellent illumination in a light colored room, but due to the .5 lux rating, it struggles in a dark colored room (IR reflects more on white walls than wood paneling or dark blue walls etc). If you're looking to use this camera pointed out of a window, do NOT expect this to work well. The IR reflection from the LED's when on blind the camera (an issue with ALL IR cameras with the LED's positioned around the lens) and the LUX rating of .5 makes this camera return a mostly black image when the IR is turned off. So, again, indoor = acceptable to great, pointed outside = acceptable during the day, worthless at night (without modifications).

First problem: From the promotion, I thought the screen would be noticeably bigger than the screen on my first Paperwhite model (which I like very much). I was mistaken: the screens are exactly the same size. Second, and bigger problem: The new "Auto-Sync" functions is truly annoying! I wish I could disable it since it causes more hassles and wastes more time than it's worth. For example: When I added some books from my cloud directly onto the new device (so I can read them without being connected to the cloud), I created a Collection for them, as usual. BUT, when I decided to go back to the cloud to find some additional books to add to my device, the stupid Auto-Sync function made a virtual copy of the collection I had made, added it as a 'virtual' collection to my device, and threw all the books I had put on my device out of the collection I had created so they were all back to being individual items again. To fix this mess, I had to delete the 'virtual' collection from all devices, then use Airplane Mode to disconnect from the Cloud, then re-create a new collection for my books. I'm afraid to turn off Airplane Mode because the same mess will recur, so I can only use the new device to read the books I already have on it. I'm very disappointed! I hope an upgrade will be made to the program to both fix this bug and also provide a disabling option to allow Auto-Sync to be turned off so I can go to the cloud without messing up my device's carefully created collection, as is possible with all my other non Auto-Sync devices. I still love my original Keyboard Kindle and my first Kindle Paperwhite and use them all the time.

REVISED REVIEW 12/07/13 of the QC818-461 (8 POE channel NVR with 4 cameras & remote) PROs: All 8 channels have POE (Power Over Ethernet) - enough to power your average IP camera. Q-SEE is well known and established. So far I get quick responses to emails from their tech support. It comes with 4, 720p IR LED (internal Infrared night lighting). Cameras have built-in mounts. The software (in firmware) looks unassuming at first but it is VERY good and VERY well thought out. Everything you need is here, if you just look for it. It comes with 4, 100ft rolls of Cat5e Ethernet cable. The DVR has expansion room for a 2nd hard drive that you (yes you) can install). ** sometimes ** (not always), one or two of my Q-see cameras that are more exposed to the elements just deliver video in black and white. When the temperature warms up (it's winter right) and/or when the sun is fully up (say 7:45am) the issue goes away. My nicer cameras that I bought separately lose color saturation by degrees - not all at once. The Q-see IP cameras are still probably better than most "Old skool" (analog) CCTV cameras out there. It was very simple for me to obtain and add an additional 1 Terabyte SATA hard drive to this unit. 10 minutes and a Philips screwdriver. You connect two cables and you're done. I now have a 2 Terabyte system since adding the additional 1 Terabyte drive. With 5 cameras in use, set to high quality,I can go easily 5-6 days of constant recording without having to overwrite any video. Have not setup motion triggering on this system and don't know if I even want to. The replay (review of recorded video) software they give you (under "Search") lets you go back and winnow things down to time slots of days, hours, 30 minute window, etc. CONS so far: *This Q-See 818-461-1 NVR does NOT transfer data and display images from my 3 megapixel Hikvision IR IP camera (which is great in every other way - I view those pics on my PC.) Q-See vendor support confirmed this re Hikvision camera incompatibility. * Only 6 character passwords allowed. It should be minimum 12. I don't like this but it's a minor complaint in an otherwise good value. * The Ethernet cable needs to be unwound carefully. Reason: Highly prone to kinking when weather is colder and you are doing cable pulls through a 3/4 or 1" hole saw hole. I can recommend this "as is" if you are in "Get it done" mode on a budget. HEADS UP / FYI: If you want to run a high current gain POE device like a PTZ camera with a built-in heater, etc, this Q-See system may not have enough POE power to cover multiple high drain devices. I bought this setup because some jerk stole two packages off my porch a couple weeks ago. The first thing the police said is: Did you see the theft happen at the moment it happened? Do you have any pictures? I immediately arranged to have all packages sent to my work location and then I immediately ordered this setup. I * was * planning on (next year) building a mega system based on a Synology NVR, but I needed something NOW for peace of mind. I will soon also have a 2nd system (Windows 7 Pro PC with Foscam "Blue Iris" software installed. So my particular system (when it's finished) will be a hybrid of this Q-See off-the-shelf setup and a Windows setup. There is another big box store in the US (W something) that typically sells this kit/package at $100 less (sometimes even $200 off) brand new. I knowingly paid the extra $200 to Amazon due to their excellent customer return policy and backing. Turns out that was unnecessary. Now knowing how reliable this system is and that I want to keep it, if I could do it over again, I might have gone with an Amazon seller to save some bucks. It's just that security camera systems were new to me a few weeks ago. THE ABSOLUTE WORST THING YOU WILL DEAL WITH * ANY * WIRED SECURITY CAMERA SYSTEM: Pulling multiple Ethernet cable runs for multiple outdoor mounted cameras YOURSELF in the winter. Not for everybody. I did all the drilling and wire-pulling and trips back and forth to the attic and outside ladders 12 feet up on my own. I drilled holes in my house in places to make this happen (involves later patching/painting, etc). It's LOT of work if you are installing more than 1 camera. Heck it's a lot of work PERIOD. Not for the faint of heart if you have no background in it or are not handy with tools, etc. If you are not up for that consider having an electrician do a "proper" Ethernet wiring pull. I would place a value on my personal aggravation of the cable pull of $500.00 easily. The amount of cussing, trips to the attic, going under the crawl spaces, yadda yadda. Do you really want to spend your free time this way? If so, yeah it works. Note: If you want to reduce the size of holes you drill in your house, you would want to acquire RJ-45 male ethernet plugs, an RJ-45 crimp tool ($25.00) and Google/download a color layout instructions for the "pin out" (wiring layout) of Cat5e Ethernet connector. Plan B, if you are in a hurry..you * could * drill much larger holes than the cable itself(i.e. 7/8") in your house and feed the uncut 100ft Ethernet cable through the hole as is and leave all the excess cable in your attic or crawl space, then recaulking, repainting the hole. It's certainly a less professional method by a longshot but you'll get it done. (Not everyone has 500+ dollars to pay an electrician for a wiring pull.) IF you really have no clue of where your 110V wiring is or your plumbing, etc - just give it up and have a professional do this. It's not worth your sanity or your health. Note: Wireless has it's own issues if you are going past a 2 camera high definition install (bandwith saturation, etc). If you want multiple high-def cameras, I suggest an Ethernet wired (POE - Power Over Ethernet) system like this. NOTE2: I'm buying an Android smartphone so I can check on the house while I'm away. This Q-See system supports remote access. S U M M A R Y: For price point, scope and function, I don't know how they did it. It's great. A lot of bang for the buck if you want to put up a working system quickly without going broke. Highly Recommended. ________________________________________________________________ Epilog: If you have the bucks to spare, improvements would go in these steps: 1. Consider either buying only the Q-See NVR without Q-See brand camera and instead purchase some Dahua cameras. -- OR --- 2. Building a fast Windows 7 PC, purchasing BlueIris software and a switch that supports 4 or 8 POE ports. Note: BlueIRIS is a CPU hog. You'd need a powerful PC for that. However this Q-see system will beat the Windows system as far as turnkey (instant use) integration and will consume a heck of a lot less power (the ARM brand CPU in the Q-SEE is a low power consumption CPU running Linux OS). -- OR --- 3. If you're going for the best, consider purchasing a mid-level or better ($600 on up) Synology NAS system with the per camera licenses and hard drives to fill it up On the other hand: The two Dahua 1.3 MP cameras I ordered were discovered almost immediately by the QC818 unit. The Dahua's deliver excellent imaging with this NVR. There is a list of 8 vendors (Axis, Arecont, Panasonic, I forget the rest - NO Hikvision) and then there's a few "generic" brand categories (Private, Onvia) for camera suppliers. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ SPECIAL NOTE REGARDING LICENSE PLATE RECOGNITION (aka "LPR"): If you have a "must do" need to pick up vehicle license plates at night (i.e. to be able to clearly "resolve" the letters and numbers when headlights and streetlights are on), then these Q-see cameras are unlikely to do that. That's not a shortcoming on their part. Neither will 99% of the security cameras out there. You have to find and purchase a special camera like this: Geovision GV-Hybrid LPR 10R 1.3MP Hybrid LPR Camera WHY? The exposure range is deliberately darkened and the shutter speed is increased to freeze cars in motion or illumunated with glare from headlights, security floodlights reflecting off plate, etc. Axis also makes a model that will reliably pick up license plates if you raise the shutter speed on it. The drawback to these specialized cameras? 1. They are relatively large and expensive [$850 on up] 2. The picture output for anything BUT the license plates will look awfully dark. There are technical design reasons for this. THIS MEANS: You don't want to purchase a specialized LPR camera as a primary view camera. You should use an LPR(License Plate Recognition) camera only as an * ADJUNCT * to a conventional camera if you are saving evidence to present to authorities. Otherwise it's difficult to argue/show the overall context of what is being witnessed. _____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ UPDATE 3-15-2014 My security camera system was instrumental in catching two gas thiefs at a neighboring business last night. The police liked having the videos with timestamps as corroborating evidence. P.S. TIP re: When pulling your files off the Q-SEE main recording unit onto your USB storage device: Make sure that, once you have marked off all the session clips that you are going to save as offloaded files, that you hit "Pause" on the unit. Reason: The file transfer(backup) will then go faster as you are not asking the ARM CPU in the unit to both render video while you are simultaneously interleaving the backup process. P.P.S. I don't use the Motion Detection on this unit. Motion Detection is tricky even on expert systems. I have no illusions that a unit of this price point with more or less fixed firmware is going to handle Motion Detection correctly. For my purposes it's not a big deal, for yours it might be. If you want Motion Detection, consider getting a powerful PC with Foscam Blue-Iris or some other more sophsiticated system.

I like memory. Lots and lots of it. So when Sandisk broke the 128GB barrier on microSD cards, I knew my next Android phone would sport one of these. With cameras getting better and higher-resolution, photo and video file sizes increase too. I was very happy to get this, the largest capacity microSD card you can buy at the moment*. My Moto X Pure Edition smartphone reads it just fine. If you're a memory hog like I am, you will not go wrong with this card. Highly Recommended! *- There are a LOT of unscrupulous dealers out there who will sell you a 128 or 256GB microSD card. Maybe even a large capacity like 512GB or I've even seen 1TB microSD cards! Rest assured, they are counterfeit fakes! They are, in reality, low capacity cards (usually 2 or 4 GB) that have been specially formatted and labelled to read a higher capacity. You could use one for weeks if not months and nothing go wrong: but eventually, you will hit the physical capacity of the card and your precious files will start disappearing into thin air, overwritten with new data and hopelessly irretrievable. Don't let this happen to you! Use a good company like Sandisk, a reputable site like Amazon, and an Android app called SD Insight. It will read deeply into your card to let you know if it's legit or fake.

Unfortunately, the user interface lacks several features that make life easier when managing the kind of large music collection this player allows. Songs are displayed and sorted by filename instead of tagged metadata, making finding songs and even knowing what is playing sometimes very difficult. Additionally, when scrolling through all music files, there is no option to skip to next letter making finding anything very tedious and frustrating. Given the lack of playlist support (only 3 playlists), you would think more consideration would be given to people wanting to hear particular songs in a large collection. Pros Good physical design (small size, robust metal case) Easy to use Large storage (for SD card) great for large collections Cons Songs displayed and sorted by filename No skip to starting letter feature when scrolling through songs Lack of above features means large collections of music are unnecessarily cumbersome to manage on this device (ADDED) Device will only recognize 4000 songs Overall, I cannot give this device any more than 3 stars. This could be a fantastic player but it's pretty much ruined by the fact the makers added a bunch of storage but didn't think through what features would make managing that many songs useful. Update: I am removing a star from the rating, lowering it to 2 stars. What I did not realize at the time of the review is that the software of the device does not recognize more than 4000 songs - which is very easy to cross in large music collections. I am personally a little sick of devices offering a great deal of storage hardware-wise but not designing software that actually lets you use the storage to its fullest. Cannot recommend this device and would consider specifications as listed to be misrepresenting what the device actually provides.

I may have gotten better results elsewhere in my house, but I wasn't going to up and move my entire desk, so I'll stick to the wifi until spring when I can run some cable upstairs.

Couldn't even pick up some channels that are less than 20 miles from my house. After buying this antenna I did some more research and found out that the term "HDTV Antenna" is just a marketing ploy. There isn't such a thing as a HDTV Antenna. There are VHF low, for channels 2 - 6, VHF high, for 7 - 13, and UHF for channels 14 - 83. There are also antenna's that combine all 3 ranges. I'm the father of a baseball pitcher (now in college and pitching for his college team). So for the last 10 years, we have tried various inexpensive devices to measure the speed of my son's fastball. We have been disappointed by the reliability and accuracy of past devices and I was really hoping that the SpeedTrac X would be different. But for the most part, it too produced less than satisfying results. Here's what I expected when I bought it: Speed accuracy: +/- 1 to 2 mph (when used correctly according to the manual) Spurious readings: less than 25% of the time Here's what I got: Speed accuracy: always 3 to 4 mph lower than actual Spurious or no readings: about 50% to 80% of the time I called the manufacturer and spoke with them about the problems (speed accuracy and spurious readings). I confirmed I read through the entire user manual and followed directions precisely. I set it up in my back yard. I threw in to a net. I positioned the SpeedTrac on a tripod low to the ground behind the net and threw directly at it, dead center. I tried both the regular mode and the "Pro Mode" to eliminate the spurious (erratic or "ghost") readings, but although this helped, I still had significant erratic readings. The Speedtrack seemed to pick up my arm and body movement every time I would go to throw and display a speed like 89 mph or high random speeds like that. Once the Speedtrack display's a speed, it won't measure anything until the reading goes away. So every time I would go to throw, just before I would throw, it would display a spurious speed. The manual suggested being at least 30 feet away from the Speedtrac so that it would not be so susceptible to body movements. I measured my distance and placed myself 40 to 45 feet away and still erratic readings before I would throw. Occasionally, when I was able to throw without the Speedtrac displaying an erratic reading, it would usually measure the ball speed about 50% to 75% of the time, but I noticed it always seemed to be low. For example, I (the father) typically only throw about 55 mph with my top speed being 60 mph. The Speedtrac kept showing about 5 mph less than that. When I spoke with the support person at Speedtac, I asked them how I could verify the accuracy of the Speedtrac. I did not have a Stalker radar gun to verify against. So they suggested measuring it against a known car speed. I tried that and consistently got readings about 3 to 4 mph that were lower than the car speed. The Speedtrac is suppose to be +/- 1 to 2 mph. I liked everything else about the Speedtrac. I liked the large LEDs. I liked the simplicity of use. I liked the housing and design. The support person at Speedtrac was helpful and spent lots of time on the phone with me to make sure that I was using it properly. So I really liked the product, but it just produces too many erratic/spurious readings and was to inaccurate for my needs. To be fair to the manufacturer, maybe there was something interfering with the Speedtrac in my back yard that I could not see. I did not try the Speedtrac at a different location (other than to test against a car speed) because even if it worked better (i.e., less erratic/spurious readings) at a different location, I bought it for my back yard, and it did not work well in that location. I would have rated this product 4 or 5 stars except for the two issues: too many spurious/erratic readings and the measured speed always appeared to be 3 or 4 mph low. To summarize, in my use in my back yard, throwing a baseball in to a net from a distance of 40 to 45 feet, with the Speedtrac positioned on a tripod low to the ground about 6 feet behind the net, and throwing directly dead center at the Speedtrac, I would get spurious or no readings about 50% to 80% of the time, and the other times, it would read about 3 to 4 mph low. You may have better success with this than I did. Everything else I liked about the product.

This is my first experience with mesh systems. It was purchased as part of a new home wifi system, replacing an existing Netgear system. The AX1800 router is installed in a home office, centrally located within the residence. One mesh unit is connected to the AX1800. The remaining 5 mesh units are installed in 5 different rooms. All units are within 20 to 30 feet of the primary unit. There are no more than 2 walls between any unit and the primary unit. All the mesh units display a green status light and and have never indicated anything other than a strong signal. The WiFi Extender (1200RPT) is installed in the garage, providing internet access for a standalone device. It also displays a strong signal. After one week of service, there are several problems that we have encountered. The main issue is random loss of connectivity between devices connected via the mesh system. During these episodes, the mesh units indicate a strong signal while the devices indicate no signal at all. This condition has occurred on devices connected via wifi as well as devices connected to the mesh units via cat 6 Ethernet cables. None of the Ethernet cables is longer than 4 feet. This connectivity issue has occurred at various times of the day, morning, afternoon, evening and late night. In most cases I’ve had to shut down and restart the router, primary mesh unit and in some cases the mesh unit providing connectivity to the device. Other issues include problems administering the system. The lack of a windows app that can access all the router, extender and all mesh units is a big problem. I find it hard to believe a manufacturer would not provide both phone and pc/laptop access. The inability to view a single screen that shows all connected devices and their status, is another problem. The user manual lacks any real technical information and is totally worthless when trying to resolve a problems.

There is a MAJOR manufacturing error involved with this TV/monitor mount. In short, you have to remove the part that swivels from left to right / attaches to the pole of the mount, and flip it upside down (as shown). The orientation of the mounting holes is incorrect out of the box. Luckily, I had a spare allen key set handy - but prepare to have one that is slightly bigger than the included keys. If this step is ignored, your TV/monitor will probably fall and break if bumped. Otherwise, this mount is SOLID. It feels really sturdy once you have it set up. It only took me like 20-25 minutes to put everything together. Side note: I saw a few negative reviews for this, that mentioned the pole being manufactured incorrectly. Those people clearly didn't read the instructions... You don't tighten the pole piece into the clamp all the way, you tighten it until the holes are facing straight ahead / in the direction you want the TV to be facing, and then you tighten down the little hex (allen) bolts to keep the pole from spinning around. READ THE DIRECTIONS BEFORE YOU SPREAD MISINFORMATION.

We purchased two of these bags at the same time, for our kids to use for school. The good news: the bag is well-designed, with ample room for large textbooks, a jacket or sweater, a lunchbox, and misc supplies. The bad news: The telescoping handle broke off on one of the bags just four months after purchasing. The handle just pulled completely out of the bag. I inspected the damage, hoping I could repair it myself. Unfortunately not. The plastic part that is meant to keep the handle from coming out of the bag had snapped on both sides, and could not be removed or repaired. In addition to the broken handle, several of the rivets that hold the bag together were missing or broken. That wasn't the worst part, though. The really bad news: the warranty service from High Sierra was a joke. The bag is advertised as having a 5 year warranty. Hoping to have it repaired or replaced with the same model, I contacted High Sierra's customer service by email. After taking two days to respond, they requested photos of the bag, the damage, the identifying tags inside the bag, and a copy of my receipt. I emailed all the requested info that same day. After two more days of waiting, High Sierra replied to say they had determined the bag could not be repaired, and would be replaced instead. But according to their email, before they would send a replacement, I had to cut a fist-sized hole in the front of the bag, take a photo, and email it to them. After receiving proof that I had destroyed the bag, they would then arrange for a replacement to be sent. I wrote to them that this was not convenient for us at all. Though the handle had snapped off, our son was still using the bag as a backpack for school, until we could get a replacement. Another three days of waiting for a reply from High Sierra. Finally they did reply, and to their credit, they agreed to send the replacement without our first cutting a hole in the damaged bag. But... they could not send us the same bag as a replacement. Instead, they told us to go to their website, and select four "comparable" choices that would suit our needs, and email them with the model numbers. High Sierra would then send whichever bag they could. We looked at their website, only to find that there was not one single wheeled "book bag" style offered. All of the bags on the site were travel luggage, or hiking/daypack style, without wheels. The bag we purchased is still manufactured and sold by High Sierra. Why could they not offer a replacement of the same item? Instead, we had to select from models that were not suited to our purpose at all. On top of that, the whole process took almost a month before we received the replacement bag. Bottom line: the bag is a good one, if you get one that is not defective in manufacturing or materials. But the "warranty", and customer service, is nearly worthless. Don't count on High Sierra coming through for you. Five stars for the bag, but none for the customer service and warranty.

Having had a 17" Powerbook for a couple years, I was keen to actually try out a bluetooth mouse. But like many other Mac users, that one button thing just wasn't gonna' fly with me. The problem was that most BT mice were too pricey just to experiment with. Then came the day that I had to buy a Windows laptop for my CAD software. This new laptop, a Sony VAIO, also came with built-in bluetooth so I thought it was now the perfect time for that mouse. After much research, I decided to make this mouse my first victim--errr candidate. The IOGear Mini Mouse functioned perfectly right out of the package with my Powerbook. It had good scrolling and good tracking. It was very tiny for this 6' guy to hold but I soon became so used to it that my desktop's Logitechs felt awkward. Now getting this thing to work on the Windows laptop was nowhere near as simple. Windows does not come with Bluetooth drivers and this mouse didn't come with them either. The drivers Sony pre-installed on the laptop could see the mouse and recognized that it was a mouse, but apparently the recognition was not mutual. After talking to Sony support a bit, I was thoroughly aware that this problem could only be solved by IOGear or Amazon Product Returns. I decided to give IOGear a shot. After an hour on the phone, I was escalated to third level support; yes, a software engineer in their development group. This guy had me try all kinds of things. About another hour later, he had explained enough about the nature of Bluetooth drivers (and Windoze drivers) that I was able to figure out a method of fooling Windows into thinking it had the correct driver already and really could understand the mouse. And that solved the problem and the mouse has been working beautifully ever since. I taught the IOGear how to use my workaround so they should be able to help anyone else who has the same problem. And eventually Mr. Software Engineer said he would write a KnowledgeBase article on it. A note on battery life: the packaged batteries are wimpy in the extreme. They are probably rated at about 200mAH. Do your self a favour and go out and buy a good set of NiMH AAA batteries with a quick charger. I happened to have a Ray-o-vac set from Costco that had an 1800mAH life. These last about 4-5 days of heavy usage before needing a re-charge as compared with the 4-5 hours of the packaged batteries. Also, it is very important that you carry a spare set of batteries (preferrably alkaline for reasons of cost and shelf life) to tie you over in a pinch. A note about construction: As I implied above, I am a mechanical product designer. For whatever that is worth, I am quite impressed by the design and quality of this mouse. It is quite durable and very robust. There is quite a bit of elegance in the design, too. The one tiny objection I have is the design of the power switch. Unfortunately, I haven't a better idea yet so I will give IOGear the benefit of the doubt. In summary, I love this mouse.

Purchased as a replacement remote for my Insignia FireTV which had stuck buttons. I got the new remote to work eventually. Instructions it came with were not very good, in my opinion. The remote did not automatically pair as it said it should. Only the power button worked initially. Also, unplugging TV and pressing the HOME button did nothing. The steps I did take required an already working remote to pair a new remote. This could be a problem for some. I could use some of the buttons on my old broken remote and also have an "Firetv Remote" app downloaded on my phone. Here are the steps I used to pair this new remote purchased: 1. Go to "Settings" with a working remote or the remote app on your phone 2. Go to "Controllers & Bluetooth Devices" 3. Go to "Voice Remotes with Alexa" 4. Go to "Add New Remote" 5. Following directions on screen, I pressed the home button on the NEW remote for 10 seconds until a new direction appeared on the screen 6. Following on-screen directions I pressed the middle circle/select button on the OLD remote to approve adding this new remote. 7. From there the new remote was added to my list of controllers. The new remote is paired and functions fine. The size is slightly smaller than the original remote but otherwise looks the same and has the same buttons and functions. Hope it holds up. XTU S3 Action Camera I have to reject this action camera for two reasons. (1) They claim that battery life is 120 minutes, but I got less than 60 minutes. (2) This may sound foolish, but I cannot open the side door without using a tool. You need to open this door every time you charge the battery or transfer files to your computer. Otherwise, this is an above average budget action camera. Good Points: Metal exterior - Camera has a solid, premium feel Three external buttons Touch screen is mostly responsive – better than GoPro Hero9 – but not as dependable as Apeman Cam Simple, intuitive Menu File transfer is simple – use the USB cable Tripod socket Photos: Photo image quality is poor, just like every other action camera. Although the colors are realistic and contrast is good, images are noisy and get worse in low light settings. At times, there is weird pink color fringing around center objects and bright areas can be over exposed. Lens flare is terrible. (See photos) Video (Compared to other action cams I used) Videos made from time lapse photos are acceptable, as are slow motion and ordinary video. Contrast is low on some videos. Hyperlapses are also decent – you can set “speeds” as low as 1/2 sec! Stabilization – is evident but not adequate. Blunders: The charger should be “Type C”, not the old fashion USB Tripod mount interferes with both battery door and the USB door. Buttons are hard to push. When trying to power off the camera the camera is likely to jump to a menu screen. I’m not certain that a WATERPROOF camera makes sense considering the trade-offs. To make the camera waterproof, the buttons and doors have to be overly sealed, making them very hard to use. There is no need for this. My Sony camera is WATER RESISTENT. Buttons and doors are moisture protected, but the sealing does not interfere with the operation of the camera. This is all you really need – protection from rain, snow, and dust. If you want to go under the surface, there’s always the underwater case.

This is my second projector. My first was the Optoma GT1080. Going from the Optoma to the Benq was a much bigger leap than what I was expecting, in every way. The high quality of this projector makes the Optoma seem like a toy. The device alone looks much nicer, the remote feels nicer, setting it up is far nicer and easier. But, to be fair the Optoma GT1080 is a good bit cheaper. Image quality wise the Benq has amazing colors thanks to the RGBRGB color wheel, it's incredibly close to the colors of my Samsung Plasma TV, which is very impressive. It also has great sharpness and clarity, I honestly did not think a 126" 1080p image could look as sharp as a much smaller 60" 1080p Plasma TV, but it very much does. So to sum up the pros, I very much understand why so many others gave this thing 5 stars. I'm loving it so far. For the cons, I don't have many, overall they are nothing major. The biggest one is when I first plugged everything up I could not get a signal with my Sony receiver. Odd thing was I had audio, but no video. It took me a while to figure out it was the HDMI cable, which worked fine for my Optoma. It turns out the Mediabridge HDMI cable I was using had a too short male connector (the tip), no idea how it worked in the Optoma, but the only way to get a signal with the BenQ was to push really hard so it would reach the back of the input, then if I barely touched it, the signal would drop. So once I got a new HDMI cable it was perfectly fine. My other problem is much smaller and has to do with the front leg adjustment. It's a bit of a pain to use and doesn't exactly have the finest positioning. This will only be a problem if you use the projector on a table though. So all I ended up doing was getting a super thin piece of cardboard and put it under the front leg so my image was positioned exactly at the top of my screen. Besides that I haven't had any other issues. I'm very much enjoying it with movies and video games. The picture is just incredible to me. The best way I can describe it is, it just looks right. It really looks like a giant plasma screen. I uploaded some pics of Horizon Zero Dawn, SteamWorld Dig 2, some colorful parrot, and a pic of some mountains from the Amazon Fire screensaver. (I'm also using a Darbee 5000S)

My goal was to have an easy way to backup my computers, especially digital photos and tax records. If I'm ever forced to evacuate my house, this is one item I'll take with me! The installation was painless. Plug the drive into the wireless router and then install the client on each computer. One laptop would not read the CD, but the download from the support site worked fine. 5 client licenses are included. Once installed and backed up, they keep the My Book synchronized with the files on each computer. By default, the client backs up all directories except the Program files (since those programs can be re-installed from their own installation disks). The setup wizard also created two shared drives, by default. This is handy with large Windows update files, like Vista SP2. I downloaded the file on one PC, stored it on the shared drive, then ran it on each computer without having to download it again. You can also set up a private drive, accessible from other computers for documents, homework, pictures and other files. One tip, use the network cable instead of wireless to initially backup your laptops. It's much faster and doesn't bog down the wireless for other computer traffic. I haven't tried to recover deleted files yet...or the iTunes sharing. My computers are not networked together, just sharing the same wireless router for internet access.

I'm writing this review after using it 8+ hours daily for over two weeks now for work and personal time. After using it for this amount of time, I have come to really dislike this headset and plan to return it. I'm leaving this review so that others can understand what some of the issues I find with it are so they don't make the same mistake. I mostly wanted a wireless headset for casual gaming/music and also be able to use it for Zoom calls for work. The flip to mute mic was a nice added bonus and these looked cute. On top of that, all the reviews I could find at the time are mostly positive so I gave them a try. For appearance, comfort and range of connection, I'd give it 5 stars. For utility and what it's supposed to be for: audio, I'd give it negative stars if I could. Pros: 1. Lightweight, comfortable, not bulky, audio quality is ok when it's on "headphone" mode 2. Gorgeous color, I got mine in pink. 3. Battery life. Charges quickly, can last 2 full days at least on one charge even if you use it all day. Cons: 1. Bluetooth only. This part I found to be a problem in all bluetooth-only headsets. What this means is, the headset actually has 2 modes/channels of audio: a high quality, output ONLY channel for stereo music, and a very low quality, voice call optimized input/output voice channel. The headset can auto toggle between between these channels automatically but what this means is that it cannot be on both channels at once. In other words, if you need the mic in any way shape or form (e.g. you're in a discord voice channel), it will FORCE you to be in the low quality sound. So if you want to listen to music or have good audio playing from a game at the same time, it won't work. Or you can have good audio, but everytime you need to use the mic, it mutes your audio. My only work around for this was to use it as only audio out and use a separate desk mic for input. 2. Really bad static on long meeting calls. Basically EVERY meeting that I've been in during these past two weeks that have lasted at least an hour, around the hour mark there starts to be static weaved in with any audio. Every time someone talks, every syllable of sound is accompanied by really bad static, and the static stops if the call is quiet. I basically have to restart my headset every time (and lose around 5-10s of audio from the call while I do this) and it'll be working good as new again. I read that this could occur if the device is low battery but my headset has never dipped below 60% battery on any of the occasions I've used it so I don't know what causes it. 3. Does not work with zoom after laptop goes to sleep and wakes up. I noticed at the end of the work day, if I do not shut my laptop down completely and restart it before next use, Zoom will stop playing the audio to this headset. Strangely it will play sounds from other parts of the computer and Zoom settings show the mic is "active" but it doesn't actually play anything unless I restart the computer completely. It's been highly annoying to have to shut down and do a fresh boot of my work laptop every day for this. 4. Auto shuts off if no audio detected for a period of time even if there is audio playing. So like most bluetooth devices, it will go to sleep if it thinks it's inactive for a while. Usually this is fine because if I'm listening to something on youtube or a music player it knows to stay connected even for hours at a time. However, for some specific applications, like Genshin for example, if Genshin is the ONLY source of audio playing (there's background music, and game characters talking), this headset thinks there's no audio so it will go to sleep for no reason every 15min or so and then I have to manually flick it back on, or I have to keep playing a youtube video in the background to keep it awake. As you can see this headset has a bunch of really ridiculous problems that destroy user experience. At this price point, it's a very disappointing buy. I don't recommend it at all unless you plan to only use it for one basic task (which even then, let's be honest, it probably will do a bad job at).
