Fantastic little gadget! I've had the Asus Chromebox M004U, the inexpensive one-$169.00, 2GB ram, 16GB SSD-for a little over a month and from using it, I'll state that it is better than advertised. When the box arrived from Amazon, it didn't look big enough for a "real" computer. Bear in mind the Chromebox is only 5" x 5" x 1.5" in size. I took out the Chromebox, plugged in the power supply and looked for a cable to hook up a monitor. Neither a DVI or a VGA plug will work. I did find an HDMI-to-HDMI cable which fits the Box, but not either of my monitors. I was thinking about buying a new monitor when I remembered that my 32" LG TV had a second HDMI port. It's mounted on a swing-arm close to my computer desk in my "man-cave" so I can catch football games and NASCAR away from the rest of the family. I pulled the arm & TV over closed to the desk, pressed the power switch and got a picture. The set-up went quickly and easily. I already use Google Chrome browser and the Chrome operating system is based on it so I was functional on that part. I entered my wifi password and, just like that, I was on the web. All my favorites were there just like on my PC. I surfed around to several sites and everything looked as normal. I should mention that everything was fast. I also already use Gmail, so the email part went fast. It's exactly the same as Gmail on my PC. I think you can set it up for Outlook, but since I use Gmail, I didn't bother to try that. It comes up fast. Someone told me 7 seconds. I have counted 1-thousand, 2-thousand... and quit because I never got over 7-thousand. You can't get to what you have on your PC hard drive. If you have saved it to Skydrive, you can easily find it with your Chromebox. I was getting worried. Everything was going quickly and smoothly, then I hit a snag. I went looking for a file, any file, and couldn't find one. Well, Toto, we're not in Windows land any more. We have to go see the Wonderful Wizard of Google. Let me give you a translation from Windows to Google for some I have picked up. 1. First, think of your Chromebox as a big Android phone. 2.There are a group of icons in the lower left side of the monitor just like Windows. Google calls this line of icons the SHELF. 3. The first icon is black with 9 little squares like a keypad. This is effectively your Start button. In Google-ese, it's your APPS. 4. You can move apps to and from the shelf. Right click on the icon in your apps and select "Pin to shelf." If the "Pin to..." sounds familiar, it's just like an Android phone. 5. Somewhere in your apps you'll see a blue, green & yellow triangle. This is Google drive. Think of it as your C: drive. You automatically get 15GB G-drive space free. When you buy a Chromebox or Chromebook laptop, you get another 100GB free for two years, as I recall. I was wondering what Big G was going to hit me for extending the 100GB. I checked and when I did, it was $2 per month. Pretty cheap. 6. I already had Microsoft Skydrive, (or is it Onedrive or is MS trying to confuse us). It also works just like Google drive. 7. If you are paranoid about storing things in the cloud, you are in trouble because everything is automatically stored in your cloud. 8. Speaking of saving, don't look for a save button. There is none. Remember, everything is automatically saved to the cloud. 9. You can hook up an external hard drive, but I haven't tried that. The Chrome computers DO NOT support CD or DVD drives yet. 10. Google Docs can read all my Word files and save as either .docx or Google files. No problem here. 11. Amazon Prime videos work just great through the Chromebox. So does Kindle for books (Kindle Cloud). Bottom line: Since I got this little jewel a month or so ago, I have been on my PC maybe a dozen times. Some of those were to start moving more pictures and notes on radio control airplanes(my hobby) to either Skydrive or Google Drive. The Chromebox makes my PC seem slow and antiquated. Sure it doesn't do Photoshop and others, but for surfing, watching videos and movies, reading Kindle books and doing the occasional doc or spreadsheet, it's been excellent for me. For what I do at home, I'll take a Chromebox over a PC any day. Added May 10, 2015: It just dawned on me that I haven't turned on my Windows PC in 2 weeks! It's still fast. It books up fast (7 seconds to the password prompt-I timed it). It shuts down fast-5 seconds. I've yet to see a prompt like, "Do not turn off or unplug your computer. Installing updates 1 to 21." Google print works fine, even from my phone-a Nokia Windows phone, no less. It goes through wifi & email. Double glad I spent the $160 for it.

I don't often write negative reviews--largely because I spend so much time vetting out my purchases prior to making them and am therefore happy with my purchases. These binoculars do not make the usual cut and here's why: Out of the box (4/28/2016): - Package was generic and smacked of Chinese import knocking off MIL-SPEC gear - Lanyard for carrying over the shoulder or neck is bright neon yellow while the binoculars themselves are MIL-SPEC green, the tote is MIL-SPEC green and the lens covers are MIL-SPEC green. - Lens covers do not maintain a tight fit and fell off when the binoculars were taken out of the box (both eye relief cover AND lens caps) First Field Use (9/2/2016 - 9/4/2016): - Noticed finger prints INSIDE of BOTH eyepieces! - Adjusted eye piece focal point for the first time and noticed plastic threading coming loose INSIDE the eyepiece--can't remove or clean that I'm aware of - Sealant over-applied to lens housings with visible oozing upon adjustment - Range-finding adjustment is loose and binds up upon rotation (like there's no gears or lubricant or anything one would expect for an optics device in this price range--just free-spinning plastic) Takeaways: - Binoculars are poorly assembled and poorly QA'd at the manufacturer - Binoculars work at their marketed range, but are nothing special - Range finding is done via calculations - not automatically (in case some of you were wondering) - Highly unlikely to withstand the test of time or hold up to typical wear and tear I would not purchase these binoculars again and regret not putting them to use sooner so as to avoid not being able to return them. The range finding feature (which is what sold me on this model) is only partially useful as you must be able to approximate the focal sources size/height prior to ESTIMATING it's distance. Further...and this is the part that REALLY makes me mad...this is clearly a private label binocular model which ANY vendor can put their name on and resale to the public under the guise of something of value. I've seen this exact model on Amazon now at least 4 times with different vendor names (exp. USCAMEL, MERYTES, BNISE, AOMEKIE, etc.), different prices, and basically the same description. For optics in this price range you can do MUCH better with Vortex and even Bushnell. Long story short, I'm VERY displeased with this purchase and wish that I had gone with a more reputable and reliable brand.

For only $50, this is an excellent and inexpensive stereo microphone for your camera. It has an earphone jack so that you can listen as you're recording and adjust the input volume (a feature I really like). It picks up sound quite well and you can change the directional angle of the two microphones. It has a two-step high pass filter that you can use if there's too much wind noise. It has a dead cat for wind noise control. Questionable issues: I am not sure that the directional angle does a lot (I do notice a difference, but it is not spectacular). I am not sure about the noise attenuation; it seems unnecessary in almost all situations. Cons: It picks up a fair amount of background noise from behind, particularly (unsurprisingly) when the main source of sound is a bit on the quiet side (i.e. it is not a shotgun or a parabolic mic). Update Nov. 28, 2015: I gave one of these to my brother, who's recording live opera music with it. He said that the quality of his recordings with this microphone and a Nikon D3300 is better than the professional recordings the opera house people do.

I have decided to buy this particular camera based on its features (particularly the "Exmor R" CMOS sensor for its supposedly good performance in different lighting conditions and 10x optical zoom) and the fact that it is currently on sale (due to this model being phased out), and after receiving it today and playing with it for several hours I think I have made the right decision. First, the good things about it: -Overall a good build quality (pretty "solid" feel, with no "loose" buttons/dials), except perhaps the battery door. The small "grip" area in front works surprisingly well even though it's not covered in any anti-slip material. -Picture quality seems to be good so far, in different lighting conditions and locations (both indoor and outdoor), using the default auto setting (Intelligent Scene Recognition - the green letter "i" with the camera icon next to it on the camera's mode dial). Of course, you shouldn't expect miracles from such tiny sensor but I think the quality is good for majority of people seeking a fully auto "high zoom" camera. If you want to see samples, you can find plenty of them on Flickr or different "professional" review sites, same goes if you want to know stuff like noise levels at different ISO values or other nonsense like this (which is irrelevant to me since I got this camera for "point-and-shoot" usage only). -Video quality is also very good, especially at maximum resolution setting (1080i at 60 fps). Of course you can use optical zoom while filming and since the zooming is somewhat "slow" during filming there's almost no "noise" from zooming motor that gets into recorded audio. Unlike the picture mode, you can modify the optical image stabilization settings in video mode (you can leave it in "standard" or more aggressive "active" mode), though just like in picture mode you can't turn off the image stabilization completely (not that you'd ever want to). -There's a useful and very user-friendly "panorama" mode which can create horizontal and vertical panorama photos very easily, all you have to do is to hold the shutter release button and move the camera to the right (or left, or whatever non-default setting you chose) until the camera indicates to release the button. -The camera's 3" display, while being somewhat low-res when compared to comptetitor's models (and newer models of HX series), is actually pretty useful for judging the overall quality of taken photos, both indoors and outdoors in moderately strong lighting. -Battery life is also very good, I've taken many photos (probably more than 50) and made several video clips in different modes and played with different camera settings and the battery life dropped to about 50%. Sony rates this camera at approximately 310 photos/charge, and I don't think this number is far away from truth. -In terms of overall speed the camera is also pretty satisfactory, there's a very little delay (I didn't time it) between turning the camera on and it being ready to shoot, same goes when switching between shooting mode and "playback" mode. I've heard some people complaining about that but I definitely am satisfied with the speed I am experiencing. -It has a built-in GPS sensor with ability to add GPS data to your photos. There's not much "tweaking" you can do for it, only turn this feature "on" or "off" or let it automatically update camera's clock, but it works good for a purpose of seeing the location of your photos on a map (if your photo management software supports it or if you're using the included Sony's photo management application). It takes fairly long time for GPS to acquire the signal once you turn the camera "on" but you can speed the acquisition time a little bit if you'll use the included photo management application to upload the GPS ephemeris data (or "GPS Assist Data" as Sony calls it) to camera's storage (memory card or built-in memory), though this data expires every month or so. Personally I keep this feature "off" since I generally know where exactly am I taking each picture and I don't really share them aside from family and few close friends. -The camera seems to work perfectly with the Eye-Fi Connect X2 WiFi memory card. Some not-so-good things I've observed: -The location of flash lamp is a little bit inappropriate since it's easy to accidentally cover it with your middle finger when "gripping" the camera, so be aware of that when taking the photos requiring flash usage. -As I've mentioned before, the door covering battery and memory card slots feels a little bit flimsy. Perhaps it just feels that way and in practice it will function perfectly for many years to come... That's basically all that I've noticed so far. Once again, I have purchased this camera for its supposedly good "point-and-shoot" performance in different lighting conditions and a useful 10x zoom and so far I am not disappointed in my purchase, especially for the current price.

I read Ken Rockwell's review of this lens, and on that basis, I ordered it. I took it to Yosemite Valley for use on a photographic workshop and was extremely disappointed in its performance. I photographed some lichen-covered boulders that ranged from 12-18 feet away and could not get a sharp image. As Rockwell points out, the lens is slow to focus. I could live with that as a landscape photographer, but the inability to render a sharp image with AF in a static environment, like landscape photography, rendered the lens almost useless to me. The inability to focus on a scene that is more than ten feet away also made the lens less than acceptable. The price point is excellent, but the lens is not. The slowness of the lens is also a drawback as far as being able to establish a narrow depth of field. I cannot recommend this lens to any shooter. I returned mine to Amazon for a refund.

Design is terrible, requires opening the plastic shell and cutting out plastic dividers. The board is designed to not use them, as there is no separation space for wide RGB plugs, while the case includes dividers that literally blocks you from plugging in your cables. So to install any RGB, you must remove the case and cut out all the dividers from the case, not to mention shaving off the edges, because the RGB pins are LOWER than the fan pins, and you have to cut out enough clearance to make the plug fit. You can buy the board without a case for like $10. Cooler Master took this board, put a logo on it, and covered it with a non functional case for over double the price. If it didn't have any dividers, the case would be fine, as it is nice to have a cover and magnetic attachment. No idea if it gets hot inside the case though. This board is a questionable design with questionable quality. The RGB input uses a 3 pin to 2 pin adapter, making me question how this is legit. Even if you didn't need the full 3 pins, the board should use it anyway for cable compatibility. This product is installed in a system I am in the process of building. I have no idea of how well it works or longevity until the PC is built. It may be better to just buy the no case $10 board that uses sticky tape. There also seems to be cheaper cased versions with functional case design that even come with remotes. Those are $5 cheaper than cooler master. So I honestly can't recommend this product, even if it works, aside from the looks and magnet, because you have to cut out plastic to plug in your cables.

===update=== I have recently installed OpenWRT on this "doorstop" (only works with versions 2 and versions 3 -- not the new version 4). It seems to have fixed many of the issues that I had with the product - except its range. Now it is relatively stable and I can connect from all 5Ghz devices that I have tried so far. It also has a much nicer GUI interface and it has significantly more configuration options. I would only recommend this for the expert users as it could be easily misconfigured to allow security issues in a home network environment and it is not very "novice friendly" (ie. if you are not an IT person in any form, avoid the advanced router firmwares like OpenWRT). I am leaving the rating at 1-star as I really feel that no one should never have to struggle so much to make a "mainstream" home device for the end-user community function as advertised... and the fact that I lost 4 years to the crappy firmware and updated firmware that TP-Link ships on the product (last tried new firmware in March 2018 with less compatibility that my initial review) and well as use of my 100USD. For a good inexpensive router, I would recommend TrendNET... for advanced features, I would recommend ASUS... and for easy of setup, use and frequency of updates, I would recommend NetGear. Steer clear of TP-Link... === I purchased this in 2014 as my first AC-class router to provide better coverage in my new house at a bargain price of less than 100USD. After switching out my Netgear N900 router for this to get better speed with devices in the 5Ghz band, I started having disconnection issues with my 5Ghz devices. Since I assumed that they were vendor compatibility issues, I kept the router and waited for updates. After configuring this router for use as an Access Point and updating it numerous times, and having tried to connect products from Netgear, Belkin, Linksys, and D-Link... the connection for any single product I have tested with it has lasted less than 1hour -- Neither can these products reconnect automatically. Unfortunately, this is basically a doorstop. I never considered that a product from a reputable networking company would function so poorly, since their power-line products and their network switches have worked so well for me. I have since utilised AC products from Belkin, Netgear and Linksys... all with wonderful results... but I am now "gun-shy" when it comes to TP-LINK wireless products. Their stability will continue to remain suspect in my eyes... and especially now that they have blocked installing 3rd party software on their devices as well. My recommendation with Wireless products is to make sure you get a connectivity and stability rating from all reputable reviews before buying any products... I followed magazine reviews and blog posts without this reference.

I was excited to order this and start using it, however it has a LONG way to go before I could recommend it heartily. Here's why. Whatever time I had hoped to save over my using my old old AT&T DVR, I pay for in waiting for this thing to respond. It takes forever to boot, load its programs or content, for menus to then load, and more buffering once the program is selected. In other words, it typically takes me almost 5 minutes from when it is turned on, to when I can actually begin to view programming. Moreover, when I try to delete programs, it takes a series of selecting individual programs, and then, sometimes up to 5 confirmations "Are you sure you want to delete this program?" before it will actually delete the program. This is time that is wasted trying to get the Tablo to accept my choice to delete something-with a single click of the confirmation button. They have indicated that there is supposedly a new firmware coming, but having had the unit for two months now, I am puzzled as to why they are taking so long to release updates that will cure some of the most common flaws of this machine. It also fails to fill the whole screen at times, at least with the menus. Moreover, it has failed to record certain programs that I have told it to, which is a big disappointment after the program has passed. Additionally, it does not seem to integrate with my Apple TV, and there seems to be no app available in the iTunes store, to add to the APPLE TV, although it does have an iPhone app. It would be far better to have the app on the Apple TV than only being able to run it through my Amazon FireStick. All of the problems I have described seem to be as the result of having flaws in the software and firmware for the product. I anticipate that when software is updated that perhaps some of these problems may be resolved. But until they are, be prepared to waste A LOT of time, spent watching the circular arrow indicating that it is buffering. I have a 50mbps, cable connection, with the unit connected by ethernet cable. I can't understand why there is ANY DELAY in loading content or programs. This is inexcusable in my view. Also, a decade ago, I had an RCA Proscan VCR, which featured the ability to identify commercials and skip over them during playback, or to be able to fast forward through them and then to STOP once the commercials were completed. I don't understand why this 2015 product cannot automatically fast forward through commercials, and then STOP when the content resumes. The inability to EASILY skip commercials is sadly AWOL in this product it takes forever to get past the commercials, and to the point where the program resumes. Mine is controlled with the Amazon FireStick remote, that allows the user to jump forward or "rewind" in increments of 10, 20 or 30 seconds, approximately, but it still involves endless punching of the remote buttons to cue the video to where you want it. What is needed, is the ability to "scrub" the video, in other words, the ability to see what it is you are fast forwarding through, like you can on ANY video online, and to resume play once you have previewed it in fast forward. So while you can skip commercials, the process for doing so is ridiculously labor intensive. This product has great potential to be THE NUMBER ONE MACHINE for cable cutters, but until their software and firmware are VASTLY IMPROVED, the hope of having a pleasant viewing experience is apparently still a long way off. Inasmuch as the machine takes endless time to buffer, they need to incorporate more "computer memory" into these boxes, so that you wouldn't need to spend several minutes a week, stuck watching the buffering indicator. If they get all of these bugs fixed, which I don't think is a realistic hope before 2016 rolls around, it would cause fewer headaches anguishing over endlessly and repetitively pushing buttons on the remote, just to get you to the location where you can resume viewing, after commercials are finished. But I so far, I am not optimistic that they have the resources to adequately engineer their software to overcome the aforementioned shortcomings that are built into the code. What a drag. UPDATE: I returned it. After waiting all summer for their firmware update, the product failed to ever provide QUICK service. After the upgrade, it began failing to record the nightly news, despite showing it as a scheduled program. I got tired of fighting it and returned it. This product should have been in development for another 2 years, before placing it in the marketplace. There are too many bugs to it, and it does not seem that Tablo has the resources to resolve MOST of these issues.

You'll hear about this lens's terrible distortion, but you'll never see it if you shoot jpeg or use Lightroom, because both have this lens's distortion profile. Maybe a little disappointing, but unlikely to affect most people. This lens really has only one downfall: It's F4. It's kind of disappointing to be paying $5-700 for a zoom that only goes to F4. Olympus, Panasonic, and Nikon all have nice F2.8 zooms on the market, why doesn't Sony? I'm sure Canon probably does as well. Unfortunately, low-light shooters using Sony are kind of forced to use primes, or live with blurry/grainy shots. Despite these downsides, I found myself taking a great liking to the lens. For me, the lens was too slow, but I did love every other aspect of it, and it was with regret that I sent it back. No doubt, for someone that lives somewhere bright and sunny, this lens is perfect.

My early impressions of this DAP using my Grado GR10e iems are very positive. Performance so far is all five-stars with a couple of four-star build demerits. Considering DP-S1 as more practical for daily on-the-go use than their flagship DP-X1A yet still awesome sounding - as it's being positioned by Onkyo - and it's a five-star result. I plan to revisit my rating after I've had this unit longer and experienced all of its features to see if I discover anything that could change my opinion, but at this point it's performing very well. Onkyo put a lot of its best DAP tech into S1's sound (thank you) and cut a couple corners for price in its body build. For example, its small volume knob lacks the precise feel you get on a more expensive player, so there isn't the user satisfaction that tactile connection can give, but it works pretty well. It's just not a premium feel. It's a pretty-good-for-the-price feel. Its power and three side button controls are plastic. They work well, but S1 is a nice design for a small, rectangular bar and metal would have been a nice touch here, but it's more costly. -Four-stars S1's back side has a faux leather-textured plastic cover. Textured plastic does serve the purpose of reducing scratching at a cost savings over aluminum. This plate feels decidedly non-premium, but somehow it looks ok. A matte-finish carbon fiber plate would be more fitting to it's design tho, imo... -lol. Onkyo is producing a $49 sleeve case for the S1 - ouch! -Four-stars Its display is a small, but legible touchscreen that responds quickly, and its UI operating with latest firmware is fast and working flawlessly so far. I haven't tried its streaming feature yet. Double slot micro SDs give it a large storage capacity -nice. -Five stars for display, UI, and storage capacity. No data on streaming yet. Sound is very good with well-recorded and mastered CD rips @44/16. The same file on iPhone 7 using same iem, Eq off, @similar volume sounds real good there's no denying, but it's nowhere near as clear and clean-sounding, revealing and detailed as thru the mini Onkyo. Experiment with the Sharp, Slow and Short digital filters on 44/16. I'm not sure which filter I like best; it depends on the recording. I leave it in Sharp for high resolution files. I also found that its upsampling feature improved some recordings. -Five-stars S1 reproduces 192-96/24 in a richly-detailed, CD-topping presentation. Exceptional original recordings and masters in 96/24 and higher sampling rates improve this hi-res presentation: new musical details from familiar recordings emerge, instrument texture increases, and there's more overall depth. The GR10e is notable for sounding open-like for an iem, presenting a soundstage. Thru S1 and hi-res, this quality is realized in a very pleasing way. Instruments sound natural/realistic and are easily identified and located. -Five-stars. DSD and MQA sound beautiful thru S1. DSD and MQA files (expensive!) thru this little player using quality iems sound like you're listening to a more expensive DAP. I haven't tried its balanced or balanced Active Control Grounds outputs, but with an audiophile-level, single-ended iem it really impresses. So my results are using just one of S1's DACs and amplifiers. I think this bodes well for its balanced performance. Music is presented against a dark background with no hiss. The implementation of its DACs, amplifiers, and related audio section is well-done for this price-point, imo. -Five-stars This DAP has very good amps, but they're not high-powered -single-ended or balanced. This power spec doesn't matter that much now days tho with four&five-star iems that are highly sensitive and @~25ohms and lower impedance, and many audiophile planar and dynamic on/over ear headphones that are, too. S1 offers headphone impedance/sensitivity input settings Low, Normal, High. Thirty-two ohms, sensitive headphones sit perfectly in Normal. S1 can drive higher impedance phones even single-ended to a degree as long as they also possess good sensitivity and are using its HIGH gain setting. Going balanced using both DACs and amps doubling voltage will help drive some cans that are not very sensitive. Both balanced options utilize its dual DAC/amps for additional headroom. Balanced on ACG setting (same power output as single-ended) promises the best fidelity this unit is capable of, but I don't yet own a balanced iem/hp to test this. All these combinations give S1 users a lot of iem/headphone choice -within reason. It is, after all, an on-the-go unit and really designed for use with high-quality (preferably balanced to access its twin dacs/amps) iems, and well-matched, high-quality (preferably balanced) portable headphones. -Five stars for iem/headphone settings feature, single-ended and balanced outputs, DAC(s) implementation, clean-sounding amplifiers, and iem/headphone flexibility. I'm not going to get into how I think this player's sound sounds. Sound is inextricably linked to the transducer in the audio chain. I've tried S1 with some other iems and full-size that I own to inform my observations re: impedance/sensitivity, but I won't review S1 with those right now. The single driver GR10e I'm using to evaluate the S1 is very good at sounding out a player's audio performance. Boiled down, DP-S1 is not really an entry-level player. It's another high-quality player from Onkyo that plays DSD to 5.6, MQA,192/32, has twin DACs and amplifiers, balanced options and more. S1 offers a more than the usual hi-res entry point portable DAP. You can tell that Onkyo isn't going for usual with this player. S1 borrows premium DAP tech from Onkyo's flagship DP-X1A and incorporates it into a more affordable and even more portable package. 11/30/17 *EXCEPT*... Onkyo streaming capability for DP-S1 is market-specific. Therefore, the Japanese version of DP-S1 DOES NOT stream in the USA! For this reason my overall stars drop from 5 to 3. As a portable hi-res DAP, I stand by my individual star ratings for its performance.

I highly recommend it to anyone that is thinking about purchasing a digital camera that seems to do everything well. Well done to Nikon for producing a great product.

Says rated for 15A. If you run 13A it overheats. It is designed with a "weak spot" in the wire, where the thickness of the conductor is reduced and it overheats at that spot. In this power strip, the weak spot is at the switch. It overheats there. It gets about as hot as a cup of coffee when you run 13A through it. Most power strips do this now. In my opinion this is totally intentional and by design. Power cords did not used to do this. The wire is rated for 15A but the connections inside are not. I purchased the Imillet HDMI Video Capture with USB3.0/2.0 Dongle to capture Raspberry Pi HDMI video onto a 2016 Lenovo X1 Yoga i7 2.6GHz w/ 16GB running Win 7 64-bit and using the Intel USB 3.0 eXtensible chipset. The Imillet dongle would only capture a few seconds of video before either freezing completely or losing sync. I tried several video packages, including current VLC and PotPlayer 64-bit, multiple USB ports and multiple Pi's as video sources. I also confirmed current USB drivers and disabled "USB selective suspend" which often cures flaky USB 3.0 behavior. All with no success. I tried the Imillet dongle on several older machines as an experiment; first an Asus G74SX ROG i7 2.2 GHz w/ 16GB using the Fresco Logic xHCI USB3 FL1000 series chipset, next a very old Motion LE1700 Intel Core 2 CPU 1.5 GHz tablet w/ 4GB with USB 2.0 only and, finally, a more recent custom built Asus desktop i7 3.47 GHz w/ 24GB using the Renesas USB 3.0 chipset; all running Win 7 64-bit. The same small group of Pi's were used for all the experiments. The Imillet dongle worked fine on USB 2.0 ports on both the G74SX and Motion LE1700 at what appeared to be 1080p resolution. As this resolution at high frame rates can not be guaranteed on USB 2.0, it may have been operating with higher latency and/or a reduced frame rate, or some frames discarded. It also worked fine on the custom Asus desktop using USB 3.0. However, it would NOT work on the G74SX's single Fresco Logic chipset USB 3.0 port! Again, current drivers were verified and at least USB power options were altered as part of troubleshooting. As the Imillet device did not meet the actual need of capturing video onto the Lenovo X1 Yoga, I ultimately purchased a Magewell XI100DUSB-HDMI USB Capture HDMI 3.0 HD Video Capture Dongle as well. The Magewell dongle worked perfectly on the Lenovo and all other systems EXCEPT the Asus G74SX's USB 3.0 port. When capturing over USB 3.0 connections, the resulting captured video from the Magewell was crisp and clear. It is important to note that the Magewell operates differently from the Imillet when running on USB 2.0 connections! The video capture software I tested opens a lower resolution window, 720p, when the Magewell is connected via USB 2.0. The Magewell is likely down sampling the 1080p video and displaying it as 720p. For example, text displayed from the Pi is not as crisp when in this mode. As I am mostly interested in capturing text screens from the Pi, or very low frame rate video, I would have preferred a compromise mode similar to how the Imillet works where some additional latency is introduced, a lower frame rate is displayed, or some frames discarded instead; but the sampled output would remain at a resolution of 1080p rather than forcing capture output to some lower resolution. Imillet, if you are listening, fix your device to work with Intel USB 3.0 eXtensible and Fresco Logic FL1000 family chipsets. Magewell, if you are listening, fix your device to work with Fresco Logic FL1000 family chipsets AND add a selectable mode where the user can choose to have 1080p displayed at a lower frame rate, or with some frames discarded, v.s. 720p to allow use with USB 2.0. I will return or sell the Imillet and keep the Magewell with the Imillet rated one star less than the Magewell and neither device considered "perfect".

I purchased this TV, partly against my better judgment, in the middle of February, 2010. I read many reviews by other consumers complaining of a "spotlighting" effect produced by the LED edge-lighting that replaces the fluorescent-style backlighting of older model LCDs. Upon receiving my TV, I was disappointed to see that the concerns others voiced were not exaggerated. The LED edge-lighting is distinctly uneven, resulting in numerous, lighter-colored "spotlights" all around the edge of the TV, most noticeably in the corners. In a darkened room, they are especially large and noticeable, covering a good five inches all around the edge of the screen. It can be distracting, as others have pointed out. One reviewer claimed to have hit upon a firmware upgrade that fixes the problem. I have been able to find no such upgrade. The only firmware upgrade Samsung has made available does not list this problem as one that it fixes. Besides this, the upgrade is from September of 2009; my TV was manufactured on December 31, 2010 (according to the serial number), four months after this upgrade was made available. I would think my TV already has the upgrade. The thing that really upsets me, though, is that just prior to writing this review, I contacted Samsung customer support via chat to see if Samsung was at least aware of the problem, even if they may not have a way to fix it. The customer service rep was enormously unhelpful, telling my to reset my TV to fix the issue. I have a feeling she probably knew next to nothing about any of Samsung's products and was just following a flow chart in response to my inquiry. She claimed that no other consumers had reported such an issue with this TV. I highly doubt I am the first person to contact them about this very real, and very annoying, issue, considering all of the reviews that have been posted on this website and others. She offered to send a technician to assess and fix the problem. Was he going to build me a different TV, I wonder? I think that is the only was to resolve an inherent design flaw. Now, having said this, let my just say that the above issue was the ONLY thing that kept me from giving this TV five stars and an absolutely glowing recommendation! The picture IS AMAZING! By far the best I have seen on any HDTV to date, and I thoroughly researched this purchase. I do not regret the purchase, and would purchase it again in lieu of Samsung's 8500 series (which has local backlighting instead of edge-lighting - this fixes the above mentioned problem, but this TV has it's own backlighting problem: google "LED blooming effect"). No LCD TV is perfect with regard to its backlighting - this is one of the major advantages that Plasma TVs have over LCD; it has always been a problem and will probably always be a problem until organic LED TVs become mainstream. Until then, you have three options: 1) Deal with low contrast ratios resulting from overly-bright, overly-white fluorescent backlighting, 2) Deal with uneven LED edge-lighting that produces "spotlights," or 3) Deal with "blooming" effects produced by local LED backlighting. I would still purchase an LCD TV over a Plasma TV with a shelf-life. I would still recommend this TV, unless you really want to splurge and spend the extra $800 to get the locally backlit LED TV - a marginally better compromise.

I own 4 Dlink cloud cameras: DCS-5020L, DCS-5010L, DCS-930L, DCS 932L for 2 years. I have a Buffalo router (on the manual, it said with a DLink cloud router, you have zero configuration!!!). The setup was very easy with all of them. This time, I decided to buy 3 DCS-942LB1 cameras because of recording on mini SD cards. I use a windows laptop for the setup. The wired connection setup was OK with the setup file downloaded from mydlink website. It took some times to install some plug-ins in order to view videos on SD card. But, the wireless connection (including WPS function) was impossible with the setup file. I read the reviews and found somebody had the same issue. One said that DCS-942LB1 setup may not be for DIYers. That's true. I finally could make the cameras connected wirelessly. Here are the steps: - Run the DCS-942LB1 setup file and choose only Ethernet connection. Then register your camera with your mydlink account. - Open your mydlink account. Update firmware if suggested. Go to Settings, then click on Advanced Settings. You'll be prompted, just trust the site and go on. - On the new window, go to Setup, then Wireless (left column). Here you choose your wireless network name, fill in the password, then Save Settings. Wait for the process, about 80sec. - When it's done, log out. - Now you unplug the Ethernet cable on your camera side. That's it. The back light may change to red, but will turn solid green in 1-2 min. If not, unplug the camera power cord, wait for 1-2 min, plug it again, wait for another 1-2 min. I still have a problem with SD recording when the camera is connected wirelessly. Whenever I insert the SD card into the camera, the connection drops. It said that the router must have at least 256K bandwidth. I did the speed test of my router and it said the download speed was 3.37Mbps, upload speed was 0.82Mbps. So I supposed (I'm not an IT pro) the bandwidth was greater than 256K. I even went back to Advance Settings to adjust the video resolution, from 640x480 to 160x112, but this didn't help at all. Really don't know how to do to resolve this issue. Regarding the difficult setup process and this issue, I gave it 2 stars. I might return them if I couldn't fixe it.

I've been using the display since April of 2020 so I've had plenty of time now to get used to it and give it a fair shake. Brightness: If you enable DyAc+ and leave it on, the brightness can be adjusted as high as 400+ nits. However, if you turn off DyAc+, then it drops to roughly 320 nits. I personally leave DyAc+ on all the time. 2D Picture Quality at 27": So a lot of people think they'll see pixelation at 1080p/27" and in my case I don't really notice it since I sit about 2 feet away from the monitor and i have it mounted on my wall. I previously had the 25" KD25F and found it too small for my liking so right now, this 27" hits the sweet spot. Remember, there is an 8 pixel per inch difference between 25" at 1080p vs 27" so all you have to do is move the 27" back a bit and you get the same view. 3D Gaming at 27": I got an FPS jump of >30% going from 1440p back to 1080p with this display which was nice. As soon as I started playing CoD: Warzone I noticed the input lag and motion was far better than my old Asus PG278Q which is a 1 ms TN panel but from 2014. With DyAc+ enabled and the ultra low input lag of this display, my K/D shifted upwards and I've been averaging 5-15 kills per match in Warzone since I bought this monitor. With my old Asus PG279Q, I had peaked and could feel the input lag. S Switch: Man what a handy little tool! I setup 2 profiles so far, one for desktop with the black equalizer set to 5 and vibrance set to 12 and DyAC turned off. When I want to game, I choose the other profile which turns DyAC to Premium while boosting vibrance and black equalizer. Very handy little tool that a lot of other manufacturers should think about copying. Colors/Sharpness: Out of the box they're a bit dull so I just set it to user define + standard and gamma at 3 and now it looks pretty good. I also had to increase the Sharpness to 8/10. You should download the color profile for this display and then calibrate it. Since it is a true 8 bit display with near 100% sRGB, you will get very nice colors from it that matches a lot of IPS displays. DyAc+: So this is the entire reason I bought this display, to have BFI that doesn't lose brightness when turned on. I can confirm that this monitor does not lose any brightness with DyAC enabled and infact gets MUCH BRIGHTER (up to ~480 nits peak) unlike every other competing display which tend to cut their brightness in half with BFI enabled. I briefly read about changing the vertical totals on these forums and since I likely won't hit 240 FPS even with a 9900k@5 Ghz and 2080 Ti in the games I play (Warzone/Apex Legends), I settled on 182 Hz with VT of 1350. I tested many different vertical total values out and 1350 just seemed to work best as the top/bottom of the screen had minimal blurring and the middle was great. It also works perfectly at 240 Hz with no VT adjustments needed. Additionally, you can enter the service menu of this display and calibrate the area/intensity using the UFO Ghost page found on blurbusters or their utility. I did this for my display by setting a custom area/intensity in the service menu and have virtually NO ghosting (see attached image of UFOs). Negatives: ------------ Yes there are unfortunately negatives with this display as there would be any display on the market. TN: Because this is a TN display, it will have limited viewing angles and you should be prepared to sit in front of the monitor with at least 1.5-2 feet distance between you and it. I have my monitor mounted and sit back about 2 feet from it which is ideal. Color: While the color is fantastic with it being a true 8 bit display, a lot of high end IPS have gone 10 bit and have better sRGB coverage than this one does so it doesn't match top tier IPS panels. If you want to do professional work, I would recommend having a separate IPS monitor for that or if you absolutely cannot afford two monitors, then buy an IPS monitor instead of this one. Overdrive: This monitor does not have dynamic overdrive which is unfortunate. What this means is if you lower your refresh rate, AMA (what Zowie calls their overdrive) only has 3 settings and so you end up with more double images at refresh rates below 240 Hz because the overdrive doesn't compensate. Some new displays (namely an AOC one) has dynamic overdrive which accounts for this and so you end up with no double images/ghosting while gaming at lower refresh rates. While not a deal breaker by any stretch, I would have loved to see Zowie include this. Price: Let's face it, this is an expensive panel for 1080p and being TN. $650 is asking a lot but if you are a serious gamer that wants the best technology, you gotta pay. Other panels offer similar performance but they lack DyAc+ which is the ultimate differentiator. I'd say if you don't care about DyAc+, then you could get a panel from say Asus that costs $200 less and will give similar performance--just be aware that Asus displays BFI is <200 nits which is pretty dark. That's it, hope you found this review helpful. If I had to, I'd buy this monitor all over again and am highly satisfied with my purchase and you will be too.

I bought two of these - one a year or so ago, and one this week. I had no significant problems with the first, but have already had to reset the second a couple times due to issues, and looks like I will have to reset again. Both have been upgraded to the most recent firmware (6.9.4). What I like: 1. From a hardware perspective, amazing value. Quad-core Cortex processor (1.4 GHz) with 2 GB RAM on-board. It has dual Gb ethernet ports with link aggregation. For the price, other than Terramaster, no one comes close. 2. VERY solid build quality. I have many NASes, from QNAP, Synology, and Asustor. This is the most solid, well-built little brick of them all. Very heavy and substantial feeling, with really nice large rubber-bottomed "feet". And the unit looks great. Door swings open to reveal removable drive caddies. 3. Compact design - shorter than most QNAP and Synology 2-bay boxes. 4. Tool-less drive installation (3.5" drives) - the inner drive bracket slides out of the drive caddy, and prongs piece the hard drive's screw holes, so no need for a screwdriver to install drives. There are screws included if you choose to use 2.5" drives. 5. Quiet fan with three speed settings (Quiet, Balanced, and Cool). I ended up setting to "Balanced" for my Toshiba drives, which run hot, and "quiet" for my Seagate Ironwolf drives, which run much cooler. Either way, fan noise is minimal. 6. Simple, decent app which makes remote file access fairly easy, though not the fastest I have seen (Western Digital's remote access is the quickest I have seen). What I don't like: 1. The operating system menu/user interface looks pretty at first, but is bizarrely and awkwardly laid out and is missing useful features standard on Asustor, QNAP, and Synology units. 2. Have had frequent "Admin page is not accessible" issues with BOTH NAS units, which makes no sense because I can see and access folders and the main summary pages for both. Sometimes a reboot helps and sometimes it doesn't. The newer unit I just bought is giving me fits and the admin page starts to load for three or four minutes, and then I get a message stating it can't be displayed. The admin page is now working for ReadyNAS #1, but not #2. My router shows the IP addresses for both units, and typing that IP address into a browser window access the admin page for one of the NASes, but not the other. 3. There is no real "system information" page which shows things like CPU, RAM, CPU & RAM utilization, etc. for this model. They say it has 2GB of RAM which I'll just have to accept because there's no way to display it on the ReadyNAS admin page. All of my other-brand NASes have detailed info in their OSes. 4. Apps I installed on my first 212 are not available for the second (Nero MediaHome, ReadyNAS Photos, etc.) are not available in the Apps list for the second unit (when I was able to access the Admin page). Other new apps are, however. 5. Resetting this unit is not straightforward like a QNAP or Synology where you hold the reset button down a certain number of seconds until you hear a certain number of beeps. 6. 16 hours later, my volume is still "rebuilding" for two 4-TB hard drives and the second NAS is molasses slow and I cannot access the admin page. To reset: You have to turn off the power, hold the reset button in, turn on the power while holding the reset button, release the reset button once the lights flash, and then click the backup button to cycle through various combinations of illumination of your ReadyNAS front panel lights, depending on your desired reset state (the power, disk 1, disk 2, and IUSB lights). Then you depress the reset button (with a paperclip) to select. Then it goes into a disk test that lasts five minutes, and then a "waiting period" that last ten minutes. You can press the backup button again to bypass the waiting period. There's no indication there's a hardware issue and no evidence of any software corruption I can see, so I'll reset the second unit again and leave the virus scanner off, and hopefully things will stay working. In any event, this thing has been far more temperamental and difficult to get set up than ANY QNAP, Asustor, or Synology device I have had. Even Western Digital's user interface is much more useful. EDIT: I did find an app that will display system info after you install it, but it's not natively displayed anywhere in the OS itself. EDIT #2: After a couple of days and a very LONG volume rebuilding process,. NAS #2 seems to be working well and is fluid and quick. Netgear really needs to do something about the rebuilding speed and unit performance during rebuilding - my QNAP NASes perform much better during this process. I have been able to access both NAS's admin pages for the past several days without issue. I also really like the ReadyCloud page. I can access my files from the app, but i like being able to get them via the rReadyCloud web page as well and being to access each individual NAS. Downside is you cannot access the admin page while not on your home LAN (I travel a lot for work). Overall, I am a lot happier with it than I was a week ago so will give back another star and give it four of them.

If it weren't for a large number of really bad errors in the map database, I'd give this unit five stars. But, having used it for several months, I have found the database to be good, but not great. I have to think of the Nuvi 350 as a nav-aid, not a navigator. I still tend to go to Google or Yahoo maps before a trip (if possible) to avoid getting routed the wrong way. Examples (though I understand at least one will be fixed in the current database update -- cost $75 -- annoying that they charge for fixing such a buggy database!): 1. Taking the NJ Turnpike north to I80 west, the Nuvi told me to stay in the right on the NJ Tpk, while the signs told me to be in the left going to I80 west. The first time, I listened to the Nuvi and had a detour (though it is wonderful at fixing things when you go wrong, even if it was the Nuvi's fault) that probably added 5-10 minutes to my trip. The second time (I drove the route two days in a row), I followed the signs instead of the Nuvi and got there faster. That such a major interchange would still have an error at this point in time is really bad. 2. Going to Great America Amusement Park in Santa Clara, CA, the Nuvi told me it was on the wrong side of the street. Fortunately, I know where it is and had been using the Nuvi mostly to find the fastest route there from an unusual starting point. 3. Going to Google's HQ in Mountain View, CA, I input the address and the Nuvi told me I was there about a quarter of a mile early. 4. There are lots of errors where small streets with blockages are concerned. On the positive side, if you make a wrong turn or are detoured, the Nuvi will get you where you want to go. Try that with Google or Yahoo maps! No fumbling for a map and a place to park and look at it. One other gripe, related to the map update cost ($75, and I think that's once per year). I bought a second unit for my daughter and she wanted to get maps of Europe for a week long trip she was making. It would have cost about $200! That was really annoying. Along the same lines, the battery cannot be changed by the user and another review said that Garmin told him a replacement would cost $225. If true, that's horrendous. I can kind of understand Apple's not making the iPod (esp the Nano) battery user accessible due to the unit's size, but here the only reason I can see is for Garmin to get a continuing revenue stream from users who don't know what they're getting into when the buy. That fits with my gripe about the database costs. A more minor gripe involves data input. I have to type the name of the city, which is a pain for something like "Mountain View". I wish the Nuvi allowed you to input the zip code instead. Often I'll know that and that's five characters instead of a city and state. Another more minor gripe is the routing software. It doesn't seem to understand that streets have stop signs and lights which slow you down. While I can't be sure, I suspect that it assumes you'll drive the speed limit on all roads, so it doesn't route you on major roads (esp freeways) as often as it should. I also saw a problem when I drove the Pacific Coast Highway (Route 1) recently. The Nuvi's ETA seemed to assume a speed limit of at least 55 mph, and maybe the actual speed limit of 65, whereas the best one can hope for on that route is about 40-45 mph due to hairpin turns, traffic, etc. It stopped trying to get me back on US101 (the faster, but less scenic route) much too early given that it was supposed to find the fastest route. Given that I wanted to take the scenic route, that wasn't a problem for me. But someone who wanted fastest routing and started near the beginning of Route 1 would have suffered by about an hour as compared to doubling back to US101. Gripes aside, I love the unit as you can tell from the fact that I bought one for my daughter. (She loves it too, though she's had a similar experience with errors in the maps.)

Did research before buying and went with Buffalo because of two big items: the enclosed software and the unit's stated burn speeds. However, this turned out to worse on-line purchase I have ever experienced. Both the software provided and the unit itself fails. I spent hours of time over multiple days, using multiple options but without successfully burning even one BluRay disk. (Made about 10 coasters though!). First the software: the overhead on the video is terrible. Have 7 gig of video? The final rendering of this results in over 22gig on the BD disk (if it actually successfully burned). I am guessing if you upgrade the software it shrinks the overhead, but wasn't going to even take that chance. The software DOES successfully create DVD's and I was successful burning a (smaller) video to my internal DVD writer using it. Also, the calculation of available space on the Blu-Ray is flawed. It stated, that the video I had created was going to need 21g for the BD, but when I burned the rendering to my harddrive the total was over 23g, which was too large for the Sony BD's I had. So you need to plan to TRIPLE whatever your current video sizes to estimate how many video clips you can burn to a BD with this software. (Another video editing software I have did not have near this much overhead or calculation poblem.) The Buffalo Unit itself: tried it with 2 laptops, one running Windows 7, the other Windows 8 (< eight months old). Neither could successfully write to the BD disks either with a very small BluRay video from the included software, or via Windows Explorer. (Also, tried using another Video authoring software tool, but it failed to burn to the unit as well.) On the Windows 8 laptop, I received "HW encode errors" during rendering, so turned hardware encoding off, and it took over 2 hours to render a file that would not burn. Note: I purchased the specific Sony BD's that Buffalo's website states provided 16x speed, so brand should not have been a problem. Very disappointed. Returned it, no I'm just out the cost of the BD discs and shipment box/packing purchase. Finally decided BluRay is not really necessary. Just going to play videos directly from laptop to TV via HMDI or Wireless.

From my Asus ZenBook Flip S13 with Windows 10, I am able to extend the laptop screen to two additional monitors and display different content on all three screens. The built-in laptop display continues to display 4K 3840x2160, and each of the external monitors are displaying their maximum resolution of 1280x1024 (these are old monitors). I am aware some reviewers complained that this device can't truly extend to two monitors from a MAC, only mirror, but I believe this is a known MAC limitation and not a fault of the adapter. You need to use a separate USB-C port for each external monitor connected to a MAC, so it would not be possible for this adapter, with only a single USB-C connection, to extend to two separate monitors from a MAC. Anyway, the product description gives fair warning about this. Fortunately, Windows 10 does not share this limitation, so as long as your laptop hardware supports this configuration, Windows 10 will support it. Some reviewers complained it didn't work at all for them. This is likely because not all USB-C ports are the same. Just because your device has a USB-C port does not necessarily mean it supports every possible protocol, like DP (Display Port) Alt Mode and Thunderbolt 3/4. The product description gives fair warning about this. I saw a reviewer give a 1 star review because they were trying to connect a Dell Latitude E5570 to 3 external displays plus the laptop screen for a total of 4 displays, and it didn't work with all 4 at once. I looked up that laptop model and confirmed my suspicion - the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) in that laptop supports a maximum of 3 displays (yes, the built-in display counts as 1), so of course it didn't work with 4. This is a limitation of that person's own laptop, and not the fault of the adapter, so the 1 star review was undeserved. I also saw some reviewers complaining they could not get the maximum resolution and/or frequency (Hz) for each monitor when all monitors were connected. Again, it's possible this is due to a limitation of their own laptop's hardware, like the GPU or USB-C port, so it might not be the fault of the adapter. There are plenty of 5 star reviews claiming that the adapter does support dual 4K at 60Hz, so I suspect the folks that couldn't achieve their desired config might have hardware limitations, like perhaps their USB-C port doesn't support Thunderbolt 3/4, so it can't provide sufficient bandwidth, or perhaps their GPU simply doesn't support multiple displays at the desired resolutions and frequencies. There are too many other variables to just blame the adapter. I saw a reviewer talk about their laptop crashing when waking from sleep, but it was not clear if they were talking about when the monitors wake from sleep, or when the OS wakes from sleep. Also, it would have been nice to know what make and model laptop this person was using, since it was likely a hardware driver conflict causing the issue. So far, I have not experienced this issue myself with my Asus. If this does happen to me, I will update this review. Some additional observations: I did notice the device gets warm to the touch, but it was not burning hot, so I'm not too worried - I think this is probably expected. So far, it seems to be a good product at a cheap price, and honestly, if it fails a year down the road, I won't be too upset considering how inexpensive it was.

Update 5/4/13: With about 70 hours on the clock, still very satisfied. Added Sony BDP-S390 Blu-ray player with wifi. Works like a charm. And it takes full advantage of the 710's HD capabilities. But the sheet I'm using is a cheap, low thread count so I can see the weave if looking closely. A good quality white bed sheet (with a high thread count) should work much better, providing a sharper image. The benefit of the "sheet method" is a very light-weight screen with a straight and flat face. Just don't let your cat (and his claws) anywhere near it. Here's the bad: I have a few persistent dust blobs. They are very noticeable when scenes go to black. I don't know if my 710 was delivered "contaminated" or if the dust infiltrated while in my possession. In either case, here's what I would recommend for every new projector user, no matter the type or brand you purchase: after setting up your projector, play a movie and freeze on a black scene (Make sure the viewing room is dark). Then operate the focus through its full range. If the frozen black image turns into a star-lit night sky your projector's optics are internally contaminated. If you see just a few and the fuzzy spots only come into view when the image is out of focus, it's not an issue. Otherwise, you may want to seriously consider if its something you can live with. The manufacturer should allow repair or replacement. (Personally, I haven't made that decision, yet.) If your new projector is "clean", do whatever you can to keep it that way. Remember, a projector like the 710 is short-throw, so it is likely to be low, near the floor when in use. The viewing room must be clean. Use a good, clean vacuum to suck up as much dust as possible. And while doing any activity in the viewing room other than using your projector, make sure the projector is covered. Update 2/17/13: I've changed my rating from 4 stars to 5. I received a replacement W710ST from Amazon and, with a total of 17 hours on the clock, it is performing perfectly, minus the speaker buzzing problem (see original review below). Getting the replacement projector from Amazon was as painless as could be. I'm very satisfied with Amazon and my new BenQ W710ST (so far). One quick comment before you move on to the review: This projector is currently $550. As I'm sure you already know projectors can be mighty expensive. Based on the performance of the 710 (at $550) I can only imagine, since I'm a beginner, how well a 5, 4 or even a $2000 projector might perform. Unfortunately, I'll probably never know. Can't really justify the expense and not able to afford it, anyway. All I can say is, based on my limited experience, the 710, in spite of a few minor quirks and/or design errors, provides exciting home theater at an affordable price. Considering a giant screen TV? Fuhget-about-it. In fact, I'll save you the time needed to read my long-winded review by offering the only best advice I can give: disregard everything and go straight to Short Throw(ST) High Definition(HD) projection. The ST technology makes a LOT of sense. And it works, very well. As for HD projection? In a word, WOW! Review 1/15/13: The BenQ W710ST does the job, but... there were a few issues. The BenQ box (inside a larger delivery box) arrived a few days ago and it looked like it had been "through the mill" (scratches, scuffs and dings). It caused me to be suspect right away. Inside the BenQ box, however, everything appeared new. The unit came carefully packed inside a black, well made and fully padded nylon carry case along with the usual extras (except component and/or HDMI cables). The "feel" of this projector is solid and precise but it's a bit chunky and odd shaped. It's not compact. Short throw is the 710's primary selling point and the main reason why I decided to try it. The BenQ is designed to be set up low and up front, not in the back over your shoulder like most projectors. It does work well and I like it. The remote is also substantial with full control and an easy-reach backlight button. A lense cap is also provided. An important extra. Upon firing up the W710ST, The fan was exquisitely quiet. Nearly silent in eco-mode...but (and here's the "but") the internal speaker was annoyingly buzzy. Starting at about 1/3 volume the plastic projector body began buzzing. Turning up the volume caused the projector to vibrate to a point where talking or music could not be understood. However, I dont intend to use the projector for presentations, only home theater, so one would not tend to use the internal speaker anyway... but (the last "but") it's still a defect (or damage) and I MAY decide to return it for that reason. Now what about the picture: it's big and bright with excellent color and good blacks. The 710 can easily be run in eco while ambient light exists. For example, you could have a 60 watt incandescent on in the back of the room (as long as it's filtered and not throwing shadows). I havn't seen the wonderful detail others have mentioned. Although I have not acheived the highest resolution yet either. I'm presently sourcing from an older standard def DVD player with component out (720 by 480), not to mention projecting on a painted wall. Planning to go to HDMI out (1280 by 720) on a new DVD player this week. I'm assuming the picture will have significantly more detail then. A problem I've found, although minor, is the lack of control built into the unit. There's no vertical keystoning and source signals are managed automatically (no manual control.). Also, a bothersome thing about the menu is it pushes you too far back when hitting return. You'll find that you're always going back then forward again, a recurring but temporary nuisance. On the up side, there is a very usefull feature that allows you to set up fast and almost anywhere without much fuss. There are auto presets built in which adjust color output for different colored walls. I'm projecting on a smooth, flat painted wall tinted a slight yellow. The projector corrected for this perfectly. Warm up time is about 30 seconds. Shutdown is quick. About 3D: The 710 has the capability but 3D doesn't interest me very much. Overall, this is what the W710ST does well: short throw, easy/quick set-up, good video under various conditions. All the extras and, especially, the very quiet fan is a bonus. On the downside, the BenQ lacks some control which, I believe, is standard on similarly priced units. It's heft, odd shape and quirky menu/remote take a little getting used to. Still, the W710ST is a fine example of quality in design and function. If not for the speaker problem, I would have gone to 5 stars for initial use and quality. Hate to say it Amazon, I'd give you 5 stars as well but the delivery took longer than originally suggested (11 days instead of 5 - 8 days). And it was obvious the package was kicked around prior to leaving the shipper (whomever that was). You were the best price, though. And the transaction was no hassle. Update 1/16/13: I incorrectly noted above the 710 does not offer vertical keystoning. It does. But not horizontal keystoning. Keystoning can be confusing and here's why: Vertical keystoning will allow angle adjustment of the displayed image on a HORIZONTAL axis; meaning the displayed image can be tilted backward and forward as if on an invisible rod laying accross the middle of the screen. Horizontal keystoning, which the 710 does not allow, pivots the image on a vertical axis. So, in essence, it's a conflict in terms. I would also like to note other pluses and minuses: 1. The 710 doesn't get hot. Compared to an Epson I tried out previously, it's like night and day. The Epson ran hot, even in eco mode. 2. The 710 user manual (downloadable and on a supplied dvd) is pretty good. What I like most is the manual provides a clear and concise explanation of each menu item. 3. The remote is very responsive from virtually any angle. 4. I haven't seen any "rainbow effect" that others have mentioned can be a problem with DLP projectors. I was very concerned about this. Fortunately, there's been no evidence of that whatsoever with the 710. 5. The 710 is a power hog (300 watts), mostly due to the lamp (220 watts). 6. The 710 audio (mono into a buzzy speaker) is extremely lacking. For my purposes (home theater) it's utterly useless. The problem here is I may, at some point, like to use the 710 as a stand-alone unit. But that is not possible because of the speaker problem. Even if there were no vibrations, I can't believe a small, mono speaker would be effective under any circumstances. Also, the audio connections in the back of the unit are not clearly marked and confusing. Why isn't the audio 2 channel pass-through and contollable from the remote (versus mono sound terminating at the projector)? Doesn't make sense. And there's no understanding why you don't get either a component cable and/or an HDMI cable with the projector. Not good marketing of the product in my opinion. Wouldn't it make sense to provide the means to demonstrate your product in the best possible way? I would suggest to BenQ that they sort these issues out (should be easy fixes) if they really want to sell a first rate projector to the masses. Final notes and buying tip: Know what you intend to use your projector for and under what conditions (what's MOST important). I don't believe there's a projector made that will do it all. For me it's home theater in a not-so-big room, so I wanted short-throw; a big, bright image with decent clarity and contrast (I'm looking forward to a new DVD player and a real screen for an even better theater experience). Plus, NOOOO distractions, meaning a QUIET fan. The 710 does these jobs admirably. But if it's complete portability with great audio capabilities you're after, look elsewhere. And a word about LED (which the 710 is not): I was hoping that might be an option for me. I liked the idea of a long life, eco-friendly (no mercury and low power consumption) lamp. Those are the primary LED benefits. It can be "always on" like a TV. But, as far as I know, it really cannot be used as such. The brightness levels just aren't there, yet. Besides, other than the benefits mentioned, what good is it to have a projector with a lamp lasting 25 years when, in all likelyhood, the projector itself with either be trashed or outdated within 5 years? Update 1/17/13: Ok, maybe I'm getting a little carried away with this review but I think I can offer an extra bit of info that may be helpful: a comment to my review noted I cannot watch high definition video on the 710 without bluray. It turns out he was very right. But being a person who has to learn for himself I decided to conduct a little (unscientific) study. I went to my local library and fortunately they had multiple copies of the same move, including one in bluray. Then I went to my local Walmart and purchased 2 dvd players (1 upscaling and 1 bluray) giving me three dvd players (as noted above I have an older non-upscaling player with component out). I hooked all three players up to the 710 at the same time, all with the same movie (Note that an additional benefit provided by the 710 is 2 - not just 1 - HDMI inputs, along with component in, allowed me to test all three at the same time.) I synced up the players as best I could and using the remote control I was able to switch from one player to the other. Bluray is DEFINATELY better; a stunning improvement over my old standard definition player, not to mention the upscaling player. The image was significantly more vibrant and clear. The upscaling player was only marginally better than my old player. But an improvement nonetheless. It was akin to making a sharpness adjustment from less sharp to more sharp. Other than that I couldn't see any real differences which, I suppose, makes my old dvd player an acceptable performer. There was no significant difference that I could see in terms of brightness, color and black levels between all three players. In fact, the "softness" of my old player had it's benefits. The additional clarity displayed potential shortcomings of either the bluray player and/or the projector. I noticed especially when using the bluray player, "noise" in the blues and grays in some scenes. This was not evident at all on the old player. I'm not knowledgable enough to know what and why the noise was there. Perhaps it's simply a matter of making an adjustment, somewhere. I dont yet know. So this wraps up my overblown review of the BenQ W710ST. I hope it was in some way helpful to you.

Once upon a time, American manufacturing was the envy of the world. Without getting into all the reasons that's no longer the case, when it came time for me to get a tripod projection screen, I was very happy to see that the Da-Lite company is still manufacturing an American classic: the "Picture King." Da-Lite and a number of other manufacturers make a cheaper version of this size screen, and most of us have seen what happens to them in normal use. The screen material is thin and funky, the tripod and adjustment hardware fall apart, and the screen quickly becomes a headache to set up and use. Don't waste your money on cheaper versions ... just spend a bit more and get the Picture King. You'll be glad you did. The Picture King is well designed and constructed with durable, quality materials, and will last a lifetime if properly used and cared for. The tripod, screen housing, center posts and adjustment hardware are all aluminum or steel, and tough as nails. It's a bit big and heavy, so it requires some strength to carry around, but nothwithstanding its heft, it's very easy to set up, and provides a great, stable projection surface for just about all viewing conditions. To set it up, you pick the screen up by its VERY beefy metal handle and set it on the tripod end; touch the toe release at the base of the tripod assembly; the tripod legs unlock and spread out by themselves; you rotate the screen housing to a horizontal position; pull up the center post and lock it in place at your desired height; pull the screen up and hang its handle on the clip at the top of the center post, and you're good to go. The center post has plenty of fixed height settings at both the top and bottom of the screen. and use the "keystone" adjuster to tip the top of the screen toward the projection source, if needed. While the maximum size of the screen is 70 x 70 in. square, it's simple to adjust it for letterbox or wide screen formats, e.g., by just pulling less of the screen up out of its housing. When you're ready to put it away, it folds up securely and neatly -- there's a fixed clip and corresponding button that holds the screen handle in place against the center handle; a pin at the top of the center post that fits in a hole at the top end of the screen housing to lock it parallel with the folded tripod, and another lock at the bottom of the tripod assembly that holds the folded tripod legs in place against the center post. The screen material is thick and durable, which you can also sponge off with mild soap and water if you ever have to. I got mine with the basic "Matte White" finish, but Da-Lite makes the Picture King with several other types of screen material as well, and their website fully explains how the materials differ. My Amazon purchase was flawless. Amazon had the best price and shipping options, hands-down. The item arrived quickly and in perfect condition. I also got the 70-inch cover bag from Da-Lite, and I strongly recommend that anyone getting the Picture King spend the extra 30 bucks for this invaluable accessory. It will extend the service life of your screen indefinitely, protecting it from dust and scratches. So far, I'm delighted with both.

Ok, this entry level home theater has the basic technology to enjoy current generation video and sound quality. To begin, the design of the player is sleek and is decently sized, the speakers are very good looking too. The materials are very glossy and I love that. I have a problem with the volume keys wich are oversized for convenience BUT, they feel rubish and the design feels kind of out of place with the rest. The unit itself feels made of standard cheap materials to be honest. Now, when it comes to the user interface, it is standard at best, probably because I am very used to play my Bluray collection on my PS3 and the XMB is very sleek and fast, this one, again, feels rubish and generic. It doesnt really use any Java trick to get smoth animations at all. The internet apps are located at the bottom of the screen and you have to go page by page to the sides see them all and you are unable to locate the most used apps in the first page for easy access. The movie tittle sprite that usually appears on the PS3 XMB is not shown on this player. and for some reason the icon to select the bluray movie is hidden until you press the yellow button on the remote, instead you are offered the options to play music, videos or photos using the online connection or USB. Very impractical taking into consideration this is a BLURAY PLAYER first and foremost. Now, the most important thing. Audio: Side note for reference: (I used to use a 5.1 LOGITECH X-530 unit. The sound is clearer and it has the same bass levels after some minor adjustment then the logitech one. The side speakers were larger thus generating a louer sound but just a minor difference, nothing that cannot be adjusted in the Samsung settings.) The main sound decoders on this player are: Dolby Digital DTS Dolby Digital Dolby True HD DTS HD Master Audio Essensials The sound is very good, I reach 50% of the volume capacity and dont notice any distortion or overload noise. Channel separation is very clear and the Cristal Amplifier Plus (Built in by default, not something you can actually turn on or off) allows for even clearer nuances in the sound track being music or sound effects. The quality of the audio will also depend of the source. You will probably not notice any difference between Dolby Digital and Dolby True HD but when it comes to DTS HD Master Audio, you will experience the same clarity but there are jumps in volume according to whats happening on screen which are very good, in short and in my own experience DTS MA is louder but not necesarily "noisy", it is loud but still very clear. Try The Lord of The Rings Extended Trilogy (DT MA), The hospital explotion scene from The Dark Knight(DTrueHD), Avatar and Master and Commander as clear examples on what to expect fromthis player I connected my PS3 using the optical in and the Dolby Digital tracks sound good, very standard to what you are probably used to hear by now (GTA V). Games that make use of the DTS Digital Surround sound louder and more dinamic in my opinion. Try using Bioshock Infinite, The Last Of Us, Tomb Raider and Uncharted 3 (Also in 3D) and you will tell te diference. Overall I am very pleased with the experience. my living room is quite small wich also benefits the experience from this small and cost effective player. I have not tried the 3D option yet but I dont think that will be a problem since that technology is very standard among brands (in 3D the TV does the difference not the player I think) so if you are on a short budget but are scared to buy this one, dont doubt it, you will not be dissapointed by the sound (the most important thing). I was obsessed with this player before buying it and when I had it, it fulfilled my expectations up to a 90% which is not bad. It's just that I am very picky with tech. Buy it!
