I bought this during the 2018 Black Friday Sale and it's like a gift that keeps on giving. I just wanted to get a really large PC monitor for my games with a 1440p resolution. I'm not a professional photo or video editor so I really can't judge the picture quality except say that it's really nice. Haven't noticed much backlight bleed and I'm glad I got one without dead or stuck pixels. I was even worried buying another monitor from Amazon because when I bought an LG monitor from them I got dead pixels on the both the original and replacement they sent so getting a perfect Philips screen made me happy. I have a GTX 1080 so I thought the FreeSync that came with the monitor is just something extra that I won't be able to use. At first I got dizzy because of the size of this thing but that's OK. It makes my previous 23" monitor look puny. Then I could play at 75Hz refresh rate! To be honest 60 to 75hz isn't really that much noticeable that I got to "I-can't-play-on-60-anymore" but having it is still nice for the games I play that are mostly racing, RPGs, adventure, action games and Elite Dangerous. Then hell froze over and nVidia decided to support FreeSync monitors via DisplayPort. At first I thought the VRR (variable refresh rate) functionality of the monitor is garbage because activating GSync-compatibility makes the display a stutterfest, like it intermittently shows a previous frame every half a second. On the first nVidia driver in order to actually get GSync properly working I had to use DDU (display driver uninstaller) on safe mode then activate Gsync then bounce the refresh rate of the OS from 60 to 75hz, then finally activate GSync on the nVidia Control Panel. Turning off the PC or restarting it breaks Gsync and it will be back to being stuttery so I have to do everything again from the top. Just today nVidia released a new driver so I deleted the monitor drivers, did the DDU-GPU-driver dance then activated Gsync. Afterwards it no longer goes bad after restarts and everything is smooth. Now that I can use VRR I can hold back on updating my GPU because as long as the framerate is 48 FPS or above I get smooth gameplay. Of course I'll be happier if games always stay 60 FPS and above all the time but money don’t grow from trees. Added 2019/02/18: I just recently discovered that the main thing that makes Gsync thru FreeSync go bad is when the display/GPU goes to sleep. Everytime that happens games would stutter really bad. When VRR is working fine I noticed that the refresh rate figure on the monitor's display information also changes. When it's not working the refresh rate just stays at 75hz. As something of an audiophile and after reading the earlier reviews, I ordered these speakers with some trepidation. For casual listening, they are a fine upgrade for subpar built-in computer speakers, but with no heavy power adapter to lug around, these compact speakers are especially great for taking on trips. (LaCie includes a padded case for safely transporting the speakers, easily worth $10 on its own!) Just plug the primary speaker into your laptop USB and connect the secondary speaker to the primary speaker, then set the iTunes equalizer to "small speakers" and turn on medium sound enhancement in preferences, and sit back and listen to what I found to be satisfying and surprisingly immersive sound. Great for when watching DVDs. (Alert readers will wonder how I could play DVDs and use the speakers at the same time on the single MacBook Air USB port. The trick is to first rip the DVD on to the hard-drive using the MBA USB DVD player, unplug, then plug in the speakers to play.) But you don't even to have a computer to benefit from these speakers. There is a Line In socket for audio from iPods and other MP3 players. LaCie thoughtfully includes a white mini-jack to mini-jack cable for this purpose. Power can be from a 9V DC source (not included) or via the USB cable. Yes, I discovered you can plug the USB cable into a small (Sonnos) iPod USB Power Adapter and it works! How's that for a complete, portable powered iPod sound system!

This seems to be a decent option for a compact USB powered travel charger. I found the charger less aggressive than the Sony A7RIII in camera charging except for a slightly higher charge rate between ~80 and ~90% battery capacity. This charger appears to be a safe inexpensive option for charging OEM batteries. Below are the results from ad hoc tests of different chargers. Testing method: USB power provided by 5v 2.4a capable Anker USB charger(s). Power draw monitored by a YZXstudio ZY1276 in line USB power meter. Tests run multiple times with two new OEM Sony NP-FZ100 batteries. (Each battery had around 3 full charge cycles at the start of these tests.) Kastar LCD Slim USB Charger (Item being reviewed.) Total charge time for a fully exhausted battery until charge cycle complete: ~4.25 - 4.75 hours. (In camera battery meter showed 100% around 4:15 but continued charging the battery itself at a very low current.) 5.1v ~1000ma USB power draw between 0% and ~90 - 95% charge. (~4hrs) 5.1v ~0 to 400ma constantly varying current from ~90 - 95% until ~99.5 - 100%. (~+15 mins) 5.1v ~0 to 130ma constantly varying current for the last .5% charge or so. (+15 to 30 mins) Notes: Between ~90% charge (as reported by camera) and the end of the Kastar charge cycle, the current being drawn by the charger was constantly varying but progressively lower as the battery neared full charge. 4200+ma of current @ ~5.1v passed into the Kastar charger during a full charge cycle. (Keep in mind that only a portion of this 4200ma made it to the battery as usable power due to inefficiencies of the charger & charge process.) Well after the Kastar charge cycle completed (via monitoring the usb power draw), the in-camera meter showed 100% charge but consumed an additional (nominal) ~40ma before the in-camera charger considered the battery fully charged. This is a strong indicator that this generic charger is not likely to over-charge OEM batteries. Vivitar dual port USB charger: (Included in a bundle with my camera purchase. Looks identical to the DSTE DUB167 dual charger.) Total charge time for fully exhausted battery until charge cycle complete: ~4.0 - 4.5 hours. 5.25v ~1300ma USB power draw up to ~80% charge. 5.25v ~1200ma from ~80% until ~90% charge. 5.25v ~700ma from ~90% until ~95% charge. 5.25v ~700ma down to ~32ma between ~95% and 100% charge. (Constant but progressively lower current draw until the end of charge cycle.) Similar to the Kastar charger, once the Vivitar charge cycle was complete I moved the battery to the in-camera charger which drew another ~32ma or so before ending the in-camera charge cycle. A7RIII f/w v2.0 in camera charging via the micro-USB port: Total charge time for fully exhausted battery: ~3.5 - 4 hours. 5.1v ~1500ma USB power draw between 0% and ~75-80% charge. 5.1v ~600ma from ~75-80% until high ~9x% 5.1v ~290ma down to ~40ma for the last 1 - 2% or so of the charge cycle. (Constant but progressively lower current draw until the end of charge cycle.)

I benchmarked using the same HD_Speed test on the same computer with same settings vs. the exact same memory card bought from a physical Costco store.... The memory I bought from "EVERYTHING BUT STROMBOLI" had a VERY UNSTABLE write rate meaning the memory quality was very poor. Also, the speed of write was HALF that of the Costco-bought version of the same exact memory. The version bought from Costco also wrote at a very stable linear rate (actually above the speed rating guaranteed by SanDisk). If in doubt, buy your memory card from a local store. It may save you a lot of hassle!

I feel like I've been dating my new Kindle HDX 8.9. I'm looking for a long-term relationship-but I am swinging between infatuation for the many things that are terrific, to swinging back to mild disappointment with the things that bother me. A partial list of the very good: * The fabulous screen (FAB-U-LOUS!) * The ulta-lightness (it feel like the battery must be missing) * The great sound * Sharp sharp sharp text * The joy of reading Kindle books on it (no rim of purple or blue) * The smooth, quick operation--no stuttering! * The really surprisingly decent cameras front and back * The straight-forward and easy process to add (and view) my photographs and videos to this Kindle (Bravo! nothing hidden or difficult!) * The placement of the power and sound buttons are perfect for me * ALL the improvements in the operating system from the previous model listed in previous reviews are spot on. Great job Amazon! HOWEVER: * The fit and finish on mine is off. Where the rubberized section meets the shiny plastic on the back is not level, so there's just enough of a sharp ridge of the shiny plastic close to the top corners on both sides to make it uncomfortable to hold. It's where I normally would grasp it, and it's irritating like a bad seam in a shoe or a tag in a shirt that has to be cut out. It makes it feel cheap and I find myself wondering if I could just take a bit of sandpaper & fix it, but one shouldn't need to fix the finish on a tablet. * The app store (you've already read about it) * I thought I would not mind the ads on the opening screen, but I find that I dislike them more and more. They tend toward unattractive or childish ads for apps in which I have no interest. Again, this cheapens the experience for me. I really wish for the ability to personalize the screens with my own photographs to take advantage of that beautiful screen. Tablets are a very personal choice and what may not bother many may rub someone else the wrong way. It's obvious that this little much improved jewel will be love at first sight for some, but I'm beginning to feel that the Kindle HDX 8.9 and I will just be friends. It's more than a 3, but maybe just shy of a 4 for me.

Yes, these fit the Sennheiser HD 280 Pro. Simply pinch original earpads, pull and remove. To place new ones, stretch the rubber inserts a little, guide around the outer edge of the earpad and tuck into the crevice. If you don't have fingernails to tuck them in, you can try using a credit card or similarly thin, non sharp object. The original earpads weren't bad at all, but over time they did begin to grow a bit brittle (most likely due to oil residue from around my ears). These memory foam earpads fit perfectly as replacements. No noticeable difference in sound signature. The pleather material retains most of the sound isolation, but does allow more sound to get it than the original earpads. Memory foam ones are also much thicker, making collapsing the 280 a bit trickier since you'll have to squeeze the pads in before folding. The memory foam is much more comfortable than the original earpads. These feel more like pillows now rather than the headphones feeling like something industrial. It's made the 280 feel like my new go to closed back headphones. Overall I'm very happy with these. I'll wait to see how their velour replacements handle the HD 598 I have.

Well I was going to get a real leather case for my iPad 7th gen, but I thought I’d give this brown version of the case a try, and I’m happy I did. It doesn’t look quite as leather-like in person, but it could fool you if you didn’t know. It seems to be well-made and the flap that covers the screen has a decent amount of cushion in it. My iPad is below the lip of the case after pushing it into the cavity of the case, and it’s settled in nice and snug. And as an aside, I must say that the white bezels of my gold-colored iPad go well with the gray lip of this case. One thing I was worried about was the hand strap that you use to make it easier to hold the iPad vertically, has a bit of a hard and rough edge where the strap connects to the case, but you can actually only feel that if you pull your finger against that connecting point. In reality I don’t think that connecting point touches the screen when the case is closed because it’s below the level of the main part of the strap, and even if it did the rough part is not the top of that connecting point. But that concern is the only thing I could call a possible flaw. I can’t comment about the fit of the Apple Pencil holder since I don’t yet have the pencil, but for those concerned about getting it out of the holder, there are two open slots at the back of the holder which should allow you to pop out the pencil relatively easy. I do wish the hand strap was a bit tighter, but it does work fine as is. The case strap for holding the flap open works fine, as do the ridges that let you prop open your iPad to watch videos and such. The slot for papers on the front isn’t super roomy, but it’s good for a decent amount of papers I would say. All of the iPad buttons and connectors fit perfectly and are completely uncovered, except for the smart keyboard connector. If you plan on adding a smart keyboard this is not the case for you, although I’m sure you can still use a Bluetooth keyboard. I suspect that this case will be reasonably durable and will be more than worth the price. It’s not too heavy, and it makes holding my iPad easy in both the portrait and landscape orientation. If I could I would rate it 4.75 stars — nearly perfect. For the price I doubt you can beat it. I highly recommend it!

I'm very happy with this purchase. My advice is to read all the reviews, because they are very informative and may point out something that for you is a deal breaker or shows it's a must have. For me, it's the latter. I teach dance and am a musician, and I actually first looked at this product to replace a lost ipod nano (!). Compared to the ipod, this is an entirely different creature; it's obviously more like an ipad. However, one of the best things, compared to the "i" products, is that the memory is upgradeable. Another bonus: the price point is a heck of a lot lower, but this is a quality device. If you're familiar with Android (I have an HTC Droid Incredible), it's great to have the real Android market open to you (and not some pared down version - beware of imitation "Android" devices!), even though I've found a few apps that have issues (not everybody plays nicely with Honeycomb). The video quality is great, although you'll quickly learn to lock the screen so the image doesn't keep shifting from portrait to landscape if you tilt the unit slightly. The speaker quality is fine for average use. After three weeks, I'm still fighting with the keyboard more than I'd like; it's very sensitive and easy to hit carriage return without meaning to. I have to admit, the battery life is disappointing, especially when my ipad user friends brag about their toys, but there are many things you can do to improve it: + set screen brightness and timeout to lower than defaults + I've found that having open mail accounts takes a lot of energy. I set them up, but when I turned off the sync, my battery life improved tons. I can reactivate the sync to use them, but I get mail on my phone and computer. Do I really need it on the tablet too? + I do use a task killer, and I set it on SAFE (as opposed to aggressive) and to kill apps automatically every half hour. Lots of apps (weather, news feeds, facebook, even clocks) check in with the web regularly. As far as I can tell, the big cons are the battery issues. Let's face it, 4-5 hours is short. I get more use, because of a light usage pattern, but it can go down pretty rapidly as I do use it. The guy on a total rant in his review regarding the charger unit does have a point - in this day and age of "folding" plugs, and charger cords doubling as USB connectors, this is not a power supply you can throw easily in a bag. It's a bummer. And it's an even bigger bummer you can't currently {ar ar ar} get a car charger. [BEWARE of USB car chargers advertised on Amazon as working for this unit; you cannot charge via USB, A100s only power up via the proprietary Acer plug. I asked at Radio Shack, it's an Acer thing...] So, it's not too much fun to have to travel with your charger. Quite a few reviewers mention the screen as a problem. While it does have some angle-related limitations, it's easy to optimize the angle - and I'm using it in class, hand-held, in varied lighting conditions. Finally, the Poetic case [[ASIN:B005PZ07PI Poetic(TM) Slimbook Leather Case for Acer Iconia Tab A100 7-Inch Android Tablet Wi-Fi (Black)]] is a useful and economic accessory I highly recommend. My husband bought an 8GB on a Black Friday special and is mostly happy with his purchase, except for battery life. He paid $199. UPDATE: July 2012 I traded in this device. I could not get around the horrible battery life. For all the cool things it does, no battery life - and such a horrible, bulky charger (and no car option) - I just realized I wasn't really using the unit. I've ordered a Google Nexus 7: lower price point, updated Android, and a battery that performs a whole lot better.

I bought this system about three weeks ago and I have to say I am very pleased with my purchase. For the price I paid, I could not go wrong. I did a lot of research and I was looking for a nice surround sound with speaker and sub for a decent price. I hit the mark with this system! I paid $244.00 for this system and the day after I purchased it the price went up to $399! It was all that I could ask for in a surround sound system for that price! It is a 600 watt system (each speaker is 100 watts). I have a smaller living room so once I ran the cables in the walls and mounted the speakers, the sound engulfs you and you feel like you are part of any movie that you watch. The speakers are very sleek and are on the small size, which is what I wanted. I did not want to mount huge speakers next to my flat screen TV. They look awesome. The sub is passive so you don't have a power cable for the device, which is what I like. It comes with an ASC mic so it auto calibrates the sound output, but to be honest, I went in and tweaked the output to my desires as I wanted the rear speakers to be a bit louder. It also comes with an iPod dock, which I have yet to use, but will eventually. This is also a 3D pass through device which was a need since I own a Samsung 51" 3D Plasma TV and a PlayStation 3. I have yet to try the 3D capabilities as I just purchased the 3D TV, but that will happen soon. All in all I think this was a great purchase at the price I paid. Would I have paid $399 for this system, hmmm, maybe and maybe not? I would have to compare what this offers to similar devices at the same price...and at this point I am done doing research :-) All I know is that I couldn't pass it up for $244.00! The only negatives for this system are the speaker wires it comes with are flimsy, so do yourself a favor like I did and purchase better speaker wires. Believe me it is worth it for the 15 bucks. I tested the system with the cables included and then with 16 gauge wires I bought and the difference is night and day! Also, the system doesn't appear to operate in standby, not a big deal to me, but someone may want this feature. The last negative for this product is that it doesn't seem to have a remote code for my Comcast remote control, which means I have to use the remote control that came with it to turn the system on and off and to toggle the inputs. This is not fun, but it's not a deal breaker for the price. Hope this helps and happy hunting.

I ordered these for a couple of reasons: 1) they looked heavy duty, which I have gone through a lot of headphones for reasons below, and 2) I love the idea of a detachable/removable cord. I also was desirous of having a headphone with really good sound quality. These Numark DJ phones fulfilled all of my desires. I received them, pulled them out of the box and had them hooked up within 10 minutes of the UPS man dropping by. The first impressions were good: Beefy construction, fit and finish is excellent, lightweight for the size, nice earpads. Then I hooked them up. I was not expecting htem to be real hifi phones. Being designed for DJ use, I figured they would be heavy, excessively so, on the bass. What I discovered was that these phones are really excellent across all frequencies. The bass is not excessive, it is simply more clearly defined than with any other phones I've used. The mid frequencies, primarily vocals, are really good. The voices seem to be really inside your head. The higher frequencies, cymbals, violins, etc., are near perfect. I love using these with classical music, which is the hardest music to reproduce due to the complexity. The Numark phones really keep up. I can pick out individual instruments in the orchestra and visulaize exactly where they are in the mental 'soundstage'. I've been a hifi nut for 38 years, and I haven't heard any phones that even approach what these can do. I've owned quite a variety of headphones through the years, including electrostatics. I'll stick with my Numarks! One thing to keep in mind. I am 6'4" tall with a 7&7/8ths size head. That translates to the phones being tight over the skull and ears. At first it was uncomfortable, but the headband starts to adjust and relax after a while. At my size, that's just the way the world is, so it is no big deal. My wife is 5'6". so they work fine for her. I did not subtract a star for it, as they are about par for the course. Summary: I highly recommend the Numark DJ phones for anyone. I'll be getting a pair for my wife soon. Best regards, John Price

Edit, AFTER ALMOST A WEEK: I started a return on these a couple of days ago (purchased at $73/pair, I got 4), but I'm starting to second guess myself and raised these a star. They DO articulate with detail and place sound (music for me) in space rather than just project it from the speaker (this is called "imaging" and "staging" respectively within the psuedo-scientific & semi-technical but-actually too often superstitious, subjective, phallocentric, insecure, & frequently juvenile audiophile world). They're fairly blank or neutral, meaning they are not coloring the sound signal much--which can make them prone to cause ear fatigue--an actual real thing. I suppressed the treble, but it only helps so much. I just don't want to sit and listen to these all day. They are a bit forward, by this an audiophile would mean that the sound from the speakers is intense--it carries, I've a good sized house, these must be behind closed doors and turned down low and STILL can be heard: these are loudspeakers. They project. No one would call them mellow or laid back, I guess if that person were used to something MUCH more intense, like maybe a studio monitor or something. They are essentially even tonally, the highs (which one expects with two tweeters, both pretty small) do not ring out and neither do the lows. They are not particularly low--but I have the SACS9 sub (which was also half-off, and not intensely great, but certainly more than adequate at $100). I worry that that .75" tweeter is making these a bit shrill in ways that I can't hear--because they were a bit unpleasant at first, but I broke them in--speakers "break-in" is not a real thing, as the folks who make and test them for the manufacturers for a living will tell you if your ask them. What I mean is I adjusted my simple EQ settings, turned on a treble filter, and now they sound, pretty good, still not warm but actually a bit resonant. I was thinking about keeping them, ending my speaker search (for now)--these aren't the look I was going for, but they look alright, I think they might have the sound I want, and they are certainly WELL UNDER the price I was willing to spend for the full system ($250 for 4.1 is hard to argue with) that sounds good and is this loud (and still sounding good) is very hard to argue with. But I can't keep them for other reasons, 6ohm that tend towards 4 is a problem for me. FIRST IMPRESSION AFTER FIRST DAY: Wanted to love these, the price was so good, impossible to pass up for 'audiophile' speakers. And maybe these sorts of speakers are supposed to be this way, but these things are unpleasant to listen to. Sure, there's a nice sound stage, solid imaging, depth, articulation, and the rest. I've seen the graph reports on these things, but it doesn't cover it, the truth is it don't sound great. I don't want to listen to them. I think I'm returning them.

I purchased the Acer Chromebook Spin 311 to use as a bedside entertainment center, so I wanted something that could stream and have quality screen resolution. I have an extensive music collection that I keep on an external SSD and I absolutely love MediaMonkey because of it's customizable interface on it's Window's app (I assumed the ChromeOS version would be very similar - my first major stumble). First, the positive: The device itself is fantastic. Everything about it feels sturdy, the touchscreen is responsive (though, I will say there are times when I feel I have to hit an app 2 or 3 times to activate). The screen resolution and sound quality are lovely for a device of this size and price - don't go expecting studio quality here, but the streaming was beautiful. The visuals are not pixelated; it's as good as watching on a television (only smaller). Oh, and I will say I love the fact that the USB-C port is on both sides, which makes it easier to plug in on any side (it's the little things). Performance is great, I get no lag and I've had no issues streaming Netflix, Hulu or Disney+. I just realized I haven't tried watching Twitch or Youtube on this. I'll download those apps and if I have any problems with them, I'll update this review and let you know. I have one grouse, and it's kind of a biggie: The apps are terrible. It was so dismaying at first, I did actually contemplate sending the device back. I slept on it and decided I was going to stick it out. In truth, part of my disappointment is that the ChromeOS version of MediaMonkey is disappointing. When it came down to it, I tried a whole slew of music apps and I wound up settling on the music app that annoyed me the least (VLC). The good: - Very happy with the image sensor. Clear image, even lighting and coloration. - Lenses are clear with relatively smooth if fast operation - Excellent depth of field. The bad: - None of the corrective capabilities I usually take for granted with consumer, prosumer, or commercial grade equipment (image stabilization, autofocus, distortion correcting lenses). In that regard, it's reminiscent of cameras on the market 50 years ago, but it's what I should expect for $100 - Low focal length has significant barrel distortion with black corners. This can be ignored for security monitoring, corrected with software for recorded videos, but can be a limiting factor for live videoconferencing use. Overall recommendation: I've used both the 2-12, and 5-50mm lenses. the 2-12 mm lens's excellent depth of field makes it a better security camera and stage performance recorder (if you can get the camera close enough). The 5-50mm lens has little if any distortion but depth of field issues limit its use for recording stage performances or teleconferencing. I wish they had a middling option that moderated the shortcomings, or better yet an upgraded lens that added some of the missing functionality. - For personal teleconferencing, camera distance from 3-5' - For group teleconferencing, camera distance from 8-15' - security camera, 2-30', though not the best low light sensitivity

If you buy this during or after 2020 you will probably receive it dead on arrival. The first one I bought was DOA so I returned it in exchange for a replacement which was also DOA. It worked when plugged into the wall but it would not charge and would not turn on under it's own power. Fed up, I held onto it for a while but I wasn't ready to give up because I had bought the waterproof case and an sd card specifically for this camera. I have experience with lithium batteries, and most electronics like this have some sort of lithium battery in them. My hypothesis was that since this product has been discontinued for years they have been sitting on shelves for years while the batteries slowly drained. Lithium batteries cannot go below 3 volts. If they do they start to become damaged and will not charge anymore. So I went to iFixit and followed their disassembly tutorial for these little cameras. And there it was. The lithium battery cells were puffed up, the clear sign of damage and too low of voltage. My multimeter read about 5 mV. Way too low. But the camera worked fine. It just didn't have power. So I was able to purchase some nearly identical lithium cells on ebay and did the tedious process of removing the wires and control board from the old dead batteries and soldered them onto the new ones. And it fired right up! I am not recommending this process to anyone. Only telling you that it is possible to resurrect this camera if it is DOA. Lithium batteries can be dangerous if handled incorrectly.

I bought this stylus for my kindergartner to do homework on her iPad (7th gen). The iPad is inside a protective case which comes with a screen protector. She mainly uses SeeSaw to draw the pictures. I don't need to put an adapter and remove cap (these are required by Apple Pencil, which are very easy to lose because they are small parts). - There is an on/off button. It helps to preserve the battery life. (You can't turn off Apple Pencil unless you are charging it) - Work with screen protector What I don't like: - This stylus works about half of the time, i.e., it doesn't work the other half of the time. For example, when my kid tried to draw on iPad, the stylus did not response randomly (like the pen doesn't draw, no response etc). We even removed the protective case and screen protector, but the problem still existed. I am pretty sure it was not a battery issue because this problem showed up randomly. Sometimes we experienced this problem after the stylus was fully charged overnight. - Unlike Apple Pencil that uses Bluetooth to talk to the iPad, this stylus mainly uses the tip (pressure) to interact with the iPad. So the accuracy is not very reliable. I guess this is one of the main reasons why this stylus is cheaper than Apple Pencil (without the Bluetooth chip). My kid felt very frustrated when this stylus failed to work. She ended up using her finger instead. So after using this stylus for about a month, I ended up returning it and got an Apple Pencil instead. My kid is very happy with the Apple Pencil because it works.

This is named a "security camera" but a combination of high image compression and motion blur render the effective resolution far less than the advertised 1080P (2 megapixel). I originally attached representative images to my review, but the review was rejected presumably because it contained "personally identifying" information. But honestly the image quality is so low you couldn't identify anyone with it. To describe the two images, in one a lady is 5' from the camera and her face is a featureless blur throughout the video. In another a car passes close by my house, and the license plate is illegible. I risked attaching that one here. Given the low image quality, it really doesn't matter that the Nest Cam doesn't support ONVIF --an open IP video surveillance standard-- because it wouldn't provide useful imagery even if it did. Without ONVIF support, the camera can't be linked with crime camera networks like a well known one here in New Orleans. This camera doesn't provide any meaningful level of security as advertised, so I'm returning it.

It works well and is clearer than I expected. Naturally it's not truly 1080p as it's only an 800x480 LCD inside, but it plays higher quality video will still looking good for its price point. It’s really useful this has a SD reader, I can load video on a card and play it with only a power cable plugged in. Great for running a single video over and over. It also has a USB charging port which is powerful enough to power a Raspberry Pi. I can hook a RPi up with HDMI and USB power and again the only wire running across the floor is the power to the projector. It’s really versatile for a low cost device. It’s quiet and gets a little warm, but by no means would I consider it “hot” when running. The noise it produces while cooling is easily drowned out by whatever you are playing. The speaker built in is a bit weak on bass but good enough for vocal tracks or game audio. I would recommend external speakers for anything requiring rich sound though. It is small and light. There is an adjustable foot on the bottom for angling it upward. When the foot is removed you can mount the projector on any standard camera mount, like a tripod for example. It works really well actually. There are rubber feet for flat surfaces. The remote control is powerful enough that you don’t always have to point it at the projector either. Reflection of infrared off your projection surface usually works. There are front and rear sensors too. In a indoor setting I could aim the remote almost anywhere but the floor to register with the projector. It’s also a nice elongated shape, which is more comfortable to use than credit-card shaped remote controls. I liked it enough I ordered two more for haunted house use. They project video onto walls and pumpkins really well. :) One tiny complaint I have actually is the keystone. The knob barely turns and only adjusts a few degrees and is really stiff. I expected a little more adjustment and it’s hard to get it dialed in. It's still useful to have keystone... granted it's only for vertical skew, not horizontal as well, like on more expensive projectors. In the end we needed a few low cost projectors for a haunted house and they will work well, are quiet, and inexpensive enough that I can buy a few for the cost of one high-end projector. Another minor complaint is that at closer ranges (3-6m) you cannot focus the entire screen perfectly. If the center and top is in focus, the lower third isn’t. If you focus the bottom, the top is a bit blurry. In the end you need to compromise for a slightly (ever so slightly) out of focus image so it’s uniform. Alternatively moving the projector back a few feet also helps correct this issue. For my use case it’s perfectly fine. Don’t expect razor sharp PowerPoint slides on this. It’s not advertised nor high enough resolution for super clear text. Though it projects old Nintendo and Sega games really nicely since they are blocky graphics already. One final little gotcha, the power cord is short. Around two feet short, maybe one meter. You’ll need an extension cord in most cases, though only a two prong US one as it’s not a grounded device. I would buy more of these without hesitation. You somewhat get what you pay for; a low cost, lower resolution projector, but overall the value is there. Thanks for reading all this.

The cutouts are just where they should be, and I confirmed that the audio jack is not obstructed at all. The power cutout at the bottom has smooth edges, nice for where my pinky usually lands when supporting the phone in portrait orientation (again, not so the Vinve case, where the edges irritated). The corners do not look quite so pronounced as they do in the product photos. They extend from the flat part of the edges just a little more than the button bumps. I like the look, and have confidence they're big enough to provide some extra protection if the phone is dropped onto a corner. I can't think of anything about this case that I would want changed..

The Mirage NanoSat, NS, is a not-quite-so-small satellite speaker. This model is slightly larger than the Orb speaker (4.2" X 5.8" H) but is constructed much like the Mirage MX. It has a 2.75" titanium/polypropylene mid-woofer and a 0.75" titanium hybrid tweeter mounted in an acoustic lens assembly. The NanoSat specifications claim the frequency response is from 110 Hz to 20 kHz with a crossover at 2.7 kHz. Measurements indicate that the 110 Hz specification is optimistic since the woofer has a resonance at 152 Hz (broken in) and a response at 137 Hz that is 10 db down while at 111 Hz is minus 20 db - too low an output to be very useful. I would estimate that the correct crossover frequency to a sub would be about 145 Hz. It has an 87 db efficiency specification but sounds like it plays louder than the MX (which also has a 87 db spec.) at the same power input. The NanoSat's power rating is 100 watts maximum (8 ohms). It also has what Mirage calls an Omni-polar design; where the woofer and the tweeter each fire almost straight up onto an acoustic lens that disperses the sound through ~360 degrees. Mirage claims the only 30% of the sound will be direct, with 70% of the sound energy reflecting from the walls, etc. While this gives the speaker a larger acoustic size, is reduces imaging ability making this speaker best suited for surround applications. It should be mounted "upside-down" if it is mounted above 6 feet off the floor to direct the tweeter output down toward the listener. It also should be mounted close (~one woofer diameter) to a wall to improve the low frequency response. Listening impressions: The Mirage NanoSat, mounted at 2.5" from a wall, has a sound that is well balanced and quite articulate with a good mid-range and mid-highs but not quite as smooth as the MX - the lower mid-bass is a bit stronger than the MX. Like the MX, the sound has little impact (It has a small radiating area of only ~ 6 sqin (almost twice as much as the MX) compared to the ~16 sqin area of common mid-woofers). It has an audible resonance at 152 Hz and a few upper mid-range resonances that make the response somewhat uneven and lead to a hollow sound especially noticeable in reproduction of piano music. Tympani sound good and the flute is nicely rendered. Strings are good and brass has some nice ring but is missing a solid bottom. The tweeter does not have quite the bite of the MX but seems quite smooth - the treble may even be a bit recessed. The Mirage NanoSat (NS) sounded a bit congested compared with the MX, but at ~$120 each it is the lowest priced speaker in this comparison test. Willie Nelson's voice sounded better on it than on the MX. Piano music was disappointing - sounds hollow - likely cause is the strong 150 Hz resonance. The Mirage MX (~$150) sounded noticeably clearer than the Mirage NS but the sound was a slight bit lightweight compared with the others - one must drive it hard to get any bite in the strings. The MX sounds much better than the NS on piano music. Conclusions: The Mirage MX sounds slightly better in balance and clarity than the NS overall, but the NS is somewhat better in reproduction of male voices. The Mirage NS and MX are pretty close in sound quality, but I would give the edge to the MX and say it is well worth the extra $30 per speaker in cost.

This is a fine pair of binoculars. The surface has a solid rubbery feel, which makes the binoculars easy to hold. Excellent eye relief. The eye cups extend with 3 distinct stops, each one with a satisfying click. The focusing dial is smooth and has just the right amount of resistance. The protective case is one of the nicest quality cases I've seen, even compared with binoculars that cost 3 times as much. Now for the optics. I certainly think these are good performers for the price. The images are sharp and clean, with good contrast. The optics are not as bright as what you'd find on binoculars with larger objectives, but this is to be expected. I compared Polaris ED glass to a similarly priced Leupold McKenzie 8x42 non-ED glass, side by side, and felt that Polaris came out ahead in terms of image quality. The only drawback is that when viewing the Moon at night, the Polaris binoculars produce two distinct ghost images of the Moon - one on each side of the main image. None of my other binoculars (Carson, Olympus, Bushnell, Leupold, Nikon, Barska) have this ghosting issue. Somewhat puzzled, I contacted the Polaris Customer Service, and here is an excerpt from their reply: "...Thank you for contacting us about the ghosting issues you are experiencing with your Polaris Optics ProBirder Ultra HD 8X32 Compact Bird Watching Binoculars. Our binoculars are specially designed for bird watching and wildlife watching during the day. Because of this they are only designed with the reflective coatings needed to have the best experience for viewing during the day. If you are using them at night for astronomy purposes you will probably not get the best image possible, because they were not designed for this purpose. For your needs, it will be best to consider purchasing binoculars that are specifically designed with internal anti-reflective coatings that are necessary for astronomy viewing..." In the end, my experience with these binoculars has been positive. Nighttime ghosting is not a big deal, and in good daylight these binoculars produce sharp ghost-free images. My daughter wanted them for her birthday, and she is thrilled to have them. I guess ultimately, it's what really counts.

After reading hundreds of reviews for Orbi; Luma & eero I was convinced the Orbi was the best (they all have good reviews). The initial installation was crazy simple. I was certain I have hit the home run of the new wave of mesh network systems hitting the market these days. My speeds were running 98 Mbs up and down (I pay for 100/100) in several tested areas in the home where I thought we used wifi the most. Now time to see how things go with our streaming devices on three different TVs. I connected all devices to the network and began streaming shows. Again everything seemed to work as expected with the great speeds I had measured. Fast forward a few days. Streaming devices started to buffer. I restarted the modem and the Orbi router and satellite, everything seemed fine for a few hours. Logged in to router to check settings and noticed a firmware update (one was installed when I first fired the unit up) was available. I thought perhaps the update would stabilize the speeds (I still wasn't sure if it was the Orbi or my ISP which is still installing fiber in the area). I installed the firmware update, restarted everything and had great speed again. In less than an hour my speed tests started to fluctuate wildly when tested in the exact same location in the house. I went and connected by Ethernet to see what speed I would get wired. I got 99/99 wired. I left everything untouched for the next several days and we continued to have buffering other issues over streaming devices along with wild changes in speed test results sitting in the same location. I contacted Orbi support via Chat (very good experience) and they had me test several different settings. Short version - still not fixed. One more firmware update an things seemed to stabilize a bit but not great. Another interesting issue that I didn't pick up on right away was that from the time I installed the Orbi I started to notice noise on our kitchen TV which gets its feed over a iogear HDMI transmitter/receiver. After some troubleshooting I determined that the Orbi satellite was generating interference with this signal (when I unplugged it the noise went away). Interestingly, network speeds (when closer to the main router) seemed to stabilize when the satellite was unplugged. I want to highlight that the 7 outlet units (non USB) are rated at 1440 joules vs the 6 outlet units that are rated at 1080. For that reason, I always purchase the 7 outlet units since there's no cost difference. Surge protectors that are rated below 2000 joules are good for basic home electronics like consumer grade printers, modems, air purifiers, and phone charging stations. For expensive home entertainment electronics, gaming consoles, and home servers, you need units rated at 2000 joules minimum. I recommend APC's backup batteries as those regulate power fluctuations as well. Surge protectors are not designed to last indefinitely. You should replace them every few years. If a surge protector is more than 5 years old or looks damaged, you need to replace it. If your building experiences frequent brownouts or blackouts, then you should replace them 1-2 years. My only complaint is the cord is off-centered. It sits a tad right of the outlet instead of dropping straight down. However, the 6ft cord is plenty long and wrapped in thick insulation. The unit has dual LED lights. One indicates that the unit is operating within parameters, and the other indicates that the power flowing into the unit is grounded. If either of the LED lights is out, there's either a problem with the unit or possibly the building's power. I highly recommend these surge protectors. I've used APC surge protectors and backup batteries for years with no issues. They offer excellent performance for the money.

The AM reception is excellent. The AM tuner seems to use a wide bandwidth which means that as the dial is scanned, the stations that are pulled in will have great fidelity. The FM tuner did not seem as sensitive as I would have liked, but the reception was acceptable. This tape radio/Tape player is also unique for one of its size in that it has a built in speaker and telescoping antenna. The speaker is very convenient and it also sounded excellent listening to an AM talk show. The lower frequencies where reproduced better than I would have expected; not tinny at all. I also tested the headphone output with a full size pair of over the ear headphone (Koss UR20) and there was plenty of power for them while playing a tape. Impressive for such a small unit. I have dozens of portable tape players going back to the mid 1980s to compare this to. Maybe I am just a fan of these in general, but I think this one is very good and well worth the price.

After reading reviews, I thought they be good, maybe not great, but good and I get two plus a charger for 30 instead of 50 for one battery. Imagine my disappointment and frustration when using each battery, after fully charged, only lasted about 30-40 minutes into a listing shoot where I spend most of the time moving and adjusting flashes than trigger the shutter or playing in settings. I can usually do 1-2 listing that take 1-1 1/2 hours to shoot on an OEM battery. At the time of this review, I have had these batteries for 3 days and shot 6 listings with them (3 each day). The first day, I used up the OEM on the first listing and some juice leftover for the second listing. I decided to swap to one of these Enegon batteries, it lasted about 35 minutes. Frustrated, I put the second Enegon in. At the "Hour mark" of the my time at the property, it was already down to 2 bars. I had to pull out my main dual charger (not the included charger) and charge my OEM and the first Enegon while I continued with the 2nd Enegon. It died shortly there after. I then wasted 10 minutes waiting for the OEM battery to have enough juice to finish the shoot. I then used the Enegon charger in my USB car charger to try and charge the OEM and an Enegon on the way to the third listing. I then continued charging batteries as I shot. The second day, I started with the Enegon and even tried strict power saving methods and they each lasted 30-40 minutes. My OEM lasted for the entire next listing and half of the last listing (roughly 2 hours and 10 minutes of use). I bet a brand new OEM will last even longer as my camera reports that my OEM is nearing the end of it's life. The charger seemed to be work just fine, but I haven't really rigorously tested it. These batteries are good to keep charged for when your in a pinch but I'll be buying more of the OEM's as soon as possible-the budget now demands it as these batteries won't cut it for my work demand.

So I did my research and specifically sought out a center pin negative replacement power adapter for my Tascam 424 MKI. The item photos and listing clearly state this adapter is center pin negative and compatible with the Tascam 424 MKI Cassette Recorder. I received my adapter today and plugged it in excited to work on some new recordings. The Tascam made a popping noise followed by a bad electrical smell and powered off / is now dead as a doornail. Upon closer inspection, it turns out the adapter they sent me is center pin Positive, reverse polarity, and quickly destroyed my vintage Tascam 4 Track. The item packaging was marked correctly, it's just the adapter polarity is the opposite of what's posted all over this listing. Sort of a large oversight. And a costly one on my end. I called Amazon Customer service, and while they offered to refund my $14 bucks for the adapter, they would not provide any assistance with my destroyed Tascam or modify / remove this listing. BUYER BEWARE: If you decide to buy this, check the polarity prior to plugging it in, or better yet, avoid it altogether and find the proper adapter. This just cost me hundreds of dollars in upcoming service repairs.

Let me start of with reviewing the products features while it worked, which was for less than an hour. It's not an actual siren but a small speaker, about the size of a hand/palm. I measured the decibels of all its sirens/chimes/sounds and got a max of about 105db when placing the measurement device right next to it. There are a number of sounds for siren/chime/alert that are ok but they definitely are not a great selection. Yes, you can configure the volume, sound, repeat for multiple "channels". Ie. One for alarm, one for chime, one for doorbell, etc. The light/strobe is very very weak. It's just an LED inside an opaque plastic enclosure. The device was included in my zwave controller easily. The device though bricked, after I played multiple sounds in sequence. It just stopped responding. Appeared as a dead node in the controller and it's light remained on constantly. I tried long pressing its action button to perform a factory reset and that didn't work either. So, yes, just like other reviewers are saying, I can confirm that this thing bricks easily, most likely due to bad programming from the manufacturer. It's not the battery that dies, not the hardware I believe. It looks like its software is the issue and there's no physical reset button that works after. I don't recommend this, not even to try it out because the refund takes extra time on this specific order.

For starters, I'm currently running a three year old Quad 9550, so the option to upgrade to a 2nd Generation i7 processor and use this cooler is a real bonus! I'm currently running at 3.8ghz, and this cooler will keep my temps under 60°C even under 1-2 Hours of maximum load bench tests. My average idle temps are about 38°C, and average load temps while playing games are now at about 50°C. Update 7/4/2011: Very, very, happy with cooler. Got my q9550 all the way to 4.2Ghz with VID at 1.29-1.3V before I could no longer stress test the computer. After an hour and a half of 100% stress, the CPU became unstable and crashed (this cpu does have a sort of overclocking "cap"). Maximum temperature from log was 67*C. I am now running it at 3.8Ghz, and I think I'll keep it that way until I upgrade. Also, this cooler is relatively easy to mount on an AMD board. I let my friend use my cooler while I was away, and it apparently works just as well on AMD processors. Duh? Update 8/18/2011: I've upgraded to an i7 2600K, and I'm now toying around at 4.2ghz. I'm actually starting to question this thing's ability to cool high-end CPUs. I realize that an i7 2600k at 4.5ghz is a chore to cool, but people have been getting there on AIR COOLERS, while I can't (at least, not without hitting 70's). Subtracted a star, this cooler needs a 10-15% percent price drop before I'd buy it again (bought it at seventy bucks). Update 12/28/2011: Turns out that my cooler may be damaged, or it's pump may be starting to fail. I'm still seeing reasonable temperatures; after working with the VID and voltage ramps, I can pull 4.2GHz without the CPU going over 60*C for 6+ hours. I'm still unable to get to the magic 4.7GHz mark without my CPU breaking into the 80's, but that could just be due to my cooler. If you're packing a big gun (i7 2600k or up, AMD 8-core, etc) you'll want to go for a higher end cooler like the H80, or a comparable setup. To credit, the cooler removes a lot of heat from my system, the rest of my PC is icy cold. My GPUs will just brush around the low 70's, even with an OC. Placed a star back on the review - the price of the H60 seems quite reasonable now! I would recommend it for anything short of a new i7. As a longtime user of the Ricoh GR, I bought an X70 to do a side-by-side test. My plan: to figure out which one to keep, and which to sell. I'd always wanted a Fuji camera, and I absolutely adore this genre of enthusiast point-and-shoots. Ultimately, my affinity for the GR won out, but there's no doubt that the X70 is a spectacular camera. WHY I LIKE THE GR BETTER: 1. I like the GR's JPEGs and even its "film simulations" better. When I was primarily shooting my Pentax and Nikon DSLRs, I always shot RAW. Always. But the GR changed that for me. I fell in love with the Positive Film JPEG preset and I've shot pretty much exclusively with it (with occasional detours to High-Contrast B&W) since. The X-Pro1 is the only Fuji I've used extensively before this (I wrote the review for Adam's other site, camera-enthusiast.com), and I liked its film simulations well enough back then. But I've played with the X70's simulations pretty extensively and I don't like any of them as well as Positive Film (not even Classic Chrome!). Then there's the actual quality of the JPEGs. I guess I just don't like the X-Trans look, but the JPEGs out of this camera look a little muddy to me at 100% and just generally aren't as crisp as my GR shots. There's also a surprising amount of NR at relatively low ISOs. I'm sure that can be tweaked, but I've never been one to do that. The GR just works for me out of the box and that's what I want. Obviously, this is very personal. 2. I like the GR's controls better. It may be that I've just been shooting the GR for too long, but the X70's manual controls (while undeniably cool) just tend to get in the way for me. They're also not laid out as well. The left button on the d-pad, for instance, is right up against the edge of the tilt screen, which makes it really hard to hit. The playback and trash buttons are way too small and finnicky. The X70's touchscreen is nice for tap-to-focus, but I'm a center point/focus and recompose guy 95% of the time, so I don't get much use out of it. 3. The X70 feels too nice. This is probably dumb, but I handle the X70 really carefully because it's so beautifully made that I'm afraid of damaging it/scratching the paint/etc. I hate the lens cap—never thought I'd say that, but I love that I don't have to worry about stashing one when I use the GR. The GR (strangely) feels more rugged and reliable, like I can just throw it in my bag and not worry. 4. I really love the GR's horizon level. Again, minor and maybe dumb, but I love the fact that the GR's level does both roll and pitch. The X70's, in contrast, only does roll. WHAT I LIKE ABOUT THE X70: 1. The screen. I think the GR actually has the better display, but the articulation of the X70's screen is a real godsend for off-angle shots. 2. It's beautiful. Going back to #3 on the dislikes, this thing is gorgeous. 3. Like the GR, it's very customizable. You can customize a total of 8 function buttons, plus the control ring around front. Pretty impressive. 4. The AF is indeed faster. This isn't a huge deal for me (see above comments about being a center point/recompose shooter), but there's no denying that the X70 has an edge here. 5. The electronic shutter is a big plus. The GR's built-in ND filter more or less does the same thing w/r/t wide-aperture bright light shooting, but being able to shoot completely silently is pretty awesome.

There are essentially two laptops available that serve the niche the Acer Swift X exists in; the other is the ASUS ROG Flow X13. That notebook is $300 more expensive...on sale. The Acer Swift X is essentially for a user who wants an ultraportable that can do a little bit of everything. It's notably smaller than a 15.6" notebook, it's light, it has tremendous CPU power, it has a usable IGP for the circumstances that require it, and it has a dedicated GPU that can offload some GPU-related tasks (i.e. video transcoding for streaming) and play games at moderate settings at the display's native 1080p resolution. It's also able to do all of this under 100W, which means it can be powered entirely via a USB-C power adapter. It's essentially about as much performance you can get while still in that power envelope. If you're strictly looking for a gaming laptop, you should look elsewhere. Speaking of performance, a few things worth noting: - While it ships with an AMD Ryzen 7 5800U (8-core/16-thread processor), and that chip is rated for ~15W, Acer actually lets it turbo up to 35W. As a result, the Swift X's CPU is within striking distance of the much more expensive AMD Ryzen 9 5900HS. For reference, it's roughly on par with a desktop AMD Ryzen 7 3700X in multi-core tasks, and a good 20% *faster* in single-threaded tasks. It's *fast.* - The notebook ships with 16GB of soldered LPDDR4X-4266. An ideal situation would have a notebook with DDR4 SODIMMs for upgradeability, but the LPDDR4X is fast and efficient, and 16GB is a healthy amount for most tasks. - The NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti is set with a limit of 35W and runs its 4GB of GDDR6 at 10GHz. 3The 3050 Ti gets a bad rap in reviews when pit against the 3060 or even the last gen 1660 Ti, but neither GPU is available at this lower power level. The RTX 3050 Ti is *really* replacing the GTX 1650 Ti, and it performs about 20% faster while adding ray-tracing and DLSS support. Ray-tracing support isn't going to blow you away, but it *is* going to give you access to current and future games that require it, and the 3050 Ti is able to make use of it in most games. I was able to play Cyberpunk 2077 at medium settings with DLSS and ray-tracing enabled in the 30-40fps range, which isn't bad at all. The DLSS support is also enormous; on a part that's power and performance constrained, DLSS makes a big difference in the games that support it and can claw back a healthy amount of framerate. - The system fan can be noisy, but more irritatingly, it has a high pitched whine at higher levels. You can ameliorate this by setting the system fan to "Quiet" in Acer's software; the performance difference between "Quiet" and the highest setting is shockingly small (<5%), but noise is vastly improved. - The display is 1080p 60Hz with a matte finish. It's not spectacular, and it doesn't support adaptive sync (FreeSync), but it's bright enough and it gets the job done. - Surprisingly, there are TWO M.2 2280 slots under the hood. That means you can actually upgrade the storage by either replacing the existing 512GB drive or simply adding a second one. That said, I strongly recommend installing a power efficient drive if you do upgrade. Phison-based drives run hot, and that heat can be felt under the left palm rest if you're pushing the drive. - The WiFi card is Mediatek Wi-Fi 6 2x2, but is user upgradeable. I'd recommend shelling out for an Intel AX210, personally, but it's not critical. On paper, the Swift X is a great laptop. Good display, cracking performance, solid keyboard, good enough connectivity (USB-C port supports Power Delivery, 10Gbps USB, and DisplayPort Alt Mode). Unfortunately, the display is good and not great, the speakers are pretty subpar even by laptop standards, and the worst part is actually the touchpad. The force required to actuate it is high and the action is really unpleasant to the point where I wonder if there was something wrong with mine. The surface also isn't especially smooth. It's functional, and you can use it in a pinch, but I wouldn't rely on it. If you're in the market for this very specific type of notebook, your choices are the Acer Swift X and the ASUS ROG Flow X13. If you can afford the extra money, the Flow X13 has better build quality, better speakers, slightly more performance, is quieter and less intrusive under load, has a better touchpad, is a 2-in-1 convertible, and has a better display with FreeSync. What you DO sacrifice is the upgradeable storage; the Flow X13 uses an M.2 2230 SSD and ships with the largest drive available at 1TB. You might be able to upgrade down the road, but for now, if you need more than 1TB of onboard storage, you're stuck. The Flow X13 also features the optional external GPU dock, but that costs more than the laptop itself. If you can get the Flow X13 for ~$300 more than the Swift X and you're willing/able to pay it, I'd probably recommend that. But that's a lot of "if," and the Swift X crams fantastic value into a single notebook. At this price point you have to make compromises, but the Swift X makes the right ones.

I tried every port on the computer, all of the multiple other peripherals I have connected to the computer both wirelessly and hardwired work flawlessly. Finally, I called Wacom “support” this is where the nightmare REALLY began. It was two hours and fifteen minutes before the call was answered. After two minutes I was abruptly disconnected. A second call and another two hour wait. Without going into all the minutiae, I was at the level of tech support where they put you on hold for “three to five minutes” while they go to Google and try to figure out what the problem is. Again, long story short, they wasted another two or three hours of my time, and did not resolve the problem. After two or three of these phone calls over two days I was told it would be “escalated” (“forgotten about and dismissed”) and I would be contacted within 24 - 48 hours. Needless to say, the call never came. This is the part of the story where you begin to attempt to track down corporate office phone numbers and reach a supervisor, but, sadly this is nearly impossible anymore as the corporate tech giants management no longer take calls from the plebians. But, I am pretty persistent so I found a corporate number in Portland, Or. and got into their global directory and kept playing keypad bingo with names until I got through to a person. Boy were they surprised! Explained the problem to the supervisor. Downloaded crash dump files and log files and sent them off to the supervisor. “I will have our engineers look at this and get back to you in a day or two” I told him that was a good one but I had heard it before. “I understand your frustration Mr. Lamm but we will get this resolved! Two days nothing , three days, nothing. I think, well maybe it is the tablet itself so I order the Intos Art and try that out, Got it the next day from Amazon (I LOVE Amazon) Same thing, different day. Tablet would not work. “No device detected” (It uses the same software as the Pro model) So, I now have two expensive Wacom beauties sitting here and over $600.00 bucks invested, and still, nada, zip. QA's suggestion is to test it on a different tablet, and see if the issue follows the tablet. Please keep me posted. Thanks XXXXXXX Customer Support Team WACOM So basically he bailed out and told me to fix it myself and keep him posted? Outstanding. I wrote him back and noted that everyone I dealt at Wacom had failed to keep their word, that it was inconceivable to me that a tech company of this size did not provide remote support. If I have a real knotty problem with one of my computers or my anti virus (Norton) that I can’t figure out they log on and usually problem resolved in under an hour. My rating would probably be more forgiving if this was a $100 Walmart telescope. For $350, I don't think it unreasonable to expect a modicum of quality control. ASSEMBLY: Easy enough, but I found the first quality issue right out of the box. The aperture dust cover wouldn't seat properly. I used a compass to do a basic roundness check of the optical tube at the aperture. It failed. Not really a deal breaker in and of itself, but still pretty lame. 2. INITAL SETUP: Again, the process wasn't difficult, but the collimation was way off. I've seen Amazon drivers perform some impressive stunt driving, but unless this particular truck did a few barrel rolls down a hill with my package in tow, the mirrors were askew before it left the warehouse. Instead, I found the a small scratch near the edge of the mirror right where the dust cap had been. 4. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS: The reviews for this model were pretty good most places I checked. When I got to the Celestron website, I saw the price for direct purchase in their online store...$189...WTF?? Something is up. I can't say for sure what it is. They're alright, but they're really not worth the price. I'm a bit of an audiophile, and this is the first time I've bought non-Bose headphones, thinking I was missing out (given all the positive reviews). The sound quality doesn't seem anymore remarkable than the normal overear Bose headphones, which will cost you $170 less. They're actually slightly less remarkable – lows aren't as nice on these headphones. These feel sturdier though, which is nice. They're more stylish looking, which is nice if that's what you're into (I could care less). Though after owning these and using them every day for 5 months, they've got a lot of negatives. One is the fact that there's a microphone built into them that you can never disable. It's the most annoying when having a Skype call – my laptop (mac) would realize that a microphone is connected and use that over the laptop's internal mic. It was noisy and annoying because the mic would sit on my shirt and scratch around when I moved while talking on my call. Suddenly though, one day (2 months into ownership), the mic stopped working. No trauma to the headphones or anything. Now I can't use these headphones at all for conference calls. This is because the mic in the headphones is still selected by the laptop over the builtin mic, and the laptop disables the laptop's builtin mic in system preferences. Given that the mic is dead, I'm just silent to the other end of the call. Now, if I'm working with my laptop listening to music with these headphones, and if I have to pick up a conference call, I actually have to take the headphones off, or switch to headphones that don't have a mic in them. Another issue is for people with long hair. Your hair gets caught, pulled, and broken in the metal fixation that the ear pieces slide around in. My hair always gets caught in between the earpiece knob thing and the metal fixation. Super painful. It happens 80% of the time I take these off. Another issue is the sturdy-looking aux connector. It broke after 4 months of use. Plugging in and unplugging from a macbook pro must've been too intense for this connector (it's a grippy socket). There's a plastic enclosure inside of this sturdy-looking metal connector, and one day, just unplugging my headphones from my laptop caused the glue holding the plastic enclosure to the metal "shell" of the connector to loosen up and the metal "shell" of the connector detached. The connector/wires were exposed and I was sliding around this sturdy-looking connector thing on bare wire/plastic. No good :( On the brown headphones, the oil from your hair will discolor the earpads. (And I have the driest/least oily hair on the planet). Sad. Bottomline: these are some really nice-looking headphones. But you could get better sound quality for a lot less. And they're not as sturdy as they initially seem...

Who isn’t searching for the holy grail of gimbals — a lightweight, compact gimbal suited for your camera of choice? The Zhiyun Crane M3 is the lightest and most compact gimbal capable of balancing the Sony A7 series. Its compact size means now I can take it almost anywhere with my A7SIII on it. I can shoot one-handed much longer than any other gimbal with the same load capacity. With the right lens, it’s capable of very fluid shots with some full-frame cameras. So is the Zhiyun Crane M3 that perfect gimbal? No, it is not the holy grail of small gimbals. It has major limitations. It is not a perfect gimbal, as the hype by YouTubers would have you believe. Despite some issues, the Crane 3M has become my go-to gimbal. I will decide if I should keep it at the end of Amazon's extended three-month holiday return period. This is a rolling review of the Zhiyun Crane M3 with the Sony A7SIII. More will be added as I use it in different situations. First impressions after two days of use… Balancing and lenses: The the Zhiyun Crane M3 motors have no problems with these relatively compact Sony primes: FE 20mm 1.8 G, FE 28mm 2.0, FE 35mm 1.8, Loxia 35mm 2.0, FE 50mm 2.8, FE 55mm 1.8, FE 85mm 1.8. The camera's eyepiece cup should be removed with these lenses for it not to hit the gimbal when tilting the camera. While the motors can handle compact lenses, the pan axis can’t be manually balanced at all. The pan axis arm is just too short. That’s the main problem with the Crane M3. If each arm could be half inch longer, it would come close to my perfect gimbal. Inverted mode: the gimbal doesn’t work well in inverted mode, because the roll and the tilt axes do not spin in 360 degrees. Getting into inverted mode by rotating around and above the camera is possible, but not practical because in inverted mode — with the camera upright — the roll motor is positioned above the lens and will hit the lens. Inverted mode is only usable by flipping the gimbal and camera upside down -- while in follow mode -- which works for the A7SIII since the LCD has auto image vertical flip. This means there’s an additional step to flip the image back again in your NLE. Adjustment wheel. The camera setting control wheel does not work at initial release of the gimbal. It is supposed to control aperture, ISO and shutter, but there is no way to test it. USB-C to Multi cable for Sony: the cable for controlling recording is barely long enough to reach the port on the side of the Sony. The pulling force on the port could eventually ruin the multi port. Quick release plate: The M3 QR plate that comes with the M3 only makes sense if you never use your camera on a tripod. The included QR plate actually slows you down. You are forced to switch plates to use a tripod or the M3. It’s not compatible with anything else. Zhiyun could have made mounting the camera truly painless if they had made it Arca Swiss compatible. Free QR plates: Ordering the gimbal from Zhiyun’s website, they send you a free customized QR plate for some cameras. Amazon customers don't receive these free QR plates. I guess Zhiyun does not care as much for their Amazon customers. Touch screen: the touch screen has froze on me several times. Powering the gimbal off and on fixes the problem…but does not fix a ruined shot. 😔 Battery: There is no indication to tell how much the battery has been charged while charging. Plug it in and the bars just keep flashing. No percentage, nothing. So far after two days of moderate use the battery has shown no drain -- that is, there is no percentage to show drain. The bad news is the built-in battery can’t be removed. Fingers crossed that the battery doesn’t go bad, because it can’t be replaced. Why white? Gimmicky white color draws attention. Who wants that when you want stealth and trying to get a shot? Audio: the add-on audio gadget is another unnecessary gimmick. Last thing I want is my gimbal's mobility limited and tethered to someone. If I need sync audio for my gimbal camera, I would go wireless. The audio attachment also adds weight to the gimbal. Just no. LED light: Have not found a use for the LED light. It could be useful for tight shots of faces in low light situations, but how often have I needed a gimbal for those scenarios? Not once. Since I am a weight weenie, I could do without the unnecessary light.

The "Ultimate Steering Wheel Racing Game Stand" suffers from a pretty major design flaw: Both the height adjustment and the pitch of the table are anchored by metal pins on large knobs, but there aren't any pre-drilled guide holes to socket them into. Securing the stand in any position requires a massive amount of over-tightening to create enough friction between the pin and the shaft to prevent the unit from shifting during use. End result: I used this thing for 1 month and 3 days (started using it on December 3 when The Crew released) and it's now worthless -- The height adjustment shaft (both the knob and opening it screws into) are completely stripped out, making it impossible to set the height of the unit above the absolute minimum. If there were pre-drilled holes in the shaft to anchor the adjustment pins instead of relying entirely on friction created by a few millimeters of screw thread, then it would probably last a lot longer.

And one more thing, a watermelon flavored sweetie. Why exactly? Why not. I haven't eaten it yet because, well, when do candy and electronics come together? Also I had a difficult time getting the potentiometer to fit into the bread board; you really have to cram it in there for it to fit. Also the rubber feat fell off right after I applied them to the arduino board, but they have stuck once I reapplied them and used much more pressure to try and make them stick properly. The first problem I have with this product is its battery life. I've had to charge my logitech keyboard that I used with the iPad 4 sparingly. Installation was easy as I used the recommended adapter plates and the adapter wire harness by crutchfield, so there was no cutting of any wires. I was disappointed by the sound after the installation, very low base and sound clarity compared to ford OEM 25watt 4ohm speakers. I left the factory tweeters plugged in because without them these kippa 62ix has very low sound. I tried switching the wires to make sure negative and positive are not mixed up, disconnecting factory tweeters, changing the +3 db / 0db on the built-in tweeters. This made no difference, seems like the built-in tweeters don't even work. I had high hopes as these were advertised as 2.5-ohm speakers boast ultra-high sensitivity so that you can power them with a factory radio or aftermarket stereo. I reinstalled the factory speaker back on passenger side door and left the kippa 62ix on driver side door just for sound comparison, and the cheap factory speaker sounds way better. I might be wrong, but as I understood these 60ix 2.5ohm with high sensitivity of 96db should manage power from factory head unit better than the OEM 4ohm speakers, at lease a lot of the reviewers had said they just swapped the factory speakers with these with existing head unit. I will be returning these back unless I can find out if I had done something wrong. I specifically wanted these low impedance 2.5ohms / high sensitivity so I don't have to install an external amp. I have 2020 ford fusion with sync 3, and 6 speakers (4 in front doors with tweeters and one each in rear doors).

I bought one of these in Jan 2014. I installed it outside under my carport, and operate it using Motion on Linux. Motion is excellent software for operating IP and Web cams, and it's simpler than the popular Zoneminder. You can also use this camera without any extra software, using just the embedded Web server to view your images in any Web browser, and the embedded FTP uploader to record images. If you have an FTP server to upload them to. You need to connect it to a wired network to set it up. The bundled software only works to set it up on Windows, but you don't need sad old insecure overpriced Windows at all; its default is to snag an IP address from your router via DHCP, so run nmap or look in your router control panel to find its IP address. Then access it via your Web browser to complete setup. ( see linux.com/learn/tutorials/762058-how-to-operate-your-spycams-with-zoneminder-on-linux-part-1- for more detail) This has been a good reliable camera for me. It is sheltered under the carport, but it is still exposed to cold, hot, and wind. It records acceptable VGA images, and the night vision works fine. There are three items that prevent me from giving it five stars. One, you have to register an email address to get firmware updates. This is an unnecessary step, and Foscam will spam you with marketing messages. Two, you get phone support and warranty only if you purchase directly from Foscam. Three, it does not support HTTPS, however it does support WEP and WPA/WPA2. This means you get a strong encrypted connection only if your wireless router is configured to use WPA2. Which it should be, but it is an extra step that inexperienced users will likely skip, leaving their connection vulnerable.
