I bought two of these, hoping to push signal upstairs and to the far end of the house. Sometimes, it has worked. But... The biggest problem that I have had was getting a bad IP address through the extender: Though the Netgear router itself seems to hand out proper (192.168.1.x ) addresses, the extender sometimes coughs up a 192.168.0.x address for the client. Customer service was not useful for this problem, and not worth the attitude and overseas gibberish. Now that I have shelved one of the extenders and dumbed down the other, I am occasionally not getting an address from the extender (ie, 169.x.x.x). Do not plan on using the same SSID as the host router (especially with two extenders, which is verboten, since one may try to chain off the other), but using the same id will also complicate problem isolation. For instance, VOIP connections are not clean over the extender, I could only determine this by checking the ssid that my phone was using. Do not buy this extender if you have or plan to buy a WiFi-6 router. It will work (with the above qualifications), but you may find the extra strength & speed of a newer router to actually be significantly faster than using the extender in a given location. I would guess that some of the problems above could be fixed with some software mods; in particular, the ability to lock the extender on a single router's MAC would allow it to share name SSID's in a multi extender environment. Something else will need to be done about the DHCP issue. Netgear also has an attractive "Nighthawk" app for network mapping and device config mods; it has no idea what to do with this device.

I purchased the Trond BT-DUO to use with a 13 year old Toshiba flat screen TV and a set of 8 year old Nokia BT (noise-reducing) headphones, something Nokia doesn't even offer anymore. I am happy to report the Trond in transmit (TX) mode paired immediately with the Nokia head phones. Once hooked up to the TV, I find I am getting excellent audio with no break up or noticeable voice lag. Turning on the head phones is all it takes to reconnect the BT link. I'm keeping the Trond powered via the supplied USB cable, so I can't comment on the Trond's battery life. I also am not using it in receive (RX) mode. The manual describes the procedure for pairing a second device to allow two users to access the same feed, but I have no way to test that. If you are wondering, I'm still using the TV because it still works well and has a built-in DVD player, which I use to watch movies while walking on a treadmill. I have wireless Sennheiser head phones I set up when I purchased the TV, but they are aging out, which is why I decided to see if I could switch over to the Nokia head phones by adding BT functionality to the TV. Given its age, the TV's only audio out is RCA jacks. The Trond package includes a cable with RCA plugs and an adapter for use with the Trond device, so hook up to the TV was a breeze. The Nokia head phones use BT 2.1 with A2DP audio, so naturally I had some concern as to how well they would play with an AptX device based on BT 5.0. That has turned out to be a non-issue. I held my breath in ordering the Trond BT-DUO, since the first device I tried, a cheaper model from another manufacturer would not pair with the Nokia headphones and had to be returned. I guess you get what you pay for. The Trond is quite small, thinner but not much larger than a 9 volt battery and comes with very clear directions for use. From what I've seen so far, for my purposes it is a 5-star product. Update: The manual says in transmit mode the Trond can transmit to two separate devices. I am happy to report this works. After I paired it to a second set of BT headphones (with the first set off), I turned off the Trond, and powered up both sets of phones. When I powered the Trond back on, after a brief delay both sets of phones were receiving the transmission. This is the procedure specified in the user directions, incidentally.

I've owned the z523 now for over a year and I use them on my flat screen TV. Needless to say the speakers in my Samsung LCD tv are weak and lackluster to say the least, especially in trying to hear conversation clearly in a movie when there is also music playing. The enhanced sound from the Logitech z523 is so much richer, louder and clearer, especially with the bass modulated downwards and the volume turned up. Not that I am comparing these to a full fledged 5.1 system through a good stereo, which I'm not. Unfortunately after about six months the speakers developed a bad hummm that is often un-noticeable when there is sound playing (although sometimes it gets very loud too) but when the TV is off (or muted) becomes very noticeable. All that is necessary to stop this hum is to walk over to the TV and place my hand on the mini-plug where it sticks in and rotate the plug half a turn one way or another. Apparently there is some short in the molded plug. It stops completely. For awhile. Then it comes back again. Several times a day. Considering that it so rarely gets plugged in or out I don't know how this happened. Just cheap manufacturing, I guess. UPDATE - one year later. Yes, the problem is still there. The solution is still the same - manual rotation or manipulation. One of the problems with the Logitech 523's is that the volume control on the right speaker enclosure is not a power switch, so you cannot turn this system off (except by unplugging it from the wall - rather a pain.) So often when I turn the TV off (and go to bed) the terrible hum may return with a ferocity just as I am sleeping. Even if the TV is off, the speaker system is still live and, yes, it hummmsss. What a pain. Finally, although I do like the sound (both bass and mids and highs) I am finally looking for a replacement. SAD, because the overall sound is really not bad for the price range. Even at 40 watts total I am amazed at how much power I get (the subwoofer will vibrate the floor) and the overall sound is fairly good (especially compared with the rinky-dink TV sound). So, now I'm thinking Klipsch Promedia or Boston Acoustics. I hate to spend really big bucks on Bose or Harmon-Kardons but then again it's also time to upgrade the TV and finally get me the BIG screen TV. Oh, woe is me! Such problems (when you think there are at least three real wars going on in the world). Correction: The volume switch is indeed an on/off switch as well. Idon't know how that escaped me but you CAN turn them off. The real problem, of course, is still there - and getting worse. So I think it's about time to get new speakers. I notice in reading reviews that many others have noted a very similar/same problem. Maybe folks just skip these speakers and get something else.

The KingPad SA8 is a very straightforward and simple tablet that hits the fundamentals that you would need out of an 8-inch Android device. It's not the best, or the fastest, nor does it come with an amazing screen or cameras or anything like that but it does everything well enough that it's hard to complain for the price. Let's break it down by a few categories: **IN THE BOX** SA8 Tablet 10W (5V/2A) Charging Brick (with female USB-A port) USB-A to USB-C cable MicroSD Slot Ejector tool Manual, QuickStart Guide, and other documentation **DESIGN/BUILD** + Metal body + Sturdy and premium feeling, it doesn't flex or creak + Only 7.62mm/0.3in thick + Weight: 310g/10.93oz - pretty light for an 8in tablet + FHD 1920x1200 16:10 screen with good viewing angles (IPS-like) and colors + USB-C port for data/charging + MicroSD Slot for storage expansion + Clicky power and volume buttons with good tactile response - The power and volume buttons wobble and make noise on my unit when you shake the tablet - No ambient light sensor - Screen brightness is fine but nothing exceptional - Screen does not get very dim for use in dark - USB-C port is charging/data only so no video/HDMI out - USB-C port only supports USB 2.0 data speeds **SOFTWARE** + Android 10 pre-installed + Clean OS build, no bloatware whatsoever + Play Store & Google services included to download whatever else you need + Nice features like face unlock (failed the first time I tried to set it up but worked on the second try) and raise to wake. + Gesture or button-based navigation options (although gestures don’t work with 3rd party launchers) + Dark mode supported + Blue light filter option (can be scheduled based on sunrise/sunset) - NOT Widevine L1 certified which means you CANNOT watch Netflix (and many other popular streaming services) in HD, it maxes out at 480p on this device. - H.264 video streaming issues with Parsec and Moonlight (you need to use H.265 for it to be functional but audio is broken in Parsec), not great for PC game streaming - Xbox Game Pass (xCloud) app kept crashing randomly so couldn’t use that for streaming games either - No wireless display mirroring/casting support built-in - Unknown long-term support and future updates since it’s a new/smaller brand/manufacturer **PERFORMANCE** + 8-core CPU (vs. 4-core often seen in this price/size range) + 3GB RAM (vs. typical 2GB in the price/size range) - about 1.1GB free after a fresh boot + Dual Band 2.4GHz + 5GHz Wi-Fi – got great speeds and latency performance! + Good speakers + Battery life seems to be pretty good, I left it unplugged in standby for about 3 days and it still had about 65% battery remaining + Bluetooth worked great with my ipega 9023s gamepad - Cameras are mediocre - Lackluster CPU & GPU performance. It's typical for the 8-inch Android tablet category which almost all use a low-end chipsets (even if it is 8-core) but still the SA8 is a little worse than comparable well-known tablets like a Fire HD 8+, Lenovo Tab M8 FHD, or Galaxy Tab A 8.4, especially in GPU performance. It's not even close to the cheapest iPads or new phones nowadays too. Benchmark Scores Geekbench 5: Single – 152, Multi – 773 3DMark Sling Shot Extreme (Vulkan): Overall – 480, Graphics – 394, Physics – 2,073 3DMark Sling Shot Extreme (OpenGL ES 3.1): Overall – 394, Graphics – 328, Physics – 1,313 3DMark Sling Shot Unlimited: Overall – 755, Graphics – 671, Physics – 1,349 **FINAL THOUGHTS** Overall, I'm still pretty happy with my purchase, it doesn't break the mold of being a budget device or anything like that but it's at least good enough for the basics and doesn't have any fatal flaws that totally ruin the experience. If it wasn’t for the H.264 video game streaming and Xbox Game Pass issues it would easily be a 5-star product for me but it just didn’t work great for the main use case I bought it for (gaming on the go) but I still plan to keep it around for other uses and recommend it if you just want a good 8-inch Android tablet that doesn’t break the bank and definitely stands out in this price range.

This review is for the 3tb drive. [see edit below] I give Fantom drives, overall, 5 stars. I LOVE Fantom drives - they seem to get good quality drives from manufacturers, throw them into their containers, and they are very reliable. There are ELEVEN of these in my room at the moment. Still of the eleven, ten are either 1 or 2 tb each. This is my first 3. For a 3tb drive, I didn't listen to Mark Solomon (the 1 star review). Thought I was immune to the "too big drive issue". Just do partitions, use a Mac, whatever. If you are not doing anything "odd", then you can probably make the 3tb drive work fine. I'm even thinking now how to use this differently than I originally intended vs sending it back. MY major issue? I can't set up a Truecrypt partition, even a small one. Same issue as Mark Solomon: can't use 512 byte sectors, or 512e emulation within 4k sectors. If you don't know what a windows image backup is, nor what a truecrypt partition is - then these drives might be wonderful. If you do, you may have trouble with these 3tb drives - they demand you do it "their way." Ok, yeah - I'm sending this back - getting another 2tb instead. Note: these 3tb drives WILL work with Windows 7, and will work under Mac OS X. It's when you try to do something that requires 512 sectoring or 512e emulation that the problem arises. Two already mentioned are Windows Image Backups, or partitioning with Truecrypt. I'll bet there are others. I don't want to give the impression these drives don't work under Windows 7 or Mac OS X. They DO work. Just that whatever company Fantom is contracting these 3 tb drives from - didn't feel the need to say these larger drives dropped one important level of support. [edit - time flies. months even. Truecrypt is dead now, and one can argue why... but 512 byte sector requirements are disappearing. So... yes go ahead and get this... still, when one crosses a barrier, it would be nice to be informed.]

So, I started exercising a lot about 6 months ago, and decided I HAD to pre-order this when it became available. Before I started exercising I owned a Fitbit Flex 2 just to track my sleep since I have sleep issues. That Fitbit is very basic and basically just a pedometer, so this was quite the upgrade. When I started exercising I realized how important a heart rate tracker was to my exercise, and also more basic fitness trackers can't track stages of your sleep, which I really wanted. I am in LOVE with this watch, and so glad I waited for this instead of getting the Ionic. A lot of people ask if they should get the Ionic or Versa. Well, it's up to you, but the Ionic is $100 more and I personally like the style of the Versa much more. It's much more sleek and elegant. However, if you have really large arms you may want the Ionic. I have tiny arms so it was an easy choice for me. The only thing better about the Ionic is the GPS, and I don't use that....so if that it is important to you then you definitely need the Ionic. Anyway, this watch is a great competitor to the Apple Watch. And you don't have to have an iPhone. Be warned, most Android devices are not "supported" by Fitbit, but will still work....however, they may be glitchy from time to time. I have an LG Stylo 3 Plus, a really new phone, and every now and then I will have syncing issues - it just WON'T sync. I have had to contact Fitbit a few times to help me, both with this and the Flex 2. Their customer support was actually surprising helpful and fixed it each time. However, I also have an iPad....so if it won't sync I will just sync to the iPad for awhile. But I know that not everyone has that as an alternative. One thing I love about the Versa is that you forget you're even wearing it. It's really, really comfortable and not obtrusive at all. It's very trendy and modern-looking. I got the special edition mainly for the lavender woven band, but it also comes with a chip where you can make payments on. I actually haven't set this up yet and be warned that it doesn't work with all banks (and almost certainly not a small local bank), but it's an interesting option I will probably get around to using eventually. I am mostly using this for the exercise and the sleep. I have to be honest, I don't care much about the music and while originally I didn't think I'd care about notifications, I actually really appreciate the notifications now because I never miss an important phone call now because I didn't hear my phone over noise or something like that. Exercise - most important thing for me, of course. I love how it tracks your resting heart rate, calories burned, the fitbit coach. I know that Fitbit has a tendency to over-count steps though, so keep that in mind. I keep my step goal about 2,000 over because of it. Sleep - One of the most fascinating things to me is how it tracks your sleep cycles. I have some serious sleeping issues so this is really helpful to me. It shows your REM, deep sleep, light sleep, and awake. Don't be alarmed to see how little deep sleep you get...the majority is supposed to be light sleep. I also noticed that when I switched from the Flex 2 to this, that I was getting a lot less sleep....both track and subtract your "awake/restless" time, but the Versa seems to be much more sensitive to it than the Flex 2. So for nights that the Flex 2 maybe recorded 9 hours of sleep, the Versa is tracking maybe 6 hours and 45 minutes, depending on the night. I know my sleep is bad, but I honestly this it may be a little TOO sensitive. Overall, I am so happy with this watch!

I use my laptop to adjust the sounds and it works pretty well to tune it in. I set the volume knob to 50% and use the remote on the source to control volume. Following Z's advice has worked out pretty well so I give him a lot of credit for my choices. its my opinion that this amp and the Micca speakers being my set up as it is, would be able to keep up with a moderately sized / powered sub woofer and not be overwhelmed with bass. I would certainly buy this again because I am happy with it but I maybe should have gotten one with more inputs.

Do not buy Phiaton MS 300 headphones. I spent months researching for a pair of sub-$200, stylish, portable headphones with emphasized mids and clear highs, and finally decided on the MS 300. It should be said that these headphones have an excellent sound: the mids and highs are phenomenal for a portable pair, and the bass manages to not overwhelm while still being present. In addition, they are quite comfortable; I was able to wear them for about 3-4 hours straight before I started feeling discomfort. I was happy with these cans for a while, until disaster struck: less than 10 months after my purchase, the plastic around where the cup attaches to the band snapped. I treated these headphones with utmost care; due to bad experiences in the past, I handled them gently, placed them back into the protective case after every use, and never dropped them or had any sort of accident. Yet the plastic broke, exposing the wiring within and rendering the headphones impossible to place on my head and use. I immediately contacted Phiaton to get a replacement (as they have a 1-year product warranty included with the purchase). After over a month and a half, Phiaton sent me a replacement pair of headphones. "Great!" I said foolishly, "My pair was probably just defective! Regardless, I'll be even more gentle this time." This time, the plastic snapped in the exact same place after only 2 months. Do not buy these headphones. I understand the positive reviews: people receive their headphones, love the quality, write a great review after a few weeks, and never come back to tell of their issues with the incredibly bad build quality, once they start. Had I written a review immediately, it would have been a glowing, 4-or-5 star affair. But as I have now owned two different MS 300's, both of which snapped in the same place, it's impossible for me to recommend this product. Go for a Sennheiser, ATH, or anything that isn't Phiaton: they simply don't know how to make headphones that last.

There are a million posts about the features of this and similar Blu-ray players. They all send gorgeous video. The BDP-S350, with an update on earlier models, will also play the latest Blu-ray sound formats, hook up with the latest HDMI cables and it is affordable. It isn't missing anything that will obsolete it anytime soon, except...read on. I think this unit is as good as anything in its price range and when Black Friday prices were sooo compelling, I bought one. It works as advertised and the both the picture and sound is really nice. Blu-ray gives the best results, even on 720p TVs. It is also modern looking with its cool blue front. Actually, the blue only shows in daylight. I thought it would look like the photos, or glow at night or something neat like that, but it doesn't. It looks black in dim light. This unit is designed to work with AV receivers that are capable of dealing with the new audio and video formats. The more expensive Sony BR players have this ability built in so they can be run through an older or less capable receiver. That is why the S350 is cheaper. The updates are just part of digital living. It is a pain, but you can improve the functionality free and that is a bonus. The problem is that you have to download to your computer and then pass it on to the player via an ethernet cable. And, this only works with Windows of various varieties. Mac owners, and others who refuse to buy cables and all, can contact Sony and they will send a physical disk. Also confusing is the subject of Blu-ray extras. You need to add special flash memory and have your player connected by ethernet cable to your internet connection. Is your connection near your TV? Or, you can buy wireless devices that do this for $75 or so. Personally, that is all too much trouble for me. I'll just watch whatever is on the disk. Too bad, because some of those extras are interesting. Sony probably came to the same conclusion. They could have built in wireless connections and more memory, but it would have raised the price and price is extremely important in making sales. They probably felt the hobbyists would add the capability if they wanted it. Sony always seems to have nice remotes. I used it to set up the dreaded modes and all, but control the S350 and my other gear with a Harmony One universal remote (I reviewed that) and now it is in a drawer. The default "Easy set-up" is indeed easy, especially if you use HDMI cables. These cables make it all so much easier and neater, and allow full functionality. If you possibly can, I suggest that you update your other equipment to use HDMI. It seems like a technology that will be around for a while, so you won't have to update tomorrow. Do get cables that are capable of 1080p, though. I would do this even with a 720p TV. Save yourself from any odd errors. More difficult, though, are the more advanced settings. No need to list them all here. Just know that there are tons of acronyms and options and on and on. Most people have no clue, nor should they. They spend a few hundred dollars and probably wonder if they set it up correctly and if they are really getting all they paid for. Likely, many aren't. This is, what, almost 2009, and the mass market consumer that Sony and others are so desperately trying to reach are still being treated like hobbyists at the home-made computer club. All this should be automatic. When you play the disk it should be expected that the best audio and video possible is sent down the line. I really resent having to figure out whether I want to "output audio signals of 96 kHz sampling as 96 kHz/24 bit..." and things like that. Look at the Amazon discussions, or the really high-end forums at AVS. Those people live for this and have the money to get the best. Even they seem very confused about how they should set up their equipment. Can you imagine an automobile forum where posters have to ask about the best way to program the air conditioning? So, as this review started, it doesn't seem that the S350 going to be obsolete function-wise for awhile, but one has to think that someone will come out with a player (and receiver, etc) that is computer-controlled and features automatic best-possible playback. There will be a day when we will never again be required to scroll silly menus, choose between unfathomable techie options or enter any mode at all except on, off and volume. THAT is high technology. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Devices like the Apple TV that use downloads instead of physical disks may well be the future and in fact many people have thrown out their disk players. But, others do have existing disk collections and do not mind renting or buying new ones. Maybe in a couple of years I will mostly be downloading, but I will still be able to play my DVDs and CDs, and owning a few favorite movies on disk might well always be the best choice. I doubt I will regret this purchase decision. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- It will get five stars when I don't have to be a sound and video engineer just to play a disk. As of today, I would not give five stars to even the most expensive player.

I bought it to use as a desktop recorder to record shortwave and medium wave radio broadcasts. My previous recorder was a JVC cassette recorder. This replaced my original tube-type 7" r-t-r recorder I used starting in 1962 as a ninth grader. I had amassed a library 7" & 5" rtr tapes - then a drawer full of cassette tapes. The Sangean DAR-101 was bought to use like the Akai unit, hooked to the line/record output of my radio and able to start recording quickly. It has the ability to monitor the input and recording as it is made, a great attribute. It's builtin amp & speaker mean you won't need any other equipment for playback, unless you need headphones, which it drives nicely. The best news is that their is no tape media to catalog and store - or tape heads to degauss or clean, or mechanical transports to clean & oil - or oddball gel cell batteries to find, either. It would be nice to know what it's audio recording capacity, ie, the time it can record at your selected audio quality, although I feel that the 32 GB card I installed may just exceed all of my previous mag tape recordings sum by perhaps an order of magnitude. It's not enough of a negative to detract from it's five star rating - I feel it was a great purchase. My unit has no USB port. I am happy.

A few months ago, I decided that since I regularly take digital pictures and upload them to my Flickr site ([...] it was about time to upgrade to a better camera. The economy being what it was, I decided that I didn't want to blow a HUGE wad o' cash--just enough to get a good quality camera that had higher megapixels than what I already had (a Casio QV-R40 with 4.0 megapixels). A Flickr friend had just bought herself a Sony Cybershot and liked it a lot, so I set about doing some research. As it turned out, Amazon.com had this particular Cybershot model on sale at the time I was looking, so I got a great deal as well as a great camera. The Sony Cybershot S750 features 7.2 megapixels, a 2.5" LCD monitor, ISO 1250 (high sensitivity) and a 3X optical zoom. In hindsight, I wish I had gone up a notch to a higher zoom but, all in all, I have been very happy with the camera. It was tremendously easy to learn to use. I am not a big fan of "reading the blanking manual," so having something that is easy to use right out of the box was a bonus. It has a very quick & easy wheel that allows you to switch between different types of shots quickly. The options are the standard auto adjustment setting for photos, a program auto setting (which I haven't tried yet), a movie setting, a snow setting for taking pictures in a bright white landscape, a waterside setting for beach and other water shots, a twilight setting for shooting in low light w/o flash, a twilight portait setting, a landscape setting, a soft background setting and a blur-reducing low-light setting. The battery supposedly would allow you to take about 280 shots on one battery charge, which is pretty darned great compared to my older camera. However, it won't take much without an additional memory card (for an additional cost, of course). I got the Sony Memory Stick Pro Duo with 8gb of memory and that has worked very well.

As the bow was drawn against the strings of the Cello, by Yo-Yo Ma, the magnificently gorgeous sounding notes were released and lifted into the air. The tone, so pure, so correct, almost made me cry. It was as if I could hear the sound created by each individual hair of the bow. The sound of Chris Botti's Trumpet, each inflection and nuance of breath, created a drama and a stirring of emotion. I could hear for the very first time not only the sound of each note, but also how the note was created. As the finger valves danced up and down it was as if they were in slow motion, I could hear all of the elements that make up a note, a tone, so perfect. Every singers voice was now real. I now know what their true voices sound like, no coloration, nothing over-emphasized, only a perfect presentation of their tone. These speakers in my environment do not add any excessive warmth to sound. And they do not add an excessive brightness to the sound. Vocal tonal character is nothing but pure joy. The sound can be Big, Very Big. All you have to do is turn them up. If you have a room that's 12 x 24 with 9' foot ceilings, these things will fill the room easily. Based on the above, these speakers, the Elac Uni-fi 2.0, are worth every penny of their full retail price, $600. Unfortunately though I sent them back, for two reasons. 1.) It was difficult to hear the snare drum or the sound of the cymbals, or the shish-shish of the high hat. I couldn't quite make out the xylophone, or the tympany. 2.) For me, I just wasn't getting the dynamics I wanted. Imagine if you have two 15" speakers and two Public Address Bull Horns surrounding you. When the symphony plays, you feel it! You feel it in your heart and soul. The Uni-fi 2.0 didn't do that for me. But to be fair nothing with a 5.25 speaker has done it for me either. I'm conflicted, I love the sound of the Elac Unifi 2.0 so much, I really want it to work for me. I'm considering buying the towers at twice the cost, and a new/used amp with 200 - 300 watts per channel. I don't know if the extra watts, and extra woofers will create the dynamics, or if I'll be able to boost the treble enough to make these my forever speakers. My system: Two subwoofers, 12 cf enclosures, loaded with dual 12 inch woofers. The subs are powered by a Behringer iNuke 3000, 440 watts per sub. My speakers are powered by a Denon 1911 avr, 90 watts/ch@8ohms. My speakers are L/C/R, Monoprice 15" Passive PA speakers with 1.75 compression horns, 8 ohm, 96db efficient. The monoprice speakers do not have the tonal character of the Elac 2.0, but boy oh boy, do they have dynamics!

UPDATE: After a few months, I'm throwing away the screw connectors. The pigtails are OK, but there is a spring clip that blocks the opening of the screw terminals and keeps small-gauge stranded wire from entering. Several have had open circuits inside, which is tough to debug. Screws continue to strip. Tried going back to valley ent, they've changed to this style also. See Item B079RBL339 for the Chanzon part I finally settled on. My initial order had all one gender of pigtail, seller was quick to replace with another complete order. All good! Until I started dipping into the pile of screw-terminal connectors. Many have screws that strip easily (I"ve been using these type connectors for years on CCTV cameras, and never stripped a screw). None have clamp openings that are actually open: I can't push in CAT5 or small gauge stranded wire because it's not stiff enough to push past the metal tab even with the screw all the way out. These commodity connectors all LOOK the same, but they're not all MADE the same.

This is my second onkyo receiver and was expecting the same quality as the first. The receiver is paired with a [[ASIN:B00752R4PK Panasonic DMP-BDT220 Integrated Wi-Fi 3D Blu-ray DVD Player]] over hdmi. This combination seems to be a problem. The receiver has problems decoding the bitstream data coming from the blu-ray player which results in sound dropping out and once in a while, the video. Research on this issue, and confirmed for my set up, was to change the data coming from the player to PCM (i.e., the player decodes the data rather than having the receiver do it). This is done in the settings menu of the blue ray player and is quite easy to do. There is no loss in either sound or video quality so that is good. But this issue was quite frustrating until I could figure out what was going on. Interestingly, the sound dropping did not happen with my other Panasonic blu ray player ([[ASIN:B0038KN114 Panasonic DMP-BD65 Blu-Ray Disc Player (Black)]]). So, not quite ready out of the box but this may not be an issue for other receiver-blu ray player combinations.

Here is a metaphor for the product - if you spend the extra cash to get the "without special offers" (just call them ads) version of the tablet, you are unable to set your own lock screen picture despite paying extra to make that screen yours rather than amazon's. The hardware overall is fine for a $150 device - the screen is low res, the back is overly slippery, there are a myriad of compromises, but hey, it was $150. The problem is that the software experience seems to have been written by a team that is at least half the size of what is needed to deliver a quality product. Trivial to engineer features like being able to customize background images are missing, nothing is really implemented in a polished manner, and the whole user interface really screams really bad android skin (which, admittedly, is almost exactly what it is). Android tablet apps are already a fairly scarce breed, but the ones made available in the Amazon app store are even scarcer, and typically far behind the official android version in terms of bug fixes and feature enhancements. Even Amazon's own apps are inferior to the versions they make available on other platforms. This doesn't seem like the product of an American tech giant but rather a low budget foreign knockoff product that's only distinguishing feature is its price, and even that is ultimately questionable if you consider alternatives. If you are willing to spend a fair amount of money on a tablet, the iPad Mini justifies the additional cost with vastly superior hardware, a much more polished operating system, and significantly better app support (and for media you are a lot less tied to the Amazon ecosystem - Amazon is still an option, but so is Apple and even Microsoft with Groove Music/Xbox Video). If $150 or so is your target, the Dell Venue 8 Pro is a better experience and I regret not buying it instead - Windows 10, despite being very new and still a bit buggy, seems like a significantly more complete and functional operating system than FireOS, Xbox Video/Groove Music are significantly better apps than Amazon Music and Video (though it would be nice if both were an option), other built in apps like Mail, Calendar, and maps are miles ahead of the Amazon equivalents, and while the WIndows App Store is small, compared to the Amazon Store it actually seems much more vibrant. With both the software and hardware it doesn't really seem like Amazon cared much about the FIre, and so I am at a loss for why would be purchaser should care either

My setup: Yamaha R-S500 receiver, JBL ES20 speakers, and this sub. All running off of my PC with an upgraded sound card. The goods: This sub is capable of clean and tight bass, if you get it set up correctly and are looking for fill instead of boom I like the aesthetics of it, but that is purely opinion on my part The connections seem solid The single-channel input to get what is basically LFE works great without too much effort Capable of being tuned to run in a pair, which would be great for a larger room. The sound is great for the price, significantly better than what I've heard from similarly priced Yamaha units. The bads: If you get the volume past about 1/3 the sound gets a bit muddy. Fortunately for me, I was only looking for fill so 1/3 volume is all I needed. Having the adjustments on the back is irritating if you place it near a wall. I spent a couple hours getting it adjusted to how I like it (no LFE on my receiver) so I was moving it every time, but now that it is set, all I adjust is the volume. Overall: I would buy this sub again, especially at the $100 price point. I didn't expect audiophile quality for this, but with careful adjustment you can just about get it there. Anyone complaining that this is boomy needs to turn the volume down all the way and turn it up in small increments until you get enough sound. I find that lower volume on items in this price range allows cleaner sound. A tip for testing; try it with a wide range of music/movies at each volume level that you try. I tried everything from classical (Vivaldi mostly) through dubstep (find something with good quality bitrate) to get it where I wanted it. The volume ended up a bit on the low side, but it fills out perfectly without being boomy. A note on good subs; they shouldn't be noticed until they are turned off. My wife constantly thinks that it's not working, but I can tell that it is through trained listening. All you should need is a good clean fill of the bottom end.

This needs clarification, because there is a lot of bad information going out on the issue, so I'm putting it at the top of this review. The Kindle Oasis DOES have text to speech. It's now called VoiceView and this is how to get to it: settings / Accessibility / VoiceView Screen Reader. It does NOT require an audiobook to use, but it does require Bluetooth headphones. And now back to the review. This review is for those trying to choose between the two more advanced Kindle offerings. I love my Kindle Voyage. I love it so much I asked for the upgrade for Christmas. I received it. I am now the proud owner of a 32g Oasis 2nd Gen, and I love that too, but not as much. I'm writing this review now, because the flaws in the Oasis 2 have shown me just how perfect the Voyage is as an ereader. They have the same PPI, but I'm pretty sure the Voyage is clearer. The Voyage definitely has a whiter background. I set them to the same lighting level of 10 and set them side by side in front of a window. The Oasis 2 is more yellow. It took an increase in the light settings of 3 levels to achieve the same look on the Oasis 2. The devices also have practical differences. The Voyage is symmetrical. There are page press buttons on both sides, so switching hands while reading one handed is no big deal. To do the same on the Oasis 2 or Oasis 1 for that matter requires you to flip the device. No big deal, except that you have to relocate your spot on the page. I suppose I could just wait to switch hands until I'm done with the page, but the Voyage does not make me strategize in order to read. The experience with cases is also different. I have aftermarket cases on both devices. The case on the Voyage makes it easier to hold. It's just too thin for my male hands without it, women's experience may vary. The Oasis 2 however feels twice as heavy once the case is on. I suspect it has something to do with the odd shape or just how wide it is, so I usually end up transporting it in the case but removing it to read. Without a case it feels like you're holding perfection though. I'm awed by how good it feels in my hands. I never get that feeling from holding the Voyage case on or not. Without the case the Oasis 2 actually feels lighter than the Voyage, a nice balancing trick that is pretty impressive. Don't worry about the weight though. The Voyage is extremely light. So in closing if you are trying to decide between these two devices, the Oasis 2 is only worth the additional cost if 1. You want the 7" screen 2. You want to listen to audiobooks on your ereader 3. You really like physical buttons If none of the above apply to you, then you're actually better off getting the Voyage.

After a couple of months, the USB connector started to flex, and shortly thereafter it failed. These long, skinny USB dongles stick rigidly out of the side of a computer, and even light pressure on the end of this drive (eg setting a laptop down on an uneven surface) bends it at the circuit board connection (see photo of this device disassembled, and the soldered connection that broke when it flexed). The "slide" feature makes this worse, and is a completely unnecessary feature (see the Kingston DataTraveller Micro for an example of an exposed USB connector that doesn't need to be "protected" by a flimsy sheath.)

Being in the audio business, I look at remotes in three categories: a) professional, personalized custom integration systems, b) the basic remote that comes with almost everything AV and then c) the middle kingdom, which is what I was looking for with a new wife and teenage son moving in. I am weak on programming anything and my old Marantz 5200 worked fine for me but was completely non-intuitive for anyone else. My wife had an old Logitech 880 I bought for her years ago that impressed me but would not work with my elaborate audio/simple video system. I wanted a tablet style remote that looked more professional than it cost yet could be programmed by me via my PC with some time but little effort. Enter the 1100 to my home. The result is fantastic for all of us. It controls what I want it to, has some if not alot of flexibility and looks really cool on the coffee table. The reason for the missing star is the effort to how I got it to where I want it. My AV "control center" is a Sim Moon I-7 pre-amp, a high-end stereo affair that I use to run other amps, three rooms of speakers and a DAC that adds three inputs to the five already in use. This is not the normal system for a Logitech remote. When I could not get the remote to recognize the Moon input toggle, despite it telling me it could, I called customer service. Player A told me I would have to deal with Player B, a level of customer service up. Player B, (I wish I could remember his name as he was outstanding in spending an hour one night, and calling me back at an agreed upon time the next night to try again). Player B identified the problem in the timing and delay needed to program the Moon's toggle input selector but could not make it happen. Finally Player C, the "highest level customer service" at Logitech, nailed it in 10 minutes. While this should not have taken three hours of my time, the result is perfect, the people were friendly and empathetic and they admitted they learned something for future users with this particular combination of gear. The only main thing I wish is that having gear I take pride in and manually wanting to touch on occasion, I could go back and forth between manual use and the remote. Can't do it without having to trouble shoot to get back in sync on the remote. No biggie, but the old remote allowed for that. I also wish I did not need the extra outboard RF transponder to make the 1100 more user friendly around tables and seating angles... because I have no place to install it, so it isn't even an option. In summary, the 1100 is a reasonably priced, aesthetically and ergonomically cool device that I can feel good about in an industry where we certainly tend to make things difficult. Oh, and my wife loves it. What else matters?

Product works exactly as advertised, and is very convenient to have and I'm glad I bought it. It's easy to configure and exceptionally easy to use. But I have two gripes about issues that I didn't discover until after I got it (but which are well-documented on Eye-Fi's website): 1) With my camera (a Nikon D40), the camera won't leave the power on to the card long enough after a picture is taken, so the pictures don't get uploaded. The workaround is easy - turn the camera off and back on. But it's annoying to have to remember to do that, because that's the point of the card - to not have to think about it. (Of course, this is really Nikon's fault, not Eye-Fi's, but it affects me nonetheless.) 2) The Eye-Fi has a feature that lets it upload both to a home computer and to a website (like Flickr or SmugMug). I knew that the Eye-Fi supported doing the uploads also to an FTP site, and I planned on using that feature to let it upload pictures to my home web server from anywhere I could get a wi-fi connection. It turned out that there were a number of problems with that plan: a) It only uses "FTPS" while "SFTP" would have been much easier for me to set up, and much more secure b) The pictures all go through Eye-Fi's servers before going to the FTP site, which I didn't realize (and this part isn't especially well documented), and I'm not OK with that c) It takes a long time for the pictures to actually make it from the card to Eye-Fi to the FTP server, so it was very hard to trust that the system was working reliably d) There's no way to tell the Eye-Fi to then NOT upload the pictures via my home wifi, if they were uploaded via FTP. So I just don't use the "upload via FTP" feature, and that's fine. So like I said, it's a good product that does what it says, so if you just want it to do the base things, go for it! On the other hand, if you have a D40, or you want to use it to upload to a home FTP site, consider this review before doing so.

I recently needed another external hard drive, and after price shopping, I got this Toshiba model for what seemed like a good price. The installation was quick and easy, it comes with a USB 3.0 compatability, and I get about 1.86 Tb of space. However, after using it for a few weeks, I have noticed a few awfully annoying things that I have never noticed with my Seagate or WD models. First, whenever I go back on a video file and come to the point I was when I went back, the video ALWAYS pauses. It seems to be quite a common problem because my mother's Toshiba hard drive does the same thing, and I have never had any issues in the past decade with Seagate or WD models. Also, at least in the case of my specific unit, I was moving some files to my mother's desktop and decided to rearrange my files while I was there. When I brought it back to my laptop, it detected a problem with the device and requested to fix it. The fix was annoying, but thankfully, nothing was deleted. However, it happened a few more times whenever I went between different computers. Both my mother's desktop and my laptop are Windows-based systems. The only difference is I'm running Windows 8 and she is running Windows 7. With just these two annoyances, I'm a bit reluctant to repurchase another external hard drive from Toshiba any time soon. I'll hold onto the one I purchased for now, because I need it and the problems have just been annoyances thus far, but I don't quite recommend this unit if you can find one from Seagate or WD for around the same price point.

A great device for the price, though not up the quality of what "mechanical" generally implies in a full sized keyboard. The switches really do have a buckling spring mechanism, and are a reasonable approximation of the feel of a Cherry Blue or Green switch, though they are NOT Cherry switches - they're some kind of inexpensive knockoff. For the purposes of a numeric pad, they work and feel great, though keyboard enthusiasts will definitely be able to tell the difference. The keycaps themselves use very poor quality sublimation (with a questionable font decision...) with lots of noticeable legend bleed and uneven dye distribution. They don't appear laminated, so I suspect the legends would be quick to wear, but I don't use the numpad heavily enough that that's been a problem. They're installed with the very common Cherry MX mounting profile, so you could trivially replace the keycaps if you felt so inclined. All in all, I definitely prefer it to the usual membrane switch device you'd typically get at this price point, and the fact that it's a legitimately working buckling spring mechanical keypad at $16 is pretty fantastic. More to the practical aspects of this device...it has a NumLock key. It does exactly what a NumLock key is supposed to do on a 90's-00's style PC keyboard (changes the 0-9 keys to arrows/page keys), and is exactly as unnecessary and confusing as that sounds. The NumLock indicator LED is oddly placed where its very difficult to see, so there's no clear indication if you've turned it off by mistake. There's also an extra top-row of function keys (a pair of brackets, =, and a backspace). These seem to use nonstandard keysyms, and haven't worked reliably or consistently in any situation that I've tried them in. They're not customizable or reprogrammable in any way, they just...don't do useful things.

Edit: After using these for several months, I made the mistake of pulling out one speaker just a tiny bit too far and it stretched the cable. Well, with any other banana cable two things could have happened: 1) The connector would pull out with no harm done or 2) The banana connector might have bent in one direction very slightly. In this case, however, the whole connector initially appeared to have bent, but upon closer inspection (trying to plug in again) it had totally shattered the outer conductors that expand to create the locking effect. In fact one small piece became lodged in my amplifier's connector and took me quite a while to fish/pull it out. Clearly this was due to my own mistake, but I promise that I only stressed the cable/connector ever so slightly - not even noticeable until I had attempted to remove/re-plug. So given that these are 'welded' (sorry forgot the term off top of head), I'm stuck either buying a new connector and just crimping or soldering (thereby losing the super duper connectivity/conductivity effect?) and having to shorten that one cable by just a tad - OR - having to buy a whole new $60 (with shipping) cable. Ugh....so for now I'm back to my old eBay Canare cables with standard crimping banana connectors. May contact Blue Jeans to see what fixes they offer. Man, the topic of speaker cables can get contentious - especially when it comes to the perception (or alleged perception) of sonic differences between (mostly) electrically equivalent cables of equal lengths. I've been using this type of Canare implementation for more than a decade on whatever system I happen to have at the time. I got a good deal on some from eBay and so far I have preferred them to every other cable I've tried - when the speaker in question allows for bi-wiring. I know there's of contentiousness about bi-wiring too, and there are folks who will tell you NEVER to use the little brass colored metal jumper that comes with your speakers if you are not bi-wiring. Personally I think that's nonsense, but I digress. The Canare 4S11 sounds as good or better than any Audioquest or Nordost cable I've ever compared them to. Each cable DOES have its own unique sonic signature - which varies with speaker and amplifier - but I cannot say that either of the expensive cables are superior to the Canares. There's a reason that professional sound guys use them. Where the Blue Jeans versions really shine is in quality of construction. In addition to the already excellent Canare conductors and jacketing, Blue Jeans takes two steps that differentiate them from other "budget" cable companies: 1) They use a form of CAD welding which basically physically and chemically bonds the cables to the connector plugs. I have worked in RF engineering in the past and we always spec'd CAD welds for sub-surface grounding loops at Tx/Rx towers. A plain weld or clamp might not conduct sufficient electricity from a lightning strike into the earth. 2) They use 'locking' banana plugs - something I'd never seen before. This prevents your plugs from being pulled out by children, pets or from coming out on their own and causing some kind of short circuit (rare, as that might be) ruining your equipment. Just set it, screw it down, and forget it. I'll return to this review over the course of the next several months with some more commentary from an "audiophile" perspective. I will have had the chance to use these cables on several speakers including "reference" models and a couple of different SET, Class D and solid state amplifiers. In the meantime, I recommend these highly. You will not get a better, longer-lasting cable for the price.

The Fujifilm XF 35mm F1.4 is a fantastic lens. It's my favorite lens (it almost never comes off), but it has its cons. The pictures are razor sharp and the quality is absolutely fantastic—The bokeh is gorgeous! For just about any casual, portrait shot, this is my go-to lens. The quality of the photos are just stunning—I can't reiterate how pleased I am. The aperture ring is also another favorite of mine. It's super nice that I can quickly adjust the aperture with a ring and not have to fiddle with buttons on the camera. I also love the feel of the focus ring. It lets you really dial in that zoom to get the perfect shot. It's also really wide, making focusing really nice. However, the auto-focus is a bit slow and a bit noisy. I can't expect the auto-focus to be as quick and fast as a regular DSLR, but there are often times I wish it was. Also you can hear the auto-focus working, and sometimes it has a tough time focusing on the subject, especially if you're rather close or in dimly lit environments. Comparing it to a traditional DSLR isn't fair, but if you're coming from one or have experience with one, you'll definitely feel a difference. All-in-all I'm super happy with it! Firstly, I love this laptop on paper. In my opinion, it is the best looking in its class at the moment, has a wonderful (although very glossy and reflective) screen, and runs silently and quickly even with the standard processor as it's sold here. I also like the placement of the fingerprint reader on the righthand side of the screen instead of sitting under my right hand while I am typing. The touchpad is also extremely impressive with it's flat (buttons built in instead of standalone) and very large (comparable to my Macbook) design. I love the keyboard too. Very nice sized keys, just the right amount of resistance, easy to let my fingers fly on. Having multitouch on the screen and on the touchpad is a whole new realm of computing comfort. Now, let me go on to say that I ordered this laptop only to receive a unit with a defective system board. The first time I turned it on the unit crashed and gave me a blue screen 4 times before I could get through a complete Windows setup. Since no one I talked to at HP knew what a blue screen was, they tried to blame Windows. After reinstalling Windows and running a bunch of tests during 5 or 6 calls to HP, the unit continued to bluescreen during or soon after startup. This is my second HP touchsmart PC (I also have the desktop, which had a defective dvd drive right out of the box) and I was disappointed in HP's inability to step up and replace this for me themselves. (In all fairness, they did offer to attempt to repair it, but I would be out a laptop for 6 weeks due to my work schedule and in the end have a refurbished unit for which I paid full price. If a refurbished unit is ok with you, I'd save a few hundred bucks and just buy that upfront. At least it's been tested that way.) So, I had to return the unit to Amazon, who gave me no hassle and offered me a full refund or replacement. Since I need a laptop now and can't wait to see the fabulous new options coming out summer 2010, I took Amazon's offer of a replacement and bought a 3 year warranty from Squaretrade. I have hopefully seen the last of my problems with this model and still like it enough to look forward to a few years of good use. Should that not turn out to be the case, I will update this review. Bottom line: If you buy this sharp little laptop, get a warranty. UPDATE 5/19/10: Got the replacement, turned it on, got through setup once, BAM - blue screen!! I couldn't believe it!! Turned out to be fixable, a problem with the fingerprint reader drivers which we reinstalled and now it's fine. Luckily we didn't have anything worse than that (or have to call HP). Now that I've used it for a few weeks, I have this to add. PROs: 1. Screen was readable in full sunlight. Better with sunglasses and not showing the vibrant colors you see indoors, but not like my last laptop that was worthless outdoors. 2. Fabulous battery life. I can go a solid 4 or 5 hours of use without ever plugging in the battery. 3. Still love the touchpad and keyboard. Both are well designed, easy to use, and beautiful to look at. 4. When in tablet mode, I like having the button right on the side of the screen that let's me manually rotate the viewing mode from landscape to portrait and vice versa. When it's time to open it back into a 'laptop' again, the screen automatically flips back into normal landscape mode, which is nice. 5. Runs quiet for the most part. I hear the fan, but it's not something that will keep my husband awake at night. 5. Wacom style pen fits inside the unit so I (hopefully) won't lose it. Very useful for hovering over a link, picture, etc to see hidden text. I usually use my finger, but the pen has been more useful than I thought it would. CONs: 1. The weight is not well-distributed, so the laptop can't sit on my lap without falling backwards. It does ok on hard surfaces that provide a little bit more support, but won't stay up on the couch, bed or on my lap. Not a huge deal just less comfortable to use in these situations. 2. On my replacement (not on the first one) the screen doesn't line up with the bottom part when it is in tablet mode, making the touchpad turn on and off all the time. This puts a pop up in the middle of the screen every time it turns on and off and I am always having to force it into place but it won't stay there. Disappointing. 3. When browsing having flash pages, computer would freeze often making it the animation less enjoyable. I'd get the better processor if I could go back and do it again. Now you it's up to you to decide! :) In the end I'm still glad I have a full featured computer in a tablet with multitouch. UPDATE 6/30/2010: Since my last update I have spent most of the time on this laptop trying to keep it turned on. It is overheating and powering off after 30 minutes of use, every time I start it I get a screen during startup asking me to do hard drive tests, and it blue screens whenever I enable the fingerprint reader. So far I have not loaded any of my personal media files or documents due to these issues. I am only running google chat and surfing the web. FYI. It has problems detecting the fan causing it to bluescreen and crash over this while running about 3 times per week and still cannot run the fingerprint reader. Overall this is a very good quality mic for the price. It's basically the MXL AC404 in a different case and $10 cheaper, so I've copied my review of that mic here. It has a slightly fuller bass pickup than the MXL. That may be good or bad, depending on the low frequency noise in your room. I compared this to the similar Soundtech CM-1000, and there are pros and cons to each. Both had better sound than my Jabra Speak 410/510 USB speaker/mic, though neither has speaker or bluetooth functions. I would also check out the Samson GoMic, which (though not a boundary mic) is good sounding, flexible, and less expensive. The Movo isn't really omnidirectional; possibly this is a function of the 3 capsule design? In any case, mine acts more like a cardioid pattern mic (the logo is the front), and I got good results orienting the mic this way. 90 degrees off axis was several dB down and sounded more distant, and 180 was even worse. The SoundTech CM-1000 was omni, and though it had a few dB more noise and didn't sound as good as the Movo on axis, it was better off axis. Thus, in a room with only a couple of people or for more distant pickup the Movo wins, but for a small round conference table the SoundTech does. The SoundTech allows you to daisy chain additional mics for better pickup for larger tables or rooms; the Movo does not. But the Movo has a headphone jack, which the Soundtech lacks. Overall, a very good mic for $60 IMO.

Note: If you just want to see my cons go to the third paragraph down. I have had the Colby 4GB MP3 player for a couple of weeks now. I don't have a lot of experience with MP3 players, I had previously only owned one in my entire life. The MP3 player I used to own was a Creative Zen Stone, I have had it for about 4 years and it was a bare bones player that also included an FM radio and microphone. I had lost it and needed a new player as soon as possible so I went with this one. On the surface I believed I was getting a bargain. This did pretty much everything my Stone did but was more advanced. While this is true, the performance of this device leaves a lot to be desired. If you are doing your research on this device I think you know the gist of what it is capable of. It plays your MP3's well, it can play low quality videos and show you low quality pictures. The radio seems to work fairly well too. Where this product aggravates me: Coming from my Zen Stone there are a few things that really bother me with this product. 1. The organization of files. Things get put into categories but the way the device chooses to file some of the MP3's bothers me. I'm used to being able to put whatever Mp3 in whatever folder I want and it being in that folder. 2. It is slow to turn on and turn off. This actually doesn't bother me a bit because my previous player was worse and I got used to it. For some people though, this could be an issue. 3. It goes to sleep very fast after being paused. I don't know if I can change this but it seems like I can't pause a song for more than 60 seconds before the deice shuts down. My last player gave me 5 minutes. 4. Very minor issues but this has no clock for the time and date. For a player with a screen, this seems lacking. My old player had this and I enjoyed it but really this isn't a big deal and doesn't effect the rating. 5. I mainly listen to podcasts while working out. That's a big reason why I needed a new player fast. When you start listening to really long files the problems really come out with this player. For one thing, the timer for some strange reason is only capable of tracking up to 59:59 minutes. That means if a show is over an hour long it will break up the timer. This is a bit confusing at first because you may download a show that's 90 minutes but you will only see 29 minutes remaining on your timer. There is a bar you can look at to gauge how far into the file you are in but this is a really tacky way to keep track of file length. Secondly, the fast forward mechanism is bothersome. After two weeks I have yet to figure out how it works. Fast-forwarding is very slow, sometimes after holding the fast forward button down for 10-15 seconds it speeds up but this doesn't always happen! I don't know if I have to apply a certain pressure or what but I can never consistently get this to work. No one wants to sit there for 5 minutes holding the fast forward button to get to a point where they were before. Now maybe you are thinking, "No big deal, how often will I need to fast-forward a podcast anyway?" That's true, especially becasue the player does remember where you left off when you turn it off. There are two problems though. A. Every time you add a new file to the system and refresh the player loses track of what you were listening to and where in that file you last listened. B. It is very easy while fast forwarding or rewinding to accidentally skip the track. Often times you may hear something you want to quickly rewind back to and if you slip up you have to start back from the begging. The rewind feature is the same but as far as I know there is no speed boost for rewind like the one that occasionally shows up for fast forwarding after holding down the control for 15 seconds. All in all this player does what it is supposed to do which is play MP3's and it does it adequately. If you only plan to listen to music it's a decent cheap option. For podcast users though, you can do better. The slow fast forwarding, poor track sorting, silly timer, and other minor frustrations that build up are not worth it. I can't give it anything lower than 3 stars becasue it does what it is supposed to do decently and for the price it is hard to beat. If this retailed at $40 though it'd be a 2 star. I suggest spending the extra 10-20 bucks to get a better product. I suspect that in the coming weeks I will be getting another player because this thing frustrates me more than I should be tolerating.

I'm not one to write many reviews, and I've only had this ASUS GTX 1050 Ti card for a few hours (purchased from Amazon), but I am super pleased with this video card. I shopped several hours over several websites and dozens of the newest video cards before I took a chance on this one. I would like to direct this review to you consumers that are similar to me. I built my desktop pc from components 6 years ago in 2011. At the time it was a decent gaming machine. Its been a decent gaming machine in all the years since. Of primary interest to this review is that back then I splurged quite a bit of money to buy two GTX 465's each with 1GB of VRAM. I ran those video cards using SLI with good results. I'm a first person shooter fan and always have been. My experience has been that if you build a pc for gaming, everything else you do with your pc will fall into place. That's all well and good, but as time passed and newer games were released, my frame rates dropped. I could compensate by turning the game's settings back, which is fine by me. Eye candy is nice, but frame rates are the difference between life and death when playing a bleeding edge shooter. The system served me well for many years and many shooters until I bought DOOM 4. DOOM 4 is a great game, but with my aging SLI video cards setup my frame rates were terrible, almost unplayable, even at the lowest of the low settings. My second most important criteria for the new card I chose is that it had to have two DVI connectors, since I want to run two LCD monitors. Back in the day two DVI connectors were common on video cards, but that is not the case now. This ASUS card is a rarity in that it has two DVI connectors, plus an HDMI connector, plus whatever that other connector is. My third criteria when shopping for a card is less aggravation and faster speed of installation. I'm older now, I don't want to break my bank, I've got a growing family and much less time to fight a pc upgrade. This ASUS video card nailed it. I removed my old GTX 465's, plugged in this new GTX 1050 Ti, started the computer, and within a tiny handful of minutes Windows 7 figured out what I needed and installed it. I followed that up with a quick NVIDIA update and now this beast of a computer and video card smoothly plays DOOM4 on ultra settings. The frame rates are over the top. The computer is quieter, the power consumption dropped considerably. I'm happy

I'd heard a lot of (mostly) favorable reviews regarding the Grundig S350, and finally broke down and bought one for myself. ($99.95 no tax no shipping). I'm very pleased with this purchase. Let's get to it..... Strong points: 1) Good overall quality. Feels solid and substantial -- especially when the batteries are in place. 2) Excellent MW (or AM) reception with the internal ferrite antenna (made even better when I hook up my C Crane Twin Ferrite Antenna) 3) Very good FM reception 4) Shortwave seems to be as good or better than any of my several other SW receivers (although none of them are high-end) from a variety of manufacturers. I find that it's best with one of those 23' auxiliary antennas (not included, but 10 to 15 bucks), but the whip works great for a lot of channels. 5) Good sound from the speaker 6) Separate bass and treble controls 7) Analog 2-speed tuning knob is fun to use 8) Clock and alarm functions are easy to use 9) Battery life seems to be excellent -- it comes with an AC adapter, but I rarely bother with it. 10) External AM and FM antenna hook-ups 10) Nice design. Not-so-strong points: 1) It's not a small radio, so it won't fit in your pocket or briefcase. 2) Some say the tuning is "drifty". I agree that there is minimal drift, but nothing that really bothers me. 3) No presets -- it's an analog tuner with a digital readout. You cannot preset stations, but that's part of the fun in my opinion, and the 2-speed tuning knob lets you either move real fast through the dial, or slow way down to pick up a weak or distant station. This seems to be the kind of radio that will get a lot of use both in the house and outdoors. It's nice, but at a hundred bucks I don't feel like I have to baby it, and being able to get AM, FM or SW means there's always SOMETHING worth listening to. I think this would make a great gift for somebody who spends a lot of time listening to AM and SW broadcasts. I know I would've loved to get it as a gift rather than buying it for myself, but I'm very pleased overall.

The Problem The problem with this arrangement is that one should never ever connect the DP_PWR of the source to the DP_PWR of the sink: it's impossible for both pins to have exactly the same voltage, so connecting them together would effectively result in a short circuit condition. In addition, if, your GPU is powered off, while your monitor is powered on, you get a problem that's commonly called 'backdrive': a sneaker path that feeds electrical components in the GPU even though nothing is supposed to have power. This can result in your GPU behaving erratically when trying to power up. In some cases, it can even damage the GPU. The official DisplayPort FAQ: Q: Why isn’t there a wire on pin 20 (POWER) on the standard external DisplayPort cables? A: The reason power isn’t included in standard cables is because both source and sink devices are designed to provide power. Captive, attached cables often include the power wire. If it is desired, for example, that a particular source device utilize the power available from the mating sink device, then that Source device could include an attached or dedicated cable that carries the DisplayPort power signal. Same could be applied to a sink device.

I'm a software developer that bought this laptop for coding in work hours and gaming in off hours. Been using it for a few weeks and overall I'm very pleased. ---BUILD AND AESTETHICS--- Build quality surpassed my expectations and I love how it looks. I find it quite light for a gaming laptop, weights around 5.5 pounds. Of course, there's that "gaming laptop" look that some people hate but I think it looks great. Never received weird looks when I pull the computer out when meeting with clients. But if you need a super conservative looking laptop maybe this one is not for you. ---KEYBOARD AND TRACKPAD--- I really love how it feels typing on this laptop (Doing it right now!) The keyboard looks great with its red backlighting and the keys have a nice texture. My only annoyance is that the arrow keys are not spaced out from others like in regular keyboards. The trackpad feels a lot like a Mac trackpad. You can use two fingers to scroll up or down, three fingers to browse all your active applications and four fingers to change desktops. It does take a bit more of force to right or left click than I'd like, but you can always use the soft taps instead of the buttons. ---BATTERY--- Battery life is acceptable, but it won't last you through a whole day. Doing mundane tasks like web browsing and watching some videos the battery will last around 4 hours give or take. Doing more demanding tasks the battery will last around 3 hours and gaming a bit more than 1 hour. ---PERFORMANCE--- Now, this is where this laptop shines the brightest. If you get the 1000$ configuration you'll get a really powerful machine. Coding in the most demanding IDE's is buttery smooth. I'm not a content creator but I hear the included i7 7700HQ it's great for editing videos. Also, the SSD it's wicked fast; Windows 10 only takes around 5 seconds to boot and applications load quickly. Perfect for productivity, which was the main reason I bought it. Do note that the SSD is only about 250 GB, so it will fill up quickly if you install many games or download a lot of media. ---GAMING--- I went for the GTX 1050 TI configuration and it can handle most modern games easily. Fan noise while gaming is surprisingly low. You can hear it but it is not distracting at all. Overwatch and Doom on Ultra play perfectly. More demanding games like Battlefield 1 will need to be toned down to High in order to get over 60 FPS. GPU crushing games like Witcher 3 and Far Cry Primal will need to be played in Medium for a really smooth experience. If you really need a laptop that can run every game on High or Ultra, I'd recommend going for a Laptop with a GTX 1060. If you don't mind lowering the graphics for some games then the 1050 TI is great for you. Of course, there are some inconveniences. The screen, although IPS, could be better, the colors are not super accurate. There's no optical drive. The IO port selection could be better (No thunderbolt). Although the front panel looks great, it's a fingerprint magnet. These cons are understandable, as the manufacturer had to keep costs low on this laptop in order to stay at an attractive price point. But overall, I think this laptop is great. Perfect bang for the buck.

I purchased this out of desperation, installed it in my attic only yesterday, but now wished I would have done so several years ago. Heres the story. I live in the Los Angeles foothills, as the bird flies less than 25 miles from Mt. Wilson, but due to my location, and my neighbors 100' tall Eucalyptus trees, we do not have direct line of sight with the broadcast towers. In1988, prior to digital broadcasts, there was a very large antenna on a 10' mast fastened to the roof but it only managed to receive a few channels and those channels had ghosts and snow. Our solution at that time was to remove the antenna and purchase cable programing. Then in 2005 we switched to equally expensive satellite TV. As television providers got greedier and greedier, prices keep rising for their services and programming becomes less and less interesting with more and more advertisements. I clocked it with a stopwatch once and in an hours worth of programming there was just about 1/2 an hour of content, sometimes even less. Finally we had enough. When I retired in 2007 I was no longer willing to pay $70 a month for basic satellite fees to watch what I call "Commercialvision". We decided to switch back to an antenna hoping to get a couple of the basic TV channels for local news and rely on Netflix and Amazon for our movie entertainment. I tried several different antennas including a Bow-tie looking one and an old VHF antenna I purchased at a yard sale, but none produced more than 3 channels. Then an electrical engineering friend of mine made a couple of directional antennas that we elevated on a 15 foot mast and rotated while watching a signal strength meter, but the most we got for all his efforts was again three channels, 7, 9 and sometimes 11 or 13….. So he made me a simple bi-pole antenna which we stapled to the rafters inside my attic and gave up, settling for three channels (its worth noting that reception would vary from night to day and night to night. The only channel I could consistently receive was the one I disliked the most, channel 7 (In my opinion channel 7, Disney owned ABC, has the least content and the most commercials of all the channels. Setting aside my dislike of anything owned by the greedy Disney corporation, it is channels 2, 4, 11 that broadcasts most of the football games, something I have not been able to watch for way too long). It was time to try something else…… I started to look at antennas again. In my research, I read the reviews on this antenna on Amazon, and thought I would give it a try. So yesterday a friend of mine and I crawled up in the attic, unfolded this antenna, pointed it in the general direction of Mt. Wilson, turned the TV on, and found I now received a total of 40 channels. Admit tingly, most of which I will never watch including Korean, Spanish, Russian, Armenian and several religious programs, but I now get channels 2, 4, 7.1, 7.2, 9, 11, and the 13's (all 3 of those). I could not be happier, and that is the reason I am taking the time to write this review… I'm hoping it encourages others to try this antenna….. it is definitely tuned for digital reception.
