This is a difficult review to write since I still own and love my LX3 and LX5 cameras. When this one was announced, I could not wait to try it. The F1.4 - F2.3 lens was the only draw for me, so that is what I focused on when I received the camera. The good things are: Great resolution for such a small sensor. The noise behavior is good up to about 400iso and manageable if you have to use 800 (better by about a stop, than the LX5 IMO). The speed of operation is great, locking focus quickly and shot to shot times are much better than nearly any other P&S out there. The screen is lovely, and you can reasonably see it in bright sun (at least enough to compose a shot). It has a distinctly better fit in my hand than the LX3/5, feeling more like you can keep hold of it. The aperture ring on the lens is great, nicely clicking into position and felling like the detents are of a quality that high end DSLR's would use/employ. The bad thing is: The lens. Yes, it is a Leica branded lens, and yes it is a faster aperture. However, that F1.4 - 2.3 are deceptive since to get the legendary sharpness from either end of this lens, you have to stop down at least one full stop. Not as sharp wide open as the LX5 I am afraid. Next, the thing seems to rear focus on all Macro shots where distance to subject is sub 6". I tried about 20 or 30 shots to have this work as this one feature is what Panny have done so well in the LX series so far. Every shot in that range, rear focuses. If you imagine a shot of a ring, where you are 2" from the ring to lens, then focus on the stone in the front area of the ring, it would consistently hit about half way through that circle of the ring before getting sharp. I loved the camera and really wanted to keep it. Alas, I cannot do so when I know that is one thing that would limit my shooting with it, and the softer images wide open would end up frustrating me. I have returned it.

This is my first home security camera, and I'm glad I chose the YI. New buyers should note that: 1. The written and verbal instructions of the Official U.S. Edition of the YI Home Camera are entirely IN ENGLISH. The instructions are short, well edited, and the camera speaks to you in English to ensure that you get each step right. 2. As others have mentioned, a 32 GB SanDisk Ultra micro SD card is included, so you should not buy another SD card separately unless you have a brand preference. Considering its small size, the scope of the picture is surprisingly wide, and you can see a bit further by dragging the picture to each side. Also surprising is the clarity of the night view; it looks like a sharp black and white photograph of an illuminated room. When I wasn't sleeping well, I checked the picture at 3 AM and could see the room in as much detail as during the daytime. Although I don't have a frame of reference after owning another camera, the high-quality and sharp YI image is impressive with less distortion than expected. Despite the instructions being in English, it did take me longer than expected to set the camera up. I had to download a QR code reader app to scan, and it took a few tries. Fortunately the QR code appears both on back of the camera and in a larger size in the instruction booklet; the scan worked on instruction booklet on my Moto G (Android) phone. I set up a YI account but didn't look up my Wi-Fi password beforehand. It took me long enough to look that up that the setup process timed out, and I had to reset it. If this happens to you, be prepared to hear the camera say, "waiting for connection" over and over. All of these delays were my own fault, due to average technical ability. After it does connect, you can plug the camera in anywhere without adjustments. The icon commands are easy and convenient, e.g. you press a picture of the camera to automatically store a photo in your photo album. I have not used the audio feature, so I can't comment on that. Overall, this camera exceeded my expectations on all fronts. Also, the YI customer service responded within 24 hours to an email query I sent, answering my question and offering extra advice. If you are another homeowner who is concerned about security and has average technical skills, you will be very happy with this useful and well-thought-out camera.

When I saw that Twelve South was releasing a new USB-C dock with the minimalist dongle solution, I had to jump on it immediate as I'm a big fan of their accessories. The hub arrived quickly and the setup is as simple as any other USB-C dongle as you would expect. The hub feels solid thanks to its aluminum shell and what I really love (and underrated) is the 3m long USB-C cable with the angled end to sit nearly flush with your laptop or tablet. This is another underrated feature as the angled designed reduces overall cable clutter and tucks in nicely either behind or under your laptop if you're using their BookArc dock. The inclusion of a built-in USB-C cable inside the hub itself for travel purposes is a nice touch as it streamlines your travel kit by not having to carry the included 3m cable. The other features of the hub is pretty self explanatory and not anything new, as the USB-C passthrough and three USB A ports (all high speeds) and HDMI that powers a 4K monitor up to 30Hz (get a Thunderbolt 3 dock if you need higher refresh rates and higher resolution). Despite the amazing design and convenience of this hub, I wished that it had an AUX out audio as it would make your desk setup even cleaner when you don't have to plug in your audio on the right side of my MacBook Pro. A minor gripe in otherwise a perfect hub solution. Update: January 21, 2020 My USB-C hub stopped working reliably a few months back but it finally got worst today. My HDMI port works (although it took a few tries to get it working), but I'm not getting any power and my USB external drive that I use for Time Machine doesn't connect. I filed a claim through TwelveSouth's warranty department and we'll see how it goes. Update: February 19, 2020 I've purchased another new 13" MacBook Pro with upgraded specs and I'm experiencing the same problem with this laptop as well, which rules out that the laptop could be an issues based on my conversation with Twelve South's customer service reps. I can confidently say that my StayGo USB-C hub's power passthrough is inconsistent and unreliable. Update: Feb. 28th, 2020 Received a replacement unit from the people at Twelve South and I was told that going forward, the StayGo will come with a new firmware that should resolve some of the inconsistent I/O issues. So far, my replacement unit has been great and I think it's been fixed. Update: Mar. 26, 2020 Since we've all been working from home, this dock has been working great and reliably with the latest firmware update that I've received from Twelve South. It works well with both my Dell work laptop and my 16" MacBook Pro. I may pick up a second one.

NOTE: I just got my K380 in today, and I haven’t had a lot of experience with it yet, so if anything changes after posting this review, I will update this accordingly. PROS: This keyboard is beautiful. You can tell a lot about a product from its packaging, and I’d say just looking at the box made me excited to give this keyboard a shot. The keyboard itself comes in a plastic film to protect the keys from scratching or getting caught on anything. Two AAA batteries are already supplied, which was a nice surprise. I was very pleased to see that the keyboard was small. I wanted something that would be comparable to the length of my iPad Pro 9.7” and this keyboard is right about there. The circular keys look very nice and aren’t a problem when typing. They’re relatively quiet, so if you’re worried about the keyboard being too loud, say, for use in a university lecture, I wouldn’t worry about it. If you want further information on the loudness of the keys, you can definitely find sound test videos on YouTube. The keys press down softly with a little bit of resistance, so it still feels like you’re pushing down a key, but it doesn’t take a lot of force, which is good for long-term typing. Mechanical keyboards can get a bit painful after a long while of typing. The keys all work on the keyboard I received. The function keys at the top are super helpful. You have a home button, an app switch button, a menu/show or hide keyboard button, a back button, and song/volume control buttons. The functions of these buttons will differ depending on which device you’re using. I mainly use an iPad, so I was a bit disappointed when the F5 app switching key didn’t work for me, but upon further tinkering, I realized command + tab is how you switch apps in iOS using this keyboard. So all is well there. That was going to be a con, but I’m glad I found that. The app switching is seamless. Takes anywhere from 1-3 seconds to switch between devices, and connecting is easy. Just hold down the button until you see it blinking and appearing on the device’s bluetooth menu. Then you can simply push the button that is connected to the device you want to use. Easy peasy. CONS: The only con I can find right now is that the space bar on my keyboard is a little squeaky. It depends on where I hit it, but I think the right-ish middle side of the keyboard has some audible squeaking. It’s not very loud, but any little out-of-place sound can be obnoxious after a while. Either I’ll have to return this for a new one or get used to hitting the space button with my left thumb, which is how I’ve been doing it for most of this review, so it’s not a difficult switch. TL; DR: My HP x360 1030 G2 arrived in pristine condition and operates flawlessly. My overall rating is 5 stars for the vendor and 4 stars for the device. I buy based on quality and value. The Tech Venture listing on Amazon seemed too good to be true ($600) and the lack of reviews made me a bit nervous. I took the plunge anyway and I’m ecstatic. The HP 1030 G2 I received from Tech Ventures looks and operates just like new. One major surprise is that my unit came with over a year remaining on an extra-cost HP Care Pack, which extends the warranty to early 2021! That’s a very, very welcome addition. Hence, the 5-star rating for Tech Venture. I’m coming from a Dell Latitude 7389 to the HP x360 1030 G2. Both convertibles use 7th-generation Intel i7 processors and incorporate 13.3” touchscreens. I purchased the refurbished Dell at Woot! for just under $1000 in 2018. It’s been a great device. I switched to the HP because I need a cellular (4G LTE) connection for work purposes and wanted at least one Thunderbolt port for desktop use. I considered the LTE versions of the Microsoft Surface Pro 5 and the Surface Go for Business (8GB RAM and 256GB SSD) as well as the new Microsoft Surface X. I also own a 12.9” iPad Pro with 4G LTE. All of these devices are substantially higher in cost compared to the refurbished HP from Tech Venture. The main drawbacks to the HP 1030 G2 are the glossy screen and the system fan. The glossy screen forces me to maximize the brightness even indoors and reduces the battery life to less than 8 hours. I’ve ordered a SightPro anti-glare privacy screen filter and hope this will remedy the issue. Also, the system fan runs even during light duty activities like word processing. It’s noticeable but not obnoxious. Overall, I give the HP EliteBook x360 1030 G2 4 stars. Recommended add-ons for the HP include the Alapmk protective case cover ($20) and the Wacom Bamboo Ink Smart Stylus ($70). The Alapmk protects my system from scratches when it’s in a briefcase. The fit is great and it’s a superb value. Next, I looked at compatible pens from HP and was shocked at the pricing. I did my research and came up with the Wacom alternative. I found a refurbished Wacom Bamboo Ink at BB for $22. I paired it with the 1030 and it works brilliantly! Here’s some additional advice. I moved a nano SIM from an older Lenovo tablet to the HP 1030 G2 convertible and had lots of trouble getting Verizon to connect. Don’t waste your time with Verizon tech support. Go to a Verizon store, buy a new SIM ($5), and have the salesperson set it up. I worked with tech support for hours. Then, they put me on hold for over 40 minutes and never came back. The salesperson had everything up and running in under 10 minutes.

I bought this speaker primarily to listen to podcasts in the shower so that I never have to be alone with my thoughts. Since playing music isn't what I had in mind, I wasn't particularly concerned about sound quality, which is why I went with this relatively inexpensive speaker. The sound quality is indeed quite poor to the point that I would never listen to music on it, and I'm no audiophile. It is loud enough that I can hear my podcasts over the din of my shower (albeit only when it is fully cranked). It's only other positive quality is the bluetooth connectivity, it always works without any trouble, even through my closed bathroom door. The speaker is quite heavy, and its suction cup is not adequate to support it. It seems like a decent suction cup, and it sticks at first, but the speaker's weight causes it to droop sharply down. It inevitably tumbles down into my tub with a jarring clatter after a few hours. Note that I have several suction cup affixed shower hooks that stay up indefinitely, so my shower surface isn't the issue here. The speaker is just too heavy to be supported by a suction cup, I think. I find the button panel interface setup to be really annoying. The volume buttons double as skip buttons, with the latter taking precedent. You must hold down the button to adjust volume; tapping results in a skip. So, if I want to adjust the volume in the middle of a podcast, sometimes I make the mistake of not holding the button long enough, which results in skipping to a whole other podcast episode. Then, there is no way to get back to my place, save getting out of the shower, drying my hands, and using my phone. Another annoying feature: when the battery gets low, the speaker starts to beep very frequently (about 3 second intervals) until you either plug it in to charge or turn it off. This means that once the battery is low enough to trigger this function, I can't simply continue to enjoy my podcast up until the battery is totally drained. The frequency of the beeping subverts any possible listening enjoyment, so at that point I just turn it off (the alternative would be getting out of the shower and plugging into an electrical outlet with wet hands). In effect, this feature just shortens the battery life by making the last stage of it unusable. A rage-inducing corollary of this feature is that, since this battery alert occurs even if the speaker is not in playback mode, the speaker will sometimes wake me up in the middle of the night with this beeping. Granted, this could be avoided by powering off the speaker after each use, but I tend to leave it on for whatever reason (I'll note here that powering off requires holding down the button for 3 entire seconds, which feels like an eternity some mornings). When I am awoken at night by its every-3-second beeping emanating from my en suite, I know that I have no other choice but to get up out of bed and deal with it, and my bedmate is none too impressed. I feel that there has to be a better option out there for a similar price point than this frustrating product. I'll continue to use it for the time being, but I wish I had chosen something else.

The thing is I don't know if I like the blueish tint of the A03 or the yellowish tint of the new A01... I'm not too sure what to do. But know that it seems fairly consistent that all the current crop of Dell U2412M monitors have a slight yellow tint to things that are supposed to appear white. It's hard to fix this with any of the settings I've tried so far. UPDATE: I've decided to keep the second one with the yellowish tint because I've found some pretty easy settings to make the color pretty closely match my the older A01 version I have. Go into the color part of the monitor's menu system and set it up to have custom color, and then adjust the Red and Green settings each to 93, leave Blue at 100. Then set Brightness to 95 and Contrast to 70. This has done it for me. The two versions I have of this monitor are now close enough in color that I'm going to keep the new one from Amazon. The yellowish tint is enough of a tint that it's visible even if you don't have two of these monitors like I do. Ah, if all my problems were this bad I would be living a truly divine life.

It is not super loud, so if you are in a noisy area, you may have a hard time hearing, but under regular conditions, it works fine. You can also listen to music from google play, and I imagine other apps as well. Off course it lacks bass, and sound quality, this is not for an audiophile, but what would you expect from the speaker on a watch? Again, I'm happy enough just with the fact that this is a feature, and you have the option to do it if you want. I like the options for changing the faces, I've already downloaded other apps, and have found a couple of great watch faces I like to customize and use, I assume you can do that with any smart watch, but this is my first, so I'm speaking for my experience with this watch. I like that it has the heart rate thing on it, and I've been observing the step counter and so far it seems accurate. I'm using google fit, there's an option to use Huawei fitness, or something like that, but for now, I'm sticking with google fit alone, just so I won't keep cramming apps and options as I have apparently been doing..hehe! The one feature I'm not thrilled about is that I can't get in the water with the watch, but I don't think this is a deal breaker. I also wish they had more options on colors, size, etc... I want to give one to my wife for Mother's day, but this one seems a bit too bulky and a bit masculine, I guess. I've been reading recent reviews about battery life, It must be an isolated issue with some units, because I have not had issues with mine... I do have to charge it every night, but I would expect that from a smart watch that does all the things this one does... but I have not had a problem with it dying on me mid day, or even by night time. Am I impressed with the watch? I'm not sure, I think there's a stretch between being impressed, and being satisfied and/or happy. I think I'm in the satisfied/happy category. What would it take for me to be impressed? I'm not sure... I guess the being able to take it into the swimming pool. But what can I say, smart watches are still a new thing, and I had been researching smart watches since before Christmas before deciding on this one, and I am happy I made this choice. Four stars because of that specific issue of not being able to get in the pool with it, but other than that, it does everything else I would expect and/or wish a smart watch would do. In a nutshell, I'm happy, I wish it did more, not so much on the software side of things, but the hardware side of things, like being able to take it into the water, but it does a lot, and I like it so much I want to give one to my wife, but I wish there were a bit more "customized" options for her. For the price, I think this is the one to go for. I cannot promise you will like it, because everybody here has their own expectations, preferences, pep eves, etc... but in my case, I don't think there was a better choice for me.

This is what the M1 through M4 should have been - essentially a mini-DSLR with good performance. You can read the specs elsewhere, so I'll focus on why this works for me where the earlier models failed. First in line is performance - finally a mirrorless from Canon that acts like it's bigger brothers. Focus time is nicer, dynamic range is on-point, and sensor quality is superb. With the right lenses it can easily keep up with the lower end D and all the Ti range. I'll frequently choose this camera over my 5D for many mobile applications - places where I don't want to lug the full-frame beast. And I don't feel like I'm missing out - I use the adapter for the larger EOS L glass I have, and while it's often the "lens with a camera attached" effect, that doesn't bother me much. And the native lenses aren't much behind either - canon has done a good job with these. The built in viewfinder also fits my usage profile, and I'm glad I don't have to mess with an externally attached one. If you don't need it, the M6 is just about the same camera with some other minor changes. I can't really comment on the consumer type features, as I don't really use them much - sure it's nice to move the screen around sometimes, but that's not really my thing 99% of the time. If you want to talk cons - battery life is too short, so get a second battery. All that screen and viewfinder eats power compared to my older DSLR's. Sometimes the screen is hard to read in bright light - maybe they could come up with a simple solution, like a shade. Making it brighter would only make the battery problem worse. And while the viewfinder is nice, it's no optical viewfinder still - almost, but not quiet. Maybe next generation?

SUMMARY: After some initial avoidable Wi-Fi set up problems (that could have been easily prevented with better Quick Start documentation), I have enjoyed using my Windows 11 x360 very much. Of the 4 I've had, I'd like to say it's my favorite, but there's ONE missing feature (right side CTRL key) that prevents it from taking that prize. More on that in DISLIKES. LIKES [[GENERAL]] - MOST of my experience of using this PC, including its being my first Windows 11 machine, have been trouble free and enjoyable, and that includes the fingerprint scanner for logging in (wish my work PC had that). It's quick, the touch screen works well, Windows 11 has presented me with no problems and the keyboard has a very agreeable feel to it (though I do wish they'd switch to dark keys with bright letters, as my home office lighting set up works much better with those (as proven on my work Dell laptop). As this is a personal PC, I only occasionally have to use it for work, but that has also been a reasonably trouble free experience once I got things set up with my work MS account apps. [[PORTS]] - equipped with 2 x USB 3.1, 1 x USB 3.2 Type-C, 1 x HDMI, 1 x Combination Audio Jack, 1 x Media Card Reader; Wireless-AX Wi-Fi 6 + Bluetooth Combo, I don't lack for ports in MOST situations on this unit, but I do advise you to pick up some port adapters (USB3 > USB-C and USB-C to USB3) as the current state of affairs, where some of our devices will require whichever port type we don't happen to have free at the moment, suggests the need to be able to convert port types will come in handy. I bought several, some simple plug-ins and some with short extender cables to Provide room for wider plug-in devices, and I haven't regretted it. A world with two or more different USB connectors seems to be something we can't leave behind. Adapters just make life easier. NOTE - SD Card Reader - I used to use the SD card readers on my PC's a lot, popping cards in and out when doing uploads from cameras or swapping data between computers, but I found that previous iterations of these readers were very fragile, so now I just drop a card in the slot and leave it there for storage of certain kinds of files I want to keep separate. So far, this reader has held up fine, but I'm not in and out of it very often, just leaving one card in place for a long time. [[SCREEN BRIGHTNESS]] - not all of my previous HP x360's have had suitably bright screens, but this one does. NEVER an issue, though I do use it indoors all the time, just in case you might need to test it for outdoor suitability. [[SOUND QUALITY]] - I'm NOT an audiophile, but it does bug me when a laptop comes with crappy sound ... this one doesn't. I've never had any complaints while listening to music or movies, but if you ARE an audiophile, read someone's review who covers that in more detail. [[FINGERPRINT SCANNER]] - Won't always work if your fingertip is a) a little dirty, b) a little wet, or c) slightly out of position or if the pc itself gets too cold, but I'd say 95+% of the time it works great. Sure beats passwords and PINs. LOVE it! [[2nd SCREEN SUPPORT]] - when I'm at my home office desk, I plug a USB-C cable into that port and extend my screen to a 2nd wide screen that sits behind my laptop. This has worked really well with only two warnings: A) not too surprisingly, if you unplug the USB cable from your laptop (disconnect the 2nd screen) while both the PC and 2nd screen are powered up, while it didn't cause any damage, it does seem to confuse Windows and re-connecting the 2nd screen required shutting everything down, reconnecting and then re-starting ... twice. Best practice would always be to power down both PC and screen and then disconnect. This is just a warning that if you don't, things can get flakey. B) Is it plugged in? Hear me out. :) Fans of the IT Crowd know that if you've already tried turning it off and back on again and it still doesn't work, make sure it's plugged in. NOT always as obvious as it seems, especially if you have cats. I once had about an hour long problem getting 2nd screen extension to work. The 2nd screen was powered on, the PC was powered on, the PC was attached to the 2nd screen via a cable from the docking station, which was attached to both PC and screen. Multiple restarts. STILL nothing. Problem? The docking station (with ZERO UX features, thanks DELL) was no longer getting power from the power strip ... seems one of my cats had stepped on the power strip on/off switch, killing the docking station, and thus no connection from the 2nd screen to the laptop. (insert eye roll here). [[RECHARGE VIA USB-C]] - This was my first HP with USB-C ports, so I was a little surprised to find I could recharge or maintain charge on my battery, even with the 2nd screen attached and live, just from the USB-C power feed. I'm not recommending we always get power from USB-C, but it's nice to know on this unit it works well. Never any issues in 8 months. DISLIKES [[NO RIGHT SIDE CTRL KEY]]: Someone at HP decided that when they gave us the fingerprint scanner, it would cost us the 2nd CTRL key on the right side. Well, as someone who uses that key about a gazillion times a day, I REALLY don't like that decision. Thankfully, my use of the right side CTRL is mostly in work apps, and my work Dell has 2 CTRL keys, but there are times when I would use it for my personal app use, and I dearly miss that key not being there. I'm not left handed, so left side CTRL+ key combinations always feel awkward. Poor choice of placement, but not a deal breaker. [[SILVER KEYS]] - My work team was declared fully remote this year, and so I'm working at home about 99 days out of 100, which means working in my bedroom, living room, dining room, or one of our 2 covered decks. Lighting in these places is very different (dimmer) than my 1.21 gigawatt overhead-lit commercial office across town. Even with the keyboard backlight turned on, it's often hard for me to read the keys clearly. I'm a touch-typist, so that's not a HUGE deal if I'm keying in text, but in other situations I find I frequently need to re-angle my head or lean forward to see which key to target. Solution? I took one of those 2-head clip-on reading lights (each light is on a flexible neck - https://a.co/d/bceKj1Q ) and clamped it to a large pencil mug behind my laptop screen, with the two light heads peaking over the top of the screen and shining down on the keyboard. Now I can leave the back-light off and see the keys clearly. Having the ability to compare this key-color/backlight combination to my Dell (with dark keys and backlight) I'd have to say dark keys are the hands down winner, allowing the backlight to provide contrast at levels light-against-silver simply can't create. Time to change, HP. Silver painted keys may look cool, but they don't work (or feel) as good as dark, rubbery surfaced keys. Oh, and judging by my previous 3 HP x360's, that silver paint wears off over time and the letters begin to disappear on the keys I used most often ("A" especially).

Admittedly, this is a bit nitpicky but it did force me to mount it in a less than ideal way. I like to top mount radiators in order to keep the pump (located at CPU) below the radiator. Since it’s at the top, I arrange fans for exhaust and my preference here is to attach fans to case and then radiator to fans (so fans are positioned above radiator). This means air is pulled through the radiator and the air inside the case is exhausted through the top. The CPU will run a few degrees hotter in this configuration than a front-mounted intake but this is a quieter, better for the pump, and isn’t blowing exhaust out the front of the case (the only alternative if it stays top mounted). The problem I ran into is that the long screws have substantially larger screw heads than the more common fan screws. This means that the filter for my case wouldn’t remain flat if I the attached fans to the radiator from the top of the case. It’s an exhaust, so I could remove the filter without too much of an issue but I like the aesthetics of the filter. So instead of a pull configuration, I had to place the fans in a push configuration below the radiator. Performance-wise, there’s no difference but this does make cleaning the radiator more difficult as I’ll have to remove the fans before hitting them with a vacuum or blowing them out with air. All that said, for this price point, it’s a great value for a water cooled AIO. I wouldn’t call it a budget pick since it’s still an AIO. If you want budget, the Hyper 212 air cooled heat sink is by far the best value for a budget build. There’s not a ton of comparison reviews that include this particular model and Coolermaster has several models with similar names (so research is confusing). From what I have seen and experienced, it performs middle of the pack for a water cooled AIO, which is roughly equivalent to a high end air cooled heat sink like a Noctua. If you’re seriously overclocking, however, consider spending 2-3 times the price on a higher end radiator.

After doing some research, I came up with what seemed to be a solid answer to the problem. The three way Infinity 351 with its five speakers was the perfect replacement for my original speaker. With the sound being split among more (and larger) speakers--five as opposed to three in the old speaker--I can keep the volume down and still hear everything with terrific clarity. A word of warning though, this speaker is large and heavy, so check the measurements of the proposed location before you drop the cash and end up needing a new entertainment center.

Let's face it, a dash cam can't be all things to all people and it can never do night vision very well without a lot of infrared lights. That said, the DrivePro 100 is a solid camera for the price. THE PROS: -"Set-it-and-forget-it" recording. When I start the car and the 12-volt outlet comes on so does the camera. -Good quality daytime image. It's like a GoPro. Keep that windshield clean though! -Battery back-up recording. It can record either 10 or 30 seconds after the power is shut off. This is great as some accidents kill your car's engine and the 12 volt power to your camera. This could mean the accident file could be unwatchable but no problem with the DrivePro 100. -It comes with a 16-gig class-10 card which is fine. According to the instructions, you can go up to 64-gig. -Size. This unit and mount pretty much fit under my rear-view mirror but I am sure this varies greatly by car. -Readable instructions. I know that sounds silly but some electronics from China have fortune-cookie like manuals if any at all. -A name-brand company. THE CONS: -Reading license plates. With a 130 degree camera lens, you can't really see plates clearly unless they are head-on and 20 feet away. I am sure with a little skill with a video program on your computer can allow you to blow the image up to see a plate. I was hoping this would be better but hey, it's $100 camera. -Night recording in low light. This does not have IR. I doubt anything short of a military grade IR spot light could help 90% of the dash-cams. A car's break-lights will change the brightness setting. Reading plates at night depend on the amount of light and proximity to your camera. On a well-light street or freeway you still can see well. -Mounting locks. If you leave the camera alone it will stay positioned but if you want to remove and re-mount your camera on a regular basis, you are going to knock it out-of-place a lot. The quick removal from the mount requires a little effort. -Nothing fancy- no wi-fi connect on your phone or GPS or speed read-outs --- I do not have the G-force recording setting on as it seems unnecessary so I can't vouch for it's performance. The free software you can get from the website is not very good. The camera records MPV-4 files so most media programs can play the file. It allows you to grab screen shots to make jpg pictures but that's about it. If you want a simple plug-and-play dash cam for $100, I would recommend it.

I was looking for a small portable radio that would also play music I already own while I am not in my house so I don't have to use up data on my phone. So far, this little radio works great. Sound/Volume: The volume is great. I only go about a quarter to midway on the volume when I am outside working. The sound is crisp – no problems if the radio station is clear or if using your own music. Radio Stations: When I turned on the radio, there were 12 stations that are uploaded based on where I am located and the signal strength. A few I wanted were not pre-loaded, so I just manually entered them. I recommend finding a list of your zip code’s radio stations and having them handy. Micro SD Card/USB Use: I purchased a 64G micro sd card along with the radio. It worked fine, but I decided that I wanted to split up the music by playlists or genre instead of playing everything. I ended up purchasing a set of 10 - 32G USB flash drives with a case. For me, the USB drives ended up being a better price than purchasing that many Micro SD Cards. You can just play them as they are loaded on your card/drive, enter the file number. You can also set it to continually repeat. Formatting of Music/SD Card: This is important – They clearly state that the Micro SD Card or USB flash drive will need to be formatted to FAT32 Format before use. I ended up having to download the format as it was not an option listed on my laptop. It only took a few minutes to find this on the internet and download it for use. Also, most of my music was not in the MP3 format and I ended up downloading an app to do this. Once I found one I liked that was also free, I was able to save the music I wanted in the new format without changing the original files. Overall, I highly recommend this product. It is small enough that I can put it in either my shirt or pants pocket when carrying it to where I am working. It also fits nicely in my purse or glove box when carrying it anywhere else. It works as advertised and I am very happy with my purchase so far.

What a delight, this Sony A7 is a photographers dream. Sony is way out front with this. Small, light, compact, tough as nails, brilliant design. The viewfinder is excellent, and I can't wait to see how they improve it in the coming years. The back LCD is the best and brightest I have ever used making back shooting in the sun a real possibility, perfect for astrophotography. The focus peaking is amazing, manual lenses come to life in real environments. Auto lenses get it done, with speed focus and aperture changes instant. I have nothing to complain about really, as usual the menus are good but not great, a few features I use a lot are hidden, and there could always be more programmable keys. Also the inability to cross use the special features like the in camera exposure stacking and HDR with timer is a little annoying. Would like to see less restrictions but I suppose that is what the will put in the next version with more memory. Write speeds on Long Exposure are about equal to the exposure time so the buffer is limited. Continuous shooting is machine gun speeds, I can rip off 10 shots and be back shooting in 2 seconds. Ok, now back to what is great, everything else. Full frame is amazing, with good glass it is mind boggling. And good glass that is manual focus is all over Amazon from Minlota's Rokkor series of the 70's, Quntaray, tamron, Sigma and Leica. Go look find the cheap adapters and see what you have been missing. Sony makes an adapter for it's alpha lenses and that even switches the focus to phase focusing for better results. I haven't bothered with that yet because the chinese adapters are so cheap and work so well even some of the automatic canon stuff will work on this. This is so much easier to carry than a DSLR, and yet the pictures are fantastic, huge, detailed, color rich. The only limitations are your lenses so start saving up. Rented an OTUS lens..my goodness I never knew such imaging was possible. Added Nikon lenses and now a canon EF from Tamron Vi VC with the Commlite addaptor, I will let you know about that auto lens adapter soon. The Kit lens (14-70mm) is actually a blast and I picked that up used as well, no regrets. There are faster sports cameras, but this thing with OSS can really grab anything short of a bullet so don't listen to the detractors. For the price it can do anything. Go buy a Nikon D4 if you are shooting the Olympics for NBC, otherwise use this and get there with twice the lenses because of the lighter weight. I bought an external Sony charger and Sony batteries, they get over 1000 shots RAW+JPG per charge. Buy Sony folks, don't go cheap on this. I do shut off the camera between shots so I get better life than some. Get a fast big memory card for this. I love the internal charging of the battery, it uses a standard Android car charger plug! I use a 64GB Sony class 14 card and am happy, though a faster card never hurts for long exposure work. CONS: Lack of built in stabilization on the sensor and Sony's slow roll out of lenses are both annoying, that being said this is one of the best cameras ever made, a game changer, and the results with good glass are ASTOUNDING. Pro quality, and I have sold stock photos already. 6000x4000 people, for under $2k. I shoot in Shutter Priority or Aperture priority with manual lenses, the AUTO feature is great with the kit lens but obviously defaults to goofy settings on manual lenses. You need to know how to use an SLR to get the results from this. A remote trigger works with my Android phone and hopefully Sony will build it into the Smartwatch 2 at some point. the buttons and dials all work very well, I think the exposure dial is almost perfect, though my Fuji x series does spoil me. You cannot find a better camera if you are looking for an all weather portable pro shooter. Well the A7R is better in some ways at least for tripod work but not for day to day shooting. Low light capabilities of this sensor are unreal. Video is great but huge files and not quite what the most serious pros are looking for in video frame rates perhaps. Still, it works great with a manual lens and puts out Bluray quality. Great headphones jacks and mic jacks! Ergonomics are spot on. Connectors rock solid. Manual programming hot buttons easy to setup. Getting out of zoom in play mode is annoying, but you will figure it out. Most menu items are well placed. So much love for Sony, such a stellar piece of equipment. Run and buy one, collect good glass. Profit.

This monitor has a lot going for it and at a price that you just can't find elsewhere (especially if you get it during one of the very frequent discounts). Main features are 4K, single-cable USB-C connection, speakers that are actually loud, full featured stand, and USB hub. After reading many of the recent reviews and what people have said, I thought I would respond with my experiences (I'm an IT guy). I've connected it to both a 14" and 16" MacBook Pro M1 via USB-C. The screen is beautiful and side-by-side, I can barely tell the different between the Liquid Retina XDR display of the MacBook and the Samsung. Fiddling with settings on the monitor, I disabled ECO mode and set the screen refresh to high (60Hz). Some report that at high-refresh, the USB ports slow to USB 2.0, but I did not have that experience. On a M1 MacBook Pro, set at 60Hz, the USB ports on the monitor report to be USB 3.0 5Gbps according to System Report on the Mac. On a Windows PC (XPS 13) via USB-C, 60Hz does slow down the USB ports to USB 2.0. Not sure why Mac and Windows work differently in this respect. Using USB-C, both MacBook's are charged via the monitor just fine. One issue I did have on both MacBook's is the monitor keeps waking up every few minutes once the MacBook and screen go to sleep. I've had to revert to either unplugging the monitor or manually powering it off via the button under the monitor. Speaking of which, Samsung's multi-button system UNDER the monitor is annoying but you get used to it. Speakers. Best speakers I've heard in a monitor. Most are so low volume, they are worthless, but not this Samsung. Nice and loud. One issue is I cannot control the volume of the monitor speaker from my Mac. The volume control is greyed out. Sort of a bummer I suppose. As others have said, disable ECO mode if on out-of-the-box to increase brightness. Colors, as I said earlier, are fantastic. Overall, I'm very pleased with this monitor, especially at a <$300 price (if you can grab a couple when on sale, do it!). You won't find all these features in a monitor at this price anywhere else.

I might have a higher opinion of the Belkin Conserve Smart AV F7C007q Energy-Saving Power Strip if I hadn't purchased it with a Kill A Watt power meter. And your particular entertainment system may see greater energy benefits than mine. The Belkin Conserve Smart F7C007q works as described. One outlet serves as the "master" outlet to control five accessory outlets. The master is monitored and when it's power draw goes up, the F7C007q applies power to five additional outlets. When the master power draw goes down, the accessory outlets are shut off. And there are two outlets that are are "on" all the time independent of the master. The point is to prevent appliances from consuming so called phantom power. That is, they're not fully off when they're "off". And it does work. When I turn the TV on, the DVD player and Wii power on. When the TV is turned off, the DVD player and Wii are completely powered off. Since I ordered them together I decided to use the Kill A Watt to see just how much the F7C007q would benefit my energy bill. The Kill A Watt showed my entertainment system consumed 13 Watts of phantom power, that is with everything turned off. With the F7C007q, the system's phantom power draw only dropped two Watts. This was my disappointment: the Belkin F7C007q works, but the resulting power saved wasn't significant. Forget about about the Conserve Smart power strip actually paying for itself on my energy bill. I could save more power, carbon emissions, etc, by changing a few incandescent bulbs to LEDs. Had I not measured the before and after with a Kill A Watt power meter, I probably would have felt it was making a big difference. So maybe it's a better green placebo than actual energy saver.

I was very excited to get this monitor, as I was coming from a pretty significant upgrade of 2x 24 in 1920x1200 monitors. Overall, the monitor is high quality, a little too gamer-ish in style for me, but I heard great reviews about the quality of it and decided to make the splurge. Unfortunately, due to some issues which I discuss below, one of which in particular being a major issue for me, I decided to return the monitor. Construction - Overall, the monitor appears well constructed and solid. The stand is definite a bit big, although I was prepared for the monitor taking up as much space as it did. Coming from 24 in monitors, this thing is definitely huge; it certainly took some getting used to the size, but it would be hard to go back to smaller monitors after this. Image Quality - Image quality is great. Images and text are clear. I was a little concerned about the curve at first, but I think for a monitor this size it is required. The corners of the screen were clear. However, there is a significant amount of backlight bleed on mine, and I am someone that has never really complained much about backlight bleeding. But, sitting here typing this up my bottom black taskbar has areas that are brighter due to the backlight bleed (and I’m in a well-lit room). Definitely disappointing, although I’m not sure if my panel is unusually bad for the monitor. Gaming - I’m sure most people looking at this monitor are considering at least some gaming. I didn’t game too much on this, as I don’t play nearly as much as I did in my youth, but the little I did do was fantastic. It definitely feels very immersive given the significant width of the monitor. Note, however, that I only ever tried playing DOTA 2 on this monitor. I never got around to playing another game (as I said, I don’t game as much anymore). However, one thing I noticed I had issues with when gaming was that I started getting a headache / nausea. I didn’t think it was related to the monitor at first, but I stumbled across many people online reporting this from ultrawide monitors. I did see one person say that issue went away after a while, but I only played games two or three times with the monitor, so I didn’t experiment enough to see if that would happen with me. Productivity - This is one area I was looking for major improvements on. I work from home as a programmer, so I wanted to explore how an ultrawide monitor would work for that. I found that I really did enjoy having the flexibility of one large canvas that I could divide how I liked depending on what I was doing. If I was working in an IDE that required significant screen space, such as Visual Studio, I would have that take up close to 2/3rds of the screen, while having the remaining 1/3 reserved for a web browser or other application. With web browsing, I typically just split the screen in half with a browser on either side. Overall, I felt this was slightly nicer in most ways than two individual monitors, but maybe not enough to say you should definitely go with an ultrawide monitor. However, there is a bit of ease lost by not being able to just maximize your window. Which option is best for you ultimately comes down to your own workflow and personal preferences. I eventually had one of my old monitors on the side as a second monitor to help with multitasking, although I imagine many people’s desks would not have the space to support that setup. Technical - While there aren’t too many input options, HDMI and DP were all I really needed. I had this monitor connected to a Windows 10 PC and a 2015 MacBook Pro. Switching between systems was relatively pain-free. When I wanted to switch from PC to Mac, I’d put the PC to sleep and could hit any menu button to bring up the input selection, hit up or down to change to the other input, press select and quickly be working on the Mac (it is slightly more difficult to change inputs when the first computer stayed on or awake, but only by a few key presses). I also enjoyed the USB ports in the monitor, as I could connect those to my PC so that I could plug the USB dongle for my wireless keyboard and mouse into the monitor when I was using the PC and quickly switch the dongle over to the Apple laptop when I was switching computers. While not a huge deal, it was a nice quality of life improvement compared to having to bend over and reach for my PC on the floor underneath my desk. There was, however, one major issue; the big deal breaker to me I alluded to at the beginning of this review. For some reason, the monitor sometimes refuses to wake up. My other monitor will wake up, but this one will not. Restarting the computer, turning the monitor off and on, pressing menu buttons, etc. all do nothing. The ONLY way I’ve found to awaken the monitor is to unplug it and plug it back in. This is extremely frustrating, especially when it can happen multiple times each day. To clarify, this doesn’t happen every time the monitor goes into sleep mode due to inactivity, but it happens often enough that it is frustrating to deal with. It is very inconvenient to have to unplug the monitor to get it working again. Overall - A high-quality monitor, with one major caveat; a serious defect with the monitor not waking from sleep. Unfortunately, this issue is annoying enough that I have trouble recommending this monitor to anyone. I’ve since read this happening to other people, although I’m unclear if this issue occurs with all of these monitors or just a select, unlucky few. While I would’ve loved to have had this work for me, this means I am returning it as there is just no way I can put up with something like that for years and years, especially given the price.

For what this monitor is and how I intended to use it most of the time, I am/was very happy with it. I must stress that its applicability to me was solely for a particular purpose. I was mainly wanting to use it connected to my mid-2014 Macbook Pro Retina 13" as an external monitor (running in "Retina" HiDPI mode... so 4K which is actually 1920x1080 in terms of real-estate, but at "high pixel density"). My use case was mainly for software development work (which, of course, mostly involves reading web pages and typing code in various IDE's) and the occasional graphical edit. At that, 24" is actually ideal for me at work, because I don't like moving my head as much as 27"+ monitors require me to do and though I'd prefer 16:10, 16:9 isn't objectionable to me. I really wanted something that was as sharp and clear as "Retina" mode on the Mac's built in display, because I find the way Apple anti-aliases text on most external monitors, even with the "EDID overrides" (to make it understand they're not TV's) severely bothers my eyes. This is true of every monitor I've tried previously with this Mac, including two 2560x1440 monitors I've tried. It's better at that high res, but still a little whacky. Hooked up to this thing, it's sharp, clear, and "liquid" as can be, exactly what I was looking for. I can't speak to color "accuracy", per se, but the colors, to my eyes, are very pleasing. The screen is rather warm, which I happen to like (my screen has a native whitepoint which appears to be closer to 5700K), and I love it. Even side by side next to my Dell 2515 and my wife's 2414 (all three are IPS) this guy's colors make me happier. In terms of refresh rate: I had some quirks... when I first plugged it in, monitor at 4K was at 30hz, much as other reviews have stated. However, at some point, after playing with SwitchResX, The option showed up (in full-on HiDPI "Retina"mode) for me to switch to 50Hz in the selection box. I clicked it, and the machine actually locked up. I had to power cycle it, but when it came back, both the Mac and the monitor itself stated they were running at 50Hz and you could tell while dragging windows across the screen, scrolling, moving the mouse, etc. I have to say, at 30Hz, it kinda sucked. The little animations looked garbage and you don't realize how many there are and how much screen movement is part of the experience until it sucks that bad. Way better at 50Hz. I honestly don't remember how I did it, but now it won't let me go back to 30Hz, and I've fine with that. (For what it's worth to other wondering, I was able to drive this at full 4K at 50Hz while driving my 2515 at full 2560x1440 at 60Hz and the internal display without any problem whatsoever... so if you have a mid-2014 or newer 13" or higher macbook retina, you can do it too!). So why 4 star? Well, like I said, outside of my intended use it didn't hold up as well. I actually wanted to use it on my PC, too, and try to play games at lower resolutions (like 2560x1440). This screen isn't up to gaming. At any resolution, the motion blur is big time. And at lower, non-native resolutions, the interpolation fuzziness seems worse than my Dell 2515 dropping down to, say, 1920x1080. I mean, that's sort of to be expected I guess, but this thing isn't up to any sort of fast moving image display. It just isn't responsive. Oh, and the monitor itself is not near as physically nice looking as my 2515 or my wife's 2414. Looks like a relic from the first days of flat panels. I ended up returning it because I need something more versatile, but, I thought hard about keeping it for use just at work. I think I'll wait until they come down in price though.

For giggles I removed the keyboard from my bluetooth devices and again followed the instructions to connect on the first channel, only to see the "d" key repeating itself again. Dropped the bluetooth connection to the keyboard, re-setup on channel 2 and it's working like a champ. Not sure what's wrong with the first channel, it's definitely kaput. That doesn't matter to me, I'm only connecting this keyboard to one device so that's a non-issue for me and not something I'd return the keyboard for. My last comments are specific to the action in the keys and the feedback they provide while typing. I typically clock anywhere from 95 - 110 wpm on every keyboard I own, whether it's an old IBM CLICKY keyboard (my favorite) an old Logitech K570 and my beloved Apple Wireless bluetooth keyboard. I'm used to the response action on all these keyboards and can switch pretty seamlessly. On this keyboard the action is lacking. The response from the time I press a key to it reverting back to it's resting state seems lacking to me. I expected the action to be similar to that of my Apple wireless bluetooth keyboard. It's not. If that's what you're expecting with this keyboard, do not buy it. The last thing I want to say is that the lack of keyboard "action" for me inhibits how quickly I can type on it. I've found my fingers "tripping over themselves" trying to type on it. That means more mistakes and backing up to correct. As I typed this review, I switched back and forth between my Apple bluetooth keyboard and this one. The difference in the keyboard action and my ability to type so much faster on my Apple keyboard vs. this one is absolutely noticeable. I'm going to give myself a little more time to get used to this keyboard and if that doesn't do the trick then I'll be sending it back. The "dealbreaker" for me isn't the bad bluetooth channel it has, it's the keyboard action and not being able to go as fast as I can on my Apple bluetooth keyboard which has a similar layout and key spacing (I measured the gaps between the keys on both keyboards, they're identical.) I never give one star reviews, but this router sucks at everything it does. I had the Nighthawk x6 before this, which is now 1/3 the price of this. Let's compare! Range: with the Nighthawk x6, I was able to get a connection outside my house. With the Nighthawk x10, I need an extender. Winner - Nighthawk x6 USB: the Nighthawk x6 has 1 USB 3.0 and 1 USB 2.0 port. the Nighthawk x10 has 2 USB 3.0. The Nighthawk x6 could not detect my 4HDD case thing. The Nighthawk x10 perfectly detects all 4HDDs. File sharing works perfectly on both. Winner - Nighthawk x10. Plex: the Nighthawk x6 does not have a Plex server. The Nighthawk x10 has a Plex server. While using Plex with HDDs connected to USB3.0 ports, the movies would constantly buffer making it unwatchable. Plex would frequently screw up the audio as well. Video glitches were also common. I noticed it down converted my 1080p videos to DVD quality. Winner - Nighthawk x6. Why? I can't get the hours of my life back I wasted trying to get Plex on this to work right. Wifi 802.11ac: the Nighthawk x10 supports a new wifi standard above 802.11ac called 802.11ad. And it shouldn't. It's terrible. 802.11ad in theory can transmit data at fiber speeds over wireless. Why does it suck? The range is 30 feet and there are no 802.11AD devices and there never will be. Winner: Nighthawk x6 because keeping it simple is better than adding a bad feature. Bands: Nighthawk x10 has a band for 2.4GHz and a band for 5GHz. Nighthawk x6 has a band for 2.4GHz and 2 for 5Ghz. This means the Nighthawk x6 essentially has twice the 802.11AC speeds and can support twice the number of devices. This also means far less collisions between wifi devices. Since wifi is the WHOLE POINT of this device is wifi speed/range/and number of devices, this is objective worse than a router 1/3 the cost. Conclusion: this router is terrible at the one thing it's supposed to do.

Update: The seller got in touch with me. They have been engaged and appear to be sincerely trying to help. I give them very high marks on their customer service. I was able to demonstrate the sync issue, repeatedly. They're reporting back to the manufacturer. They've asked me to increase my rating here, and I wish I could. But, the sync issue really is a big deal. It's a flaw in the SQ12 product coming from all the sellers here on Amazon. What I've found is that the sync is fine on the first clip. But every subsequent clip, it's off by a random amount, from 5-30 frames. That's up to a full second, and that's enough to make a difference. That's three or four words in conversation, which is very annoying to watch. If you're editing these clips, it's possible to shift the audio to sync them back up. But, it's an added step. ---------- I have an oddball application for this camera. I am using it as a hockey helmetcam. This camera does, indeed, have a wide angle lens. Many of the listings for cheap Chinese cameras get this wrong. I have a face cage that has a large enough gap that the camera fits between the bars. I cut a piece of sheet metal to mount on the cage screws and bend it under the brow of my helmet and in front of my forehead. I glued velcro (Actually, EZ Pass mounting strips) to the mount and the camera. The size and location works well. I mostly don't notice is during my games. One major disadvantage of this camera is that it only has a 60 minute record time. My games are routinely about 75 minutes. Longer if there's overtime and a shootout. Including extra time from when I fire it up in the locker room, and I really need at least 120 minutes, to include a little leeway. Given my the size constraint I'm working with, I could live with the camera being 1/4" longer front-to-back in order to increase the size of the battery. While the camera can record while plugged in to power, I have no good place to hold the battery. Also, I've had issues with past cameras with the cable coming out of the side of the camera and interfering with the face cage. There's not enough clearance. That interference results in the cable disconnecting and connecting in quick succession when the helmet gets bumped. Often, that will cause the camera to just give up and stop recording. I ended up solving this by buying two cameras. I have to try to remember to swap them during the second intermission. They're inexpensive enough that it's not too painful. But, sometimes I get distracted, so it's easy for me to forget, and then I'll lose the end of the game. Another frustration with all of these cheap Chinese cameras is the button incantations necessary in order to start recording. I've worked with more than a half dozen of these cheap Chinese cameras, so I understand the general concept. But, they are just incredibly cumbersome. The timing on the button pushes makes it too easy to get the camera into the wrong mode, and it's difficult to tell. The light goes out while recording. So, I can't always tell if it has started recording, or if it has locked up for some reason. Or, if I turned it off by accident. (Already happened in my second game.) One not-so-cheap camera that appears to use the same underlying technology is the UHWK helmet camera. I have one, and it's nice. The problem is that most refs won't let me wear it on the outside of my helmet. And, it's a little too large to fit inside my cage. But, one thing they did on that camera is they have a physical switch and a record light to make it obvious that it's recording. I greatly prefer that. I wish these other cameras would use a switch to turn on power. And another switch to start recording, with an LED indicator. And then use the pushbuttons for setting the mode. And now to the biggest problem with this camera, and it's a huge one. The sound is not properly synced with the video. One of the cameras is about 1/4 second off and the other is nearly 1/2 second off. This is a problem I last saw about three years ago. I think that the delta appears to be consistent for the duration of the recording. So, it can be corrected in the editing software. But, it's still annoying. This should be a solved problem. I have tested the sync with multiple players and multiple editing programs on Windows 10, and on multiple computers. The sync issue is present with all of them. So, two stars off for the sync problem. One star off for the cumbersome controls. Half star off for the battery life. Half star back on for the size. Another half star back on for the price. And then I'm feeling generous, tonight, so I'll round up.

Here is where I dropped the ball. I assumed, yes I said assumed, that this router was like every other router I have ever owned. Default settings out of the box and leave it up to the user to tweak things here or there. Not. The. Case. This router is clearly made for the novice end user. The user interface is bubbly and limited. There is no real advanced features and the back breaker for me is the Guest Network. I will never allow any device on the main network that I do not personally know. That includes Roku, Alexa, Samsung TV or any other smart device. Way to many security holes. Even our phones are on the Guest network. There is NO NEED ever to allow access to any computer by an unknown source. EVER! That being said, the guest network for this router is Unsecured. Yes, Unsecured! Not a happy situation for me as I'd like to keep my private home, private but not a deal breaker so long as I use a strong password, right? Wrong. The guest network is web-based, meaning anyone who wants to use it must go to a web-page and sign in. Not good for a smart TV or a Roku or Alexa or any other non-web based device. Crud. This device is not for the advanced user. If you require any deviations from what Linksys has enabled, your out of luck. There is no Expert Mode here. This fancy, expensive router is now an Access-Point (Bridge Mode). And my old Netgear is still running the show until I can get a new one to replace it. Over all this device does as promised. The speed is near the advertised limits. The range is also as advertised. The performance for me is superb. There is no downside except what I mentioned in my review above. If you are Ok with limited security feature (Please do not be!) then this is a good buy. If you prefer to be as secure as you possible can, then no, this is NOT the router for you. -Ron

The Clearstream 4 antenna [[ASIN:B008PBTPOI ClearStream 4 Indoor/Outdoor HDTV Antenna with Mount - 70 Mile Range]] has served me well for a couple of years providing quality TV reception. Therefore the Clearstream was on top of my list for installation in a new location. However the number of channels with quality signal were scarce. I therefore tried the 1Byone amplified antenna. It performed better and gave me 40% more channels and higher signal quality on the channels already received by the Clearstream. We are surrounded by trees and 1Byone behaved more like a rifle shooting through the trees. FOR THIS INSTALLATION THE 1BYONE PERFORMED BEST. I consider both antennas of good quality, however the Clearstream seems over engineered and heavier than the 1Byone. Both antennas were installed in the attic thus mounting hardware did not have to stand up to wind. However for installation outdoors I would prefer the hardware that came with 1Byone over the Clearstream also considering that the wind pressure on the Clearstream will be higher due to larger windswept area.. The 1Oneby one is light weight and easy to hold on a broom handle while checking signal strength in different directions. The antenna construction appear strong due to its central core made of plastic. It is also much easier to assemble than the Clearstream. The Clearstream is very noticeable when mounted indoors whereas the 1Byone is smaller and less noticeable. The short coax cable that comes with the 1Byone is very skimpy, but you will want to replace it with a longer higher quality cable anyway. Normally you want to mount the amplifier as close to the antenna as possible, but not to worry, the 1Byone has the amplifier integrated in the antenna. The power supply (injecting the power into the coax cable) can be mounted next to the TV and will power the amplifier integrated into the antenna plastic housing. This location of the amplifier is optimal compared to an ad-on amplifier. Signal Quality Signal quality is affected by noise sources and degradation if it has to go through materials, especially if they they contain water, such as trees and leaves and rain. In my experience, on a rainy day I must have 50% or higher signal quality as reported my TV to consistently maintain a quality picture without pix-elation. Anyway I am glad that I tried the 1Byone antenna. ... better result for less money.

I was excited to finally see a case that's made for the Surface Pro. Not to mention one that supports both keyboards. I will make it simple and break it down for you. PROS * Amazing for the price. I pre-ordered it for $13.95 and free shipping a few weeks ago and just got it today. I think the release date got delayed. But the price may go up soon now that it's out and the good feedback rolls in. * Nicely made and looks good for the material that is used. It stays closed with a nice thin magnet inside the top flap and backside of the case so it lightly connects and just feels "executive like". Reminds me of the kickstand of the Surface in a way. Looks really nice when closed and folded up and adds a professional look to your Surface. The top flap actually covers the crease that is created when you use the case as a stand which was a really nice touch. It keeps the case looking clean and sleek. * Adds stability for the keyboard especially if you are using the touch cover. Using the touch cover on my lap usually resulted in missed keys or it feeling like it's bending while I'm typing on it. With this case it gives you a harder more stable surface underneath the keyboard. I am typing on the touch cover right now and it feels great. It also fits the Type cover as well and makes that a better experience too. * The case can hold the Surface up and a few different angles with or without the kickstand. I've been messing with it and it seems to improve viewing when you have it on your lap. The "starting point" can be farther forward than what the kickstand offers which is great for your lap. So far I've also been able to get multiple additional viewing angles since the Velcro can be adjusted by tiny bits beyond the kickstand angle to make it angled back more. * The case doesn't block any of the ports and you have easy access to all of them. You can even still mount the stylus pen on the side like usual. The cutouts on the front area around the screen leave enough room to do swipe gestures off the sides and top of the screen, as well as the windows button. No issues there. CONS * It's a little tedious getting the Surface into the standing position. You have to sort of keep pushing the Surface into the holster while you are wrapping the Velcro strips around the bottom and trying to get them in the right position. It is kind of annoying because the Surface keeps wanting to slip out of the holster. This feels like a design flaw but if you are patient I'm sure it'll become second nature. * There is a slight annoyance if you have two keyboard covers or just want to remove or attach one. The magnet connection is underneath the Velcro area so you have to lift up on the tablet and pull it out from underneath. All while making sure the Velcro doesn't detach and make the Surface fall back flat. * I wish it came with a slot to keep the stylus pen when not in use. That way while you're charging you can keep it in a tiny loop hole or something at least. It would of been a perfect case AND solved one of the few annoyances with the Surface as a bonus. They would of had 6 stars if possible if they included that. But I'm sure other case makers or maybe Minisuit themselves will come up with a new one that has that feature. All in all I recommend this case as it's the only case actually made for the Surface Pro WITH keyboard specifically. It looks nice, protects your device, and the issues are forgivable for the current price tag. You don't have much to lose. I am VERY picky when it comes to cases to the point where I avoid using them if possible. So if I say this is a nice case then I really mean it. Hope you find this review useful!

I've only had this for a day, but I'm very happy with it. I use it with a MacBook Pro 15" retina, so I have full Thunderbolt 2 connectivity. Contrary to some others' experience, I had no trouble getting the computer to recognize it at full 3440x1440, 60 Hz. Again contrary to others, I find no disturbing backlight bleed in the corners: no doubt due to the fact that I don't use it with black backgrounds, but when I did display something with black on the sides, I didn't notice anything in the corners. It's wonderful to have so much screen real estate without the discontinuity between two monitors. I use this for "office" tasks: the way I write, it's ideal to have four full windows open side by side, and with this display I can do that while leaving Mail open on the MBP's screen at the same time. The curve is hardly noticeable, but probably contributes to the impression of a uniform big screen. On the mildly negative side, this isn't of course 4K resolution, and the difference between what I see on the big screen and the resolution on the retina MBP screen next to it is noticeable. If I were doing video editing or the like, this might be a problem, but for me this really isn't an issue: the screen is not so big that the pixelation is noticeable. The experience is at least as good as on the 30" cinema display in my office, and I'm quite happy with it. It would be nice to have height adjustment. Not sure why that isn't here, given that the flat screen equivalent has it. The plastic cover over the cables on the back is no problem for me, since I don't plan on changing the cable connections often. The one thing that might produce problems in the long run would be if I had to get to the on/off switch often. So far, it looks like the display sleeps nicely when the computer does, so no apparent problem there. Overall, this seems to be the display I've been looking for. I do wish Apple had produced a 4K TB display, but even if they had, it probably wouldn't have met my needs (screen real estate) as well as this one does. Update, 10 December: I have downgraded my review from 5 to 2 stars now, not because of the monitor itself but because of Quality Control issues. When the monitor arrived and I set it up, I was delighted with all that screen real estate, and the initial experience was very positive. My MacBook Pro-Retina recognized the monitor and its ideal resolution (3440x1440, 60 Hz) immediately, and only a tiny bit of calibration seemed necessary. On the second day of use, though, I began to notice display artifacts on the right half of the screen: a pattern of closely spaced vertical lines that appeared in solid color areas such as window titles, solid areas in the background, etc. Just how much and where varies with which windows are in focus, and maybe other things. The effect is subtle, but once you notice it, obvious and wrong. I contacted Amazon and they arranged to ship a replacement right away. Great, I thought: wonderful customer service (and I have no reason to retract that). But when the replacement arrived, it was DOA: wouldn't do anything when powered on. So now I had two of them to return, and since the second one had come in a box that was too big and that therefore got destroyed in shipment, I only had one carton in which to return them. I sent the DOA one back, and I'm still hoping to find appropriate material to send back the other defective one. But now Amazon is out of stock, so they can't send me another one (they have arranged a refund), and the only source they list wants a significant premium over list price and doesn't offer Prime shipping. Phooey. I really like this monitor, in theory, but it does not look as if LG is doing a great job producing it. Edit this post | Permalink

I live in an apartment and wanted to limit the sound while watching movies at night so as not to annoy neighbors. I'm not picky. I have a cheap computer monitor with HDMI and some cheap computer desktop speakers. I'm an audio engineer so I was about to spend 100 bucks on a normal rack compressor. Why not? But this thing, as cheap as it was, seemed worth the risk. I'm not picky, right? Well, this thing is in a dump somewhere now and I have an Alesis rack compressor in front of my speakers. :) The problem with compressing audio for video is that low frequencies like explosions, booms or a kick drum in the background music, aren't as perceivable to our ears but are extremely loud in actual energy. They trigger this thing to reduce the volume drastically right when you're trying to hear the dialogue. Audio gear nerds: There are no adjustments - not even on the circuit board. The compression threshold is set too low. There is no makeup gain so you must turn your speakers up to ridiculous - hence the hiss some mentioned. The attack rate is ketchup slow and the release rate is molasses slow. It's less "pump and breath," more "pummel and break wind." If you're gonna to do this then you need fast attack, fast release and adjustable threshold. A cheap Alesis or Behringer rack compressor does fine. Ok, enough nerd talk. Don't. Just don't. Thank me later.

If you are having problems opening the back cover of the remote to put in the batteries, here's how to open the back cover. Place the remote between your palms as if you were praying. The bottom half of the remote should be on top facing the ceiling (so the Amazon logo is upside down). The part without any buttons should be in the palm, so really you have the remote only half way in your hand. Now slide your hands in opposite directions forcing half the remote to move down and the other half to move up. That should dislodge the back cover enough for you to open it and place the batteries. Hope this helps.

I purchased this to carry when traveling, primarily to use with my Fujifilm X-T2, which is a light camera. Out of curiosity, I tried it with my full-frame Nikon with a 28-300mm zoom attached, which highlighted a design flaw in the tripod. The legs to not have a positive lock to hold them in any other position than the lowest height (50mm). With the tripod in a higher position (e.g. it's advertised max height of 135mm), the legs collapsed under the weight of the heavier full frame camera with a larger lens. It will support the weight when the tripod is in it's lowest position. To assure stability and the safety of my camera, I don't expect that I will be using this tripod at anything other than it's lowest position. In this low position the legs are spread to their widest which requires a surface of about 12" (30cm) in diameter. I would have given them a 5 star rating if they had included a positive lock to hold the tripod legs firmly at their highest position. I don't regret the purchase, but other buyers should consider the weight of their camera and lens when deciding whether this tripod will be of use to them.

Last month I had the toughest time deciding if I should save $ to buy a new Archos MP3 Jukebox Recorder or bite the bullet and get the iRiver iHP140. I hardly ever encountered playback problems. It was usually very reliable for downloading music from the internet. The biggest issue I had with the Archos MP3 Jukebox Recorder was the display. If I recorded music using the Line Input, eventually the display would wig out. It wasn't that big of a deal. If I restarted the unit, the display would return back to normal. All the minor problems I had with the Archos MP3 Jukebox Recorder have yet to happen with the iHP140. The iHP140 performance has been flawless. Not only did the iHP140 play back the entire wave mix nonstop, the battery indicator still showed that the battery was fully charged afterwards!! The sound quality is excellent. When I feel like cranking up the volume I set it at 30 (75% of maximum). That's more than enough volume for me. The preset EQ's sound descent. I only wished that the iHP140 had AGC or normalization for playback in noisy environments. That's a big issue for me, especially when listening to music in the car. That's why I rated the iHP140 four stars instead of five. The reception on the FM radio works better than I thought it would. I wasn't expecting much. I've listened to all the file formats the iHP140 supports. I have to say ogg files sound the best compared to mp3 and wma files. I hope this review has been helpful.
