In a [coco]nutshell: PROS: —> >> Well made, premium materials, splash resistant (untested!) and stylish! —>>> Great sound quality, especially for a Bluetooth device. On par with— and similar sound signature to— my Klipsch Image One wired headphones (about $80 here on Amazon 2 years or so ago). Decent bass, but won't beat Beats in this arena. Clear non-strident trebles and nice vocal midrange. I would add that this sound profile feels easy to listen to for long periods of time. —>>> *Strong* noise isolation, but no active cancelling —>>> Great range, likely upwards of 100' or so clear line of sight! This is *much* farther than my small Plantronics in-ear BT headset (both tested with an iPhone 6plus), which maybe gets 30'. —>>> Light weight and comfortable; not too much tension on my medium-sized noggin. Nicely adjustable with flatly folding earpieces. Comfy ear pads; they feel memory-foamish. —>>> *Really* good ergonomics in terms of button layout and intuitive ease of use. The outer ring of the left cup rotates slightly clockwise and anti-CW for volume up and down with about 6 steps up and down from neutral. The center button on the left (easily identified via a finger-sized depression) pauses and restarts tracks. Anterior and posterior buttons on the left cup serve as track control/FF/REW. They're all well separated with a nice positive 'clickiness'. The right cup has a single center button for placing and ending calls or for starting Siri. You can't miss it. On the rear of the right cup is a slider that clicks once up for power on/off and then when on if you slide it up and hold its spring loaded position, it enters pairing mode. Let go and it returns to the 'on' position. Pairing's quick with up to two devices. There's also a mute button on the bottom of the left cup. —>>> It charges via micro USB (included) with no rubber cover dongle to get lost. Supposedly it lasts 18 hours, but I tend to charge it when not in use...I believe the figure though. When you turn it on, it chimes with a pleasant C-chord and tells you the battery level in High/Medium and I presume 'Low' increments, but I've never been able to drain it to that point! This is a step back from my small Plantronics in-ear BT earpiece (M90) which tells you battery life in 1 hour increments up to it's 11 hour max. It also tells you which phones/devices are connected (calling them 'Phone 1' or 'Phone 2' no matter what type of device you've paired). —>>> Remove them and a sensor (hence, the Backbeat SENSE moniker) pauses your music. Put them back on and it usually starts up where I left off but on occasion requires a re-press of the 'play' button on the left cup. I get the feeling the 'sensor' is in the elasticized tension band on the headpiece. —> >> If the battery's dead, you can plug in the included 3.5 mm standard audio cable and it runs just fine. CONS: —>>> The biggest negative for me—and this is a BIGGIE—is *huge* (insert Trump inflection) noise transmission. When the cups are well placed over your ears with the music off, you immediately sense strong external noise isolation—surprising given the 'on-ear', not 'over-ear' nature of the beast. This usual plus markedly heightens clear transmission of any slight touch or brush against the earcups or the head band and I'm talking *loud* here! Nearly *any* head motion, even normal straight-line walking, and you get copious transmitted rubbing/low-frequency squeeking sounds the worst of it arising from motion induced slight bouncing/rubbing of the elasticized cushiony head band. The metallic part of the head band then transmits—nay *amplifies*—this noise better than a tuning fork! It's the Ta-Majal of headbands where a 'whisper' on one side of the building's audible a hundred feet away. This is highly annoying to me and *much* different from my Sennheiser or Klipsch wired phones. I find these characteristics *intolerable* when the phones are paused, acceptable with normal volume '' music '' playing and moderately *distracting* when listening to Books on Tape/Audible where dead-air abounds. OTOH, if you're relatively motionless then all is great! —>>> The included case is as uber-awkward as the phrase 'uber-awkward. It's soft with weird angles on the smallish separate zippered pouches and'll end up being one of those things I'll just never use. —>>> Cost? $200 for the 'splash resistant' model and $190 for the vanilla. There are way cheaper phones out there with decent sound and comparable battery life, but none I've found with such intuitive switch-gear and excellent range. SUMMARY: —>>> Primo materials, sound, battery life, styling, weight, range and switch-gear ergonomics. Pricey with major touch/brush/bounce sound transmission issues with even slight head motion. ~ UPDATE: Returned them for the noise issues above.

This is a very pricey tablet, to be sure. But it delivers on the qualities it promises. The screen is bright and clear, the battery keeps going and going, and the housing is exceptionally rugged. This tablet is aimed at drone fliers and that's why I bought it. And I'm glad I did. It's far easier to view this screen than the excellent but not nearly as bright display on the Pixel 4 XL that I'd been using to fly my drone. Both the the size and brightness of the Tripltek make it far easier to see what my drone camera is viewing, even on a sunny day. And although the tablet is fairly hefty, I don't find it awkward when mounted on the drone controller. It all comes together pretty well. One hitch is that you may have connectivity issues if you don't use the purpose-built Tripltek cable, available from them at extra cost. Using a suitable short Amazon USB C to USB C cable, I found that I couldn't launch a DJI drone using the takeoff button. Then, the screen went completely blank (i.e., no signal from drone camera). Reinstalling the DJI Fly software made no difference. Everyting worked when I swapped the Pixel phone in for the Tripltek. So I knew it wasn't the controller or drone itself at fault. Using the very short DJI cable (too short to mount theTripltek to the controller but able to connect temporarily with controller and tablet just sitting on my lap), everything worked fine. So, I isolated the problem to the cable. Other USB C cables of various lengths that I tried failed to work. Looking online, I saw that others had contacted DJI and been told the cable was at fault. So, I bit the bullet and spent $9 for the short cable from Tripltek. After that, everything worked perfectly. But this was an annoying extra step. At the price Tripltek is charging for the tablet and its marketing aimed at drone users, they should just throw in that cable or make it available for a nominal cost to those who request it. Had they done so, they would have gotten a fifth star from me. The tablet itself is great. But it's very expensive. Having an additional hidden cost leaves a bit of a bad taste. UPDATE: Tripltek reached out to me and refunded the cost of the cable and shipping. More importantly, they said that they will soon include the cable with the tablet. This kind of responsiveness to customers is very admirable. I said that had the cable been included, I would have given the tablet 5 stars, so I'm adding that fifth star now. I'm also very pleased that Tripltek will proactively resolve the cable issue for future purchasers. It speaks to their commitment to customer satisfaction and support.

First off the device looks fairly elegant and modern and it works with some USB based devices. That's about the only positive thing going for this. The device, is bulky, so I assumed it is intended to be primarily used near a docking station or desktop. The issue with that is that the provided USB cable is ridiculously small at around 1/3 - 1/4 the length of the power cable. So it becomes difficult to get the thing on your desk even when your desktop ports are <6 ft away. Which brings up another point, with such a bulky power cable setup I would expect all the ports to provide the USB 3.0 spec'd 900mA (0.9A). This is clearly not the case as external hard drives that need the full 900 mA simply start spinning up and shutdown (rinse and repeat until your HDD dies), this causes any device that requires USB3 or USB2 powers specs to not get power or charge (so 7 ports wasted). The 3 "POWERIQ" ports provide essentially ordinary USB3.0 power so you get the same rate of charging on your phone as if you plugged it directly into the computer, but unlike plugging it directly into the computer, you can't access your phone while plugged into the charging ports. I spent the month testing this and USB sticks and external hard drives with their own power seem to work just fine, but the rest is a real disappointment.

We bought this jukebox for our upstairs bonus/billiards room. The jukebox is great fun to use and really adds the right flavor to the room. It adds the right amount of size/height to the jukebox and really makes it stand out. The jukebox seems much smaller without it. NOTE: if you order the base then be very, very careful during the unboxing. The drawer is not secured in the base (or the box) and it slid right out while we were unboxing the base, crashed into our hardwood floor and took appreciable damage to the top left corner. Good news - I contacted Arkrocket, told them what happened and we already have the replacement drawer that they shipped to us at no cost! They provided excellent customer service. As for the jukebox, the only way to get better is to spend a whole lot more money. Overall I'm quite happy with this purchase and pleased with how it accentuates our adult play space. NOTE: This jukebox has an SD memory card slot and a USB port. However, it cannot use any memory card greater than 32 GB. And the SD card and/or USB thumb drive must be formatted to the FAT32 standard. FAT32 is just a method for storing data on SD cards, USB drives, hard drives, etc. So, if you get an ERR when trying to play from either then check and make sure you're not exceeding 32GB and that the memory card is formatted correctly. This is one very enjoyable device. I lived happily enough with the original Explorer for three years, but recently decided to upgrade in order to do MQA through Tidal. I'll give my impressions of the DAC using its line-out capabilities in a living room stereo and a headphone amp. My experience is that, yes, it's a worthwhile upgrade. MQA tracks range from good to exceptional on my simple living room system of Mac laptop, vintage Marantz receiver and KEF LS-50 speakers. I won't say streamed MQA files sound better than well-mastered 24-bit releases (or even necessarily better than the finest CDs, such as those artfully engineered by ECM Records). In practice these days, the event horizon for "better" in this hobby is close and getting closer. I only claim that in terms of my pleasure, MQA hits the mark! The question of whether playback improves by being "unfolded" by the ME2 instead of by Tidal alone is easy for me to answer: yes, it's better this way. You can sum it up as holographic, dynamic sound. I grew up with LPs and, for better or worse, their sound lingers in memory -- casting a long shadow, really, across my digital wanderings. MQA recalls their easeful, romantic quality. To be sure this is hotly disputed in some quarters, but you can only go by the testimony of your own ears. So far in my listening, it has proved true on contemporary recordings such as Simon Rattle conducting the BPO in 2008 in Berlioz's Symphonie Fantastique, on much older ones such as the Warner Classics remasters of Herbert von Karajan in the 1960s, and (stunningly, in the case of The Smiths) on pop music I know so well I could sing it in my sleep. Leaving aside MQA, how does this new version of the DAC compare to its predecessor? Where better recordings are concerned, I don't hear a vast difference but two qualities are noteworthy. The first is a pleasant increase in imaging width and depth. Instruments spread out in air is my audio holy grail, so this is a definite plus. Secondly, this version is slightly brighter and markedly more dynamic. My impression is that the original Explorer is more rolled off, more polite, a signature I'd grown accustomed to (and a little tired of). The difference was mildly eyebrow-raising at first, but not for long, thankfully. If you weren't doing a direct swap-out, you'd never know. In an unexpected twist for me, the ME2 is also being used to feed an Oppo HA-1 headphone amp. This is a more than serviceable solution for MQA playback when Oppo (along with other manufacturers who are hoping the format fails) isn't in a hurry to pay costly licensing fees to Meridian. Does the ME2/MQA duo pumped in over RCA inputs rival the satisfaction from hearing DSF recordings, until now my high-water mark for headphone listening? Yes, actually! Color me pleased and impressed.

It looks like the Divoom Voombox-travel has recently been updated with a more powerful 5 watt driver. This must be a very recent update as the official product description still shows 4 watts and all of the reviews seem to be referring to the less powerful 4 watt version. I purchased this one sold by 'Divoom Official' and fulfilled by Amazon and I got the updated 5 watt version which I was not expecting. I assume that if you purchase from the 'Divoom Official' you'll get the updated 5W version as well. In addition to being more powerful, they changed the inputs so there is a port for charging and a separate port for an audio connector. It looks like the version in the pictures has just one input for both the audio and the charger so you were limited to using their proprietary cable if you wanted to connect a non bluetooth source. Now you can use any 'male to male' audio cable to connect to a non bluetooth compatible source. I learned about this speaker in a CNET article that listed the best affordable bluetooth speakers available. CNET (and most other reviewers) loved it when it was 4 watts, and now it is even better as the power has been increased by 25% to 5 watts. 1. Sound Quality - This is really what you care about and I am VERY impressed with the sound quality for something so portable. Given that some reviewers complained that the speaker wasn't loud enough, I can only assume that the increase from 4W to 5W has improved the volume as well as the quality of the sound at higher volumes. I have never actually heard the older 4W version, but I have listened to a lot of other bluetooth speakers like the JBL Clip Portable, the Bose Soundlink, Bose Soundlink Mini 2, the Harman Kardon Esquire Mini, the Jawbone Jambox Mini, and several others I can't remember off the top of my head. I'll revisit some of these speakers as a point of reference in this review. I won't be referencing the Jawbone Jambox Mini because I hated everything about it and believe that almost any bluetooth speaker is better. A. Volume: I can't imagine anyone being unhappy with the volume at this small size. You need to be realistic with your expectations here. If you want to host a dance party in an empty warehouse, then look for something bigger. B. Clarity and Distortion: Just like any small speaker, there can be distortion at maximum volume - there are zero distortion-free alternatives at this size no matter how much money you spend. HOWEVER, after reading some reviews, I was expecting (and would totally accept) more distortion at maximum volume. I am actually surprised by how little distortion there is at high volumes. Of course some songs (usually with mucho bass) distort more than others, but really not that bad - I suspect that the 5W version has improved quite a bit from the 4W. Below maximum volume (about 80% and below) the clarity is very good. You will notice that certain genres play better than others, but nothing is bad. Mids and Highs are likely a bit better with the Bose Soundlink ($129) and Harman Kardon ($150), but not by much. And those speakers have a MUCH higher price tag and pathetic bass. C. Bass: When properly placed, this little thing seems to have better bass than most anything I have heard for this size and wattage - in fact the bass is much better (louder and clearer) than many bluetooth speakers that are bigger and more expensive. The bass blows away the Harman Kardon Esquire Mini, the Bose soundlink, and the JBL clip. More expensive speakers like the Bose Soundlink Mini 2 and the UE Mini Boom have better bass, but they are MUCH more expensive ($199) and usually bigger/less portable. The "good bass in a small package" comes from the Voombox-travel's well-thought-out design with an active speaker on top of a passive speaker that faces down. So keep in mind that the best bass comes when you have it sitting on a solid surface so the bass from the passive woofer can be reflected (it sounds really good on the hood of a car). When the speaker isn't on a solid surface the bass goes down by a significant amount (like 50% or more in my opinion). 2. Size/Weight/Design. This is a very convenient size and shape and I love the versatility the top clip gives you. If you're looking for super slim/thin - like to carry in a pants pocked or slide into an over-stuffed backpack or purse, then you would do much better with the Harman Cardon Esquire Mini. That thing is crazy thin and probably would be the most convenient to carry around. Of course the thicker design is 100% the reason the Voombox has good bass and the Harman Kardon has none. The Harman Kardon has great sound with no bass if you are into that - It seems better as a speaker-phone than music-player. The Voombox is heavier than it looks, but it's not inconvenient. If anything the weight speaks to the quality of the unit. For me, the Voombox is 'Just Right' size/shape/weight for the sound quality. I actually think that this is the best bluetooth in this size category, regardless of price. 3. Durability: I have only had it for a few weeks, so I can't comment on long-term use. I will say that it feels very durable and I love the water/shock resistant design. It opens up MANY more applications than most bluetooth speakers (shower, outdoors, whatever). If anything is going to break, it will probably be the top clip (like another reviewer had happen to him) That said, it doesn't seem cheap, it's just more vulnerable than the rest of the unit. I would guess that to top clip will be perfectly fine for 90% of users. 4. Features: Bluetooth works great - easy to pair and good range. The speaker-phone feature was something I didn't care about at all... but I was PLEASANTLY surprised how well it works. It's such a great feature I never knew I wanted. If you're within about 8 feet it works great. Haven't tried it beyond that. I also haven't tried it with massive amounts of ambient noise, but my spouse could hear me fine even with kids playing in the background. 5. Battery life: I haven't done specific tests on this, but at 50% volume I would guess it'll go beyond the stated 6 hours. It will go several hours on full volumes. The nice thing is it will display how much battery is left on your phone next to the bluetooth icon. So convenient. I don't know if they updated the battery in the newer version, but I listen to it for an hour or two here and there and it will last for days. 6. Price: Really this is an incredible value for such a high quality piece of equipment that performs all-around better than most speakers three to four times the price. Yes there are better bluetooth speakers (like the UE Boom and Bose Soundlink Mini 2), but nothing near this price point and portability. By the way, this DOES INDEED come with a carrying case, a USB cord, and an audio jack cord so you can plug this directly in to a sound source that doesn't have bluetooth capability. One reviewer said that the description was misleading because it didn't come with those things. That reviewer either didn't notice the carrying case and cords in the box, or somehow got a used one that didn't include them. Rest assured those things come standard with the product. You will not be disappointed with this product. Go ahead and buy it. If you think there is a better or equivalent speaker within this size/price range, please comment on my review with the info. I'd love to know.

If you use a D2 series camera, this is a must-have item. Essentially, it eliminates that "tunnel" effect created by puny crop-factor viewfinders. Crop factor viewfinders are, of necessity, 1.5x smaller than full-frame or 35mm film viewfinders, giving an annoying tunnel vision effect when looking through them. This item magnifies that 1.5 crop viewfinder by 1.7, making it in effect 20% LARGER than a film or full-frame viewfinder view. You are still seeing what your lens sees, and your photos will still be the same 1.5x crop factor, but manual focus, composition, and reading the HUD readouts inside the viewfinder are all vastly improved. It does not stick out too far at all, in fact, if anything, it makes your nose not have to press so hard into the back of the camera. Very great item, especially if you shoot all day, as I do, in low light (weddings, events, etc.). Eyestrain is reduced because you don't have to squint so hard to see what you're focusing on. I'd recommend using this with a Katz Eye split-image focusing screen for even more brightness, clarity, and focusing ease. Conclusion: a great (and small) investment that goes a long way, especially if you're stuck without the full-frame goodness of a D3 or D700. I'm sure some pessimist may find something to whine about, but overall, this item is a great help to me, and probably will be to you as well. Got a D200/300? Received the Seagate IronWolf 10TB drive, box was fine, physically no issues. Started Seatools to test it, passed the short test. Started the long test, a several minutes later walked past and noticed the drive activity LED wasn't even flickering, turned the monitor on and found that it failed, "likely due to unreadable sectors". Luckily I ordered this to expand my NAS storage and not to replace a failed drive so not time critical. I have requested a replacement via Amazon and will update this review after testing that one. This purchase was giving Seagate hard drives another chance after several drives failed in the past (spread over years). If the second drive fails, I'll have to switch to WD Red Pro 8TB, only a $11 cheaper than the IronWolf, but 2 TB smaller in storage. The real test will be if the replacement drive passes testing and works in the array, I'll order a second 10TB IronWolf drive in a few weeks, hopefully that drive will pass testing also. 4/24/17 Update: Changing stars to 4, as the drive seems quite nice. SeaTools short passed, but the long test passed, but only took a few hours, not trusting that. Ran DBAN 3 passes, took a few days, passed that, and SMART info looks fine. Just put it in the Synology NAS, currently rebuilding, looks like it will take around 16 hours. Interesting thing is that the NAS shows a IronWolf testing button (says beta, and the drive passed), and has a IronWolf logo instead of the generic hard drive logo. Will be ordering 2 more in a while one so the array can expand to use the new space, and a third so I can have a tested spare ready to go. Considering it takes so long to test huge drives a spare is a good thing to have handy. 5/9/17 After the first (replacement) drive tested good and incorporated into the array just fine, ordered another 10TB drive, it tested good and also went into the array just fine. Ordered a third drive (fourth if you include the original that was exchanged). Took longer to test than I thought the others did by about a day maybe a day and a half. Ran Seagate tools long SMART test and when I went back a few hours later it had failed with a code, just got done doing the return process for the drive, and awaiting another. Two failed drives out of four, not great. The two in the array passed an additional test pass after they finished the array rebuild. I'll keep an eye on the two in the array, and update this with whatever happens with the next drive when it arrives and hopefully passes its tests. UPDATE 5/17/17: Fifth drive tested good, and will be a spare, waiting for one of the other drives to die someday. It was packed in a box without any packing material, unlike the other drives I ordered, but it looks to be fine this time. Conclusion, 2 of 5 drives failed testing using Seagate tools tests, then DBAN for multi-pass wipes, then Seagate tools again. One of the drives failed the Seatools long test quickly. The second only failed the long SMART test after being wiped for almost 5 days. As with all drives test them before you put them into service. This is the last update as I am looking for a new job and shouldn't be wasting money on more drives. UPDATE: 2/7/21, took away a star, my experience so far, been wanting to write up my findings for a while, then today I got an email that drive 1 now has 8 bad sectors, great way to wake up in the morning. I had 8 10TB Ironwolf drives total (ST10000VN0004-1ZD101, FW: SC61). All drives are in a Synology 8 bay NAS, powered via a large UPS for power protection, reboots/shutdowns are exceedingly rare, maybe once or twice a year. One that was drive 1 failed after about 2 years power on time. 9/2019 1 bad sector, 12/2019 12 bad sectors, 5/2020 57 bad sectors. Test failed, wiped the drive, then it seems it cleared the counters and passed. Untrustworthy, so put it in the scrap pile since the warranty expired by a month or two. Swapped in the spare drive (Always keep a tested spare drive handy!). Drives that are currently in the NAS: Drive 1, 10TB, 8 bad sectors 2/2021 (just happened today), power on hours is 0.7 years. Drive 2, 10TB, 0 bad sectors, power on time 2.7 years. Drive 3, 10TB, 16 bad sectors total, 8 in 11/2020, 8 in 12/2020, power on time is 3.8 years. Drive 4, 12TB, no bad sectors, power on is 0.4 years. This is bigger as I gave up on Ironwolf drives, trying a more expensive enterprise grade drive. Drive 5, 10TB, 24 bad sectors in 11/2020, power on time is 1.8 years. Drive 6, 10TB, 8 bad sectors in 12/2019, power on time is 2.0 years. Drive 7, 10TB, 24 bad sectors total, 8 in 8/2020, 16 in 12/2020, power on time is 1.8 years. Drive 8, 10TB, 0 bad sectors, however 1 re-connection/re-identification error, power on time is 1.9 years. The reconnect error occurred upon power up after the NAS was powered down while I was rearranging/cleaning up the wiring closet, power cycled it and it came up clean. Overall I am not impressed with the Ironwolf 10TB drives, perhaps I would have had similar issues with another 10TB drive brand/model. This is a home NAS, used for backups and file storage, not exactly a high utilization environment that would stress hard drives into a early grave. Currently the increases in bad sectors over the last several months have been during times when backups grow to double or more of their size before being cleaned up. New unused areas get written to and it finds bad sectors. Ironwolf tests always come back normal, and extended SMART tests all complete fine, quarterly data scrubbing completes without issue. As my array is only setup for one drive failure, I am now in a position where I either need to replace a drive, hope I pick one that would have failed first, and hope the rest do not increase their bad sector count while rebuilding. Or buy eight 12TB enterprise drives, and the new 2021 Synology (SHR, and migrate the data over. That would be far less stressful, although much more expensive. YMMV, just what I had happen so far in a home 8 drive NAS, that is in a basement wiring closet, no vibration, powered through a UPS, and no temperature issues.

If you look at the spec sheet for this camera, it looks like a dream come true. Although if you have experience interpreting specs you'll realize that the combination of a small sensor, a relatively slow lens, and too many megapixels will pose challenges in low light. This Fuji can't can't compete with the luxury compacts that have larger sensors, much faster lenses, and fewer megapixels: costlier pocketable cameras like the Canon S95, Olympus XZ-1, and the Panasonic LX-5. But then none of those offer more than a 5x zoom or more than 720p video. In a pocket size camera, the choice is a fast lens OR a long zoom, but not both. But the most tantalizing promise of this camera is its unique (to Fuji EXR sensors) ability to take two different exposures simultaneously. These can then be combined to capture more dynamic range than otherwise possible. In contrasty situations this gives you both shadow detail and highlight detail where most cameras would show areas of all black or all white. There are other cameras (and more coming) with "dynamic range mode", but they take 2 (or sometimes 3) varying exposures in sequence to do the same thing. But any movement between these exposures ruins the result. Apple's iPhone 4 camera has such a feature, and in shots where you manage to hold it still, the results are spectacular. I used my iPhone4 to snap some shots in a redwood forest where there were areas of sunlight alternating with deeply shaded areas. Amazingly, almost all the detail was captured in the HDR shot (the iPhone 4 takes both normal and HDR shots automatically) but the normal shot "clipped" the shadows and highlights leaving many areas all black or all white. But 2 out of 3 of my shots were blurred in spite of my best efforts to hold the phone steady. Fuji's EXR sensors can take 2 different exposures at once, making it possible to get high dynamic range shots reliably without needing a tripod. Other sensors can't do this because their pixels are in rows and columns, whereas Fuji's pixels are laid out like interlocking hexagons. Because cameras capture 3 colors, this three-axis layout means there are always two adjacent pixels of the same color. So half the pixels take one exposure and the other half take the other. You lose some resolution, but with the F550's 16 megapixels, you're still left with a 8 megapixel picture. Still very high resolution. At least theoretically. The EXR settings do indeed capture incredible dynamic range. They can maintain detail in contrasty scenes that other cameras would lose. From a hill in San Francisco I took some shots of the city scape lit by the late afternoon sun where buildings were directly lit and foliage areas were deeply shaded. The EXR settings kept the detail in the brightly lit buildings while the other settings did not. There was just one problem. If you zoomed into the pixel level you would see alarming amounts of noise everywhere below the brightness midpoint. Not enough, perhaps, to be bothersome in a small print, but at page size it's very disturbing. The obvious solution to this would be to lower the ISO settings and use a longer exposure. Almost all digital cameras allow this adjustment, as does this Fuji, EXCEPT when you shoot in EXR mode where you can not set ISO below 400. Though this setting is a maximum ISO none of the shots I took used anything lower even when the high setting was unnecessary. Instead I got unnecessarily fast shutter times. I might have accepted this as a limitation of the technology except for one thing. I happen to own Fuji's first EXR camera, the F200exr. It has the same technology and EXR modes, and it uses lower ISO settings for EXR exposures, but even when EXR exposures occur at ISO 400, the noise is only a tiny fraction of what you get with the F550. True, the F200 has a larger sensor, a slightly faster lens, and 25% fewer pixels. Even so, the difference in noise is just too great. I strongly suspect there is an engineering flaw built in to this design and I hope it can be remedied with a firmware update. The other possibility could be the sensor itself which unlike the CCD sensor of the F200 is a CMOS type which facilitates the full HD video. Before you let this ruin your enthusiasm for this camera, I'd like to report that the non-EXR results are quite good. Noise is way lower, especially at lower ISO settings. I get the same tonal smoothness as with the F200, which is why I can't believe the EXR functions are working properly. And that 15x zoom is addictive. Sitting on a park bench in the late afternoon I noticed a half moon above so I snapped it at full zoom. You can actually see the craters on the moon. The lens seems quite sharp although I noticed some intense reds seem to bleed. Because the F550 can capture RAW format files, I suggest using this format instead of the EXR for high contrast scenes. You can get quite a bit of the clipped information back this way, although you'll have to struggle with the powerful but alien converting software that comes with the camera. Adobe RAW will not open Fuji RAW files. You can use the Fuji software to create 16 bit TIFF files to import into Photoshop if you prefer and do the processing there. It's quite a chore and I wouldn't blame you if you didn't want to bother. Incidentally, the in-camera processing (except for EXR mode) seems quite excellent. The JPEGS strike a nice balance between resolution and noise. I'm not a professional but I don't think you can get better results processing RAW files in Photoshop, so why bother? There are some video issues I saw covered in other reviews so I won't repeat them. Another fun and useful feature is the panorama shooting. You can make it work using it handheld, but the probability of success if far greater with a tripod. If you don't keep the camera level while sweeping the scene the stitching will malfunction. Overall, this is a great bright light camera, even without the EXR function.

I've got machine tools though so using a band saw, drill press, and bench grinder, I was able to shorten up the post area of the finger to allow them to be adjusted "thinner" and get them to work. It took 2 of us to get the thing mounted though as you have about 10 different things that have to be tightened at the same time or your monitor will fall out and crash to the floor (only happened once to me ;-) ). Your next best solution if you have non-vesa mounting holes would be to use a thin sheet of steel or aluminum and fabricate yourself an actual adapter plate. If your monitor doesn't have any provisions for rear mounting...this setup may be your only choice short of replacing the monitor.

Before installing this radio, take a look at my updated diagram. The original one they give you has many errors, doesn’t include the full back-up camera hook up, and throws a lot of unnecessary information on the page. Also if any of my methods or codes doesn’t work for you, check the FQAs for this radio on Amazon and look at the reviews from other people. I installed this in a 2007 Toyota Highlander. I soldered all my connections properly and used heat shrink to cover them, and on top of the heat shrink also used electrical tape. Needless to say, I spent A LOT of time double/triple checking everything and did a quality job. Here’s what you need to do this job: 1) Cable harness for your specific vehicle (you can find one on amazon for approx. $5). 2) Method for connecting cable harness wires to radio wires (I soldered all mine). 3) Two wire taps for back-up camera positive + power (see attached updated diagram). 4) Method for connecting ground wire of back-up camera (I drilled a small hole in the vehicle’s metal frame, and soldered my black ground wire into the hole, see attached picture). 5) Electrical tape to wrap around RCA connections from back-up camera (Just to keep them together permanently). First of all, if you think the radio is defective at all after doing the full install, contact the seller (JBY Tech) on Amazon. The first radio I got from them was defective (the radio function didn’t work), and after about 9 messages exchanged between me and them, they finally agreed that it was defective and told me to send the radio back to amazon, or send it to JBY Teck for an exchange. Well I already had the car taken apart and the wires soldered and everything so obviously I was going to do the exchange. The only thing is, they made ME pay the return shipping cost which was around $23. I even told them that I shouldn’t have to pay more money because their item is defective. They came up with some excuse that made absolutely no sense and was in broken English. In the box I returned to them I even put the receipt for the shipping cost, but they still didn’t refund me. They sent me a different radio after they received my defective one. So this whole ordeal took about a month and 13 messages back and forth. Not cool. Anyway, I received the new radio and everything works. Secondly, the length of the cable of the cable that goes from the radio to the camera in the back of the vehicle was just barely long enough. Literally could only spare maybe an inch or two. I installed this in a mid-size SUV (only two rows of seats), so if you have a big SUV you’ll probably have to get more cable. Third, the red power connector (the one with a red and black wire) for the camera was not even close to long enough to reach the back-up light’s wire. I had to use 2 ½ times more wire to reach, so that’s annoying. One thing I have to mention: the default settings on this radio are so stupid. When you first hook up the radio and turn everything on, the radio volume is going to be super loud, and there will be loud beeps every time you push any button. The beeps can be turned off in the settings. Here’s something that they don’t tell you anywhere in the useless instructions, and you’ll most likely need it: There’s a factory settings page. Go to “about device”, then “Factory Setting”, then type in either “5839” or “3711”. In here you can adjust a lot of things, including default start-up volume settings, radio settings, and adjust the different BT, radio, or CD volumes (hint, make them all the same so you don’t have any surprise volume blasts when switching between them). After you’re done in factory settings, save everything then exit to main menu, then turn off your car/radio. Wait around 10 seconds then turn the car/radio back on. Your factory settings changes will be in effect now. The loud beeping will be on again, so turn that off in settings. Go into your GPS function, then go into its settings and turn all the volumes down or off. They are extremely loud and abrupt and can surprise you if you’re driving down the road and using the GPS. There is no Aux connection for this radio. That Mic hookup in the back is indeed an extra mic hookup. I confirmed this with JBY Tech. I wish it was an Aux connection though, because there’s already a mic in the front of the radio. For the boot logo set up, try 3506 or 0000 for the code. I didn’t hook up the 4 following wires, because my vehicle doesn’t have these hookups: Brake-In <pink> (I don’t think anyone needs to hook this one up, believe it’s for the parking brake), Amp Con <Blue/White>, Key 1 <Brown>, Key 2 <Brown/Black>. I’m giving this radio 3 out of 5 stars. If I had my updated instructions to start off with, I would have given it 4 stars. I usually wouldn’t take off stars for things like defects/default settings/bad instructions, but after you spend $180 and hours putting this thing together, it’s frustrating to not have a perfect working radio. Here are the Pros: touchscreen is good and has a good response, they have actual physical buttons on the sides as well, many different capabilities (DVD player, extra monitor hookups, GPS, Games, BT, Radio, etc.), camera resolution is good, GPS works pretty well (google maps on your phone is still the best though), radio is very customizable, overall not bad quality of the material used and seems durable. Here are the Cons: seems that quite a few of the radios have defects (based on my experience and reading other people’s reviews) so be prepared to have problems if you buy one, no Aux connection, camera lens needs to be wider, connecting to the BT can be difficult sometimes (usually it’s great though), a BIG issue I’m having right now is that the radio reception has decreased significantly. I installed a radio signal amplifier, but not sure if that helped at all.

I received my order today. My first impression was "jeez, these things are 'kinda small' for 30A use!" Because the contacts are "barrel" type, make sure you have a PROPER crimper! NOTE: the maximum usable wire size is 10 gauge (thus, the "30 Amp" rating). Assembly notes: 1) depending on the wire used, you may have to "shave down" the insulation (1/2" behind the strip line) so it'll easily enter the rear of the connector. 2) the contact is a "one-way" insertion! do not try to insert it "upside down". 3) when inserting the contact, push hard enough until you hear/feel a "click" - this indicates the connector is fully locked! 4) DO NOT allow wire strands to protrude past the "wire stop" on the contact! this will prevent the contact from locking. 5) DOUBLE-CHECK YOUR WIRE "POLARITY" BEFORE INSTALLING A CONTACT! if you use the "wrong color" body (i.e., black when you wanted red), it's a REAL BITCH to remove the contact and you may need to cut it off and apply a new contact. Anyhoo, they do seem to Do The Purpose for which they're designed.

The case holds the tablet and pen perfectly. It is well designed and will prevent things in a backpack/messenger bag from scratching up the screen. For this style of a case the protection is exactly what you would expect, especially considering the price. Here are the caveats: * The case is NOT designed to be "quick" to use. IE you will have to open it, pull the keyboard physically off of the case, and then the case will function as a stand. * There is nowhere for additional accessories or anything (like a dock or charging cable), but this should be obvious. It would be a nice-to-have. * Apart from the grip inside the case and the relatively weak magnets, nothing keeps the keyboard from falling out of the sides of the case. I would have liked to see a better mechanism to hold the keyboard in place and stop it from falling. * The "stand" feature is pretty terrible. It works fine if you make sure the keyboard is wedged against the tablet, it iwll not work otherwise. There isnt enough weight/grip for the tablet to stand properly. * There is no way to use this case while holding the tablet comfortably. You have to pull the keyboard off of the case for thigns to fold up properly and be comfortable to hold in non-keyboard mode. Overall the keyboard itself is cool and all but this is a VERY uncomfortable case to use. The way it was designed, it seems you have to make a choice between using a tablet like a tablet or like a laptop. I feel a case should enable both methods of usage, and this one does not. Others might want to consider a separate unattached folding bluetooth keyboard or a keyboard+trackpad or a keyboard that comes with a little carrying case, and then have a separate case that lets you stand the tablet up in portrait or landscape mode. While this is convenient for those who ONLY want to use the tablet in laptop mode, it does not allow for proper S-pen usage/access with a comfortable grip. It has nowhere to store/attach a mouse (not even like a keyring type of thing, not that i'm knocking points for that). But since you have to carry a mouse with you anyways, why not have a case with a proper stand that lets you use the tablet hand-held in portrait OR landscape, or in your lap while laying in bed, and then have the keyboard/mouse separate in the bag, to pull out when/if you actually need it? Also, the case doesnt prevent the keyboard from coming in contact with the screen. TERRIBLE design flaw there. a screen protector is mandatory if you use this product.

I bought this mainly of curiosity, as I have a portable music player with a 2.5mm balanced output and a powered speaker with a couple of XLR inputs. To be clear: the music player's balanced output is intended for use with headphones. What I'll write about should not be taken as criticism of the cable (or the player or amp that I used). The reason I was curious about this cable is because there's no way that the cable could establish a ground reference for the device attached to the 2.5mm plug. This is a TRRS plug; the four connections are used to establish two balanced connections. (If you take a look at the 4.4mm balanced plugs, you'll see that they're TRRRS; that fifth connection is used as a ground reference.) My tests confirmed suspicions: there is some hum introduced by the player. How loud that hum is depends upon a lot of factors, including both the attached gear and the environment in which it operates. I suspect that if I was connecting a player that had its own ground reference (e.g. a 3-wire mains connection), the hum would have been absent. For a battery-powered (or worse: powered by a wall-wart) device, you should expect the connection to hum. If you're handy with a soldering iron, you could run a lead from the ground pin of one of the XLR connectors to a clip that you could simply attach to some bit of chassis metal on the player. In the case of a portable player like mine that has both 3.5mm TRS and 2.5mm TRRS jacks, you could run the ground reference to the sleeve terminal of a 3.5mm plug leaving the other pins unconnected. Other than the questionable application, I have no concerns regarding this cable. It does what it claims to do.

I got this monitor based solely on reviews regarding its incredible picture- all of which are true. However, coming from the Dell Ultrasharp series - a relationship that ended when the u2713hm had more backlight bleeding than picture - I can only say that almost everything else is disappointing at this price range. Sure, there's plenty of connection options like the dell, but no PiP, PbP, or any other options. Yes, the (awkwardly shaped, space-consuming) stand is rotatable, tiltable and height-adjustable, but where as the dell's flow smoothly from position to position, the viewsonic plastic just feels jerky and liable to break (I tried to rotate the monitor once and stopped halfway in fear of breaking it). Yes you can adjust things in the menu, but over an extremely limited range of options and with a very counter-intuitive and un-friendly interface. Yes, there's a USB hub, but it's awkwardly placed. Yes, There's allegedly a software component, but that hasn't been upgraded since windows 95 and I couldn't install it. And at least for my money, the cheap "touch" buttons are an annoying and poor alternative to quality mechanical buttons. So why 4 stars? Because really, the picture is incredible and requires very little tuning, there's minimal bleeding (which almost any monitor at these sizes will have), and an otherwise very uniform picture quality. And while all the rest is very nice, a great picture should be the main consideration when getting a monitor. So I'd highly-recommend this one over the dell, at least until they get their s*** together regarding the major issues with the 2713hm series. However, people who regularly use the rotation and height-adjustment should consider carefully before getting this monitor.

Though I bought these earbuds 6 months ago, due to the annoying volume control, I've decided to give this product one star. The sound quality is decent, as far as Bluetooth earbuds go. They aren't as good as Air Pods, but it's not like Air Pods are 10x better either. For the price, the sound quality is good (hence the 4 stars) These earbuds don't have active noise cancellation, but they do a decent job of isolating the sound. A lot of that has to do with making sure to choose the proper size ear piece to fit your ear canal. My ear canals are large, so I use the largest one that came with this product. So 4 out of 5 stars is a fair rating imo. The battery life is also good for the price range. It seems like a charge lasts for a pretty long amount of time. 4 out of 5 stars. Now, on to my biggest complaint. I have two actually. The first is that these earbuds are terrible for phone calls. When a call comes in, I just turn off the Bluetooth on my phone, and answer it that way. That's not a deal breaker though. For some people, it might be. The worst feature of these earbuds are the volume up and volume down controls. If I have these in my ears, and literally touch anything with them (a pillow, my hood in my sweatshirt if it's up) these earbuds will either turn all the way down, or all the way up. Or say I'm trying to adjust these earbuds in my eardrum because they are heavy, and sometimes fall out of my ear. To add to the irritation of that, there's a voice that either repeats, "minimum volume" over and over, or "maximum volume" over and over. If you try to fight the earbuds with your phone's volume control, these earbuds will literally keep on turning the volume up or down (depending on what was selected). The pause control of just tapping the earbuds to pause or unpause seems to only work 50% of the time, and sometimes you get the lovely minimum or maximum volume command instead. I didn't use these earbuds much for the first few months after I bought them. Maybe a couple of times a month. They had the same problem then as well, but I wasn't quite irritated enough to review them. I usually use wired earbuds, just for the simplicity and convenience of them. It's true that the wires can become annoying and cumbersome, but the sound quality is superior to Bluetooth imo. Plus, they don't decide to turn the volume up and down whenever you touch them. I'm not saying these earbuds sound terrible, and not saying the battery is bad. I am saying they are poorly designed, and that poor design does negatively affect the listening experience.

In this orientation, the camera picture was rotated 90 degrees (don't remember which direction). Just remember not to push the camera in all the way til you get the image lined up; it helps to hook the camera up to the monitor, turn it on and watch the monitor from the rear window as you rotate the camera. I'm powering my camera from the reverse lights, which I measured at about 10VDC with the lights on (across the light bulb); I will likely switch to an accessory power wire so the camera is powered when the key is in the ACC position or higher. This will allow me to view the camera from my Kenwood head unit without having to put the car in reverse. I measured the camera current draw at 110mA, which is too high (for my tastes) to leave it connected to an always-hot battery line. Picture's pretty clear, colors seem a bit washed out, but that *may* be due to the lower voltage... not sure. I'd probably recommend this camera to others.

These have been excellent fans so far! I personally use one of them as a 3D printer part cooling fan. I needed higher static pressure and higher CFM than the cheap sleeve bearing fan I had been using. Plus: -The motors are beefy and able to provide solid static pressure. Air velocity at the nozzle of the part cooling duct has to be at least twice what it was before. -The bearings on these fans are quite smooth, and there is very little slop in them. -In my use case, this fan absolutely rips. Cons: -They are still somewhat noisy, even if the bearings are smooth. -The aforementioned beefy motor adds a bit of heft to these fans. Other Considerations: -These fans have a radius to the edges of the exhaust. If you plan on installing these, make sure you take this into account, and modify your design or use a sealant/putty. Solid unit (well, in this case, two) of a fan both in terms of weight and performance. If your goal is to shave weight, may want to go a different route, but I'd say the extra weight is worth it in terms of cooling performance.

In my experience simple problems almost always have a simple solution..take a tiny square piece of hockey, medical or duct tape and stick it to the bottom of the hot shoe mount and fold it over the edges. I purchased this unit along with a Cambridge CXA81, and I am very happy with it! To be clear, I am happy with the way it sounds - clear and rich. The media player aspect... not so much. I'll clarify: Pros: * Exceptional pre-amplifier will allow you to listen to Tidal Masters at an up-sampled rate that sounds absolutely fantastic. * The DAC seems extremely capable, and seems to be a step up from the one built into the CXA81 Amplifier based on my experimentation of plugging directly into both (although, this may be the pre-amp doing most of the heavy lifting, I'm not totally sure...) * As previously stated, this unit will noticeably improve the quality of your music over using the Cambridge CXA81 amplifier alone. * Just about every wireless protocol is supported here. I can stream Plex, Google Music, Tidal, Spotify - you name it, this unit will likely support it! Just connect via your phone and you're playing music. * The LCD layout is really great when playing music through the media player - it's got a well designed layout (which is clearly shown in the product image) * The remote that comes with the unit is high-quality, and effective. It allows for 8 customer-selected pre-sets, which is great! One click to turn on USB mode, one click to return to the media player, one click to do whatever else you may want to do. * No software was required for my Mac Pro's Tidal App to play music through the unit. I plugged the unit in, and Tidal immediately let me select it as an output. Cons: * The LCD panel is extremely dim. It does its job, but it leaves a LOT to be desired. * Tidal Masters can ONLY be played at full quality through a connected device (in my case, a laptop). Tidal is built into the unit, but it will not natively play masters quality. This was a huge disappointment for me, but it does play perfectly through USB, and the screen actually shows the quality (which is not always the same between masters recordings, I was surprised to learn! Some are higher quality than others.) * When in USB mode, only quality is shown and it's shown in small white text. This is a bit disappointing. I wish they added a visualizer, or something else that would make it a bit more exciting when playing music in the best mode possible (USB is the only way to get the highest quality, after all!) * I see no value at all in the supporting app, but that being said, I don't really know what value it would ideally have? I guess it would be neat if the unit had a visualizer, and that sort of thing could be controlled there.

The MobileLite has two key functions: 1. A wireless reader of SD cards or USB flash drives 2. A power bank to recharge a mobile device As a power bank it is limited - the product data sheet mentions 1800mAh battery, which when fully charged, would suffice to fully charge an iPhone or iPod Touch, but not iPads, SGS3, SGS4 and most other high-end smartphones. So I personally wouldn't buy it for its power bank capabilities, but it is nice addition to a wireless reader if you need one. As a wireless storage device, it is similar to Kingston's WiDrive product, but instead of the embedded memory in the WiDrive, the MobileLite comes with SD card slot, USB 2.0 interface and no memory. As such it leaves the consumer the freedom to use existing memory cards/usb drives, with the SD card slot especially useful for inserting the card from your digital camera and sharing photos via your mobile device without the need to carry with you a laptop... To get going you simply download the app, go to the wireless settings of your mobile device and connect to the WiFi network the MobileLite is creating when turned on, and that's it. You would be able to browse content loaded to an SD card or a USB flash drive inserted to the reader. It takes the MobileLite about 30 seconds to get up and running - a pretty long time for a flash based device. The MobileLite is about the size of iPhone 5, but twice as thick. It has a clean design and is surprising light-weight. In the box you will find the reader, a USB cable, an SD-microSD card adapter and the quick start guide. It has 3 LEDs indicating battery status, wifi access (middle blue), and internet access (side blue). A different Internet LED could be helpful as from a short distance I may not be able to tell which of the two blue LEDs are on and what it means... SD Card: The MobileLite supports SD, SDHC and SDXC cards. This means it supports ExFAT, so if you would like to load it with files larger than 4GB (think full length HD movies) or simply use high capacity cards (anything higher than 32GB) this feature would come handy. I was experimenting with it with a 64GB SanDisk Extreme Pro card and could access content on it with ease. The USB 2.0 receptacle works with USB 2.0 or 3.0 flash drives, so no problems here. Mobile Apps: To fully enjoy this reader you'd like to use the native iOS or Android apps. Unfortunately, it seems Kindle app is not available for this product. I accessed the MobileLite with iPhone 4, SGS2 and my laptop (at the same time). I viewed photos, streamed videos and listened to music so it can be used as a memory expansion device to memory-challenged devices where you could put a few full length movies and thousands of songs (depending on card or USB you plug in) for a long trip. The manufacturer claims up to 5 hours of operation, but I haven't got the chance to check how long it would stream continuously. You can also offload photos from your iPhone (Camera Roll) or Android (Gallery) if you are running out of storage on your mobile device. The apps shows content on the drive in two ways side by side - as files and by media type (Photos, Videos and Music). While mostly stable, I found the file/folders order on iPhone confusing and the both apps have some quirks I hope Kingston will fix quickly (photos and music I downloaded from the reader to my iPhone don't show in the Files view, only in the corresponding media tabs, content in media tabs is not searchable in the Android app etc.). You can download files from the reader to your mobile device for later access (though if you will buy this product to offload content from your mobile device you are less likely to use this feature). In the Settings menu you can check the status of the device battery, password protect your reader, rename the wireless network it creates. You can and should protect your MobileLite wireless network unless you'd like anyone in the wifi range of the device to be able to access your content. Password protection is available from the apps' settings menu and is as easy as it is on your home router. The Settings option to make the network invisible also helps preventing incidental access to an unprotected wireless network. The MobileLite features "internet pass through" - basically allowing you to maintain internet connectivity (receiving emails, browsing the internet) while connected to the drive. When doing so, you would see the reader's IP address under the device name in the application home screen. You can also access the reader via any web browser without a native app, but the functionality is much more limited. The MobileLite allows playing iTunes purchased content (by devices authorized to access this content), but only music will play directly from inside the app. To play Movies or TV shows you MUST browse the reader from Safari (typing the drives [...] Documentation could be improved. The quick start guide is targeting iOS users and there is no User Manual for Android users at all. Also, the user manual and quick start guide provide conflicting descriptions regarding battery status (the manual says red means less than 50%, while the quick start guide says it is means less than 25%). Pros: 1. ExFAT support and its expandable storage interfaces (think of 128GB SD card + additional capacity on a USB if you really need more) makes it a good candidate as a movies-stash on the go. 2. If you already have such a device - being able to using it as a power bank is nice. 3. iTunes content is generally supported. Cons: 1. At a price of $70 with no memory, if you consider it as a memory expansion device - you should consider buying other products (Kingston's own 32GB WiDrive for example is cheaper than this reader...). 2. To access iTunes videos and TV shows - you would need to browse the drive via Safari. 3. As a power bank - it's really limited. 4. No Kindle Fire app. 5. No user manual for Android.

I have owned two Sangean HDR-14 portables. I used the wrong adapter on the first and blew a circuit board to heck. So be careful when plugging in your radio. My second HDR-14 has improved performance on both FM and AM. Pros: Sensitive FM. This radio picks up HD signals better than my HDR-16. While it isn’t quite as selective on FM as the 16, its standard FM and FM HD sensitivity is quite good. Even weak FM stations are clear on this radio. Fringe stations that are in mono still sound clear. Small size and a lock switch make this radio convenient for travel. So far, have had good battery life. Cons: AM is noisy. Lots of radio noise hides weak signals that can be heard on other radios. From my location, good AM radios get WLW AM 700 in the daytime. The HDR-14 can’t, and I believe it’s because of the noise generated by the radio. FM selectivity could be a bit better. With a local station on 101.5, I can’t hear a weak station on 101.3. The HDR-16 can pick up the weak signal. Conclusion: Price, size, very good performance on FM and FM HD plus adequate AM reception make this radio a good buy in my view. If AM was less noisy, I would have easily given this radio 5 stars. Update 07/06. I traveled with this portable. Its FM is quite sensitive. On standard FM, it was more sensitive than my C Crane Skywave radio. In a market with strong signals, you may hear a weaker image of a strong FM station .4 MHZ above the signal. While in St. Louis, from my location, got weak 93.7 signal on 94.1. This radio is sensitive enough that this drawback doesn’t reduce my rating. Still very happy with it, especially on FM.

I purchased this TCL HDTV after doing extensive research, reading tons of reviews and shopping around. I decided to give it a try. The price was very low, the reviews were pretty darned good, and this specific television offered LOTS of connections for the price (a good number of HDMI ports, Composite, PC video input, USB, etc). Well, I'm not sure if the UPS delivery driver dropped this baby on its "head" en route, but we experienced problems right out of the box. It is a shame, too. I had high hopes for this set based on other's GLOWING reviews and positive experiences. Upon first glance, my husband was really excited about this TV, too - especially after hearing what I had paid. (He IS a thrifty guy - not the type to think that the more expensive brands are always the best.) Well, maybe the old addage IS true after all. "You get what you pay for." My husband set it up and tweaked the settings to his liking. It was connected to our AT&T U-Verse box, and also hooked up to a PS3. Now I'm no technophile, but my husband is pretty savvy with electronics. HE set everything up, so I know that it was done properly. At first glance it DID have vibrant colors and crisp Hi Def picture (watching the evening news in HD.) Our enthusiasm was short lived. Suddenly (a few days in), every couple of hours - the screen would go completely black. The sound simultanously cut out. A few seconds later, it would all come back on. We read the owners' manual, poured over all of the info (thinking maybe it had something to do with a "Sleep" timer function or some energy saving feature.) Nope. No explanation for this phenomenon in the owners' manuel. My husband un-connected and re-connected cables, re-set the television (and our U-Verse box), tried MANY different things - for about two days - to no avail. We called customer service at AT&T (our cable provider) - thinking maybe there was something wrong with the U-Verse box or the HD channels, or the connection... SOMETHING. It was not a signal or connection problem. I had several new HDMI cables - so we tried different ones... it wasn't the cables. During our time trying to figure out what was causing these "black-outs", we DID continue to use the television to watch occasional HD movies, or play a game here and there. As the days went on, the black-outs went from randomly - every 3 or 4 hours... to a more consistent bout of occurrences - like every 30 minutes or so. It was getting to the point where I was afraid that one of these times, the screen and sound would go "Off" and simply never come back "On". Like not wanting to stop and ask for directions on a road trip, even my husband (who is an engineer) finally gave in... and called TCL customer service. They first offered potential solutions (trouble-shooting) and after about 20 minutes, they told us about a "Firmware Update". We downloaded the update from their web-site, uploaded it to the set and gave it a couple of days. It went from BAD to WORSE! Finally, after numerous days of frustration, I contacted Amazon Customer Service. They simply said "Send it Back". Thankfully, I kept the box and packaging materials. Amazon was wonderful about it - the UPS driver was here the following day. Luckily, I was able to return it directly to AMAZON, and not have to rely on TCL's 2 year warranty (because I'd only had the set for fewer than 30 days). Also, Amazon did not charge me for the return shipping, even though I explained that I had no intention of exchanging it for another TCL. I truly felt bad about it - because this television DID have a lot of the things on my husband's "Wish List" as far as features. But the aggervation it had caused... and the wasted time that was spent trying to make it work... was NOT worth the few dollars I was "saving" versus buying a slightly higher priced (but reputable brand) set. Also, the time that we DID have it up and running, there were several OTHER issues that I noticed (not related to the "black-outs".) These are things that will affect my decision when buying a different set to replace this one. Maybe it will help someone out there, too. The first was an issue with the remote control and settings. We have an AT&T U-Verse box, which has HD Channels, Wi-Fi and Ethernet all running through it. Even with our old 150 lb RCA 32" television (circa 1990's) ... the U-Verse box & remote recognized our old TV set and was able to control everything with the one AT&T universal remote. Unfortunately that was not the case with this TCL television. So right off the bat, it required the use of TWO separate remotes... the U-Verse remote to change the channels, and then the TCL remote to control the sound. Kind of a pain. Speaking of sound... the actual VOLUME of this set was okay... but background noises seemed to drown out voices, especially with action movies or sporting events. I suppose this MAY have been remedied by adding a sound bar or additional customizable speaker system... but for casual viewing (especially as a third set for my husband's den) it was not a good thing. Something else I noticed - was with ANY with fast-action content (movies or sports) - it was extremely pixilated. Again I'm no pro, so maybe this is the norm with 60 Hz sets? However, as a casual viewer, the more I looked at different types of media (video games, HD movies, and sports) I felt that the transitions were choppy and boxy. Again, it's a shame because when we originally hooked it up - at first glance it DID have vibrant colors and a crisp clear picture. (Watching the evening news - the set& anchors behind the desk were clearly in HD.) Too bad it didn't do so well with fast paced movements on screen. Finally, one last issue - and this is another reason that I will be searching out a different brand - as opposed to simply exchanging this defective set for another TCL. Here on Amazon, I read the title of this television set: "TCL L40FHDF11TA 40-Inch 1080p 60 Hz LCD HDTV with 2-Year Warranty, Black". HOWEVER, as I scrolled down to the Item Description, it says "--this LED television makes it easy to watch a photo slideshow in brilliant color..." SO - which is it... an LED or an LCD? Maybe this could explain why some customers have nothing but GLOWING reviews... and others (like myself) seem to have a horrible experience! (I did not think to actually CHECK the model number on the outside of the box and compare it to what's listed here on the product page.) Did I even actually receive the "40FHDF11TA"? Let's face it... if "Firmware Updates" are required RIGHT OUT of the box (in order to prevent black-outs, or in the event you'd like to use an HDMI cable, and ultimately to prevent COMPLETE failure of this set) at the LEAST they should include some instructions or explaination in the Users' Guide. Or better yet... they could include a simple CD-ROM for the computer (or web address for their site) where customers can easily download the necessary "Updates" - without sending clients on a wild-goose chase to simply get the darned thing to work as advertised. With the myriad of different options out there -(1080p, "True HD", 60Hz - 240Hz, 100,000 :1, LED or LCD... versus Plasma... etc, etc) it's tricky enough to find that perfect balance between price, options needed for your specific room and applications that you will be using this set for. Even though other people have had great experiences with this TCL television, maybe it is a GOOD thing that we got a "glitchy" one. Ultimately, I'm going to check out other brand sets in the $500 - $700 price range, with 40" to 42" screen (to fit our furniture). I DO know what we want and need for our space. Besides the obvious "black-out" problems, this set was just not a match for our needs or expectations. I do not claim to be an expert on HD televisions. However, I DO feel that NO ONE should have to go through SO much effort and aggervation - right out of the box... even if this TV WAS only priced at $400 bucks (when I purchased it). I think it's only fair to let people know EXACTLY what they will be getting from this company. Again, maybe we got a "lemon". Who knows? At least, hopefully my review will help someone out there and save them the time, money and aggervation that I experienced with this TCL television set. As bad as it was, I'm not willing to take a chance with another TCL. I can only IMAGINE how it must be when a customer attempts to call about their "2 Year Warranty". Luckily, Amazon was wonderful. They were truly helpful... No hassles to return the TV... SUPER fast(and FREE) pick-up and return processing.

Amazon’s, order confirmation email was acceptable. I sent all this and, at first, it didn’t seem to go through. After about 15 minutes they found my reply. Here is what I now expect to happen. After a day or so, they’ll send me an email telling me where to ship the defective unit (at my expense). After they receive and examine my unit, they will ship me a replacement. INFORMATION FROM SEIKI: The five "buttons" on the front of the TV are touch sensors and do not require any force to use. To remove all power to TV, press the power switch on the back of the TV. Leave power off for a few hours or more to completely lose charge. 2) There is also an option to do a factory reset on the TV, but this requires the use of some of the buttons. I'm not an audiophile, and currently have one good headphones (AKG K701) that are not really portable and I use them mostly when working from home (sound leakage, open design). I am looking for polyvalent wireless headphones, mostly to listen while working 8h / day. Tried the [[ASIN:B075749KHR Skullcandy Hesh 3 Wireless Headphone, Black (S6HTW-K033)]], the [[ASIN:B01MSZSJE9 Sennheiser HD 4.40 Around Ear Bluetooth Wireless Headphones (HD 4.40 BT)]], the [[ASIN:B074KBWVYT Sony Noise Cancelling Headphones WH1000XM2: Over Ear Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Case - Gold]] and the Bose QC35II. Did compare them on various musics, rock, pop, classic, ... . Bottom line: The only one I kept are the Hesh 3! Not for myself as I felt the comfort was not great (too tight / clamping pressure, burning ears after 1h listening), but for commute / smaller listening periods (i.e not full workday), they are great. Bluetooth is stable, sound quality is good. I'll keep looking for a comfy work-polyvalent headphones, probably give up the bluetooth criteria as I'm disappointed by the sound quality of the Sony & the Bose, and I'm not ready to put 350$ for 100$ audio quality level. Sound quality: Sony and the Bose are OK, but that's it, just OK, not great and not what I expect from 350$ headphones. Hesh3 have well defined bass (not too boomy, just what's needed to make it a fun headphones to listen to). Very good spatialization. Grabbed them at 80$ on black friday, and for my uneducated ears, they compare more to the Sony & the Bose than with my AKG K701 (not in the same category :-)). TBH, the sony & bose are a bit more clear than the Hesh3, but ... I feel the Hesh3 are more "fun" and would be my choice here. The clear looser here are the Sennheiser. They are disqualified from this review. Stay away from them, my 10y-old 15$ Koss are better. No spatialization, bad for rock, for pop, for classic... Might do for techno / podcasts. Build / comfort: Hesh 3 feels a bit plastic like at opening, but you quickly forget it. Comfort is so-so, you definitely feel them more than Sony & Bose. More clamping pressure, lower quality ear pads. Sony feels good and are probably the winner, I'm just a bit worried about the touch control thingy, what happens after the warranty expires ? Do you pay 200$ for repair if this stop working or bug ? Bose earpads feel less durable, BUT, they are the comfort winner. If you have money and want to buy a light, comfy headphones, go for it. Sony are the 2nd best in these models. Bluetooth: Hesh3: all good. Sony: I sent them back because... they kept jumping on my macbook. If I looked left or right, the sound will jump. If I walk 2 meter away from the laptop, it will jump. Worked good with my iPhone, but ... it's the only BT headphones I tried that was disqualified because of this. Not acceptable for this price range. Bose: did try them only 30min, but they seemed good. Sound leakage / isolation: Hesh3: no active noise cancellation, but cost 5 time less than the competition. I don't need that much noise cancellation and what they provide is enough to work in a open space, very little sound leakage. Sony / Bose: amazing. You put them on, and feel isolated from a lot of background noise. If you're looking for peaceful commute, they are worth it. The mic from the Sony did seems to pick less background noise in the few calls I tried.

If they have an auto-focus lens, you better have your lighting at studio quality like you are shooting a soap opera or it will focus in and out every 2 seconds. If they have manual focus, you won't have that problem but the auto-white balance may be whacked like this webcam. Too much light and the footage starts flashing and flickering all over the place like you are watching a found footage horror movie. I was wearing my wedding ring while recording some tabletop gameplay and the reflection from the ring caused the feed to start flashing as if it was having a seizure so I had to remove my ring. At least with this weird white-balance problem, you can always reduce something that you have in excess. The other problem with auto-focus? Good luck with that unless you are friends with Michael Bay. So this cam falls into the better cheapy webcam category. It's not going to replace a high end Logitech, but it's usable and serves its purpose.

For whatever reasons, manufacturers of M.2 devices "forget" to include the stud and screw needed to install the device to the computer instrument it needs to be attached to. Amazon sells several of these kits, in different configurations. In my experience, this is the better of these kits.Depending on your hardware, there are several different size fasteners needed for the task. Some other kits give you enough hardware for one or two installations, but not necessarily the right sizes. This kit comes with three sets in three sizes. When installing the M.2 device, start wit the new M.2 safely in the package it was dispensed to you. Instead, find a little magnet, and spread all the pieces in the magnetic tray or over the dace of a magnet. Then, with a good light, a dose of patience, and perhaps a magnifying lens (as your age and health dictate). Find the area of your computer (Mother-Board) where the card is supposed to be mounted and study it a bit. A YouTube short presentation may help. This system is a bit unusual and it will not hurt to get acquainted with all the participants before the fin begins. Next, install the heat-sink to the device, paying attention to pesky details. (Assuming the <.2 device is to be mounted parallel to the MB), measure the length of the M.2. This will hel0p you decide which mounting hole to use. Almost without exception, you will need a stud; the M.2 needs to go over the mounting holes/bases pput there for the shorter sizes. Going over them without touching; the studs are metal, the bottom of the M.2 is full of signal traces, metal to metal contact means trouble, etc. Install the stud in the appropriate hole. Finger tight is good enough, unless you have the proper tools. Next, the M.2 card needs to be gently inserted into the special socket (about 30 degrees angle), and then gently lowered onto the stud you just finger-tightened above. Hold the M.2 down and start a screw into the stud. fasten the screw gently. No need to torque anything, jsut tight enough so normal handling will not loosen it. Suggestion: Get yourself a tiny magnet. If it is small enough, attach it to the shaft of the tiny screwdriver that came with the kit. If not, try to rub the screwdriver with the magnet, a few times, but not back and forth. The goal is to make the screwdriver slightly magnetized. This way you will be able to pick up the screw with the screwdriver. Whatever you do, do NOT drop the screw or the stud into a crevice in the computer. If you do manage to do that, make absolutely sure you find the screw before you apply power to that computer. None of this has anything to do with this kit, but it is information surprisingly many do not possess.
