We eventually upgraded to an [[ASIN:B0013N3T7O Altec Lansing inMotion SoundBlade Bluetooth A2DP Speaker/Speakerphone (Black)]] which works great for that purpose, but a small problem remained, if the netbook crashes or needs to be rebooted for any reason, the music will stop. So we started looking for something else. Another feature she has always wanted was multi-room audio and just thought it was out of our price range; then we found the internet radios and thus the Squeezebox. This seemed to fill all our needs and then some and is still within our budget. After learning that it supported multi-room audio with additional devices it sealed the deal. We decided to go with the Radio version of the Squeezebox line because it had built-in speakers. When it arrived I was impressed with the heft of this device. It feels well made and has a nice fit and finish. The knobs have a velvety rubber feel to them and are of the continuous rotary kind, meaning that they don't stop turning at a certain point. You will use the main knob/button to enter in all the requested account information for the various services, including the Squeezebox account that it requires that you create the first time you turn it on; in fact you will be doing a lot of this with your various accounts and it can get tedious using the main knob/button. Before you can sign up for an account you will need an internet connection and if you don't plug into the ethernet you will be prompted to join a wifi network. Again, you will need to use the knob to input your wifi password. Pandora is one of the available services and the reason we purchased this device so I'll tell you how it works great for that purpose. It's a nice upgrade to have dedicated buttons to skip tracks, pause/play and volume as well. It will also link to online photo accounts like flickr and display random photos, or ones from your library or facebook, on the small, clear LCD. The sound quality is better than I expected for a small radio and never really distorts, even at max volume. Everything sounds rich and has fairly good bass response for a unit this size. This device really allows you to get more from your Pandora account. I will update this later as we become more familiar with it; we've only had it just over a week now. If they seem to be as good as I think they are right now we will be buying additional units for other rooms in her salon to enable a remotely-controlled, synced-up, multi-room audio system for far less than a [[ASIN:B001CROHX6 Sonos ZonePlayer 90 Wireless Multi-Room Music System for Home Theater or Stereo]].

The product features are good: This hub, and others identical to it, are great for tying a number of devices together, particularly if you want to run the hub some distance from your computer, so need the hub to be powered in order to maintain signal strength (quality/speed). It has on/off buttons for each port, which is nifty so you can power devices down without having to stress the cord or the internal connections unplugging connectors. It also functions unpowered, which can be nifty if you're traveling, and don't mind your computer/laptop pushing the power to your devices. The manufacturing may not be quality, and the customer service is significantly sub-par in my short experience: Unfortunately, the feature to operate without the power adapter can be a bit of a "gotcha", as in my case, I didn't notice for several months that the power adapter did not work properly.. my devices still worked most of the time, and they'd just flicker out occasionally, leading me to suspect cords, devices, computer processing and such. Once I noticed my laptop battery was draining while plugged in, but occasionally recovered and held a charge unplugged, I started investigating for a power draw, and quickly realized the hub was not operating correctly. If I pushed the DC cable into the hub firmly, or held it at an angle, the lights would stay bright, but if I did not apply pressure, the lights would randomly dim or brighten over time/jostling. These symptoms, which I described to technical support on my first contact, indicate that there is either a short in the DC power cable, or the DC plug is not making adequate connection to the port on the hub, or the solder joint of the port on the hub has failed. In other words, this requires a new power adapter connector (as I offered to solder the replacement into place), or a new hub to resolve. Despite describing an even more in depth set of trouble shooting which I used to absolutely identify the point of failure, they asked questions I had directly answered already. That's fairly common with the first line of "techs", so I answered their question, and again pointed out how the symptoms make it clear what the problem is. Their reply this time was fairly identical, saying if the problem was the hub, not to worry as they'd honor the warranty exchange. I replied answering their questions again, confirming the problem is the hub or the power adapter. Their next reply came several days later, and it was a notification that they were closing my case as I had not contacted them in several days. I replied, and said please don't close my case as I am waiting on you to reply and complete the warranty exchange. They never replied to that final message. I enjoyed using this hub, and promptly found a replacement with a few more ports manufactured by a slightly more reputable company who's customer service hopefully won't play the language barrier run-around, which it's hard to say if that's an innocent failure, or a more malign cost saving strategy.

I ordered it on 9/12/14 (Friday), and received it on 9/15/14 (Monday). For starters, I use this strictly as a HTPC: I purchased this primarily because I wanted to use my PlayOn digital media server application on a separate PC, so it would run faster. I didn't want PlayOn to continue hogging up the CPU resources on my laptop, while I was trying to use the laptop for other things. I wanted a DEDICATED device to be able to use PlayOn to watch TV, and also watch other streaming media online via Internet, Youtube, etc. I thought the price on this was really within my budget, plus the $20 rebate was an added bonus. This was EXACTLY what I needed!! I plugged the PC into my Samsung Smart TV via HDMI, before I even booted the device for the first time – no issues at all. The overall setup was pretty simple – just a small note: I did not realize I had to use a Microsoft Account to set it up – I guess this is specific to Windows 8 (???) – not sure. Anyway, I had to dig around to find my old Microsoft account info – an account I set up YEARS ago, for my Zune MP3 player – never really needed to use it again, until now. This was my first time working with Windows 8, but I became quite comfy with it fairly quickly. I did not use the wireless mouse or keyboard that came with the VivoPC – instead, I used the Logitech Wireless Touch Keyboard (K400) with built in mouse pad that I previously purchased for my Samsung TV – it works beautifully with the device…another plus. Now, I must say, as much as I REALLY like this device, unfortunately, and I am sorry to say this, but I have to take off stars because of the WIFI – it is TERRIBLY SLOW. When I initially noticed the slowness, I tested it using a popular speed testing website and it was horrible via wifi. However, while it is plugged in directly via Ethernet, I get GREAT speeds. I am not sure if others experience this wifi problem, but this is quite disappointing for such an overall quality device in other areas. I tried testing the speed problem further, after first ensuring that I had the latest drivers from the Asus drivers website - everything was already updated to the latest drivers. From what I could determine, it seems that the DISTANCE from the wifi router is a real problem for this PC. I have the PC sitting in the living room, next to the TV, which is about 30 feet from the wifi router, with 3 walls in between. With that amount of distance, I am experiencing VERY slow speeds. To further test the speed and signal, I moved the device DIRECTLY in front of my wifi router and tested the wireless speed – I got TOP SPEEDS (30MB down / 6 MB up) – with no problem at all. Afterwards, I moved the PC back to it’s original spot in the living room: 30 feet away – yes, I actually MEASURED the distance (by the way…I really like the PORTABILITY of this PC.) I tested the wireless speed again from 30 feet away: VERY SLOW SPEEDS – 0.5 MB down/up, being the SLOWEST. However, I did get a max of 2 MB down / 3 MB up at one point, which was surprising – but overall poor speed, and not the top speed that I’m currently paying for with my ISP. Now, my Vaio Laptop which is ALSO sitting in the living room (30 feet away) and running WIRELESSLY, gives me top speed (30MB down / 6 MB up). That is the EXACT same speed the VivoPC gave me when I sat it DIRECTLY in front of the wifi router to test the wireless speed. So sadly, distance is going to be a problem with the wifi capabilities of the VivoPC - that is about the ONLY negative thing I really have to say about this device. Other than that I really like it so far. So while I would love to give this about 4.5 maybe even 5 stars – I am going to have to deduct a star for the Wifi performance. I am sorry to say, it is terribly disappointing, and quite unexpected. I’m not sure if it’s in the hardware or the software, but maybe Asus will provide an update in the near future (wishful thinking, I guess.) Other than that, the VivoPC is VERY nice, as an HTPC and will probably do well for basic computing needs as well. But if I were remotely thinking of purchasing another one of these, the quality of the wifi performance alone would definitely be a deterrent for me, because there may be instances where you truly NEED the wireless capabilities. Even with this affordable price such as this, I wouldn't shell out another $229 + tax and not get a decent wifi signal, when the other devices in my home work fine with the wireless connection at the same distance. I’m sorry but that’s just unacceptable. It’s a little disappointing because years ago, I previously owned an Asus EEE Netbook, which was very nice, and it really made me take notice of the quality of the Asus brand, and even led me to later buy an Asus Slider Tablet which I still own. However for this particular Asus device, and for my home entertainment purposes, I’ll stay “plugged in” via Ethernet for now. If you’re going to basically leave this plugged in, wired via Ethernet, and use it for computing and/or HTPC purposes, then it should be FINE. Otherwise if using wifi, then the device should be placed fairly CLOSE to the router (or possibly purchase a Wireless USB Adapter with a better signal as a workaround.) Other than that, I am fine with this using device as an HTPC (connected via Ethernet) and I am satisfied overall with my purchase. It’s “officially” 3.5 stars for me. Thanks for reading and I hope this helps with your decision to purchase.

UPDATE 2022: Today, while I was watching Netflix, my computer shut off. Thoughtlessly, I pressed the power button to turn it back on. Immediately, I was met with sparks and a literal flame coming out of the top vent of my computer case, then the smell of burnt electronics. After taking the whole thing apart and checking individual pieces, I found out the motherboard was what had caught fire, and now did so every time I tried to turn it on. Literally nothing had changed - this computer had been sitting on the same shelf, unmoved, for months. I have no idea what happened. ORIGINAL REVIEW: This motherboard has been great for me so far! I could talk about all the nice features, but the product page does a pretty good job of that. Only problem was that something appears to be wrong with my USB and Bluetooth connections. Windows sporadically ceases to recognize the Bluetooth module and temporarily disconnects all of the devices, and the same for my mouse and keyboard that plug in via USB. Something must be defective in the motherboard, since I've upgraded all the drivers and OS as much as possible (instructions on manufacturer's website). Because of this small problem, I'm returning mine for a replacement, which hopefully is super easy with Amazon as always. UPDATE: I thought it was just a defective unit, so I actually tore my computer completely down, returned the motherboard, and installed a new one -- just to find the exact same issues again. I've tried several versions of Windows (including reinstalling Windows from scratch), every Bluetooth driver I could possibly find, and a variety of other things to no avail. It turns out this problem is not uncommon - you can find many mentions of it on this motherboard and other Gigabyte boards across the internet, if you look. I'm very, very dissatisfied that a company as well-known as Gigabyte would let this happen for so long, across multiple products.

I owned the Antennas Direct DB4 for roughly 3 years and was very happy with its overall performance. Its roof mounted(outside) on the J-30 mast and it held up very well to some of the nasty winds and weather we get here in upstate, NY. Anyway, I had my roof done so I figured Id give the DB4 to my bro-inlaw and buy the latest unit, the DB4e. With a limited amount of testing I feel like the general performance of the DB4e is *slightly* better for channels that I was receiving already. We had a few fringe channels that appear to come in a little better now and actually stay clean the whole time so thats an improvement. However, we didnt gain any new channels so this new version(DB4e) is NOT a revelation or anything. People are probably wondering if they should upgrade or not. I say for most users its not neccessary to upgrade if your current DB4(older model) is working well and you are happy. I dont think this one will do a heckuva lot. If there are some channels that you wished came in better then the upgrade is probably worth it. Lets summarize that: Its WORTH the upgrade IF - certain channels do get picked up by your current DB4(old model) but the reception is a little dodgy at times or you need that little extra boost to have it stay clean and clear the whole time. Its NOT WORTH the upgrade IF - You are hoping to pull in channels that you never received before. This new unit wont likely help. The DB4e is larger than the orignal by a decent amount but still works with the same J-mount mast. Build quality is about the same which I always felt was pretty good. Of course if you dont currently have any antenna or have an older crappy one, by ALL means get the DB4e - its a good product that has always served me right and its held up well in the weather too. Its priced right too, IMO. Id also suggest trying to mount it outside as high as you can. That alone makes a HUGE difference with any antenna. Good Luck!

[[VIDEOID:36510611]]Ever since I picked up my [[ASIN:B001OI2YNS Canon VIXIA HFS10]] camcorder, I've wanted to add a wide angle lens converter. Of course, the macro converter that Canon sells (the [[ASIN:B001UDHGMQ WD-H58]]) is pretty expensive and since I wouldn't use it very often I couldn't justify the cost. Then I noticed this Zeikos lens and thought at this price it was worth a try. I'm pretty happy with it. First, it looks great on my camcorder. It doesn't look cheap, and matches the style and look of the Vixia HFS10 very nicely. It comes with a "fit on" cap for the Wide Angle end of the lens and a "screw on" cap for the attachment side. It does what I was looking for, expanding a bit on the angle I can capture up close and extending the range of imagery that's in focus on a longer shot. The main thing I wanted was to be able to shoot a bit wider up close, since I sometimes use a green screen in my office and can't get my camera back very far from the screen. Though I was hoping it would go a bit wider than it does, this definitely helps. I'm not exactly sure what the .45x means, since as far as I can tell (based on measuring the relative size of objects with and without the lens on) this really gives about .8x magnification. I assume it may have to do with the fact that what you really have here is a "Macro" lens + a .45 Wide Angle lens and the net effect is to give a .8 magnification. What I didn't know when I bought this is that the "Macro" component of the lens and the "Wide Angle" component are separable. With the "Macro" filter alone you can get VERY close to objects like flowers and insects - and you can ONLY focus on things that are very close (between an inch or so to about half a foot). If you wanted to fit only "Wide Angle" component onto the Vixia HFS10 you'd need another adapter. Anyhow, the roughly .8 magnification of the whole set up is not quite as wide as I'd hoped but it does mean there is pretty minimal curvature effects around the edge of the frame - if you look closely at the attached video you'll see there is SOME curvature at the edges, noticeable on the right and left hand sides when the converter is attached. Anyhow, I wondered why Canon only sold a .7 converter when you could get an inexpensive .45 converter from another company - I assumed to begin with that was because .7 is as far as you can go without vignetting (change in light levels from the center to the periphery) or fisheye-like curvature, and so I worried a bit that this lens would show those effects. Luckily it doesn't show them to an unacceptable degree, but what my tests suggest is that this lens with its roughly .8 magnification is probably pretty close to what you actually get with Canon's own lens, and their numbers likely assess the "true" conversion rate of the lens as a whole, whereas the .45 only applies if you were to use only the "Wide Angle" portion of the lens. (If anyone knows more about this than I do I'd love to read about it in the comments.) One thing that is probably evident from this footage is that with the lens on there seems to be a slight loss in the light levels. That's to be expected, but it's something you can compensate for in the settings. I can't compare this to Canon's own lens, but since I picked this up at less than 10% of the cost, and it does most of what I wanted from it, I'm not complaining.

If you want an 5.1/7.1 amp with HDMI switching (6) phono amp and generally easy set-up to display on one screen this works well. If you want to make use of the second zone or A/B speaker features read on. They are very limited. A little background I have a PC, XboX and cable box all with HDMI outputs. I also use a projector and would like to also use a large tv (monitor the speakers don't work.) The PC and monitor are side-by-side and have a set of speakers. The projector is in the same room but to the right (90°) with at the full 5.1 surround system. I had a Yamaha amp HTR 5750 and many others over the years. The previous set-up used the A/B switch A - main system B - PC/monitor and both used the same input for sound. So if I wanted to play Xbox on the projector A or monitor B same for the PC or cable box. But I had to manually plug / switch the HDMI cord. (Side note part of the reason for this is the Kinect cable is not easy or cheap to extend the 50' that would be needed. Plus there are times when it would be nice to listen to music and watch something different - very possible with the Yamaha set-up.) Hurray! the VSX-1131 has 2 HDMI out and an A/B speaker setting or second zone. Should be perfect right? Nope. The A/B setting is not a simple button like the Yamaha (and Sony systems I have had in the past). It is a remote button press, selection (on screen not visible on the face of the receiver) and another selection. That's not very useful. I thought well I'll just set to A+B and use the PC internal volume control... BUT here is the kicker if you have A+B selected then system A is only 2 channel. Well the HDMI output (again several clicks in the on-screen menu) can be set to main / sub / main+sub. This is okay(?) set to main+sub now I get twin output. I can just turn the projector or monitor off. Guess what the sub output is stripped of sound! The only AV sound sources that can go to zone to are ANALOG - that is right. No digital sources to zone two. So if you want to use zone two to monitor the ball game while listening to music or just pipe music (analog) but if you actually want to watch and listen to the same thing in both places you need to have a device that will output the sound via TWO sources - one which you must convert to analog. But this completely kills the switching ability. While the set-up manual tries to be helpful and are generally nice the zone 2 / A+B speaker settings are not done well. Partial instruction located in several places. They are available on the Pioneer website. I encourage you to check the limitations. Summary Pros - works well for single screen - phono amp - 6 HDMI inputs (7 if you count the front) - easy set-up (multi-channel sound leveling) Cons - Zone 2 / Speaker A+B not well documented - Speaker A+B switch setting buried in menu - use of A+B speaker eliminates multi-channel on Speaker set A - 2nd HDMI output (sub) stripped of sound - only analog sources available for second zone - second zone switching and volume changing requires pressing poorly marked/located button - Android app has been hit or miss for connecting I have had this for about 4 months and have set and reset and thought through this several times. (My last idea was strip the sound out of the HDMI sub and feed back into an analog port...) At this point it really only 1/2 meets the needs I had when I purchased it. So I need to either get an HDMI switcher that can pass through audio and split off analog audio or just go back to manually switching HDMI cable.

These are solid connectors. One warning though: make sure you have everything setup before screwing them into place. If you have to unscrew them you might strip the little screws. That happened to me. I used heat shrink to seal them off and on a couple of wires I forgot to put it on before screwing down the spades, so I had to unscrew them, put the heat shrink on, and then screw them back into place. Doing so, a couple of the screws got stuck and a little stripped. Fortunately in each case it only happened to one of the two screws, and I was still able to get the problem screw all the way in, so the connection remained solid. The gold plating in the screw holes flake out and likely hamper the screw when screwing back in. That said, I would consider these as set-once and let-them-be forever. I don't know how they will hold up but based on the solid construction, the gold plating, and copper, I expect these will last a lifetime. I tested one channel with, and one channel without (bare wire), and the sound was either better or the same with the spades. I swear it sounded a little more open with them. This could have been due to slight oxidation forming on the bare wire channel. The reason I decided to go with spades was to permanently prevent oxidation over time. It feels good to know I will likely never have to re-trim wires again. One other little niggle: out of 16 spades, one might not have been perfectly flush, but I'm not sure if it was the particular spade or the angle I was connecting it, as I had poor access to the back of my amp. That said I did get it snug and all sounds good. The rest of the spades were completely flush when mounted making for a super solid connection. I would have given these five stars if not for the screws, but if you don't run into that problem then these are 5 star in my opinion. P.S. For those with an older model car like myself (mid 90s) or for those that just don't have bluetooth capabilities built into their car, this is the device for you. Siri/voice assistant is easy to use and is activated by pressing and holding the middle button for 3 seconds. Other features that are great to have include a USB port to access music via a thumb drive, a USB-C port that supports quick charge on newer model phones, a regular USB port for charging, a slot for music/media playback from micro SD card, and digital displays that allow you to view current radio station and current battery voltage. The LED light feature is an added bonus with an option to rotate through all the colors, however, there is no option to turn off the LED light. I am someone that does research before making any purchases and I am not disappointed with this bluetooth device. I would definitely recommend it for anyone looking to listen to music/media wirelessly in their car via bluetooth. Below is just a quick summary of the pros and cons I have found while using this device. Pros: -great audio quality, no noise feedback issues -easy pairing with smart phone -ability to use siri/voice assistant -shows current battery voltage -USB-C and regular USB charging ports -USB port and micro SD port for music/media playback -buttons on bluetooth device to change songs, play/pause, answer calls, adjust volume -multiple LED light options Cons: -no option to turn off the LED light

I wanted to give a good, qualified review of the Lomokino, so I waited to write this until I had loaded, shot, digitized, edited, and posted a movie from this camera. The entire process can be tedious, but the results are very unique. The camera is a lot of fun to shoot with too, but not without a few difficulties. First, the good: Finish: For a toy camera, Lomography put a lot of polish on the fit and finish. It is encased in a sort of faux leather, which actually lends the camera a pretty good aesthetic. It's small (about the size of a large orange), and although it feels like it would not withstand a beating, it did feel durable enough to use without worrying about breaking it. Image Quality: The image quality is what makes this camera truly unique. It shoots in a super-wide aspect ratio and uses a plastic lens, meaning that each frame you shoot has 25% area volume of a standard 35mm frame and its lens is far from sharp on the edges and corners. However, this is all part of the charm, and the look is uniquely Lomo. If you've ever shot through a Holga or Lomo camera, it's pretty much of that quality (although most of what gives any shot a "Lomo" aesthetic is the film, let's be honest). The Neutral: Film Loading: I couldn't call this one bad because each camera loads a little bit different. The loading mechanism is counter-intuitive, using a wrap-around method to position the emulsion side of the film behind the lens. What makes this difficult is that, unlike most cameras, the natural curl of the film must be overcome to get the film to load correctly. I'm sure Lomo did this to keep the size of the camera down, but it takes a time or two to master. Editing: This is what I really wanted to post about this camera. Not too many reviews fill in the details on how to digitize and edit your shots into a movie. Mostly, this topic is just glossed over, leaving you to just guess about how to do it. I'll share my technique. First, I use color-negative film, which if you're planning on using the kinoscope would not be a good idea, since all you'd see is a color negative. Once the film is shot and processed, I take the negative and digitize each frame using a Wolverine F2D Super film scanner. I line up each frame to the edge of the scanning area and digitize the shot. That process is repeated for every single frame. Once I have the shots digitized, I then need to trim off the excess so each picture is the same size. Since the digitization process yields the same size file, I can automate the crop process for each frame using Photoshop. This will make the crop for each image the exact same size. Once that is done, I grab all of the cropped images, rotate them 90 degrees, then drop them into a video editor. I usually give each frame about 6 frames' worth of time, which makes the motion fluid enough to watch without being overly choppy. Finally, I drop in a black bar matte of 3:1 aspect ratio to eliminate the jerky change in aspect ratio you see a lot with Lomokino films on the internet. I do this because, no matter what you shoot with, if your aspect ratio changes in your film (and you don't mean for it to), it's going to make what you shot look like garbage. Finally, I drop in some title cards and music and the process is done. The Bad: The Crank: I don't have high hopes for the crank. It seems awfully frail. That's pretty much it for this camera. If you can adapt to the neutral points, live with the bad ones, and enjoy the good ones, you'll get along famously with this camera. It is a lot of fun to shoot and the end result of the process is unlike anything I've shot with, but be warned it doesn't come easy and it requires a good attention to detail.

This sound bar from Wohome has been wonderful, and we’ve been very happy. We had been wanting one for some time, probably more than a year. I’m glad we did our homework and waited until we found this one. The 38” length is the perfect size for a 55” TV, and the 105dB output is perfect in a large great room. It has superior quality with a total of 6 built-in speakers and provides a rich full sound. The built-in subwoofer produces a deep bass. The sound bar offers pre-set equalizer modes for music, movie, and default. It also has adjustments for bass and treble. It sounds great for tv, movies, and music. Hookup of the sounder was fairly simple with the easy-to-read instructions provided. I am a 65-year old woman and completed the connections and startup easily. The sound bar was up and running in a few minutes. Operation is very straightforward. The sound bar includes options for many different audio connections on the back of the sound bar. It has Optical, USB, RCA, Aux, and ARC(HDMI) ports. It is also a nice option that you can use the 5.0 Bluetooth connection to play music from your phone or other bluetooth devices. The ARC port has been invaluable, and I can’t say enough about that. ARC is the best option if you have a newer tv model that supports it. There are a lot of sound bars on the market, with a higher price tag, that do not include an ARC port. Once you are connected to the ARC port, and you have selected it as your Input, your tv remote control turns the sound bar on/off with the tv and adjusts the sound level as well. I’ve seen several complaints about needing a separate remote. However, when using the ARC option, the remote is not necessary unless you want to fine tune your sound preferences or change the input (to bluetooth for instance). However, if needed, the remote works flawlessly and allows you to customize the sound to your preferences. There are a number of comments and questions related to the speaker volume. After the speaker is turned off, the volume is then way too high when it comes back on. We had the same problem. Some people have stated that their volume came on at the maximum level, but our volume came on every time at a 37 level. You can contact Customer Support at Wohome through their website or by sending an email directly to support@wohomeshop.com. Be sure to include your Amazon order # for their reference, the model number (S29), an accurate description of your problem, your name, and your email. They responded with instructions and an update file that I could upload to the sound bar through a flash drive to the the USB port. It took them less than 4 hours to respond. The instructions were easy to understand, and I had this “fix file” applied within minutes. The fix worked, and our volume now comes on at an acceptable level. We have truly enjoyed the Wohome S29 sound bar. I would recommend it to anyone, and I was once a real audio snob, if not an audiophile. We really didn’t see the need to mount the sound bar, even though hardware is included. We decided to leave it on the console, and it is very attractive. There has also been an unexpected added benefit, because the sound bar has kept the cat away from sitting and walking in front of the tv!

Summary: A well designed case that will definitely protect your Mini. A few minor issues (hard to take apart, dust getting trapped under the screen) means it's a solid 4 star product. The excellent price here at Amazon more than makes up for any shortcomings. Note: Be aware... this is NOT a waterproof Otterbox case, which is disappointing. UPDATE (Nov 2013) - ATTACHING & REMOVING THE CASE: ** REMOVING THE SILICONE COVER 1.) Start by pulling back the little tab covering the charging port 2.) Now slide your finger under the silicone piece covering the home button and pop it up 3.) Working from the center bottom of the case, remove the lower corners of the silicone cover 4.) Work your way up and around the case, being sure to carefully pull back on the tab above the volume keys (it covers the mute switch) 5.) At the top, carefully pull back on the tab covering the headphone jack ** OPENING THE CASE 1.) Look at the corners of the case, there are a few bigger connectors you need to free up... there are other smaller ones that are harder to see around the case --NOTE: NEVER push directly on the screen of the iPad Mini. The case WILL come apart WITHOUT ANY PRESSURE ON THE SCREEN. It is very difficult to get apart, but make sure you are only trying to seperate the case on the edges -- 2.) At the bottom, there is an opening for the charging port and speakers. Use this to provide leverage to get one corner of the case apart. In my experice, getting this first corner free is the toughest part 3.) Once you have one corner apart, slowly work your way around the case opening it (I generally work from lower right corner up to the volume keys and around counter clockwise ** PUTTING IPAD IN THE CASE 1.) Put your iPad Mini in the bottom half of the case 2.) Clean the inside screen of the top half of the case and the iPad Mini's screen 3.) Put the top half of the case on the Mini and secure it from the top corners down ** PUTTING THE SILICONE COVER ON THE CASE 1.) Start by putting the silicone cover on the top corners and work your way down 2.) Make sure all the edges are "tucked in" nicely 3.) Secure the cover over the home button 4.) Secure the tabs covering the headphone jack, mute button, and the charging port 5.) Make sure all your buttons work (be aware they are very stiff the first few days of use) !!! BACK TO THE REVIEW !!! Pros: - Good protection (hard case surrounded by silicone case) - Extra cover doubles as a viewing stand (it took me a few days to realize the stand allows the iPad Mini to be viewed in landscape modes at TWO heights... you can either have it laying almost flat or turn it 180 degrees and it's almost vertical -- very cool) - Built-in screen protector - Looks like a part of the Mini (without the extra cover) - All buttons/ports covered by the silicone cover - Cost Cons: - Dust collects under screen protector fairly quickly - Difficult to disassemble for screen cleaning - Silicone cover over charging port difficult to use, gets better with time - Volume buttons hard to press Review: This is our third iPad Mini... Yes, you read that right. The first one had no case, and was dropped 4 days after purchase (four days!!!) resulting in massive screen cracks. So it was replaced under Apple Care. The second one was immediately put into a Speck leather folio case. It lasted about a year with a couple of drops and no damage. Unfortunately, it took a drop right on the face (with the case open) and it was game over for the home button. Enter Apple Care and Mini number 3. We decided to up the protection and agonized over the Otterbox vs. Trident Kraken (what I have on my phone) vs. Lifeproof. Lifeproof is just to expensive. Yes, I know I've now spent more than $100 on the two replacement Minis and cases... It's still wrong for a case to cost that much. At $60, I'd buy it. But it's not, so... I love the Kraken case on my phone (and the silicone cover is Orange!), but I'd heard raves about the Otterbox case so we went with it. Essentially you get the same protection as the Kraken, but in reverse. The Otterbox is a two piece hard case that snaps on fairly easily followed by a silicone shell. (The Kraken is a silicone case that is then covered by a two piece hard shell). The Otterbox comes with a second hard cover that can snap on the front (for transporting and protecting screen) or the back. That's a nice bonus feature. The Otterbox looks very natural on the Mini. Especially without the second hard cover. It just about doubles the thickness and weight... But that doesn't impair usability. It does a nice job of slightly recessing the screen so hopefully a full face plant means the screen stays intact. The full outer silicone cover gives me hope it would bounce without further damaging the case. My Kraken case took an eight foot fall onto asphalt and protected the phone, but it left a small crack in the case. The only issues I've had are the volume buttons are difficult to press. Kids especially will not be able to work them. All the other buttons (power & home) work fairly easily, though I don't get tactile feedback with the home button anymore and that takes a little getting used to. The mute toggle (just above the volume buttons) is neatly hidden behind a silicone cover/door and is accessible by pulling back on the silicone door. In contrast, the Trident Kraken Case buttons on my phone are all easy to push and have a little "click" with each press. The charging port is covered by a silicone cover that is easy to pull back, but difficult to put back. It gets a little easier with time. My only real gripe is the screen protector. In the first week, I had to remove the entire case twice to clean the screen of dust particles trapped under the protector interfering with screen responsiveness. A couple of more times and I'll just remove the protector with an Exacto knife altogether and install a Ghost Armor or Invisible Shield. Bottom line... Overall, I'm very pleased with this case. Very good protection (equivalent to the Trident Kraken) in a much more aesthetically pleasing design. Loses points for difficult to press volume buttons and dust quickly collecting under the screen protector (and not being waterproof). Gains points back for its very competitive price, especially here on Amazon. If you're on the fence, it's a good choice.

Undercabinet TVs are not very common. The big boys really don't make them. When a relative moved into a new house, she wanted to have one in her kitchen the same as the kitchen she just moved from. So I went on this search to find one that looked reliable and had good features. This is the one we settled on. The LCD seems of good quality and with and HD picture source the screen is pretty good. The input is basically limited to coaxial cable and does not have an HDMI port. I don't think the screen is true HD resolution, but it is pretty close. Getting around in the features is not the easiest thing in the world but it's workable. If you are looking for your first feature being undercabinet and don't care much about the rest then you are good. The biggest problem I have with it is that the TV plugs into a GFI circuit in the kitchen. Whenever the circuit should happen to trip, which it has twice in the past month...the unit completely forgets everything about itself. Not just the clock, but all the channel programming, settings everything. So I have to rescan for channels again, set the clock again, etc. This is very annoying even if it were to happen only once a year after a storm. However, you get what you get when there are limited choices in this type of product. Buy this if you really need the unit to be undercabinet and have a DVD player built in. If you can just get away with a regular HDTV on the counter I would recommend it instead. Since this screen is so big, when its open it basically forces you to move everything under the unit that you might want to keep there to someplace else anyway. You really don't get to use the counter space there if you plan to use the TV every few days or so. Why not just give up the counter and have a TV that remembers its programming?

I have been shooting with Canon Vixia's for years and they've always been winners! Recently my oldest one (as in mini DV tapes) started having problems with the shutter not opening all the way and I was told it would cost more to replace the part than to buy a new one, so I bought a new one, and by new one I mean this refurbished one. Mostly what I use these cameras for is to record local concerts and arts events to make performance videos for different groups like high schools and colleges. A few of these cameras set at different places in a concert hall really make for a nice finished product! You should know however that I don't use the built in audio. I either pair it with house mic recordings when available or use my own pair of stereo mics with a zoom H4N recorder. That being said, the audio on these isn't half bad for the price! I also use this to shoot video for a YouTube channel. I sing and tour with the Salt Lake Vocal Artists all over the world and record our audio and video as we perform in different churches and venues and need equipment that is light and easy to pack/travel with/set up and this Vixia is perfect for that purpose! If you want to see a sample of the kind of end result I get with these Vixia's go to YouTube and search Salt Lake Vocal Artists if you want to see a sample of what the finished product of this camera looks like. ALL of these videos were shot with Canon Vixia's. I love how easy these cameras are to use, but it would behoove any first time user to spend a little time with the manual going through and arranging the settings one by one to make sure everything is set just how you want it for your purposes before you start shooting. That being said, you can use it right out of the box without messing with anything if you don't feel like it. I love the touch screen and that you can flip it around to face you if you're filming a YouTube video for instance, so you can see what is being captured and frame your shot correctly. The picture is sharp and clear! My only complaint is that I wish the battery life were longer. That being said, I don't know that it's any worse than other similar cameras at similar price ranges, and it will last for an entire concert which is mostly what I use it for anyway. If you need the battery to last longer, I suggest buying one of those plug in batteries that you can connect to an outlet and use as long as you want. I also have to say I'm REALLY thrilled that these are offered refurbished on Amazon! If you're nervous about the word "refurbished" don't be. These cameras come looking and working like new and you save a boat load of money! I buy refurbished on Amazon whenever I can and I've never been burned! I highly recommend this camera for all kinds of uses, especially for entry level YouTubers or those who don't have enough room on their smart phones to capture everything they want to capture. For the record I paid full price for this! Hope this helps!

EDIT-- +1 star for having awesome support! I was provided a functional firmware, which I like! Its not perfect, but it certainly resolves my issue. :) I practically lost my mind when 66 Audio released an update to their previous 66 Audio BTS+ model! I needed a pair of headphones that were both comfortable, and technically advanced enough to more advanced Bluetooth audio codecs such as AptX and AptX-LL-- even purchasing two of these! Compared to all the clones out there, the quality certainly feels great—plastic but feels solid, with metal accents (which I suspect is the antennae themselves, kudos for adding an external antenna—if that’s the case!) The ear cushions are a sort of memory foam, covered with synthetic leather material. The antenna range is AMAZING, especially if you pair it with a Bluetooth audio transmitter with an antenna which I have-- it covers nearly the entire first floor of my home. Audio quality also sounds amazing compared to my older pair, though it’s a little heavy on the low-end for me, flattening my EQ levels solves this problem for me and works perfect for gaming. Works and pairs perfectly with my OnePlus 3, connects with my PC bluetooth and Bluetooth audio transmitter with no problems at all, even using it in my gaming sessions. I have even taken it on my long jogs and it has handled moisture/sweat easily—just remember to clean it with a damp cloth, as your body’s salts and other residue will remain once the liquid dries, which can damage the unit over time. One big reason I purchased a pair of these is because of the AptX-LL protocol. To me, the AptX-LL audio codec is a godsend-- making audio delays near indiscernible (~30ms vs. 80-150+ms on A2DP / SBC audio codec) and eliminating lip sync delays on both my movies and games on my PC! Unfortunately, for reasons unknown the headphones came with this very feature disabled on the firmware level. I have a small collections of AptX-LL Bluetooth audio transceivers, some with displays to show the status of the Bluetooth connection. Other AptX-LL enabled receivers connect via AptX-LL with no problems except for these headphones. Unfortunately to date (firmware 1.06), this feature remains disabled for some reason, which is a HUGE disappointment for me. I waited a few months to see if this improves and unfortunately I have lost confidence that this can be fixed. If audio delay is important to you then look elsewhere—otherwise these are one of the best behind-the-head style headphones I’ve ever owned.

Purchased this USB extender on 4th-Sep-2021 and died 12th-Dec-2021. In life, it worked great, but in death it would only work for a while and then required that I reboot my computer. Now on 14th-Dec-2021 it refuses to work with my flash drive with or without rebooting. A 3 month lifespan is too short to justify the money I spent. I will explain will how the determination was made: Possible problems are bad computer USB port, or bad USB flash drive or this USB extender is bad). I used this approach: I took the questionable flash drive out of this USB port extender and plug it directly into an unused USB port of my computer--flash drive worked fine -- so now I know the flash drive and the previously used computer USB port are both good. Unplugged this USB extender from my computer and inserted the flash drive into that USB computer port that had previously been used for this USB extender -- the flash drive works in both USB computer ports. Plugged this USB extender into the other USB port (not the one that had been previously used with this USB extender) -- flash drive still working where this USB extender had been used. Move the flash drive back to this USB extender -- flash drive not working in this extender, again. (Also had same results with my 5T USB external hard drive.) My conclusion is that the problem moves with this USB extender. (No data was lost. Both of the storage devices I used for troubleshooting were simply not recognized when plug into this USB extender.) A three month lifespan is not good enough!!! It would have been better if it never worked, because Amazon would have refunded the purchase. I will make it a point to never buy this unreliable brand again, but I will buy from Amazon again.

I purchased the Archerfish solo from Amazon.com after reading the excellent reviews. Setup easily done with a Mac and a Belkin wireless router. The problems began after disconnecting the Archerfish from the ethernet and attempting to set it up at the surveillance spot. Got that blinking orange light - no connection. I called the support line (excellent service - the guys tried hard) and after about an hour of troubleshooting he recommended trying a different router, as some models of Belkins had a history of connection problems with the Solo. I then purchased a Netgear N600 dualband router. Same story. This time I was on the phone with the support person for almost 90 min, which happened to be 30 minutes past his closing time. He tried hard, multiple shenanigans via remote access to my ip address and router settings - again he was able to connect it via ethernet, but once unplugged, even when placed adjacent to the router - no connection would happen. This is about day 12 into my purchase. The support guy assured me that since I had addressed the network problem within a short time of my purchase that Archerfish would refund my unit if I continued to have problems. I fiddled with it for a few days, reluctant to call support again as each call takes about an hour of dedicated phone time. I then left for Cambodia for 2 weeks (the main reason I wanted a surveillance cam). Upon my return, the unit continued to be nonfunctional. Called support again -we worked remotely for a third time, at which time I asked to return the unit. The answer? If bought from Amazon.com I must be compliant with their return policy (30 days). I was 2 days over Amazon's return period and the Archerfish company refused to take it back, despite a well documented history of problems. SO BE CAREFUL!! If it doesn't work, return it quickly despite reassurances that the problems can be solved. Don't rely on the Archerfish customer service to help you. I now have a nonworking expensive camera after spending hours on the phone with them. Yes the remote support person is a great help, but no they cannot solve everything. Addendum - I have modified this review after Archerfish sent me out a replacement - the replacement unit worked perfectly and was simple to install and use. I was pretty sure that the first unit was defective, but had to discuss this with customer support at least 4-5 times before they would send out the replacement unit. I wasted a lot of time on the first defective unit and I wish they would've been able to recognize the problem sooner. Other than that, we love it. I have used this card both in my Windows Vista setup and Linux. The digital side of the card is brilliant - crystal clear picture and no noticeable system performance hit while it is recording. Granted, recording digital is just transferring a stream of 1's and 0's over the PCIe bus. I have only recorded over-the-air digital broadcasts (ATSC) on this side of the card. Analog cable reception was reasonable under SageTV, although somewhat less clear than the same analog cable channels on my LCD TV. My antenna and cables are cheap, which I found hurts the signal considerably more for this card than when attached to the TV. If I just wanted to record digital, which may suffice for many people, I would have opted for one of the software-based cards at half the cost. I still have enough analog cable channels to warrant the hardware encoder. One feature I have yet to use is the composite IN. If it goes well, this should be a nice feature for digitizing old VHS tapes. I can warn that I had no real success in setting up this card in MythTV (MythBuntu, to be precise) although a small no-nonsense TV application called MeTV did a great job recording hours of sharp over-the-air Olympics broadcasts for me off of a channels.conf file. If it weren't for the latter success, I would assume the card isn't supported in Linux. But despite the ambiguity of web sources on this point, the digital tuner of this card is in fact supported in kernel 2.4.

I can see how people have been getting very frustrated with the installation of the thin plastic pieces included for cable management. They're meant to be bent into 2 diagonal grooves in the wood that hold it in place in a curved shape. The cables then slip between the plastic and the wood. The natural way to try to install this is to put one side into the grooves completely and try to work the other side in little by little. This method is WRONG and will lead to complete frustration. THE CORRECT WAY: Put the 2 end corners of the plastic piece into BOTH GROOVES at the SAME TIME. Then, work your way down the plastic piece with 1 finger on each side, guiding the edges of the plastic into the both grooves together. This makes the installation 100x easier. If you try the other way, you'll bend up the plastic piece and want to throw it across the room. It took me one stand assembly to realize this, the second one I did the correct way and it took all of 20 seconds to install.

I picked up the Otterbox Defender for the S7 because the phone by itself felt too slippery. The Otterbox promised to toughen up the phone so it could survive drops as well. The case comes in 3 pieces, an internal shell that goes directly around the S7, a rubber bumper that goes around that shell, and then a holster. The shell and bumper weigh 81g, and I didn't bother weighing the holster because it was so bulky as to be unusable. The resultant phone inside the bumper felt very grippy. So much so that when I slid the phone into a pocket, it would grab the sides of the pocket and not go all the way into the pocket! Extracting the phone from a pocket had the same feeling. The rubber bumper has flaps for USB charging and the headphones, and these are the most solid flaps I've ever seen. They definitely will protect the phone! The biggest flaw with the case is that the top and bottom lips interfere with the functions of the phone. The top lip prevents you from using the "pull down" gesture to drag down notifications. The bottom lip prevents the finger print reader from registering all the time. I don't know how this could have been prevented --- one possibility is that there's so little bezel space that any lip would have intruded, but without trying a slew of cases there's no way to find out. Ultimately, I returned the S7, but I'm pretty sure I would have to return it for the gesture interference problems anyway.

I purchased this remote to use with a Pentax K20D & when I got it there were NO instructions. SO I want to try to help anyone else out who may not know how to use this remote with their camera. On my camera you have to change 2 different settings. The first one has to do with AUTO FOCUS. On my camera I have to push the menu button & then scroll over until I come to the "Custom" menu & hit ok. Then scroll down the Custom menu until you see "Auto Focus Remote" & switch that to "ON" & leave it like that. Now when you use your remote, it will auto focus first. Otherwise it won't & you have to look through the viewfinder & press the shutter release half way to lock focus. The 2nd setting is under the "Fn" menu & then press the up arrow to choose your "drive" mode (single, continuous, self timer, or remote). Set it to remote & choose "single, 3 sec delay, or continuous." This you will have to change every time you use the remote. It's now set & you can use it to auto focus!

I was excited to get this light as an affordable step up to a strobe from speedlights. I wanted strobe power but with a battery - something portable that I could easily take on outdoor shoots. This was not my first choice, but the price was right, and it was worth trying this out. What I love: It is powerful - 300ws of power, enough to overpower the sun when shooting in bright conditions. Easy to use - with very little experience using a strobe, I was able to quickly start using this without pouring through the (small) user guide. Excellent battery life - I've not yet been able to run down the battery after at least a couple hundred shots. Durable - as others have noted, it is built like a tank. Reliable - With over 200 shots, I've not noticed any misfires, and the light, as best I can tell, has been quite even. What I'm less thrilled with: Size & weight - while very portable, this has some heft to it; not something you want to lug long distances. Trigger - extremely low build quality and no options to adjust the light remotely. Features are limited - modeling light controls are limited to on/off and it will only stay on for around 1 minute; unless I'm missing it, you're limited to full-stop adjustments from 1/1 to 1/128 - 1/3 increments would help; and most importantly, no support for HSS and TTL. One of the benefits of a powerful light like this is the ability to add light in bright environments, but without HSS, you're left wanting/needing an ND filter for shooting at wider apertures. I'm honestly on the fence about this light. For the price, it is hard to imagine a better value. I've not come across a light this powerful, especially one with a trigger (yes, it's cheap, but it works), for anywhere close to this price. But that is where I am wondering about keeping this. For a little more money, you can get the Godox/Flashpoint AD200. It is not as powerful, but is way more portable and has a variety of affordable modifiers available. Portability is probably a little more important to me than power, but I'm so pleased with the light and what all that power can do that I'm inclined to keep this. BTW, I've had pretty good success using this with cheap speedlights set as optical slaves. This opens up a lot more shooting options.

Having had the Cavision finder on a previous shoot, I thought it wouldn't be ridiculous to "brand-upgrade" to the Alan Gordon. Mechanically, it's identical, from my observations. Cosmetically/functionally, I like the knurling on the aspect ratio ring better than the Cavision. However, on the particular model I received, there are two major differences between this and the model I'm familiar with: The sensors/film sizes labeled on this dvf are anamorphic, S35, S16, 1/2", and 2/3" - it lacks the 1/3" size that is in the manual. Which is a problem if you shoot 1/3" with interchangeable lenses. However, this isn't really an issue for me. Just something for other users to consider. [For those looking for a viewfinder for their 35mm-stills sized sensors, this isn't for you. If you try getting measurements out of this, you'll go under (S35 and below) or over (anamorphic). Look for a model that says it has "full frame," instead.] The other item is in regards to the aspect ratios. Now, the aspect ratios it has labeled are 1.33, 16:9, 1.85, and 2.35. However, the device has all the ratios described in the brochure as hard stops, including the two slightly-different 1.33 ratios, a 1.66 ratio, and the 2.55 ratio - they are just not labeled. Could be a little annoying, but, if you're on a shoot, you're probably going to live on one aspect ratio - and, unless you're the type to shoot in obscure aspect ratios (or extremely narrow ones), you probably won't even need these unlabeled ones. Quirks aside, it's still a solid little item, and I recommend it to any directors and cinematographers who haven't yet developed the reflexive knowledge of what lenses to use, and even those that do, in case you need an analog reminder of your framing. I mildly prefer it over an app, simply because it's one less battery to worry about. Long and short: Would recommend to any and all filmmakers, if you don't shoot with a 35mm-stills sensor. APS-C or S35 is all you can do with this finder. Update: Not long after posting this, I dropped the viewfinder, which threw the aspect ratio mattes off their tracks. Spent a lot of time trying to repair it, but wound up losing a metal ball and spring, which made the hard stops I described above. I scratched into the metal to mark these spots previously, so I can still eyeball those aspect ratios. Bit of a hassle though. Could be better constructed, but easy enough to repair, provided you don't lose the ball and spring in a carpeted room.

So what do I love about the Sennheiser momentum 4 headphones: I love to fit and feel. I love its design and the way it looks I got the white version. These headphones stay on my head no matter what I'm doing. These are the first headphones that have done that. I love its call quality. It's not as good as the Sony XM5 but very good. I love it's noise cancellation. It's really good. The touchpad is very responsive, easy to use and you have one button for the assistant on your phone. Very helpful and user friendly. Excellent battery life. People think you don't need 60 hours. That's the only pair of headphones that I have. I need those 60 hours because I use them daily for many hours a day. And I don't have to charge them but more than once a week sometimes depending on my usage. It's 7 to 10 days. I like the fact that the sealer on my ears is almost perfect. No wind or any other noise gets in behind my ears which sometimes can cause sputter if you're listening to music. I also love how the case works as a de facto off switch. You could place the headphones in the case and it will automatically turn off the headphones. You can then remove them from your case and it will turn them on and then connect to your device. I love the sound quality with this one Caveat, if you experienced the power of the Sennheiser momentum 3, you will be missing that with these headphones. Sad to say, but it appears that Sennheiser has decided to be mommy and daddy and tell us how loud our music should be. I don't like that. It's still a great sound but it's just not as powerful as the momentum 3. As for what I don't like: I don't like it's multi-point connection. There's something weird that happens. What is connected to two devices and you try to use the other devices connected to it starts making this weird beeping noise. I have to literally turn off the audio on one device so if I'm using it while connected to another device, it won't make that noise. I don't like that. I still don't like the three band EQ. It's 2022. Most headphones that have an EQ have at least five bands come on Sennheiser. The app is a little wonky. Sometimes it doesn't connect when the headphones connect. Sometimes you have to go to the app and tap it two or three times before it will connect. But to be honest, those are really minor problems that aren't daily annoyances. Overall, these are some of the best headphones I've ever had and I've had a lot. Most of everything that you need works well, including the head sensor for the autoplay and auto stop. Also, the head sensor is good for muting the caller. These headphones are just great. They are definitely worth the purchase. Between these and the Sony XM5 they are only headphones I really need.

The TL;DR is simple: I have found the SW321C to be a phenomenal, no-compromises, nearly flawless monitor. Great stand, great user interface (I love the puck), outstanding image quality, even backlight, no backlight bleed. It's superb for work and leisure. There's IPS glow, but that's unavoidable. I'm a programmer who spends most of his time on his computer -- reading/writing text, watching video, and playing games. Previously I was using 2 Dell U2518D monitors, which, even after calibration with an iDisplay Pro Plus, had the following issues: * Crushed blacks * Poor contrast * Uneven colors * Uneven backlight * Backlight bleed * Glare, despite the matte surface After deciding I didn't want to put up with those issues any longer, I did a week or two of research on what the best no-compromises monitors were in late 2020. That led me to the SW321C, a professional monitor rather than a gaming/consumer monitor, because consumer models -- no matter how fancy they claimed to be or how slick the marketing -- all seemed to fall short and require me to resign myself to compromises in at least one area (and I didn't want FALD). The BenQ SW321C is expensive (though not as expensive as the EIZO and Dell screens that it's often compared to), but I consider the money well spent. The image quality is outstanding. Colors are stunning. Images and text are markedly sharper and crisper than they were on my 25" 1440p monitors (though this would be true of any 4k 32" screen). The backlight is the evenest I've ever seen. There's no backlight bleed that I can detect. I love the shade hood and never take it off. The matte coating is far and away the best I've seen/used. For the movies and tv shows I've watched on it (Blade Runner, Ex Machina, The Witch, The Expanse, The Man in the High Castle, The Midnight Gospel), I couldn't be happier with the quality of the picture. The HDR may be "fake," but it still massively improves the viewing experience, especially in regard to handling of darkness/shadows. Last year I bought and returned the BenQ SW271. I loved it, but the backlight was uneven, there was backlight bleed, and 27" was too small for 4K". (32" is, for my eyes (late 30s), the perfect size for a 4k screen.) If I was going to spend $1,500, I wasn't willing to put up with those issues. The SW321 isn't as bright as the SW271, which is a shame, but it also fixes every issue I had with the SW271. == Update: the blacks aren't as dark as I'd like them to be. (EDIT: correction, for $2k you can NOT get a very decent oled tv with perfect blacks. You will experience burn in.) The monitor also seems to produce a lot of heat. I'm not sure I regret the purchase. It still ticks all the boxes for me, and I consider the money well spent, but if I could do it again, and my living quarters allowed it, (EDIT and recantation: I would not opt for an OLED) Update #2: Scratch that. I still wish the blacks were darker, but this is as good as it gets on an IPS panel. OLED TVs aren't meant to be used as PC monitors, and if you use one that way, there will inevitably be burn in. I'm still quite happy with the purchase, despite the one, single, occasional stuck sub-pixel. I've seen a few reviews here that fault the hardware calibration, but for me it has been superb -- certainly better, to my untrained eye, than the i1 Display Pro Plus's software calibration. That being said, I encountered a couple of bugs/problems when using the Palette Master software: it didn't detect my calibrator until I set colors to 10 bit, full output, and I had to plug it into a USB port on my desktop, not one of the SW321C's USB ports. Update #3: The stuck pixel started to occur more frequently, so I contacted BenQ customer service and asked them to service the screen. The customer-support staff, who were phenomenal -- prompt, professional, understanding, knowledgeable, and incredibly to work with -- helped me, despite a couple of mix ups (which weren't their fault), resolve the matter to my satisfaction. Update #4: The top review is... awful. What on earth sort of person brags(?) about bossing around delivery people? The top item in this person's list of pros is "high Quality Display Monitor," but the review also states that the screen was defective, that s/he has seen better image quality on $200 monitors, and that the colors look "horrible." Garbage. Neither of us is an expert. Ignore amazon reviews. Read reviews written by professional photographers, for whom this monitor is intended. Dec 2022 update: my sw321c is one of my favorite possessions. Even my partner who isn't finicky about screen quality loves it. Watching movies or shows on it is always a treat. I can't praise it highly enough. And I can't believe I omitted from my review that its cardboard box is the nicest, most thoughtful I've encountered for anything I've purchased. It's huge but well worth keeping, as it protects the monitor perfectly and stores and organizes everything incredibly cleanly and effectively. No loose cables. No textured carton compartments. Everything has its isolated section, or its own box (which perfectly fits into only one place). My only complaint with the monitor concerns the shade ood, which has started to fall apart easily. I doubt it's meant to be handled, put on, or taken off as much as I have though. I cover the screen with several layers of cloth when I'm not using it, e.g. at night, because I want to keep it pristine, and they don't fit over the hood.

Ok, so I replaced my internet/voice/TV package from Frontier Communications (formerly AT&T Uverse) with a triple play package from Comcast including Xfinity Blast Internet at 105Mbps. The location of the modem/router was originally in the center of our center hall colonial, but Comcast could not easily accommodate this central location so the equipment had to be placed in the corner of the ground floor. This location presented an issue for the bedrooms upstairs and on the other side of the house. I could still connect but I was not getting anything close the xfinity "blast" speed that came with the package. I considered an extender but decided to invest in the Nighthawk as they claimed to have the horsepower in their signal to cover a lot of territory. I received the product and set it up which was quite simple as with all Netgear products, however the farther away bedrooms upstairs got only a nominally better signal than with the Netgear WNDR4500 router I was replacing. In the rooms furthest away from the router the signal strength on the 2.4Mhz radio went from 40% to 50% after the upgrade; the connection speed remained about the same @ about 14mbps (vs over 100Mbps in the room where the new router was placed). I spoke to Netgear technical support a couple of times. We upgraded the software and changed some of the channels but nothing improved. The first guy I spoke to said that I should just return the Nighthawk and keep my WNDR4500 router but add an extender. I decided to keep the Nighthawk and add Netgear AC1200 range extender. Given the ever increasing number of connected devices we have in the home I think that the Nighthawk is better suited to handle the multi device load and the extender should boost the degraded signal on the opposite side of the house. All in all though the cost was way way over what I would have expected to pay for wireless access ($279 for router + $126 for extender). When the range extender comes in today I will test it with both the new Nighthawk and the Wndr4500. I may change my mind and send the Nighthawk back. Update 3/11/2015 I got the range extender (ac1200 aka model ex6200) and had all sorts of issues getting it to work with the router. Tech support ultimately suggested I return it for a new one which I did. The new one did not work either. I could get it to connect on one radio but not both (2.4 ghz and 5 ghz). Since I really wanted to improve network speed all over the house I tried one more shot. I returned the ac1200 extender and went for the top of the line AC1900 Nighthawk range extender (model ex7000). I thought that since they were both tagged with the "Nighthawk" brand that they might actually work together. I was correct on this; I got it installed and connecting from extender to router to modem on all radios. I have noticed so far that while all is working and I have achieved good high speed connectivity all over the house the connections to the extender has dropped from time to time requiring a reconnect. I will be contacting Netgear on this issue. Given that this is their top of the line consumer router / extender combination which i spent nearly $500 on I hope they will finally resolve this last issue.

To sum it all up, android was not made for head units. This Dasaita promises to do a lot of things, and for the most part, it delivers. Contacting support felt extremely disconnected, it took two days to get a reply and most of the messages seemed unprofessional and rude. Another ding against Dasaita is that they do not own any of the software on this head unit. Carplay is through an app called "Zlink" which is another Chinese company that licensed their software for this application, that is why SWC didn't work, Dasaita didn't make the app so they couldn't fix it. To add on top of that the stereo glitches and acts up when it is brand new out of the box. Carplay can sometimes take a minute to sync; if this is how bad the software is now, imagine how it will be in 5 years when the software is out of date. The credibility of Dasaita comes to mind when looking at the flawed interior design of the radio. The heat spreader on the board is terrible at managing thermals, during the summer months this radio will certainly overheat and die within 2 years, who's to say Dasaita support will even be around then. For the money just get a Pioneer or something like that. The screen may be worse but at least it will be a product with some thought and care.

I did professional photography in the ancient days of film and 35mm. I've never been very happy with the quality of digital (though the convenience of it is really nice) and have a love of eating regularly, so I gave up professional photography in favor of working for a living. Fast-forward 30 some years. Digital photography is beginning to approach the quality of 35mm and the affordability of the working-class slobs like me, so I decided I needed something illuminating for inside work. After much consideration and research in value, quality, cost, etc. I settled on this bundle. Keeping in mind that prices often change, I found it to be an excellent little studio for the kind of limited, inside shooting I do. The good: - Set-up is relatively simple. - Very portable. - Decent lighting included. - Backdrops are large enough for most indoor purposes. - Very affordable The bad: - No clips to hold backdrops (they can drape, but you get wrinkles if you don't clip it). - Cords for lights could use an extra six feet or so each. - Case doesn't even come close to holding everything - only the backdrop stands. - Not exactly professional quality. When I ordered this, I added the cheapie clips (currently unavailable now) [http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005CRKZOM], white umbrellas [http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005AKF0XM] and a large gym bag to carry it all. For indoor, non-professional photography of people, this is an excellent kit for those looking to expand their photography skills. It's one thing to point and shoot. It's another to work in a "studio" environment and hone one's skills in capturing the right lighting, pose, composition and other aspects of photographing people. It CAN be used for pets, but they had better be sedated or really laid back about it. It provides more than enough light for non-flash photography, which makes composition simpler prior to taking the picture. With a little thought (flipping the umbrellas around, or putting them on one side), lighting effects are easy to accomplish. For pros: If you have a static studio and need portability, this will be a "do-for". It's not great, don't set it up in anyplace with a draft and you're set for some good shots. The backdrops can be layered to eliminate light bleed-through and with sunlight and lighting effects, the results can be pretty stunning. Just make sure you have the clips and some patience since the way the backdrops are folded, there are creases that need to be ironed out. Back in the days of Coken filters and losing money on every bad shot, I was rather anal about making sure things were "perfect" before I ever pressed the shutter release. Today, the fudge factor is much higher (thanks in part to a general lack of manual focus in prosumer digital cameras), but the cost of taking, and examining, a photograph are nothing if you already have the camera. Assuming I get back into photography as heavily as I used to be, I'll be getting better cameras. But since I don't plan on doing it professionally, I think this studio starter bundle will provide excellent service for my relatively modest needs. So for non-professionals who want a touch of professionalism in their photos and to inexpensively get into studio photography, this is five stars. For pros who need something in the field, this is three, since it will not replicate a full static studio in someone else's home, but it's adequate if you're a good photographer to begin with.

It works as described, with catches. This product is developed by the company previously known as Elgato. I forget the name of of the company before that. I have used their Tuner on Mac many years ago. They are pretty much the only company making these devices, so there isn't any option. There isn't competition. I purchased this Android adapter before looking deeper into the Manufacturer. Was looking for a simple way to add a HDTV tuner over USB, and here it is. The catch, the software is clunky, the tuner may need an extension cable, and it over heats super easy. If the usb connection shifts at all while in use you will loose signal and it requires physical disconnect. There is no driver so the phone sees this OTG as a a battery that needs to be charged and I cannot change that. To resolve the issue of the plug not fitting my USB-C jack, I purchased an extension. I recommend something 1 no more than 2 inches, but most flexible C to C extensions start at 6 inches and cost the same as 3ft. Next there is the issue of the heat, I took off the plastic snap fit housing, then applied a layer of Phase Change Material to both sides, Over that I pined a few bits of smoothed metal for making video card heat sync shims. Metal office clips hold it all together, and now the device runs for hours as long as the battery in the phone holds out. My phone has a 8000mAh battery, but the Tuner will still run it down in about 2 hours. With the mods it is stable. 1st run: You have to click on the flag in the Channel Search window to find USA. That was confusing. If the channels cant be found, try the bigger antenna. But chances are, it's already over heated and it wont find anything. You will need to let it cool and try again, be quick about it. Don't touch it while it is searching or the software will lockup. If you got lucky and the channels were found, and you started using it but now it says no signal or no channels found, its over heated. The no channels error is almost always its over heated and shut down. If you can self resolve the heat issue, the device will work just fine. Although I did not reach out to the Vendor, I did try to contact the Manufacturer, and of course there was no reply. My suggestion to the Manufacturer is to get more feed back on the Software interface and make it better. Also fix the heat issue on the tuner. I am assuming this an onboard amplifier that is over heating.

I went ahead and spent the extra $4.00 to get the USB3.0 version for future compatibility. To address part of Andrei's review regarding the hidden clip, it's certainly there - see the pictures for details. Part of the problem is that it's very difficult to release, since the only avenue you have to it it via the bezel itself, and you can really only pry it "wrong." I carefully used a (very) small flat-blade screwdriver to free it, and the rest of the assembly was easy. As to the enclosure itself, it's solid on the outside, plastic for the drive carrier, but stamped steel to handle the PCB and connectors and uses an initio INIC-3619PN bridge chip. Overall build quality was good, it had only a single overspecced (16V) electrolytic cap in it and the soldering looked to be of average quality.. The only other fault I could find would be that it's pretty easy to push the drive just that LITTLE BIT too far into the cage, so that it binds when attempting to eject. I would recommend the following: 1 - Make the drive cage completely out of stamped metal to reduce "wonkiness" of the molded plastic 2 - Get rid of the back bezel configuration, and add some simple ejection mechanism for the drive itself. There shouldn't be any reason to twiddle around with the clip stuff, and would make swapping drives easier. Overall, it's certainly worth the $20-odd bucks and gives me a nice looking external drive.
