If you've recently purchased a Macbook Pro and want to ensure that your investment stays aesthetically pleasing for the long run, then this product is something that you should consider buying. When I got my 15.4" Macbook the last thing I wanted to do get it scratched, dirty, or blemished; so I browsed around looking for protective products to help me avoid these kinds of problems. I came across the Moshi PalmGuard and after a bit of deliberating, decided to pull the trigger and buy it. That was 10 months ago and in retrospect I'm really glad I made this purchase. The PalmGuard is semi-rigid film that is sticky on one side, just like a sticker. It comes with two separate pieces (both perfectly pre-cut to fit the Macbook Pro) which are surprisingly very easy to install. Don't be discouraged about getting the placement perfect on the first attempt; the sticker is not meant to be permanent in the sense that it will easily peel away without leaving any residue. I'm not saying that the film is going to slip and slide after you install it (trust me, it won't move unless you want it to), but rather IF you need to remove it then you can do so without hassle. Moshi did a great job of matching the PalmGuard's color to the Macbook Pro's aluminum unibody. Few people even notice I have anything added to my palm rest area and those who do happen to see it are impressed by how well it blends in. For some, the the thought of the trackpad sensitivity being impaired by this additional layer of material is a concern. I can say that the trackpad will behave just as it should, even with the PalmGuard over the top of it. However, it will feel different to the touch. This turned out to bother me enough to remove the trackpad cover altogether. I preferred the feeling of the glass trackpad over the rigid plastic feel of the PalmGuard. It all depends on what your preference is, but with or without the trackpad being covered, it will still respond perfectly. So now, 10 months later, my Macbook still looks like it did out of the box and my palm rest area is free from dirt, scratches, and stains. Good job Moshi!

I’ve been using my phone’s GPS to track my runs and play music for many years, but finally had gotten to the point where my distances were long enough that the cumbersome bulkiness of my phone and an armband prompted me to look at a GPS watch. I started my search in January, just at the first reviews for the Forerunner 645 Music were coming out, and was so excited that a watch designed for runners was not coming with on board music. I ordered my watch through Amazon not long after it became available and wore it for a few days alongside my Fitbit Alta HR that I’d been wearing to track my daily activities. The sleep data from the Forerunner was not as detailed and naps are not tracked, but this data was not my priority, so I could live with it. The step and heart rate agreement was pretty good, and I like the additional information I was getting, like flights of stairs. For the first couple of weeks I had the watch, I ran without music and liked the in-run information I was getting. Again, accuracy seemed good, I was getting used to the buttons, and even programming my workouts. There are a lot of features I like about the Forerunner 645 Music, and they are captured in other positive reviews; however, the Music feature is not one of them. I’d been using my Plantronics Backbeat Fit headphones for about a year and a half and have never had any problems with them, except maybe when getting a mid-run phone call and the music not automatically restarting. Despite some of the reviews that have been coming up about the music feature, I was optimistic my trusty headphones would work just fine. Well, boy, was I wrong. First, when trying to load music onto my phone, the I Heart Music app was not even available yet (how do you roll out this device without that being ready?), so I had to load music from my computer which was an incredible pain. The interface was slow and difficult to browse through. I could not find/add my iTunes playlists so I had to manually search for each song I wanted to add and then transfer. Each search was really slow, so I only had ded about 40 songs. Next, pairing my headphones – I have to re-pair every time to get the headphones to connect. Rather than my phone, which automatically connects when I turn my headphones on, I need to first go to my music, select play, then while the watch is “connecting” to my device, I need to turn the headphones on in pairing mode. Pain. And, it’s true, the music does drop out quite frequently. Despite Garmin’s handy table recommending better performance for Backbeat Fit headphones with the watch on the right hand (bizarre) I did not switch my watch to my right hand because I am right handed. So every few songs, the music drops out for a beat, but does come back without losing the connection, so I figured I could live with that. ***What I cannot live with, however, is the watch re-setting in the middle of a run, as it did this weekend.*** A little over 3 miles into a 12 mile run, the music cut out, I looked at the watch, and the blue triangle was displayed as the watch rebooted. I was furious. This is absolutely inexcusable in a running watch and no serious runner should buy this watch. Yes, when it rebooted, I was able to resume my run. However, my headphones were no longer connected so I had to go through the process of turning off my headphones, starting up the music (finding the controls mid run was not straightforward), then turning on in pairing mode, and I was “running” again. After a lot of bad luck in the past, and a little research; I recommend the "Transcend High Endurance" micro SD cards - they are rated for dash cameras. The "save video button" doesn't stand out, like it does on this cameras predecessors, the B40, A118, and A118c. I had to contact "Technical Support" in order to get a link to the firmware for this camera - it took a couple of hours to get an email response with the link, and only after I supplied my name and order number. You'd think they'd print the link on a slip of paper, and slip it in the package. Don't let the negatives stop you from buying this dash camera, or from buying it from Spy Tec - They're minor complaints, and Spy Tec is a great company to do business with. This is a lot of value in a great little camera, for not much money. If you have technical issues, or need instruction, Spy Tec is there for you. I have contacted them several times in the past, and they have always provided excellent support for their products.

I expected more from JBL at this price point. The base response seems fleeting and over emphasized in narrow frequency ranges to try to trick the ears into hearing sufficient bass. I blame that on the absolute waterproof nature of the speaker. The design is portless to prevent water intrusion, so the only design option was to add passive radiators 0n the sides to enhance base. The TiVo Bolt OTA for Antenna is a great product. The setup was rather lengthy, but worked well with patience. I subscribed to the TiVo service, which was around $75 for the year, tax included. The most important thing, if you use this for on-air TV, is you MUST have a good antenna and/or be in an area where you can pick up a good TV signal. Without that, this box will not be your friend. Digital TV is different than old analog - you either get the signal or you don't. That being said, the recordings are great. You can set it to record a single show or a series. The menu is a lot like cable TV in that the grid displays all the programs by channels and notes if they are new. There are options to display all the channels in your channel list (like NBC and the local subchannels such as Grit, Bounce, MeTV, etc.) or favorites you select can be displayed alone. Results have been very good for recording my favorite programs, which was my purpose for this purchase - getting rid of cable and saving money while still enjoying the time-shift recordings of TV shows. Many shows also have the skip option which is awesome for not having to wade through commercials. For programs without the skip function it's easy to fast-forward through the ads, just like I did with cable. I'm very happy with this box, except for one simple thing. It has the Amazon app and I am a Prime Member, but the app will not play the movies - the screen just goes black. I still have my Fire Stick to watch Prime, but it would have been nice if this worked. Thus, the 4-star rating instead of 5. I do recommend this TiVo box. It's great for saving on the price of cable. Just be sure you can get a good TV signal BEFORE getting this. Otherwise you may be very disappointed at the channels you can actually receive and watch.

It was with MUCH research that took me to finally choose this unit - I was looking at an Onkyo, Denon and the Pioneer. I had an older Pioneer receiver with no HDMI and based on my satisfaction with that kept me towards this model. Being that it was going to be installed in a cabinet I wanted to try Onkyo but their constant heat reports concerned me. That and I liked the features offered for apple integration. I only have 1/2 of my 7.1 speaker setup completed and with just the front channel, I connected my ipod touch and was shortly playing my Iron Movie video from my iPod Touch with acceptable quality. Now - on to what they don't tell you in the review - 7.1 as per DOLBY's own site (check if you don't believe me) 7.1 setup is FRONT(left,center,right), CENTER(LR), REAR(LR) and SUB! That's it - where did Pioneer all of a sudden decide that "THEIR" 7.1 setup actually put's 5 speakers up front and includes FRONT HIGH left and right. Their manual almost implies that by doing the "dolby" method isn't optimal. One of the main selling points on this receiver is for 'stand-by hdmi pass-thru" - well what again is not explained is this apparently called "HDMI Control" - but what they don't tell you is that it sounds like it's not a standard. I spoke to a Support person and basically he said that you enable it on the receiver, but then you must also have devices that allow you to enable it on the DEVICE side as well - which means probably my older 50" Samsung DLP won't have it. And what that means is now I need to have the receiver turned on if I want audio AND video to process to the TV. I hope when I try later that their suggestion to allow Audio pass through to work will work as shown so I don't need to be blasting all speakers, just the TV in normal use. After a day's research, it seems like this HDMI Control is about 3 years too early, and most people that finally get it working turn it off because it causes other issues. I wished there was support for 2 HDMI outputs and I have the DLP TV and an overhead front projector. I had to buy an Splitter box to run that, now it sounds like with this HDMI Control "feature" I should reconnect the external HDMI Switch. That being said - so far these are the main drawbacks of the unit - and a few items that can no be accessed (system setup) from the front panel and instead you have to use the remote.

I purchased the Chuwi Hi10 Go back on August 16th 2021 for a total of $298.81 plus shipping. I also purchased the Hi10 Go keyboard case and H6 Stylus pen, both of which I recommend that you consider if you're thinking of purchasing the Hi10 Go (particularly the keyboard case). So far the Hi10 Go has performed exactly as I expected of a sub $300 Windows tablet. In fact, it's more than met my expectations in that regard. I use it almost every night for casual browsing and sometimes catching up on office work (it's easier to carry around than the office laptop PC). Some minor quibbles: 1. Battery life is a little low for a tablet. You can extend this a bit by configuring the tablet to go into hibernation when not in use. This does mean however that it takes a little longer to be usable after you press the Power button. But it also means that the battery won't be dead if you want to use it after you've put it down for awhile. 2. The power button is a bit close to the volume control buttons. I have turned the tablet off a few times when trying to lower the volume :-). 3. The protective screen on the tablet is a bit "soft" and seems to scratch easily. Using the pen on it can lead to some scratches on the surface, but these are not visible when the tablet is on. 4. Windows activation isn't automatic, which apparently has let some to believe that it's a pirated copy. It's not. The process to activate it requires the product key, which you can retrieve this way : Open “Start” menu, Enter "cmd", select " Command Prompt" and the the "Run as administrator" option, and enter the following command: wmic path SoftwareLicensingService get OA3xOriginalProductKey. 5. It supports up to BT 4.2. The latest version is 5.1. 4.2 however should be enough for most people. 5.1 would have been nice though, for its extended range and possibly higher audio fidelity. Still, with all of the minor quibbles above, this is a great deal for a sub-$300 Windows tablet, particularly as it does offer pen support!

Here are my initial impressions of the Fire HD. (Me: I'm an IT professional, have an android phone and older android tablet.) Pros: The display is very nice! Crisp and bright. It's fast and the actions are smooth. Sound quality is very good for a small tablet. Video quality is very good. Photo display is very good. It was nice how the three main Google apps (mail, calendar, contacts) were immediately set up once I selected Gmail in the default email app. Cons: - The main reason I decided to get the Fire HD was for the Lending Library. (I'd gotten a trial Prime account and read about the many thousands of ebooks available for free through Prime on Kindle devices.) However, there is no way to search the Lending Library! If you click on the link for the Lending Library, in the Book Store, you get an unsearchable list of almost 200,000 books. Which is almost entirely useless! You can sort by popularity, customer review, etc. but that's it. I called Support, and the best they could offer is that I go to the overall book store search, put in a search, and scroll to look for the books marked as Prime. VERY disappointing. However, I did discover that you can enter "<search criteria> kindle eligible" and that does work. The selection is also quite disappointing. - The action of re-selecting the search bar doesn't work very well. I tap and tap the search bar and wait and nothing happens. Eventually the search bar is active again. - VERY few apps available. I thought that the apps listed in the Amazon app store (while on PC) would be available on the Fire. Not so. It seems there are only a handful of useful apps. (I don't know about gaming, I don't do that.) Going from the hundreds of thousands of great apps available on an android, this is very disappointing. - Again, if you're used to android, the lack of flexibility and actions will be frustrating. For example, click on the "apps" link and you get a screen with HUGE 3/4" app icons. There is no way to either size the icons or move them around. There are only links to order by title or recent, no long-press and move. - When on the Home screen, I don't like all those "suggestions" running along the bottom. I will experiment with the Fire some more. But based on my impressions so far, I'll be sending it back. I do see how this could be a good tablet for a very non-technical person, or for a non-technical young person that just wants to play the available games, videos, music. Update: I "sideloaded" a number of android apps -- just did a backup of apps from my phone (via Astro), copied over the .apk files (on phone, /backups/apps) to my PC, and then copied over the files to the Kindle. Click and the .apk files install the apps. I installed the ADW Launcher EX app that gives you a regular android user interface screen instead of that awful carousel. [...] But the launcher slowed down the process of bringing up an app. And it was all just a bit too kludgy. If I were going to watch more videos, or listen to music, I would have kept the HD because the picture and sound quality are fantastic. But after also trying out a friend's Nexus 7, I liked the size of the Nexus (fits in hand easily), the speed (faster than Kindle), and the flexibility since it's not locked down like the Kindle. But the picture and sound quality of the Nexus doesn't come close to the Kindle HD.

Update I've been using this great little radio in my kitchen for the past three months, and I have to say it's just excellent. The audio quality really impresses me. It's rich and warm, and sounds far superior to any tabletop radio I've ever owned. Obviously it won't replace a full audio component system, but for what it is -- a small radio -- the sound is great. The rotary dial is cool. A digital display is of course more convenient for dialing in stations, but the rotary dial is easy to use. And it's better suited for fine-tuning. The bluetooth works just fine. As I mentioned in my original review, you have to pair your device every time you want to use it. It sounds like a major chore, but in practice it really doesn't bother me. It takes less than five seconds to pair an iPhone/iPod. Great little radio. # # # I got this little radio for the kitchen, to replace an alarm clock-stereo that always seemed out of place. The audio is fantastic. HUGE improvement over the cheap table-top radios you buy at Target or wherever. Between the solid wood cabinet, the large speaker and the bass port underneath, the sound is fantastic and much richer and bigger than you'd expect from such a small package. Also, it's clearly better to have one big speaker (mono), than two little ones (stereo); with a unit this size, stereo imaging isn't possible anyway, so two speakers are unnecessary. The Bluetooth works great. Only gripe -- and others have noted this -- is you have to pair your BT device EVERY TIME you want to use it. The unit doesn't automatically pair. It only takes a few seconds to go into Settings/Bluetooth/Pair, but it's kind of a drag. The only workaround is to pair one and only one device; if you do this, the unit will automatically pair to that one device. If you pair another device, you'll forever have to manually pair whatever device you want to use. Anyway. Great product. Happy with the purchase.

I was planning to purchase a Sony soundbar for over $1200 for use in a bedroom setup when I came across numerous reviews on audiophile internet sites which praised the audio quality of this soundbar to the skies, often rating it higher than units costing several times as much. The only acknowledged trade-off with the Pioneer was the omission of surround-sound effects to get pristine stereo quality at a budget price point. However, in almost every review and in the comments following the reviews were indications of a plethora of problems with the early-production units of this soundbar, including bluetooth connectivity, woofer syncing, and woofer turn-on issues. However, the issues were reported to have been resolved by the manufacturer one by one, or users had found some kind of work-around to address their individual issues. Figuring that the soundbar had been in production long enough (almost two years now) for all these problems to have been resolved by Pioneer, I decided to purchase the unit. Now that it has arrived, I can say this is easily the best-sounding audio device for its price that I have ever heard . . . when it is is working properly. Alas, my unit is plagued by yet another of the apparently endless problems with this soundbar. When I bring it out of standy mode by activating a source device through either the digital or the bluetooth input, only the subwoofer produces sound. (This is the opposite of one of the earlier reported problems in which the soundbar came out of sleep mode but the subwoofer did not.) In order to get the main soundbar to produce sound, I have to turn off the master power switch on the back of the bar, turn it back on, and then hit the power button on the front of the bar. This is annoying enough, but my plan was to mount the soundbar on a wall (there are brackets on the unit for doing this, so it is not an unheard of plan). However, since I need access to the back of the soundbar to turn it on, I've got to figure out another placement if I'm going to use this thing at all. I really cannot understand why Pioneer would engage the talents of a well-respected speaker engineer such as Andrew Jones to produce a product that is so plagued by ancillary defects that owning it is an annoyance rather than a pleasure. It just doesn't make sense to use the name of someone such as Jones to draw reviewers and customers and then irritate them all of with dirt-cheap manufacturing and poor quality control unless the underlying strategy is to destroy the brand's reputation. In this, at least, they seem to be succeeding with this product.

The problem with the product on my computer was that Win 8.1 recognized it as a (Logitech Unifying USB Receiver). New USB card drivers were ignored by Windows due to this mistaken identity. Inateck needs to fix this. I came up with the following work around; Go to Start, Control Panel, Device Manager, then select Universal Serial Bus controllers Select the (Logitech Unifying USB) item with the (yellow triangle error notice) and double click to open it. Select (Driver) tab, (Update Driver), (Browse my computer for driver), select (Let me pick from a list) and finally select (USB Composite Device) and then okay. The product now works Once I got the driver to work the card operated without incident. Tested it with my fastest USB 3.0 device, a SSD with a USB 3 adapter (see results in photo). Its speed was limited by the SSD to 188mb/s. Supplies a decent amount of current but not enough to charge my phone at full amperage. The maximum current it could provide was 0.71amps and that dropped the voltage from 5.00v to 4.68v. Even at that low voltage I was able to transfer files to and from the computer.

I want to warn purchasers here that there are TWO versions of this bag. I ordered this bag, it broke and so I ordered it again with the intention of returning the first one when the new one arrived (I had nothing to take my laptop to work in otherwise). I was hoping it was just a manufacturer defect on the swivel clip on the first bag. When the new bag arrived, ordered from the exact same seller here on Amazon, it was almost an entirely different bag. I want to detail the differences here along with some photos so other purchasers can be sure they get the 'authentic' bag. First off the thickness of the leather is significantly different. The real bag feels thick and kind of stiff actually, the fake bag is pretty thin. Stitching on the real bag is CONSIDERABLY thicker as you can see from the photos below. Fake bag has a 'devil hunter' logo square stitched on the front flap. Front flap on the fake bag is also missing an extra slide pocket on the front flap (behind the zipper). Fake bag has smaller snaps than the thicker versions on the real bag. Real bag has double stitching on the bottom seams, fake bag has single stitching. Real bag has leather trimming around the inside of the 'laptop' portion, two additional pockets, and has pen holder loops as well. Fake bag just has nylon untrimmed area around the laptop pocket and just a chintzy zipper pocket. Real bag has an extra leather snap thing around the handles so they can be secured together, fake bag doesn't have this. Huge difference in the quality and thickness of both the leather AND nylon webbing on the shoulder straps. Fake bag has single 'ply' leather loops holding the shoulder strap D rings to the bag, real bag has double thick leather loops. D-Ring quality and the clips on the real bag are way thicker, and the attachment points on the clip swivels are designed differently. Real bag has a sliding pad on the shoulder strap, fake bag doesn't have this. Adjustment point on the strap is beefy on the real one. Zipper quality on the real bag is also smoother feeling, fake bag kind of has binding zipper in comparison. In short I'm glad mine broke at the chintzy clip swivels on my fake bag, otherwise I would never have reordered and noticed the differences. In terms of rating, I really likely would have given the fake bag a 3 star rating. It's not terrible, but really a bit overpriced for 140ish bucks, AND it broke. I did like the looks and design of it though, which I why I reordered hoping it was a defective version. COMPARED to the real bag though, it should be a 1 star. The real bag I'd rate at 4-5 stars and is the kind of quality I expect for 140 bucks. In the included photos the fake bag strap had broken at the swivel point so I'm able to show the weak part of it (the ring) the real bag wasn't broken so it was harder to show the stronger swivel point. I hope it's clear below which bag is which, but if you can't tell from a photo the fake one has dark, small stitches, the real one has thick light colored stitches.

I won't need to list the specs as you can get them off the site. What I wanted: - A powerful enough machine to check into and work on my office projects when on holiday and very portable (I need the Adobe suite for production.) - A laptop that turns into a tablet - mostly because I don't have enough devices already, LOL - I really wanted to learn how to use one that I can do both work and play (watch videos on the couch, play Candy Crush, with headphones - I didn't even care about how its speakers are as I will always have an external connection for that.) - Needed to be "affordable" - Something that would last for a few years - A gift to myself during these times. - A couple of USB ports and a working Bluetooth, wireless connectivity and RAM - We cook a lot so it's nice to take this into the kitchen and already have the recipes readable off the screen and use a stylus pen without having to dirty the screen. - Price: I'm okay with a refurb as it will be cheaper. What I don't care about: - Charging brick - a huge number of complaints was that it couldn't charge via USB-C, which I didn't even know was an option. A first-world problem, don't let anyone tell you otherwise. - I don't need my touchpad to charge anything - I wanted to watch movies and play Candy Crush but I didn't know that you could download those apps and not have to watch within a browser window, THAT'S A HUGE PLUS for me that I wasn't even aware of!!!! - The S pen. I have lots of other stylus pens that I can use. - Speaker quality; I will always use headphones, airbuds, etc. What I liked: - Gorgeous QLED screen, colors are vibrant! - Feels pretty luxe - doesn't feel cheap but also pretty light. - Expandable micro-SD card (so glad I went that way with memory selection 10yrs ago) - Backlit keyboard for the dark. I didn't know I needed this a few years back until I started working in the dark! This is not a deal-breaker but very nice to have. You can force the backlit keyboard to light by covering the light sensor, which is pretty cool. - It works really well with my own stylus pens with no issues as well as using a mouse for apps and games simultaneously. - With the iPad and other tablets, they don't ignore your resting hand so you get stray marks. With this in tablet mode, it knows you are resting your hand and just notes your writing/drawing marks. That was unexpected for me. - I have nothing to compare but the hinges seem sturdy enough and they stay at 40 degrees (anything less and the screen turns off and it starts to close but who's using it at that angle?!). Any point beyond 90 degrees does seem to stay in place so I can simply lay the keyboard down and open the screen to, say, 290 or more with no issues (so I can play Candy Crush while eating and using a pen or cook with the recipe open). - The virtual keyboard: there are three or four options so I love moving the smaller keybd off to the side rather than covering the lower part of the screen and can move it around. - You can set this to always check for tablet mode, I don't have to worry if the virtual or physical keyboard is available. - Speakers are better than expected. What I don't like: - The physical keyboard keys are really flat and my hand positioning is off but I guess you need that when it turns into a tablet. It mimics Apple's keyboard, which I'm used to so I have no qualms with the design. I can learn to get use to it. The point of YouTube is video, not the description of videos. [Update: I upgrade to Win11 and this is no longer an issue. I noticed I can set up side-by-side windows. - PC/Tablets don't work as intuitively as smartphones so I expect them to respond the same way when in tablet-mode but you are still in the Windows ecosystem, which isn't always logical, as I'm finding out. Still, Candy Crush is crushing it ... I haven't taken notes with it at this point as I'm WFH. Would like to see which apps work well. [Update: I'm using this less as a tablet and more as a laptop, surprisingly. Still, there are a number of apps that make this worthwhile.] - I don't want every app to be always be full screen, I'm working on a laptop, the window should be the size I need, but maybe they aren't smart enough to know the difference. I realized I need to keep everything in a split screen for my personal productivity. [Update: see note above.] - I have to create an Outlook account. It's one thing to create a login user but another to not have a choice unless it's connected to MS. I will use this new email account for newsletters and unimportant things. - And the MAIN thing I don't like is that I seem to hit the on/off button on the side more often than I care to. It's in the exact middle, where my finger often sits and presses. VERY ANNOYING!!! OVERALL - I'm very happy with this product, more so than I thought I would. Heavier than a tablet but I don't have to hold it! It comes with it's own "stand." - There's a learning curve for me since this is my first PC-tablet--I'm so used to smartphones and expecting the tablet mode to act the same way so it's taking some time to learn the differences but I will say it is great to be able to use a stylus, a mouse or my finger(s)! - As a laptop, I think it works well until it thinks it's a tablet when I'm still in the laptop mode.; I must have hit something to change the setting. - In general, I like having the keyboard available when I need it. - It's only been one week and I haven't loaded all my apps (Adobe Creative Suite) and use it for actual work - enjoyed watching movies on half the screen and typing on the other OR able to cook with the recipe open. [Update: I bought a screen cover so no problems since.] - Not all apps respond to finger pinching - I haven't traveled with it yet and I'm not far from a plug so I haven't really tested it on a plane or anywhere. It can certainly live on one charge a day - I'm on this about 2-3 hours actively and it sits idle for another hour before I put it away and use my phone or watch the actual TV. [Update: the battery life is pretty decent. I think I can make it to 3 hours one on charge. I often plug it in before it dies.] - As it has been only a week, I can't give it 5 stars just yet but so far it excels. The complaints are pretty minor at this point. Let's check back in after a month or two. [Update: Works like charm. I found some good games and apps (like Myst but the 3D makes me nauseous!) and has handled the apps for work as well. I did have to get in touch with Samsung customer service and re-enable my video for Zoom and has continued to work like a charm! I'll give it a 5-stars now.]

The Good: It's got lots of screen real estate, which is helpful for capturing gestural sketching or having a bunch of tool pallets open simultaneously. It's got a reasonable amount of resolution, though, compared to the Retina screen it's currently sitting next to at my workstation, it looks a bit dated. The pressure sensitivity is great, much better the ancient Intuos3 it replaced. The tilt-adjustable stand feels solid and is easy to adjust. *Lot's of hotkeys. **Customer service is helpful. The Bad: The OSX install instructions are in Engrish. You may get through them in one piece; I did not. The supplied USB-C cable on my copy doesn't inspire confidence. They stick out further than they should in my iMac. It needed to have the plugs rotated, flipped, etc. in order to get the tablet running. **Reaching out to XP-Pen for help will be a bit of an exercise in patience and persistence. I've needed to uninstall/reinstall the tablet driver, and dump my prefs file for Adobe Illustrator 2020 alarming often since installing this equipment for the first time. *The hotkey and scroll-wheels haptics feel cheap. The Neutral: Before buying ANY screen tablet, think about your lighting situation. If there are lights directly above your desk, the reflected glare is going to give you a migraine. This is just a personal anecdote, but the lighting in the cube-farm in which I work significantly reduces the number of positions the tablet (and my head) can be in without catching reflected glare from one or more lights. Because my job allows me some freedom/authority over my workstation, as a solution, I've removed the lights above my desk. This may not be feasible for some. Conclusion: If you NEED the extra screen real estate and don't have the budget for a Cintiq, and you're willing to deal with some headaches and downtime, this is a good fit.

This Megaboom 3 is nowhere close to what UE advertises. First off, the "megaboom" is not there. Basses are OK until you bring the overall volume to 60%. After that, forget about the sound quality, the crispiness of the sound, the nice bass frequencies. What you are left with is a jumbled mess of sounds. In addition, the EQ is not a real EQ. From what I hear by changing it, it sounds more like a Frequency band compressor. If you bring up the bass, all the other frequencies "disappear", exactly like they were compress down to "make space" to the bass so that the energy level of the signal stays the same. If you know a little bit about audio, you will understand what I am saying when you try it yourself. In conclusion, Megaboom 3 is not worth the money. If you don't plan on tumbling your BT speaker in sand or throw it in the pool, then you will be most likely better off with a JBL. For the same money (or a little more), you will get a much better sound overall.

Sounds great, solid build, was so happy I bought another pair for another connection, really opens things up. 6/24/16 update: I have started to identify the sound these have, and while some may not think cables can have a "sound", they can (anything within a circuit, cable included, can impact the overall system). I find this cable has a great balance, and while some have said they are bright, but I didn't find that. what i found was clarity, highs that may have been suppressed were now present, think leading edge of a drumstick's strike upon a cymbal, the "click", and being able to tell if that was a wooden or nylon tipped drumstick. I haven't noticed any excess sibilance (think adding an extra "s" on everything), just clarity. The other thing I noticed was balance, but at first it seemed like less bass, but the very lows were still there, but upper lows/ lower mids were now more present than before (the absence gave the impression of more bass), this didn't detract from the sound, but in fact brought more coherence into everything, lower register instruments now sounded "fuller" without being tubby, like hearing a knock on different woods, slight variations now come through. Like many things in this world, we have become more accustomed to an overly saturated world, brighter colors, more brightness from TV's, enhanced everything, making truly "neutral" look bland at first, but after some time, you come to treasure honesty and purity.

I've had this router for a short time so far but I've already had the wireless become inoperative after approximately 1 week of use, it should be noted that a couple of days prior to this I noticed some drops/reconnects but thought nothing of it at the time... Upon the rebooting the router, wireless functionality returned... Unfortunately I didn't have more time to trouble-shoot the wireless at the time, next time I'm hoping to have the time to see if I can reach the router via Ethernet to check logs and such... Documentation is lacking as far as some of the features such as printing as noted in a previous review... Zyxel should include additional functionality within the GUI to disable/enable and view the status of various services, i.e., telnet should never be enabled by default due to the availability of secure alternatives... Firmware is based off of OpenWRT which opens the potential for significant flexibility in the future assuming it gets to the point where you can install the full version along with any additional packages you may want/need but I reiterate POTENTIAL, I've seen no forums indicating any success while Zyxel indicated is was against policy to provide any guidance(not to be confused with actually requesting support) without approval from HQ which they wouldn't provide approval without the demand from owners so if this is something you want then you should request it... Speaking of OpenWRT, Zyxel should utilize a more recent version, they are utilizing a version released in July of 2014(keeping in mind it appears they were utilizing a release candidate which was released much earlier than the "official" release)... Wireless performance, when functioning, outstanding... I am concerned about long term stability given my previous statement above and the fact I got this to replace my pre-existing E8350 which has consistently unreliable wireless functionality... Edit - About a week after this initial review, I experienced a router crash, it did seem to recover on its own this time. My suspicion is that there may be a firmware/software issue. I did observe steady memory utilization on the router which has dropped back down. Given the router's use of some very dated openwrt release its very possible this is something addressed long ago.. Logs don't seem to indicate what the issue may have been, then again, they probably rolled, the device doesn't seem retain much locally which is a shame given the amount of storage present on the device. I may need to resort to remote logging for better retention... Update - 11/29/2016 - Noticed a firmware update was available this morning, figured I'd give it a try, this was a mistake on my part. I wrote a comprehensive breakdown and first impressions of the Kindle Fire on my website when it was first announced back in September. Well, the day has finally come and mine has arrived! I am also planning to do a full video review and hands-on demo in the coming days, but just wanted to post a quick review now that my newest toy is finally in my hands. First impressions "out-of-the-box" is that it is a VERY solidly constructed device, that feels great in the hand and has a really nice weight to it. I have already begun to play around with: Streaming Video: Smooth, no stutters, very crisp and clear. I tested on Amazon Instant Video and Netflix. The display is quite beautiful, packing more pixels-per-square-inch than the iPad. Apps: Limited due to availability through the Amazon Appstore (and not the Google Market), however there are thousands of apps available that are optimized for the Fire...which is what Amazon wanted, in order to ensure the best customer experience (not dissimilar to what Apple does). I haven't had any trouble finding most of my favorites (i.e. Evernote, Pandora, Politico, Comixology, RSS Readers etc). I also side-loaded and installed the Spotify apk, since it is currently not available in Amazon's Appstore...yet. Music: I have been using and recommending Amazon's Cloud Player for a long time, therefore as soon as I turned on my Fire, I had access to the thousands of songs I already had stored in Amazon's cloud. All streaming perfectly and clearly, displaying the album art and other listening options. The ability to download your music directly onto the device is clearly displayed and a snap to do, but I doubt that I will do that, since I can simply stream all of my music and let Amazon do the storage heavy-lifting it for me. Books: Looks great and shopping for books is SO much nicer / easier than on the previous Kindle's monochromatic display, but when it comes to reading, nothing can beat my 2nd generation Kindle and E-Ink display...I'm just not a fan of back-lit displays when reading a book. Therefore I do not plan to read many books on the Fire unless I'm reading in bed as the girlfriend sleeps. :) The new Silk Browser: Disappointingly a little choppy in places, especially when using pinch-to-zoom or scrolling on pages with a lot of images; however according to Amazon, this will improve as more and more people are using the Silk Browser and it learns predictive surfing (in which Amazon cache's and pre-loads pages on their farm of servers). Basically, as more people use it, the faster it will get. It's not a bad experience by any means, just currently not as smooth as on my iPad, which I have become accustomed to. However, in the days since I have received my Fire, I have noticed the Silk Browser getting faster and faster when it comes to loading the pages of websites that I frequent often. During the next few days, I will be spending a lot of time with the device in order to take it through some trials, data-loads and "real world" usage before giving my final word; which will come shortly in a comprehensive video. I also stated in my original 'First Impressions' write-up that I did in September, that I do not plan to compare the Fire directly to the iPad, as they are entirely different devices, that appeal to different people. There are simply those (millions) who will never pay over $500 for a tablet, but who want to enter the tablet market...for those people, Amazon just became your new best friend. Frankly, you sound like an idiot if you think a $200 device can be compared to a $500 - $800 device. And for $200 - and judging from my initial time with it - the Kindle Fire is absolutely BRILLIANT when you compare that low price point against what it is capable of.

I am the kind of person that likes a laptop for mobility. I'm not stuck in one room where the computer is I can take it with me. Also, I am a gamer which means I can't have the laptop sitting just anywhere - I need it on a solid, comfortable surface that offers stability and airflow...this desk hit the nail on the head for my personal ideal desk needs. Here is my pro and con list of it all. Pros : - LOVE that it's ultra lightweight - It is the perfect size for my Toshiba Satellite , haven't tried it with the thicker dell but for the Toshiba it's just great - I have a larger laptop and it fits perfect with some space to spare (an inch or two to spare on the side) -It's made of aluminium so it's tough and durable! - The black vented lap desk comes with a little side tray that attaches easily and effortlessly for your mouse and the plus in that is you don't even need a mouse pad with it but I do choose to use one. - The table section has enough of a ledge to keep the laptop from sliding off even when the desk part is on an angle BUT they have provided you with two slip on clips for added non-slip/ to accommodate thicker laptops. - This desk does have two fans and they seem decent enough quality. They are extremely silent and do a great job keeping my laptop cool as a cucumber while playing a cpu/gpu intensive game like Rift. Normally an expensive fan would be needed to play this game while on a desk BUT your laptop is supported in the air with clear and easy air flow, no wood or stone desk suffocating your pc so the fans on the desk are more than enough to please any gamer. Now, if you have a dinosaur of a laptop and are trying to play system intensive games...this won't be ideal for you as most likely your laptop is not up to par and barely qualifies to play such games so expect your laptop to run beyond HOT - there is no fix for "old" laptop outside of getting a new one sadly. - I adore I get the option of turning the fans on or off with a flick of a switch. Facing the user and under the table top is a little black on/off switch. Also, there is a usb cable that attaches to your laptop for a power source, it is removable so it's not dangling under your table if you aren't using it. - The legs on the desk move in the most incredible ways. There is no angle these little suckers can't move AND they can be positioned differently from each other to literally accommodate any angle/incline/decline. There are times when I have one leg positioned one way and the other leg positioned on another angle to offer me stability on strange inclines. Sometimes I am on a surface where the right side of the laptop is lower than the left and this laptop is the answer...stability on every angle for me. - This lap desk doesn't really jiggle or shake, I mean if you kick it or hit it it will but it never tips over (anything tips over with enough force though), it's never come close to it thank goodness. - It folds up very, very thin. I can slip this under anything and no one would really see it it's so thin. Under the bed, under the couch even. It's not bulky one bit. Cons: - I wish the side tray mouse pad was a tad bit bigger, it is more than enough for me in the time I have used this lap desk but I like having roaming space. - The aluminum legs have plastic joints, I am unsure if this plastic is a cover for the aluminium or if indeed it is plastic. It seems like a hard plastic but I just have bad luck with plastic altogether. I am a bit worried it will break in the future. - I am a woman with long nails and the buttons on each leg to adjust it give me a bit of a hard time. They are sometimes difficult to press when only my nail tip can reach the button to press it. Some times my nail bend in a hurtful way, other times my nail just breaks so I've started using small things made of metal to press the buttons in for me. Over all I love this desk and am extremely pleased with it on every front. It's lightweight and stable, easy on the eyes and just looks cool! Anything that allows me to use my laptop comfortably on the floor or in bed, sitting up leaning against the wall or on the sofa, in a chair or anywhere else is amazing to me. One of my best purchases to date! If this broke tomorrow I would order another the very same day I am so pleased with this. 15 out of 10 thumbs up from me.

First off... this thing is amazing. I originally bought the BOOM and while it was great too, it just wasn't enough for me. After almost a month with the MEGABOOM, the $100 difference between the two was totally worth it. I spent about a week with the UE BOOM, and the audio quality was great. I'm certainly no audiofile, but I know how good speakers should sound. The lows were so-so, a bit punchy and monotonous. The mids and highs were great, very clear. They remained clear just about all the way through the volume spectrum. The thing I didn't like was that it really didn't get loud enough for my taste. And the music I listen to is complimented well by good sounding bass. So, I forked over the extra hundred for the MEGABOOM, and ahhhhhhh. This thing sounds so good. I've brought it to parties, pools, the river, and everywhere in between. It always catches everyones eyes, and most importantly, their ears. This thing will easily fill up a backyard of loud people with plenty of sound. The bass is so much better. A bit boomy, but the equalizer can fix that problem pretty quick. As someone on here mentioned, the equalizer is not so much an equalizer (it seems to just slightly mute the frequencies that aren't turned up the most), but it does the trick all the well. The features this thing has are amazing. It is full IPX7 waterproof (I haven't fully tested this yet, I'm kind of scared. But, its good to know it has it in case something happens), 100 foot of bluetooth distance (I have tested this, and I can take my iphone at LEAST 100 feet away with no issues), it has 180 degree sound which is one of my favorite things about it (all of my previous bluetooth speakers didn't, and it was one of the things I hated about them. You had to literally be right in front of them to get good sound), the battery life is crazy long, and it has an amazing app with bluetooth 4.0 that adds so many more features. I now use this thing as my morning alarm, and with the app you can set it to play music from any source on your phone (iTunes radio, spotify, stored music, and even music stream you can find a url for). At first I worried something would happen and it wouldn't wake me up and I would miss work (which really would have been nice), but it never happened. Every single morning, this thing wakes me up with a gentle ramp up in volume of my favorite music. I press the bluetooth button, and it snoozes for 9 or 10 minutes, and then when I finally get up after 4 or 5 snoozes (I know, I have a problem), just hit the power button to turn it off. Sometimes it will lose the stream or the music app your using will close or something, but it will wake you up with a default built in alarm which isn't as pleasant to wake up to, but at least it still wakes you up. I probably listen to it for at least 4 hours a day. And I charge it MAYBE once a week. Thats crazy. Great water-proof speaker, awesome software features that continue to get better, and amazing sound. Worth the price? In my opinion, ohh yes. EDIT: Do not purchase this thing until Logitech fixes the firmware. This speaker has gone from my favorite speaker I've ever owned, to pretty much useless over 2 firmware updates. No, you can't roll back the firmware, and no, Logitech doesn't seem to care to fix it. Issues that exist now that didn't exist before: 1. Double up (now called Party Up) doesn't work at all. There is now no way to connect multiple speakers. It was supposed to be a new "feature" that you can now connect more than 2 of these, but it turns out now you can't connect any of them. I guess I will be the contradictory voice in the reviews for these. I bought the ATH-IM02's based on all the positive reviews I found online (both here and at other sites). It's rare to see a product rated so highly by nearly everyone who reviewed it. However, I have to break that trend. Let me preface by saying I've been doing Pro Audio stuff for 20+ years and know good sound. I was hoping these would give me sound similar to my studio monitors or over the ear headphones, but in a much more portable package. Good: The mids sound fantastic (excepting a bump at 2-2.5kHz). The mids are very rich and full with midrange instruments sounding fantastic and most vocals filling out very, very nicely. Bass is rich and present, if not very loud. Bad: The highs are not very flat. There is a sharp dropoff above 7kHz, with a little bump around 11.5kHz. While the mids and lows can be made to sound better depending on placement, the highs always stay just as bad. Corrective EQ can make up for some of it, but not all. Placement is VERY important. Lack of a good seal in the ear canal will result in loss of nearly all sound below 450Hz. Getting a good seal will fill in the low frequencies, but it still won't be ruler flat (see attached image). That said, the sound that is there sounds fantastic, but you will not be happy if you're looking for loud bass. I did multiple tests with my measurement equipment on these earphones. I'm sure if your google-fu is strong, you can find my far more detailed post at a certain audio forum. Suffice it to say that these are good earphones, but not great. They are also very dependent on placement and in-ear fit. I really wish manufacturers would give more detailed specs regarding frequency response, but I guess if they did that, people wouldn't buy models like this because they would see that they aren't nearly as flat as what they want people to believe. People have a habit of hearing with their wallet... the more expensive it is, the better it sounds to them because they have to justify their purchase (hello Bose, anyone). Now, in fairness, I can't really say that these are bad and that you should pass on them. In all likelihood, any of the "professional" IEMs (in-ear monitors) are going to have similar frequency limitations. It's quite likely that these are markedly better than similarly priced offerings from other manufacturers, but I can't say that for certain since I haven't tested any other IEMs. Just be aware that these aren't the holy grail as other reviews may make them out to be. Edit Jan 9, 2015: I've had these for over a month now and my impressions have improved a bit. I ordered a set of the large sized Comply Foam tips and they have changed the in-ear frequency response some. The sport tips actually made the sound worse, but the large size comfort and isolation tips do sound better in my ears. The bass and mid range sounds almost flat now, as opposed to the gradual roll-off of low frequencies that you can see in the graph I posted with the original review. Granted, it's not ruler flat, but it is pretty close. Bass is much more punchy and I can actually feel a bit of the sound pressure from the bass notes now. Now that said, it's not like a teenager's car stereo, but then, I don't want that kind of bass in my ears. The change in the low end response just reiterates my earlier comment about how important placement is as well as getting a good seal in your ear canal. However, the highs still have the uneven response and sharp drop-off, and changing in-ear placement and/or ear tips is not going to change that. Overall, I would bump up my rating a bit, but I still don't think that they are worth four full stars. They also aren't anywhere near the five-star, ruler flat perfection in my ears that I was hoping for, but in the end, I am happy with them.

With my usual remote-work setup, my laptop's built-in camera isn't an option, as I use attached monitors instead of the laptop screen. That's really no loss, as the built-in camera is...let's go with poor quality to be charitable. But that means I'm in need of a decent webcam and a light, as my workspace does have a window that faces me, the daylight can be obscured by the trees outside, the shadow of my monitor and plain old clouds or darkness. While I'm not so sure it's necessarily a good thing for my colleagues that this camera/light combination is good quality, as they're stuck seeing me relatively clearly, it does provide a professional appearance that's a step up from the older, lower quality webcam I had been using. With the light built in, it also saves me space atop my monitor, and a USB slot since I need only one. For some context, my most usual conferencing service is Teams, and I use a separate headset/microphone. With that in mind, I've found this camera to be reliable, easy to use and capable of delivering a high-quality video call. I also use a portable green screen behind me most days so that the background feature in Teams works a little better, and this camera is far better than my previous one at making the background look smooth--few weird bits of my room/screen tend to show on the screen, just me and the backdrop. The 1080p quality is noticeable, and that's the step up from my older 720 camera. I look...less fuzzy, for lack of a better term. I can still soften the focus with Teams's filters. I always looked a little harsh on the previous camera, now I look more "real," without the odd sort of jagged edges. The built in light also helps with that, as it directly surrounds the camera, instead of needing to be mounted next to it, and angled awkwardly, creating an inevitable "Phantom of the Opera" type shadow effect on my face. I also wear glasses, and while I do sometimes see some reflection of the light with this camera and light, it is nowhere near as bad as the annoying circle of light I would see reflected in my lenses before, with a fairly standard ring light setup. The light has three modes (I usually prefer the cool mode) and you can control the brightness by holding the button at the top of the camera (a light tap switches mode, a press and hold changes the brightness). I'm also a fan of the somewhat narrower field of view on this camera, 78 degrees. While still considered wide, this is, to me, far better for a single user than the 90+ degree cameras out there. Those tended to make me as one person on screen look ridiculously small relative to the background. It also might be better to have a narrower field of view if you want to keep people from having too much of a look around you at home. Also easy to use is the built-in privacy slider. In lieu of an obvious cover over the lens, you simply slide a lever and a red disc slips over there camera letting you know it's covered up and should slide it back before trying to go on camera. All things considered, I'm quite happy with this webcam/light combination. It's been an improvement to my remote working, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

Free music, delivered wirelessly whenever you want. Create your own stations. All in a small, portable player. What a great idea. Unfortunately, the Slacker portable fails to translate this idea into reality. Why? Primarily because of its el cheapo components. First and most egregious: my unit died completely five weeks after I purchased it (and just 3 days before Amazon's refund deadline). I did nothing to harm it; it simply died. Second, the port for the headset was ultra-flimsy and if I so much as breathed on the connection when the headset was plugged in I lost sound in one or both earpieces. Had the unit not died, I'm sure this connection would have cut out soon. And finally, the wi-fi downloading feature was nice, especially since you can't use a wire to hook this unit up to a Mac desktop to download music. However, it took ALL AFTERNOON to download four stations. And the wi-fi sucked energy out of the battery at a furious pace. Battery life wasn't great to begin with, so wi-fi downloading meant finding a hotspot at the office early in the day, plugging the unit in, and trying to remember to pick it up at the end of the day after the downloads were (hopefully) complete. My advice: listen to Slacker on your BlackBerry or iPhone and forget this cheesy "personal radio player." The BlackBerry is much sturdier and its Slacker app seems to run fairly well.

I was looking for economical headphones I could use to watch TV in my family's common area with various ambient and conversational background noises, including a snoring pug sitting on my lap... I found these by searching "Top 10 Noise-Canceling Headphones" and reading all of the reviews before purchasing. I am a Bose CQ-Line long-term owner, so my expectations are pretty high. 1. Comfort: I have a medium head, so there is no tightness for me. Being my ears also stick out, I found the over-ear cups to be roomy and not create any kind of ear fatigue. 2. Sound: I did not notice any bias to upper or lower frequency at the normal setting without activating the bass feature. I am watching TV shows that don't have scenes that require much bass, so I opted to leave this off. 3. Noise Canceling: All the ambient noise is definitely mitigated. However, people talking still bleeds through, but it is at a much lower DB level than using non-ANC headphones. They do not have that background hiss that the Bose CQ line has that some people find annoying. The level of NC that these headphones offer fits the bill for my use case. 4. Volume: When the volume is at the Max, it is just above a level that I would find unacceptable. This might be an issue with my Samsung TV which has no device control in addition to the Bluetooth device volume. Unlike a phone where you can increase the sound input above the max of the headphones volume resulting in 2x volume output. So far, I am 4.5 Stars happy. If you need a 5-star product look at Bose QC or Sony ANC products. If you want an economical pair of ANC headphones that are simple to use, look no further.

Not only does the stand manage to accommodate my monstrous 30" screen (WQHD, about 15"x26.7"---my aspect is 16:9, *not* 16:10 that is more common among computer monitors so I can't speak authoritatively for all 30" screens), it does so while supporting all the different rotation modes (I do have to slide it as far above the desk as it goes and tilt it all the way back when switching between portrait and landscape orientations---but this wouldn't be necessary for most smaller screens, including all sizes that this is actually designed to mount.), and it's capable of enough spring counter-balance to make it reasonably one-handed to adjust! There are two screws that adjust the tension of the weight-balancing springs; between these, essentially any screen that fits can be given the right level of spring to balance gravity---granted, my very heavy monitor isn't effortless to raise, but I can still manage it one-handed and it stays put at whatever height I like. Let me say this again: If you adjust the two springs in back correctly (Yes, it can take many turns of the screwdriver to get there...), this *CAN* support any weight screen staying put at *ANY* height/angle, up to at least 1.5 times the rated screen weight. Reviewers saying the spring is too strong or too weak for their screen's weight have not made this adjustment. One spring is hidden under a plastic cover by the "main" angle hinge, the other is in the middle of the vertical support column, accessed from below. Google "3M MS110MB" (no quotes) and the 3M company page for it has links to useful PDFs of dimensions and specs, plus the end user manual. Thankfully, the plastic covering the base and main column is purely aesthetic. All load-bearing internal structure is metal (from the look of it, something ferrous---probably steel). Overall, quality is excellent, style is understated if you have dark hardware (and as elegant as matte black plastic can be). Unless you have very demanding positioning needs, this completely obviates the desk-attached arm you may have been considering. tl;dr (a.k.a. "Summary"): Is your VESA-mountable monitor less than 30" diagonally, weighing under 24 pounds? This is *the* monitor stand to buy; all advertised features will work with your screen.

11/27/2017 **************************** After much research, chatting with various online Nikon groups and Googling, I decided to buy this Godox Ving V60IIN flash. Given the specifications, a comparable Nikon Speedlight would have cost me anywhere from $600 and up, while the Godox was a flat $200 (with a spare battery). Got the flash on September 7th, as promised by Pergear. I charged the battery, threw the flash on my D750, and ran some basic tests - all seemed well at the time. I didn't really have time to use the flash again until early November, so I read the manual and played with the various adjustments. (More on that later). When I took the flash to actually use it, I was about 30 minutes into the kiddie party when the flash started throwing an "Error 3". (I found out later that this meant "over high voltage on contacts", with a recommendation to return to a repair center.) I cleared the error many, many times by powering the flash on and off, and it finally seemed to clear... but then I started getting "Error 2". I figured out this error through the screen on the flash, which showed the flash as overheated... which was rather odd to me, since I'd only shot a little over 100 images in a 2+ hour period. But... the bend on the flash was actually hot to the touch, so I figured I had simply over-used it. The error 3 bothered me when I discovered what it meant, and I reached out to Pergear even though the Amazon return guarantee time had elapsed. They immediately offered to replace the flash with a new one - which I accepted gratefully. The new flash arrived today, and since I already had a charged battery (I had bought an extra, because it's always good to have a spare), I decided to mount the flash on my new D850 and give it a run. The new flash performed brilliantly - no errors. I decided to REALLY put it to the test, and flipped my dial to CH (7 frames per second) and shot 48 images in a continuous stream. When the buffer started slowing the capture down, I let up on the shutter... now, I had been watching the flashes without bothering to look through the viewfinder, so I could see how well the flash kept up with the continuous shooting. It never missed a single shutter click. (I verified this by viewing all the images one after the other - all had successfully flashed.) The bend in the flash was... cool. Not warm. Not hot. Ambient room temperature. So - moral of the story is this - great service, great flash. My first copy had a problem, but the vendor made good on it without any hesitation, and the new copy looks like it will work exactly as expected. Should anything change, I'll update this review. In the meantime, I'll be playing with the flash this coming weekend, and exercising it thoroughly - so if you don't see any updates, you'll know all is well. :) Now, regarding the manual and settings... do yourself a favor. Save your eyes from the incredibly tiny, light print in the Godox manual and search Youtube for how to do settings. Trust me, you'll get your answers a LOT faster, and understand them a LOT better. This Godox flash does everything the high-priced Nikon flashes do, but... I have to say that the controls aren't the most intuitive. Don't be put off by that - buy the product, watch the Youtubes, and then enjoy. :)

I recently switched my DSLR kit over to all Canon 1D series bodies. The biggest downside of this is that the DSLRs are no longer anywhere near convenient for travel photography. For a while, I was using the Canon 16-35 F/4 IS on my A7R with an adapter, but that's not really an optimal solution in the long run so I picked up a copy of this lens for a recent vacation. First let me start off by saying that this lens is not quite up to the amazingly high standard set by Canon's latest 16-35 F/4 IS, especially at the long end, but the gap between the two is not enormous. The Good: - Excellent performance at the wide end, almost as good as the Canon everywhere except the extreme corners. Nobody will be anything but thrilled with how sharp this lens performs at 16mm. - Fantastic build quality. The lens is all metal and feels extremely solid and smooth, well done Sony. - Excellent control of flare. You can shoot directly into the sun and not experience any flare. Good luck doing that with a Nikon 14-24. The Mediocre: - The AF with this lens on the A7R is not very fast. I also found it seems to miss more often than the 35 2.8 and 55 1.8, but I thinks that more of an A7R issue than a problem with the lens. - The OSS is there but it's not terribly effective at the wide end. I'd give it somewhere between 1-2 stops effectiveness at 16mm, as compared to the Canon versions which is easily at 3 stops. - The price of this lens is noticeably higher than the competition while performing a bit worse. The Bad: - The image sharpness at 35mm is fairly poor, even stopped down to f/8. For travel photography this doesn't matter, but I wouldn't expect to make giant prints based on images taken with this lens at 35mm. These adapters plug into a 2017 Jetta SE with basic audio. However, the polarity is reversed. Simple fix. Pull the pins and reverse them. Warning for you folks with limited car audio knowledge....polarity is important. Proper phasing gives your system a fuller sound. Reversed polarity will cause your speakers to move in the opposite direction when firing. In a very basic 4 speaker system this isn't a big deal. However, if your system is expanded with perhaps a sub or additional speakers polarity will be a factor for you. In general you want your system phased the same all around. Audiophiles may take exception to this statement.....but I'm not talking to them. This is for all the folks that just want that crappy sounding factory system to be rejuvenated a bit lol. These adapters are perfect for replacing those factory VW speakers with anything aftermarket.....but you need to reverse the pins.

Overall I'm happy with the kit. Yes I would recommend it. No it's not perfect. Read below for pros, cons, some things I learned, tips, a little explanation on it's features, and see the my photos as I explain. I'm a complete newbie with electronics, this is not my first time soldering, but it's my first time soldering on a pcb board and putting something like this together. I wanted a kit to practice on, and I bought this as my first since it might become useful on other kits or projects. I learned that my helping hands I bought saved me a lot of time, and I need to buy an adjustable iron. Currently I have a 60W Weller and it got way too hot. I did damage the board, but I was able to make things work, and everything does work. After a few solders I found out that my smallest tip doesn't transfer heat as fast and I was able to finish the rest of the board with no damage. But my joints weren't very clean. The kit is just thrown into a bag, and I did have a couple things bent, but nothing broken and I was able to make everything work. It does come with assembly instructions, but no manual for using it. Thre instructions were not printed well so they were almost unusable, but they did still help. Forget the photos on them, they were too blurry to make out, and the schematic is very hard to see. But the pcb board seems decent quality and very well labeled making assembly fairly smooth. The heat sink is painted, so I scratched off the paint hoping for better heat transfer from the lm317. I don't think it matters though since it can only draw .1 amps. The instructions explain this, but poorly, it took me a few minutes before it clicked in my head. Desolder the wires from the voltage segment display, and solder on leads that you clipped off of diodes and resistors. This gives a better way to connect the display to the board, but you can still manage with using the wires, or leave the wires to put the display on the case. (See my photos for a detailed view of the leads). I was also confused with the LEDs and terminals, so here's what I found out (see my photos). Block P1 is voltage out and ground. Block P2 is buzzer input, switching output, and logic input. The blue led is power, yellow corresponds to your switching output (that's why it blinks), red and green correspond to the logic input, red for yes and green for no. So you can connect the switching terminal to the logic and watch the red/green LEDs blink accordingly, or connect it to the buzzer and it will buzz accordingly. The adjustable resistor changes the switching speed. I'm glad I bought this kit. I learned a lot and had fun making it. I do wish the instructions were better, but it helped me learn more since they were garbage. And i wish this could put out more amps; i connected it to a computer fan and it died on me, but did come back to life once disconnected. The fan is brushless and rated 12V and .6 amps.

OVERALL: The keyboard/mouse combo for the price is quite great, and would buy again in a pinch. It looks nice, feels nice, and just works. I bought this keyboard to give me a mac-like experience on Windows, and I'm overall happy with what I bought, but may replace the keyboard at some point. PROS: - Keyboard feels durable. The keyboard is heavier than both my windows and mac keyboards - If you are used to typing with flat keys, or if you're accustomed to the mac keyboard, this keyboard is a natural transition - The DPI switch on the mouse is perfect; it typically takes buying an expensive gaming mouse to control the sensitivity of the mouse with a button-click. - The mouse moves smooth as butter and it's very easy to control - Clicks are QUIET but can be felt. The mouse buttons CAN be sensitive, which can take some getting used to, but overall, the mouse is smooth and feels very natural to use. - the number keypad is super useful; I missed having this on my mac keyboard. - The keyboard looks and feels kinda like metal, in spite of being 100% cheap plastic :) CONS: - The keyboard requires the use of the 'fn' key to use the function keys; not ideal if you rely on function keys to do work (coding, media editing). The manufacturers could have moved the media buttons to their own row, and preserved the function keys. - The mouse and keyboard both fall asleep after some short idle time, and will wake on button/key press. This is fine for the keyboard, however, if you're used to clearing your screensaver by moving your mouse, that won't work here. You will need to physically left or right click. This sounds like a petty complaint, however, it is annoying to have to change an intuitive behavior because of poor engineering. Waking on mouse-move would have been nice - The keys on the keyboard require more strength than other keyboards. Many times have I hit a shift key, or a back space, or a space bar, and saw nothing happen on the screen. Compared to the mac keyboards especially, this keyboard requires a bit of force when pressing the keys. - There appears to be a delay when comparing to my logitech/mac keyboards. Keypresses feel much more responsive when typing. As someone who writes code on a regular basis, and powers through tasks using a plethora of keyboard shortcuts, this can really put a damper in my work flow, if key presses are being processed out of sync. - Windows key is positioned and labeled poorly. The key itself is much smaller than other keyboards. and says 'Win', rather than the icon you may be used to. If you use the keyboard shortcuts for Aero-snap, or if you tend to navigate/search the start menu solely with your keyboard, you may get frustrated. I find myself having to stop and stare at my keyboard to make sure I'm hitting the right key - not ideal for power users. - Not all keys respond equally. Certain keys, specifically the CTRL keys, shift keys, Windows keys, Enter key, and really, many of the larger keys, require additional force to get the key press to register. The reason for this, is that the actual button under the key is small, and the larger keys themselves will simply move AROUND the button. You must hit each large key with additional force or dead-center on the key. As such, prepare for your typing speed and quality to significantly reduce. SUMMARY: This keyboard is ok. It excels in its physical design and comfort, but lacks performance in its basic functions. especially when comparing to other brands of wireless keyboards/mouse. THIS PRODUCT IS GOOD FOR: 1. Home PC's 2. People who simply need SOMETHING on a budget, but cannot afford name-brand alternatives 3. People who navigate primarily with a mouse, not a keyboard 4. People who do not use function keys in their workflow 5. People who do not like mechanical keyboards 6. My parents THIS PRODUCT IS SUBSTANDARD FOR: 1. The keyboard is terrible for gaming and editing anything 2. Power users 3. Multimedia professionals (video editors, audio editors, etc) 4. Software engineers 5. People who do not type heavily/hard

I bought this board to get better OpenVPN performance over that of the Raspberry Pi 3. Out of the box, the only general purpose operating software available did not support OpenVPN. Also, the Linux kernel supplied with it did not use kernel modules. Everything is compiled into the kernel directly. This means if you need any feature that is not already included, you have to compile a new kernel from scratch, and build an install image yourself. While I was eventually able to do this, but it took 2 weeks of effort, and the help of a couple of knowledgeable people in the Libre/Firefly community. Not for the faint of heart. After all that, I was able to get 90 megabit per second throughput, as opposed to 30 megabit with the Raspberry Pi 3. The Renegade could probably do more, as I was hitting the limits of my ISP. I am very happy with it, despite all the extra effort needed to get it to work. If you only need the base functions that come with the vendor supplied OS, this board is worth the price. If you need additional features beyond what is supplied, then get ready to delve deep into Linux development. Hopefully, they will get the software up to par in the future. But right now, it really seems half baked.

I bought this, along with a Fence Clip to record my son's baseball games. As expected, the included battery only lasts about 90 minutes. I use an external 10000 mAh power brick to keep it charged. That's enough to last through five games. My 256 GB micro SD card can record 9 hours at 4k/30fps, which is good for four games. An aside. I really want to record at 4k/60fps, which this camera can do, but the storage requirements are prohibitively high. I wouldn't mind getting multiple micro SD cards, but I just don't have enough storage on my PC to keep all the games in highest quality. I'm not too concerned with image stabilization since my primary use case is having it attached to a fence. Wind noise reduction is nice, but I haven't really tested how good it is. I like being able to select between wide/medium/narrow lens angles to ensure I can capture the whole field. The only real minor issue is the minor blip in recording that happens whenever the camera starts a new file. The camera uses FAT as the card format, which restricts file size to 4GB. As you are recording, when the file reaches this limit, it will automatically switch to a new file. When it does so it misses a fraction of a second of recording, which is noticeable when you stitch them all together later (Quicktime player makes this super easy). My other issue with the camera is my secondary use case. I ride an electric scooter to work every day and want to use this camera to record my commute (in case of accidents, belligerent pedestrians, etc). The problem is that I sometimes forget to turn off the camera when I reach my destination, leading to a dead battery the next time I go to use it. I'd be great if the camera had a mode that helped me overcome this. Not sure how it would work. Some kind of auto-shut off under certain conditions. Dunno. I can't use an external battery because I keep it in its waterproof housing in case of rain (and just to protect it). So the 4 out of 5 stars is due to the 4GB file size limit (switch to FAT32 please) and subsequent blip in recording, and the problems using it on my commute. If those don't matter to you then it's still a great camera. And less than half the price of an equivalent GoPro.
