Much sturdier/high-end construction than I expected. The people who say these are of odd construction either have very simple ears or have never had to work with real ear pieces or hearing aides. About half my job is inserting and removing hearing aides, checking fit and accuracy/efficacy. These just need to be inserted at the correct angle to be comfortable and effective. The problem with mainstream ear buds is they rely only on the outermost part of the ear and many people are not equipped to accommodate that or at least to allow for optimal sound quality. (And they are usually cheaply made.) Short of custom molded ear pieces/IEMs to account for the exact nuances of the human ear, this is the best shape available, in my opinion. The shape allows for for the eartips to slightly slide past the conch of the ear and behind the tragus, while sightly resting on the anti-helix. See Wikipedia: Pinna (anatomy). This allows for a remarkably similar experience to that of ear pieces that rest more in the ear canal (though not exact -- that is pretty much impossible or at least not recommended without a custom fit!) To anyone having fit problems, try twisting the earpiece from the outer edge. Do this slowly and by feel -- most likely counterclockwise, but as always, it depends on the person and the ear. I think the fit of these is the real highlight. I have had a lot of difficulty with headphones in this respect and have almost always opted for huge, over the ear models. These are comfortable and very light. They are really easy to insert and remove. The sound is great. As others have said, you're probably going to want them a little louder if you're extra bass-humgry, but chances are, if that's what you like you're a "louder the better" type of person. For the record, I've been more than happy at less than .25 and .5 capacity on all devices from phones, to mp3 players to laptops. I think the sound is highly precise has a great range for the quality/price range, but keep in mind that that also depends on your file. Plenty of others have gotten into more detail about the specifics of sound and quality, so I wanted to focus more on fit, because that's what I know well. Overall? The sound is what I expect or better, regardless of music type. Great range/precision. The fit makes possible a remarkable, intimate and weightless listening experience. But don't expect to feel like you're completely in another world in really high traffic areas. I, like other reviewers, still can't believe these are priced as low as they are. It pains me to spend more than $20 on about anything. I'm cheaper than I should be, and I'd buy these again in a heartbeat. Don't have $300+ to spend? Think you'll be happy with superb rather than transcendent? Get these. This is one of those few times where you get a fair bit more than you pay for.

It's no DSLR, but the start up time, shot to shot speed, autofocus performance, and low light picture quality are perfectly acceptable for this class of camera. What I love about it: the size, price, zoom range, video quality, optical image stabilization, remote control by wifi, and battery life. What could be better: ISO, white balance, and exposure compensation adjustments require a deep dive into the menus. No manual control of aperture or shutter speed. I realize this is pretty normal for point and shoot cameras, but a little work on the software could make this a better camera. I also don't see why the camera can't be used while it's charging. My cell phone can do this, why can't my camera? What's wrong with it: flash pictures in auto mode are generally overexposed, often blowing out highlights. Exposure compensation has no effect on this. There is no flash exposure compensation. Workarounds include going into P mode and manually decreasing the ISO value, or putting a one stop neutral density filter over the flash. The first means it's no longer a point and shoot, and the second decreases the reach of the flash. Either way it's a hassle, whereas Sony could easily fix this with a simple software change. (My camera has version 2.00 of the firmware.) I deducted one star for the flash exposure problem. Others might not mind it, or might consider it a deal breaker.

In my last truck, I installed an earlier version of this stereo and loved it. So, when I traded that vehicle in, I decided to purchase this stereo for my new truck. I could not be more thrilled! This stereo is everything that its predecessor was and more. Firstly, the AUX line is a must-have. Being able to hook up the kids' iPods or the sound output of a portable DVD player is worth the purchase price alone. The USB port is great, and I can pop in a USB thumb drive and have hours of music at my fingertips. The CD player of course plays MP3 encoded CD-ROMs and others, so you can fit several albums onto a single CD if you are so inclined. The real reason I purchased this stereo was the Bluetooth, though. I use the stereo as a speakerphone, and I use it to wirelessly stream music from my phone. It works unbelievably well--much better even than the previous version of this radio! Firstly, the stereo comes with an external microphone which can be mounted on the visor or near the driver to make the conversation more clear. The sound is so good that people that I call can't tell that I'm talking to them on a speakerphone. The stereo apparently incorporates noise-cancelling technology, because the microphone will not pick up and loop the sound coming from the speakers. Amazingly, the stereo communicates with my phone (LG Lucid in my case) and can display my contacts' info right on the faceplate of the stereo. I can flip through my contacts and recent calls without pulling my phone out of my pocket. There is even a voice dial feature that will call a contact by name without me having to flip through all the contacts! The Bluetooth audio feature is just as impressive. In the previous version, I could wirelessly play music from my phone, but could not control the phone from the head unit. Now, I can play, pause, skip backward and forward, and explore different tracks and albums from the faceplate. The artist name, song title, etc. are all viewable from the display. There are other features that I have not explored yet. I do not currently use Pandora, but apparently the stereo is equipped to control the Pandora application on both iPhones and Android devices. There is a second AUX port on the back of the stereo, which can be used to route a cable to the inside of a center console or similar. That way, you don't have to have a cable strung from the console or back seat to the radio when piping in audio from non-Bluetooth devices. The only criticism I have is that the secondary functions of the memory buttons (buttons numbered 1 through 6) are not illuminated. These secondary functions are things like pause/play and such which are used when the tuner is not active. Unfortunately, these are impossible to read in low light, and this can be frustrating if you are using a non-tuner mode and you do not have all the functions memorized.

"Designed for Linux Developers & Open Source Experts" is marketing spin for "our router is broken and you'll have to fix it." For starters, this router is marketed toward Open Source fans, but when you first start the router, it takes you through one of those 'configuration wizards' for setup, and it REQUIRES Internet Explorer. There's IE-specific JavaScript on the first page of the setup wizard, which is simply asking "Do you want to run the setup wizard?" and has yes and no radio buttons and a continue button. There's no reason for even having scripting on this page, but they put broken IE-only script there and the continue button doesn't work. Absolute incompetence. After getting past the wizard, though, the normal web interface works in Firefox. But there are more problems to come. The router's DNS server is buggy and slow, and the router FORCES you to use it. I often couldn't get through to websites. It hijacks any DNS requests destined for a server on the Internet and handles them itself, so you can't go around the problem. Someone made modified firmware with a different DNS server. You need this custom firmware for the router to be usable at all. It will still hijack DNS with the modification, but it won't be so broken. This router is terrible. I initially thought that my DS Lite didn't work at all with this router, but I found out quite unintuitively that you have to configure it in 'g-only' mode. The original DS and DS Lite are both b-only, so this is the only setting that logically shouldn't work, but it's actually the only setting that does work. I also had connectivity issues with my Wii, but I seem to have sorted those out, and I'm not even sure what I did. The router would crash sometimes when I connected a device (Wii, DS, my laptop) and I've have to manually reset it. I have it mostly working now but it just wasn't worth the trouble. If I knew in advance how much work it would be, I wouldn't have bothered. Only buy this if it's the cheapest router available, you have hardly any money, you desperately need a wireless router, it doesn't need to work well, and you've got plenty of free time to sink into tinkering with it. This router is terrible.

There is a huge thread over at "Kindle Fire won't connect to my WiFi" in the Kindle Customer Service Q&A forum where people are discussing the connectivity issues going on with the Kindle Fire. I'm one of them. This device has great potential, but it just won't connect to the internet through many people's wifi routers. Because of this, I give the KF a 1 star rating. Currently, the only way I can use it is by going to a semi-local Starbucks. You can also do a Google search for "Kindle Fire router" and find a LARGE number of people online posing questions about the issues they're having getting their Kindle Fire connected to the internet through their Wifi routers. This is a systemic problem that really needs some publicity so Amazon will see it as a real issue that needs to be addressed. EDIT: After 4 solid days and nights, spending every spare minute I had reading hundreds of forum posts, reviews, web sites and more, and trying numerous "fixes" to gain connectivity between the KF and our router, I was finally able to get it to work by resetting our router back to the factory default settings. Once I did that, the KF miraculously connected to the internet and worked. {and the angels began singing in the background} And now, after a week of using the KF, adding apps, setting up email, watching a show through Netflix and other assorted fun, I felt it was important to come back and revise my one star rating of this product to a 4 star rating. It would have gotten a 5 star rating if it hadn't been so darned picky about the routers it connects to and the settings on those routers. However, the resetting of our router back to the factory default settings did the trick for us (my husband has a KF too) and now we're both happy campers with our KF. I'm just glad I was persistent with my attempts to fix the problem instead of doing what my husband wanted me to do within the first hour of router troubles: "Send the **** things back to Amazon!" For those of you who are having router troubles, you might try these potential fixes: 1. Enter the correct wifi password/passkey/passphrase and make sure its less than 15 characters long and does not contain any special characters 2. Try setting your wifi access with a static IP address (I tried it and it still doesn't connect properly) 3. Enter the MAC address of the KF if your router uses MAC addressing for part of its security 4. SSID should be less than 10 characters, again with no special characters 5. Kindle is currently on version 6.1 or version 6.2 (we received ours with the current version) 6. Reboot router 7. Rebooted KF 8. Completely turn off router firewall and see if that helps 9. After a BRIEF success with changing router channels, I then tried all channels, 1-11, and had no additional success. 10. Be sure your router's SSID is broadcasted to the public (some people have posted it doesn't work if it's not a broadcasted SSID) 11. Change wifi security settings from WPA2 to WPA or vice versa 12. Updated the firmware on your router to the current release. 13. Reset your router back to the factory default settings. Good luck to all having troubles, and it's really a nice device once you get past the router connectivity issues.

So many smaller consumer devices come with USB cables that are "charging" type cables and do not have data lines or do not have the data lines connected to the Type A and MicroB pins on the connectors. This saves the manufacturer money. This also causes havoc with consumers that think all USB cables are created equally. They are NOT. So if you have an item that will not connect to your computer via USB, then you are probably the victum of a charging USB cable. You need to order a couple of these cables to get the real deal. These cables will charge AND will pass data from your device to your computer. Amazon should re-think the description of these cables as the phrase "charger cable" appears as a marketing word yet discounts the value of the cable since it has all USB data lines available.

This 11.6" laptop is great on battery life, has stellar performance, and houses a sleek and portable form factor. Chrome OS is limited to some, but with a constant internet connection and a computer at home that you can remote desktop to (not entirely necessary), there isn't much you can't do with a Chromebook. The dual-core Intel Celeron (Haswell) CPU inside isn't power hungry, it doesn't put out much heat at all, and it powers Chrome OS like a boss. The C720 also carries 2GBs of RAM, which is plenty for most of what you'll be doing inside of Chrome. You won't have any stuttering or lag with multiple tabs open in Chrome, a video playing or music in the background while blogging on social media. At the time of this review I currently have 6 tabs open, including a livestream on Twitch.tv, and there is no lag whatsoever. Battery life is also fantastic. With social media, email, music, and word processing, you can expect anywhere from 7 - 9 hours with the C720, slightly less if constantly streaming video. I had a day where I unplugged the laptop at 7am, used it for notes and videos through school till around noon, then used it all day at work researching tech and playing videos; I ended the day at 10pm with around 49% battery, I then proceeded to use the laptop most of the next day at home before it finally dying around 3pm. So you can expect to get through a whole day with this Chromebook. Another additional benefit is USB 3.0. There is 1 on this laptop, as well as a single USB 2.0 port on the other side of the laptop. You also have full HDMI out for running an extra HDMI enabled monitor/tv. This greatly improves functionality if you enjoy having multiple displays. It's lightweight, portable, looks great and the build quality is superb for a sub $200 laptop, but there are a couple downsides. The original carried a full-size SD card slot (when inserted, the card would be flush with the laptop, making portable storage easy), the C720 lacks this, and only carries a half-depth SD card slot, minor downside. Also, there are no function keys as well as no caps lock key, like the original. I would like to be able to ALT-F4 out of Chrome, instead I have to CTRL-W to close each tab/window individually. The screen is 11.6" and has a resolution of 1333x768, which is just fine for a 11" laptop. Viewing angles and color reproduction wasn't the best, but you won't have many complaints sitting in front of the laptop for a few hours. Another downfall out of the box was the keyboard, the keys were shallow but well spaced. After a couple days of use I got completely used to this and am now typing this review on the C720 at 60+ WPM. To conclude, if you're on a budget looking for a laptop, already live inside of Google's ecosystem or are okay with living in the cloud (no classic Windows applications/limited storage), then this laptop will serve you well.The C720 has the best battery life for a Chromebook on the market, other than Dell's Chromebook 11 ($100 more than the C720 at the time of this review),which only carries a couple hours of battery life over the Acer here. Other than that, you won't find better performance, battery life and a simple, utilitarian design in any other sub $200 laptop. Pros: Performance Battery life Portability Loud speakers Good trackpad with easy-to-use gestures Cons: Screen viewing angles and colors Lack of caps lock key and F4 key. (Search key can be swapped with Caps lock in settings) Keys are a bit shallow and hard to use at first If you reading this feel I didn't cover some aspect of the laptop, feel free to ask a question on this review, I'm very active in replying to Amazon questions. Thanks!

I bought the RT-AC66U as an upgrade for my very old WRT54GL. I decided it was finally time to move on from 802.11G to allow for far better media streaming around the house. Additionally, I just upgraded to 50 Mbps internet service (and a new SB6141 modem), and my old WRT54GL couldn't even handle the bandwidth on the WAN port, limiting me to about 30 Mbps. I did a lot of research before purchasing this router, because it's probably one of the most expensive home routers you can get. I considered the RT-N66U for a little cheaper, however I figured if I was going to spend that much, I might as well go for the RT-AC66U and probably not need to upgrade again for many years. The range and speed of this router are fantastic. I live on 2.5 acres and I can go all the way to the back of my property and still have a little signal left on my phone. On a laptop I'm sure I'd get enough signal to be usable anywhere on my property, and that's pretty impressive, especially since half of the exterior of the house is thick stone. I never have an issue hitting 50 Mbps down and 5 Mbps up dead on, which is what my package is. Speaking of phones, I just got an HTC One so I finally have a device to connect to the router over 802.11ac. Not much to say other than it works and is pretty fast, though it's kind of hard to utilize that kind of bandwidth on a phone. I don't expect to run out and buy any network adapters that are 802.11ac either seeing that 802.11n is still fast enough for most anything I'd do, but like I said, I consider it well worth it to know that this router should satisfy my needs for 5+ years easily. And one last thing, being a long time DD-WRT user, I strongly weighed my options of what routers had what capabilities. This router with Asuswrt-Merlin firmware is fantastic. I haven't even really begun to use all of the features, but I do use the OpenVPN server regularly with no issues at all. If you're willing to spend a little extra money, this router will do everything you want, and anything you will want for years to come.

I've used these headphones for quite a while now and they are very comfortable. Wearing them for 8hrs a day has not been a discomfort. After that the phone was turned on and they quickly paired. It was really nice listening to Prime music in Chrome, having a call come in, the music pausing automatically whilst the call is in progress on the cell phone and then the music resuming after the call. This makes it great for the office - listen to music at the computer but no more frantic rushing to find which chrome tab has the music streaming as the call comes in. Having said that, the call quality has been hit or miss. About 50% of the calls I've made or received have suffered from bad sound artifacts that have meant I have been unable to continue the call with the bluetooth on. .I have had to switch bluetooth off, continue the call on speaker or handset but i did find that switching back to bluetooth for the remainder of the call has worked pretty well. Edit: I have had to stop using these headphones for calls as everyone was complaining that they couldn't hear me on the phone calls. The headphones are still decent enough for listening to music, but I got these to work with my phone and that is just not going to work. The sound quality hasn't been too bad when streaming from the computer but the range of the device does vary. I can go upstairs from the computer and still hear the music, but if i go into another room on the same floor I get told that the device is out of range. The indicators with this headphone are very useful though - the above mentioned out of range along with a vibrating feedback (in case the earbuds are not in your ears) and the audible cue when you turn them on that tells you the battery life is very helpful.

I've tried the wired Sharkoon X-Tatic, but hated the bulky, heavy wire and the constant hissing background noise. I then tried the wireless Logitech F540 - loved the wireless (can never go back to the wire) and overall great headset EXCEPT I couldn't tell front from back as they are only stereo. This is my third try at a headset for the PS3. I think I'm glad I did - love the wireless and the sounds are comparable to the Logitech, and now I can tell front from back. It's certainly not full surround sound immersion, but I do gain an edge over regular stereo headsets. I can't say the build quality and style are as good as the Logitech, but they're just as comfortable and functional. I took away a star as I find the mixer and volume controls to be difficult to both locate and use; they're too flush with the side and takes more time and effort to adjust, especially during a match. But I find the onscreen status display to be very useful, such as checking if my mic is muted. I'm not sure why some have problems with the chat/gameplay sound settings and volume. Leave the mixer in the default (it's got a tactile stop in the middle) and it's perfectly balanced. Slide it all the way down to instantly mute all the gabbers and rappers without having to actively mute each one - very convenient! And I actually find the volume too loud - I have it dialed all the way to minimum, to the point of muting it entirely. And bass is definitely there - not sure why some say there isn't enough; it's almost too much at times. If I had to choose between the Logitech and the Sony, I'd pick these - they're comparable in comfort, sound, and function, but the Sony wins with the virtual surround and better integration with the PS3. I just wish they were available a few months earlier so I saved a Benjamin.

A split keyboard really is the way to go. You're in more comfortable posture and slouching less. The only drawback is there is no one-handed typing, ie if you want to quickly type a search term while still holding onto the mouse. As an added bonus a split keyboard is also more portable. Two halves can be packed into a backpack much more neatly than one whole. As to Kinesis Freestyle2 specifically, it is the most affordable split-type keyboard I was able to find. Not counting the R-Go Split which is compact-form and has shallow keys (ie it is a completely different type of keyboard) there is nothing else on the market anywhere near its price point. Everything else is at least $150 (including the mechanical Freestyle Pro) but can easily exceed $300. So at $90 the Freestyle2 is the cheapest way to test out the split-type. For me personally, the function keys on the left get in the way, as does the page-up row on the right. I'm used to there being empty space to the left of Tab and to the right of Enter, but in Freestlye 2 there is another 1 row beyond Enter without increased empty space in between. (And 2 more rows beyond Tab.) I find it disorienting and it increases the learning curve. Users may end up blaming typing difficulties on split-type that are really caused by Kinesis opting to cram a high number of keys on a relatively small board and sacrificing separation space. Just look at that enter key, it's small and surrounded on all sides, good luck finding that in a hurry.

I just switched from another hybrid drive, I believe a seagate model also 1tb. The big draw to this hard drive is the 120gb SSD vs my 4 or 8gb ssd. I have a late 2011 macbook pro 15" which has been holding up quiet well for its age. Pros: -Price. I purchased for ~ $150 at the time of this review. For a 1tb drive alone it would be steep, but paired with a 120gb SSD, a steal in my humble opinion. -Performance has been great so far (~1 week of use). I noticed faster boot times and general UI response, you mileage may vary. -Option of Fusion drive or SSD + HDD via osx software. -Comes with a very hand SATA -> USB adapter for duplicating your old drive. -Looks like some sort of black ops hardware or something. Very cool case design (reversed PCB all black). Cons: -Tricky install, I read some threads on an apple forum talking about how to install, I'll list my procedure below. -I don't like that the 120gb SSD shows as the only drive out of the box, you need their software to reveal the 1tb platters / partition. How I would've installed mine (2nd time around): 1. download the osx tool 2. physically install the drive 3. use their SATA -> USB Adapter plug in your old OS drive 4. boot mac holding down "Option" key (lets you choose a boot device), select your os drive 5. once in osx, run their utility, to create either a Fusion drive or SSD + HDD partitions. (Fusion drive described below) ** DO NOT initialize the drive when OSX boots and asks to initialize the drive, the WD software will initialize it for you properly. 6. create and boot a mavericks USB thumbdrive install. > boot it > use diskutil to "Restore" your old os drive to your new fusion drive. 7. profit :} Fusion drive vs SSD + HDD. Basically it comes down to do you want to manage the 120gb SSD or let the OS decide what files get used the most and move them to the SSD for you. A Fusion drive takes note of what files get used most and moves them to the SSD partition, the drive shows up in diskutil as a 1.12TB drive. Some people may want to setup the drive in SSD + HDD because they want to put VM's or something that needs lots of IO onto the SSD. This drive setup shows up as two partitions in diskutil, 1tb and 120gb. Personally I trust the science and chose the fusion drive. I hope this helps, if it did please select "Helpful".

I am a "professional" photographer in the sense that people pay me to take photos sometimes, but I don't pay the bills with my camera - it's really more of a self-funding hobby. I spend the money on good gear when it makes sense to do so, but I am always looking for performance at a reasonable price, and the price/features balance on this filter seemed worth the risk.I was initially pleased with the performance of this polarizer. However, after some use in the field, it is obvious that in this case you get what you pay for. The filter provides effective polarization and does not cause any visible color cast as is common with many inexpensive filters. Using it on a 16mm prime lens (APS-C camera, 24mm equivalent) showed no vignetting, and I took the combination on several backpacking trips to shoot landscapes. The first indication of trouble was when I tried to use it on my 70-200 f/2.8 when shooting an outdoor wedding in fairly bright light. The camera seemed unable to autofocus properly, and every shot had a visible level of blur and serious lack of sharpness. Remove filter, problem solved, so I tossed it in my bag and kept moving. My next hiking trip covered several miles through changing lighting conditions, and I removed the polarizer for several shots. Later, when editing the photos from the day, I found myself admiring the sharpness and clarity of the photos taken in conditions where the filter was not needed. The photos taken with the filter were not "bad" but when compared to unfiltered images from the same day it was obvious that the lens was better without. The attached photos will illustrate - the trail shot is unfiltered, the waterfall is filtered. The loss of sharpness may not be visible at this resolution, but the overall feel of the waterfall photo is not one of good detail and clarity. The trail photo has much better detail and sharpness and was taken with the exact same gear, on the same day, minus the filter. I decided to test by taking an identical shot with and without the filter. When I compared the two side-by-side, it was obvious that the filter caused a significant loss of sharpness and detail that was visible to my 14-year-old son at a glance. Too many photographers agonize over pixel-peeping levels of perfect sharpness; I am not that person, but having good clarity in your images matters, and this filter will not get you there. Spend more and get a better product.

DO NOT BUY THIS! Pay attention to the return policy on battery backups like these. Ensure it says returns accepted. If you're purchasing it to use with a desktop or laptop you also need to make sure that the power supply in your desktop or laptop will work with a simulated sine wave ups battery backup like this. Even though the item's description says it will work with desktops(see the screenshot that I took directly from the product descript) it doesn't work with certain types of PC power supplies. Find the model number of your power supply and look up if it has PWF(power factor correction). If it does then this battery backup won't work properly with it and in fact can damage it and other parts of your PC. The item description is misleading and doesn't clarify at all that this battery backup won't work with power supplies with power factor correction, which a good majority of modern power supplies have now. This is a clear misrepresention of the operation of this item. When I discovered this battery backup causes my desktop to turn off during a power loss rather than stay on long enough for a proper shutdown I contacted cyberpower and the manufacturer of my power supply(cooler master). Both companies confirmed that a simulated sine wave battery backup won't work and is in fact unsafe to use with a power supply with power factor correction. When I contacted Amazon for a return they forced me to try some troubleshooting despite me making it clear and providing links to articles about this issue proving that no amount of troubleshooting will work to fix this. They told me this was unreturnable and that they will have to send it to a specialist team to approve the refund and that I should wait 24-48 hours for an email from them. Well it took them less than an hour to decide they were going to steal my money and I got an email refusing to refund me despite the item's complete lack of an accurate description, not even a generic disclaimer. Now I have to deal with filing a dispute with my credit card because Amazon decided they'd rather steal from me than do the right thing. Even if your power supply doesn't have power factor correction it's worth it to just get a pure sine wave battery backup. That way you'll always know it'll work with what you plug into it.

Confident this is a very good AIO liquid cooler, but be very concerned about who you purchase it from. The Arctic II 280 model is in high demand and out-of-stock from many distributors. I suspect this Amazon distributor shipped me a unit that might have been dropped/damaged in their warehouse, because the external shipping box seemed fine, while upon closer inspection the retail box was damaged in the exact same zone as the radiator. When I return it for a refund they might box it up again and send it out to you !!! Great .... was looking forward to using this Arctic Liquid Freezer II 280 in a new computer build. When I removed it tonight from it's factory retail package the radiator frame 3" from the end with the hose attachments was crushed in approx 3/8" deep x 2.5" wide, damaging fins and frame. This is not slight cosmetic damage - the radiator probably will not maintain a seal over time and could leak inside my build. There was no hint outside the shipping container, so I had no reason to worry until I removed the radiator a couple weeks later and saw the crushed in frame and fin damage. As my photos show, something hit the radiator frame with a lot of force in one spot also causing a crease in the thin retail box which has NO side protection for the radiator. There was nothing else in my shipped order except the radiator, which is why I am suspicious the distributor shipped the unit without inspecting it or sadly knew it maybe fell and hit the edge of a pallet rack and just didn't care, making it now my problem. Will follow up on the Amazon site for this item to report what the distributor or manufacturer has to say. Radiators and their fin assemblies are rather fragile as metal case items go. The manufacturer: Arctic, protected the CPU heat exchanger pump assembly reasonably well inside the retail box, but the radiator frame and fins had only the thinnest cheap single skin cardboard layer for shipping protection, that is wholly inadequate. Maybe they think ... well it's metal, what could happen. Hello - it is a labyrinth of ultra thin metal fins, a zillion tiny tubes filled with water and a soft metal frame..... a lot can happen that is bad for customers like us if they don't protect it properly during shipment.

We just bought this for our young son who had spent the last year testing the integrity of my wife's ipad air 2 case. She'll be happy to get her ipad back and I'll be happy knowing that Amazon's worry free kid warranty is covering this one. Now to the meat: Three stars is a middling review for sure, but I really an happy so far, since this is such a good value. I can see upgrading to four stars later after the set up pain is behind me. More on that below. Technically it's better than you'd expect from a fifty dollar tablet. Not top of the line, but one tenth or less of the price of top of the line, and for a kid to play on is just fine. I will say the one clear place where they cut cost was on the cameras. My 2005 flip phone took less noisy pictures. Maybe in bright daylight they would be worth a hoot. Too bad for only one reason--my son loves taking my phone (and my real camera) and playing and playing photog. Mostly is just blurry feet and unintentional Dutch angles, but every once in a while he gets an interestingly framed capture. This tablet camera will let him play and explore, but we probably won't be submitting these pics to Flickr lately. Set up wasn't impossible, but there are pitfalls. We have ipads, and I use android, but I was able to figure out how to get around the fire os and the freetime app pretty quickly for it being my first experience with either. That said, I doubt my parents would be so lucky. There are some nonintuitive steps for people unaccustomed with fearlessly banging away on touchscreens, especially with regard to controlling, adding, removing freetime content within the adult profile. I had read in another review about a father's severe frustration with trying to remove the thousands of preloaded titles in freetime. It is all true. You must manually select every individual icon from a settings menu on the adult side. There is no "select all" or other shortcut. It takes forever, and it is necessary if you don't want to crash the tablet or run out of space immediately. Also without reading that review, and knowing I needed to go looking for this painful task, I might never have figured it out at all. The gist is that the freetime app which is the default environment when you set up initially has literally thousands of terrible book, game, and video titles displayed as icons on the home screens. They aren't installed though, not bloatware exactly, just there as bait. If you press any icon however, it begins downloading and installing automatically. Trouble is, it's that easy. So a child, especially a young one, would likely just start by pressing every icon in sight. Far better as a parent to start by whittling down the selections to, you know, less than a thousand apps of dubious quality to start with. So I went tryng to figure that out, did, and then was annoyed that they seemingly designed the software to make it harder to avoid than it could be. Simply adding a "Clear All" button in the settings menu would earn a while star on this review. Also as an aside, I was disappointed that Amazon video or a version of it can't be added into the kids freetime profile. Or at least I could not get it to. The kid can navigate the full app on the iPad just fine--somehow he finds every truck video. It's a shame that the free and "Included with Prime" content isn't available on freetime. Those gripes aside, this is a fantastic value for what it is, especially with holiday discounts.

Okay, I decided to wait a little bit before I reviewed the Paperwhite - I knew moving from the [[ASIN:B004HZYA6E Kindle Keyboard]] to the Paperwhite would involve some changes that I would have to get used to, due to the differences in hardware. So overall, I am very much enjoying this Kindle - the quality of the eInk screen is great, and if you turn on the Page Refresh option, there is no noticeable ghosting. My husband is also enjoying my ownership of the Paperwhite...because I am an insomniac who reads herself to sleep, and he needs a pitch-black room to sleep in. I've tried many different book lights over the years - including the [[ASIN:0641077491 LightWedge Reading Light]] - but if they were dim enough for him to sleep by, they were too dim for me to read by (or in the case of the LightWedge, it's highly annoying to move the wedge from page to page so it still leaks light into the room). This Paperwhite has completely eradicated that problem. If you are someone who has a similar problem, you should seriously consider the Paperwhite, even if you've never had an e-reader before. You may have seen some reviews complaining about the small areas of darkness near the bottom of the screen with this light; they come from the light dispersion from the LED's embedded in the bottom of the device screen. I won't deny these are there. However, I mentioned the LightWedge above for a reason - it had the exact same problem, except on a much larger scale since you could see light rings throughout the whole lens. But as with the LightWedge, I have personally found that I notice this problem less and less as time goes on; especially as I drop the intensity of the light as my eyes adjust to darkness. For the most part, those areas of darkness don't intrude on the text you are reading so it is a minor quibble in a product that has to obey the laws of physics and try to sell at a decent price point. I am also really enjoying the "X minutes left in chapter" feature at the bottom left. For someone who frequently says "one more chapter before I go to sleep", it's nice to know how much time I have left. :) That being said, there are some small issues that keep me from giving this 5 stars. The biggest is something you have probably heard elsewhere - the bezel for this device is too small to hold comfortably without a cover. The Kindle Keyboard had a nice, wide bevel - partially because of the physical page turn buttons - that meant you could hold the device on its own quite easily. That simply isn't the case here - and I have pretty small hands. If you are planning to buy this e-reader, you need to also plan on buying a cover. (I have one from Etsy, so I can't comment on any provided via Amazon.) Moving from the Keyboard to the Paperwhite has mostly been painless, though I do wonder if it is possible for Amazon to look into adding physical page turn buttons to the bevel. Because as noted above, the small bevel makes the product uncomfortable to hold, but it also has returned page turning a two handed process. In reality, turning the pages of a real book also involves two hands, so I shouldn't criticize. But with the Keyboard, you could use the physical bezel buttons to hold the book and turn the pages easily with one hand - which was nice when you were reading on your side and it was easier to use one hand rather than two. I don't know if this is possible, but from reading reviews, I don't think I'm the only person who would find this desirable. It is not a deal-breaker though, as you can use a thumb to turn pages forward once you get used to it (if you're right handed) - it's going back a page that definitely requires two hands, as that's a narrow strip along the left side, and in a case, that's usually where the hinge/spine is which makes it harder to stretch your fingers over. As a software/user-experience issue, there is one thing I'm finding annoying - turning the WiFi on and off. In the Keyboard, it was the top-level item on the home screen menu to turn it on and off. In the Paperwhite, you have to go to Settings and turn the Airplane mode on or off. Considering turning off WiFi is a major way to keep from draining the battery, it's annoying this isn't the top-level item here. I would love to see it return there. Also from a user-experience issue, I would love it if - as in the Keyboard - collections could be sorted by recent viewing, not just alphabetically. I use collections to organize all of my reading, and sometimes what I'm currently reading is in a collection that's several pages in. If I hadn't experienced it another way before, I doubt I'd be as critical, but if an earlier version of the Kindle put your most recent collection at the front/top of the list, there's no reason they can't do that here. One final user-experience quibble: on the Keyboard, you could use the 5-way button to advance a book from chapter to chapter. There does not seem to be an equivalent here - you must use the "go-to" function in the main menu. I really liked being able to quickly go back to a previous chapter using one hand, and I miss the feature more than I ever thought I would. Without a physical button, I'm guessing there's no way to add this in, which is a shame. As far as the light goes, again - can't say enough good things about it. But for someone who does several hours of reading a day (if my Paperwhite isn't on my nightstand it's in my tote bag or on my coffee table) not just the one or two Amazon used to calculate battery life - I will say that I've learned to only use the light at night. It undoubtedly improves the reading experience during the day time, but leaving it on for hours when I don't need it does appear to drain the battery. When I started turning the light off during the day, my battery life also improved, so keep that in mind. It's not as if eInk is difficult to read to begin with, so it's not a huge sacrifice. I think I've seen some people complain about how easy it is to accidentally forward your pages, because if you touch the screen, the page turns. But honestly, I had the same problem with the Keyboard - if I was carrying to Kindle by its bezel, I frequently found myself in a completely different section of the book. I consider it an occupational hazard of using a Kindle in general, and no worse than forgetting to note your page if you walk away from a physical book. I am going to enter a plea to Amazon here - please make it a normal part of functionality to let users swap out the screensaver images. I admit I jailbroke my Keyboard so I could use my own images. And that the wallpapers here are better than the ones that came with the Keyboard. But this is a really little thing that helps you personalize your Kindle, and I can't imagine it would take much to allow users to personalize them. All these are pretty small quibbles, though, in the larger scheme. This is a great e-reader with a wonderful built-in reading light which means I no longer consume AA or AAA batteries at a rapid pace :) Well worth the purchase.

I bought the Reecom 1630 with high hopes that it would manage my needs for timely weather alerts since I live on a barrier island off the NC coast. I read the manual and then systematically went through the setup. I selected my county's alerts along with a neighboring county that is nearby. I selected the voice setting but that is supposed to give me a 8 second siren, then switch to voice, then reset so it doesn't drive the dog insane. But in all the weeks I've had it, I've never heard it or seen a warning LED light up, even as Hurricane Earl brushed past us last week. When I reviewed the settings: sure enough, the warnings are enabled. They just don't seem to work. On the plus side, I can always manually turn the radio on and hear the weather broadcasts but I expected more. Update: I finally found the proper combination so that I now receive the warnings I was looking for with about 15 seconds worth of siren followed by the voice message. The radio does in fact do what it was advertised to do. Since I bought this, I finally found the First Alert WX-167 radio I had lost when I moved here and have now had an opportunity to compare the two radios directly. Of the two, the First Alert wins on audio quality (the Reecom speaker buzzes at normal volumes) and for ease of setup. To set up alert areas, on the 1st Alert, you choose the state, county, and subdivision. On the Reecom, you visit the NOAA website and get your location digital code from them, then enter it laboriously. The end result will be the same for both so the annoyance is fleeting in nature as once you've done it, you're done with it. The First Alert has a pivoting display panel that allows you to angle its display to the most appropriate position. The Reecom allows you to scroll through past alerts easily, something the First Alert doesn't (or I haven't found the feature yet). Of the two, I prefer the First Alert. And yet the Reecom is quite serviceable. You'd do fine with either or these.... just maybe a little finer with the First Alert.

This product arrived in a neat little box with simple directions and all the necessary supplies. I cleaned the screen of my A6000 and applied the protector without any issues. Since I install every screen protector for my family, and have done it quite a few times (glass and plastic), I've become pretty good at it (I even have a little kit just for that). This install went really well. In fact, it was perfectly aligned and had no trapped dust or bubbles except for a tiny one along the right edge of the glass. So, just like with any other screen protector I've installed I used my thumb to squeegee the bubble out. While running my thumb along the edge of the glass (with very little pressure, as it is a LCD screen that I didn't want to damage) I heard the tiniest crack. I lifted up my thumb and there was a tiny little triangle crack right where my thumb had been. It was pretty cheap so I wasn't expecting anything special, but I would have expected it to withstand mild thumb pressure. Imagine if you had your camera strapped on your shoulder and it accidentally bumped up against a chair corner. This would NOT protect against that. Ironically, the shattering of the glass protector would more likely scratch the screen it's supposed to protect. I decided to count this one a loss and began trying to take it off. Every time I lifted a corner the glass would crack even more. What started off as a little 1 cm crack on the side quickly turned into something resembling the product photo on the listing page. Needless to say, I wanted this thing off my camera before it caused any damage. Luckily with a little patience holding the opposite corner slightly off the screen the whole thing eventually came off and left no damage to my camera. All in all, no harm no foul and all I've lost is a little time and $7. Probably not worth the cost of shipping it back. The product's description only states that it will protect from "casual scratches" and fingerprints, which I can not deny. I wrongfully assumed it was like the glass protector I have installed on my D600 which can flex quite a bit without cracking, and can therefore protect from more than just fingerprints. For that reason I give it 2 stars. Pros: - It's very clear. Would have been very nice if it wasn't so fragile. - Install was easy and instructions were decent enough. - Came with a neat little box. Cons: - Incredibly fragile. It couldn't protect my screen from my thumb :-/ - The glass didn't have a front plastic tape on it (as the description says it should). Because of that, it had 2 minor blemishes that weren't really noticeable. I wouldn't have worried about it if the glass hadn't cracked. I didn't have it long enough to test it's fingerprint protection. At least now I get to use the little box it came in to house my screen protector install kit :)

I bought this backpack for several reasons, the most notable being that: 1. It's genuine leather. 2. It looks awesome. 3. I've been wanting a nice quality backpack that I could put all my stuff in. And let me say it was totally worth it! PACKAGING: Great product, arrived packaged nicely and undamaged. SMELL: You can smell the leather before you've even opened it all the way, and though I'm sure some might find it repulsing or 'too strong' I love it and can't get enough. I've had it for a few weeks now and I can still smell the leather. STRAPS: The straps are adjustable and really long, so you don't have to worry about it not fitting if you're a larger (or smaller) person. The backpack itself is a little on the smaller side, so if you're a big person it might look a bit odd, but people will be so blinded by how awesome you look wearing it that no one is really going to notice. POCKETS: Like other reviewers say, the front pockets are indeed hard to use/find a function for (though they do look ridiculously attractive on the front of the backpack, so even if you couldn't find a use for them you'd still look cool wearing it). If you stuff one thing into one pocket, it makes it kinda hard to open up the other pocket and get into it, partly because of the size of whatever you put into it and partly because of how close together the pockets themselves are. The only pocket I have no problems with out of the main four is the tiny zippered one. I have found a use for all four, though, finding that I can fit my wallet, Batman knife, iPod charger and cord (I put those in the zippered pocket), and change purse (which I'm not gonna lie is a pretty good size) into each of them respectively. I put my Apple Pencil and pens and whatnot into the topmost pocket and it all fits with plenty of room to spare. Also the metal parts you see holding the front straps of the pockets in place are indeed metal, and not plastic. The pockets on the sides for water bottles and such are pretty narrow, so I wouldn't expect anything more than a pop can or regular-sized water bottle to fit in either one of them. There's actually an extra zippered pocket on the back of the backpack as well, which you can use to store relatively flat things (like cards, cash, notepads, etc). ZIPPERS: Let me first say that ALL the zippers on this backpack work like a dream. I've read countless reviews on this thing from other brands/sellers (like Polare and S-Zone) saying that the main zipper is absolute crap. I would be lying if I said this didn't make me wary of purchasing because of this fact, but I know that there are differences in design between the Texbo and S-Zone (and Polare too, probably) because the front pockets on the S-Zone are only held together by the leather straps and the ones on the Texbo have velcro patches on the flaps for extra security (which is nice, but it tends to scratch my hands whenever I'm reaching in for something). I find that the zippers thus far are fairly good quality, they glide easily with no snag whatsoever. The only thing I could see being a problem is the little flap covering the main zipper, which I'm sure is there to protect it from getting gunk and whatnot in it. I have to bend it back all the way before I unzip it, otherwise I feel like it stresses the zippers. So I could see it coming undone pretty easily and needing to be replaced/fixed if someone continuously tried to unzip it without getting the protective flap out of the way first. Most people said they had theirs for either a little over or under a month before theirs broke, though, and I've already surpassed that mark with no problems to speak of as of yet. THE INSIDE: They weren't kidding when they said it would fit a 17" laptop. I have a 17" that is quite heavy, and it slid into the larger pocket, no problem. There are two main pockets, one large and one small, both with a stretchy sling over the middle with a velcro patch to keep whatever you've got in there...well, in there. I use the larger one for my laptop. the smaller one for my iPad and journals, and the main middle pocket for my sketchbooks and art stuff. I use the zippered part to hold my bag of art tools (pens, pencils, erasers, etc). I don't really use the two pen holders, but I'm sure they'd hold up to their purpose. The two open pockets below the zippered part are a nice touch for things you just want to throw in there (I use them for nail clippers, chapstick, candy, and a little compact mirror), but I kinda wished they were deeper. The things I have just kind of fling around in there. BUT they've always stayed in place and I've never had a problem with anything falling out thus far, so I guess they knew what they were doing when they put them in. STAINING: A couple reviews I read said that wearing the backpack stained their shirts. I wore it loaded up with everything I wanted in it and walked a mile in the sun on a relatively hot day, and didn't have any such problems (the leather actually kept my back nice and cool). Though to be fair, I didn't try going out with it on a rainy day. But of course, I can't imagine why anyone would want to go out with a backpack on a rainy day in the first place, except maybe for hiking in all kinds of weather. I've never gotten any kind of residue or anything like that when I touch or handle it, though, so I'd imagine it'd be fine in light to moderate rain (just don't head out into a storm and you'll be fine). OVERALL QUALITY: The quality of the backpack itself is pretty undeniable. I mean you can look at it and just know that it's topnotch. The leather is nice, heavy, and sturdy, the stitching is reinforced and neat, and you can just tell that it's at least a $100 backpack. WORD OF CAUTION: I bought the dark brown one and it's a tad bit darker than in the picture. I ended up giving that one away for Father's Day and buying myself another one, going for the light brown since I figured that one was probably a bit darker than pictured, too. It does NOT look like in the picture at ALL. The picture looks like a nice light-ish brown, but the actual color was more of a bright yellow-ish brown, like the color of construction worker's boots. It's more of a bright mustard brown. I'm sure that may be the color some people would like, but it wasn't for me so I sent that one back and got another dark brown one, though it seemed just as durable as the first one I bought. Just a word of caution in case you decide to get the light brown one so you know what to expect. OVERALL IMPRESSION: 5/5 stars. Extremely pleased with the quality of this backpack, as well as the fast shipping of the seller and painless return/exchange of the second backpack. Would buy again from them in a heartbeat!

First off, as to the out of the box directions or to those without any networking knowledge, have a friend help you. If you like to tinker, have at least an entry level knowledge of what a router is and how networks work, this is by far one of the best options out there. I've setup half a dozen of these (and older WRT54G v1-4) routers running on Tomato for friends and family. It's not that great on it's own, what it is great for is being able to use the 3rd party firmware of your choice, which offer far greater features than pretty much any out of the box router. It is worth noting that this router does not have N support, for that I use a standalone Wireless N access point in conjunction with this router. Second, No router out there has the community base of support that this router (and the prior series) has had. It isn't the best looking option, but it is by far the most functional single-purpose device you can get. For years, I and others have hoped for a proper successor to this series, and even the WRT160NL falls short of that promise. This is, at the moment the single best option, if you want to own your hardware, vs. having your hardware own you. As others have mentioned consumer level support from Cisco/Linksys falls short, fortunately this is a great product on its' own merit. For 3rd party firmware, search for Tomato, DD-WRT or OpenWRT, there are other options out there. My preference is for Tomato for the best front end application.

I had previously purchased a Rexing V1P Pro camera, which I liked, but the GPS encoding on the video files was in a proprietary format, so I returned it and bought this. Whereas the other camera is bulky, but lightweight, this camera is small, dense, and surprisingly heavy. One feels like a toy when compared to the other. I chose to use the default power connector, as parking mode is not important to me. The kit comes with a lot of extra mounting tape, so if you mess up your placement, or move it, you are all set. Be careful to leave room for the power cord when mounting the GPS block. I almost mounted it too close to where the rear-view mirror mounts on the windshield, and had slight difficulty plugging it in. The wiring with this camera is thick (heavy duty), and holds it’s shape well, which makes it real easy to install. This is only the 2nd time I’ve ever installed front/rear dash cams and it literally took me less than 15 minutes. Because the wires are so thick, they hold their position well, and hiding the wires from the front dash cam into the header is real easy. The kit also includes a tool to help install the wiring, which is real nice if you haven’t done it before. The memory card slot is on the left side, so removal is convenient. Just be sure to use two hands when ejecting the media. The camera will slide off the GPS mount if you push too hard. This is the one thing I think I would have designed differently. If the mount clipped on and slid to the right (instead of left), you could remove the memory card easier. This camera shuts off the screen when you’re driving, which I wasn’t used to at first. After running it around for a little while, I actually prefer this to other dash cams, as it is less distracting while driving. The iOS software is very good. I found only one bug, whereas if you put the camera resolution into 1080 x 1080 mode, the app will crash immediately when you try to connect to it. The app functions as expected under all other circumstances (so far). The 5GHz wifi is FANTASTIC. Download times for clips are blazing fast as compared to the other camera I had used. Note that 4K files are huge (1.6GB for 5min), so it’s going to be more efficient to remove the memory card and plug it into the computer. Speaking of which, VOIFO even provides a USB adapter for the memory card. Video clip options are great with this camera, offering 1,3,5 and 10 minute clips. Personally, I like to divide the clips into 5 minute segments so this camera does exactly what I need. The only thing that I wonder long-term, is how well the card slot will hold up from constantly removing the memory chip to retrieve the footage. For this reason, I purchased a warranty for the camera. The 4K video quality is absolutely amazing, and the 130/140 field of view front/rear is perfect. Unlike other cameras, there is no fisheye effect due to the wide angle. The mic on the camera also exceeded my expectations. The only annoying/missing feature on the camera is the lack of a daylight savings time setting. You must switch the timezone offset to match your timezone when daylight savings comes and goes. This is a software setting that could easily be addressed in a future firmware update. Not a dealbreaker for me. 4K video playback is choppy in dashcamviewer on macOS due to Quicktime. Too bad, as that’s the whole reason I bought this camera. I’m hoping that newer builds will read the H.265 codec. RE: H.265 codec, there is an undocumented feature where you can change the encoding from H.264 to H.265 by holding the mic button for 4 seconds. H.265 encoded videos will play smoothly in Quicktime on macOS, whereas the H.264 videos will not. Both formats play perfectly in VLC, so if you don’t care about following your footage around the map while you play it, even better! The software has options for displaying speed and GPS coordinates on the footage if you want, and you can hide the camera model from the footage if you prefer not to show it. I have not seen that feature on other cameras. Additionally, you can add a custom label to your dashcam footage which might be useful. If you’re looking at other cameras, and you’re wondering if the cost differential for this one is worth it, I would say go for it! The worst thing for me is the poor 4K playback support in the software I wanted to use, but I’m confident the developer will solve that as more 4K cameras hit the market. Virtually everything else about this camera either meets or exceeds my expectations.

DO NOT PURCHASE THIS PROJECTOR ( Panasonic PTAE8000U 1080p Full HD Projector) - for long term use. The specific issue is with the main board (the one with the CPU). The main board appears to be a weakness with moderate use over a period of time and when it fails - PANASONIC DOES NOT OFFER A REPLACEMENT BOARD. Yep, you heard right. They expect for you to come out of pocket to purchase or a $3000.00 projector that the manufacturer does not service !! I know, right ?! Check on Ebay and you will find tons of these Panasonic PTAE8000U units for sale for "parts only" for pennies on the dollar . The common denominator seems to be (you guessed it) - they all have a bad main circuit board). I purchased the projector from Amazon in December of 2013 for home theater use the unit had less than 3700 total hours on the projector with approximately 3400 hours on first bulb and 300 hours on the second (replacement bulb. So, moderate use - mostly home theater stuff with the occasional gaming session mixed in. Other than the recommended filter cleans (it has like 4 filters ) and the expected replacement of the original bulb - no issues. Until a couple of weeks ago - when while watching a movie then projector cut off and went into "Safe Mode". I had a Projector come out and ultimately take it with him for further diagnostic. I got a call last week that the main board was fried. After more than a week of looking the tech calls me back and confirms that the replacement board is not available though the manufacturer, refurbished, aftermarket - nowhere and nothing! I did some checking myself (trust , but verify - for this kind of money - am I right? and confirmed that no reputable (or non reputable for that matter) source supplies a replacement main board. I now have a $ 3K projector (with an almost new $300.00 replacement bulb in it) that is worthless as anything other than a boat anchor. So , to summarize - unless you have money to burn, Find an alternative brand at this price point, with these features - DO NOT purchase this projector.

UPDATE 11/20/2010: I ended up getting the TV replaced by Sharp because of the defective backlighting (the first bullet below). The new TV has perfect backlighting and I'm very happy with it. The blacks and overall quality of the picture does seem better on the replacement. I have to commend Sharp for their excellent customer service with the replacement process. I also found a way around the audio delay that can happen with this set with Film Mode and other video enhancements enabled. If you run your audio and video directly through your external stereo receiver, it should fix the problem. However, if you run your video from your DVR or Blu-ray player directly to the TV and the audio separately to your stereo receiver, you will probably get a delay because the video takes longer to process than the audio. Also, if you just use the TV speakers, you shouldn't have any audio delay either. ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW: I can't give this TV a perfect 5 stars for the following reasons (note that these issues may only be an issue with my set): - There are 2 very faint lighter areas that stretch horizontally across the screen when the TV is completely black. They are hardly noticeable except during dark scenes, but once you know they are there, you start to see them more. - The "Fine Motion Enhanced" doesn't appear to do anything to reduce motion blur (but on a positive note there isn't much blur on this set). BUT, this is the mode that sets the TV to 240hz, apparently with no effect. - The Film Mode option (soap-opera effect) does a good job at eliminating almost all motion blur, but at the cost of audio delay. The audio delay was so bad (words not matching up with people's lips) that I can't have this feature enabled. The last Firmware update was in May. Sharp might release a newer one eventually that solves this. Some of the other video options are interesting to play around with, but I found that most of them don't work well enough to be used. A good example is Active Contrast. I wish this had different levels you could set for it because it makes things too dark. My recommendation would be to change the video to "Movie" and turn off Film Mode and most of the other settings or go with "Game" mode (note that Film Mode is turned on by default). To do this, you have to open the bottom part of the remote that has more buttons hidden. You can also reset any of the video modes to their factory defaults if you mess something up with them. Even with the above issues I do still recommend this TV as a cheaper way to get a high quality 60" LCD 1080p TV. Black levels are excellent. Blu-rays look stunning. There are plenty of connections in the back to hook up all of your components (make sure you attach a good sound system as the TV speakers are horrible). The menu system is also very well done. Overall - 4/5

Excellent package for the price but, as pointed out by many, many, other reviewers, the instructions are nonexistent. The monitor appears to be very good quality and the size offers a very good image. Before going into any further detail, I must offer my thanks to reviewer Jessica S. Chamberlin (2/12/2012). Her wiring insights were invaluable. I offer my comments in the hope they may help others. I installed this unit in my 2008 Nissan Frontier King Cab with automatic transmission and dealer installed tow hitch. I wanted the camera / monitor to act strictly as a backup camera so all wiring was done to activate the system only when backing up. Based on prior experience, I decided to solder all electrical connections instead of using "splice connectors": 1. Camera: Luckily, the tow hitch had a wiring diagram embossed on the electrical connection cover. I connected the camera Red wire (12v +) to the reverse light power light and the Black wire to the hitch ground wire. Soldering the connections allowed me to fold all the wires back into the tow hitch's wiring harness "case" resulting in a secure and clean install. 2. AV Cable: The Yellow AV cable was just long enough to reach the engine compartment. I ran it along the existing cabling down the driver's side and secured with cable ties. 3. Monitor Fuse Box and Wiring: Since my truck has an automatic transmission, I needed to go under the hood to the smaller relay box located on the passenger side to find the reverse / backup lights relay and wiring. All the wires were way too short for my desired install so I lengthened all wires. I soldered connection terminals to the Red and Black leads coming out of the monitor fuse box. I connected the resultant Red terminal to a sub-terminal on the truck battery connector and the Black terminal to a good grounded bolt. The green wire I soldered to the Yellow wire found in the terminal box (this is the reverse light wiring for the trailer hitch). I could have also used the Light Blue wire which is the wire for the actual truck reverse lights. My final entry point into the cab and monitor was a small rubber plug located on the driver side firewall, adjacent to the entry point of the wiring harness. I drilled out the plug just enough to push the monitor cable through and replaced the plug into the firewall. Plugged everything in and the unit works as advertised. I would never have found the proper wires to connect to without stumbling onto a post submitted by "micl9" on the "clubfrontier.org" website entitled "2005 & up reverse wire - AVIC-D3 install complete! ". He posted complete with photos. The link, if Amazon allows, is: [...]

Hejnar Photo makes a long conversion plate that is designed to place the optical center of the camera directly over the central axis of the tripod. The first portion of this will be the technical -- well, as technical as I ever get -- discussion of the device in comparison to my K2 and then I'll move on to book readers and the overall Kindle experience. My husband and I both had Kindles 2 and loved them and I decided to get the newest version. I was so happy with the K2 that I didn't have to make the change -- I wanted to. The K3 retains most of the great features of the K2 -- like the ability to read anywhere, the ability to change fonts, the built in dictionary, and access to more books than can be read in a lifetime -- adds some new ones that through updates are now available for the K2, too -- such as being able to share favorite passages and organize books by collections -- and brings exclusive improvements. 1. The print, which was always easy on the eyes, is noticeably crisper. I found myself reading a smaller font than I'd been reading on the K2. 2. The print is also darker than it is on either of the K2 in the household. 3. Lighter. Somewhat easier to hold in the hand for long periods of time. 4. Smaller. We set the K2 and the K3 side by side and the difference is marked. The screen size is the same, but they've rearranged buttons to save on room. 5. Page turn speed, which was always pleasing before, is even faster. 6. Markedly better battery life. After I charged it I was arranging collections and left the wireless on. With my K2, there would still be a lot of battery, but there would have been depletion, and so I decided to top off the K3. The light immediately went green, fully charged still. I routinely turn off the wireless, only turning it on once or twice a way, to receive subscriptions or new purchases. I didn't need to leave it off, but liked the extra battery life. With the K3, I'm more inclined to leave it on. According to the details, the battery life should last a month or so with wireless off, which is just wow! The only issue I have, and it's simply because it was perfect on the K2, are the buttons to the left and right of the screen -- the page forward and page back. They're smaller, which I understand, and more along the side than on the face, I imagine to further save room. The placement is awkward at the moment -- at least until I get a cover, which will offer more ways to hold the device. It makes it too easy to hit the buttons by mistake and when holding with one hand a bit more dangerous as you are more holding on to the edge than before in order to turn pages. I do prefer the K2 in this one regard. I find it disappointing. As with my K2, I'll have a cover for it when the maker I like releases their designs, and that should help, but it's definitely a minus if you have to buy another product to improve a design flaw. This was a step up -- the improvements do outweigh the flaw -- and I was happy before. With the even better pricing, Kindle is still the one to beat and Amazon is still making their device with the serious reader, as opposed to the gadget junkie, in mind. If you want bells and whistles, nope. If you love reading, yep! People, readers, are skeptical about eReaders. I was one of them. The Kindle ads used to bug me, and I imagine some people reading this who are still on the fence, understand that. I had all the sentimentality expressed when folks talk about the smell of books. What I think though is that the experience of reading is what makes the smell and other tactile memories so tempting -- the pleasure imprints itself on the other aspects and becomes associated with good memories. Most of the adult readers today do have good associations with print books, like their parents reading them bedtime stories and then doing the same with their own kids, like those Scholastic Book newsletters from school. Like reading Jane Eyre on a rainy day, holed up somewhere like she was in the beginning of the book. What I've found matters most though are the words. What the author wants to say to you. If the worst book in the world has the best cover in the world and the old book smell, it's still the worst book in the world. The Kindle, and other readers to some extent, gets out of the way and lets it be about the words. Stephen King talks about what happens between the writer and reader as a form of telepathy. He can reach across time and make you see and feel what he has in mind. That magic is still there with an eReader and made easier. Barriers are torn down when you can adjust the font or make the device read to you, if needed. Ever hear someone mention a book, see it on a talk show, and you forget what it was when you get to the book store? Or you order it from Amazon, but even with the fastest shipping are still impatient? (For pubs, the purchase can beat the bad reviews ::grin::) The Kindle allows you to preorder the next book by your favorite author. You can finish one book, realize that you found a new author you like, and have another book by this writer in your hand in the time it takes you to click a couple buttons and and your yourself a glass of iced tea. If you're like me, and keep a few books going at a time, they're always all there to be continued. Every time I sit down I can ask, "Okay, what do I want to read now?" I can do that because I have hundreds of books in the palm of my hand and countless other books I can access. Just like everyone else in a waiting room, you can be reading Time or Newsweek or the New Yorker, only you're reading the current issue and they're reading a dog-eared, grimy looking one so old that the big story is about the cold war. If they do become interested in an article, they're leaving it behind if they're called for their appointment. Your article will be waiting for you to continue. If your appointment isn't called and you're reading about the latest strife in some country with which you're not familiar, with the dictionary feature you can find out the basics and your understanding is instantly improved. My husband and I have the same Kindle account. I'm the one who buys the majority of books. He stumbled onto the Jack Kilborne book,[[ASIN:B001VLXNWO Afraid]], in the archived books and loved it. He then ordered another book by the author. I realized the author also writes as J.A. Konrath and so I bought a couple of those books and sent them directly to his device. The next time he turns on turns on his device they will either be their instantly or within a minute. I really could discuss it for paragraphs more, all the things I love about my Kindle! I'm sure other people will do that in my stead. I'm not going to say these devices are for everyone, but I do think that some of the readers most opposed to them are the ones who would adore them the most. I'm a year and a half in to owning Kindles, and there is no going back for me. Maybe brief vacations if someone lends me a book or there's another reason to do print, but my preference is now for a book reader.

I have been using this tablet for several months and have mixed feelings about it. I had high hopes when ordering this device based on my positive experiences with the HD8. It is a good device for media consumption due to the larger display but not for productivity applications. The good: It has a great 1080 display, with a size that enables a comfortable viewing, good colors, good brightness, good contrast. Several people who have seen the screen in action while I was watching a movie were impressed with quality of the display, including an ophthalmologist. The display compares favorably with an iPad Air 2. The sound output of the speakers (volume not quality) is similar to the iPad Air 2. Has voice activated Alexa. In my earlier review I stated that some apps that work on other fire tablets (I.e., TCM) did not work on this tablet. After recent updates this statement no longer seems to apply as TCM now works as do other apps I use. =================================== Very good price compared to other tablets in this size range. If you can wait look for sales like Prime Day. Battery life is good, about 5-8 hours depending on apps used. Internal data storage is very good (I chose 64gb) and with the external storage option used (I added a 128gb SD card) makes for a lot of storage availability. I have downloaded about 9,000 songs, 100's of books, 6 HD movies, a lot of photos, about 20 apps and still have about 50 gb of free space. The bad: Audio volume is weak and distorts when the volume is pushed to an adquate listening level. Low volume seems to be the bane of most tablets and phones, but not distortion. The Amazon Fire HD 8 and 6 have much better audio and the volume can be increased using booster apps without noticeable distortion. The Fire HD 8 (6th generation) has Atmos Dolby audio and works to provide a nice surround sound effect, the HD 10 is also presented as having the same audio but I cannot detect the same surround sound effect (is the effect decreased due to the increased spacing of the speakers). For some reason the HD10 is not able to maintain a connection with WiFi even though my other decices don't have this problem using the same WiFi network. I get constant displays that I do not have a WiFi connection. Maybe this will be resolved with a software update? The bottom line: If you want a 10" tablet display to watch videos or for reading at a reasonable price (even better when on sale) this is a good choice. The under performing speakers can be compensated for with Bluetooth speakers or headphones (note: also has a plugin connection for headphones/speakers).
