I had a specific purpose for buying a BT portable speaker. When I am out of the country for an extended period I load my Mac Book with movies. It is often noisy where I stay. Mac Book speakers are not anywhere near loud enough to listen without headphones. I also did not want to have wires all over. I bought and compared the Logitech UM Mobile Boombox with the JBL Flip. I compared music (classical piano, opera, voice, & movies). The Logitech had a flatter, more muted sound. The JLB Flip sounded clearer, if a tad tinny up at high volume. The JLB Flip was a clear winner on volume. It is designed to push out more air and it certainly sounds like it does. Sound quality in normal volumes was more pleasing to me in the Flip. But the real tie breaker was listening to movies. JBL Flip was the hands down winner. Excellent quality & extraordinary volume. The Logitech has some features and facilities that the Flip does not. Logitech Boombox allows pairing up two separate devices, handy but not essential for me. It also claims longer battery life (though I did not test that out). The comparison is 5 hours for the Flip, which is apparently less than the norm, and 7 hours for the Logitech. For my purpose this was not a deal breaker. The Logitech was nicely shaped with a confidence inspiring "rubber" kind of finish. The JBL had a metal mesh and looked good as well. The Flip comes with a protective case. The Logitech sits firmly on your surface. The Flip can lie down or stand upright. The upright position is not my favorite as it stands like the Leaning Tower of Pizza. They are both compact & light weight for travel - about a pound. Blue tooth pairing with the Logitech was straight forward. I had 2 tech calls to JLB with regard to pairing. There is an issue with the JLB Flip's Bluetooth. It seems to be more sensitive to obstruction. I was able to play music in my study and listen with the speaker in my bedroom - about 25 ft apart. All was well until I walked between the two devices. The speaker got upset, but recovred. I cannot address longevity as I have only had the Flip for two days. The warantee is 2 yrs on the Logitech & only one on the Flip. The Logitech comes with a generic charging wire & USB TO AC plug. This allows you to use the wire to charge the speaker from your laptop. The Flip comes with a proprietary plug. Not a deal breaker for me as I would normally charge it overnight. Bottom line - The JLB Flip is a keeper, based on volume and sound quality. The Logitech UM Boombox went back. By using my American Express Card I doubled the warrantee on my Flip. Just a note. These Bluetooth portable speakers run on Lithium rechargeable batteries - which limits their life span as the batteries are not replaceable. Price was the same for each of these items - $99.

Since I'm having a hard time trusting their over priced products now - as I recently went on a search for some Bluetooth Headphones I visually saw and tried on the BOSE Bluetooth Headphones at BEST BUY; you can quickly see that they look cheap and of course have an inflated price tag, which I now know is usual. Word is from 90% of the peeps I spoke with in stores is that Dre's headphones are more hype than anything else; so I decided to give the JABRA Bluetooth Stereo Headphones (Amazon) a go because while I was internet hunting for a pair that were wireless the online reviews about the JABRA stuck out like they were the Bentley of Bluetooth headphones. One guy wrote such a great article (review) that I started to tear up at how wonderful these priceless gems were - and at a stiff punch-in-the-lip ($200) price tag I figured that I had found the holy grail. My ears were sore, which is strange because the material on the actual earpiece is very subtle and soft but I still experienced a sore feeling after taking them off. The next day I put them on again, not leaving my apartment and this is where the epic fail stuck out like a sore thumb, better yet it stuck out like a sore ear. The headphones would not, could not and DID NOT - stay on my head. Let me make this clear, I am a normal sized man and I mean I measure as close to a normal size as you can get and the headphones while bending over to pick up a pillow would slide off my head. For the next few days I would try them in 10 minute intervals and then I actually started to get really pissed off. I mean if you think you're going to work out or better yet even if you think you're going to bend over to pet your dog Lassie - chances are they will not stay on your head. All of a sudden my BOSE with the annoying-ass cord and the cheap material and the inferior sound, became all-of-a-sudden BETTER. It's possible you may have a different experience but for $200 the one thing that I want the Headphones to do is stay on my skull. The Amazon seller took them back no-prob and I'm not disappointed I gave them a try. I imagine some reviewers that write articles in magazines can be listening for the bass and the treble while they're sitting at their desk, but if they get up off their ass... LOOK OUT. So the frustration I had by just trying to wear them around a very small space while walking on egg shells and them refusing to stay on my dome, they should be valued at half the price in my opinion. My search continues...

We have a couple of other projectors, a high-end BenQ W1070, a lower-end Fugetek FG-857, and I purchased this Xinda mini for above my bed as a replacement for an Aaxa ST200 (which I will explain later in case you're considering the two). Display quality: the Xinda at 800x480 has the lowest resolution of the 4 projectors (BenQ ~$500 1980x1020; Fugetek ~$160 1280x800; Aaxa ST200 $250 1280x720), but at $100 it is the cheapest and, considering its small size, I think it's acceptable for me. As long as your expectations are realistic this may be an excellent purchase for you. For watching movies and TV the Xinda is absolutely fine. Better than I would have expected at this price point. However, I am mainly running my laptop to it and initially Windows 10 was duplicating the display from the laptop, so the lowest resolution I could set within Windows 10 display settings was something like 1024x768, which was difficult to use, especially with small text. After I went into the Intel graphics card properties and separated the displays I could set it to 800x600 and that was much more usable for seeing taskbar icons, web browsing, spreadsheets, and Steam games. I can also point it at the wall 9 feet away and get a nice, clear display. I'm including 3 photos of the Xinda hooked to a Win10 laptop and displayed on my ceiling at 4 feet distance from where it's mounted: 1) with blinds and black-out curtains closed, 2) blinds and curtains closed but headboard lamp on, and 3) blinds closed, curtains open on an overcast afternoon. You can see the Xinda above me in the second photo. After switching the resolution to 800x600 you can see text is fairly legible. The available keystoning works, but it distorts and blurs the display with a computer, especially because my display is about 4 feet from the projector. For movies and TV I really don't notice the blur. In contrast, the Fugetek is about the same in its keystone action (mostly useless), the Aaxa ST200 was a bit better, and the BenQ you can keystone all you like without ever incurring noticeable blurring of the display. Obviously the BenQ is my favorite on this count, but I just can't justify spending $500+ on a bedroom projector. The Xinda is about on par with the Fugetek and maybe a little better than the Aaxa for viewing during the day without lights on. It also looks okay when the light on the headboard is on, but turning the ceiling light on next to where the display is on the ceiling obviously blows out the image terribly. I have blinds and black out curtains on the two windows in the bedroom, so I just shut those and it looks great. But it is also okay with just the blinds shut and some ambient filtered daylight. It actually performs a little better than I expected. The built-in speaker sounds tinny and because it's right above my head I really don't enjoy it. I use a separate bluetooth speaker paired with my devices for sound. In contrast though, the built-in speaker on the Xinda is a bit louder than the speaker on the Aaxa, about like the BenQ, and quieter than the Fugetek. You definitely need a separate speaker for the Xinda to sound decent. The fan noise is maybe a little quieter than the other projectors we've had. None of them are silent or, if they are, they probably won't have great longevity. I've fallen asleep with the Xinda on. It is about the same loudness as and sounds like a desktop pc fan. The display space between my headboard and ceiling is limited to about 4 feet, which makes the display from the Xinda about 40" on my ceiling. Originally I had it on a tripod next to the bed and the size was good, probably 70" to 80", but I couldn't leave it there because it was in the walkway to the laundry room. So I got an Erisan wall mount with an extension and mounted it above the headboard. In contrast to the Aaxa ST200 the displayed image on the Xinda is a lot smaller from the same distance. The resolution is significantly better on the Aaxa, which I do miss. However, the Aaxa is built so that the lens is recessed behind the white plastic case, which causes horrific light reflection on the surrounding white plastic that appears as about a 1 foot box of dimmer white light around the actual image displayed by the Aaxa. That one thing was so profoundly annoying I simply couldn't live with the Aaxa. On top of that, the lens on the Aaxa ST200 I received was misaligned, so you could never get the left and right sides of the display in focus at the same time. While that was an easy manufacturer warranty fix apparently, the white box around the display was extremely annoying. I sent back the Aaxa and my search for a mini projector began all over again. The Xinda's lens is flush with or sticks out past the plastic case, depending on how it's focused, so no weird light bleed, and its resolutions was on par with other similarly priced projectors. The overall reviews and customer satisfaction with the Xinda were higher than others, so I took a chance on it. I'm glad I did. It is totally acceptable for an above-the-bed projector for my computer and Chromecast. I'm trying to do away with heavy TVs in my home because of earthquakes and thanks to regular power outages we go on generator a lot and LED projectors eat fewer watts. This Xinda replaced a 42" flat screen that was taking up wall space in my bedroom. The image quality took a hit, but I can lay flat on my back and play games. Can one really put a price tag on that? No. If you are only buying one projector for serious movie and TV viewing and can swing a few hundred more dollars, you should look at something else, like BenQ or Optoma.

I videotape 1 to 2 hour concerts. I would often put my GoPro Hero 4 on the pianist or other unique angle. The normal GoPro batteries would only last about 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes and they would die, even with the screen set to turn off after 2 minutes so that it used as little power as possible. The camera would often die before the end of the concert, or if it was a 2 hour concert with an intermission, I'd have to change out the battery at the break. I got this Suptig 7800mA/h battery bank and I never run out of battery now. It makes it 2 hours no problem with plenty of charge left (again with the screen shutting off after 2 minutes). Unfortunately, at the moment I don't recall how much charge is left after 2 hours, but my guess would be it could easily do 4 hours or more of recording. However, if you do time-lapse shooting, I have GREAT news. Yesterday and today I set up my GoPro for a construction build and set it to Time-lapse 2.7k, wide angle, with it capturing an image every 1/2 second. I kept the screen set to turn off after 2 minutes to conserve power usage, and after 12 hours of recording (didn't touch it again until I turned it off), I still had about HALF battery life left (2 of the 4 lights are still lit up indicating 26-50% of battery life left). That was awesome!

It’s not the end of the world, but it is distracting -not full HD -very little detail in the blacks, can be really hard to make things out in dark scenes. Things tend to look a bit too crunched. The drain wire is shown in the diagram as running next to the shielding, which makes sense: ground the drain wire and you ground the shielding so it can absorb some RF and shield the conductors. Like another reviewer, my drain wire is not next to the shielding but instead it's separated from it by a layer of clear PE tape. I can't make reliable electrical connections to plastic-backed aluminum foil so the shielding is useless. If this is true for other rolls, it might be why other reviewers had crosstalk. The cable seems top notch otherwise: thick shielding (really thick) apparently properly twisted pairs, rip cord, solid copper, all nice stuff. People who are claiming great coverage with these should -- the power output on the one I received was many times over the FCC legal limit -- be aware. Also, the one I received the little A/C adapter cube did not function at all. ZERO power output from the adapter. Which was confusing anyway, as the FCC Certification tests (available at the TAW website and the FCC database) state that the mini USB plug had been disabled and no longer was used for anything, but yet it will run off power connected here (once you get a working adapter). I imagine it had to be disabled since the cable acted as a counterpoise and sent the output way over the limit. Adding the necessary audio cable, or using AC power created a counterpoise to the antenna creating a signal ever more over the FCC legal limit. Further, is does NOT have an SMA antenna connector. It has a reverse thread BOLT. It is in NO WAY a connector. Additionally the included antenna is not a carefully designed "helically wound" antenna like a REAL rubber duck style antenna and like it is explained on their website, it's a piece of braided wire in about a 5 inch plastic antenna. The FCC limit for signal strength of these transmitters is 250 uV/m at 3 meters. This clocked in at 1102 uV/m at 3 meters, more than 4 times over the legal limit. Adding the audio cable brought the output to over 4000 uV/m about 16 times over the legal limit. I am a broadcast engineer with over 40 years of experience, and tested this with commercial grade test equipment. If your goal is to be broadcasting illegally, this will do the trick.

Okay, several things - a) The QNine SD-to-IDE44 adapter is based on the KTC FC1307A bridge chip, which is a bit of a hit-and-miss with various SD cards and IDE controllers on various hardware. So if it doesn't work, it's either the card or the IDE controller. Possibly even both. In general, Class 10 16/32GB SDHC cards are okay. Anything else (U1, U3, A1) might cause it not to work, and as for SDHC/SDXC? I am not even sure. I had 64GB SDXC cards work in certain cases, and not in others. b) Watch out for DOA components - I got one that did not work regardless of what I tried. c) Be careful of Pin alignment - Make sure that you know where Pin 1 needs to be. d) The FC1307As are limited by a theoretical transfer speed of 25MBytes/sec. Not quite UDMA6 speeds nor would it be up to the U1/U3/A1 speeds of certain cards.

I've owned this lens for four+ years now and used it on two bodies and it's remained my favorite. My other lenses: -Rokinon 14mm f/2.8 -Canon 16-35mm f/2.8 -Canon 24mm f/1.4 -Canon 70-200 IS f/4.0 -Canon 100mm IS f/2.8 macro -Canon 400mm f/5.6 Because you will be wanting to shoot at f/1.2 a lot, I suggest buying an ND filter (think of it like sunglasses for your lens), which will let you open up to f/1.2 to get your nice bokeh, which after all came at a high price, so you want to use/abuse it when you can. If you don't shoot with a ND filter, for instance, your camera will complain that its shutter speed isn't fast enough. There's just too much damned light in the scene. Now, that's usually a good thing with cameras, but not when you want to shoot wide open at f/1.2 in broad daylight. Advantages: -bokehlicious -very fast lens, even in near-dark conditions. Bloody great, and corny as it sounds, it puts a smile on my face (almost) every time I'm in difficult lighting conditions. -great big aperture for astrophotography, though the focal length is a bit weird for that application (not too telephoto for closeups, not wide enough for big Milky Way shots) -low profile, not big enough to attract much attention. One of the reasons this is my favorite. -USM ultrasonic motor (also on f/1.4 version). My biggest gripe with the f/1.8, other than the gorgeous shots it was capable of achieving, was the noisy autofocus. That doesn't work well if you're trying to photograph animals or trying to remain inconspicuous. An upgrade to the f/1.4 or this f/1.2 model will fix that, since you'll get the fast and quiet USM focus. Disadvantages: -heavy. This is definitely heavier than my 70-200 f/4.0 and 100mm f/2.8 macro -expensive. 16x more expensive than the f/1.8 I upgraded from, but I've never once regretted it. -not paired well with some cameras, though this is more of a gripe with the camera and not the lens. Open wide at f/1.2 on my older Canon 7D, I had focusing issues which required me to guesstimate microadjustments I had to select in the settings of the camera (based upon the distance between the camera and the subject). This was especially difficult with off-center focus points, which seemed more touchy. I got pretty good at guesstimating the microadjustments needed for each shot, but when I changed distance between me and my subject I had to reset it again, which was annoying. All of these problems went away when I moved to the Canon 5D Mark III, where a greater percentage of my shots now come out in-focus, even off-center focus points. That being said, most of my favorite shots that DID come out well with my Canon 7D are gorgeous - it was just much more difficult to achieve. -because you paid more, you will want to justify your purchase by always shooting at f/1.2. Don't do that. For instance, this lens is great for food photography, but you'll want to go to around f/2.8 for that usually. On the plus side, the f/2.8 on this lens will be sharper than on the cheaper models. -lots of shots end up out of focus full open at f/1.2, at least on the Canon 7D. I have had a MUCH better success rate with the Canon 5D Mark III. Also, a quick tip for portraits: focus on the person's eyes, not their nose. Select your autofocus points. At f/1.2 it matters a lot.

I purchased this headset and the Kidz Gear wired headset for my children. I also reviewed that set and have a slight preference for it. However, I do feel this is an excellent headset and that is well be enjoyed by my kids for several years. We have had this headset for a week now and it has seen a good bit of use by my 5 yr old and my 1.5 yr old. This headset fits the toddler better than the Kidz Gear set, and it also fits my 5 yr old nicely. It does not fit me, an small-average-headed woman. I can listen it comfortably if I rotate the headband around to the back of my head, though, as could my large-headed husband. The interchangeable pictures are a cute idea, but the clear covers that hold the pictures on want to come off easily, especially when dropped on tile. They are a solid, clear plastic and I fear them being stepped on and broken before they are seen. A little bit of rubber cement should make this problem go away, and still allow them to be removed easily. A redesign on Griffin's part would be nice, though. I shouldn't have to mod things to get them to work right. But, it's easy, free and doesn't make it look bad, so it's a minor quibble. I really like the headband design and the way the size adjusts. Folding would be a nice feature, but none of the contenders folded, either, so that wasn't a choice for me. The headphones come in a clear plastic "carry case" as their packaging. I think they should do away with this. Honestly, it's just more trash. It's a hard, clear plastic, very thick, but thusly also will prove brittle. The first time you or your kids drop it on the way to the car, it will surely crack enough to render it useless. And, that's if you actually got the kids to use it, which I imagine is unlikely. Less packaging would surely be nicer for the environment and for shipping costs. If they want to include a case, a fabric bag or soft, zipper case would be MUCH more serviceable. Despite the cons, I would recommend this headset for the younger set.

I wanted to love this product and to start I did. The Garmin r-10 is beautiful looking all the way to the carrying case and the set up is extremely easy. The Garmin app that pairs with it is fantastic. I only used the Driving range feature and it's awesome how it shows you shot dispersion for all your shots, your metrics for individual shots and averages per club. It's also very cool how you can record video straight to the app through your phone and observe your swing with the data right beside it! The only problem is I found the data to be questionable. I tried it once in my backyard hitting into a net and 3 times at my local driving range. The distances in the backyard seemed to match up to my usual distances but of course I had no way of verifying those. So I took it to my local range. It seemed to worked fairly accurately with shorter clubs but began to give a lot of questionable carry distances for longer irons and longer clubs, at times 10 to 15 yards off what I could pretty plainly see with my eye. As someone who also has the tendency to pick the ball or hit up on the ball, I questioned also the accuracy of the attack angle readings (which are calculated based off the measured metrics). So I scoured the internet for reviews on its accuracy. Many golf blogs give it glowing reviews without giving it much rigorous testing. I found one "professional" reviewer with much more robust testing equipment than my naked eye, that seemed pretty critical of its spin measurements being off by the thousands. As someone who bought this to improve his swing and understand all these kinds of metrics for the first time, I feel the lack of confidence in the accuracy could derail and mislead my progress, as beautiful as the interface on the app is. Amazon accepted it as a return before 30 days which I respect and appreciate, though UPS had to pick it up at my home which made it a little trickier. For me $600 is a lot of money, and I would probably stop using it overtime if I doubted the accuracy too much. I wonder if anyone else here has questioned its accuracy. For me, I'll hope they come out with an R-20 or improvement down the road that I'll consider because as I said the app and interface and the promise of all these metrics at that price is very appealing!

Update 2/15/2013: My iPad accidentally fell about two feet from a table onto a vinyl floor. It hit corner first, but suffered no visible damage. Now the top left of the back portion has become loose and no longer holds that corner of the iPad securely in place. I expected a little more durability than that, but the case did its job protecting the iPad. -- I've had this case about a month now for my 4th gen iPad, and overall it functions great with only a few minor downsides. Pros: - Back portion holds iPad securely in place by the corners with virtually no overlap on the front surface. - Microfiber/suede-like inner lining won't scratch screen and helps keep it clean. - Magnetic sleep/wake feature works correctly and front cover doesn't flop open when closed. - Front cover folds all the way back and even from the rear the magnet holds it in place. - Appropriate openings for connectors/buttons/camera/microphone/speaker. Cons: - Cover-hinge durability is questionable if it's going to be folded back and forth all the time (as mentioned by a previous reviewer). - Tri-folded front cover for upright landscape viewing sets the iPad nearly 90 degrees/perpendicular to the surface. - Speaker opening might be a little small, but shouldn't affect volume levels. Other considerations: - To reinforce the cover-hinge, I've added a strip of black duct tape along the spine. It should help with the repeated opening and closing of the cover over time. - If you want to use the camera without the cover flopping around, just fold the cover halfway onto itself (microfiber side touches each other), then fold that all the way back. - The tri-fold cover design is inherently flawed since it exposes the microfiber lining to whatever surface you set it on - this is not ideal if you have dirty table for example. To minimize dirtying the microfiber lining, I actually tri-fold it inwards so only the leatherette side touches the table. However, this only works with the typing position, not the upright landscape viewing position (it won't stand up if folded that way).

This is a compact unit ideal for travel. We used it in Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Netherlands, Belgium, and France to plug in multiple US-style chargers that auto-switch 110/220. We used an appropriate adapter to fit the plug into the wall. This came in very handy when there were limited outlets or we wanted to unplug everything at once. The cord is short and body small -- disadvantages in terms of flexibility, advantages in terms of fitting in luggage. I noticed some reviews complaining of purchase and inability to use on a trip (product DOA) -- I have no idea why anyone would buy electronics and not test it before a trip. Ours was fine right out of the box. I saw another review that complained this unit does not convert 220 to 110. That fact was pretty clear to me when I purchased it; my electronics autoswitch (I checked each unit). We powered a laptop, AA/AAA charger, camera battery charger, and cell phone charger (USB out) from this unit at various times. The only reason I do not rate this with 5 start is that it became very difficult to insert US plugs into one of the outlets. I was able to continue using that outlet by using our backup European adapter plug in the outlet. The little swinging covers were fine with rounded rods (European plug) but not blades (US plug). It did see pretty heavy use during our 3 weeks in Europe. We had no reason to test the circuit breaker nor surge protector. I will continue to use this as a spare/backup powerstrip at home/when I travel.

It was with a heavy heart that I recently laid to rest the Wacom tablet that's served me faithfully since I got it as a gift more than ten years ago. As much as I wanted to replace it with another Wacom, they're way beyond my hobbyist price range, so I decided to just bite the bullet and try one of the more affordable competitors - clearly I chose Acepen, and I'm glad I did! What has impressed me most is the tablet's size. It's comparable to a sheet of paper, which makes it so much easier for me to draw naturally. Even after years using my previous tablet (which was considerably smaller), there was always a learning curve when I switched between physical and digital sketching. This tablet is roomy enough that I don't have to change my natural hand movements to fit its dimensions. Installation was another bonus. The Acepen website was easy to navigate, and I had the correct driver downloaded and installed within minutes. It's good to go right from there, but if you take a minute to program the hotkeys on the tablet itself you can customize them for easy access while drawing. A number of accessories are included, like replacement stylus nibs, different USB connectors, and a half-glove ostensibly to keep your hand from triggering the tablet surface as you work. I haven't needed it yet, but it'll be useful to have available if and when I do! The cord is fabric-wrapped to keep it from getting tangled, which is much appreciated. There are some drawbacks to this tablet, of course, the biggest being the responsiveness of the stylus. Because it isn't battery-powered or rechargeable, it's nowhere near as full-featured as, say, an Apple pen. Tablets at this level just don't offer the pressure sensitivity of the higher-priced options. However, that's just par for the budget-conscious course, so I don't consider it a drawback to the product itself. Overall, this is a big, easy-to-use, functional tablet at an excellent price, perfect for beginners, students, and casual artists. Honestly, you can't go wrong!

This is a fine 12 inch Win10 2in1, with unique features that give it the edge over other options for my use. Lots of goodness: +m7 (that's core m, not core i) low voltage part, but still good speed. Not blazing, but plenty fast for all my software up to and including lite video and graphics editing. The m7 variant pushes core m performance up just enough to be a good option in a 12inch tablet. +very good screen, brightness is plenty for all the places I use, including shade outdoors. 1920x1280 is a very good resolution on a 12" form factor, and the 1280 vs. 1080 vertical is noticeably better for viewing and scrolling content. +upgradeable storage. Replaced the 512GB ssd with 2TB Samsung 860, then bought the new 1TB microSDXC from Sandisk for too much money, but solved my storage needs for now. The disassembly to replace the SSD is not difficult once you see it done on youtube. The slot for the microSDXC uses a tray, which I really prefer when using SDXC storage on going. Thoughtfully, the SDXC tray is separate from the SIM tray. Good design! +Excellent security. HP provides pre-boot security and drive encryption via hardware with biometric unlock for both as well as for Windows Hello. Only hassle is that you have to have keyboard attached to unlock the pre-boot security, and the screen goes full bright at this point, kinda blinding, but these are minor compared with the benefits of real pre-boot security. +WLAN/SIM slot. Critical to me for secure connectivity on the go. Using Verizon, $20/mo unlimited data on my family unlimited plan. +Excellent touch and pen responsiveness. Fortunately this model also works with active pens like the one for my Lenovo Flex5, providing options in terms of styli. +Good removable keyboard. I can type almost full speed on it despite the compact dimensions. Nice backlight, very strong magnetic connection that pops into place quite easily. +Nice kickstand. I really prefer this approach to some of the other much less flexible ways to support a 2in1 screen on other designs. I can balance the unit on one leg and my lap using the kickstand, and type pretty comfortably. Not many others are capable of this. +Total wt is very low for all the power and flexibility you get. The size and weight make me willing to just grab my X2 and go to a meeting even in fairly social settings, since it says "tablet", not "laptop" in appearance. +USB-C charging is great, and unlike some other HPs, is not too terribly picky about chargers. Works with all 45W and above USB-C PD chargers that I've bought, except one from NekTeck https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B0719KV9PH/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1. Tried other more powerful NekTecks and they work. Will not charge from 30W USB PD adapters, so not as flexible as Samsung 2in1s, but overall pretty good and definitely workable. +USB-C PD power banks with 45W output will charge the X2 as well, and can double or more your run time depending on which you get. I've got two that work well and the one I like best is the Zendure A6PD. Improvement areas -no place to store pen, so I bought an adhesive pen loop and put it on the back on the left side. Working well, but not nearly as well as a small internally stored pen like Samsung does on some models. -good but not great battery life. 4-5 hours on "balanced" power plan. Worth the time to create a couple other power plans to extend battery life a bit more where you think through your own usage scenarios and turn off other features. If I put the X2 to sleep regularly during the day when not in use, I can usually go all day, and sleep/resume are really quick, but is also worth carrying something like the Zendure power bank mentioned above, will just about guarantee all day + performance. -ports. One USB-C 3.1 with PD and Thunderbolt 3 is a plus, but there is only one other port, one USB-A 3.0, at best just adequate. I quickly acquired a number of USB-C multifunction hubs with PD charging, hdmi out, etc. and consider this essential to carry along in my bag. Net, I'll be keeping this baby for a while, no plans or needs to upgrade other than storage. This frees me to look for a replacement for my Flex5 14". Will likely be an HP, especially something under 3 pounds with Optane, so I can discard the Optane and have a dual SSD lappy.

We had a huge lightning strike with a surge coming in from the Spectrum cable. We also had a huge (induced?) surge come in on a temporary outdoor network cable from temporary IP security cameras on a tree. The net cable was protected by this Gas Discharge Ethernet Surge Protector before it gets to the DVR. The cable was destroyed up to the arrester but NOT beyond. The DVR was apparently NOT damaged. I have included photos showing the destroyed cable areas and burned input side of the arrester so you can see how bad the surge was. In the photos... The gray cable comes from the security camera tree and wraps around the base of another tree before it comes up under outside stairs. You will notice the strike blew the cable open at the base of the tree. Under the stairs, the gray cable went through a simple coupler to a yellow cable which goes into a utility room through the window. The coupler was inside a ziplock bag and was twist tied up under the stairway platform. You will note that the strike blew open the coupler in the baggie and blew it off where it was hooked under the platform. It also blew one cable connector right out of the coupler and burned everything to a crisp. From inside the window, the yellow cable goes to the lightning arrestor bolted to a well grounded metal electrical box in room. That end was burned where it enters the right side of the arrestor. (It did not blow it out of the connector. I manually disconnected it to better see the damage.) The right side of the arrester is charred and pitted. The white network cables from the left end of the arrestor go about 15 ft to the security camera DVR in another room. *** The DVR was NOT damaged from what I can tell so far. *** I am amazed how much punishment this arrestor took and still protected the DVR. I have not opened the arrester yet but I'm going to consider it destroyed no matter what I find. $25 well spent! I just ordered more of them! UPDATE: I opened the arrestor up and it was totally destroyed. A small price to pay for what it did.

I bought this iPad jacket because I wanted something a little more stable than the stock Apple model. The Apple iPad jacket works really well if you are looking for something to cover the iPad, protect the screen when you stuff it in a briefcase or backpack, or when you prop it up so that you can use the virtual keyboard. But it has one weakness, when you stand the iPad up in landscape mode, the narrowness of the bottom flap makes it unstable. So when the Ctcstore jacket came out, I looked over the specs and saw that it was designed to allow you to prop up the iPad in landscape mode at various viewing angles, and it had a wide base, so stability wasn't an issue. So, if you are looking to use your iPad primarily as a video player or a picture frame, this is the jacket for you. However, you have to trade form for function. The Ctc jacket is very thick, which makes it difficult to hold and use the iPad as a reader. The same flap design that provides such stability in landscape mode proves to be a disadvantage in portrait mode. Its bulkiness also makes it weighty, again a disadvantage. So in the end, you have to choose: function or form.

In a way, this is a remarkable item. It's truly a testimony to all the effort that must have gone in to producing such an inferior product. Usually, there's SOMETHING in even a shoddy product that makes you go "mmmmhhh, I guess I'll keep it." Not this time ... Okay, to connect to your wireless (don't use the 5G, as I found out the hard way; the software in the Kindle doesn't like it) you'll need a brain surgeon because only someone with very steady hands is going to get the Kindle's screen to register the correct touches. There's no option (that I can find) for adjusting sensitivity. So be ready for keys to either strike too often or not enough. What's that? You've had products in the past that gave you the option to adjust sensitivity/screen points right at the start? So you could ENJOY the product? Not in Jeff Bezos' world, pally. When you get in, the home page is an inelegant mess. Lots of images of book covers (if you've owned a Kindle of some sort before) cluttering up the rather small screen. Also, the screen is grayscale. Yes. You read that correctly. 21st century and the thing's grayscale. They offer comic books on this thing. And. It's. In. Grayscale. Scrolling? Nope. As you drag your finger, the screen jumps, row by row. There's a scroll bar down the side that's merely ornamental. It moves to show you where you are relative to the total page, but you can't use the scroller to move the page. So all those decades of simply click-and-drag by the active portion of the scroll? Not on this, pally. What else. Oh, right. When you go to the books to search, they let the business development team -- the ones who never took an English literature course after sophomore year -- handle it. One section is "Literature and Fiction" (yeah, think about that for a second. What's that? You always thought literature was, by definition, fiction? Nope. Not in Jeff Bezos' world.) By the time you finally figure out where the stuff you want is, you're so ramped up with frustration and anger that the last thing you want to do is read anything. There's a lot of pushing of "offers" and a nearly endless litany of hosannahs to "Kindle Unlimited." "Recommended For You" is apparently code for "what we're trying to sell you based on contracts we've worked out with publishers, because some of these books, you not only have never heard of, they're nothing you're interested in." What's that? Didn't I pay extra to not be molested by ads? Yes. Yes I did. The Web browser (and I'm already sweaty with dread over how bad that'll be) is preloaded with bookmark tags for yahoo, facebook, twitter, and a few other items. There's a selector that indicates remove, but when I clicked that and then touched the facebook selection, I ended up on the facebook log in page and CANNOT get back to the remove page. I feel so dirty knowing that somehow, Facebook has managed to get my data with Kindle's help. If this were the 1980s, this would be a top-notch product. But now? It's like something a high school computer club put together over a weekend as a proof of concept. A big, expensive disappointment.

I love good quality pictures and have purchased quite a few small cameras (the kind you put in your pocket). Sometime they're ok, sometime not so much depending on the lighting. I really appreciate the fact that the shutter speed is fast and it worked under low light so well that it brought me great joy! The flip screen saved me a lot from difficult position and it can be the saving grace from taking a good picture from different angle. Also, the battery life is quite good. I took about 300 (1080p quality) pictures before I need to recharge the battery. But, if you use flash a lot, you may want to have a spare battery. I found that this camera was quite popular too. I saw 2 other people during the cruise that used the exact same camera. It also takes good quality video (with sound). Many people said, "Wow, nice camera!" after they took our pictures (my wife and I). There are many features that have been discussed in the previous reviews. If you were like me (who didn't want to spend too much but want to have a quality camera that will not disappoint), I recommend this camera. I've done a lot of research and I'm very happy with my decision.

I've been wanting to try out a ChromeBook for a while now, to see how it fits into my computing needs. I chose the Acer because of its speed, allegedly faster than others that are out there. I wasn't as concerned with the display, which reviewers have said is not as good as those of competitors. Overall, I'm very happy. It's definitely fast, a combination of Chrome OS and the chipset. Chrome OS lets me set up several different Google accounts at the login screen, so I can keep my personal and business computing separate. The display is just fine for my needs. I'm using it with a BlueTooth mouse, which works well when I'm at a desk; the touchpad is adequate for laptop use. The reason for four stars rather than five is simply due to the (current) limitations of Chrome OS. It's just not as versatile as the more complex -- and much slower -- Windows and Mac alternatives. And, despite being able to do many things offline, it really needs to be tied to a good wi-fi connection. I knew this going in, so it wasn't a surprise. Fortunately, the wi-fi sensitivity seems very good, picking up signals that my iPad doesn't even see. Bottom line: I'll be taking it with me when traveling by car. My iPad mini beats it for size and convenience for air travel, but when I sit down at the end of the day, I like having a mouse and keyboard, and relatively easy access to gigabytes of data on Google Drive(s) that I can access with all my computers. It fills an intermediate position between my Win7 desktop and iPad mini. It's a keeper.

I now have two nights of completely useless video that looks and sounds horrible. Fortunately I also file a separate angle with another better quality camera for close up and fade shots that I can at least edit and use. I have learned to always have two cameras filming at all times. I am grateful for this camera, it has taught me that cheap cameras deliver cheap audio and video. Cameras need to be properly stored and transported and handles with care when filming. Although I have not had a major bump, drop or crash incident with this camera, I did keep it in a hard case in my truck with all the other equipment and it gets hot in Texas, which may have caused the problems I'm experiencing. I have also been able to learn some techniques and it helped me decide whether to continue to pursue this hobby or not without having to shell out a lot of money. I'd considered a GPS many times but was put off by the absurd number of available units and manufacturers. I did not want to have to become an expert on GPS just to make an intelligent purchase. I envisioned getting something where I could just plug in a destination and it would guide me there and back. Pictures? Video? BLUETOOTH? What does any of this have to do with directions and maps? Ultimately I relied on Consumer Reports and went with their recommendation of the Garmin Nuvi 260W as a top pick for features and size. It has all the GPS features including turn by turn vocal instructions in American English and NONE of the junk that adds to cost. After the usual Amazon super-fast order processing, the box arrived. The "W" in 260W is for widescreen and it is. Great graphics, clear and bright screen. The manual was laughably short. At first I was actually annoyed that it ran all of six pages and most of that discussed how you shouldn't soak it in water or throw it against a wall, etc... Turns out, Garmin was showing off. The user interface is so simple and easy to understand that a detailed manual is pointless. I know nothing about GPS units but still had this up and running in seconds. The on-off button is the only button on it. Everything else is touch screen. So how's it do? Brilliantly! I have tried, HARD to mess it up. Blown through turns, gone the wrong way, left it on while the car was parked. None of this phased it in the least. It constantly tracks your position and gives ETA and MPH. If you continue past a turn, it takes about 2 seconds for it to recognize what happened and then the voice tells you "Recalculating". In no more than another two seconds, it has mapped out an alternate route. (The speed of this thing is stunning.) Mind you I'm not talking about it saying "Turn around bone-head, you blew that last turn." It literally maps out the next best way to your destination in a flash. Driving with it is very cool. It tells you to prepare for a turn and then tells you dead on the money to make the turn. By the way, it doesn't say "Turn left in point two miles." it says "In point two miles, turn left on Main Street". Then when you get there it repeats it as "Turn left on Main Street." This means that if there is more than one left turn coming up, you know exactly which one to take. It also monitors the road itself and advises of bends and twists. As an example, I was on a major highway that bent to the left with a single lane exit if you kept straight. As I approached this spot, it told me to keep left! This thing is nailed down. It is dead nuts simple to operate, does what it should in real time and seems to be without vices. Great device.

The Product Description should state up front that it is a "UART Serial Cable" and what exactly this means. The Product Description was not wrong per se, but not clear enough for me, and I made a mistake by purchasing it and then wasted many hours contacting Tech Support for my Laptop Notebook company, the Cable's Driver's Manufacturer, and my Internet Provider trying to figure out what the problem is that keeps it from giving me internet. The cord says that it connects RJ45 (like a phone jack that you find on the back of modems) and routers and Cisco (which makes routers) with USB (like on laptops) and works on Windows. So I thought that this should transfer internet to my laptop. I even remember it working on one of my computers to transfer internet 2 months ago, but I could be misremembering. I am a person like your average internet user. I don't know if all internet from modems that are not dial up is Broadband, and if all Broadband is Ethernet. My guess was that I was using Broadband. And my guess was that it would work. Maybe I thought that it would convert ethernet internet to laptop internet. I must not have paid enough attention to the fact that the Description says that it is not an Ethernet cable. It did not provide me internet from my modem to my ASUS Notebook Laptop. The product showed up in my Device Manager as an "FT232R USB UART Driver," so I called the FT232R Manufacturer called FDTI, and told them that I had ethernet (I guessed). FDTI replied that since it is a "UART Serial Cable," then it only transfers UART computer data, not ethernet, and that they think that this must be the problem. I called up my internet provider and they replied that I do get Ethernet internet from them, so that I need to have an Ethernet cable. A second problem is that the device apparently needs to be manually installed on your computer because even aside from the fact that it did not give me internet connectivity, it still had a Driver error in my Device Manager. The problem is that I needed to find someplace to download the Driver and install it manually and that took a bunch of steps too. I had to install it BOTH under USB and in the Ports Com section of my Device Manager to fully install it. These steps should be given in the Product Description or in the packaging when the item arrives. I have a hard time rating the product because my problem came from the Product description, and I guess that the product would work if you set it up between the right products. But there is also the installation issue and the fact that I wasted money on a product that I didn't need.

This wonderful headset completely improved my ability to move about while listening to my favorite programs without interruption. Switching between music and phone is easily accomplished with buttons that are easy to find, and it has a boom mic that swings conveniently up and out of the way when not using the headset for conversation. So what more could you possibly want for providing good listening and reliable communications? Well I found some room for improvement, one being to provide a better set of instructions. It took me a little while to determine that the button on the swing mic boom is the Multifunction Button. Once I figured that out, pairing was immediate. I don't really see a need to fold the earphones inward, but the ability to size the headset by extending the earphones downward would probably help to improve the wearing comfort. The packaging includes an AC charger with a detachable USB cable that can be plugged into any other USB source for charging its built-in rechargeable batteries. I would prefer the batteries to be user replaceable with the possibility of using rechargeable batteries. But the first charge was rapid, taking less than an hour, and the headset can't be used while charging. How long the installed batteries will continue taking a charge is anyone's guess. Otherwise, the headset is shipped in excellent packaging that opens easily and it can even be used for storing them. And the one and only real downside I found about this headset is the tendency to be somewhat uncomfortable after wearing them for awhile. The non-extendable harness is somewhat short and must rest on the rear of my head in order for the speakers to sit directly over my ears, and the generously padded earphones are a tight fit. UPDATE: The speakers will extend using a little more force than I tried initially. It made all the difference for wearing them comfortably for an extended time. These are excellent earphones if you are in constant contact over the phone and you want to switch to stereo radio or mp3 when not engaged in a conversation.

I purchased this cable specifically for a USB DAC (HRT Streamer II). It certainly meets the price point for a decent, but not too expensive audiophile cable. Pangaea is one of many companies in the audiophile USB cable market ,you can spend literally hundreds to nearly a thousand more. After reading a LOT of debate and questioning the engineer of my DAC, I am not convinced that spending one hundred to a thousand dollars makes a huge discernible difference in audio quality. Granted, I am not feeding a 10 or 20 or 100,000 system either. Some say the USB cable makes absolutely NO difference in sound quality since it is simply transmitting data, which any cable can do, so just use a cheap one. Some say that better cable (somehow without any measurements to prove it) makes ALL the difference, despite the fact that the cable remains on the digital side of the DAC equation. That, at minimum, in the clocking, anti jitter, and other "mechanical functions" a good cable is invaluable. Personally, I did not hear a huge jump in terms of sound quality, I may, at a later date swap between the two (cheap and the Pangaea) I don't think you can go wrong spending 20 bucks for a quality cable, like the Pangaea but if you are going to spend 900 or more on one, I would just put the money into an upgraded DAC, speakers or amp.

Great features include: * More than enough to drive 300 ohm headphones. * Integrated power supply, so you don't have a brick or need to find an extra USB connection. * Included useful remote. * Quality feeling front button. * BT is easy to pair and fine for convenient streaming when not engaged in critical listening. Things to keep in mind: * Included USB cable is a bit short. You may want to purchase a longer USB input cable. Reasons to look elsewhere: * You need to drive a high impedance headphone, such as something with 600 ohm impedance. * You want a DAC/AMP that is internally balanced. * You need something portable to with a built-in battery that fits in your pocket to use on the go. * You need your DAC/AMP to have a sub out, for ease of connection to a sub. (2) The mount got fairly close to my wall. The ability of the mount to bend backwards allowed me to go a little closer giving me about a 5 inch gap from my wall. (3) The 27" monitor mounted without any issue. The 32" monitor did mount properly and maintained it's position HOWEVER, if I pushed a little bit on the bottom of my monitor the whole screen would quickly tilt downwards as far as possible. In the pictures you can see, I wedged a piece of cardboard between the mount and my monitor to prevent this from happening. My 32" monitor weighs 11.2lbs which is far below the 26lb claims. OVERALL: Price (5/5): This cost me $30, can't beat it. A gas spring mount to accomplish the same feat costs approximately 3x more. Stability (3/5): As mentioned before it didn't properly support my 11.2lb monitor and I also notice that when typing, my screen jiggles a little. To fix this I pushed the monitors together to "support" one another and it's pretty much gone. Installation (5/5): Very easy to install, took me roughly 15 minutes, by myself, and another 15 minutes to adjust my view angles. Overall (4/5): I would recommend this. The construction is pretty sturdy and I don't feel scared that my monitors are going to fall and break. It clears up so much space on my desk and gives it a clean feel. If your situation is like mine (2 different sized monitors), I would recommend.

The results consistently showed that the stick in question (the stick itself and not the remote nor the TVs nor the WIFI networks) worked intermittently for a few minutes then the TV screens went blank. Contacted Roku as follow: 1. Logged a ticket on Roku website indicating the problem as such. No response for several days until after calling them in next step. 2. Called technical support explaining the problem and the troubleshooting process above. They said they'll send an HDMI extender. 3. Received the extender 2 weeks later, but it did not work at all - no audio, no video, just blank screen. The problem was actually worst since using the stick without the extender would at least work for a few minutes then stopped. 4. Called them the following day. They admitted that they had sent a bad part and will make sure to send a "working" HDMI extender. It never arrived. Probably never send it. 5. After 2 weeks of waiting, called them again and explained the troubleshooting process all over again (for the 4th time). They said they will send a remote. With patience running thin, asked the tech support rep why would she send a remote when the stick is the problem. After a brief silence, she asked to wait for a few minutes then came back and said an email with instructions on how to return the stick for a replacement will be sent. 6. Three days later, still no email. And no, it's not in spam folder. Simply put - they lied the second time. Frustrated but decided to give them a final chance to rectify the problem and called one last time. After 25 minutes, a rep finally answered then the line got cut off immediately. Coincidence? Bottom line: The problem had been reported for over a month and still no resolutions. The average wait time for each call is 30+ minutes due to the so called "heavy call volume". They sent bad part and lied their way out of honoring their warranty. The Extraordinarily Good: Amazon Customer Service Frustrated and planned to just throw away the stick, but also decided to give Amazon a call to inform the type of service Roku had provided with the hope that if this is the norm, Amazon will think twice before selling Roku products on its site. I messaged the company and they were going to send me replacement batteries, then sent this response: "PS：we don't recommend leaving radio in charger after charged. Although the battery is lithium ion battery, it also has the memory effect, but its merory effect is much more lower compared to NiCad battery. People have believed lithium ion batteries don't have memory effect for a long time, but it has been proved by scientists that lithium ion battery also has memory effect recently. I find an article titled "Memory effect now also found in lithium-ion batteries" in a physics website (Amazon probihits writing website links in the message, so I can't write the exact link in the message). If the battery has memory effect, it will remember how many quantity of electricity it was charged last time, and the battery will accept the same quantity of electricity next time it is charged. This is the reason why leaving radio in charger after charged has a problem. It takes about 2.5 hours to fully charge the battery if the battery is fully run out, and charging them for a whole night will be too long for the battery. When you don't need a walkie-talkie, you can put it there without removing the battery. When you use it, you have to fully charge it and use it. By the way,our battery is lithium manganate battery which is a kind of li-on battery. And lithium manganate battery's charging and discharging cycle is about 250-400 times. It means lithium manganate battery will eventually be dead when it reaches its maximum charging time. " Arcshell HAS TO KNOW that there are battery issues (considering the MANY, MANY reviews that state there are problems), yet they STILL sell this item and just expect people to waste their time contacting them for new batteries. Then upon wanting to send me replacement batteries, basically they tell me it's our fault for leaving the walkies on the chargers for ANY time more than it takes to charge them. Am I supposed to sit there for 1 to 2 1/2 hours staring at them, waiting for them to be charged so that the finicky batteries don't overcharge and mess up?! NO WAY! The ONLY reason I am giving this 2 stars instead of 1 is that WHEN the batteries were working, the item worked well and had good range. We are returning these and buying from a different company.

I have had these speakers for a couple of months. They are mounted in my backyard and produce a very nice and crisp sound. I am very pleased and happy about the speakers and sound quality. So, the speakers get 5 stars! The grills however, are a different story. The industrial designer that came up with this idea probably looked at the sketch on the CAD/design program and figured it's very cool and they moved forward with it, without making a few prototypes and testing them for a period of time to see whether or not there are any issues. The perforated metal screen has very short lips and they fall out of the cut in the body of the structure easily, especially when the speakers are hanging at an angle from the wall. The mechanical engineer would have caught this, had they held a design review meeting, and they could have resolved this if they had seen the prototypes in action during the design phase. I'll have to look at them and see if there is a way to fix them so that they don't fall off, but then why did I pay the hefty price for these speakers in the first place? I hope the folks at Polk read this review and think twice next time they release a product. So, if you don't care about the grills, go for them, they are nice speakers, but the grills will not sit on them unless you use "superglue" or something else to hold them in place (not a recommendation obviously!!!)

I had issues with some of these cables as they arrived and had to replace many of them. There are a few 100mb devices that I left in place on these but they will be replaced soon enough and I’ll have to buy better patch cords. As an example of issues, I use Ubiquiti Wi-Fi access points with PoE injectors. The AP’s would frequently (several times in a few minutes) lose network link and all devices connected would lose internet connectivity, renegotiating with the next AP. The link would spontaneously recover, the Wi-Fi devices would see a stronger signal and hop back to the nearer AP then the cycle would repeat. The power seemed to hold but the Ethernet link would die. Sometimes after many drops the AP would just fall offline and I’d have to reset things to my aggravation. I finally realized what was happening and replaced these cables on both sides of the PoE injector. The APs have been stable since. I learned why the signal was terrible shortly after seeing this behavior. I wanted to shorten several of them so I cut a few in half and attempted to re-terminate the cut ends. I’ve terminated cable for years and have never seen such thin and were flimsy wire in Ethernet cable. It reminded me of stranded cat2 phone wiring in RJ12 cables. Lesson learned with cheap cables. They’re low priced for a reason. Pay a little extra and get better cables.

After further research I realized that my monitor had a max resolution of 1680x1050, and unfortunately my TV stick cannot go below 1080p. So I had to buy another device (the Blackbird 4k Up and Down Converter) which took in 1080p HDMI input from my TV stick and downscaled it to 720p HDMI output. Also, I mounted the monitor upside down, and neither the TV stick nor the monitor had an option to Flip 180 Degrees, so I bought another box (TV Rotate Controller) to flip the picture upside-down. Overall, I had to settle on using 4 components (the UGREEN adapter, the Up and Down Converter, the Rotate TV Controller, and the TV stick) which all have separate power adapters, plus the monitor itself creates an additional cord, so that's 5 plugs on my power strip and a lot of clutter. It would be nice if the UGREEN adapter included some of these features (180 degree flip, resolution downscale/upscale). But if you know what you're buying and you don't need any of this stuff, it's a great standalone product.

It’s a very good hybrid camera, I said “very good" , but not excellent. There are some features in video and photo that are lacking in this camera, making it looks like Panasonic is clearly “holding/neutering" the camera's full potential. Some examples of that in video: Doesn’t shoot full hd 24fps, doesn’t shoot full hd at high bitrates (24 mbps is outdated in 2022), Crops in 4K even more than the micro 4/3 crop (it means that it has to shoot very, very wide, to look a little bit wide), does not record 10 bit in full hd or 4K to an external device, the focus peaking for manual focus lies a little bit (does not works perfectly), little noisy in the shadows (but this is common even for far more expensive cameras). For photography in my opinion it’s a fine camera, I only felt it lacks HDR pictures, and as I said in video, the response is a little noisy in the shadows. So if you are searching for a great camera for video in a similar price range, go with the GH4 or GH5 (used), X-S10 Fuji (body only), Sony A7s2 (used, body only). But there are good points on this camera, that makes me believe it’s surely costs what it costs: Beautiful 8 bit colors, no limit of recording time, stabilized sensor, great photos files (comparable with much more expensive full frames).

I bought this TV as an upgrade from an older 42" LCD Panasonic, which I was happy with until it died with a lightning strike. I've had this 50" LED model for about a month now, and I am very happy with the picture and sound quality. I really love the ultra-thin bezel. It means the TV fits in a smaller space (actually a space not much bigger than where my 42" sat) while still maintaining a huge 50" picture. SCREEN & PICTURE: The screen has a semi-gloss finish. I wasn't sure how I would like this because I was used to a matte finish on my old TV. I have windows at ninety degrees to my couch (and TV) so I was concerned about glare. As it turns out the semi-gloss screen on the 50" model does not reflect the window glare as I had feared. Happy about that. I didn't do much tweaking to the default picture settings except for a little contrast, brightness, and temperature changes to complement the lighting of my room. I found the default settings were good for me. SOUND: I'm not an audiophile, so the TV speakers sound fine to me. I would eventually like to attach this TV to a sound bar for enhanced features, but for the moment I find the built-in speakers do a great job. I do not use the Surround Sound feature. APPS: One thing that drew me to this model was the built-in apps, particularly Amazon Prime. I was familiar with using the Amazon Prime app with my other devices (game console, computer, tablet), so I was a little disappointed to discover that the Amazon Prime app on this TV does not include access to My Watchlist. It's really a very basic app that I feel could be improved. Likewise, the YouTube app. It allows sign in to access my subscribed channels, but to do this, the TV app supplies a code that I must enter via my computer. This wouldn't be too bad if it retained my sign in settings, but I must get this code from the TV and sign in via my computer EVERY TIME I run the app. Honestly, it's more trouble than it's worth. The VuDu app works well with my VuDu/Ultraviolet account. The web browser is basic and lacks Flash capabilities, so it won't work with various movie pages that rely on the Flash player. I don't use Netflix or Hulu so no comment on them. HOME PAGE: I wasn't sure I'd like having a TV with a home page, but turns out I was wrong! Love this feature. I love being able to customize it to show my most used apps. I also love being able to have more than one Home page. It's very easy to set up and use, although I recommend turning off the "Viera Connect Banner" advertisements via the settings page to prevent seeing ads when using the remote. CONNECTIONS & PORTS: 3 x HDMI 2 x USB 1 x Component input (red, blue, green) 1 x coax input (cable) 1 x RCA audio output (red, white) 1 x Digital audio output 1 x Ethernet port Built-in Wi-Fi I like that all these connectors are on a back panel, not "up under a lip" as I have seen on other TVs. This makes all the connections easily accessible. I can even reach over the top of the TV to access them without having to swivel the base around. I teamed this TV with a [[ASIN:B00BP5KOPA Logitech Wireless Combo MK270 with Keyboard and Mouse (920-004536)]] which connects via USB. This allows better couch internet navigation with a keyboard and mouse. OVERALL: This 50" LED TV from Panasonic more than meets my needs and expectations. Could not be happier. Recommended.

I really enjoy using these headphones. I use them as my main DJing headphones, and being [[ASIN:B000TDZOXG Sennheiser HD25-1 II Closed-Back Headphones]]'s at heart, this is the classic pair of headphones many DJ's have come to love, now with a little bit of flair. Sound quality: Really good quality. The sound is crisp, the lows reach deep and the highs have great clarity. The sound feels very closed in though, being tightly closed headphones, so I definitely prefer my open-backed [[ASIN:B0011UB9CQ Beyerdynamic DT 990 PRO Open Studio Headphones 250 Ohms]] for leisurely listening. In the DJ booth, though, these sound great. Isolation: These headphones keep out sound pretty well. As you'd expect it cannot match the isolation you'd get from most in-ear earbuds, but as far as conventional headphones go these do a great job. You'd think that over the ear headphones would do a better job than on-ear ones, but this beats out my old headphones, [[ASIN:B000P62ND6 Audio-Technica ATH-M50 Professional Studio Monitor Headphones]] (excellent headphones by the way), as far as isolation goes. As for leaking sound out, I don't really care about it so I don't know (I use different earbuds when I'm on the go) but they're decent at that, too. Comfort: They are more or less comfortable, although over time they start to get a little painful since, in the name of isolation, they clamp down on your head fairly hard. I can't use these for easy listening usually just because my head starts to hurt over time, as these press my ears against my head hard. Style: This one is really up to you. I think they look pretty cool (the all black original version of these headphones are pretty bland if you ask me) though they can rub people in two ways: a) some people presume they are cheap and plasticky (which perhaps is a plus against thieves!); b) they look a little immature/tacky. Sure, I can see where you're coming from, so if you ascribe to these groups, try the original [[ASIN:B000TDZOXG Sennheiser HD25-1 II Closed-Back Headphones]] Hope this helps those of you who are deciding which headphones to go for!

I just received my new Kindle 2 today and I must say I love it. I love my original Kindle as well, but I am very happy with many of the small improvements made, especially the improvements in navigating the periodical material. Being able to jump to the next article from any place within the article is a fabulous improvement over the way it was done in the original. I LOVE the new quick menu selection to get to a book's details in the Store. I can't tell you how many times I wished for that feature for books I had purchased weeks in the past. I frequently buy multiple books at a time just to have for future reading and like to browse the book's descriptions when looking through my library for something new to read. However, I think it would be nice if the Kindle detail page indicated if I had already purchased the book I am looking at the same way the main web site at amazon.com does. I have a horrible memory and a large library ... I can easily picture myself buying a book a second time if browsing the store on my Kindle. Actually, the whole menu system seem slightly improved. Lots of little conveniences sprinkled here and there. Other things I love: Images in the periodicals are clear and not pixalated like they were on the orginal. The new case is symetrical and can be propped up against something if reading while your hands are doing something else, say like eating. The new cover attaches much more securely then the original 5-way button is a huge improvement over the old vertical scroll wheel. Dictionary look up is much quicker and less intrusive I am, however, disappointed in a couple of missing features. The first feature appears to actually have been removed and that is the ability to display the current time by pressing alt-t. I didn't realize how much I used it until today when I was reading in the bath and realized it wasn't there. Also, I was really hoping to see a way to organize my library in this release. Especially with the increased capacity on the new device. Being able to create my own groups/categories and assign books to them would be very helpful. My own personal use of this feature would be to group books in a series together so I could easily get to them or to group books on the same topic e.g. the Civil War. As my digital library grows, my list of books is becoming quite overwhelming and my memory isn't what it should be. I can't always remember the specific name of a book I am looking for and would love to be able to organize them much like I do with my paper books on my bookshelves. Lastly, since I am also an owner of the original Kindle which my daughter is anxious to inherit, I am disappointed that the original Kindle's firmware isn't being updated with some of the new features. Although some of them I understand are not possible without the new screen or the 5-way button, I think many of the improvements could also be given to the loyal early adopters as well, especially things like the new menus. Much as Apple did for the first gen iPhones. I can tell you they made me a much more loyal customer by making sure my first generation phone had all the cool software features as my husbands 3G phone. All in all, I loved my original and I love the Kindle2 as well.

Whomever designed this NEVER exercised, it’s horrible and the reason has everything to do with the location of the controls and microphone. For comparison with its predecessor the BeatsX, I’ve included a photo to show location of old vs new. Here are the problems: 1. The controls for volume, function, and microphone have all moved further away from the ear and now rest on the neck. This means fumbling around trying to find them. You can’t see the controls, so it forces you to find the cord, then slide your fingers down the cord until you locate the controls resting somewhere on your neck. On the predecessor, the BeatsX, they were higher up towards the ear, making them easier to find, fingers needing only to slide an inch or so. That may not sound like a lot of extra effort, but imagine you’re running. Your arms stop swinging not for a second or two, but several. It’s not just locating the controls, it’s problem two. 2. Problem #2 is the actual design of the controls. On the predecessor, the BeatsX, the controls sat on a tapered rocker design. Once you found the controls, they were easy to operate. The center point of the rocker was pressed and held to call up Siri (or Hey Google), to advanced to the next song track, go back a song, or answer an incoming call. On the new Flex, the buttons have been separated and moved far apart. The up/down volume is on the side, unnatural to the position of easy use. You have to first find the controls, then rotate to side, then feel again for the rocker switch. It’s a 3-step process now and is clumsy. Think about doing that on a run. It takes several seconds and 100% will throw off your stride. 3. What was the center function of the rocker on the BeatsX has now moved to a stand alone button, but there’s little elevation to the button height AND it’s next to the mic. This means it’s difficult to find, then distinguish from the mic itself. And because it’s small with little elevation off the left side battery, it’s very difficult to depress, especially when sweating. It’s all around a very crappy redesign of the controls making them difficult, if not impossible to use during exercise. 4. Finally, Apple has moved the mic from about 3 inches below the ear where it was nearer the mouth, onto the left battery as shown on the image. This means it’s sitting on the neck. AND, because of the design placement relative the earpiece, the mic actually sits up against the neck itself. This means the mic is obscured and noisy if moving. Try noisy as all heck. It’s impossible to carry on a real conversation while moving. Overall this is a horrible redesign for anyone using them for sports or any moving activities. Don’t even consider them for a moment, run from them. They’ve been reengineered for sitting at a desk. They’re not even usable for simple walking. The added battery life would be a big plus if functional, they’re just not. The sound quality is about the same. No real change. Overall, BIG Apple misfire on this redesign. You’re gonna see a pretty quick redesign soon, these problems are highly noticeable. BeatsX were out for years. I’ll be surprised if they don’t hit reset in 18 mos. on the Flex. Until then, don’t buy if you’re using for a workout. Total waste of money, you can do better for half the cost. While I was willing to pay $100 for BeatsX, the BeatsFlex are a poorly designed product equivalent to the low end $25 or less products you can find from China. They’re really that bad, so don’t say I didn’t warn you if you get em!

I ordered this shortly after the arrival of a brand-new MacBook Pro, enticed by the prospect of being able to dis- and re-connect my external monitor, Ethernet connection, headphones, and USB accessories via a single cable. The first one arrived and... didn't register at all. My laptop was oblivious to its existence. A quick look at the power supply suggested why: the green LED wasn't lighting up. Borrowing the power supply from a colleague's Belkin Thunderbolt Dock confirmed that my own power supply was DOA. I wrote it off to bad luck, and went about ordering a replacement dock from Amazon. The second one did not have a dead power supply. Instead, it had an Ethernet port which, after a few days of seemingly-reliable service, started behaving erratically, ultimately wasting roughly a day of my time and productivity. (I made the mistake of initially assuming that my network connection had been broken by my IT department, which is a sadly-reasonable prospect in my case. It wasn't until I switched over to Apple's Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter that I realized the problem might be a mere couple of feet away from me.) I hesitated while filling out the return form for the second dock. Should I go for another exchange, and hope that a third unit would work reliably? I decided that actually, no, I shouldn't. I wasn't paying $160 for the privilege of being Belkin's quality-assurance lackey. I'd rather have to occasionally fiddle with a bunch of cables than worry about what new and innovative way Belkin's hardware will find to waste my time.

The value proposition here was really good. I've been using this for a while now to make sure that everything works well, and overall, I'm really happy with this purchase. The kit is really quick and easy to put together, perfect for a first time Raspberry Pi user. As always, be careful with static electricity when you are working with open circuit boards. There are a couple of things to keep in mind if you also buy it though - so here's a summary of my experience: 1) There are no silicon sticker bumps to install on the bottom, and that means this could scratch up something it sits on. These are really cheap to buy yourself though, and as long as you know to get them, it's no big deal. Honestly though, I'd really rather have these than the included stylus. 2) The airflow could be a problem if you use this LCD in a case that isn't open air. Because this case is open, there's tons of airflow - if you put it in a more traditional case, that fan is not going to have anywhere to draw cooler air from as the giant LCD is sitting right on top of it. This is common to pretty much any large LCD that is GPIO mounted, and nothing against this particular model. There were some parts I really liked though, and I would like to point out: 1) The heatsinks were a great addition to this kit. I have a half dozen Raspberry Pi's hanging around, and it seems I'm always buying a new one. Having some heatsinks come with the kit means I didn't have to buy another $10 part. Thumbs up to Miuzei here! 2) It's a small thing (literally, and metaphorically) but the addition of a screw driver can be make or break. Using the wrong size screw driver on these small screws can make an easy build turn into a painful trial. Really liked the simple precision screwdriver supplied, and it went straight into my electronics kit bag after I was done. 3) The LCD really was plug and play. No drivers to install, no headaches trying to get Linux to recognize it. I've used various GPIO LCD in the past, and there's always a worrisome driver to download from a less-than-reputable site just for video. Not here. This is perfect for beginners! Overall, the pros massively outweigh the cons with this really nice screen. I couldn't be happier with my purchase. I'm a repeat customer of Miuzei, and I can't say enough nice things about their customer service. If somehow you do end up running into trouble, they will get you back on track again, guaranteed! Hope this helps someone!
