Context: I do photo & video editing. Thus I wanted to buy a new card reader - and replace my 'old' Transcend one because it feels a bit flimsy. Except, guess what? It outperforms this Ugreen one... It was a big let down because I liked the aesthetic of the Ugreen & the outside build. BUT it doesn't perform well at all. I've included screenshots comparing the two card readers along with the micro SD card itself (a high end one). The only one I've not included is the one in my DSLR but that one too is a high end SanDisk 64GB Extreme PRO... So when the results continue to be persistent despite using all equal high end Flash storage- it means the fault and the problem is with the reader. Key things to note: - The Ugreen only performs the same as the Transcend during SINGLE file transfers. Meaning if you're only copying and pasting ONE item at a time it's *usually* going to perform the same. Not faster- just the same or close. - The Ugreen's construction feels nice - If you value aesthetics more than transfer speeds (which you shouldn't) then go for it. However I cannot recommend this product when there's another out there for a few cents cheaper and outperforms this one in every occasion. Here's a link to the one I've had for years: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009D79VH4/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1 If you need to copy and transfer multiple files of significant sizes or simply in quantities- you need a reader that provides a consistent experience. The Transcend may not be the prettiest but holy crap does it simply just work and there's no BS. I was wishing this review would have been different- unfortunately Ugreen falls almost more than 50% behind in speed when compared to Transcend. So something's definitely wrong with the internal card reader itself and should be AVOIDED.

Wont waste your time with wordy paragraphs, lets do this: -Sturdy, works great, clamps strong. Great cable routing features. -Works with XP-Pen 22e Drawing monitor. Mine sits up straight and high when not drawing, then lowers and angles over the desks edge when I'm drawing. -The movement isn't quite fluid but not clunky either, its reasonable enough. -To the people who claim that the tilt is broke/monitor is stuck facing ceiling - I had this issue as well, here's what I did: ---Attach monitor and adjust tension in everything as needed, turn the up/down tilt tension screw all the way loose, then tight, then loose....remove monitor. grabbing the VESA plate directly with your hands, adjust it up and down a bunch to loosen it up (it will be stiff but not locked solid if you are doing it correctly, if its solid you may have left the tension screw in the TIGHT position instead of LOOSE). After breaking it in a bit up and down....leave it in the position you will want the monitor in. re-attach monitor. gently tilt monitor up and down a couple times to further loosen it up(don't grab your monitor in a way where you will crack it if the tilt is still too tight). After I did this it now just works fluidly. I understand this might not work for everyone. Pro tip for drawing monitor users: Grab an extra Keyboard Wrist Wrest, use it under the monitor bottom when you lower it on the desk edge for padding if needed/desired. You may need a USB extension cable as well or longer full cable(see below) Pro tip for everyone: Buy longer cables for whatever you are mounting on this. You will want to route your cables through the arms and your going to want to leave slack at the joints. I would say 10' cables as a standard for most users is a good idea.

I heard a tapping noise one morning and found several buzzards on my back patio, pecking at the sliding glass doors. After quickly checking my pulse, I realized they weren’t here for me. Wife was not cooking, so… wrong house? Turns out they think there are other buzzards in the mirrored glass. I chased them off, but they kept coming back. And they’re messy. This PIR switch was just what I needed. I didn’t want to hurt the birds, so I decided to use this PIR switch to build a motion activated sprayer. It has adjustment pots for both sensitivity and duration, and now when critters come onto my porch, they get sprayed with water for about 1 or 2 seconds at a time until they leave. I love that I can adjust the length of time they get sprayed. Most switches available in 12-24V can’t be adjusted down past 30 seconds, which is way more than I needed. This one goes all the way down to one second, which is just what I needed. You could use this for lighting in a cabinet or safe, and adjust the time to any length you want. It’s super sensitive, and I’ve seen it chase away everything from squirrels to raccoons to buzzards. But I also like that you could reduce the sensitivity if you only wanted to spray maybe dog, or even mother-in-law-sized things. This isn’t waterproof by any means, but it was easy to seal from the elements with a little silicone. Mine has been rained on many many times with no problems. The back pops off easily so you can adjust the pots on the circuit board for sensitivity and duration with a small screwdriver. Love it, and would order again. Pros - + Adjustable for sensitivity and duration. + Highly sensitive – effective on things as small as birds. + Can reduce duration to as low as one second, much shorter than almost any other switch available. + Perfect for any trigger from 12 to 24V. + Flat ends allow use of zip ties, or there are screw holes in tiny side wings. Cons - - None.

I already owned one of these (in fact, as shown in the image on Amazon). I wanted a second one, so I ordered it here. What I received is a "model upgrade" from the version I owned. However, I actually prefer the older version. The new version is smaller, and may well be superior when working with standard EIDE or SATA drives, but for 2.5" EIDE drives, the functionality is reduced. The old version had a power supply with two adaptors... one to go to SATA and the other which plugs into the adapter itself to provide power to the 2.5" EIDE (laptop) drive. The new version has a smaller power supply (perfectly suitable) with the addition of an in-line power switch (a nice addition!) and ONE adaptor, so you can use it with a 3.5" or 5.0" EIDE device, or with a SATA device. But if you want to use it with a 2.5" laptop EIDE device, you have to rely on USB bus power to power the device and the hard drive. Since, right now, I'm transferring the contents of an old laptop drive to a replacement drive, both 2.5" EIDE, this is inconvenient. I ended up using the on-motherboard EIDE port and a step-down plate I have to handle the second device, instead. I realize most users won't be worrying about 2.5" EIDE drives. Just be forewarned if you are... unless you have a tremendously good 5V power line on your USB, and a very-low-power-draw drive, this won't work for that purpose. On the other hand... if you have SATA or full-size EIDE, this device is nice. The physical size of all components is significantly reduced, and the device seems to be recognized more easily than the older device was. Just realize... the image on the Amazon page is NOT the device being shipped. It's sort of like thinking you're buying a cherry 1970 'vette and getting the current one instead. It may be a nice car, perhaps a NICER car... but it's not the SAME car.

I have purchased several sets of these cables in the past, and by and large been pleased with them… until now. When I attempted to connect these cables to their perspective hardware, I noticed a distinct difference in the brand/style of plugs they used. They were all the proper type of plugs, but were obviously mix and match as far as the actual style and/or manufacturer. All 3 plugs on the 24 pin ATX cable were distinctly different in cosmetic appearance. Of the two that plugged in side by side on the power supply, one was noticeably shorter in height than the other, creating a major eyesore for the $3000+ custom rig I’m building. There were similar issues with mix and match plugs on the PCIe and SATA cables. Seriously… if you’re going to charge $100 or more for a custom cable set, you should have a little more concern for the plugs you use to assemble them. I see no problem with buying plugs from different sources to insure the best pricing and quality, but you should take the steps to insure that mismatched plugs do not get mixed together in a bin for assembly. These are not what I would consider “Cables Perfected”, as your motto implies. Edit: Lowering review to 1 star for this purchase. The more I examine these, the more problems I find. Since my first review, I've found two pins on the ATX connector where the ends of the sleeving were not properly crimped to the pin. One was frayed so bad, it was pluming out the back side of the connector, causing yet another eyesore. Using leftover cables from a previous set, I've been able to fix all the problems I've found so far, but sincerely wish I would have sent this set back at the first sign of trouble. These things are too expensive to have this many defects. It makes me question whether CableMod has any quality control in place, and if so, how did they miss so many issues with this set?

Honestly I’m not even confident that the dongle is USB 3.1 certified. I would doubt it. Second, the dongle does not have a power supply or outlet. Since dongles use the power outlet on the iPad to connect most include a second power outlet on the dongle itself so you can use devices and charge the IPad. This can also speed up transfers because you are not relying solely on battery. Unfortunately this dongle lacks a way to charge the IPad, meaning you either use the dongle or you take it out and charge the device. Third, and lastly, this dongle does not have a magnet nor is it designed to fit onto the ipad. Instead the dongle just hangs off the ipad. Unfortunately the dongle cord is not long enough to even sit evenly on a table. You will always be hanging from the ipad. This cannot be good for the outlet long term. If you can get past these cons then BUY the device. I use it for quick transfers only and so it meets my needs. BUT if you need to have external devices connected to your IPad at all times DO NOT BUY THIS DONGLE.

I am another that purchased this laptop as part of Prime Day, and I have experienced what others here have as far as the horrible choice of mechanical drive for this PC. Thankfully, I was in a position to put in both a 500GB Samsung 950 Pro m.2 nvme SSD as well as a 500GB Samsung 850 Evo 2.5" SATA SSD. The laptop, after these upgrades and a clean Windows 10 install, runs perfectly and I am extremely happy with it now. As happy as I am with it now, I can't give it more than 3 stars due to the out-of-box experience; on first boot with the original hard drive, after an hour of waiting it wouldn't even show me the desktop. Eventually, when it got to the desktop, even Task Manager was locking up due to how much was going on vs how slow that mechanical drive was. I wanted to at least see how things were before doing the upgrades, but I couldn't even get to that point. This was expected, however, as I planned on upgrading the drives either way. What really irked me was 1.) having a warranty sticker in place before being able to remove just the bottom cover, and 2.) having to remove the motherboard of the laptop to get to the m.2 slot. I have repaired several laptops to this degree before so thankfully I was well equipped to handle the process, but it's inexcusable to put this level of difficulty to change the storage config. And while I realize that it has been said by multiple people that the warranty sticker being broken that is over one of the screw holes on the bottom of the laptop won't necessarily prevent you from getting warranty service, MSI still puts it on there in hopes to scare people away from making these upgrades (replacing just the 2.5" drive should not present any risk of losing your warranty, that's ridiculous). As I said before, after making these upgrades I love this laptop now. Games run well (they run much better with power plugged in, couldn't maintain over 60fps in Diablo 3 on battery even after changing the power profile and disabling battery boost in Geforce Experience, plugged in it stays over 100fps), and battery life is around what I'd expect. I also love the form factor of being a powerful machine but being nice and light/thin. The keyboard has been just OK, though, as the space bar seems to not like my default right-hand thumb position as it sometimes misses inputs, and after setting the RGB backlight to all white you can see bright green and blue colors on the bottom row of keys, so not perfectly white. Overall, I would not recommend someone buy this particular configuration unless you're ready and willing to replace the hard drive with at least a 2.5" SSD and do a clean install of Windows. If that process doesn't scare you, then this is a great machine.

I've tried a few of the low cost security cameras around including ones by blink, ring and wyze and they all fell short in some way in terms of annoying detection issues or app problems. The camera is made by Anker, a company that is known for making power banks and chargers. First off, it does offer 2fa security by email and phone to secure the account. It also lets you choose the server you want it to interact with. The video image quality and sound quality is very good. The night vision on it is black and white but it has good clarity. So far detection is flawless. It can detect sounds as well as motions. It is easy to disable detection or turn off the camera completely. Updating the firmware was also simple The Eufy securiy app from the Apple app store is nice and works well. I especially like that you don't need to buy some plan to see or download your videos. They do offer a cloud plan for $2.99 a month, which I guess could be useful, but you don't need it. I just put a 32gb memory card in it and it works fine. I can even download the videos to the photos app on my iPhone. The head of the camera swivels so you can easily position it. You can turn off the indicator light in the settings. I unplugged it once from power and thought it might be a hassle to reconnect it. Nope. Plugged it back in and it reconnected all by itself. To top it off, it's also a nice looking camea. In my view, so far at least, this is a far superior product compared to other similar security cameras offered here.

The AT-LP120 is a really impressive and fun turntable. I upgraded from a Sony TT so I could buy nicer records and set the tracking force lighter as to not damage them. I researched thoroughly (Steve Hoffman, Audiogon, etc...) and it came down to this one or a vintage one. Vintage TT's seemed too finicky for my laziness, and this one seemed like a solid performer out of the box so I went with it. It took minutes to set up (watched a video on Youtube which was helpful) and sounded perfect right out of the box. However I noticed the bass was lacking a bit. I did more research on how to dial this TT in and found out that it is important to upgrade the platter mat to the 1/4" Technics rubber mat (available on KABUSA) and get an external preamp (ART DJ PRE II from Amazon). That fixed the bass issues and it sounds Amazing now. Some great records to play: Postal Service - Give Up; Beck - Sea Change; Sigur Ros (anything by them); Radiohead (all, but especially OK Computer and Kid A and In Rainbows); Peter Gabriel - So. Those records blew me away when played on this turntable and now I'm permanently hooked on vinyl and will pretty much only get music in this format from now on. The awesome thing is nearly all new albums also come with a digital download of the entire album on mp3 so I can load it on my ipod too. Pros: Price (nothing beats it under 300 dollars. You'd have to spend at least 400 to get a better model) Easy to use and set up, not finicky at all. Looks beautiful Sounds really really good. I can't imagine a Rega P1 or Project Debut Carbon sounding any better (but perhaps they do, but I doubt it's enough to justify 2-3x the price! Spend that money on these expensive MFSL records or the Beatles Vinyl Box Set) Performance better than listed specs - apparently the listed specs aren't that great (w&f < 0.20%) but I've listened to this turntable for over 300 hours and it keeps speed perfectly and I haven't heard any warbling or fluttering during piano or long-held notes. I also don't hear any rumble in the speakers. In between songs you can kind of hear the subtle motor purring if your ear is right next to the speaker and it is up loud but as soon as music starts that goes away completely. Again, is that worth an additional 400 dollars to get rid of? Not to me.) Cons Construction - It's a plastic top and hollow inside, not well dampened (will get to that next). The tonearm clip broke already (no big deal, but not awesome). The feet are not adjustable (I replaced them with adjustable brass spikes that screw right in). Thud - tapping the TT makes a very loud, deep, audible thud. When the music is up loud, I can't help but to hear a subtle hollowness in the bass notes that is a result of this construction and poor dampening. I created an isolation platform from solid oak with sorbothane feet, and though that isolates the TT from the rest of the world (footfalls), it doesn't prevent the effect of resonance on this super thud-y plinth. I am still working on ways to silence this behavior. Of all the things worth spending more money on, I think this might be it. Personally, this hasn't affected my enjoyment of the music because I typically don't have it up loud enough to experience this coloration (I play it pretty loud though). But if you plan to really blast your music, this might be an issue for you with this TT. Also enabling the low cut feature on the preamp does help this I noticed. But still, it's a weakness in the TT. You shouldn't need to use a low cut feature on a preamp at all. Those con's may sound pretty bad, but I'm only taking off one star because the pros so far outweigh them. At the end of the day this turntable is brilliant and musical and engaging and and and... So if you don't want to spend 400 dollars or more on a turntable I highly recommend the AT-LP120. If your budget is higher, I'm sure you'll be rewarded with less thud, quieter motor, and modern looks, but I just don't think your music will sound significantly better than this. At that point your speakers (and maybe your amp) become your bottleneck. So if those are super high end, only then will the differences in those 500-600 dollar turntables become noticeable.

This review is for the "Quiet" version, the 400Q. I ordered two of these to build fan-only (no water cooling) workstations using full-size ATX motherboards. I am extremely happy with these cases, as they fit my use case perfectly and there are very few other options on the market at this price point. They're quiet, they look great, and they're pretty easy to work with. That being said, the "five star" review reflects their value and quality *at the price point*. If this the kind of case you're looking for, you're probably going to be satisfied. First off, quality control for Corsair seems to be improving. The two cases I ordered were free of any obvious manufacturing flaws (no broken tabs, finish is even, things that I've had issues with with some Carbide series cases in the past). They look identical, they're solidly put together, and they arrived well-packaged. The 400Q cases have dampening material on the inside. Reviews I'd read online were vague about what this material actually was. It's a sort of rubberized black mat about 1/8" thick that is evenly adhered to the inside of the sides, the top magnetic panel, and the front panel. It feels high quality and does not look like it will degrade during the life of the system. The interior of the case is fairly easy to work with. The plastic shrouds for the power supply and disk bay are held in play with thumbscrews, and can be easily removed. There's no reason to leave them in place in a "no window" build with the 400Q. The drive bay itself and the 3 SSD mounts on the backside of the motherboard mount plate are just OK. Easy enough to use, not as precisely molded as some other cases I've tried. Not a big deal. The backplate includes pre-installed standoffs. One of the standoffs has a slight protrusion that "locks" the motherboard to the backplate before you screw it in place. Fine. The standoffs in both of the cases I ordered were all precisely installed (something I've had issues with in Corsair cases in the past), and anodized black (you could remove them and install your own if you wished, but I didn't find it necessary). I used Cooler Master Hyper 212 Evo CPU coolers in both cases. No issues with clearance. If you use a large CPU cooler like this, you will not be able to install additional cooling fans on the top of the case. Not an issue for me. There's a front fan installed in the 400Q, but it's well above the 3.5" hard drive bay. Especially if you keep the shroud in place, this means you have no direct cooling over your hard drives. This wasn't an issue for me, since I already knew about this and installed another Noctua 120mm fan at the bottom. If you are planning on using spinning disk, you *must* relocate the fan or install a second fan, unless you like killing disks. The front of the case is a bit weird. It has a very nicely finished metal front with large plastic vents on the sides. The backing plate for the front is plastic and plugs into the rest of the case with large plastic clips. If you want to access the magnetically removable dust filter, you have to take both sides off and gently push in three plastic clips on both sides to remove the entire front before you can access the filter. Which...OK. For me, this is acceptable at the price point, and the clips all seem relatively robust. Overall, I'm very impressed with these cases. They look sleek, they have reasonable cable management and fan mount options, and the fan/dust filters are on par with much more expensive options. Recommended.

I have used Garmin Streetpilot C340 for about 2 months now. My decision came down to TomTom and this model. I could have easily gotten either one, I guess, since both items are highly recommended on various web sites. I wanted a GPS because I was driving to Washington D.C. (from central PA) for a 6-week training and I had never been to D.C. before. The unit was easy to use right out of the box. I read the quick reference sheet for less than 5 min and was ready to go. The map was very accurate and I had absoluately no problem driving around D.C.. It even knew which street was one way and led me to the correct turn. One small problem I had was that if I drive too fast on the city street, the voice warning maybe a bit too slow and I would had to make a quick turn at the last minute or missed the turn completely. Once I learned to pay attention both the monitor (it tells you the distance you have left before the next turn) and the voice, I had no more problem. Besides the unit recalculate a new route quite efficiently if I did miss a turn. The pre-loaded data, which are broken down into various categories (food, shopping, gas, parking, major attraction, etc) is very helpful, though not all business are listed, of course. But if I have a specific place to go, I just type in the exact address (which is relatively easy to do with the touch screen) and it leads me to the correct location without fail. I drove around D.C. and suburbs a lot and felt like I knew the city well. It is 100x better than trying to use a map and had to constantly look for street name/signs. Highly recommend for people who travel to unfamiliar cities often. I'll be going to San Fran next month to visit my brother, and can't wait to see what this thing can do. The only minor issues (basically two) i have with this are the same other reviewers mentioned already. 1) On the trip calculator, it displays the estimated arrival time only. I wish it also displays the distance left to the destination. 2) The power source does not plug into the unit itself directly, instead it only plugs into the supporting base. By the way, love the internal battery which allow me to use it outside of my car. The unit is small enough that I can carry it in my jacket pocket. A few times I used it as a map while walking around D.C.. It's kind of geeky, I know, but it got me where I needed to go.

I spent a great deal of time researching multi-channel receivers to replace my 10+ year old Denon AVR-3300, which still sounded as good as the day I bought it. However, it just wasn't up to delivering modern codecs and didn't have HDMI inputs. My requirements were: I wanted at least 6 HDMI inputs, analog multi-channel inputs to hook my SACD player to, and pre-outs to allow routing to an external amplifier in the future. I also wanted at least 100 watts into all speakers with low distortion and a receiver that sounded as good with music sources as with movies. I first considered some of the lower priced receivers, but quickly ruled them out due to quality control issues reported. They also didn't deliver the power I wanted to all speakers and even though they had a lot of functionality, I knew the wouldn't deliver the sound quality I wanted. This then made me look at higher priced receivers. I liked Yamaha, as I had a lower end receiver in the past that was very nice sounding. I was impressed with the features, build quality and positive reviews of the AVENTAGE line of receivers. At the time I was considering Yamaha receivers, their new X030 line was out. The biggest difference between the X020 and X030 line were the DACS being used and the price. I found I could purchase a 1020 for substantially less than the 1030. The power was the same and the DACS in the 1020 were Burr Brown vs. ESS Sabres. (I figured how could you go wrong with Burr Brown?) If anything, Yamaha chose the ESS DACS as they had similar specs for a lower unit cost. (That's my theory anyway) Sure - on paper it probably has better specs, but would the average Joe hear the difference? I highly doubt it - especially as good as DACS are these days - especially 192khz sample capable Burr Browns. I was tempted to pay a little more and get the 2020 model for the extra wattage and higher quality video upscaler chip, but in the end, I really didn't need anymore than 110 watts of power and would probably never use the upscaler as my PS3 and HD DVD player both do upscaling themselves. So I decided to save money an went with the 1020. (Knowing what I know today and the very small price difference - I would have chosen the 2020 if I had to do it over again) I'm just too lazy to disconnect everything, ship the 1020 back and then have to re-hook everything back up again. :) Nothing against the 1020 - I'm really happy with it and also saved a few bucks. It's highly doubtful whether you would notice the 30 watts difference between the two amplifiers anyway. The 2020 does offer 9.1 channels if you decide to go nuts with surround speakers later. Rather than do a total review here, I thought I would tell you where I got confused and frustrated and hopefully save you the same challenges if you decide to get this receiver. Here goes: YPAO, which automatically sets up your speaker distances, levels and equalization is both good and bad. I found I hated the sound of the equalization it set my speakers at. I chose "FLAT",(I didn't like "Front or "Natural any better) but at the end of many hours of fiddling with this thing, I ended up setting it to "Through" which effectively turns the equalization off. I just didn't like the compressed sound of how it set the equalization for my room. I did like how it set the distances and left it to do this task as it was very accurate. I also didn't like how it set the output levels of my speakers. I ended up using my Radio Shack SPL meter and set them manually. (75 SPL DB at an AVR output of 0 DB) This one really threw me for a loop. I have a nice Schiit Asgard Audio headphone amp which I use to drive my Sennheiser HD-650 headphones that I wanted to use through the receiver. So how to hook it up? At first I thought from the PRE-OUT Front R/L RCA outputs to the headphone amp. Wrong! Unless you have the speakers disconnected you won't get any output from the same pre-outs that you have speakers attached to. The manual didn't state this. I had to call Yamaha three times to figure this out. You can either connect it to zone 2 outputs and then turn on "Party" mode, or do as I did and connect it to the AV/Audio output jacks. The Pre-outs are only designed to ouput to an external amp. If you don't have four sets of surround back speakers make sure you choose "surrounds" not "back surrounds" It's easy to make this mistake. I did. At first I couldn't get an HDMI signal to my Panasonic Plasma TV no matter what I did. I finally disconnected all of the HDMI cables and pulled the power out of the receiver. I hooked them back up and then it worked. Go Figure. Not sure what the problem was there. (Something must have gotten corrupted in the initial HDMI handshake) I haven't had an issue since. Version 1.6 is the latest firmware for this receiver. It's best to update it by downloading to a USB drive and install it from that. You won't get Pandora and some other networking functions with older firmware. Just make sure your USB is formatted to FAT 16/32 and the Firmware file is the only thing on the USB drive. I initially had a hard time understanding how to use straight codecs like Dolby Digital without the sound effect programs. You simply choose "Straight" on the receiver. Make sure the device that is playing is set for "bitstream" output to the receiver, otherwise your receiver will just tell you it is receiving "PCM". That means your blue-ray player, etc. is doing the processing, not the receiver. I had this problem with my Playstation 3. It was setup to send bitsream out via an optical cable, not HDMI. Once I changed it to output "Bitstream" to HDMI the receiver started displaying the proper codecs. Pandora works great with this receiver. Pay the additional bucks for the yearly membership to get 192kb streams. The free version is only 128kb. (It also eliminates the commercials) Otherwise it won't sound very good. The DLNA service also works great. I was able to access my FLAC albums directly from the receiver to my media PC using Media Monkey software. I probably won't use this as I find it easier to manage my albums from my media PC to the receiver instead. Even so - it worked without a hitch. Network radio also works great - but most stations don't output very high bit streams. You can search on the internet on which stations have higher bitrates. It's very cool checking out many foreign stations. The receiver's strengths are in it's surround sound output. Movies with good sound tracks blew me away with this receiver. I watched Batman the Dark night on Blueray and it was stunning how good the sound was. The receiver displayed it's true capabilities with this soundtrack. The sounds were instantaneous, enveloping, powerful and incredibly accurate. Two channel Audio through this receivers DAC is just stunning with a good source - see update below. The bad. The manual is not very well written in my opinion. For example, not explaining how the pre-outs work and exactly what the YPAO is doing as an example. It just doesn't explain why certain things work the way they do. It is also delivered on a CD. I printed it out in order to explore it easier. Call me old fashioned, but I think Yamaha should include the paper manual for receivers in this price range and with this much functionality. I am also not a fan of the remote. You need a magnifying glass to see the labels on the tiny buttons. They are just crammed together too tightly. I didn't even know some functions existed until a Yamaha tech pointed them out to me. I still get confused as to where certain buttons are. It also isn't back-lit on this receiver in case you were wondering. You will definitely need a light when watching something in the dark. I should mention however, that there is a very cool app you can download for free that networks with the receiver from either and IOS or Android device. I used it on an Android device and it works extremely well. This is a nice concept that Yamaha developed and relieves some of the concerns with the poor remote. There is also an audio mode called "pure direct". Basically, it turns off of all the sound processing features and just sends the signal directly to the amp section. When I had the receiver using the "FLAT" equalization settings I really liked the pure direct setting with my audio but kept wondering why the "straight" mode sounded so bad. After I turned off the equalization from "Flat' to "Through" - it sounded just as good. I also turned off the Adaptive DRC function which automatically adjusts peak volumes at different sound levels. It sounded muddy to me. Just because this receiver has a lot of "bells and whistles" doesn't mean you should necessarily use them. In the end, experiment and change settings to what sounds best for you. I spent a lot of time reading the forums. They were very helpful and explained things I couldn't get from the manual. They tell you to set all your speakers to "small" if you have a subwoofer and for the most part they are correct. I have Boston Acoustic 975 monitors which have their own side firing subs and amplifiers. In my situation, setting the front speakers to "small" was the right decision as you can control the crossover frequency to the subwoofer this way. When the speakers are set to "large" there is no crossover setting to choose. Some people, who have front speakers capable of handling the full range of frequencies and a separate subwoofer might be better off setting the front speakers to "large" when listening to music. Do to the architecture of my speakers, it didn't make any difference - the bass was being sent to the side firing woofers regardless. Yamaha's support is very good, When I called I never waited more than about 5 minutes to get a real live person. Depending on who you talk to, however, you are likely to get different answers. (Some were unfortunately wrong or they didn't understand what I was trying to do) I recently contacted a Tech via e-mail support and he gave me the best advice of all. I ended up asking him several other questions via reply and he again quickly responded to me. So - techs will vary in experience and knowledge as usual. Overall, Yamaha's support was very professional and responsive. You can't say this of many vendors these days. Update: January 26 2014 I recently purchased an OPPO 103D to be able to play Blue Ray, DVD, SACD and DVD Audio discs. I'm feeding both SACD DSD streams and high resolution DVD Audio directly to the internal DACS of this receiver. Not only can this receiver handle al of these audio formats, (including direct DSD from SACD discs), but the audio quality is more than excellent, so much so that I retired my Cambridge audio DACMAGIC DAC from my audio system. The DACMAGIC is an excellent DAC, but in my opinion, the Yamaha's Burr Brown DACS are better. The more I use this receiver, the more impressed I am with it. There hasn't been anything I have fed it that it wasn't able to handle and with excellent results. If the new 1030 is any better sound wise I just can't imagine it. I'm glad I saved hundreds of dollars by buying this older model. If you are looking for a great receiver, save some money and pick this one up. You aren't giving up anything sound wise and the features are almost identical. Now that I am over the learning curve, I find every setting very easy to find and use. I also like the "Scene" modes that let you push a single button on the remote which then allows you to turn on the receiver, select the right input and sound settings you made for that particular mode. I just wish Yamaha would have included a Macro function to turn on other devices along with it. The remote does allow you to control other devices like your TV or DVD player from the remote, however, you can't input macro functions vial the "Scene" function. The remotes function of other devices are also very limited. (Turn on/off, volume, etc.) This is an excellent AVR and I highly recommend it. In my opinion, you should view a surround sound receiver as a long term investment and spend some money on it. After all, it is the heart of your entertainment system. This receiver is built like a tank and it is also aesthetically pleasing to look at and very well engineered. The front door allows access to most controls that you would use from the remote. You can also hook up external devices there like camcorders. I could go on for hours on everything this receiver can do. I'm sure 10 years from now it will be viewed as a dinosaur, due to technological changes - but I'm betting I can get 10+ years out of it just like my last Denon receiver. My Denon can still be used as an excellent audio receiver for another room and will eventually get relegated to just that. If you are looking for receiver with just about every feature you could wish for, great build quality, (note Yamaha feels confident enough to put a 3 year warranty on it) and great sound - this receiver will get the job done. I'm a big fan of Yamaha as a Company. They make great musical instruments and products. (I have one of their acoustic pianos and many synthesizers and digital keyboards as a musician) They understand how to build quality products and this receiver is a good example of this. My previous Denon receiver cost me a lot more money than this receiver and can't touch the capabilities. I call this a very good value. Money spent on the Yamaha AVENTAGE line is money well spent in my opinion. Update Dec 8 2013 I spent some more time tweaking this receiver - mainly the two channel audio portion. I was using a Cambridge Audio DAC Magic as my DAC from my PC which streams all my FLAC files. I know the DACMAGIC to be very good and have been very happy with it. I also know that the USB input supposedly has more jitter than the optical connection, (which is the way I have it connected.) So, I got to thinking, why not connect my PC via the HDMI input from my PC directly into the Receiver's DAC and see how it sounds? In doing this I heard a noticeable improvement in the sound quality. The depth, sound-stage, detail, and overall dynamics improved. I can attribute this to the excellent DAC in this receiver and the lack of jitter due to the direct digital input. I am running it in "Pure Direct" mode and have never heard my sprakers sound better. (Boston Acoustics 975's) I no longer feel this receiver has a "clinical" sound in listening to music since I switched connections. (I removed that from the original review) When you play a really good source through it it really shines. The FLAC album I auditioned was "The Tord Gustavsen Trio- Being There". This is one of the best recorded CD's I have ever heard. Maybe the new 1030 is even better with the new ESS DAC's but I just can't believe it can get much better than this. It's like splitting hairs. If I could I would rate this receiver a solid 5 stars for audio quality and features but would still deduct 1/2 a star for the not so good documentation and Yamaha not printing out the manual. Once again, I don't like the YPAO equalization. In my opinion the YPAO is really only good for speaker distance. I realize it may smooth out the sound when listening in less than optimal room acoustics but it just kills the audio detail when listening to music.

I was so excited to score this innovative TV! My intent was to put it up on my wall and use it as a computer monitor in my office, watch some Netflix programming and have some cool wall art when I'm away. The box arrived and my excitement was furthered. It was a slim box and everything packed nice and neat! As I unboxed it my confusion grew a little bit. Instead of a standard power cable with various video ports in the TV itself, this thing is complicated with a control box. I suppose it could be to simplify the wall art idea (i.e. 1 fewer cable coming out of it maybe?) But in pursuit of this engineering miracle, the brilliance of Samsung introduced unnecessary complexity - there's a giant cable that must be connected from the TV into the control box. Your power and HDMI, etc. then plug into it thus adding an additional connection point that could fail. Anyways my somewhat complicated setup was complete! I installed the batteries into the oddly shaped remote control Then, with my excitement reaching a crescendo that could only culminate in the beautiful "SAMSUNG" blue and white image splashed on the screen that I so eagerly anticipated, all that remained was the simple, final push of the power button. With a measured flick of my right thumb, this newfound pleasure would be mine! AND..... Nothing. A little red light flashed on the remote. "Hmm" I thought. I flicked again. Nothing. After a third flick brought no change I checked all the connections, un-doing and re-doing in the overly specific and risky order that apparently is required of such an amazing engineering marvel. I plugged and unplugged the power. Flick. Nothing. Being a veteran of years of PC support, I seemlessly and ever so carefully moved the unit to another power outlet. Triple checked the connections. Flick. Nothing. DOA. Patience worn thin, frothy anticipation turned completely flat like a 3-day old beer, I packed up the unit and sent it back never to buy one of these again. Turns out my experience was like that of the 1995 film "Waterworld". Couldn't wait to see it, couldn't have been more disappointed once I did (in fairness the movie projector actually worked at the theater and at least I did see Waterworld, but still...). Sometimes even Samsung, the Kevin Costner of electronics can't thrill you. Save your money. This thing is probably cool when it works. That is, if you can ever power it on.

My rack arrived missing more than half the pieces, including several of the large and heavy pieces. Literally all of the small pieces were gone. The packaging is flawed in its design in that it clearly relies on the carrier never tipping it towards its side at all, which every carrier does all the time, in spite of the tiny sticker on the box that requests them not to. The context to understand this is that while I've had plenty of boxes arrive in questionable condition, and have even had much heavier boxes delivered by Amazon (hello, treadmill!), this is the first box I have ever, in 10 years of such deliveries, had missing or damaged items that were clearly due to problems in transit. To understand how much of a failure the packaging truly is, one must understand that this is not a true box, at least not as it arrived at my residence. What arrived were a bunch of metal pieces that had been laid on a piece of cardboard that was essentially "rolled" into a square and zip tied to keep it from coming apart. This part was actually effective and the cardboard seems to be of an appropriate strength, as is the tape, zip tie, etc. However, the ends were only taped over, and that only partially. There were, to be clear, very large holes on both ends of my package that appear to be by design. The rack pieces that have arrived are in great shape! They feel sturdy and I have no doubt will serve me well once the rest of the rack arrives. However, today, I feel let down by the entire supply chain that led to this scenario, as I am hardly unique. Amazon, as the seller, failed to adequately package the material before it left the warehouse. The carrier mishandled the package by disregarding the instructions on it to not tilt the package. StarTech (the manufacturer) created a terrible, awful design for their packaging that should never have been approved. I know 7 year olds that would design sturdier boxes. This whole experience has been an exercise in frustration that I hope no one else has to experience, so I am rating this 1 star.

Out-of-the-box the case has a clean monolithic appearance. Opening it left me a bit disappointed. The internal layout is similar to other mid-tower computer cases. Power supply sits on the bottom with ventilation below it. Ventilation on the left side includes a large fan. Two ventilation ports on the top allow for 240mm radiator/2 x 140mmfans. Some Pros and Cons: +The ventilation ports have good airflow. Front and bottom ports have filters. -The fans run quite noisy, even at low-speed. I replaced some of the stock fans with Thermalright 140mm and Noctua 120mm units. +The matte paint has a textured finish and resists fingerprints. -The paint scratches easily. +Removable hard drive cages allow for long expansion cards or mounting radiators in the lower front. +Lots of black screws, uniquely shaped for different functions (case, hard drive, fan, etc.) -The sheetmetal is quite thin and flexes easily. -The faceplate did not align properly during reassembly. The friction pins loosen up and result in a small gap between the faceplate and chassis. Closing Remarks: The case has good cooling for air or water cooling setups, but also results in bad acoustics. **Not directed solely at Corsair, but I wish case manufacturers would include a bay to mount a slimline optical drive. I'll try to keep this as short as possible. I bought this camera a month ago directly from the Kodak online store. Upon arrival, the camera displayed noticeable vertical lines in all of the modes except 1080p. These vertical lines appeared both on the external LCD display as well as when the files were transferred to a computer. I tried three different SDHC cards (all class 6), and upgrading the firmware. No dice. Additionally, the internal microphone had that high pitched whine sound that has been mentioned a lot (contrary to what many say, the firmware did NOTHING to fix this problem, at least for me). I called Kodak's tech support, and they told me the camera would need to be sent in for repairs, covered under warranty. I had to pay $20 non-reimbursed shipping to send it off, but I did anyway. The facility, an outsourced repair center called Precision Camera and Video Repair had the camera for about three weeks. They claimed they replaced the main CPU and power circuit. I received the camera yesterday, exactly one month after I initially received it, and the same exact problems persist. Once again, I tried different cards and upgraded firmware. No help whatsoever. Additionally, the repair facility scratched the external screen up pretty good, something that was NOT there when I sent it in. So I called tech support again, and said I want a new camera. They said they can't do that, and that I would need to send it back...to the SAME repair facility, and spending my OWN shipping costs again. I said that was unacceptable, and they transferred me to store customer service. They said that they could not replace the camera since it had been repaired...something that tech support assured me would fix the problem. I was livid at this point, and demanded a supervisor. After re-explaining the situation for what seemed to be the 50th time, she supervisor told me that she would need to get authorization from upper management, and that she would give me a call back tomorrow (today...still no call, but it's early). She said if they approved it, I would get an email with a shipping label and to send the camera back. Once they receive the camera, I will be refunded, and can reorder a new camera. I will be refunded my initial shipping costs, but not the cost I paid to send it in for repair. So not only am I a month into this, with no working camera, but I spent an hour on the phone, with no ultimate resolution...yet. Here's the moral of the story. First, don't send it in for repair, demand a new camera. Second, go through Amazon, and avoid Kodak's customer service at all cost. Third, don't buy this camera. The 1080p mode is nigh-useless (it zooms the frame in, narrowing the viewing angle and shooting width, thereby giving you a clearer picture...but much smaller and more narrow), the internal mic is garbage, and more likely than not, you're going to have a sensor problem (look in the forum below or google "Zi8 vertical lines." You'll see many people with the same problem I had) that isnt going to get fixed for you. I dont mind buying an SD card, but when you factor in an external mic, tripod (the electronic image stabilization is also useless), and the headache of actually getting a working product, you're going to spend upwards of $300 and have a heart attack. At this point, I will be taking my refund and running. I will never buy a Kodak product again. You send me a defective product, make me pay for the return costs for repair, DO NOT REPAIR THE ISSUE, and then try to tell me that I cant exchange it or get a refund...even though it's covered in the money-back warranty? I don't think so. Never again. All that potential, and this camera is a cheaply made bust. I think I'm going to take my money, buy off Amazon, and get the Flip MinoHD 2nd Generation. I have an Ultra HD and it's great, but bulky. Only would like a mino for the portability. I would have loved for the Zi8 to work. External mic, expandable storage, 7209/60fps (this was the feature I was most jazzed about since it offers a much smoother video in "action" shots. Too bad this was the very thing that was defective...twice), thin, sleek design, large screen...almost the perfect camcorder. But as it stands, the issues with this camera far outweigh the benefits. I would prefer something more versatile than the Flip line of cameras, but it's looking like thats a pipe-dream at this point. Thanks for reading. The short version: In a ten-minute test at 100 percent CPU load, core temps never exceeded 54C. The slightly longer version: Intel Core i9 processor Gigabyte Z390 M Gaming motherboard Thermaltake Core V21 case Noctua NF-P14s redux-1500 PWM rear cabinet fan Win10Pro I was actually a bit skeptical about the ability of a 120mm fan to cool the i9, but the dual fans, copper base, and fairly massive fins kept the core temperature to 54 degrees C at 100 percent utilization on all 16 logical processors. Of course, the V21 case has a massive front intake fan, the added Noctua NF-P14s rear cabinet fan (blowing out) insured plenty of airflow across the CPU cooler, and I wasn't overclocking; but still, 54C is pretty decent, especially for a 120mm fan. The sound level is not quite silent, but not excessively loud at any speed. Unless you're one of those who can't handle any fan noise at all, I don't think you'll be unhappy. Overall build quality is excellent, and the installation was as easy as one can expect from a large air cooler. You have to install the backing plate, the standoffs (make sure you use the right ones -- they're different for different sockets), and the mounting bracket. That takes maybe five minutes. Next you apply the heat sink compound (which is included), press the cooler straight down onto the mounting bracket, and tighten two screws, a few turn at a time. The screwdriver is also included. Finally, reattach the fans to the fins with the airflow in the same direction as what's already going on in the case (typically front-to-rear). All in all, I'm pleasantly surprised. This "little" cooler does a great job of cooling my hot CPU.

All the bits that you touch are well-made. It’s a nice form factor. It’ll probably survive lots of car camping. If you’re looking for playback controls - forward, back, play/pause - look elsewhere. (Why not add three buttons?) The Bluetooth connection buttons are baffling, but, hey, that’s the exciting new world of Bluetooth connectivity for you. But - this took me a while to figure out - it’s got an internal power supply instead of a wall wart. 120V AC to 12V DC converter circuits are NOISY by nature and can bleed over the 60Hz hum in our mains supply in to the audio amplifier circuits, especially if they’re not well engineered. In that regard, this is not a well engineered product. I have to silence my phone when I’ve got the BT connection active and nothing playing, because the key clicks make the amplifier circuit fire up and whine in the background until the unit detects it’s been quiet for a few seconds and shuts it off again. It’s not LOUD, but it’s easily in hearing range, and I don’t have great hearing due to loud concerts and the occasional power tool use without ear protection. It’s unacceptably loud, though. How many pennies did they save on components to put in a cheap internal power supply? For a three hundred dollar speaker? If it wasn’t for the whine-hum, I could overlook the other annoyance that in most situations, I have to go into my Bluetooth settings to connect to the speaker. In comparison to my only other BT speaker, a JBL Charge 3, the Kilburn here is a little louder (yay!), sound quality is about the same - a different color, but by and large the same (at least, until my charge developed a slight bass rattle). Keep looking, though. As a gift it’s not bad. But it’s not worth the price tag.

For the first time ever, I upgraded from a 27 inch monitor to a... 27 inch monitor. I decided to go for an IPS panel with at least a 144hz refresh rate and <2ms response time, and this one fit the bill. Plus, it's made by Gigabyte, one of my favorite component manufacturers. I opted for a 1080p set, which to me looks perfectly crisp at the distance I sit from my monitor. The installation took me much longer than expected, which brings me to the first small issue - even though the monitor is VESA-mount compatible, with a standard 100x100 pattern, the mounting holes are recessed in the back. This meant that the M4 screws from my existing universal wall mount were too short (by about a half inch) to work, even though they worked perfectly with my previous monitor. I scrounged around my tool box, odds and ends drawer, and cable bag and lucked out by finding one the perfect length and diameter to lock the tilt, and three that were too long, but still worked as support screws. Once the mounting was done, I connected it to my nvidia 1060 card via HDMI cable, booted the computer up, and crossed my fingers. To my surprise windows correctly identified the monitor, and I was up and running in no time. I had no luck getting G-SYNC to work over HDMI, so I switched to the included Display Port cable, and it worked like a charm. Knock on wood, no dead or stuck pixels! I did a little adjusting of the image (mainly lowering the brightness and switching to a different gamma setting), but I was impressed with the image quality out of the box, to be honest. Great colors, more than bright enough, and no ghosting. The only issue with the quality is light bleed - it's noticeable on the left side of the screen during very dark scenes/transitions (not uncommon with IPS panels), but not enough to make it lose more than half a star. I was also impressed with the included cables - HDMI, DP, USB, and an alternate power cable. I would highly recommend plugging the USB cable in even if you don't use the built-in hub - it lets you run OSD sidekick (Google it to download it from Gigabyte), meaning you can control the monitor's features and settings via mouse + keyboard, using the OSD program. You can even set up hotkeys for various features, so you don't have to fiddle around the back of the monitor to mess with the joystick control. So far I am very happy with my first Gigabyte monitor, and it's an easy recommendation if you plan to stick around in 1080p land for a while longer.

First off, I have to say that this is a stunning design. I build speakers myself at home and I picked this up to get some design ideas myself. I love the passive radiators they use on this thing! But overall, I was looking forward to testing it out for myself as I had heard great things about this unit and I'd love to have a great sounding portable speaker. Modeled after the Sony SRS X77 and tuned much better in my opinion, picking this up for $89 was a no-brainer and I tip my hat to DOSS for adopting this design. But... It's not quite there yet. The DOSS Soundbox XL suffers greatly from the enclosure not being totally deadened and dampened against the vibrations of the sub-woofer. The passive radiators in place will do their job thoroughly if the box was to be sealed better and deadened completely. Again, This is a great design, It's just executed somewhat cheaply. These currently available units are not deadened enough stop the buzzing fart noises from the ports in the back and the enclosure as a whole. The grill on these models now seem to have additional dampening to address some original complaints about grill vibrations. My units did not have grill vibrations or rattles. In my testing of this speaker, I decided to actually purchase two units and I've now sadly returned them both. I originally listened to Oluv's YouTube videos on this unit and when compared to other units I thought this was a good choice for my intended application. But they definitely suffered from the same issues you hear about in some of the written reviews as well as in Oluv's commentary. The first one arrived and sounded fine in the beginning. With only the loudest techno tracks being played at max volume causing this buzz like fart that you hear about. This began to get worse though over the course of the past few days and as I listened today, it seems like the Soundbox XL wants to literally vibrate itself apart. The buzzing from the back became very noticeable especially with the unit against a wall. It was not like this when I began using it and that was why I picked up the second unit. I really liked it at first. The second unit I bought though was much louder overall. It also had a much more distorted sound at lower volumes. It also buzzed a lot more from the back ports than the first unit. It also had a noticeably louder Bluetooth hum. I had two very different offerings of the same item. Still, with the second unit purchased, the left driver hissed loudly with a static like harshness when playing music and videos. The right driver operated closer to normal but was muted and less clear. This particular unit was obviously internally setup just a little differently than the first one I bought and the little 2 inch main drivers were possibly improperly sealed within their isolated enclosures. I boxed it up pretty quickly for a return as the sound was just unacceptable. I boxed the first unit up today for a return as well. If DOSS would dampen and deaden the enclosure better to eliminate the vibration issues, double down with some back plane absorption material, seal and deaden that back port better, pay stricter attention during the process in which they lay the foam seals around the drivers, specifically the sub-woofer. Then and only then will the Soundbox XL be a winner. Especially when the overall intended sound stage and presentation is easily on par or better than other portable units costing hundreds of dollars more. They should also probably use lock-tight on their screws too. Honestly, the normal listener might be OK with the shortcomings of this portable speaker. They may not even notice. But as stated, I build high-end bookshelf and tower speakers and based on my own 35 years worth of experience. I would stay away from this portable speaker until DOSS specifically addresses the issues that their production practices have introduced to the unit that should not be present. I was truly excited about it and I still want one. It could be the best in class! It looks amazing and if built just a bit better, it would surely be the one to beat... But in the long run, in its current state, I am a bit disappointed.

It's been about two months since I've had this laptop and I feel like I've had enough time learning and reviewing it so heres my review: Pros: - i7-7700 HQ Quadcore CPU up to 3.8ghz - Nvidia 1050ti with 4GB DDR5 - Both an SSD and HDD (Although you can always add these yourselves, it was nice to have come with both) - Cooling system is one of the best Ive seen so far (Includes an Ultra-Boost button to give you extra cooling, but never needed to use it.) - Fan disperses air away from the back screen of the laptop, rather than the side of the keyboard. (I prefer this design better) - Red Backlit keyboard (Color cant be changed, but I wasnt specifically looking for a flashy laptop so this is just a plus) - Overall Matte Black texture around the laptop with pleasing MSI dragon logo on the back screen. - AntiGlare Screen - Num. Pad keyboard - Comes with 1 year manufacturer warranty(US) (You'll have to activate it online yourself.) Cons: - Although aesthetically pleasing, the Matte Black Plastic Finish is a FINGERPRINT/OIL magnet and takes more than just a dry cloth to remove - 8GB RAM (I intend to add on another 8GB stick in the nearby future) - Battery life is ridiculous when playing games - Fans are REALLY loud when playing games (Not much of a problem if you wear headphones, and is expected as it does a splendid job keeping the laptop cool) - Speakers are subpar (Again, not much of a problem if you wear headphones) Overall, I was in the market specifically for a laptop that had a good CPU/GPU, and both an SSD and HDD. I stumbled upon many competitor laptops along the same price range however, some were missing an SSD or HDD, or had the regular 1050 GPU which comes with only half (2GB) of dedicated memory of what the Ti model has (4GB). If I had purchased those laptops instead, and added on a separate SSD OR HDD, the total cost spent would be above $1000. The laptop is surprisingly light for a gaming laptop, and comes in a sleek yet aggressive theme, which wasn't what I was in the market for but is a plus to me. Most people who game on laptops would know that you get better frames while plugged in to the charger (This is due to bottlenecking of either the CPU or GPU demanding more power, yet the battery cannot provide that power alone), so the low gaming battery life is not much of a problem considering you should be plugged in to get the best performance, and the battery life outside of gaming is average (4-6 hours) depending on what work you'll be doing. Ultimately, the laptop met more than my needs and was in my price range ($899, $960~ after taxes), and I expect to be using it throughout and well after the years of college.

OK so I bought an Amazon Recast on Prime Day for $100 off, and on the whole, am very glad I did! I must say, I really do like the way it integrates live TV into the Amazon Fire ecosystem of Fire sticks, TV cube, & Fire TV boxes of varied generations that I own and have deployed on the 7 different TVs I have in my household. As you may be able to tell from my headline, I am a long time cordcutter, who has never been entirely satisfied with my DVR hardware & software setup for streaming and OTA TV recording and viewing. I am still not satisfied, but what I do have today, thanks in part to the Recast, is pretty darned good. You see, i have tinkered with Tivo, and HDHomerun from the earliest of days, using PC software and external, or internal hard drives for storage. This pre-dates cell phones, "apps" and any fire tv hardware device or software app. Tivo software remains the gold standard for it's channel guide and recording capabilities; as well as season passes, it's wonderful remote, and lack of UI clutter. With Amazon it's ads, ads, ads and what else can you sell me next, but I digress. I am a pseudo slave to the Amazon ecosystem as a Prime member, but there are viable alternatives. i must say the AirTV by Sling does a reasonably good job of integrating its channel guide with OTA & your subscribed package for Sling, if you have one. The drawback may be no internal hard drive, but you can easily get the max 2tb for an additional $50 making it very competitive with the Recast. It also does a better job of organizing your recorded content by season. With Recast you only have tiles in no particular order, with no way to sort, so you must scroll until you find the episode or season you want. What is nice about Recast is it purportedly would support an external 10TB hard drive at this point, so that's much more than AirTV hardware I currently have, and its easy to skip 30 seconds forward with a single click, like a Tivo which is not easy to do with AirTV and Sling. The reason I personally deploy both AirTV from Sling with Recast is to increase my tuners. I also have my Tivo so potentially 5 tuners streaming or recording OTA channels concurrently on 5 different Tv sets is now possible with my current setup, thanks to the distribution amplifier that runs from my OTA antenna to Recast, AirTV, and Tivo. Unfortunately my 1st generation HDHomerun is like a first generation firestick, not capable enough or suitable for todays HD OTA viwing needs, so it has been fully retired. I am looking forward to further evolution in the DVR market, and hope Amazon developers will be reading this review.

It appears the makers of Goovis will now be furnishing timely upgrades as they become available so here's hoping this product will become even better. I received an email from my ISP (Cox) stating they'd upgraded my connection from 150mbps to 200mbps. As a heavy internet user (average of around 2,000GB transfer per month), I was pretty excited. In order to make use of these speeds, though, I needed a new modem. My current one was already DOCSIS 3.0, but with only 4/4 downstreams/upstreams. I decided to purchase this unit as my solution, as it has 16 channels down. Using identical speedtest servers, I compared the old modem and new modem. I observed that pings and upload speeds did not really change, as expected. The download speeds definitely saw an increase going from about 107mbps on the old modem, to 177mbps on the new modem. Definitely substantial. For those without much experience with network transfer speeds, "mbps" stands for megabits per second. This is the measurement used in speedtests and advertised by ISPs. Your browser measures download speeds in bytes, you'll see things like MB/s (megabytes per second). They are different, but related, measurements, so be careful not to mix them up. There are 8 bits in a byte, so to compare the two, you'll either have to multiply your BYTES measurement by 8, or divide your BITS measurement by 8. In this case, 177mbps (megabits per second) translates to 22.125 MB/s (megabytes per second). I have indeed managed to download certain files at 20MB/s after this upgrade, but you'll often be limited by the server which you're connected to rather than your download speed when it comes to things like http (your typical web) downloads. --- The rest of this review below is preserved for the sake of history, but no longer relevant. See the EDIT at the end for more details --- Now, here's where the big con comes in... It seems that this modem is not properly cooled. Regardless of the speedtest server, or speedtest type/provider, it appears that this modem begins throttling after sustained high speeds. Speedtest, for example, and with a good local server, will hit a peak of 195mbps pretty consistently, but after the test has been running for a while, it'll begin dropping about 3mbps every second. This is how I end up with 177mbps instead of sustaining the 195mbps. I've checked the Cox Cable's policies and they state that they do not shape or throttle their connections, so I'm fairly certain this is a heat issue with the modem, and it's resultant throttling or performance degradation due to the heat. I have not contacted Netgear yet, but may do so in the case that I received a faulty unit. If that turns out to be the case, I will update this review accordingly. EDIT: Netgear responded in a comment below, and I got in contact with them over email. One of their recommendations was to contact my ISP to ensure everything was set up correctly and I initially brushed it off, figuring it was all fine, but still called to hold up my part of the deal. It turns out that Cox Communications had forgotten to update my internet package code in their system when they did automatic network speed updates, so I was running off of the previous 150mbps plan with BOOSTS up to 200mbps. The following slow drop in performance was the boost slowly going down to the normal 150mbps speed. Once Cox updated the codes, everything run much more quickly and even though my speeds are rated for 200mbps, I'm seeing 300-350mbps download and 30-40mbps upload. Much, much better. I can confidently say this was a great upgrade now!

I am very pleased with the TIVO Bolt. I happy to be able to use just one set top box for access to everything I watch on TV. I was able to cut the cord from Direct TV and still be able to record my favorite major network shows such as Survivor. Once the unit is fully functional everything is great. However, some of the menu functions took 24 hours to become operational. There is a message during setup that there may be a delay of 24 hours before the unit is fully functional. The device would still record programs after initial activation, but it would display very little information able what you are recording. Once the 24 hours passed, everything on the Bolt worked perfectly. If you are planning on cutting the cord, the TIVO bolt is the device to buy. It can be used with cable or just an antenna. I am using it with only an antenna. You have to check with your local cable company to find out if they will support a TIVO device. I found out the Charter will no longer support TIVO. In order for the device to work with cable TV, your cable company must give you a special card that inserts into the TIVO. If you cannot get this card from your cable company, the device will not work with cable. The Bolt comes with all the major streaming TV apps such as Netflix, Hulu, and many more. So you can switch to streaming and back to live TV anytime. Your Bolt can record live TV while you are watching Netflix or other streaming apps. I looked at several other choices for the TIVO, and found the bolt is the most cost effective. The other TIVO models cost much more. The TIVO Bolt is on Amazon at $ 155 and $ 199 on the official TIVO website for the 500 gig model (white). You must purchase the $ 15 monthly subscription to have complete functionality of the device, although recording live TV is still possible without a subscription. Of course, all you could do is push record when you actually see the show on TV in real time. Recording a future show would be almost impossible with out the TIVO show information you get with the subscription. Finally, I would have to say that I am exceptionally pleased with the TIVO Bolt. It does everything I needed to cut the cord from satellite TV and still have plenty of TV to watch when I am ready. This TIVO Bolt is saving me $ 81 a month after leaving Direct TV. I highly recommend it to everyone looking to cut the cord. It is worth every penny.

This gets amazingly close to their state-of-the-art LS50 powered system which is probably the best small amplified speaker system ever made – but at $2K, the LS50 has a price to match, while the LSX has about 95% of its big brother's DNA for only 50% of its price. Relative to its bigger brother, the LSX shows only a modest reduction in built-in amplifier power (and probably something like ~3 db in terms of max volume levels), with somewhat less reach into the lower bass fundamentals below 60 Hz, and a bit less cabinet volume, but with a more streamlined and more pleasantly styled cabinet in the LSX. The LSX system realistically does not have much bass below ~50 Hz but, mitigating this, its midbass is excellent and very articulate, making it very easy to follow any bass line or instrument in your music selection. Speaking of selection, it appears that almost all the negative reviews around this system relate to difficulty people have with either connecting it to streaming or some other aspect of its streaming software – not with the audio quality of the speakers – which are simply phenomenal. I think you'd be hard-pressed to find small pair of speakers that sound as good, and outside of KEF's own LS50 systems (powered or otherwise), in my opinion, there isn't one. It's not perfect however, and I would dock KEF for their failure to duplicate at least the basics of the control architecture of the remote on the back panel of the master speaker – this leaves you with an inability to turn the system out of its suspended or sleep mode without the remote control. If you lose your remote control or it becomes inoperative (which is going to happen to more than a few users, given how often this system is likely to be placed outdoors on patios and lanais and thereby potentially exposed to moisture at least accidentally), you cannot either turn the system on from suspend, or adjust volume, except through your Bluetooth source. Re-initializing the system by unplugging it still brings the system up in a suspended mode. We may attempt to secure a second remote control from KEF. Also one has to admit to the somewhat buggy nature of some of their apps. However, since we drive the speakers exclusively from a Bluetooth source streaming lossless files, potentially buggy interactions with streaming software are a nonissue. Pros: 1) Superb tonal balance and neutrality, including remarkable fidelity on vocal material, consistent with virtually all of KEF's recent high-end designs 2) excellent bass, given small cabinet size and one half cost of state-of-the-art LS 50 powered system 3) with decent subwoofer the LSX becomes relatively inexpensive full range system with very small footprint 4) attractive range of colors to match room interiors (plus the white color no longer contains a hideous copper driver seen in LS 50) Cons: 1) you're SOL if you lose the remote or it becomes nonfunctional 2) Streaming app can be a chore to get operating properly 3) not much else to complain about In summary, it's a nearly perfect small compact system for small to medium-size rooms and spaces, it will play decently loud, and it is an exceptionally faithful and accurate transducer. If you've got a high quality source, it can approach a state-of-the-art system for way less than state-of-the-art money, especially with the addition of a decent subwoofer.
