History I own and am happy with the the 1st gen Echo. It serves my life nicely in our kitchen for measurement conversions, timers, weather reports, and the occasional family dance parties when eating snacks and deserts. I was compelled to add more Echo devices to my 2017 Christmas list after Amazon announced drop-in calling and multi-room music features. I previously used Apple's Airport Expresses to create a multi-room music experience and the idea of using my voice to control my music in multiple rooms was a hard one to pass up. Pros + Better sounds than Echo gen 1 (as of latest update - post Christmas 2017) + Smaller form factory, color, and style (I got the gray fabric) makes it a better looking device than the 1st gen, especially as a stand alone shelf unit (versus sitting next to your other black plastic electronics) + It performs most of its advertised features pretty well + Multi-room music works great with Amazon Unlimited and/or Spotify Neutral * Sound as a whole is comparable to most mid-range price bluetooth speakers. You can't really compare it to a Sony or Bose, but then again you pay a price for that quality. Sound is pretty much what I expected (maybe even a bit better) for their 80-120 price point * Sometimes the Echo doesn't respond when I call for Alexa, other times she responds without being prompted. Since this is new-ish technology I give it a pass here as it's features far out-way the occasional hiccup. Cons (mostly with new added features, could be improved based on updates or Amazon offerings) - 1st gen and Echo Plus offer the ability to change volume with a large dial built-in to the top of the speaker. This version only has plus or volume buttons (similar to Echo Dot). The large dial is far superior to the buttons, in both speed and ease of use when changing volume - Intercom or Drop-on Feature is not that great When speaking between devices on the same network there is some delay (for today's standard anyway) and on nearly every call whole words or sentences don't get picked up, prompting you to miss some of the conversation. The quality is similar to my cheap IP camera's intercom feature that I use in my kid's room. - Multi-Room Music and Amazon's music upload feature (or lack thereof) do not allow you (any more anyway) to stream your personal music library natively through their Echo ecosystem. (Read more below why this feature changed my mind about owning multiple Echo products) Why Multiple Echos won't work for me... I don't rely on any one streaming music service as my only go-to home music choice, I enjoy a variety of artists that may or may not be on certain services. When I added multiple Echos to my Christmas list I was counting on taking advantage of Echo's new multi-room music feature along with Amazon's music upload service to play music from my personal library throughout my house. Amazon's music upload service allowed you to upload 250 free songs or thousands of songs for 25 a year. Unfortunately I didn't do proper research and found out that Amazon had just recently shut down this service (12/2017) which is the only way to play your music through their ecosystem. While you can use skills such as "Plex" or "My Media" to play your library on one speaker, only Amazon Music and Spotify currently support multi-room music. I am disappointed that Amazon took this service away right after adding multi-room support. Both Apple and Google offer upload features and if I would had realized this before the Christmas season I would have a Google Home and Google Home Mini under my tree instead. Google's Home devices offer most of the same features, cost the same, and Googles allows you to upload up to 50,000 free songs from your personal collection to Google Play. Conclusion The Echo 2nd gen works as advertised and most people will probably appreciate everything Echo has to offer for the price, especially if you are an Amazon Unlimited or Spotify heavy user. However, if you are looking to play your personal library on multiple speakers, this is no longer an option for you.

To detect & play MP3 files in the overall order you wish, see below (after review) for a method I found to do an alpha-numeric sort of your MP3 tracks for playing on this type of player. Always appreciate feedback ... If you find this review helpful, please feel free to give it a quick 'Yes'. Thanks. Additional items required in order to use this MP3 player (not included): 1) Micro SD card (up to 32GB, FAT32 formatted) to store MP3/song files. Player does not come with any internal storage memory. A micro SD card-reader is also recommended (for adding/editing .mp3 files), since the MP3 Player gives an unreliable computer connection. 2) USB 2.0 cable with Mini Type-B 5-position plug (called 'Mini-B' or 'USB-Mini5B') to charge player (similar to https://smile.amazon.com/C2G-Cables-Go-27329-Mini-B/dp/B00006B6PH ). The USB cable needs to be plugged into a computer or standard 5V USB charger for player to charge. 3) Earbuds or external speakers (standard 3.5mm stereo plug). Player has no built-in speakers. 4) And of course your own collection of MP3 files to play (no tunes are pre-installed on this player). Player PROs: - Received my Mini Perman MP3 player in about 2-weeks. Faster than the month estimated. - Very basic MP3 player that is compact and lightweight. About 2" x 1" x 1/2", and weighs next to nothing. - Player detected all 1,548 MP3 files I had on the SD card. Including those buried deep inside a series of folders. Did take a short time to accomplish this detection before being able to play tracks for the first time. Have had the occasional annoying 'No File' indicator when starting or switching tracks (usually need to restart player &/or reinsert SD card). I did run a file/volume error-check on the SD card and defragmented the files to encourage smooth sailing. - My 320kbps MP3 files play fine with good stereo sound. Player volume goes up to 30 ... I use 05 - 15 for comfortable listening through my earbuds. - Player remembers last MP3 track number played when turning OFF. However, may start back at the first track (0001) if MP3 collection on the SD card is changed (added to, renamed, re-arranged, etc). - System menu has a 'backlight' function to set how long display backlight stays lit (after last button is pushed). Set to 00 to have display light always on (uses battery much more quickly). Set from 05 - 60 seconds to leave display on for that many seconds after last button was pushed. First press of any button turns on backlight. Display also has a 'contrast' function to set display appearance (00 - 16). High contrast display is surprisingly easy to see in bright sunlight (more difficult in low sunlight). Backlight is needed to see display indoors or at low light levels. I've found a Backlight setting of 10 seconds, and Contrast of 16 (full) to work well. Player CONs: - No instructions. Use is pretty basic, so not a big deal. - Play time of the battery is fairly short. With minimal display backlight time and a volume of around 10 (of 30), I can listen to my 320kbps MP3 tunes for only up to 2.5 hours (around 3 albums). Full-charge time is then in the neighborhood of 2 hours. The player charge indicator is pretty useless. Still indicates 3/4 full when empty, also indicates full long before actually being fully charged. - No track sort, shuffle, or scan features. Starts playing at track 0001 (or wherever you last left off), and can only move/skip forward or backward 1 button-click at a time. Doesn't even have a button hold-down feature for fast-skipping of multiple tracks. Kind of a pain if you want to get from track 0005 to track 0500. Skipping forward is definitely quicker than skipping backward. Does allow going around the corner (... 0002, 0001, 1548, 1547 ...) in either direction. - Player puts tracks in the order that the folder/file was added to the unseen FAT32 directory-system of the SD card (this took me a while to figure out). Has nothing to do with the date the folder/file was created/modified, but has more to do with the order in which they were added to the SD card. See below for the best way I found to rearrange/sort this directory-system so tracks are played in the order you desire. - Equalizer is limited to 3 settings: Natural, Pop, and Rock. IMO, Natural is the only setting worth listening to. Both Pop & Rock sound muffled even at higher volumes. - Can not play MP3 files while player is charging. Can charge with player power turned OFF or ON. Can access the SD card if player is turned ON and connected to the USB of a computer (shows up like a card-reader on the computer). However, I find the connection unreliable so instead I use an actual SD card-reader when editing the MP3 content. - Display is very tiny. No track titles show up ... just shows a line of asterisks with .mp3 at end (like in the product images). The number of asterisks (up to 12) change depending on the length of the MP3 file name, but if there is a way to get actual track names to show on this player I have yet to figure out how. Opinion: It's a cheap little $4 ($2 + S/H) bare-bones player that does it's basic job of playing MP3 music. With a play-time just over 2 hours, a light-weight player for taking on a walk or listening to over a lunch-break. Giving it 3-stars as an inexpensive way to listen to some tunes if you already have the extra required items laying around (SD card, charge cable, etc). Might've given it 4-stars if not for the occasional 'No File' connectivity issue, or if it allowed fast-skipping by just holding down either skip button, or the track names actually showed up, or updates were available online for the ht2836 v1.0 firmware to address some of these issues. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Hope this file sort method helps other bare-bones MP3-player owners to get their tunes sorted out. If so, please feel free to give this review an always appreciated 'Yes' &/or maybe a quick comment below. Thanks. Note: This MP3 Player puts tracks in the order that each folder/file was added to the unseen FAT/FAT32 directory-system of the SD card. Free software is available to quickly sort these system entries to get things in alpha-numeric order. To sort the .MP3 files on the SD card, for playing tunes in your desired order on this type of MP3 player: Step 1 - Download/unzip (or install) a free FAT directory-system sorter like Anerty’s Lair - DriveSort (for Windows) to perform the sort. Note: FAT sorters usually will not work with other drive formats (e.g. NTSF). Step 2 Arrange folders and MP3 files in the alpha-numeric order you want - Connect your SD card (containing the MP3 collection) to your computer. I suggest using an SD card-reader, since the USB connection of the MP3 player tends to be unreliable. - Edit any folder &/or file names (e.g. add 01, 02, 03 ...) to get them in the order you want when sorted by name. - Can also use subdirectories/folders to further divide/arrange MP3 files. One option for getting things in order (>> also see attached photo/image): >> ##Genre folder(s) [optional], then Artist folder(s), then YearAlbum folder(s), then ##Track.mp3 file(s). For example: 03 Alternative \ Soundgarden \ 1994 Superunknown \ 08 Spoonman.mp3 In this case will sort by: Genre number given, then Artist alpha, then Album year, then Track/file number. Step 3 (takes only about a minute to do this when needed) As always, it is a good idea to make a backup copy of your MP3 collection before proceeding ... Note: The steps below are specific to using the Anerty’s Lair - DriveSort program (other sorters may differ slightly). With your SD card (containing the MP3 collection) connected to your computer: - Use the sorter program to Open… desired disk (containing the MP3 collection) on your SD card. - Locate the overall folder (or entire disk) containing your entire mp3 collection to sort, and highlight this folder in the left-pane. The folder/disk highlighted in the left-pane is what will be sorted in the directory-system. - Under the Sort icon, select Long Name Sort, Order Ascending, Directories Before the files, AND include Subdirectories. Under the Save icon, select include Subdirectories. - Click Folder Sort, then click Folder Save (program will freeze for up to a minute while completing). This quickly and automatically rearranges the basic directory-system entries on your MP3 SD card to detect & play files in order. Note: I avoided using DriveSort's ‘Playlist Mode’. - Close the disk, and Quit/Close the sorter program. I usually run a quick file/volume error-check on the SD card, but this usually does not find any problems. Eject/remove the SD card from computer. The MP3 player should now see your track list in the same order as you see it when viewing on a computer that sorts by name of folder/file. Sorting your MP3 collection can make it much easier to find a specific album/track to play. Of course, with the limits of this MP3 player, can still be a pain skipping to the right section if you have a lot of music saved.

This has turned out to be a great little gps. I bought one to replace my old Garmin street pilot that was acting up. I liked it, and it was so inexpensive I bought a second one for my wifes car. For less than a hundred bucks its a great product. I had originally thought I would skip gps altogether and just rely on my phone but I'm glad I got it. Its very easy to use, gets a good signal so far has been very accurate. So why not 5 stars? A few things: 1) There is no dash mount kit. Only a suction cup to stick it to your windshield. I dont care for that plus I am not sure its legal in CA. I have a beanie dash kit from my previous Garmin but was disappointed to see this unit does not fit. I would have buy a new beanie for this one. That bummed me out a little, it would have been nice if they kept the mounts the same size people who had previous accessories. I wound up placing the gps in the sunglass holder behind gear shift. It fits good there and still gets a good signal. 2) The map update process is...a process. You have to install update software, you register the device, it downloads, it installs, it reboots, etc. . Mine went flawlessly but it takes a good 30 mins to complete. I hate having to install software on my computer because you never know how its going to interact with your system, what info its collecting, etc... But the update went well so its not a big negative but wanted to mention. 3) There is no instructions or documentation. The unit is easy to use after you play with it but I would have liked at least a little cheat sheet. I had to go online and get the manual. Once I got the manual I learned a few features it had that I would never have realized. These are minor drawbacks and its probably what helps them keep the price so low so I really cant complain too much. Its a great unit, gets a good signal and is accurate. UPDATED A YEAR LATER - NO LONGER WORKS The GPS worked great until I made the mistake of trying to update my maps. My device is now a paperweight. DO NOT try to update your maps, its not worth the risk. What a mistake. I got a pop up on my computer saying map updates avail. The unit had been working fine but I thought its good to keep it updated. I plugged in gps and it says sorry you dont have enough space to update your maps that I must get an SD card. Hmmm....bummer. OK, I went and got an SD card and inserted it into the gps and tried again. This time it began the install. It went got about 10% installed and an error came up saying could not communicate with device. I tried 3x more and same error and which point I said forget it I'll just stick with old maps. Not so fast buddy...I discover that my device has no maps!! NONE. I tried for 2 hours and same thing..the gps seems to go into sleep mode, the screen goes dark and the install fails. I now have a paperweight. I hope Garmin support can help. I am frustrated because it was an unforced error. I should have just left it alone.

Despite other reviews warning that the Samsung T7 SSD runs hot, I bought it based on the assumption that it would do so only under heavy use, such as large video file transfers. It's also dead silent, vibration-free, and trouble-free (so far). I have discovered however, that even when it's not in use the resting temperature hovers around 100 degrees F (41 degrees C). This will of course depend on the ambient room temperature. The cooler the room or the larger the heat sink you set it on, the cooler it will run. It also has a built-in protective circuit that will reduce transfer speeds if the heat approaches 48 C (118 F). I have yet to experience this, but it's good to know the T7 is unlikely to die without notice. That said, if the heat aspect makes you nervous you should probably consider something else.

I'm giving this 2 stars because you HAVE to buy a $100+ program to use it, to be fair every Z-Wave USB controllor MUST have one of these programs so don;t think that a "Z-Toller" or an "Aeon Z-stick" would be any better. But there are also no instruction..... anywhere... in the whole world.... for the Tricklestar. Ok so this is my second write up of a review on this product. To summarize it comes with no instructions. Not in the box, not on the web site, not on any of your internet. I spent six hour getting it to work but with what I found it can be done in 3 minutes. so what follows is a write up of the instructions you need. I used the HomeSeer program, so thats what HS means. Well so it's a serious #$*&$% but it works with HS just great but heres what you need to know. This is NOT a usb device, It's a serial device. You plug it into a usb port and instal drivers but there are no TrickleStar 300SW-US-W drivers. The drivers are for a "Prolific" Usb to serial converter. The 300sw is two seperate devices. First a data converter that needs driver. Then a Z-Wave that does not need drivers. Confused? you should be. There are no instruction anywhere on the web besides the ones that follow. To use the 300sw -Instal HS -Plug the USB stick into your computer -Go to the "prolific" web site [...] Download and install PL2303_Prolific_DriverInstaller_v130.zip, it's the third on the list. you have now installed the data converter but you don't know what the computer has desired to call it. When a computer uses "Serial data" it creats a "Com #" port but you don't know what # it is yet. YOU MUST IDENTIFY THE COM PORT. -Figure out what com port the usb made. This can vary depending on your version of windows so I'm going to throw out some word and you may have to Google them. +Go to "[B]Control Pane[/B]l" +Go to Hardware +Go to "[B]Device Manager[/B] *Scroll down the list until you see ""Ports (COM & LPT) and click on it to expand the tree. You will see "Prolific USB-to-Serial Comm port (COM#) [B]Write down the # that com.[/B] -OK now we go even faster! Run HS and open the website control thingy. +Go to setup +Go to Interface +Go the the drop down menu "Built-In Interfaces" "Z-Wave Interface" +clicky on COM Port and wait for it to auto update +type in the # you wrote down -[B][I]CLICK SAVE[/I][/B] your done.

I installed the HDDBoost with an Intel 40GN SSD onto my C drive. It worked, but a separate physical data drive was lost to Windows. The physical drive was present, and correctly recognized in the CMOS setup, but it was listed in Diskmgmt.msc as "Dynamic disk". I uninstalled HDDBoost & SSD, converted the lost data drive to "Basic disc" in Diskmgmt (thereby wiping out all data), and re-partitioned it. Then it was recognized. I copied its last backup onto it. I reinstalled the HDDBoost and SSD. All was now OK. I timed the improvement in speed: 1) Windows end of BIOS POST to fully loaded: from 140sec down to 103 sec (improvement of 26%); 2) load Firefox, 15 sec to 10 (33%); 4) load Word 4 sec to 3 (25%); 5) load WordPerfect w file 6 sec to 2 (67%); 6) Windows shutdown 27 sec to 20 sec (26%); total for six processes, 212 sec down to 143, or 69 sec faster, or 32% speed improvement. Not bad. However, after a month, my PC failed to boot. I could not find my C drive, even in BIOS. I removed HDDBoost (again), and the BIOS found the C drive, and the PC booted OK. A few days later, after finally removing the HDDBoost from the case, where it had been sitting unattached electrically to the rest of the PC, the PC would not POST at all. I zeroed out the CMOS, but the PC still would not POST, giving instead continuous short beeps (24 of them), then shutting down and restarting, 24 beeps, etc. The troubleshooting code for my Gigabyte motherboard said this was a "power error". I disconnected all cabling in the PC and reconnected. No good. Gigabyte said my symptoms generally indicate unstable memory, so I removed all memory from mobo, removed the onboard cell battery to clear the CMOS, then put in a single stick of memory in the slot closest to the CPU. The system booted into BIOS. I reset the BIOS to load fail-safe defaults and optimized defaults. I then added the remaining 3 RAM modules, and the PC booted successfully. This history may be two separate problems (loss of the data drive; bad RAM), but I'm not taking a chance. I'm not reinstalling HDDBoost. And I'm out $160 for the HDDBoost & the SDD, and the loss of troubleshooting time. And this was supposed to save me time.

The USB adapter is fine -- install the drivers and switch to Windows and you will be fine (SO FAR - one post complained about bad memory leaks). Price is right for a dashcam and a rear/backup camera. Don't think this price can be beat. Cons: 1. The gold colored camera lens is awful. This sticks out like a sore thumb. This should have been black. I'm afraid this can cause someone to break into my car and steal the unit. 2. Lack of instructions in user manual. 3. Blue tint 4. Glare won't let you see the LCD screen during daytime The kit does come with a 1 year warranty. Before I start my review, I have to make mention of how amazing this company's customer service is. While I can't recommend these headphones, you will be in great hands with this company. But now to my review of the headphones... I have been looking for a nice bluetooth set of headphones for a few weeks now as my current wired headphones (V-Moda LP), which are amazing and have lasted me a good eight years, are starting to show their age. And I anticipate I'll eventually have to break down and buy one of those stupid new phones with no headphone jack. I originally wanted some around the ear headphones as I primarily use them at work, but these had such stellar reviews, I figured I would give them a try. The packaging is very nice and simple. And, like any good pair of headphones, they come with a nice case. The headphones themselves feel pretty nice, and have a nice weight to them, but I found the buttons on the side to feel plasticky and have a cheap-sounding clicking noise. While I know I have a pretty big head, these were immediately uncomfortable as they pinched my ears. My roommate, whom I assume has a pretty normal sized head, tried them and said the same thing. I think this could have been prevented with soft-touch material around earpieces, rather than the hard plastic. The ear pads seemed quality and were very comfortable though. Pairing with the phone was simple, and the Motion iOS app is very cool, though I had trouble getting the headphones to pair with the app at first. The sound is very good, especially for this style of headphones. And they do a good job of blocking outside noise. Unfortunately, after a while I began to notice a pretty obnoxious high-pitched whine during quiet points in songs and videos. A minor annoyance, sure, but not when you pay $130 for the set. The battery life seems to be amazing. I listened to them for a few hours and the battery meter in the app barely moved. Unfortunately, after less than 24 hours of owning the headphones, they froze with the orange LED light stuck on after I attempted to turn them off. No matter what I did, the orange light stayed on. They would no longer pair with my phone. Sadly, my search for the perfect pair of headphones would continue, but 66 Audio made returning the headphones for a refund very simple. They sent me a prepaid return label and even offered me another product, free of charge, just to make sure I was happy. While these didn't work out for me, it seems people have had pretty good luck with them. And I would definitely purchase from this company again, given their excellent customer service. I'm interested to see what they do next.

I've been very happy with this watch as an upgrade from my Writings Steel HR. Unboxing and setup was simple. Tutorials within the app walk you through each feature of the watch. ECG. There's an activation process for the ECG function depending on where you live. I had to take one ECG reading and wait for the feature to be unlocked. The app explains exactly what's happening and why. It took a couple hours before I could view my ECG results, and after it's activated the results are instantaneous. It will only categorize your heart rhythm if your heart rate is between 50 and 100 beats per minute. All of my readings within that range have been categorized automatically. HEART RATE. Accurate when compared to my previous watch, a Withings Steel HR. I checked that watch against a pulse oximeter and got similar results. ScanWatch takes your heart rate every so often and displays a reading in the app for every half hour. STEPS. Again, I get similar step counts compared to my Steel HR, which was similar to my previous Fitbit. Steps are graphed in the app for every half hour and totaled for each day. The ScanWatch also counts the number of floors of stairs you climb, and they show up in the app similar to steps. BLOOD OXYGEN SATURATION. Taking your blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) manually is simple and returns a percentage in 30 seconds. It also takes your SpO2 during the night and averages it for you each morning if you enable that feature. BREATHING DISTURBANCES. The watch uses the blood oxygen saturation sensor to determine if you're breathing well at night. The section where you activate this feature warns you that it will shorten the battery life, and it definitely does. One night's sleep with the feature on "Always On" mode took 15-20 percent of my battery, which is a lot considering it should last 30 days on a charge. I changed this to the recommended "Automatic" setting and will have to wait and see on the battery life. FITNESS. I haven't used the fitness features of this watch yet. I've used the fitness features of the Steel HR and this watch is the same. It doesn't have built-in GPS, so you'll need to have your phone on you to track your location on a walk or run. My experiences with this feature have been good. The ScanWatch should be no different; I'll update this review if my expectations aren't met. BATTERY. My experience with my Writings Steel HR's 25-day battery life was always solid, so I'm expecting the same from the ScanWatch's 30-day claim. Some of the features I've activated might shorten it slightly, but I'll update this review if it doesn't meet my expectations. NOTIFICATIONS. The Withings Health Mate app monitors your phone's notifications and calls to alert you via your ScanWatch with a little vibration and text snippet on the watch screen. This feature can be enabled on a per-app basis, so you'll only be notified by the apps you want. DESIGN / COMFORT. The ScanWatch feels durable, has a stainless steel case and fluoroelastomer band. The FKM band is much more comfortable than silicone; it feels similar to leather but is waterproof and a little stretchy. I've found the watch to be very comfortable after wearing it a few days. The stem is easy to twist and click, and makes navigating the menu much easier than the Steel HR's single push button. The sapphire glass is nice and clear. The packaging is pretty Spartan and has very little instruction. I found it nice and clear, but I can see where other reviewers were disappointed. OVERALL this is a great watch I'd recommend to anyone wanting a smart watch experience with long battery life and classic styling.

If you are purchasing this for use as a security camera, keep shopping. I have had nothing but trouble with these cameras since the day I installed them. I am tech-savvy and have very strong and reliable wifi, so the issues are not operator error or system instability. I have a total of 4 Netvue cameras. The 2 older ones (wireless, no batteries, used indoors) work great and record constantly. The 2 Vigil Plus wireless cameras I purchased in February rarely work properly. The most common issue is not being able to connect to the camera at all - and that usually happens when I am not at home. It is VERY frustrating to receive an alert and see a picture of someone standing on your porch, but not be able to interact or even connect to the live camera at all (2-way sound is useless if I can't connect to the camera before the person leaves). Other issues: The date and time stamp on my alerts is off by several hours on both cameras, even after double-checking the time zone settings on both cameras and my home wifi connection. Battery life is a JOKE! I got the cameras in February and have already had to charge them, even after fully charging them for an entire day and night before installing them. Considering they rarely work correctly, I'm certain it isn't excessive activity using up the battery life. The timing of the snapshots on the alerts is way off. It snaps a series of 3 pictures as long as 10 seconds after the actual activity began - usually a picture of someone walking away from the door and 2 more pictures of my empty porch. It takes a very long time for the live feed to load, so if an event is happening and you need to quickly check in, you cannot. Sometimes it takes multiple attempts to load the live stream - up to 2 or 3 minutes. That is a long time to wait if somebody is ringing your doorbell or stealing a package from your porch. If I only had one of them and it consistently failed to work, I would keep trying to troubleshoot this. I have 2 and they BOTH consistently fail to connect, fail to record, and just fail.

From the '90s I've been using wireless speakers to extend my stereo throughout my apartment. The original pair, Recoton 900 MHz, were giving up the ghost, and I originally purchased a strong Bluetooth transmitter and two Bluetooth speakers to replace them. That was a mistake because 1) the Bluetooth process causes an audible delay in relation to the hard-wired and older wireless speakers, and 2) the transmitter interferes with other Bluetooth signals, creating static. I was pleased to find the Wolverine system, one of the few non-Bluetooth wireless systems I could find. At $70, this system is a bargain compared to my previous wireless systems. Compared to the other wireless speakers I've owned (I also have a pair from The Sharper Image), the Wolverines produce a surprising amount of bass. On the flip side, the treble isn't the clearest, but overall the sound is satisfactory. Yes, all of the system's components use the legacy AC adapter plugs, which take up space on one's power strip. I'd recommend to Wolverine that they adopt the trend I've seen with laptops, where a cord is provided between the wall and the transformer. But the use of an AC adapter is understandable, given the output of the speakers. USBs won't do the job; all of my previous wireless speaker systems employ AC adapters. Overall, I'm pleased with the system. Its performance is better than either the Recoton or The Sharper Image systems, with less static than either (the Recotons had to be manually tuned). The sound quality isn't going to knock your socks off, but they're just fine for what they are. For audiophiles, get an expensive Bose system.

The likely cause is due to the CPU choice of a Z8350, as bay trail/cherry trail has been historically buggy on Linux. I'd recommend spending just a little more for a mini PC that uses newer gemini lake CPUs (ex. N4000). Otherwise, this mini PC is it's one of the cheapest offerings on the market and offers good value if you are willing to accept this one caveat.

This tablet is much faster than I expected and the build quality is great. I used to have an ASUS M81C and this feels and acts much better. Having the 4GB of RAM along with a relatively higher end atom processor, 64GB of storage, and Windows 10 Home 64-bit, runs most applications surprisingly well. I'm able to play older and even some relatively recent games like Oblivion and Skyrim at a respectable frame rate of around 30 fps on lower settings and resolution. Video playback on youtube has also never had any real stuttering problems. The Intel HD Graphics 400 integrated GPU seems to run similarly to my first and oldest desktop with an Nvidia 6800 Ultra (both using around the same 256MB of memory, the Intel obviously being shared). Other less demanding games like Deponia run well at full resolution. I also ordered a separate micro SD card (a Sandisk 256GB ultra) that pairs well with it. I've used it to store Steam and whatever games I install with the access rate being perfectly reasonable. I assume the 128GB max specification mentioned is due to larger micro SD cards not being around when they first tested it because I've had no issue with the 256GB after formatting it to NTFS. I seem to get around 6 hours or so of actual usage while gaming, but it might be a little better if being used for only basic web browsing. It would be nice to get a little bit bigger of a battery, but it is still acceptable without worry about it running out too soon. It feels a little long to charge fully at around 2-3 hours, but it's still acceptable in that aspect as well. The additional/separately purchased keyboard with trackpad doesn't seem to hurt battery life either. Overall I'm very pleased with it after owning it for a few weeks now and the build quality seems to be great with it's unibody metal frame. It feels like it will last quite a long time and is great for putting on my lap when I want to relax in bed while watching movies/shows and basic gaming. It might not be as fast as some laptops, but it is far more portable and nice to be fanless.

I purchased the 4-bay version. The reviews span several very different versions of this enclosure with different strengths and weaknesses. This is a sold JOBD enclosure that has several critical design flaws. The worst is that the unit shuts down my drives after less than 30 seconds of inactivity. That is just crazy. The constant power cycling will shorten the drives' lives considerably, and absolutely kills performance, and may endanger RAID integrity. I have not found any way to disable this horrible "feature" other than using VOVSOFT's Prevent Disk Sleep program to force out a write operation to each drive every 25 seconds. Really stupid design. The next worse design flaw is that the drives will remain offline once power is restored after a power failure. This makes the enclosure no good unless you can always be around to manually turn the drives back on one by one. You can't could on this enclosure being available when you are away and power is anything less than 100% reliable. Finally, the cheap fan, while working well to keep the drives cool, is much louder than it should be. At least that hardware issue may be fixed by replacing it with a quality fan, but why should I have to do that hack? A variable speed fan and temperature sensor would have been a better design choice. Such a shame as the enclosure is otherwise a solid unit. Heavy metal housing, nice smooth drive housings. Decent construction and materials.

How bad and misleading can reviews in Amazon get ? Half of these reviews are by those who get the product at "discounted" or free. I had two Sony Bluetooth headphones. One I returned due to tight fit and low volume but the other MDR-XB950BT/R is good. It has some lip sync delay but it's manageable. These Avantree cans are really that - cans. Hardly any bass response, volume is severely limited - especially if you connect to a Bluetooth transmitter or go to a TV headphone jack. Again I compared with the Sony - at the same time using a splitter directly from the TV headphone jack - no contest - the Sony was good - not great - but these Avantrees were bad. Then I compared with both connected to a Homespot BT transmitter - terrible flat response from these. The Sony was actually good. I even tried the dual link mode and it was the same result. I quickly packed it up and am sending it back to Amazon. No doubt I will hear from the reseller or vendor asking why I had problems and offering another one at discounted price for an "unbiased" review but I'm not playing that game. Update: I switched my Homespot BT transmitter to Toslink Optical Audio input (though I had to use a Optical RCA to Toslink converter for my TV). What a difference it makes to my Sony headsets - the volume is high, noise is gone, there is no lip sync delay and bass is deeper) So my recommendation is to skip the TV headphone out jack and connect to the optical output to get the best out of your headphones.

All in all, this is a well designed keyboard that helps my hand positions. I want to mention some details to supplement some of the other comments floating around. The GOOD: Ergonomics and OSX Compatibility The nice thing about the keyboard is that the curve on the Y and Z axis really seem to improve the positions of my wrists as opposed to the traditional keyboard. I used to have a Microsoft Natural Keyboard but that thing is particularly large. This is a good solution if size is of concern. It sits low on the desk and doesn't have the large wrist supporting frame like the Natural Keyboard. This works for me. I find that the profile of the keyboard and my wrists/arms on desk position are natural. That said, ergonomics have a lot to do with not just the keyboard but the desk and chair you use. I am using an Ikea Galant desk that is height adjustable and a Herman Miller Mirra task chair. I have both adjusted so that my posture is planted pretty optimally, with my elbows 90 degrees to my sitting position, resting on the arm rests and the desk height level with my arm/hands. My arms are comfortably horizontal when approaching the keyboard. Before this, my desk was too high forcing my arms into a "snake ready to strike" / hook-like position which was starting to hurt. It's good to prevent RSI. Mac OS X somewhat compatible: Most keyboards will work sans the extra functionality of special keys. I wasn't expecting the play, volume up and down buttons to work but they do! (The calculator button doesn't do much and the num lock doesn't seem to work, so I guess 3/5) The BAD: Possibly key press feel, number pad or not to number pad I just recently purchased this product and my opinion on this is still in the air. The main issue I have with this keyboard is the feel of the key press / tactile feedback. It is quite mushy. I come from both Mac, Dell, and Microsoft keyboards and this one has a very damp, muted key press feel rather than a crisp one. Imagine putting a piece of felt underneath your keys. That's the best way I can describe it. As a consequence, the keys feel heavy. It is quiet though. I'll have to give it a week or so of use to see if I can get used to it. The second problem (that I can't solve) is the number pad or not number pad question. Actually it has less to do with the number pad and more to do with what is between the num pad and regular keys, the arrow keys. Since I use this for programming, I need to use the arrow keys a LOT to navigate my code. A full-sized arrow key set is nice. If you want full-sized arrow keys, usually this means a full sized keyboard. However, the inclusion of a num pad leaves little desk space immediately in front of me for my mouse and mouse pad. Thus my mouse is way off to the right and I have to shift the keyboard and mouse left when I want to use it naturally. With a chopped off keyboard like the Mac bluetooth keyboard, my mouse resides in that position that would otherwise be taken by the num pad. This is more natural and productive. But then I have to deal with a small arrow key pad. You can't win at everything and I suppose you need to make compromises somewhere but these are some of the issues I've run into. The OTHER: Some people complimented that this keyboard is small. It's not that small. As a matter of fact it's a tad bigger than my non-ergonomic Dell keyboard which includes a numeric pad. You can tell that the engineers spent a lot of time thinking about the user experience with this product. It's the little details that make this product not only easy to use, but also an experience I enjoy every day. Here are a few of the things I love about this product: - There is a physical switch on the back to switch to "clock set" mode placed out of view on the back of the device, but located right next to the power cable's plug. When you first plug in the radio you are sure to see it, and there is no need to hold down some combination of buttons to try and set the clock - Bluetooth pairs easily with NFC and even when I turn the clock-radio off (standby mode), I can still wake it up and start playing music from by phone without having to turn on the radio or press any buttons to repair - Physical buttons and knobs (instead of cheap capacitive touch ones like many electronics use these days) feel spectacular, are easy to find in the dark, and LEDs under the buttons illuminate to guide you on what buttons to press next when doing actions like setting the clock, alarm or radio presets. - You get five radio presets for each FM and AM stations, and it comes with a nice AM antenna that can be removed if you don't use it. - 3 display brightness settings from really bright to really dim and a fourth setting that automatically adjusts to the ambient lighting of the room. The auto mode works great: easy to read in the daylight but doesn't disturb at night. I also love the orange LED color that feels less annoying than red or blue. - A touch of the snooze button enables a sleep mode for 30, 45 or 60 minutes to listen to music while you fall asleep. But the best part about this is that it will disconnect your bluetooth connection when the timer is done, allowing your phone's music (or audio book) to be paused when you fall asleep. - The speakers sound great, even with radio or Bluetooth. I'm impressed considering the small size of the device. - You can download a free "DTA Controller" App for Android or iOS that let's you control the volume, radio station, etc. from your phone. It also let's you sync the clock or set different alarm times for different weekdays. There are only a few cons that I see to this product, and they are all really minor: - When bluetooth is connected there is a bright blue Bluetooth logo LED displayed. I just find bright blue LEDs annoying personally. - There is an included USB port to plug in your phone at night. This is a great extra feature, but the USB slot is on the top of the device which means you have a cable sticking up vertically out of the top of the radio. This is sort of ugly and feels like a last minute feature that was crammed in, but they did have the excellent foresight to provide a plastic plug to cover the USB connector when it is not in use. I simply use my standard wall charger so it is no big deal. - Some people complained about the fact that the AC adapter is a power block external from the radio itself. I don't really mind this because it means it is easier to replace if there is ever some sort of power surge that damages it. I suspect the decision may also have to do with the design of the speakers in the device and keeping the overall size small, so I think that is a reasonable trade off. - It would be nice if it supported the feature to "auto set" the clock based on the radio signals, but it does have a nice feature to sync with your smart phone if you install their "DTA Controller" app so I didn't need to worry about adjusting for daylight savings. - The "DTA Controller" app doesn't seem to be able to connect and change the volume when the alarm is going off. Not sure if this is a bug in the App or the radio itself. Overall, I just really love this product. So much in fact, that I want to buy another one to have in my garage. This is my second really positive experience with Yamaha products. The design and engineering reminds me what really good consumer electronics can be and inspires me in my own work to make high quality, great experiences for my customers.

Pulled the trigger on these and I am satisfied. Keep in mind, I already have the Bose QC35, Sony 1000XM2, and Plantronics BackBeat Pro 2 SE, so these were more for knock-around headphones at the gym, etc. That being said, I actually enjoy these headphones quite a bit and the sound quality/signature. There are conflicting reviews on the bass, some saying there is a lack of bass and others indicating they are bass boosted. I can confirm they are definitely bass boosted when the ANC is activated. They were certainly tuned with ANC as the typical use scenario. They have the same general signature when ANC is off, but turning it on, there is a bass/mid/treble boost, which may be a little more accentuated on top of the canvas created by the ANC. I actually enjoy the bass more on the Anker than my QC35, as I find the bass on those to be loose/flabby and a bit sloppy overall. The Anker has a really nice deep, hard, round bass (ANC on), which I really enjoy. If any of you have the Anker SoundBuds Surge, the sound signature is very similar, especially the bass. If I were to compare sound signatures to the headphones I have, they are most similar to the Plantronics BackBeat Pro 2 SE, except the Anker is a little warmer with less sparkle and sub-bass, which is not surprising, since the Plantronics have great treble performance with some top end push (10kHz) and one of the deepest boosted (7dB) low-bass out there. The sound is by no means "muffled" and does open up a bit after a break-in period of about 8 hours. If you like bright headphones, these are not for you (I actually don't like bright headphones at all). The ANC itself is about average, definitely not what Bose or Sony (1000XM2) will give you, but it's still decent. I'd say the effectiveness is about equal to the Plantronics BackBeat Pro 2 SE, the Sony MDR-ZX770BN (or MDR-ZX770DC from Costco), and the newer Sony WH-CH700N. The ANC does not create much white noise and the effect itself is unobtrusive. The build quality and fabrication of parts is very good, so they don't have a cheap feel and the headphone joints move smoothly. Although mostly plastic, the grade of plastic seems to be very good. Ear pads are made of thick and soft memory foam. The protein leather ear cups and headband are soft and smooth and feel nice against the skin. The MIC works well for calls. My voice is loud and does not sound distant at all. The headphones also seem to have a bit of a side tone, as to prevent the wearer from speaking too loudly. The side tone is mild, however, so it's not as good as the QC35 for hearing your own voice during calls. My only gripe is play/pause on the touch pad does not work 100% of the time. Vol +/- and track skip work fine, but it seems you have to hold your finger down to play/pause a bit longer than what's "natural". There is a slight delay in response when compared to the Sony 1000XM2 touch pad, but for the price, I can't complain. Overall, these are a great buy and could legitimately compete against headphones 2 to 3 times more. Under $100 is a steal for these.

Using this to help with big blind spots due to large c-pillars. Installation required removal of many lining bits in the trunk and drilling one hole. Overall, not too difficult but take patience to invisibly route camera, power and GPS cables. I won't do a rehash of what other owners have already written, but here are a few points that are good to know. - LCD display is semi-transparent mirror. It is intended to be used as LCD display or physical mirror. When used as a physical mirror, the reflected image is about 50% that of a regular mirror. I do NOT have any vibration problems, probably because my OEM mirror is a thick one and gives the elastic bands plenty to hug. When used as an LCD display, the physical reflection will badly wash out the LCD image. Because I am using this as a full-time rearview mirror, I simply angle the X2 downward. The physical reflection is a view of my rear seats, rather than out the rear window. If I want to use as physical mirror, one simply tilts the X2 up. I only need to use it as a physical mirror when sunlight is directly hitting my back seat. - Rear camera view covers my blind spots well. Cars don't leave the camera view until the front of the care is visible beside my car in my peripheral vision. Makes it a LOT easier to verify next lane is clear before changing lanes. The rear camera video looks quite good on the X2 display but is very aggressively edge enhanced. You notice that as edge ringing and detail obscuring noise when rear camera video is played back on your computer display rather than the X2 display. The rear camera's video is 1280 x 720 resolution during playback. - Rear camera video is 25 FPS. There will be visible motion jitter on the X2 display. Takes just a bit and you learn to ignore it. - Parking lines of rearview camera are not very useful because you can't adjust their position to match your vehicles mounting height and angle. - Front camera will pick up up a LOT of interior reflected off the windshield. This can be DRAMATICALLY improved by adding a circular polarizing filter. I fashioned a DIY one from a black bottle cap and piece of polarizer from a Real3D theater glasses. Huge improvement for free. I'd say a circular polarizer is a must have for this dashcam. Either make one or buy one. - Hardwire kit for power is worth getting. Just be sure to get the right one for your vehicle's size fuses (ATO vs Mini) - The hardwire kit's mini-USB connection is a straight connector rather than right angle. Depending on your mirror mount, that may mean the plug will jut too far up to fully clear mirror mount when you have the mirror in use position. A right angle, mini-USB adapter is a good idea if you are going to use the hard wire power kit. - Although the front camera is on a gimbal, it may not point far enough leftward once you have the X2 angled for use. This will be more of an issue if you sit relative forward and must angle the X2 more rightward to get correct mirror angle. Without sufficient leftward gimbal range, center of forward camera will point too far right. I had to modify the camera mount to add another 15 degrees leftward angle. Cautious melting and bending of the housing support was performed to get things just right. As a result, mine won't slide the camera in or out any more, but more importantly it has the correct left/right aim angle. Yep, nichrome wire and an adjustable power supply lets you do crazy things with plastic. - Lane Departure Warning System works for me on the highway. I would not DEPEND on it, but it might save the day if one nodded off and drifted out of lane. I score it as a bonus feature. - Clock lacks DST vs SDT ability. You have to change time zone manually to adjust for daylight saving time. - The rearview camera display does not include speed display, but it does show heading and time. - If your stock mirror housing is light colored, the X2's black mounting bands and casing stick out like a sore thumb. They draw attention to the X2. My solution was to painting my stock mirror body and mount jet black. No longer do highly visible black bands against a bright background invite a car break-in. With the mirror body painted black, my X2 install became nicely camouflaged. UPDATE: AutoVox customer service directly answered about two details that may be confusing. 1. The rear camera sensor is a 720P sensor. That is why the rear camera recording is 1280 x 720. It is NOT a 960P sensor! 2. Parking Mode requires always-on power to be supplied to be used. The built-in battery doe NOT power Parking Mode. One must manually switch in and out of parking mode. The device does NOT switch it automatically because power is always on.

Let me start by saying I'm not a professional photographer and I wouldn't even qualify as an "amature". I did purchase a point and shoot a few years ago (paid a pretty penny for it) for a trip to Iceland. I can honestly tell you my old iPhone 4s trumped the point and shoot on trip. I'm so glad I did. I've only had it for a week and I already, LOVE it. The picture quality is fantastic and you can definitely tell this blows a camera phone out of the water. This is exactly what I was looking for. And for someone who knows next to nothing about photography it is easy to use with its Automatic adjustments. For now, I plan leaving on automatic until I have more time to dedicate to playing around with it and/or purchasing additional lenses. I will also say I am millennial so SMART technology and WIFI is extremely important to me. This camera absolutely delivers on that front. I can upload my photos instantly to FB or even to my One Drive. I LOVE this feature for two reasons. 1. I can share immediately. As a millennial baby I rarely print out pictures but I do upload them constantly. This allows me to do this quickly and effortlessly. LOVE this. 2. Accidents happen with camera all the time. They break, something happens with SIM card (happened on my trip to Iceland and lost 1/2 of my photos including one which was supposed to appear in my local newspaper) or even worse, they get stolen. But because these pictures can be backed up quickly to FB, sky drive, or even your camera phone it helps transfer the risk of losing all your pictures if something where to happen. That alone makes Samsung cameras worth it! I did review a few other cameras that had "WiFi" settings only to find out it was very limited and hardly even qualified as "WiFi" and the internet connection was limited at best. If you are in the market for a camera with capabilities of sharing I highly recommend you review ALL the camera manufactures out there and I think you will also find, regardless of what model you select Samsung is pioneering the camera with wireless technology. It truly is a camera for the 21st century. But with anything, this camera isn't perfect so here are the cons. The battery drains FAST. Honestly I don't know how it fairs in comparison to other cameras so it maybe more of a technology issue rather than an issue specific to this manufacturer but it does drain quickly. If you are going to make this purchase, expect to buy more batteries to keep on hand/charge because this fully charged battery won't even make it a day, especially if you are connecting to the internet. Another con, (although some places I have seen this cited as a Pro) is the size. Don't get me wrong I'm all about "smaller is better" but the camera size in relation to the lens size and weight is awkward so I don't love that. (Also would suggest buying an after factory camera strap. The one that comes with it doesn't feel secure at all). Also the size again is an issue in terms of taking pictures and comfortably in the palm of your hand. There are so many buttons/ features on this camera that its compact size makes it impossible not to hit several of them accidently. I definitely think making he camera slightly bigger would be beneficial. I can't imagine how someone fares using this camera that has larger hands. I could never see a man using this to be frank. Lastly, the reason I did not give it 5 stars was because I've only had it for a week. It is hard to judge anything after only a few days and durability is an important factor to me when making any purchase. But even in consideration of the cons I've mentioned I'd buy this camera again and I'm very happy with it. I also forgot to mention I sell clothing/ household items online as a hobby and of course quality pictures/ great staging sells the product. Yesterday I used the camera for the first time to list of some furniture I was selling. I had SO many inquiries it was hard to manage (I sold everything within 30 minutes of listing it) and believe me it wasn't because the furniture was anything amazing-- it was surely the pictures. If you are in the market for a camera for any of the same reasons I was I'd highly recommend you purchase this camera. It really delivers on quality, price point, and progressive-integrated technology.

I could not get this to work with Windows 10 Pro "Windows Hello" (sign on). I have been working with computers for a long time, and I am pretty sure I did everything according to the manuals. But the sign on message says: "After a restart or logoff the device requires verification before using it." It also does not work at all with Bitlocker. The documentation and setup programs are abysmal. The worse I have seen since the early 1980s. You follow the instructions from one dead end after another. They direct you to a program which tells you it does not work, and it directs you to another program which says it is "depreciated" (meaning obsolete). That program told me I am not an Administrator, although I am, and it would not install. Restart the computer and hey-presto, I am an Administrator after all, and it installs. Ah, but it generates an obscure error message, "Failed challenge-responses. Is the YubiKey configured for HMAC-SHA1 challenge-response in slot 2?" No indication what that means or how to configure it. A Google search finds another program they forgot to mention, which -- oh yes -- configures it, sort of, if you follow the directions exactly, with dire warnings if you don't. (It "sort of" works meaning the screens complete as shown in the manual, but it doesn't actually work in the sense of making the product functional.) It also doesn't work because it turns out you you have to run the first program again, which gives no indication that it worked, except that when you run it yet again, it says you already assigned this name, so I guess it did work. But anyway, after this merry chase down the rabbit hole from one program to the next, with the Windows sign-on you click on the device and it says: "After a restart or logoff the device requires verification before using it." I have to say, this takes me back. It gives me a weird sense of nostalgia for the dawn of the PC era, when software was terrible, ridiculous installation procedures went out to lunch or did not tell you they would fail until you get to the end, documents were loaded with obscure computer jargon, and programs were oft "depreciated." Yikes.

I purchased the RT-AC66U router several months ago based on very high company reviews for previous products and personal recommendations from friends who have used ASUS products. I was replacing a trusty old Linksys router that finally died. It ended up being a big mistake and this ASUS router has been very problematic. I started having issues about a month after I purchased the router with the wireless signal suddenly degrading significantly for no reason (yes I checked for interference and that my internet connectivity was OK). This then proceeded to get worse over time so that the router would completely drop the wireless connection and only a reboot of the router would fix the issue. At first this only happened every couple of weeks but has become more frequent to the point that it's happening every few days (if not every day). I have tried contacting ASUS technical support and become incredibly frustrated. I have taken every step they have recommended such as upgrading the firmware, changing the control channel, changing the bandwidth settings, changing the power transmission levels, unplugging all other devices that might even possibly cause interference, etc. with absolutely no luck. After each of these failed attempts, I would have to wait a while to monitor the results and then call back to ASUS support. Their wait time for their support line is exceptionally long no matter what day or time I call. In several cases, after waiting for over 20 minutes, I was kicked into an automated voicemail system and told that I would be called back. As I sadly learned to expect, I never received a return call from ASUS. Today, I finally reached the end of the road with ASUS. I can't upgrade the firmware, I can't remove any additional devices that "may" cause interference, I can't continue to change the control channel and expect anything different. The service representative could only offer that I send the router for them to diagnose and potentially repair. They refused to send a replacement router, which means that I will be left without anything for a week and probably much longer. For me (and I'm guessing many others), that is a completely unacceptable solution given that I must have connectivity for work. This will mean that I have to purchase a replacement router just to cover the time that my ASUS router may be getting repaired. Now that I've read through many other reviews on Amazon and other websites where people are experiencing the same problems I'm convinced that there is a hardware design problem with this router. Unfortunately, ASUS is refusing to stand behind their product. Yes, there are a lot of 4 & 5 star reviews for this router out there. Perhaps a lot of people have been lucky and haven't run into these issues yet. My advice is to not gamble your $200 on this router because you will eventually, most likely end up very disappointed. Read the details of the many 1 star reviews and you'll start to see the pattern.

I will say this, it's more sturdy than I was expecting. However, there could've been some more thought in the design and manufacturing. The screw to keep it locked in place does not go in straight, so it's definitely not threaded correctly. However, what really caught me off guard was this has to be slid on to the rail from the front or the back. Well, that's great, except for the barrel nut prevents you from sliding it on from the rear in most cases. If you have a bipod, pistol grip or other grip, laser, etc. at the front of your rail, you'll have to remove that or place the mount on top of your weapon and invert the GoPro's orientation. For me, I have a fixed front sight like many AR-15s and because of the design of this product, you can't slide it on the top of the rail from the front if you have a fixed front sight either. In my case, I ended up having to move my foregrip and make room for it in the front on the bottom and it's literally the only spot I could slide this mount on without taking my gun apart. In short, if you want to permanently have this mount affixed to your rifle, you're probably going to be fine. If you have easy/open access to the bottom or top of your rail in the front or rear, you're going to be fine. BUT, if you have stuff on your rails already and/or want to add/remove this mount frequently, bring your tools with you.

Cons: -Made of highly brittle and inexpensive plastic (The Fold-out rotating extension arm on mine was already broken as it came brand new in the box!) For example, when I simply panned from left to right, with no tension on the screw lock, it got stuck a few times due to pieces not being smoothly joined, and also not very well built. \ -Upper rotating parts are so poorly made, they don't work that well. It seems to frequently get stuck in any operation, either tilting the D-SLR camera to shoot in portrait mode, or just raising/lowering the camera view angle. -When tightening and releasing the tension on the locks of the camera head movements, plastic makes slight squeak due to imperfections and flexible nature of the plastic. It is brittle in areas that exceed 1/4" thickness, and somewhat flexible in areas that are 1/8" thick or less. -Top mounting track encounters frequent fluctuation in tightness when panning longitudinally. Even when the tension lock is completely open, as the mount is rotated 180 degrees, there spots where it gets stuck and requires more effort to push, thus creating a shaky and uneven panning motion. -Paint on steel/aluminum legs was already scratched on my product, and easily scratches off, leaving unsightly appearnance. -One of the two included bubble levels was off... requiring an extreme tilting of the whole tripod up to 17 degrees simply to center the bubble in the level. Completely inaccurate! -$40 price for overall poor quality. So, in conclusion, I have bought $20, and $30 tripods that were much better quality than this.... but I had no way of knowing since all the previous reviews were misleading. I'm not a heavy gamer or video watcher, mostly internet and some " light" games like words with friends. I really like the notification bar. Another thing that has worked way better than my last tablet is watching the HD video I took on vacation this summer. On the vtab I could only watch bits and pieces with no audio at all. On the Excite they play perfectly beginning to end. The preloaded apps are kind of annoying as I don't use most of them and they can't deleted,but since there is no limitation on the space you have for apps, this isn't really a big issue. That was a nice surprise on this tablet as I had very limited space for apps on the old tablet and was always deleting to make more room for new apps. Once I solved the overnight battery drain problem, I am 100% happy with the Excite. I happily recommend it to everyone who asks about my tablet, which is everywhere I go - conferences, the airport, etc. Can't live without my tablet so hope it lasts a long time!

A couple of general comments. Rating the sound quality from a speaker system is somewhat subjective. All people have a natural frequency response in their ears that will bias them towards a particular sound. And sound quality at the low end of the frequency spectrum is more about moving air than reproducing detail. All of that said, I still hold out hope for a light, portable speaker system that makes me happy when I'm sitting in a hotel room on yet another business trip. After much research and listening to various models in electronics stores, my dreams are yet to be realized. So here we have the TravelSound 400. I bought these because of a $[...], and that's probably the main reason I'm going to keep them. First, the positive. The industrial design is very nice. They are compact: 6 1/4 L x 2 3/4 H x 1 5/8 D. The swivel down position protects the drivers nicely. Battery life seems to match the specs, with one caveat. When traveling, I leave them on overnight so I can wake up to music on my iPod. Unfortunately, these speakers don't seem to have an auto-off / auto-on feature, so the batteries still drain. Now, the negative. If you're looking for a miracle in big sound from a small package, this probably isn't it. These speakers sound like a slightly upgraded version of laptop speakers. They get reasonably loud, enough to fill a hotel room and irritate the neighbors, but they really lack a good low-end response. When I say they lack low-end response, I'm not saying they can't handle rap music, I'm saying that they don't even handle the normal amount of bass you'll find in most music. You end up with what sounds like an exaggerated midrange, and an EQ can only partially compensate. You should really try to listen to these (or any other speakers) before you buy. Bottom line, if you like portability over sound, these will do. If you're picky about sound, you're going to be disappointed.

This review is for DS4 Mini Tower (wish Amazon would stop combining reviews for different products that may or may not be similar or interchangeable) Good: - Quiet while providing decent cooling (I added a 120mm Gelid fan on top too). - Lots of storage bays (I'm using 5 HDDs, one DVD RW and there is one external bay left, one internal bay and 2 locations for SSD or slim 2.5" HDD left). - Allows for good cable management (I ran most of the cables behind the mobo) - Looks decent. Bad: - Short I/O panel cables (had to run the audio cable diagonally to reach the header on the other corner of the mobo; the USB 2 cable only reaches one header port but not the other 3). - One USB 2 front port but the connector takes the full 2 port header connector. - One rubber foot fell off while installing the mobo; it looks like cheap glue was used. - The side panels leave gaps, not flush to the main frame when closed. - No speaker, not even a $0.25 on-board 2-pin buzzer. I'm trying to use this for a headless server and need to know when it reboots - had to order one from Amazon ($4 with shipping). - I/O panel on top will surely gather lots of dust, potentially causing issues. - Flimsy materials; removed the sound isolation panel on top to install the extra fan - the weight of the fan bends the top of the case(!) so the fan leans on the motherboard connector (it probably straightens when the side panel is in place). - Small clearance on the sides of the motherboard (micro-ATX); the top fan sits on the connectors at the edge of the mobo, also the bottom PCIe slot can only be used for thin cards (without side connectors or fans) due to very small gap to the PSU. Other: - No real use I see for the 2-channel manual fan controller. Most motherboards already have 3 or 4 fan headers and allow advanced fan speed setup function of temperature, also allowing RPM monitoring. I did not connect it. - I don't really know whether was made in China but it surely feels like it. EDIT: It is Made in China, says so by the UPC!

Amazon Review Passes all of the tests I was reluctant to buy because some of the details on Amazon’s product page seemed a bit vague. I didn’t want to end up with a refurbished nightmare. I’m glad I made the plunge! It arrived on the promised date. The packaging was typical high quality Amazon. I was glad to see a pristine Apple box complete with shrink wrap in place. The Apple box was in pristine condition just as though I just brought it home from my local Apple store. So far, so good. After removing the heat shrink and sliding the box apart, I was greeted with Apples typical new device presentation. The iPad was enveloped in the clear plastic wrap and thoughtful tab used to lift the iPad up and out of the box easily. I carefully examined the iPad and it was free of fingerprints, scratches, dings and dents. In short, just like it should for a brand new Apple device. I smiled. After charging the battery, I proceeded to the set up. This was super easy as most of the set up info was transferred from the iPhone. It went smoothly with no glitches to speak of. The only “work” was to reactivate a few non-Apple apps. That went quickly. As much as I love the iPad bare back (Space Gray) I am aware that due to size and weight, surviving even small drops could yield far worse than than an iPhone. So, I installed an Otter Box Defender. Visually as ugly as the iPad is beautiful bare back. Small price to pay for protecting the iPad from me. LOL! After reading reports of broken screens even in Defender cases, I opted to get AppleCare as a backup. After fiddling around in Apple Support and getting nowhere, I called Apple and a very helpful service rep walked me through the process. He even helped me set up a few other things and I had AppleCare in less than an hour. It took longer because I’m still adapting to how things work. I come from the world of PowerBooks and desktop Macs. The ability to purchase AppleCare also tells me that this is not an Amazon or 3rd party refurbish. Only new devices that have never been registered sold are eligible for AppleCare. And only for 60 days after warranty start date. I smiled again. I tested the battery by topping off the battery and disconnecting the power. Then proceeded to watch movies, read emails, cruise the web, etc. The low charge warnings appeared at the 10 hour mark. I smiled. Exactly what is expected for a new iPad. Should you get one? Depends on how you plan to use it. For the average user, this will cover all the bases. If you are more of a power user, then you may need to move up to the iPad Pro series. Based on my experience, I’m satisfied with Amazon, and this iPad. If you have no heavy use needs I’m sure you will be just as happy. Highly recommended!

I used the mount in conjunction with an Sanus SLF9-B1 heavy duty articulating wall mount, along with a 55" Samsung TV and a Sonus sound bar. Sonus recommend mounting the soundbar at least 2" above the TV. The back of the Samsung TV is curved and uses 'top-hat' spacers, and the TV is attached to the wall mount with an "X" style mount, with each cross-member extend about 4 inches beyond the M8 45mm mounting screws. Sanus recommends screwing the soundbar mounts directly to TV. That might work without a TV mount, but attaching one bracket to another would require a 55mm screw (which I did not have, and was difficult to find) or a 60mm with washers. Instead, I mounted soundbar mount to the ends of the "X" TV mounts, using 2 16mm M8 screws on each mount for stability, and washers and nuts from the hardware store. The Sonos soundbar now sits about 2" above the TV. While not a pretty as a flush mount, if follows the Sonos soundbar recommendations and sounds a lot better than mounting below the TV, and the sound follows the angle of the TV screen. The mount is wide enough to hide the power, Ethernet, and optical cables. Sanus will ship you additional screws at no charge if the included screws do not fit. I also tried the highly rated Mounting dream MD5420, but it did not fit well.

it, this is a very good mount (as long as the weight limitations are respected),and if it is used as intended.for me is doing what I was expecting, It is ideal for small telescopes, the hand control from orion and sky safari, with the same result, I contacted iOptron, but they could not give me a proper solution, because of this issue, I am giving 4 stars, otherwise I I'll give them 5 stars I think for the price it worth it ,but is not a bargain, as a second mount to have fun is perfect,, , but if you are looking for a serious mount, I would recommend other options, the mini tower and if There's been a lot written about these headphones, most of which I feel no need to reiterate. The noise canceling is class-leading, the sound is excellent, if a bit bass-heavy, and battery life is top notch. Overall, I really love these cans, but they have a major problem for anyone that lives in cold climates.... Anytime I am outside in sub-freezing temperatures (less than 32F or 0C), the touch control cup starts to pause, skip, volume up/down - all on its own. The touch controls become completely unresponsive to user input, which negates a pretty major feature of the headphones. I specifically bought these to use in winter as a pair of ear muffs (in summer I use buds or I'll show up to work looking like I swam a few laps). Google this problem; I am most definitely not the only one. If you live somewhere that never gets below freezing, I really have no reservations with the WH1000XM3's. Unfortunately for me, they are not a long-term solution and while I generally prefer the Sony's to the equivalent Bose model, I have no choice but to go with the latter.

UPDATE: As I've continued to use this I've concluded that the iA features still need tuning, most likely via a firmware update. Where this camera seems to shine over the 150 are in the custom settings. Finally, as someone pointed out, the lens hood takes some getting used to. Once you force it on and off a few times it starts to get easier. It does click into place firmly with some effort. I'm still irritated by the lens hood closing on my fingers, but the reality is that the lens hood isn't something I really use frequently. I've seen some absolutely amazing shots taken with the FZ-200 by those that know what they're doing. Thus, this camera may be better suited for more advanced users or those looking to take their photographic knowledge up a notch from the 150. See some of these shots, and you may just click the 'buy' button. [...] I've updated my rating to 4 stars. -------- First of all, this is an evolution from the prior model. I've been using the FZ-150 since December of last year, and was excited to hear about the full range F2.8 of the new FZ-200. The FZ-150 is a fantastic camera, and I've been incredibly impressed by the photos I've captured. I'm not here to discuss megazooms vs. SLRs, but I can tell you that having this much range in such a small package makes it worth the trade off in my opinion. I received the FZ-200 on Saturday, and took it to Mt. Jefferson in Oregon to catch some scenic shots. Some early observations: Low light performance seems better, but the program menus are completely different. I was unable to test long exposures, despite trying to find the feature for 10 minutes straight. The new viewfinder is AMAZING. That being said, it's still a digital viewfinder. As such, performance in dark conditions is non-existent. You'll be guessing at where you're aiming your shot. In good lighting, it's crystal clear. A massive improvement over the 150. Fit and finish seems on par, but the glare shield seems loose compared to the FZ-150. In fact, it barely stays on. Which brings me to a major issue. Because the barrel is considerably larger than the 150, get ready to feel like you're going to get your fingers amputated. If the glare shield is stored on the camera (which is normal), the barrel will try to retract when the camera goes to sleep. Because the gap between the grip and the barrel has been dramatically reduced, when the lens retracts the glare cover tries to close around your fingers. Holy **** it can hurt. I also suspect it's terrible for the motor. Leave it off, and the problem is solved. Still, what were they thinking? Panorama Mode: Useless. Use Photoshop or anything else. Images were incredibly pixelated for some reason, especially in bright light. It also takes the image from an incredibly narrow field of view. Video: Same as the 150. I've not really seen a huge difference, although the slow motion functions are nice. Is it worth upgrading? Probably. But the FZ-150 is a ton of camera for the money, and it's now at a lower price.

As a case, the Dell Venue 7 snaps into a tray that is custom molded for it. This means there are no unsightly corner clips and nothing touching the front plate. When the case is closed, it appears like real leather, although it is not, and has a rich look and feel. There is nothing cheap or flimsy about it even though it is an inexpensive case/stand. I like how the Dell logo shows through the case. Cut-outs are in all the right places and all connectors and controls are assessable. Only the SD door is hidden. The case is held closed by a strap which is not my favorite. There are no magnets. As a stand, this is one of the few case/stand combinations that is usable in the portrait position due to the rotation capability. Most others are landscape only. The stand is a bit top heavy in the portrait position and falls over easily. It is also prone to collapsing in landscape position if doing some serious tapping. It is best to use one hand to stabilize it and the other for touching. Although tipsy, like some of my friends, I would still recommend it as a very good value for the money.
